0.title: Revelation: The Unveiling of the Victorious Lamb
0.overview:
Revelation is the most debated book in the Bible. In the third century Dionysius of Alexandria questioned whether the apostle John wrote it — not because he rejected the book, but because he found it so unlike the Gospel. In the centuries since, the book has generated more controversy, more speculation, more bad charts, and more genuine spiritual comfort than any other portion of Scripture. Before we open a single seal, we need to understand what kind of book we are reading.

The word that opens the book — apokalypsis — means “unveiling.” Revelation does not conceal the future in cryptic code to be cracked by clever scholars in the final generation. It unveils a reality that was always there but hidden from ordinary sight: the reign of the slaughtered Lamb over all of history. The book was written to be read aloud in congregations (1:3), probably by a lector standing in a first-century house church. Its images were designed to be heard, felt, and worshipped — not diagrammed. If your primary response to Revelation is to reach for a chart, you are already in danger of missing the point.

Revelation belongs to three overlapping literary genres simultaneously. As an apocalypse, it uses symbolic visions, cosmic imagery, and heavenly perspectives to reinterpret earthly events — a thoroughly Jewish genre with deep roots in Daniel, Ezekiel, Zechariah, and the rich inter-testamental literature (1 Enoch, 4 Ezra, 2 Baruch). As prophecy, it speaks the word of God into a specific historical crisis, calling the church to faithfulness and warning the world of judgment. As a letter (1:4; 22:21), it is addressed to real congregations facing real pressure, and it carries all the pastoral weight of Paul’s epistles. Missing any one of these three dimensions distorts the whole.

The author is John, exiled to the island of Patmos “on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus” (1:9). Early Christian testimony overwhelmingly identified him with John the Apostle, the beloved disciple. The book was most likely written during the reign of Domitian (c. AD 95–96), when the imperial cult was being aggressively promoted in the province of Asia and Christians were being pressed to acknowledge “Caesar as Lord.” Seven actual churches — in Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea — received this letter. They were living under the crushing weight of Rome’s total-sovereignty claim. Revelation is the pastoral response of an exiled pastor to congregations in crisis.

Four Frameworks for Reading Revelation

Faithful, Bible-believing, Christ-loving readers have understood the overall structure of Revelation in four main ways. The reading followed here is the amillennial/idealist position — the historic Reformed mainstream — with the other frameworks noted at every major structural decision point. All four frameworks agree on the non-negotiables: Christ has decisively won. The church will endure to the end. History is moving toward a fixed and glorious goal. Jesus returns in visible, bodily glory. The wicked face final judgment. The righteous receive a new creation. Where they differ is in the timing, sequencing, and nature of the visions.

The Preterist framework holds that most — or all — of Revelation was fulfilled in the first century. The great tribulation is the Roman-Jewish War of AD 66–70, culminating in Jerusalem’s destruction. The beasts represent Nero and the Roman imperial system. “The things that must soon take place” (1:1) and “the time is near” (1:3) are taken with strict literalness: the book addresses events imminent to its first readers. The partial-preterist position (R.C. Sproul, Kenneth Gentry, David Chilton) holds that chapters 1–19 are largely fulfilled while chapters 20–22 remain future. Preterism’s great strength is its seriousness about the book’s own time-markers. Its challenge is explaining how a largely-fulfilled Revelation speaks with permanent power to the church in every age.

The Historicist framework reads Revelation as a symbolic map of the entire sweep of church history from Pentecost to the Second Coming, with the seals, trumpets, and bowls charting the rise and fall of empires. The Reformers broadly held this view, identifying the papacy with the beast. Though now a minority position, historicism produced generations of courageous preaching by men who believed they were living inside the very story Revelation was telling.

The Idealist (Amillennial) framework — the reading followed here — reads Revelation as a profound symbolic portrayal of the cosmic conflict between Christ and Satan, the church and the world, that characterizes the entire period between the first and second comings. The visions do not map a sequence of datable historical events; they depict recurring spiritual realities — the pressure of empire, the suffering of the saints, the apparent triumph of evil, and the certain victory of God — that are enacted in every age. The seals, trumpets, and bowls are best understood as parallel series (recapitulation), each sweeping from the cross to the Second Coming with increasing intensity. This reading takes seriously both the first-century occasion and the book’s permanent relevance. Its advocates include Augustine (City of God), B.B. Warfield, Geerhardus Vos, William Hendriksen, G.K. Beale (whose commentary is the fullest scholarly treatment available), Dennis Johnson, and Michael Wilcock.

The Premillennial/Futurist framework holds that most of Revelation (especially chapters 4–22) describes events still future, culminating in a literal thousand-year reign of Christ on earth after his return. Two major streams: Historic Premillennialism (George Eldon Ladd, Wayne Grudem) teaches that the church goes through the tribulation before Christ returns to establish his kingdom on earth, followed by the final judgment. Dispensational Premillennialism (John MacArthur, Charles Swindoll, J. Vernon McGee, John Walvoord, Charles Ryrie) adds the distinctive of a pre-tribulation Rapture — the church is caught up before a seven-year tribulation falls on an unbelieving world, with that period constituting God’s final dealings with national Israel. Shaped by John Nelson Darby in the 1830s and widely popularized through the Scofield Reference Bible, this is the dominant eschatological framework in much of evangelical America. It deserves full respect as the honest, Scripture-rooted reading of millions of sincere believers, and its specific interpretations are noted at every key junction.

How to Read Revelation

Three principles will guide us. First, let the book’s own genre shape how you read it. Apocalyptic literature communicates through symbols, not newspaper reporting. When you read of a dragon with seven heads and ten horns, you are not meant to visualize a literal creature — you are meant to feel the horror of satanic power in all its many-headed, grasping form. Second, hear the book through first-century ears. Most of Revelation’s images come from the Old Testament — Daniel, Ezekiel, Zechariah, Isaiah, Exodus — and from the Roman world of the first century. When John’s original hearers heard “the great city,” they heard “Rome.” Third, read for comfort and courage, not for curiosity. Revelation was written to sustain the church’s witness under pressure. It was written to answer one question above all others: Is Jesus really Lord, or is Caesar? The answer, given in vision after dazzling vision, is: the Lamb who was slain is Lord of lords and King of kings. Everything else is footnote.

When was it written, and by whom? Most early writers place it near the end of Domitian’s reign, around AD 95; Irenaeus, who knew men who had known John, says the vision was seen near the end of Domitian’s reign, almost within his own generation. Some argue for a date before AD 70, under Nero, pointing to the temple in 11:1–2 and the seven kings of 17:10. The later date is more likely: the churches have had time to decline (2:4; 3:15–17), and Smyrna’s church seems to be well established. The author calls himself simply John, a servant who needs no introduction (1:1, 9). Dionysius of Alexandria doubted that he was the apostle, because the Greek is so different from the Gospel’s. But Justin and Irenaeus, the earliest witnesses, say it was the apostle, and the difference in style suits a different kind of book written in exile. The more likely conclusion is that the apostle John wrote it.

How should the thousand years of chapter 20 be read? Premillennial Christians hold that Christ will return before a literal thousand-year reign on earth. Postmillennial Christians hold that the gospel will so prevail that a long age of peace will come before he returns. Amillennial Christians hold that the thousand years is the present age, from Christ’s first coming to his second, in which Satan is bound so that the gospel goes to the nations and the saints reign with Christ, followed by one return, one resurrection and judgment, and the new creation. This commentary takes the amillennial view, because Revelation repeatedly tells the same story from different angles, because the rest of the New Testament speaks of one return with resurrection and judgment together (John 5:28–29; 2 Pet 3:10–13), and because the binding of Satan matches Jesus’ words about binding the strong man (Matt 12:29).

1.title: The Son of Man Among the Lampstands
1.overview:
Revelation opens by naming itself three ways: a revelation, a prophecy and a letter. All three are in play at once, and forgetting any one of them leads to misreading. Within three verses the Father, the Son, the Spirit, an angel and the whole church have all appeared.

The chapter moves in three steps. The prologue (vv. 1–3) gives the book’s source and urgency. The greeting (vv. 4–8) is a Trinitarian blessing that gives Jesus titles of the kind Caesar claimed for himself. Then the vision of the Son of Man (vv. 9–20) shows John, before any seal is opened, who stands at the centre of history, and the rest of the book unfolds under his authority.

The vision is drawn almost entirely from Daniel 7 and 10, and its first readers, schooled in the Hebrew Scriptures, would have felt the weight of every image. It shows the eternal Son in his glory, the conqueror of death and the ruler of history, and the first thing it tells any congregation about itself is that he walks among the churches.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Three verses position the whole book. The revelation passes from God to Jesus Christ, to his angel, to John and on to the churches: nothing here originates with the writer. Verse 3 pronounces the first of the book’s seven blessings, on the one who reads aloud, on those who hear, and on those who keep what is written.

Apokalypsis means an unveiling. Revelation is not a code hiding the future until a clever generation cracks it; it is the cloth coming off the throne, so that a church which can see only the magistrate and the emperor’s temple may also see who has been governing the world all along. The word “soon” is taken up at the verse itself. And the blessing is attached not to understanding the book but to keeping it.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Book to Be Kept

The revelation comes from God through Christ, his angel and John, to the churches. It is an unveiling, not a code, and its blessing falls on those who hear it and keep it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: One reader stood before a listening house church.

Now: After any chapter of this book, ask whether it left you with an opinion or a resolve.

verseByVerse.quote: The revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to show to his servants the things that must soon take place. He made it known by sending his angel to his servant John, who bore witness to the word of God and to the testimony of Jesus Christ, even to all that he saw.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Revelation 1 introduces the whole book and the Christ at its centre. The book is an unveiling God gave to Jesus Christ, sent through an angel to John and on to the churches, with a blessing on all who read it aloud, hear it and keep it (vv. 1–3). John greets seven churches of Asia with grace and peace from the eternal God, from the sevenfold Spirit and from Jesus Christ, the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead and the ruler of earth’s kings (vv. 4–5a), and breaks into praise to the one who loves us, has freed us from our sins by his blood and made us a kingdom of priests (vv. 5b–6). Christ is coming on the clouds, seen by every eye (v. 7), and God declares himself the Alpha and the Omega, the Almighty (v. 8). Exiled on Patmos for the gospel, in the Spirit on the Lord’s day, John hears a voice like a trumpet telling him to write to seven named churches (vv. 9–11). Among seven golden lampstands he sees one like a son of man, robed as a priest, with white hair, blazing eyes, bronze feet, a voice like many waters, seven stars in his hand, a sword from his mouth and a face like the sun (vv. 12–16). John falls as though dead, and Christ lays his hand on him: do not be afraid, I am the first and the last, the living one who died and lives for ever, holding the keys of Death and Hades (vv. 17–18). The stars are the angels of the churches and the lampstands the churches themselves (vv. 19–20). To a small, persecuted church the message is simple and immense: the risen Christ is alive, he rules, and he walks among his churches.

The setting. John was exiled to Patmos, a small island off the coast of modern Turkey, most probably near the end of the emperor Domitian’s reign (about AD 95), as the early church writer Irenaeus reports; some date the book earlier, in the late 60s under Nero. The churches of Asia faced pressure from three sides: the imperial cult, which expected citizens to honour the emperor as lord; trade guilds whose feasts involved idols; and hostile local synagogues. Some Christians were compromising, some were growing cold, and at least one had already died (2:13). Revelation is written to them, and to the whole church after them, to show who really rules.

What kind of book this is. Revelation combines three kinds of writing. It is an apocalypse, a genre full of symbolic visions, numbers and heavenly scenes, like Daniel and Zechariah. It is a prophecy (v. 3), a word from God calling for response. And it is a letter (v. 4), sent to real congregations with real problems. Each shapes how it is read. Its images are symbols, not photographs: Christ is not literally a lamb with seven eyes (5:6), and the sword from his mouth is his word. Its message calls for faithfulness, not speculation. And whatever it meant, it must first have meant something to those seven churches.

Five links in a chain. The book does not begin with John. It begins three steps above him. God gave the revelation to Jesus Christ; Christ made it known by sending his angel; the angel brought it to John; John bore witness to everything he saw; and the churches heard it read aloud. Before a single seal is broken the reader has been told exactly where this material came from, and it did not come from a lonely man’s imagination on a prison island. Evidence is only admissible in court if someone can say who handled it, in what order, from the scene to the courtroom, with no unexplained gap. John opens with the chain of custody. The first name on it is God, and the last name on it is a congregation crowded into a room in someone’s house.

The revelation of Jesus Christ. The title word sets the register for all twenty-two chapters. Apokalypsis means an unveiling, a covering pulled off something that was already there. It is what happens when the sheet comes off a statue. Revelation is not God encrypting the future so that clever readers in the last generation can decode it. It is God taking the cloth off the throne room so that a frightened church can see who has been running the world all along. And “of Jesus Christ” is meant both ways at once: it is the revelation that comes from Jesus, who gives it, and the revelation about Jesus, who is its subject. The book has many beasts and many angels, but above everything else it unveils him.

To show to his servants. See where the chain ends: his servants. The word is douloi, bond-slaves, and it means all believers, not a spiritual elite. John puts himself in that same category in the same breath: his servant John. The disciple who leaned back against Jesus at supper signs himself as a slave. That fixes the posture of everyone who comes after him. This book is not a document we stand over with a highlighter and a chart. It is a word we sit under, with our shoes off.

Must soon take place. The small word must is doing quiet work. Dei in Greek means necessity, the same word Jesus used when he said the Son of Man must suffer many things (Luke 9:22). It is not the blind necessity of fate. It is the necessity of a Father’s settled purpose. The phrase echoes Daniel 2:28, where Daniel tells Nebuchadnezzar what will happen in the latter days. Daniel saw it far off; John says it must happen soon. Nothing in the chapters ahead is a surprise upstairs. When the horses ride out and the seas turn to blood, no angel will be improvising.

Soon. This is the first hard sentence in the book, and smoothing it over would be dishonest. Nearly two thousand years have gone by. Was John simply mistaken? Three things can be said, and all three are needed. First, the Greek is en tachei, which can mean soon but can also carry the sense of speed rather than of the calendar: when it starts, it will not drag. Luke uses the same phrase of God, who will give justice speedily (Luke 18:8), in a parable that is explicitly about waiting a long time. Second, the New Testament measures nearness from the cross and not from our diaries. The last days did not begin with a headline we are still waiting for; they began at Pentecost, and every generation since has lived inside them (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2). And third, the plainest point of all: a great deal of it did happen soon. Within a few years of this letter, Christians in the towns it names were losing their trade, their standing, and in some places their lives, exactly as the book says they would.

By sending his angel. “Made it known” is esēmanen, signified, showed by signs. The verb is related to the word for a sign, and it is a hint at the form of everything that follows. God communicates in pictures here. He did not choose pictures to hide the meaning but to drive it home, because a picture of a Lamb on a throne stays in a frightened mind long after an argument has faded.

Who bore witness. Witness is one of the great words of this book. Christ is the faithful witness (v. 5), and believers are killed for their testimony (6:9; 12:11). The Greek word for witness, martys, is the word that became martyr in English, and the slide in meaning happened because so many witnesses paid for what they said. John is in exile for exactly this. He is a faithful reporter: he writes all that he saw, no more and no less.

Where Christians differ: how to read Revelation. Preterists see most of the book fulfilled in the first century, in the fall of Jerusalem (AD 70) or the Roman Empire. Historicists read it as a timeline of church history, often identifying the papacy with the beast. Futurists place most of chapters 4–22 in the last years before Christ’s return; dispensationalists among them set it in a seven-year tribulation after a secret rapture of the church. Idealists see it as timeless symbols of the conflict between good and evil. (A secret rapture is the belief that Christ will first come unseen to take believers out of the world before the final troubles.) This commentary’s view: the best reading combines the strengths of several. The book spoke first to first-century churches about their real enemies. Its visions then show, in a series of repeated cycles, the conflict between Christ and Satan through the whole period between Christ’s first and second comings. And it ends with a real, future, visible return of Christ, a final judgement and a new creation. This is often called the modified idealist or eclectic approach, and it fits the amillennial reading this commentary follows: amillennial means that the thousand years of chapter 20 picture Christ’s present reign through the whole age between his comings, not a future earthly kingdom of exactly a thousand years. The reasons are the book’s own: it was written to seven real churches about things they would face (1:3, 11), and its visions run in repeated cycles, each arriving at the final judgement (6:12–17; 11:15–18; 14:14–20; 16:17–21). It keeps the book relevant to every generation without losing its historical roots or its real future. Many faithful Christians read the book as futurists, and some expect a rapture before a final tribulation; they share the same great hope of Christ’s visible return, and this commentary honours them as brothers.

Who wrote it, and does it matter? The author calls himself John and nothing more, which suggests a man so well known to these churches that he needed no title. From the second century the church identified him as the apostle John, the son of Zebedee, who also wrote the Gospel and the three letters, and the shared language (Word, Lamb, witness, the one who conquers) supports the link. Some scholars think of another John, a prophet of the same circle. It matters less than it might seem. The book’s authority does not rest on John’s name but on the chain he describes: it is the revelation that God gave to Jesus Christ. Whoever held the pen, the voice is Christ’s.

How should an ordinary Christian read the symbols? With three simple habits. First, look for the book’s own explanation: it often tells you what a symbol means (1:20; 5:6; 17:9, 18). Second, look back to the Old Testament, because nearly every image comes from Daniel, Ezekiel, Zechariah, Isaiah, Exodus or the Psalms, and the first readers heard those echoes. Third, ask what the picture does rather than what it would look like in a photograph: a sword from the mouth is not a deformity but a statement that Christ’s word conquers. If a reading needs a newspaper to make sense, or would have meant nothing at all to a Christian in Smyrna, it has probably gone wrong.

Is this book too frightening or confusing for me? No. It was written for people most of whom had little education, some of them slaves, many unable to read, and it was meant to be understood when heard once in a church meeting. You will not grasp every detail, and nobody does. But the main message is not obscure at all: Christ is alive, he reigns, he sees his churches, he will come, evil will be judged and his people will be with him for ever. Start with chapters 1, 4, 5, 7 and 21 to 22. The frightening parts are real, but they are written to the church as warnings and comforts, not as threats against the people who belong to the Lamb.
verseByVerse.note: John wrote on Patmos, probably in the mid 90s AD under the emperor Domitian, though some date it to the late 60s under Nero. “Revelation” translates apokalypsis, an unveiling. The book is full of Old Testament imagery, especially Daniel, Ezekiel, Isaiah and Zechariah.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of this prophecy, and blessed are those who hear, and who keep what is written in it, for the time is near.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Most early Christians could not read and did not own books. Scripture was read aloud in the gathered church, as in the synagogue (Luke 4:16; Colossians 4:16; 1 Timothy 4:13). Revelation expects to be read aloud, from start to finish, to a listening congregation. Heard this way, its patterns, repetitions and climaxes work like music.

The first of seven blessings. Seven times in this book a blessing is pronounced, and here is the first of them (1:3; 14:13; 16:15; 19:9; 20:6; 22:7; 22:14). “Blessed” is makarios, truly happy, favoured by God, the word of the Beatitudes. Even the book’s blessings come as a complete set. Put the scene together before taking the sentence apart. It is the first day of the week, somewhere in Asia Minor, in a room that is somebody’s house on every other day of the week. Most of the people present cannot read. There is one copy of this scroll in the town, and it has just arrived by courier. A man stands up with it. For perhaps an hour and a half he reads, and nobody moves.

The one who reads aloud. The one who reads aloud (anaginōskōn) is singular: one lector, one voice, the public reader in the church service. Those who hear is plural: the room. Revelation was not written to be studied privately with a pencil; it was written to be heard in company, which is why its images hit like hammer blows rather than unfolding like an argument. If the book has ever felt airless to you on the page, that is because you are reading a script for a performance while sitting alone in a chair.

The words of this prophecy. Revelation calls itself prophecy (prophēteia), God’s word through a prophet, carrying the authority of the Old Testament prophets. Prophecy in the Bible is never only prediction. Isaiah and Jeremiah said a great deal about the future, but they said it to call people to repent and be faithful now. That is what this book does.

Those who hear, and who keep. The blessing does not fall on the one who understands. It falls on the one who keeps (tērountes: observes, obeys, holds fast). A man may hold every chart ever drawn of the seventy weeks and the seven years and miss the blessing entirely, while a widow who could not tell a seal from a trumpet walks straight into it. Revelation is to be kept, like a command, not solved, like a riddle. It is a marching order. Keeping is not the price of the blessing, as though obedience bought God’s favour; the blessing is pronounced before a single command has been kept. Keeping is simply how a person who has heard it holds on to it.

The blessing in his own voice. At the close of the book this first blessing returns, and this time it is Jesus who speaks it: Behold, I am coming soon. Blessed is the one who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book (22:7). The blessing that opens the scroll and the blessing that closes it come from the same mouth, because the prophecy is about him: the testimony of Jesus, the angel tells John, is the spirit of prophecy (19:10). Its visions are many, but its subject is one. To keep these words is to keep hold of him, and to be kept by him.

How do you keep a vision? You cannot obey a dragon. But the book answers this itself, two chapters later, and the answer is completely concrete. Keeping Revelation looks like refusing to say the words that would restore your trading licence (2:13). It looks like not eating at the guild dinner where the meat has been offered to an idol, even though missing the dinner will cost you the contract (2:14, 20). It looks like holding on to what you already have when you have little strength left (3:8, 11). It looks like staying awake in a church where everyone else has drifted off (3:2). It looks like worshipping the Lamb and nobody else, whatever the market demands (13:16–17; 14:12). Every one of those is something a person can do this week without owning a single commentary.

The time is near. The verse closes with the pressure that makes the whole thing urgent. The word for time is kairos: not clock time ticking away, but the appointed moment, the hour that has been set. Near is engys. A soldier waiting for the order to move does not need to know the minute. He needs to know that the order is coming and that he must be standing where he was told to stand when it does. Because the end is near, the response cannot be postponed.

Do I need to understand Revelation before I can be blessed by it? No, and the verse is built to say so. The blessing is promised to hearers who keep, not to scholars who decode. Understanding does matter, and the more you know the Old Testament the more the book will open to you. But you can receive what it says about Christ, about worship and about faithfulness on your first hearing, and act on it. Many parts of Scripture are like this: a child can obey what a lifetime of study will never exhaust.

Should our church read Revelation aloud? It would be a good thing to do, at least once. The book was written for it, and it takes about an hour and a half from beginning to end. Heard in one sitting, its repeated cycles and its great songs of praise (4:8–11; 5:9–14; 7:10–12; 11:15–18; 19:1–8) carry the hearer along in a way that reading a few verses at a time never can. Many Christians who have found the book baffling have found it suddenly clear when they heard it all at once.

On a Tuesday. Think of the last time this book came up in conversation. Was the subject a headline, a war, a politician, a date, or your own faithfulness? Revelation has often been used for the first, sincerely, but everyone who set a date by it was wrong. It was written for the second. Ask what in this week would look like keeping it: a compromise refused, a cold heart warmed, a hard thing held on to.
verseByVerse.note: The first of seven “blessed” sayings in Revelation. Letters were read aloud to the gathered church.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–8 — Greeting to the Seven Churches
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
What looks like a routine letter opening is a declaration of allegiance. Grace and peace come from the eternal Father, from the Holy Spirit in sevenfold fullness and from Jesus Christ, whose three titles make him prophet, priest and king, in language of the kind the Roman emperor claimed for himself.

Then the greeting breaks off into praise. The tenses carry the doctrine: Christ loves us now, has freed us by his blood once for all, and has already made us a kingdom and priests (Exodus 19:6). Verse 7 announces his public, universal return, joining Daniel 7:13 and Zechariah 12:10 as Jesus himself did at his trial (Matthew 26:64). And in verse 8 God the Father speaks in his own voice, one of only two times in the book, naming himself the Almighty.
verseByVerse.theology:
Loved, Freed, Made Priests

Grace comes from the eternal God, the sevenfold Spirit and Jesus Christ: faithful witness, firstborn of the dead, ruler of kings. He loves us, has freed us by his blood, and has made us a kingdom and priests.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Churches under pressure heard Caesar’s kind of titles given to a crucified man.

Now: Endurance grows from hearing that he loves us now.

verseByVerse.quote: John to the seven churches that are in Asia: Grace to you and peace from him who is and who was and who is to come, and from the seven spirits who are before his throne, and from Jesus Christ the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and the ruler of kings on earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Asia here means the Roman province in the western part of modern Turkey, with Ephesus its leading city. The seven churches are named in verse 11.

To the seven churches. After the majestic prologue, the ordinary furniture of a letter: sender, recipients, greeting. That in itself says something. Whatever else Revelation is, it is mail. It was addressed, carried and delivered to seven congregations in seven real towns, and those towns sit on a road. A courier landing at Ephesus would go north up the coast to Smyrna, then further north to Pergamum, then turn inland and swing south-east through Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia and Laodicea, a rough circle of a few hundred miles. John lists them in exactly that order (v. 11). This is probably a messenger’s round, not a numerical code.

Seven. Seven, all the same, is the number that governs this book: seven seals, seven trumpets, seven bowls, seven beatitudes, seven spirits. In Scripture’s symbolic arithmetic seven means fullness, the complete set. There were more than seven churches in Asia; Troas lay on the coast, and Colossae and Hierapolis were both within a day of Laodicea. So these seven are real congregations, and at the same time they stand for the whole church, in every age, which is why the letters keep saying that he who has an ear should hear what the Spirit says to the churches. Plural, every time.

Grace and peace. Grace (charis) is God’s undeserved favour, and peace (eirēnē) is the wholeness and reconciliation that favour brings. It is the standard Christian greeting, the one Paul used in letter after letter. But think what it means here. A book about to describe seals, trumpets and bowls of wrath opens by wishing the church grace and peace. Whatever the coming chapters hold for the world, for the people of the Lamb the first word and the last word are grace (22:21).

Him who is to come. Grace and peace come from three sources, and John names all three. The first is God the Father, described with an expansion of the divine name given at the burning bush, I AM WHO I AM (Exodus 3:14), stretched across time. In Greek this phrase is deliberately broken. The grammar requires the words to change their endings after the preposition “from”, and John simply refuses to let them. He leaves the divine title standing unchanged, like a boulder in a stream. The effect is untranslatable and unmistakable: this name will not be bent to fit our sentences. And the third term is a surprise. Not “who will be”, which is what the pattern demands, but who is to come. God’s future is not merely more existence. It is arrival: his coming to judge and renew (11:17). The emperor’s power was passing. This name was there before Rome and will be there when Rome is a ruin for tourists.

The seven spirits. The second source is the Holy Spirit in his sevenfold fullness, and two Old Testament pictures stand behind it. One is the description of the Spirit resting on the Messiah in Isaiah 11:2, the Spirit of the LORD, of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and might, of knowledge and the fear of the LORD. The other is the lampstand of seven lamps in Zechariah’s vision, which the angel explains with the words not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts (Zechariah 4:2–6). Later in this book the seven spirits are the seven eyes of the Lamb, sent out into all the earth (5:6). So the greeting is Trinitarian, Father, Spirit and Son, and the Spirit is placed between the other two because he is the one sent out from the throne into the world where the churches live, and by him, not by might or power, they keep what they hear.

Where Christians differ: who are the seven spirits? Some take them as seven angels, the highest angels standing before God (compare 8:2). Others take them as the Holy Spirit in sevenfold fullness. This commentary’s view: the Holy Spirit. Grace and peace come only from God, never from angels, and the seven spirits stand within a divine greeting from Father and Son. No angel has ever had grace to give. Revelation’s symbolic numbers make sevenfold a natural way of picturing the one Spirit, perfect and active everywhere (5:6).

The faithful witness. The third source is Jesus Christ, and he gets three titles where the others get one. The three echo Psalm 89, the psalm of God’s covenant with David, which promises a son who will be firstborn, highest of the kings of the earth, with a covenant that stands firm like the faithful witness in the skies (Psalm 89:27, 37). The faithful witness (ho martys ho pistos): Christ told the truth about God, and held to it before Pilate unto death (John 18:37; 1 Timothy 6:13). He testified in front of a Roman governor and it killed him. The persecuted churches are to be faithful witnesses like him; in 2:13 a believer named Antipas, already dead, is given the very same title. Christ shares his own name with the men and women who die for him.

The firstborn of the dead. Not the first to be revived, since others had been raised only to die again, but the first through death and out the other side permanently, into resurrection life that can never end. His resurrection is the beginning and guarantee of ours (Colossians 1:18; 1 Corinthians 15:20). Firstborn (prōtotokos) also carries the sense of rank: the eldest son and heir, with supreme status (Psalm 89:27), of a family that will eventually be enormous. Every believer buried since has been buried as a younger brother or sister of this one.

The ruler of kings. Present tense, written by a prisoner of the empire, about the man the empire executed. Ruler (archōn) is the word for the one in charge. Psalm 89:27 promised that David’s son would be the highest of the kings of the earth. Jesus already is. The emperor in Rome, who seemed to rule the world, is under the authority of the crucified Jew whose followers he persecuted. The book will show the kings of the earth in rebellion (17:2), defeated (19:19), and finally bringing their glory into the new Jerusalem (21:24).

Prophet, priest and king. Put the three titles together and they make a portrait. The faithful witness speaks God’s word, as a prophet. The firstborn of the dead has passed through death on our behalf, as a priest offering himself. The ruler of kings reigns, as a king. And titles of this kind belonged to Caesar in the public language of the empire; lord of the world was simply a description of what Rome claimed to be. John gives them to their true owner, in a letter, in the opening greeting, before he has said anything a censor could object to.

If Jesus rules the kings of the earth now, why does the world look so out of control? Because his reign is real but not yet visible to everyone, and it works in a way the world does not recognise. He rules as the Lamb who was slain, carrying out his purposes through the very evils that seem to defeat him, as he did at the cross, where the worst thing human rulers ever did became the salvation of the world. He restrains evil, sets its limits (2:10 gives a persecution a fixed ten days) and will judge it fully. The kings do not know they are subjects. That does not make them any less so. The book’s visions exist to let a struggling church see the throne behind the headlines.

On a Tuesday. Whoever holds power over you, an employer, a government, a culture, is under the rule of Jesus Christ. Faithful witness is worth it, because the faithful witness rose again. When you are asked this week to shade the truth, to keep quiet about Christ to keep a contract or a friendship, remember whose title you share. The faithful witness lost everything in Pilate’s court, and he is now the ruler of the man who sentenced him.
verseByVerse.note: The seven churches lay on a circular road in the Roman province of Asia (western Turkey). “Seven spirits” probably stands for the Holy Spirit in his fullness.

verseByVerse.quote: To him who loves us and has freed us from our sins by his blood and made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father, to him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sentence that breaks. Something happens here that the English cannot quite show. John is in the middle of a sentence, grace and peace from the Father, from the Spirit, from Jesus Christ, who is this and this and this, and then the sentence breaks. He never finishes the greeting properly. The mention of Jesus derails him into worship. The gospel would not wait its turn. And see the order: before Revelation shows a single judgement, before one seal is opened, it tells the church it is loved.

Him who loves us. Three things are said about what Christ has done, and the tenses are the whole sermon. To him who loves us: present tense, a participle that keeps running (agapōnti). And has freed us from our sins by his blood: past tense, a single completed act. And made us a kingdom, priests: past tense again, already enacted. Take the present tense first, because it is the one a suffering reader needs. John does not write “him who loved us”, looking back to Calvary as a historical kindness. He writes loves, and he writes it from a prison island to people who may be dead within a year. That is the tense that has to hold when a diagnosis comes back, when a congregation shrinks to nine, when the trade guild strikes your name off the list. Not he loved me once and I must make that stretch, but he is loving me now, in this, while this is happening.

Freed us by his blood. The verb (lysanti) means loosed, released. Sin is pictured as a chain, and Christ’s death is the price that broke it. The vocabulary is the exodus. Israel came out of Egypt because a lamb died and its blood went on the doorframe, and the whole nation walked out of slavery in the morning. Christ is the greater Passover lamb, and the slavery he breaks is not Pharaoh’s but the one underneath it: the guilt that no change of address can escape. And see what purchased it. Not his teaching, not his example, not his miracles. His blood (en tō haimati autou): the actual, physical cost of a real death in our place. Penal substitution is assumed here: Christ bore the penalty of our sin in our place, so that the sentence God’s law passed on it was carried out in full on him instead of on us (Isaiah 53:5; 1 Peter 2:24), and the song of chapter 5 will say it again, that by his blood he ransomed people for God (5:9). That is why the chain is truly broken. A debt that has been paid cannot be charged again.

A kingdom, priests. The third clause is lifted straight off Sinai, where God told a nation of former brick-makers that they would be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation (Exodus 19:6; 1 Peter 2:9). Now it is said of shopkeepers in Thyatira and slaves in Laodicea, Jew and Gentile together: the church is the people God promised Israel would be. We are a kingdom (basileian), the people over whom Christ reigns and who share his reign (5:10; 20:6). We are priests (hiereis): every believer has direct access to God and offers spiritual sacrifices of praise and service (1 Peter 2:5, 9; Hebrews 13:15). And it is said in the past tense. The church does not get promoted into royalty and priesthood at some future ceremony. It already is both, right now, in its weakness, with its dwindling numbers and its debts.

What does a priest actually do? Suppose he is a man who fits doors for a living. He does three things, and none of them requires a robe. He has access: he walks into the presence of God without an appointment and without an intermediary, which no ordinary Israelite could ever do. He carries other people in there with him: that is what intercession is, standing at the throne holding somebody else’s name. And he offers sacrifice: praise, and a life laid down for others, and the money that could have been spent elsewhere (Hebrews 13:15–16). A man who prays for his neighbour on the way to work has performed a priestly act, whatever his payslip says.

Glory and dominion. Glory (doxa) is the honour and splendour due to him. Dominion is kratos: raw ruling power, the root buried inside words like democracy and autocracy. It was an imperial word. And here it is being assigned, for ever, to a man who was flogged, stripped and nailed up outside a city wall by the very power that thought it owned kratos. Jews reserved such a doxology for God alone. John gives it to Jesus without a pause, because he worships Jesus as God.

Amen. Amēn: so it is, so let it be. The hearers in the church were meant to say it with him. A doxology in Revelation is not a decoration on the end of a paragraph; it is the room answering.

Textual note. Older manuscripts read “loosed” (lysanti); later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “washed” (lousanti), a difference of one letter in Greek. The older reading is stronger. Both are true in Scripture (7:14 speaks of robes washed in the blood of the Lamb). Similarly, older manuscripts read “a kingdom, priests” and later ones “kings and priests”; the meaning is close. They also read “loves” (present) where later ones read “loved” (past).

Where Christians differ: the priesthood of all believers. Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches hold that, alongside the shared priesthood of the baptized, there is an ordained ministerial priesthood that offers the sacrifice of the Mass. This commentary’s view: the New Testament never calls church leaders priests in a sacrificial sense. Christ is the one high priest, who offered himself once for all (Hebrews 7:27; 10:12–14), and every believer is a priest with direct access to God through him. Elders and deacons are servants who teach and care, not priests who offer sacrifices.

What it does not mean. Being a kingdom and priests does not mean Christians rule now by political force, or that the church should take over the state. Our reign is shared with the slain Lamb, and it now looks like faithful witness and suffering (v. 9). It will be fully seen in the new creation (22:5).

If every believer is a priest, do we still need pastors? Yes. The priesthood of all believers means no Christian needs a human go-between to reach God, and every Christian has a ministry of prayer and service. It does not mean every Christian has the same task in the church. Christ himself gives pastors and teachers to equip his people (Ephesians 4:11–12), and calls the church to honour and follow its elders (Hebrews 13:17). The difference is that a pastor is not a priest standing between you and God. He is a fellow priest whose particular work is to open the word and care for the flock, so that all the priests can do their work.

How can I say Christ loves me now when my life is falling apart? Because John said it to people whose lives were falling apart, and he based it on the cross, not on their circumstances. The evidence of his present love is the past act: he has already freed you by his blood, and a love that paid that price will not lose interest halfway (Romans 8:32). His love is not measured by whether this week has gone well. It was proved at Golgotha and it continues at the right hand of the Father, where he intercedes for you now (Romans 8:34). Feelings rise and fall. The tense of this verse does not.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him, and all tribes of the earth will wail on account of him. Even so. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. This verse combines two Old Testament prophecies, as Jesus himself did (Matthew 24:30). Daniel 7:13 shows one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of Days, to receive an everlasting kingdom. Zechariah 12:10 shows Jerusalem looking on the one they pierced and mourning for him as for an only son.

The announcement the whole book exists to make. John did not invent the weld of the two Old Testament texts. Jesus made it himself, under oath, in front of the high priest who was about to condemn him: you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven (Matthew 26:64). The court heard it as blasphemy and voted to kill him. This verse is that answer coming back.

Coming with the clouds. “Behold” (idou) means look! “Is coming” (erchetai) is present tense: his coming is so certain it is as good as under way. Clouds in the Old Testament are not weather. They are the vehicle of God’s presence: the pillar that went before Israel (Exodus 13:21), the cloud on Sinai (Exodus 19:9), the cloud that filled Solomon’s temple so densely the priests could not stand to minister. A figure who comes with the clouds is not travelling by an unusual method. He is arriving as God arrives. And he will come as he left, personally and visibly, for a cloud took him out of their sight on the Mount of Olives and the angels said he would return in the same way (Acts 1:9–11).

Every eye. No phrase could be more comprehensive (pas ophthalmos). This settles a question that recurs in every generation, because in every generation somebody announces that the Lord has already returned quietly and only the initiated noticed. Jesus dealt with this himself: his coming will be like lightning flashing from east to west, and no one will need to be told to go out into the wilderness to look (Matthew 24:26–27). Nobody will need to check whether it happened.

Those who pierced him. A soldier at Golgotha put a spear into the side of a man who was already dead, to make certain of it (John 19:33–37). To him it was very likely one more day’s work. This verse says he will see him again. So will the men who held the hammer, and the ones who chose Barabbas, and the councillors who agreed the verdict at night, and all who share their rejection of him. Nobody involved has been lost track of. And the Zechariah passage John is quoting is even more staggering than the English shows: there it is the LORD himself who says, when they look on me, on him whom they have pierced. John applies the line to Jesus and offers no explanation at all, apparently because he sees no difficulty. The one who was pierced is the LORD.

All tribes will wail. The verb is kopsontai: to beat the breast, the violent public grief of a funeral. Which kind of grief is this? In Zechariah the mourning is unmistakably repentance: God pours out a spirit of grace and pleas for mercy, and the people weep as for an only child. Here it seems to be mainly the grief of the unrepentant facing judgement, as in Matthew 24:30, where the same mourning reads much more like terror, though the book also hopes for the nations’ conversion (11:13; 15:4). The same sight will produce both. The face that one man has longed for all his life is the face another has spent all his life avoiding, and when it finally appears, neither of them will be able to look away. For believers, the same coming is the day of joy (22:20).

Even so. Amen. John ends the line by saying yes twice, once in Greek and once in Hebrew, nai, amēn, as though one language could not carry the agreement on its own. It will certainly happen.

Where Christians differ: one coming or two? Dispensationalists (Christians who read the Bible as a series of distinct eras, keeping Israel and the church apart) distinguish a secret rapture, when Christ comes for his church before a seven-year tribulation, from his later visible coming with his church to judge and reign on earth for a thousand years. This commentary’s view: Scripture teaches one visible return of Christ. Every eye will see him; there is no secret coming. The gathering of believers to meet him (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17) happens at that same public, trumpet-sounding return, which brings the resurrection, the final judgement and the new creation together (Matthew 24:29–31; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). Revelation itself shows the church on earth through the tribulation, protected but not removed (7:3; 11:1–2; 12:6). Many earnest believers hold the rapture view, and they love the same Lord and long for the same appearing; the difference is about the order of events, not about the hope itself.

What it does not mean. This is not a spiritual coming in someone’s heart, nor Christ’s coming in judgement on Jerusalem in AD 70 alone. Some do read it that way, taking those who pierced him as the Jewish leaders and the tribes of the earth as the tribes of the land. But every eye and all tribes of the earth point to the universal, final return.

Will people who died long ago see him too? Yes. The ones who pierced him have been dead for nearly two thousand years, and this verse says they will see him. At his coming all the dead are raised, the righteous and the unrighteous (John 5:28–29; Acts 24:15), and everyone who has ever lived will stand before him (20:12–13). No one escapes the meeting by dying first. That is a sobering thought for the unbeliever, and a glad one for the Christian whose loved ones have died in the Lord: they will see him too, and he is bringing them with him (1 Thessalonians 4:14).

Should a Christian be afraid of the second coming? Not with the terror of the unrepentant. For those who belong to him, his coming is the day the bride has been waiting for, and the book ends with the church crying Come, Lord Jesus (22:20). There is a right seriousness: we will give account, and we should not want to be found careless or compromised (1 John 2:28). But a believer’s fear is the fear of a child who wants to please his father, not of a criminal awaiting sentence. The one who is coming is the one who was pierced for you. You will be looking on the wounds that saved you.

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the Alpha and the Omega," says the Lord God, "who is and who was and who is to come, the Almighty."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. This is one of only two places in Revelation where God the Father clearly speaks directly in the first person (the other is 21:5–8). He sets his signature on the introduction.

Two brackets around everything. God speaks in his own voice here, and again at the very end, when he says Behold, I am making all things new (21:5). Two sentences, twenty chapters apart, bracketing everything. The first says who he is. The second says what he will do. Between them come the dragon, the beasts, the famine, the martyrs and the burning city, all of it inside those two brackets, none of it outside.

I am the Alpha and the Omega. Alpha (Α) and Omega (Ω) are the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, and therefore they hold everything in between: every word ever formed, every sentence ever spoken, the whole alphabet of history. God is the source and the goal of everything. He is not merely present at the start and waiting at the finish, like a man who sets a race going and then walks to the tape. Every letter in between belongs to him as well. Isaiah heard the same claim in Hebrew form: I am the first and I am the last; besides me there is no god (Isaiah 44:6).

Says the Lord God. Kyrios ho theos is the Greek form of the Old Testament title the LORD God. Israel’s covenant God speaks, the God of the burning bush and of Sinai, the God who made promises to Abraham and kept them.

Who is and who was. The threefold name returns from verse 4, and the order rewards a second look. Our instinct would be to start with the past: was, is, will be. John starts with the present, because that is where a frightened church is standing. God is not principally a memory from Israel’s history or a hope for a future generation. He is, in the present tense, in the room where the letter is being read.

The Almighty. The last word of the verse is the heaviest. The Greek is pantokratōr: ruler of all, holder of all power. It appears nine times in Revelation and only once in the rest of the New Testament (2 Corinthians 6:18). In the Greek Old Testament it was the word chosen to render LORD of hosts, the God who commands armies. Set that against what the seven churches could actually see. They could see the temple of the imperial cult on the hill at Pergamum. They could see the magistrate who decided whether their case went further. They could see the empty chair where a brother used to sit. What they could not see was the throne. So God says it himself, out loud, in the first person, before the visions begin: whatever your eyes report, the one who holds all power is not the man with the seal ring, and he has not been away.

The Almighty and the Lamb. The book never lets the Almighty stand alone for long. Four chapters on, John looks at the throne of the one who holds all power and sees, standing at its centre, a Lamb looking as though it had been slain (5:6). By the end the river of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb (22:1), and the city needs no temple, because its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb (21:22). The power of verse 8 does not stand apart from the cross. It shares its throne with the slain Lamb, and that is why the word Almighty is good news for a church and not only a terror to an empire.

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add “the beginning and the ending” after Alpha and Omega, borrowed from 21:6 and 22:13. The older manuscripts do not have it. The meaning is unchanged.

Who speaks here, the Father or the Son? Here it is the Lord God, the Father. But at the end of the book Jesus claims the same title: I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last (22:13; compare 1:17). That is one of the clearest testimonies in Scripture that the Son shares the Father’s deity. Isaiah said there was only one first and last. Revelation gives the title to the Father and to the Son, and does not think it has said two different things.

If God is almighty, why does he let his people suffer? Revelation never pretends to give a full answer, but it gives enough to stand on. God’s power is not in doubt; the book’s point is that nothing happens outside it. Suffering is allowed for a purpose and a limit (2:10; 6:11), it refines and proves the church’s faith, and it is never wasted: the martyrs under the altar are told to rest a little longer, and their cries are heard (6:9–11; 8:3–5). Above all, the Almighty answered evil not by staying distant but by sending his Son to suffer it, and he will finally wipe away every tear himself (21:4). We may not know why this sorrow. We do know who holds it.

On a Tuesday. Begin prayer with who God is. When life feels out of control, confess that the Almighty is the Alpha and the Omega of your story too: he was there before the trouble began, he will be there when it ends, and he holds every letter in between.

For worship. He is the Alpha, before whom nothing existed and by whose word everything that does exist came into being. He is the Omega, after whom there is no further chapter and beyond whom there is no appeal. He is the one who is, and who was, and who is on his way. He is the Almighty, and there has never been a single second in which that was less than completely true. Let the seals be opened. He is not braced for what is in them; he wrote them.
verseByVerse.note: Alpha and Omega are the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet.

parallels.desc: I am the first and I am the last

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–20 — The Vision of the Son of Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Before a seal is opened or a trumpet blown, John is shown a person, and everything in the remaining chapters happens under his authority. Exiled on Patmos and keeping the Lord’s day, John calls himself his readers’ brother and partner in the tribulation, the kingdom and the patient endurance, three things that arrive together.

He sees seven golden lampstands, the temple’s single lampstand now scattered along a Roman road, and among them one like a son of man, robed as a priest, doing the priest’s daily work of keeping the lamps burning. Every feature of the figure is drawn from the Old Testament, and features that belong to the Ancient of Days are given to the Son of Man.

John falls as though dead, and the hand that holds the stars is laid on him. The one who claims Isaiah’s title for God (Isaiah 44:6) is a man who died and now holds the keys of Death and Hades. The chapter closes with Christ explaining his own symbols: the stars are the angels of the churches, and the lampstands are the churches. Whatever the angels are, they are in his hand.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Son of Man Among the Lampstands

John sees the glorified Christ, clothed as a priest, walking among the churches, holding their stars in his hand, and holding the keys of Death and Hades.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: An exile kept the Lord’s day alone on Patmos, and heaven opened.

Now: The one too glorious to look at is the one who says, “Fear not.”

verseByVerse.quote: I, John, your brother and partner in the tribulation and the kingdom and the patient endurance that are in Jesus, was on the island called Patmos on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus. I was in the Spirit on the Lord's day, and I heard behind me a loud voice like a trumpet saying, "Write what you see in a book and send it to the seven churches, to Ephesus and to Smyrna and to Pergamum and to Thyatira and to Sardis and to Philadelphia and to Laodicea."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Patmos is a small rocky island in the Aegean Sea, about 40 miles (65 kilometres) southwest of Miletus and some 60 miles from Ephesus. Early church writers (Irenaeus, Eusebius) say John was exiled there under Domitian and released after Domitian’s death in AD 96.

Your brother and partner. He could have written I, John, apostle. He could have written the disciple whom Jesus loved, which is how the fourth Gospel refers to him. Instead: your brother (adelphos) and partner. The Greek is synkoinōnos, a fellow sharer, someone holding the same thing you are holding. Before he tells them anything they do not know, he tells them he is standing where they are standing.

Tribulation, kingdom, endurance. What are they all sharing? Three things, and in the Greek a single article gathers them into one bundle. Not three separate items on a list, but one package, delivered together. That arrangement is the theology of the whole book compressed into a single phrase. Tribulation (thlipsis) is pressure, affliction, persecution. Kingdom (basileia) is the reign of Christ. And the kingdom does not arrive after the tribulation is over, and it is not an alternative to it. The three come in the same envelope, and the middle one is the one nobody expects to find there.

The kingdom in the tribulation. A Christian under pressure very naturally concludes that the pressure is evidence of God’s absence: that if the kingdom were really here, the tribulation would not be. John, who is in more trouble than any of his readers, says the opposite. He is in the kingdom and in the tribulation, and both are in Jesus. The Lord said the same thing without a single softening clause: In the world you will have tribulation (John 16:33). And the apostles told the young churches that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God (Acts 14:22). Tribulation here is not only a future seven-year period; John and his readers are already in it. And the kingdom is not only future; they are already in that too.

That are in Jesus. The last three words hold the bundle together. Tribulation, kingdom and endurance are not John’s private lot, nor his readers’; they are in Jesus, because he had them first. He walked the road of suffering into his glory, as he told the two disciples on the Emmaus road that the Christ had to do (Luke 24:26). The kingdom is his, and he shares it (1:6). And the endurance is his too: to Philadelphia he calls it my word about patient endurance (3:10). A believer under pressure is not on a strange road. He is walking in the footprints of his King, and those footprints lead out of the grave.

Patient endurance. The third word in the bundle is the one that gets the reader through: hypomonē. It is not resignation, and it is not the vague cheerfulness we mean by patience. It means steadfast endurance, and its roots picture just that: remaining under the weight rather than stepping out from under it. It appears seven times in Revelation, and every time it describes the saints (1:9; 2:2, 3, 19; 3:10; 13:10; 14:12). The great Christian virtue in this book is not brilliance or influence. It is still being there.

On account of the word of God. Patmos is a bare volcanic island of about thirteen square miles, close enough to the mainland that on a clear day the coast is a smudge on the horizon. Rome used such islands for banishment: not a labour camp so much as a life shrunk to nothing, no assembly, no way home. John is careful to say why he is there. “On account of” (dia) means because of: he was not there as a missionary or a tourist, nor for theft or violence. He was sent for a sermon. His circumstances look like the end of a ministry, and they are in fact the beginning of the church’s most extraordinary book.

In the Spirit on the Lord’s day. “In the Spirit” (en pneumati) describes a state in which the Holy Spirit gave him prophetic vision, as he did with Ezekiel (Ezekiel 3:12–14; 11:1). The phrase marks the major sections of the book (4:2; 17:3; 21:10). “The Lord’s day” (tē kyriakē hēmera) is the first day of the week, Sunday, when Christians met to worship because Christ rose on that day (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2). This is the first time the expression appears, and it is dropped in without explanation because the readers already knew it; early writings such as the Didache use the same term for Sunday. The adjective lord’s was also used of things belonging to the emperor. Christians claimed the day for their true Lord.

Keeping Sunday on a rock. Picture what it means in his situation. As far as we know, there is no congregation on Patmos. There is nobody to read to, nobody to break bread with, no lampstand in sight. And an old man keeps the Lord’s day anyway, alone, on a rock, because the Lord rose whether anyone else on the island cares or not. That is where heaven finds him.

A voice like a trumpet. The trumpet (salpingos) recalls Sinai, where God spoke with a trumpet blast so loud that the people trembled (Exodus 19:16–19). A voice behind him, as Ezekiel heard (Ezekiel 3:12), and it will turn out to be Christ’s own.

Write what you see. The vision is not for John’s private edification, and it never becomes his possession. Within a sentence of receiving it he is a courier. And it is one book (biblion, a scroll) for all seven. Each church would hear not only its own letter but all seven, and the whole book.

Where Christians differ: is the Lord’s day Sunday or the day of the Lord? Some have taken it to mean that John was transported in vision to the future Day of the Lord, the day of judgement. Others hold that Christians should keep Saturday as the Sabbath, and that the Lord’s day is the Jewish Sabbath. This commentary’s view: the Lord’s day is Sunday. The Old Testament Day of the Lord is always expressed differently (hēmera kyriou), and early Christian usage of John’s phrase clearly means the first day of the week. This commentary’s view is that the Sabbath command is fulfilled in Christ, who is our rest (Hebrews 4:9–10; Colossians 2:16–17), and that the Lord’s day is not a burden of rules but the privilege of gathering on the day of resurrection to worship, rest and hear God’s word. Many godly brothers, with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold that the Sabbath command carries over to Sunday as the Christian Sabbath (Westminster 21.7–8; 1689 22.7–8), and their view deserves real respect. But Christians set the day apart gladly, out of joy and wisdom, and no one may bind another’s conscience about it (Romans 14:5).

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add in v. 11 the words “I am Alpha and Omega, the first and the last” and “which are in Asia”. They are absent from the older manuscripts.

What it does not mean. Being in the Spirit is not a technique for producing visions that Christians should seek today. John’s experience was a unique prophetic revelation, given to write Scripture. Now that the canon is closed, we meet the Spirit’s voice in what he wrote (22:18–19). And this verse should never make an ordinary Christian feel second-rate. “In the Spirit” describes something God did to John, not a technique John had mastered. He was not meditating his way upward; he was keeping Sunday, and the trumpet sounded behind him. A normal Christian life, prayer that feels flat, a psalm sung badly, a sermon half remembered by Tuesday, is not a lower grade of the same thing. It is the same Spirit. The dullest act of worship performed this month was performed in him.

If I suffer for my faith, has something gone wrong? No. John puts suffering inside the Christian life, not outside it. If you are mocked at work, passed over, cut off by family or worse because you follow Christ, you have not left the kingdom; you are sharing what John shared and what Jesus promised (John 15:18–20; 2 Timothy 3:12). That does not mean every hardship is persecution, or that we should go looking for trouble; much of our pain is ordinary, and some of it is our own fault. But where the pressure comes because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus, it is a mark of belonging, not of abandonment, and the right response is not panic but endurance.

How should I keep the Lord’s day? Keep it as the day of resurrection, centred on gathering with God’s people to worship, hear the word, pray, sing and share the Lord’s Supper. Christians differ over how strictly Sabbath rest applies, and the view of this commentary is that the command is fulfilled in Christ, so the day is not a list of forbidden activities. But it is still a gift to be received rather than a gap to be filled: rest from ordinary work where you can, make room for fellowship, mercy and quiet, and do not let it become just another day for errands. If, like John, you are cut off from church by illness, work or distance, keep it anyway. The Lord is risen on Patmos too.
verseByVerse.note: Patmos is a small rocky island in the Aegean, about 40 miles off the coast of Asia. “The Lord’s day” is Sunday, the day of Jesus’ resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I turned to see the voice that was speaking to me, and on turning I saw seven golden lampstands, and in the midst of the lampstands one like a son of man, clothed with a long robe and with a golden sash around his chest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I turned to see the voice. The ESV keeps the oddity rather than tidying it, and the oddity is the point. You do not see a voice. But this voice is so massive, so evidently coming from somebody, that John turns to look at it the way you would turn towards a shout in an empty house.

Seven golden lampstands. What he sees first is not the figure. It is the furniture. Anyone raised on the Hebrew Scriptures would place it instantly. In the tabernacle and the temple there stood a lampstand of pure gold with seven branches, the menorah, and it burned continually in the holy place before the veil (Exodus 25:31–40). Zechariah saw it in a vision (Zechariah 4:2–6). But something has changed, and the change is the point. In the temple there was one lampstand with seven branches. Here there are seven separate lampstands (lychnias), and verse 20 says they are the seven churches. The single light of Israel has been broken out and distributed: one in Ephesus, one in Smyrna, one in Pergamum, and so on up the road. The holy place is no longer a room in Jerusalem. It is a house in a Roman market town, and another a few days’ walk up the road, and the lamp is lit in both.

Golden. And they are gold. Small, struggling congregations in pagan cities, some of them compromised and one of them nearly dead, are in God’s sight precious metal. The world looked at a few dozen tradesmen meeting in a house and saw nothing worth counting. Christ looks and sees gold.

A lampstand makes no light. That quietly settles what a church is for. The stand holds the lamp up so the room can see. It is not admired; it is not the point; it is judged solely by whether the light is high enough to be useful (Matthew 5:14–16). The church is not the light itself; it holds up the light of Christ to the world. A congregation that has become impressive at everything except that has misunderstood the shape it was made in.

In the midst. This phrase carries the weight of the whole vision (en mesō). Not above them, inspecting from a height. Not outside, waiting for results. Not far away in heaven, out of reach. In the middle of them, close enough to touch the gold. He walks among his churches (2:1), seeing all. This is both comfort and warning: he is present to strengthen and to correct.

One like a son of man. Then, in the middle of them, a figure. The phrase (huion anthrōpou) comes from Daniel 7:13, where one like a son of man comes with the clouds into the presence of the Ancient of Days and receives a dominion that will never pass away. It is the title Jesus used of himself more than any other, and its power lies in its double edge. On the surface it means simply a human being. Underneath it means the figure Daniel saw receiving the worship of all peoples. He is truly human, and more than human.

A long robe and a golden sash. The long robe is podērēs, reaching to the feet, the very word the Greek Old Testament uses for the high priest’s garment (Exodus 28:4), and a golden sash was part of the priestly dress. The figure in Daniel 10:5 is clothed in linen with a belt of gold. Christ appears as the great high priest, ministering among the lampstands, and also as a king, since such robes signified dignity. The sash is not round his waist where a working man would knot it, but high across his chest, probably the way a man wore a sash when he was not labouring but presiding: dignity and rest, a task completed. The sacrifice is finished. What remains is the tending.

The priest at the lamps. The first picture John is given of him is a priest among the lamps, and it recalls the humblest priestly work there was. Morning and evening in the holy place a priest trimmed the wicks and topped up the oil so that the flame never went out (Exodus 27:20–21; Leviticus 24:1–4). That is the place the glorified Christ has taken among his churches, and the letters that follow are his tending of them (2:5). The one with eyes like fire and a face like the sun is first of all a lamp-tender.

Is Christ really present in my small, ordinary church? Yes. That is exactly what this vision says. Take the smallest, coldest gathering your church has had in the last year: the wet evening when eleven people came and the singing was thin and nobody could think of anything to say afterwards. He was standing in the middle of that room. He was not disappointed at a distance. He was there, doing what he does, keeping a wick alight that anybody else would have written off. He promised it where two or three gather in his name (Matthew 18:20), and the seven churches were not large. His presence is not measured by the size of the room or the quality of the music.

Is this vision about churches, or about me personally? Both, but in that order. The lampstands are congregations, and the picture is of Christ among his gathered people. Revelation does not imagine a Christian on his own with his private faith; it imagines believers held together in local churches, which is where Christ chooses to be found. Of course he is with each believer always (Matthew 28:20). But if you have drifted from church and kept your faith as a private thing, see where John sees him standing: among the lampstands. To find him most clearly, go where he has said he walks.

verseByVerse.quote: The hairs of his head were white, like white wool, like snow. His eyes were like a flame of fire, his feet were like burnished bronze, refined in a furnace, and his voice was like the roar of many waters. In his right hand he held seven stars, from his mouth came a sharp two-edged sword, and his face was like the sun shining in full strength.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Every feature here comes from the Old Testament, mostly from Daniel 7 and 10 and Ezekiel 1 and 43. The startling thing is that features belonging to the Ancient of Days, God himself, are now given to the Son of Man. John is showing, in pictures, that Jesus is God. He is not describing a face; he is assembling a theology out of the Old Testament’s greatest visions, and each feature tells a hard-pressed congregation something it needs to survive the week.

White like wool. In Daniel 7 there are two figures in the throne room: the Ancient of Days, whose clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool (Daniel 7:9), and the son of man who is brought before him. John has taken the description of the first and put it on the second. He does not argue for the deity of Christ here. He simply hands the son of man the Ancient of Days’ own hair and moves on to the next clause. The white is not the white of decline. In Daniel it is the mark of one whose existence has no beginning to date: eternity, wisdom, dignity and purity. Christ shares the eternal majesty of God, because he is God the Son (John 1:1; Colossians 2:9).

Eyes like a flame of fire. The phrase (phlox pyros) comes from Daniel 10:6. Fire does two things at once: it illuminates and it consumes. Nothing survives it and nothing hides from it. More than once in the letters that follow, this Christ will tell a church something about itself that it had managed not to know: Sardis thinks it is alive, Laodicea thinks it is rich. The eyes of flame are why. To Thyatira he introduces himself this way, as the one who searches mind and heart (2:18, 23). And the same fact lands two ways depending on where you are standing. To a believer keeping faith in a town where nobody notices, it means that nothing done in obscurity has gone unrecorded. To anyone maintaining a respectable front over something rotten, it means the front has never worked for a moment.

Burnished bronze. Burnished bronze (chalkolibanō) is a rare word for a fine, glowing metal alloy, a picture drawn from Daniel 10:6 and Ezekiel 1:7. Bronze glowing from the fire, and therefore bronze that has already been through it. These are feet that have stood in the heat and come out harder. And these feet stand firm, in contrast to the feet of iron and clay on the statue of earthly empires in Daniel 2. Feet also crush; that image will return when the winepress is trodden (14:20; 19:15).

The roar of many waters. Ezekiel heard exactly this sound and named it: the sound of his coming was like the sound of many waters, and the earth shone with his glory (Ezekiel 43:2), the glory of God returning to a temple it had abandoned. For John on an island, the image is the endless crash of the sea on the rocks. Stand at the foot of a waterfall in spate and try to hold a conversation. You cannot. Every other sound in the valley is simply taken away. That is the volume at which this Christ speaks over the empire, the accuser, the rumour, and the voice in a believer’s head at three in the morning.

Seven stars. The right hand is the hand of power, authority and possession. The stars are not orbiting nearby; they are held. Verse 20 will say they are the angels of the churches. So the churches are in his hand: they are in his power, and they are safe, and no one will snatch them out of it (John 10:28). And Roman coins used stars to advertise imperial divinity; Domitian issued one showing his dead infant son as a god, seated on a globe among seven stars. John has seen the real hand.

A sharp two-edged sword. Not in his hand; from his mouth. The sword (rhomphaia) is a long one, and the weapon of this King is speech (Hebrews 4:12). Isaiah said the coming ruler would strike the earth with the rod of his mouth (Isaiah 11:4), and the Servant says that God made my mouth like a sharp sword (Isaiah 49:2). At the end, Christ defeats his enemies with this sword alone (19:15, 21). The Roman governor had the right of the sword, the power of execution; Christ’s word is greater. The church has therefore been given no other armament, and needs none: not political leverage, not cultural weight, not numbers, but the word, spoken by people with no power, which has outlived empire after empire that banned it.

Like the sun. Three disciples, John among them, had seen it once before, on a mountain, for a short time (Matthew 17:2). Here it is not a glimpse permitted and withdrawn; this is simply what his face is like now, permanently, unbearable glory. And it is the last detail because nothing can be added after it. Every other feature has been an image drawn from somewhere. The face is just the face.
