He is the light that the lampstands were made to carry, standing in the middle of them, shining at full strength in a province that thought it had put the gospel out.

Is this the same Jesus who took children in his arms? Yes, entirely. The Jesus who welcomed children, touched lepers and wept at a grave is the eternal Son, and this vision shows what was always true of him, now unveiled. The tenderness was never weakness; it was the kindness of the Lord of glory stooping. And the glory is never cruelty; it is the strength of the friend of sinners. If you know only the gentle Jesus, you will find him too small to trust in a crisis. If you know only the blazing one, you will be afraid to come near. The next verses put the two together: the same right hand holds the stars and rests on John’s shoulder.

Why should the eyes of fire comfort me rather than frighten me? Because they see everything, including what no one else sees. They see the faithfulness nobody thanks, the prayer nobody hears, the temptation resisted in private, the injustice done to you that no court will ever examine. Nothing is lost to him. They also see your sin, and that is meant to bring you to honest repentance, not despair, because the eyes belong to the one who died for the sins they see. For a believer, the searching gaze of Christ is the safest place there is to be known completely, because it is also the place where you are loved completely.

For worship. The friend of sinners is the Lord of glory. The hair of the Ancient of Days is on the head of the man from Nazareth; the eyes that wept at Lazarus’s tomb blaze through every disguise; the feet that walked the roads of Galilee are bronze from the furnace; the voice that said Little girl, arise drowns the sea. He holds the churches in his hand, he conquers by his word, and his face is the sun. This is who walks among the lampstands, and he is ours.

verseByVerse.quote: When I saw him, I fell at his feet as though dead. But he laid his right hand on me, saying, "Fear not, I am the first and the last, and the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As though dead. This is the man who leaned back against Jesus at supper and asked him a question about the person sitting across the table (John 13:25). Some sixty years later he sees the same person and his body simply stops holding him up. That reaction is the normal one, which is itself instructive. Isaiah saw the Lord high and lifted up and said, Woe is me! For I am lost (Isaiah 6:5). Ezekiel fell on his face (Ezekiel 1:28). Daniel fell into a deep sleep with his face to the ground (Daniel 10:9). Peter, in a boat with more fish in it than it could hold, said, Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord (Luke 5:8). Nobody in Scripture who actually sees the glory of God finds it comfortable. Holy fear is not a lack of faith; it is a true sight of who he is.

Near this Christ, or near a picture of him? Which raises a question worth putting honestly. If a congregation always leaves a service feeling pleasantly warmed and never once leaves it undone, has it been near this Christ, or near a picture of him scaled down to a size that would not disturb anybody? The answer is not to manufacture fear. It is to preach and sing the Christ of the Bible at his true size, and let him do the rest.

His right hand on me. That is the hand from verse 16, the one holding the seven stars. He does not put them down to reach for John. The hand that governs the churches is the hand that steadies one frightened man on the floor, and it does both at the same time without strain. It is a hand of power and a hand of tenderness, as in Daniel 10:10, and as Jesus touched the frightened disciples on the mountain and told them to rise and have no fear (Matthew 17:7).

Fear not. Mē phobou: stop being afraid. The first words the glorified Christ speaks to his church in this book are the same words he used in Galilee to frightened disciples on the lake, and among the most frequent commands in Scripture. The voice like many waters says the gentlest thing in the vocabulary. And the order matters, because sentiment gets it backwards. The comfort does not arrive by reducing the glory. John is not told that he over-reacted. He is left flat on the ground, and lifted there. The awe remains, but the terror is removed. The glorious Christ does not destroy his own servant.

I am the first and the last. In Isaiah, twice, this is how God distinguishes himself from every rival: I am the first and I am the last; besides me there is no god (Isaiah 44:6; compare 48:12). It is not a phrase that can be shared out. Jesus takes it, unedited, and applies it to himself, the same divine title the Father used in verse 8 (Alpha and Omega). Jesus is not a lesser god; he is the one God, with the Father. And then he adds something Isaiah could not have said.

And the living one. Ho zōn. God is the living God, in contrast to dead idols, and Christ has life in himself (John 5:26). He does not merely have life, as we do, on loan. He is the one whose very definition is life, the source of it.

I died, and behold I am alive. No other being in existence can put those two clauses side by side. He does not say I was dead and now I am not, as though death had been an interruption to be got over. He says I am the living one, and then: I died. The Greek is literally I became dead (egenomēn nekros): a real death, in history, outside a city wall, with a spear to prove it. Life itself went into the grave. And came out, not restored to a life that could be lost again like Lazarus, but alive into the ages of the ages (eis tous aiōnas tōn aiōnōn). His resurrection is not a return to ordinary life but entry into endless life. Death can never touch him again (Romans 6:9).

The keys of Death and Hades. Keys (kleis) are not decoration; keys are authority. Whoever holds them decides who goes in and who comes out, and holds them because the door is his. Death here is the event and Hades is the realm, the state of the dead (hadēs, the Greek equivalent of the Hebrew Sheol): the two things every human being fears in different ways, the dying and the being dead. Later Jewish teachers, in the Talmud, said that the key to raising the dead is one God never hands to an agent. Both sets of keys hang from one belt, and they were taken by the only man who has ever been inside and walked out under his own power. He will open the graves at the resurrection (20:13), and in the end Death and Hades themselves will be thrown into the lake of fire (20:14).

A locked room with the key in a loving hand. Which means this, exactly and without softening. A grave is not a locked room with the key lost. Somebody has the key, and he loves the person inside. For anyone who has stood at a graveside in the rain and heard the earth go down, that is not a decoration on a hard fact; it is the hard fact. The one holding the keys is not a stranger who might be persuaded. He is the one who wept at a tomb before he opened it (John 11:35, 43–44). And for anyone who lies awake afraid of their own dying, the fear is not answered by being told that death is small. It is not small. It is answered by the keys, and by whose hand they are in.

What it does not mean. The keys of Hades do not mean Christ went to hell to suffer further after his death. His suffering was finished on the cross (John 19:30). The keys mean authority over death, won by his death and resurrection. Nor does this support the idea of a second chance after death; the Bible gives none (Hebrews 9:27).

Does Fear not mean I should never fear God? It means you need never fear being destroyed by him if you belong to Christ. Scripture still calls believers to fear the Lord (Proverbs 9:10; 1 Peter 1:17), and that is not the opposite of this verse but the other half of it. The fear of the Lord is reverent awe: taking him seriously, trembling at his word, not daring to treat him lightly. What Christ removes is the terror of condemnation (1 John 4:18). John stays on his face, and he stays unafraid. That is the posture of a Christian before Christ: low, and safe.

What happens to a believer who dies? He goes to be with Christ at once. The soul does not sleep or wait in a holding place; to be absent from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23), and the souls of the martyrs in this very book are awake before the throne (6:9–11). There is no purgatory to pass through, because Christ’s blood has already freed us from our sins (1:5). The body rests in the grave until the resurrection, when he will use the keys and raise it, glorified, to be reunited with the soul (1 Corinthians 15:42–44, 52). So the grave is real, but it is temporary, and the one who holds the key is coming.

On a Tuesday. If you are sitting with someone who is dying, read them these two verses. And if you are afraid, do what John did: stay low before him, and let him put his hand on you.

verseByVerse.quote: Write therefore the things that you have seen, those that are and those that are to take place after this. As for the mystery of the seven stars that you saw in my right hand, and the seven golden lampstands, the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven churches."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Christ repeats the command to write (v. 11) and explains two of the symbols.

Write therefore. “Therefore” (oun) ties the command to what has just happened. Because Christ has conquered death and holds its keys, John is to write without fear. The man who was lying on the floor is put back on his feet and handed a pen.

After this. “After this” (meta tauta) echoes Daniel 2:29 and 45, where Daniel tells the king what will be after this. The book concerns both present realities and future events, and both are mixed throughout. Many read this verse as a three-part outline: what John has seen (chapter 1), what is (chapters 2–3) and what will be after this (chapters 4–22). It is a serious reading of a genuine feature of the text, and 4:1 does open with almost the same words: come up here, and I will show you what must take place after this.

Where Christians differ: is this verse an outline of the book? Dispensationalists, who expect the church to be taken from the earth before a final tribulation, often take it as a strict outline, with chapters 4–22 entirely future, after the church is raptured at 4:1. Careful teachers in that tradition have worked it out at length, and any reader in a church shaped by it will have met it. Others hesitate, for two reasons that should also be given fairly. The same phrase, what must take place, is used in verse 1 of the entire book, chapters 2 and 3 included, so it is not obvious that it marks off a section beginning at chapter 4. And the contents resist the split in both directions: the letters to the seven churches are full of the future (a crown, a hidden manna, a pillar in the temple, the coming of Christ himself), while chapters 4 to 22 are full of the present (a throne that is occupied now, martyrs who are already under the altar, a Lamb who has already conquered). This commentary’s view: the phrase is better read as describing the whole book: what John saw includes things that are and things still to come, all mixed together. Chapter 12, for example, goes back to Christ’s birth and ascension. The book is not a strict timeline but a series of visions, each showing the same age between Christ’s comings from a different angle, and each ending at or near the final judgement. Nothing essential about Christ rests on the question; readers who differ here can and do sing the same hymns, and where it changes the meaning of a passage the options are set out again at the verse itself.

As for the mystery. Then Christ explains his own symbolism, and that fact is more useful than the explanation. The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven churches. Twice in one sentence the pattern is: this image means that reality. A reader who wanted a rule for handling the rest of the book has just been given one by the author. The word mystērion in the New Testament never means a riddle nobody can solve. It means something that was hidden and has now been told (Ephesians 3:3–5). The visions are not locked; they are explained, sometimes on the spot, and almost always by the Old Testament.

The angels of the seven churches. Angels (angeloi) can mean messengers, and each of the seven letters is addressed to the angel of that church (2:1 and the others).

Where Christians differ: who are the angels of the churches? Some say they are human messengers carrying the letters, or the pastor of each church; they point out that each letter is addressed to the angel and then rebukes him and calls him to repent, which seems a strange thing to say to an unfallen angel. Others say they are guardian angels assigned to the churches. Others suggest they personify the spiritual life or heavenly counterpart of each church, its corporate character as heaven sees it. This commentary’s view: they are most likely heavenly angels connected with each church, since every other use of “angel” in Revelation (over sixty) means a heavenly being, and Scripture speaks of angels watching over God’s people (Daniel 10:20–21; Matthew 18:10). Yet the letters are clearly aimed at the congregations themselves, who are rebuked and called to repent. The angel represents the church before God, so to address it is to address the church. In practice, the messages are for every believer (2:7).

The seven lampstands. Christ calls the church to shine for him in the darkness. The lamp is his to light, and his to take away.

Held and surrounded. What is not ambiguous is where the stars are and where the lampstands are. The stars are in his right hand. The lampstands are around him, and he walks in their midst. Whatever pressure is coming in the next twenty-one chapters, and a great deal is coming, it will arrive at churches that are already held and already surrounded. That is the chapter’s last word before the letters begin, and it is the reason the letters can be as searching as they are. He can afford to tell Ephesus the truth. He is not going to lose it.

What it does not mean. The seven churches are not seven ages of church history, as some have taught (Ephesus the apostolic age, Laodicea the last days). Nothing in the text suggests it, and every church in every age needs all seven letters.

Does my church have its own angel? Possibly, though we should hold it lightly. Scripture says angels are sent to serve those who will inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14) and speaks of the angels of little ones (Matthew 18:10), and this verse most naturally pictures an angel connected with each church. But the Bible never invites us to identify, address or pray to such angels, and it forbids worshipping them (19:10; Colossians 2:18). The point for us is not the angel but the hand: the star is in Christ’s right hand. Your church is watched over, but it is Christ who holds it and Christ to whom it answers.

Can Christ still remove a church’s lampstand today? Yes. A congregation can lose its witness and even cease to be a true church if it abandons the gospel and refuses to repent, and history is full of buildings where Christ was once preached and is preached no more. Ephesus itself, the leading church of Asia, is now a city of ruins. That does not mean any true believer is lost; Christ never lets go of his own (John 10:28). It means local churches are not guaranteed to last. The remedy he gives is simple: remember, repent and do the first works (2:5). The warning is given so that the lamp will not go out.

For worship. The Lord of the churches does not leave his servants guessing at what they are. He takes a star and a lamp, the brightest thing in the night sky and the humblest thing in the house, and says: this is you. The mystery hidden for ages is now told to his saints, and its heart is Christ himself among them, the hope of glory (Colossians 1:26–27). The one who died and holds the keys counts a few struggling congregations as stars worth holding, and the light they were lit to carry is his own.

1.text: <sup>1</sup>The revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to show to his servants the things that must soon take place.<sup>2</sup>He made it known by sending his angel to his servant John, who bore witness to the word of God and to the testimony of Jesus Christ, even to all that he saw.<sup>3</sup>Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of this prophecy, and blessed are those who hear, and who keep what is written in it, for the time is near.<sup>4</sup>John to the seven churches that are in Asia: Grace to you and peace from him who is and who was and who is to come, and from the seven spirits who are before his throne,<sup>5</sup>and from Jesus Christ the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and the ruler of kings on earth. To him who loves us and has freed us from our sins by his blood<sup>6</sup>and made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father, to him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.<sup>7</sup>Behold, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him, and all tribes of the earth will wail on account of him. Even so. Amen.<sup>8</sup>“I am the Alpha and the Omega,” says the Lord God, “who is and who was and who is to come, the Almighty.”<sup>9</sup>I, John, your brother and partner in the tribulation and the kingdom and the patient endurance that are in Jesus, was on the island called Patmos on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus.<sup>10</sup>I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s day, and I heard behind me a loud voice like a trumpet<sup>11</sup>saying, “Write what you see in a book and send it to the seven churches, to Ephesus and to Smyrna and to Pergamum and to Thyatira and to Sardis and to Philadelphia and to Laodicea.”<sup>12</sup>Then I turned to see the voice that was speaking to me, and on turning I saw seven golden lampstands,<sup>13</sup>and in the midst of the lampstands one like a son of man, clothed with a long robe and with a golden sash around his chest.<sup>14</sup>The hairs of his head were white, like white wool, like snow. His eyes were like a flame of fire,<sup>15</sup>his feet were like burnished bronze, refined in a furnace, and his voice was like the roar of many waters.<sup>16</sup>In his right hand he held seven stars, from his mouth came a sharp two-edged sword, and his face was like the sun shining in full strength.<sup>17</sup>When I saw him, I fell at his feet as though dead. But he laid his right hand on me, saying, “Fear not, I am the first and the last,<sup>18</sup>and the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades.<sup>19</sup>Write therefore the things that you have seen, those that are and those that are to take place after this.<sup>20</sup>As for the mystery of the seven stars that you saw in my right hand, and the seven golden lampstands, the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven churches.”

2.title: Letters to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, and Thyatira
2.overview:
Chapters 2 and 3 hold the risen Christ’s seven letters to real congregations in the Roman province of Asia. Before the visions begin, he speaks to each church by name, with exact knowledge of its condition.

Every letter follows a pattern: Christ introduces himself with a feature from the vision of chapter 1; he says I know; he commends, rebukes, or both; he calls for repentance or endurance; he bids whoever has an ear to hear what the Spirit says to the churches; and he makes a promise to the one who conquers. Conquering (nikōn) is the key word of the letters, and it means faithful endurance to the end, not occasional spiritual triumph.

The seven towns lay on a courier’s circuit, running roughly clockwise from Ephesus. Seven also signals completeness: these churches stand for the whole church in every age, and every congregation since has found itself somewhere in these letters.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — To the Church in Ephesus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ephesus was the first stop on the courier’s road: a harbour city famous for the temple of Artemis, where Paul had spent three years (Acts 20:31). Christ comes as the one who grips the seven stars and walks among the lampstands. He commends the church at length for its toil, endurance and testing of false apostles (vv. 2–3), then charges it with abandoning the love it had at first (v. 4). The remedy is to remember, repent and do the first works, or lose the lampstand (v. 5): not salvation withdrawn, but a congregation ceasing to give light. The letter ends with praise for hating the works of the Nicolaitans and the promise of the tree of life (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology:
Orthodox but Loveless

Ephesus had sound doctrine, hard work and endurance, but had abandoned its first love. The cure is to remember, repent and do the works it did at first.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A second-generation church kept the truth and lost the warmth.

Now: Ask what would remain of your faith if the things others can see were taken away.

verseByVerse.quote: "To the angel of the church in Ephesus write: 'The words of him who holds the seven stars in his right hand, who walks among the seven golden lampstands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Revelation 2 holds the first four of Christ’s seven letters to the churches of Asia. Each follows a pattern: Christ introduces himself with a feature from the vision of chapter 1; he says, I know your works; he praises and rebukes; he calls for repentance or endurance; he bids anyone who has an ear to hear what the Spirit says to the churches; and he makes a promise to the one who conquers. Ephesus is sound in doctrine and tireless in work but has abandoned its first love, and must repent or lose its lampstand; the conqueror will eat from the tree of life (vv. 1–7). Smyrna is poor, slandered and facing prison, and receives no rebuke, only the call to be faithful unto death and the promise of the crown of life (vv. 8–11). Pergamum, where Satan’s throne is, held fast when Antipas was killed, but tolerates the teaching of Balaam and the Nicolaitans, which permits idolatry and immorality; Christ will fight them with the sword of his mouth, and promises hidden manna and a white stone with a new name (vv. 12–17). Thyatira is growing in love, faith and service but tolerates a false prophetess, Jezebel, who leads believers into immorality and idol feasts; Christ, whose eyes are like fire, will judge her, and promises the faithful authority over the nations and the morning star (vv. 18–29). Together the letters show a Christ who knows his churches completely, loves them enough to rebuke them, and calls every believer to conquer, not by willpower but by the blood of the Lamb (12:11), holding fast to the one who first loved them.

The setting. Ephesus was the leading city of the Roman province of Asia, a great port of perhaps 200,000 to 250,000 people, famous for the temple of Artemis (Diana), one of the seven wonders of the ancient world. Paul spent nearly three years there (Acts 19; 20:31), and a riot broke out when the gospel threatened the trade in silver shrines of Artemis (Acts 19:23–41). He warned the Ephesian elders that fierce wolves would come in (Acts 20:29–30), and Timothy was left there to oppose false teaching (1 Timothy 1:3). Early tradition says John himself later lived and ministered in Ephesus. By now the church was probably about forty years old, into its second generation.

The pattern of the seven letters. Every letter identifies its sender by lifting one feature out of the vision of chapter 1, and the feature chosen is always the one that particular congregation most needs to see. In every church, Christ’s knowledge is complete and his promises are rich.

To the angel of the church in Ephesus write. The angel (angelos, messenger) is probably a heavenly angel who represents the church before God, but that question need not be resolved to read the letter, because the message is for the whole congregation and, beyond it, for all churches. The letter closes by telling whoever has an ear to hear what the Spirit says to the churches, plural. All seven letters were sent to all seven towns. Ephesus read Laodicea’s mail, and so do we.

Holds the seven stars. “The words of” is tade legei, the prophets’ formula for the LORD’s own speech, Thus says the LORD: Christ speaks with the authority of God. Both halves of his title come from 1:13 and 1:16, and both are sharpened. In chapter 1 he simply held the stars; the word here is stronger (kratōn): he grips them. To a church that may lose its lampstand, he presents himself first as the one who holds the churches firmly in his power.

Walks among the lampstands. In chapter 1 he stood in the midst of the lampstands; here he walks among them (peripatōn), as an inspector does, and as a priest went from lamp to lamp in the temple. He is not stationed at the front of the room. He is moving through it.

Where he is standing before he speaks. Christ does not begin the correspondence by naming faults. He begins by saying where he is standing. Every hard sentence in the letters that follow is spoken from inside the room, by someone who has not left and is not going to. Correction from a stranger feels like an attack. Correction from the one who holds you in his right hand is love.

What it does not mean. The seven letters are not a forecast of seven eras of church history. Some teachers, many dispensational Bible teachers among them, have said that Ephesus represents the apostolic church, Laodicea the lukewarm church of the last days, and the others the ages between; they hold it out of a sincere wish to see Christ ruling all of history. But these were real congregations with real problems, every letter ends by sending its message to all the churches (2:7), and the scheme only works by reading history in hindsight, so most interpreters, including this commentary, do not follow it. All seven speak to every church in every age.

Which of these letters is written to my church? Very possibly more than one. Any congregation that has ever existed will find itself somewhere in this chapter and the next: correct and cold, poor and hunted, compromised, tolerant of what it should have confronted, asleep, weak and faithful, or comfortable and self-satisfied. Before reading on for the interesting question of who the Nicolaitans were, ask the more useful one. Read all seven and notice which commendation you would most like to hear, and which rebuke makes you most uncomfortable. The discomfort is usually the clue. And remember that the letters are also personal, because each ends with a promise to the one who conquers, singular.

For worship. The hand that grips the seven stars has never once opened to let a church fall. He does not go through his churches as a landlord goes through a property, but as the bridegroom who loved the church and gave himself up for her, so that he might present her to himself in splendour, without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:25–27). Paul wrote those words to this very congregation. The one who now walks among its lamps is the one who first paid for every one of them, and he is still at work making his bride beautiful.
verseByVerse.note: Ephesus was the greatest city of Asia and home to the vast temple of Artemis. Paul had spent nearly three years there.

verseByVerse.quote: "'I know your works, your toil and your patient endurance, and how you cannot bear with those who are evil, but have tested those who call themselves apostles and are not, and found them to be false. I know you are enduring patiently and bearing up for my name's sake, and you have not grown weary.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Travelling preachers moved from church to church, and some claimed apostolic authority they did not have (2 Corinthians 11:13). Churches had to test them (1 John 4:1); an early church manual, the Didache, gives rules for doing so (Didache 11).

I know your works. Every one of the seven letters begins there (oida), and it cuts two ways: comfort for the faithful, warning for the compromising. To Ephesus it opens a commendation that runs for two full verses before a word of criticism.

Your toil and your patient endurance. What he commends is impressive by any measure. Toil is kopos, labour to the point of exhaustion: not activity, but the kind of work that leaves a person emptied. Patient endurance is hypomonē: staying power under pressure, remaining under the weight.

Cannot bear. “Cannot bear” (ou dynē bastasai): they practised church discipline, and did not tolerate evil in their midst as Pergamum and Thyatira did.

Tested and found false. “Tested” (epeirasas) means put to the proof; “false” (pseudeis) means liars. They measured the claims of teachers against the apostolic gospel and exposed the frauds, and that took nerve, because rejecting a self-proclaimed apostle in the first century meant a public fight. This is exactly what Paul had asked of them. He had warned this very congregation, in tears, that after his departure fierce wolves would come in among them and that men would arise from their own number speaking twisted things (Acts 20:29–31). A generation later, Ephesus was still acting on it.

Bearing up. Verse 3 says it again from a different angle, and the repetition is deliberate. There is a play on words: they cannot bear evil people, but they have borne (ebastasas, carried a load) hardship for Christ’s name. And another: they laboured (kopos) without growing weary (ou kekopiakes). Christ says all of it before he says anything else, and he means every word.

For my name’s sake. The motive Christ names is himself. Ephesus has carried its load for his name, and that name is not a label but a person, the one who first carried a heavier load for them. He endured the cross, despising the shame, and weary believers are told to consider him who endured such hostility from sinners, so that they may not grow weary or fainthearted (Hebrews 12:2–3). That is the secret of a church still on its feet a generation on. And the tests they ran on travelling apostles were tests of loyalty to him: false apostles are false because they preach another Jesus (2 Corinthians 11:4, 13).

Why the praise comes first. This makes what follows in verse 4 far more serious than it would otherwise be. If Christ had opened with the fault, a reader could dismiss the commendation as softening. He opens with the commendation, and it is genuine. The problem at Ephesus is not that the good things are unreal. It is that a church can have all of them and still be in danger.

What can be counted and what cannot. There is a warning here for anyone who has ever measured a congregation. Everything in these two verses is visible from outside: the workload, the doctrinal spine, the longevity, the discernment. A visitor could count all four in a single Sunday. What is about to be named cannot be counted at all, and only the eyes like a flame of fire could see it. That is why the same church can be commended by every observer and corrected by its Lord in the same letter. And there is a quieter danger inside a church like this. It can come to love its own correctness, the feeling of being the ones who got it right, more than the Lord it is right about. That is trusting in religion rather than in Christ, in its most respectable form, and from the outside it looks exactly like faithfulness.

How do I test a teacher without becoming suspicious of everyone? Test what is taught, not the personality. Ask: does this teaching agree with the plain meaning of Scripture, read in context? Does it confess Jesus Christ as God come in the flesh, crucified and risen (1 John 4:2–3)? Does it lead to holiness, or make sin easy (Jude 4)? Is the teacher’s life consistent with what he says (1 Timothy 3:2–7)? And does he point people to Christ or to himself? You need not interrogate every sermon in a hostile spirit; most faithful teachers will make small mistakes. Testing is for protecting the flock from real error, and it should be done humbly, with Scripture open, in the company of your church and its elders.

verseByVerse.quote: But I have this against you, that you have abandoned the love you had at first. Remember therefore from where you have fallen; repent, and do the works you did at first. If not, I will come to you and remove your lampstand from its place, unless you repent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Paul had praised the Ephesians for their love toward all the saints (Ephesians 1:15) and ended his letter to them with grace for all who love the Lord Jesus with undying love (Ephesians 6:24). Now, a generation later, that love has cooled. Jesus had warned that because lawlessness would increase, the love of many would grow cold (Matthew 24:12).

Abandoned. One sentence undoes the tone of everything before it, and the verb matters. It is not that their love has cooled by degrees, the way a room cools when the fire goes out. Aphēkes is the word for leaving something behind, letting it go, releasing it, the same verb used of the disciples leaving their nets. Ephesus has not lost its first love in the way a man loses his keys. It has put it down and walked on.

What is first love? Two answers are usually given and there is no need to choose between them, because the letter itself refuses to. Love for Christ, plainly: the astonishment of a person who has just discovered he is forgiven and cannot get over it. And love for one another, which is what the same apostle spends his first letter insisting cannot be separated from it (1 John 4:20–21). A church that has stopped marvelling at grace will, in short order, stop being gracious. The two go together, and they leave together. The church kept doing the right things, and kept believing the right things, but the warmth of devotion that once drove it had gone. Its battles against false teachers may have left it suspicious and hard, defending the truth without the love that the truth produces.

Picture the difference. Imagine a young congregation in the fifties of the first century taking in a runaway slave and hiding him at real legal risk, because they cannot get over the fact that they were themselves bought out of slavery. A generation on, the same congregation, in the same city, correctly identifies a false apostle, writes a careful refutation, and is right in every particular, and nobody in the room would take a risk like that any more. Nothing has been believed that should not be. Nothing has been added to or removed from the creed. The doctrine is exactly what it was and the temperature is not.

Remember. Christ’s remedy is three verbs in a deliberate order. Remember (mnēmoneue, keep remembering): not try harder, but look back, and compare honestly what you were with what you are. And “fallen” (peptōkes) is a strong word: losing first love is a fall, not a small matter.

Repent, and do the works. Repent (metanoēson) means turn round, and it means this is a sin and not a phase. Coldness towards Christ is not a temperament; it is something to be confessed. Then do the works you did at first: not wait for the feeling to return, but act.

The heart reached through the hands. That last instruction is the practical hinge of the letter, and it is enormously freeing. Anyone who has ever tried to manufacture affection for God by sheer effort knows that it does not work and that failing at it produces despair. Christ does not ask for the feeling directly. He asks for the deeds, and he identifies them from the record: the visit you used to make, the giving that used to cost you something, the praying you used to do before anyone was awake, the conversation about Christ you used to be willing to start. Do those, leaning on the Spirit who first kindled that love. The heart is not reached by being lectured; it is reached through the hands.

The love that did not leave. Set the charge beside the one who makes it. Ephesus has let go of its first love, but its Lord has never let go of his. John, who wrote down this letter, had written in his Gospel that Jesus, having loved his own who were in the world, loved them to the end (John 13:1). And he had told the churches where love begins: we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). That is why the remedy starts with remembering. The way back to first love is not to stir up a feeling but to look again at the love that came first, his, which went to the cross and has not cooled for a single day since. And no church has ever loved him as it should, not even Ephesus in its first warmth; only he has loved the Father with all his heart and his own to the end, and that perfect obedience is counted to all who trust him (Romans 5:19). A cold heart confessed is a forgiven heart (1 John 1:9).

Remove your lampstand. Then the threat, which is severe and precise. “Come” (erchomai) is probably not the final return here, but a coming in judgement on this church in history. Not I will remove your salvation: this is a letter to a church, and the lampstand is the congregation as a light-bearer (1:20). To remove it means the church would cease to be a witness and finally cease to exist as a church. A church that keeps its doctrine and loses its love does not immediately close; it can run for years on organisation and memory. But the light goes out, and eventually so does everything else. Historically, the church at Ephesus did continue for centuries, which suggests it heeded the warning; but the harbour silted up, the city was abandoned, and Christianity there long ago disappeared. The lampstand stands in a field of ruins.

What it does not mean. Losing the lampstand does not mean true believers lose their salvation. Christ is speaking about the church as a community and its witness. True believers persevere because God keeps them (John 10:28–29); and one way he keeps them is by warnings like this one, which they heed.

How do I know if I have left my first love? Ask a few honest questions. Do I still marvel that I am forgiven, or has it become a fact I simply know? Is prayer something I want or something I manage? Do I love my fellow believers, especially the difficult ones, or mostly assess them? Am I quicker to spot error than to show kindness? Is my service still for Christ, or has it become habit and reputation? No one passes such a test perfectly, and the point is not to measure your feelings on a bad day. It is to notice drift over months and years, and the direction you are moving in. And if these questions trouble you, take heart: a heart that worries about its coldness to Christ is not a dead heart, and the concern itself is the Spirit’s work.

What if I never had a dramatic first love to go back to? Then do not try to recover a feeling you never had. First love is not a particular emotional experience at conversion; many believers came to Christ quietly, as children or slowly over years. It is the love that answers grace: gratitude, delight in Christ, love for his people. The way into it is the same as the way back to it: look at what Christ has done for you, confess your coldness, and do the works of love. Read the Gospel accounts of the cross slowly. Serve someone in his name. Feelings often follow obedience; they rarely come before it.

On a Tuesday. Correct but cold rarely announces itself; it looks like an ordinary week of doing the right things. Somewhere in that week is a small work you once did gladly for Christ or his people and quietly stopped. Picking it up again is not a way of earning back his love. It is a way of walking back into the warmth of a love that never left.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet this you have: you hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. To the one who conquers I will grant to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. The Nicolaitans are mentioned only here and in v. 15, where they are linked with the teaching of Balaam: eating food offered to idols and sexual immorality (v. 14). Early writers (Irenaeus) connected them with Nicolaus of Antioch, one of the seven in Acts 6:5, but this is uncertain, and later writers simply repeat him. They seem to have taught that Christians could join in pagan feasts and the trade guilds’ idolatrous life, perhaps claiming that what is done in the body does not matter. In Ephesus they were rejected; in Pergamum they were tolerated.

Yet this you have. Christ returns to commendation before the letter closes, to a church he has just warned with the removal of its lampstand; the rebuke is not the last word. The Nicolaitans were most likely not a doctrinal sect in the abstract but the party of accommodation, the people arguing that a Christian could keep his guild membership, attend the dinner, join the ritual, and privately not mean it.

Hate. Take the word seriously (miseis), because it is used twice and the second time Christ applies it to himself. This is a church commended for hating something. That sits awkwardly with a sentimental picture of Christian love, and it should. Love that cannot hate anything is not love; it is indifference wearing love’s clothes. A father who watched his child being fed poison and felt nothing would not be gentle. And the object of the hatred is stated with care: not the Nicolaitans, but the works of the Nicolaitans. Christ hates the works, not the people; some things are right to hate, whatever destroys his people. Ephesus has got that distinction right while getting first love wrong, and Thyatira will get first love right while getting this wrong. Neither church is asked to trade one for the other.

Whoever has an ear. Jesus often said, He who has ears, let him hear (Matthew 11:15; 13:9), after a parable. The words are Christ’s, yet John reports them as what the Spirit says: Christ speaks by his Spirit, and the two are not in competition. And the Spirit who speaks the command is the Spirit who lives in every believer and gives the strength to keep it (Ezekiel 36:27). And it is churches, plural. Every letter is for every church.

To the one who conquers. The participle (nikōnti, from nikē, victory) ends every one of the seven letters. It is a fighting word, and it will be defined precisely later in the book: they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death (12:11). The Lamb conquered by being slain (5:5–6). Conquering, in Revelation, is not winning by force. It is holding on to Christ, at cost, to the end. And the conquerors are not an elite class of super-Christians: everyone born of God overcomes the world through faith (1 John 5:4–5). Every true believer conquers. There is no other kind. Theologians call this the perseverance of the saints: everyone God has truly brought to faith he will keep in faith to the end, so that the believer’s holding on is the fruit of God’s holding him (Philippians 1:6; 1 Peter 1:5).

The tree of life. Trace the promise back and the reach of it becomes clear. The tree of life (xylou tēs zōēs) stood in the middle of the garden (Genesis 2:9), and after the fall a guard was set on the way to it so that fallen humanity could not reach out and take and live for ever in its ruin (Genesis 3:22–24). For the whole of Scripture after that, nobody eats from it. It reappears in the last chapter of the Bible, in the middle of the street of the city, with its leaves for the healing of the nations and no sword barring the path (22:2, 14). Paradise (paradeisos, a Persian word for a garden or park) is the word the Greek Old Testament used of Eden. Here the exile is declared over: Christ promises to restore what Adam lost, eternal life in God’s presence.

The true tree and the true refuge. And see who opens the way back. It is the one who was himself hung on a tree. The shrine of Artemis is said to have begun at a sacred tree, and her temple was a place of asylum where fugitives could claim protection. Christ offers the true tree, and the true refuge, and the cherub’s sword that barred the path to it fell on him.

Am I a conqueror if I still struggle with sin? Yes, if you belong to Christ and keep coming back to him. Conquering in Revelation is not sinless perfection or a life of visible triumphs. It is persevering faith: trusting the blood of the Lamb, holding to his word and refusing to give up on him (12:11). A believer who falls, grieves, confesses and gets up again is conquering; the one who gives up on Christ is not. The victory belongs first to the Lamb, and you share it by faith (1 John 5:4). The struggle itself is a sign of life, because the dead do not fight.

Is it ever right for a Christian to hate? Yes, but only what God hates, and only in the way he hates it. Scripture calls us to hate what is evil and hold fast to what is good (Romans 12:9), and to hate even the garment stained by the flesh (Jude 23). That hatred is aimed at sin and the lies that destroy people, never at the people themselves, whom we are to love, even our enemies (Matthew 5:44). The test is simple: if your hatred of a false teaching makes you want to rescue its victims, it is godly; if it makes you enjoy the downfall of its teachers, it has gone bad.
verseByVerse.note: The Nicolaitans are unknown outside Revelation; they seem to have taught that believers could take part in pagan feasts and immorality.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–11 — To the Church in Smyrna
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Smyrna, thirty-five miles north, was a beautiful city fiercely loyal to Rome. To a church about to face death, Christ comes as the one who died and came to life (v. 8). He knows its tribulation, its poverty and the slander it suffers, and in his reckoning it is rich (v. 9). He does not deny the suffering to come, but sets bounds on it and gives it a purpose the devil did not choose: that you may be tested (v. 10). The faithful will receive the crown of life and will never be hurt by the second death (v. 11). Smyrna receives no rebuke at all.
verseByVerse.theology:
Poor, and Rich

Christ, who died and came to life, knows Smyrna’s tribulation and poverty, and says they are rich. Suffering is coming, bounded and purposeful; the faithful will not be hurt by the second death.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Polycarp, bishop of this church some sixty years later, served Christ to the fire.

Now: Grace for a trial is given on the day of the trial, not in advance.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to the angel of the church in Smyrna write: 'The words of the first and the last, who died and came to life. "'I know your tribulation and your poverty (but you are rich) and the slander of those who say that they are Jews and are not, but are a synagogue of Satan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Smyrna (modern Izmir) was a wealthy port about 35 miles (56 kilometres) north of Ephesus, a beautiful planned city that called itself the first of Asia, with a paved street running from the harbour to the temple of Zeus and a ring of public buildings along the ridge of Mount Pagos that visitors called the crown of Smyrna. It was fiercely loyal to Rome: it built one of the first temples to the goddess Roma (195 BC) and won the honour of a temple to the emperor Tiberius (AD 26) in a competition among eleven cities. Emperor worship was intense, and refusing it was seen as disloyalty. The city had a large and influential Jewish community. Destroyed around 600 BC and refounded three centuries later, it was said to have died and come back to life.

Who died and came to life. This letter takes the two clauses about death (1:17–18) and hands them to the church that is about to face it. To a congregation being told to prepare for prison, the credential offered is not power in the abstract. It is that he has been where they are going. The one giving the orders has been dead. As the city had, in a sense, died and lived again, the true Lord has truly died and risen.

Tribulation and poverty. Tribulation (thlipsin) is pressure, persecution. The word for poverty is ptōcheia: not the modest means of a working family but destitution, the poverty of a beggar with nothing. In a rich city. That is not an accident of economics. A Christian who would not join the guild ritual lost the guild’s work, and a Jewish believer disowned by the synagogue lost the legal protection that exempted Jews from emperor worship. Some may have had their goods seized (Hebrews 10:34). Their poverty was very likely the invoice for their faith.

(But you are rich). Into the middle of that sentence Christ inserts a short clause in brackets, and the parenthesis is the whole letter. He does not deny the poverty; he has just named it. He sets a second balance sheet beside the first and says the second is the real one. They are rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom (James 2:5). Laodicea, in the next chapter, will get the mirror image: rich in its own eyes, but wretched, pitiable and poor (3:17). Two churches, two account books, and the figures inverted in both.

Two instruments of measurement. Of the seven congregations, the two that receive no criticism whatever are Smyrna and Philadelphia, and both are poor and under pressure. The one that receives no commendation whatever is the wealthiest. Nothing in that pattern says money is evil or that hardship is holy by itself. It says that the instrument we habitually use to assess spiritual health is not the instrument Christ uses, and that the two readings can be exactly opposite.

The slander. Slander (blasphēmian) is abusive speech. Local Jews apparently denounced Christians to the authorities. Jews had legal tolerance in the empire and were excused from emperor worship; once they disowned the Christians as not Jews, Christians were exposed. In the account of Polycarp’s martyrdom, written by the church of Smyrna itself, the crowd gathered wood for the fire, and Smyrna’s Jews were said to have joined eagerly in it.

A synagogue of Satan. The description is functional: by accusing God’s people, they were doing the work of Satan, the accuser of the brothers (12:10), and whoever brings accusations against the people of God is doing the accuser’s work, whatever synagogue or church he attends. Christ says they are Jews in name but not in reality. As Paul says, the true Jew is one inwardly, by the Spirit (Romans 2:28–29); and all who belong to Christ are Abraham’s offspring (Galatians 3:29).

What it does not mean. This is not antisemitism, and must never be used to justify it. Christ, John and the first church were Jews; the same apostle wrote that salvation is from the Jews (John 4:22). The words are aimed at a particular community that persecuted Christians, and the charge is spiritual, not ethnic: rejecting the Messiah and accusing his people. Reading this verse as a statement about Jewish people in general has done terrible damage in the history of the church, and it is a sin to be repented of. Scripture holds out hope for Israel’s salvation (Romans 11:25–29), and Christians are called to love their Jewish neighbours and pray for them.

Does this mean faithful Christians will always be poor? No. Scripture does not make poverty a badge of holiness, and it records faithful believers with property who used it for others (Acts 16:14–15; Romans 16:23). The point is that Christ’s accounts differ from ours. Faithfulness sometimes costs money, as it did in Smyrna, and when it does he counts the believer rich. Prosperity is not proof of his favour, and hardship is not proof of his displeasure. Ask not how much you have, but whether anything you have has been bought with compromise, and whether you are rich toward God (Luke 12:21).

Is calling the poor rich just a way of keeping them quiet? No, and the letter itself shows why. Christ does not tell Smyrna that its poverty is fine or that injustice does not matter; he names the poverty plainly, and he names who caused it. Nor does he offer a feeling in place of bread. The riches he speaks of rest on a fact, that he died and came to life (2:8), and a risen Lord can make good on his promises in a way no slogan can. The same book that calls these believers rich pronounces God’s judgement on the merchants who grew fat on a cruel trade, slaves and human souls among their cargo (18:11–19). This is not comfort that excuses the oppressor. It is comfort that outlasts him.

On a Tuesday. If you are slandered for your faith, do not answer in kind; leave the accuser’s work to the accuser and keep doing your Lord’s.

For worship. The Lord who calls Smyrna rich knows poverty from the inside. Though he was rich, for our sake he became poor, so that by his poverty we might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9): laid in a manger because there was no room, owning no place to lay his head, slandered, falsely accused and stripped of his clothes at the end. Every coin his people lose for his name is entered in a book kept by one who gave up everything for them, and what he has made them heirs to no magistrate in Smyrna can confiscate.
verseByVerse.note: Smyrna (modern Izmir) was a wealthy port, loyal to Rome, with a large Jewish community, some of whom were slandering the church.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not fear what you are about to suffer. Behold, the devil is about to throw some of you into prison, that you may be tested, and for ten days you will have tribulation. Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. In the Roman world, prison was not usually a punishment in itself; it was a place to hold people before trial or execution. To be thrown into prison often meant death was coming.

In the flow. This verse is the heart of the shortest letter. It takes the word John used of himself, tribulation (1:9), and tells this church that its share is coming. It takes the comfort Christ gave John on the floor, do not be afraid (1:17), and gives it to them. And it looks ahead: the martyrs under the altar (6:9–11) and the saints who conquer by not loving their lives even unto death (12:11) are Smyrna’s faithfulness seen from heaven.

Do not fear what you are about to suffer. Not do not fear, you will not suffer. The suffering is confirmed in the same sentence in which the fear is forbidden. “Do not fear” (mēden phobou) is literally fear nothing. Christ does not promise to stop the suffering; he tells them not to be afraid of it.

The devil. The agent is named. Devil (diabolos) means slanderer, and behind the slanderers and the Roman courts he stands: persecution has a spiritual source. Some of you, not all, which is worse in one way, because it means the congregation will spend the coming months not knowing who. Yet even the devil can act only within the limits God allows, as in Job 1–2.

That you may be tested. Then the clause that turns the verse over. It is a purpose clause, and the purpose does not belong to the devil. He throws them in to destroy their faith; that is what he is for. The sentence says the imprisonment has another purpose running through the same event, and that purpose is the proving of something valuable (peirasthēte, tried, proved). The devil is permitted to strike, and while he strikes he is unwittingly doing the assayer’s work. Job was the first man to live inside that arrangement (Job 1:12), and Peter said the same to churches in this same province: the tested genuineness of your faith is more precious than gold that perishes though it is tested by fire (1 Peter 1:6–7). The same event has two purposes, and only one of them will prevail.

Endurance, not stoicism. That clause is the difference between endurance and mere stoicism. A believer facing something frightening does not principally need to be told that it will end. He needs to know whether it means anything. This says it does: the thing coming at you has been given a purpose it did not choose, and the purpose is not your destruction.

And for ten days you will have tribulation. Ten days is short. In a book where numbers carry meaning, ten is the round figure for a complete but limited stretch; Daniel and his friends were tested for ten days (Daniel 1:12–14). Nobody should press it into a calendar. The point is the shape: the suffering is real, but it has a stated duration, and the one who states it is not the devil. There is a fence around this, and the devil did not build it.

Be faithful unto death. Faithful (pistos) means loyal, trustworthy. Unto death (achri thanatou) can mean faithful right up to the end of your life, and it can mean faithful even to the point of being killed. Both were true in Smyrna.

The crown of life. The crown is stephanos, the victor’s wreath of leaves given at the games, not the royal diadem. Every athlete in Smyrna knew that the wreath was brown within a week (1 Corinthians 9:25). And the ring of buildings on Smyrna’s skyline was, it is said, called the crown of the city. Christ takes the local word for a beauty that lasts a generation and a sporting trophy that lasts a week, and offers instead a crown that is life itself (James 1:12).

The faithful one asks for faithfulness. The command comes from the one who kept it first. He is the faithful witness (1:5), who became obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:8), and who introduced himself to this church as the one who died and came to life (2:8). He does not ask Smyrna to walk anywhere he has not walked. And the crown is his to give because he won it: the life he holds out is his own resurrection life, which the firstborn of the dead shares with all his younger brothers and sisters. Faithfulness unto death is following him to the place where death was beaten.

Is the crown of life only for martyrs? No. It is eternal life itself, given to all who remain faithful to the end (James 1:12). The Smyrnaeans faced death, but the promise is for every faithful believer, including the one who dies quietly in a hospital bed after a long life of ordinary faithfulness. What the martyr shows openly, every believer shows in his own way: that Christ is worth more than life.

What if I am afraid I would deny Christ under pressure? Many are, and the fear is not a sign of unbelief. The question is not whether you feel you could face a prison. Nobody feels that, and Peter, who was certain he could, could not (Luke 22:33, 57). Grace is not issued in advance for a trial you are not in. It is issued on the day, in the cell, at the fire, which is exactly what Christ promised (Luke 21:14–15). Smyrna was not being asked to generate courage in the weeks before the arrests. It was being told who would be with them when they came. Your part today is faithfulness in the smaller costs; his part is the strength for the great ones.

On a Tuesday. Pray today for believers in prison for Christ; there are many, in many countries, and they are your brothers and sisters.
verseByVerse.note: “Ten days” probably means a short, limited time.

verseByVerse.quote: He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. The one who conquers will not be hurt by the second death.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second death. “Will not be hurt” (ou mē adikēthē) is the strongest form of denial in Greek: will certainly never be harmed. The phrase second death occurs four times in Scripture and all four are in this book. Revelation explains it as the lake of fire, final punishment after the resurrection and judgement (20:6, 14; 21:8): the first death is physical, the second is eternal separation from God under his judgement.

The smaller of the two categories. Set that against the situation on the ground. The magistrate can compel the first death and has no jurisdiction whatever over the second. The devil can throw them into prison and cannot follow them past the grave. Everything the enemies of this congregation are able to do to it is contained inside the smaller of the two categories. Jesus had said it in one sentence: do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul (Matthew 10:28; Luke 12:4).

What is not promised. Something is conspicuously not promised, and the honesty of it is part of the comfort. Smyrna is not told it will escape the first death. Several of them will not. Christ does not offer his most faithful church protection from the thing it fears; he offers immunity from the thing it has not thought about. It is the only kind of consolation that is actually true, and the only kind that holds when the cell door shuts.

Polycarp. Polycarp was bishop of this church about sixty years after this letter arrived, and he may well have heard it read as a young man. When the proconsul at Smyrna urged him to swear by the fortune of Caesar and revile Christ, he answered that he had served him eighty-six years and Christ had never done him wrong, and asked how he could blaspheme his King and Saviour. They burned him in the stadium. The account the church of Smyrna wrote afterwards says that when they came to nail him to the stake he asked them to leave him unfastened, because the one who gave him strength to endure the fire would give him strength to stay still in it. The letter to Smyrna had done its work.

Where Christians differ: is the second death the end of existence? Annihilationists hold that the second death means the wicked cease to exist after judgement; some sincere evangelical believers hold this, pointing to texts that speak of destruction (Matthew 10:28). This commentary’s view: Revelation describes the lake of fire as torment day and night for ever and ever (20:10; 14:11), and Jesus spoke of eternal punishment alongside eternal life (Matthew 25:46). The second death is called death because it is the final loss of all that makes life life: God’s presence and favour. It is conscious, eternal punishment, which is exactly why the promise here is so precious.

How can a loving God allow a second death? Because he is also just, and sin against an infinitely holy God is not a small thing. The second death is no outburst of irritation in God; it is his righteous judgement on those who refuse him to the end, and Scripture says it will be seen to be right (16:5–7; 19:1–2). But see what this verse actually does with the doctrine: it turns it into comfort and invitation. The second death has no power over anyone in Christ, because Christ bore the judgement in their place (Romans 5:9; 1 Thessalonians 1:10). The way out is open to anyone who will come to him now.

On a Tuesday. If someone you love does not yet know Christ, let the reality of the second death make you pray and speak, gently and soon.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–17 — To the Church in Pergamum
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pergamum, the seat of the Roman governor, was where the power of the sword resided and where emperor worship in the province began. Christ comes with the sharp two-edged sword (v. 12). The church held fast his name even when Antipas, his faithful witness, was killed (v. 13), but it has let some remain, unchallenged, who hold the teaching of Balaam and the Nicolaitans: the guild feasts with their idol meat and immorality (vv. 14–15). The whole congregation is called to repent, or Christ will come and fight the false teachers himself with the sword of his mouth (v. 16). To the conqueror he promises hidden manna, a white stone and a new name, each the reverse of what the compromisers wanted (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Second Strategy

Pergamum held fast under the sword but tolerated the teaching of Balaam, the invitation to compromise at the idol feast. The whole church is called to repent of its silence.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Guild banquets tied a man’s livelihood to idol meat.

Now: The argument for compromise is always reasonable. Christ offers hidden manna and a new name instead.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to the angel of the church in Pergamum write: 'The words of him who has the sharp two-edged sword. "'I know where you dwell, where Satan's throne is. Yet you hold fast my name, and you did not deny my faith even in the days of Antipas my faithful witness, who was killed among you, where Satan dwells.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Pergamum, about 65 miles (105 kilometres) north of Smyrna, was the old capital of the province and probably still the seat of the Roman governor, who had the right of the sword: the power to execute. It stood on a huge cone of rock about a thousand feet above the plain, crowned with temples, among them the first in Asia to the emperor Augustus and the goddess Roma (29 BC), which made it the centre of emperor worship in the province. Its library was second only to Alexandria’s, and parchment (pergamēnē) is named after it.

The sharp two-edged sword. Christ introduces himself to this city, and only to this city, with the sword from 1:16. The governor of Asia held a sword by delegation and used it on Antipas. There is another sword in this letter. It comes out of a mouth, and its owner did not receive it from anyone. The governor has the sword of Rome, but Christ has the sword that really decides life and death: his word. And he will use it against the false teachers in the church (v. 16).

Satan’s throne. Three or four things in Pergamum have been proposed as the throne, and a first-century Christian climbing that hill would have seen them all. The Great Altar of Zeus stood on a terrace near the summit, its frieze carved with gods destroying giants, and from below it looked like a throne on a mountain. Below that lay the shrine of Asclepius, the most famous healing centre in Asia, whose god’s emblem was a serpent and who was worshipped under the title Saviour. The governor’s seat of judgement was there. And Pergamum had built the province’s first temple to a living emperor, which made it the birthplace of the imperial cult in Asia. The best explanation is the city’s leadership in emperor worship, combined with the governor’s power to condemn Christians: Satan’s power was concentrated there. Political power, false salvation and a serpent, all on one hill.

Where you dwell. The verb Christ uses of the church is katoikeis, the word for settled, permanent residence, not for lodging somewhere temporarily. And at the end of the verse he uses the same root of Satan: where Satan dwells. They live there. He lives there. They did not choose the place, and Christ knows how hard it is.

Faithfulness on hard ground. Christ does not tell this congregation to move. The address is not the problem. Faithfulness is measured on the ground a person is actually standing on, and some believers are standing on very hard ground by appointment rather than by mistake.

Hold fast my name. Two verbs, one positive and one negative, and in a city with a governor holding a sword they mean something specific. Hold fast (krateis) is to grip firmly: holding fast the name means still saying it in public. Deny (ērnēsō) is to disown: when the question came, and in this city it came formally, with a magistrate and a written record, they did not give the required answer. The test in the Roman world was rarely a demand to renounce Christ in a long speech. It was usually a demand to say Caesar is Lord and offer a pinch of incense, and perhaps to curse Christ, after which a man could believe whatever he liked in private. Pergamum would not do it. “My faith” (tēn pistin mou) means faith in me, or the faithfulness owed to me.

Antipas my faithful witness. This is the only place in the Bible where the name occurs, and nothing else is known about him with any certainty; later tradition says he was roasted in a bronze bull. What is known is the title Christ gives him. In 1:5 Christ himself is the faithful witness (ho martys ho pistos). Here he hands his own description to a man from Pergamum who bore witness the same way, to the death. Nobody remembers who the governor was. There is one name from that courtroom that the risen Christ has kept, and it is not the man who held the sword. Killed (apektanthē): martyrdom had already begun.

Among you. Two words remain, and they are among the most consoling in the letter. Not in your city, not in that period: among you. They had watched it happen, and Christ names their friend in front of everyone. Nothing done to the church at Pergamum happened out of sight.

Should I move away from a place, or a job, that is hostile to my faith? Not necessarily. Christ did not tell Pergamum to leave, and Christians are scattered into hard places on purpose, to be light there (Matthew 5:14; Jeremiah 29:7). Hostility alone is not a reason to go. But there are times when a wise believer should move: when staying would require you to sin, when your family is in real danger, or when a door opens elsewhere that does not depend on running from faithfulness (Matthew 10:23). Ask whether you are leaving to escape the cost of faithfulness or because faithfulness itself leads you on. Pray, take counsel, and wherever you are, hold fast his name.

On a Tuesday. When you are asked for your small pinch of incense, the sentence you do not believe, the silence that keeps the peace at your Lord’s expense, remember Antipas, whose name is known in heaven while the governor’s is forgotten.

For worship. The Lord of Pergamum once stood where Antipas stood, before a Roman governor who held the power of the sword, and he told the truth and was killed. He told that governor he would have no authority at all unless it had been given him from above (John 18:37; 19:10–11), and now the governor’s seat is empty and the crucified one holds the only sword that decides anything. The records of Rome lie in the dust, and the name of one faithful man from Satan’s hill is read aloud in every church on earth, because Christ chose to keep it.
verseByVerse.note: Pergamum was a centre of emperor worship and home to a great altar of Zeus — perhaps why it is called the place “where Satan’s throne is.”

verseByVerse.quote: But I have a few things against you: you have some there who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before the sons of Israel, so that they might eat food sacrificed to idols and practice sexual immorality. So also you have some who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I have a few things against you. The problem is not that Pergamum has denied Christ under pressure, because it has not. The problem is what it has permitted inside the room while standing firm at the door.

The teaching of Balaam. The reference is to one of the strangest episodes in the Old Testament. Balaam was hired by Balak, king of Moab, to curse Israel and tried three times, and could not; every time he opened his mouth a blessing came out, and a fourth oracle followed unasked (Numbers 24:10–17). Curses had failed. So, as Scripture states much later when Moses is accounting for a disaster, Balaam gave different advice (Numbers 31:16). Israel was invited to the Moabite festivals, ate the sacrifices, committed immorality with the women of Moab, bowed to Baal of Peor, and twenty-four thousand died in a plague (Numbers 25:1–9). What could not be cursed from outside was seduced from inside. And it is called teaching (didachēn): not merely bad behaviour but a doctrine that justified it, taught within the church. The sword did not work at Pergamum, so the strategy changed, and the second strategy was working. That is why the New Testament remembers Balaam as the prophet who led God’s people into sin for profit (2 Peter 2:15; Jude 11).

A stumbling block. A stumbling block (skandalon) is a trap, the bait stick that springs it, something that makes people fall.

Idol food and immorality. The two specifics named were not two unrelated vices. In a Roman city they usually arrived in the same evening. Trade guilds were also religious associations; the carpenters, the dyers, the bakers each had a patron deity, and membership involved attending banquets held in the temple precincts, where the meat had been offered on the altar and where the later part of the evening often involved sexual licence. Refuse the dinner and you are outside the guild. Outside the guild there is no work. Food sacrificed to idols (eidōlothyta), eaten in the temple as part of a feast in the god’s honour, was taking part in idolatry (1 Corinthians 10:19–22), and the Jerusalem council had asked Gentile believers to abstain from both (Acts 15:29). Sexual immorality (porneusai) is sexual relations outside marriage; the Old Testament often calls idolatry adultery, but here the literal sense is clear.

Two tables. Behind the guild dinner stands the question Paul had already put to another Greek city: whose table are you sitting at? The cup of blessing is a participation in the blood of Christ, and the bread a participation in his body (1 Corinthians 10:16), and a Christian cannot eat at the Lord’s table on the first day of the week and at the god’s table on the next feast day as though both meant nothing. The compromisers said the idol was nothing, so the meal was nothing. Christ’s answer is that his own table is not nothing. He gave his body and blood for his people, and no guild in Asia had anything to set beside that.

Balaam’s argument today. The party of accommodation in Pergamum was not arguing for wickedness. It was arguing that a man has to feed his family, that the ritual means nothing to a Christian anyway, and that God looks on the heart. Almost nobody reading this is being asked to burn incense. A great many people are being asked to say something in a meeting they do not believe, to stay quiet where speaking would cost a promotion, to let a client’s arrangements go unquestioned, to laugh at the table, to sleep with someone they are not married to because everyone does. The stumbling block is not laid in front of people who want to fall. It is laid in front of people who need the work. Underneath the argument lies a quieter question each person has to answer: what do I believe I cannot live without? Whatever that is, the income, the approval of colleagues, the place at the table, is where the stumbling block will be laid, and it is the thing to hand back to Christ before the moment comes.

The Nicolaitans. “So also” (houtōs, in the same way): the Nicolaitans’ teaching is the same as Balaam’s, or very like it. And the parallel with verse 6 is exact and pointed. Ephesus hated the works of the Nicolaitans; Pergamum has some who hold their teaching. The same error, a hundred miles apart, met with rejection in one church and hospitality in the other. Between the two letters Christ has now criticised a church for being loveless and a church for being tolerant, which forecloses the comfortable assumption that one of these is the safe direction to err in.

You have some there. He does not say some of you hold this teaching, which would be a charge against individuals. He says you have some there who hold it: the charge is against the church for having them, unchallenged, in the membership. Pergamum’s sin is not that a few people were wrong, but that it let them stay.

Does this contradict Paul, who allows eating meat bought in the market? No. Paul allows eating market meat without asking questions (1 Corinthians 10:25), but he too forbids taking part in idol feasts: you cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons (1 Corinthians 10:21). Here the false teachers were leading Christians into idol feasts and the sexual immorality that went with them; that is what Christ condemns. For us the principle is the same. Ordinary things in an unbelieving world are not defiling in themselves. Taking part in worship of another god, or in sin dressed up as custom, is.

Where is the line between living in the culture and compromising with it? Ask three questions. Does this require me to do what God forbids, or to deny or hide Christ when faithfulness calls me to own him? Does it involve taking part in worship or celebration of something false, rather than simply being present among unbelievers? And is my real reason fear of loss, dressed up as wisdom? Christians can work in secular jobs, attend a colleague’s wedding, eat at a neighbour’s table and share in the common life of their town; Jesus ate with sinners. But when the price of belonging is sin, the answer must be no, even if it costs the job. Take counsel from mature believers when the case is not clear.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore repent. If not, I will come to you soon and war against them with the sword of my mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Balaam himself was confronted by the angel of the Lord with a drawn sword (Numbers 22:23, 31).

Therefore repent. Two words (metanoēson oun), addressed to the whole congregation, including the majority who have done nothing wrong except let it happen. The church must repent of tolerating the faction, and the faction of its teaching. A church is answerable for what it tolerates, and silence is a decision.

I will come to you soon. As at Ephesus, this is a coming in judgement on this church in history. Soon (tachy) carries the sense of speed rather than of the calendar: without delay once the decision is taken, and not left indefinitely. God’s patience is real, and the next letter will show him giving a false prophetess time to repent, but it is patience with a purpose, not tolerance without a limit.

War against them. Then the wording is unexpected. He comes to you; he wars (polemēsō, makes war) against them. The pronouns separate, and the separation is deliberate and faintly terrifying. Christ will arrive at the congregation and conduct a battle inside it, against the false teachers, and the faithful majority will be standing in the room while he does. Refusing to act against error does not exempt a church from the action. It simply means the action is taken by someone else, in the middle of the assembly, without consultation. The faithful do not need to fear his sword, but they will see it used.

The sword of his mouth. The sword is the one from 1:16 and 2:12: his word of judgement, which exposes and condemns false teaching. It is not a metaphor for something gentler; in 19:15 the same sword strikes the nations. But it does tell a church what the instrument of correction is, and therefore what its own instrument should have been. Pergamum was not asked to expel anyone by force or to organise against the faction. It was asked to say the true thing out loud, which is precisely what nobody there was doing.

The sword they could not see. Pergamum is where the sword of Rome lives, and the believers there have already faced it and not flinched. The sword they could see did not move them. The danger they had not noticed came from a sword they could not see, and it was pointed the other way: not at their bodies, which were brave, but at the purity of the church, which was unguarded.

Balaam’s end. Balaam himself is a warning attached to this. He is one of the few figures in Scripture who spoke true prophecy, blessed God’s people four times against his own financial interest, and predicted the star that would come out of Jacob (Numbers 24:17), a line this chapter picks up at verse 28. And he died by the sword among the kings of Midian, on the side of the enemies of the people he had blessed (Numbers 31:8). Getting the doctrine right and saying true things about Christ is not the same as being on his side, and a man can do the first for years while drifting into the second.
