Does Christ really fight against people inside his own church? Yes, against those who lead his people astray and will not repent. Not everyone on a church roll belongs to Christ (1 John 2:19), and he will not let wolves feed on his flock for ever. His war is waged by his word: the false teaching is exposed, consciences are troubled, judgement falls, and sometimes those who persist are removed. For the faithful this is protection, not threat. And for anyone who has been drawn into error, the first word of the verse is still open: repent. The sword is the last resort of a Lord who would much rather heal.

What should I do if my church tolerates false teaching? Begin with prayer and with your own heart, and make sure the issue is real error, not a matter of preference. Then speak, humbly and privately, to the elders, with Scripture open (Matthew 18:15; Galatians 6:1). Be patient; churches often move slowly. If the leaders themselves teach serious error about the gospel, or refuse to deal with open, unrepentant sin, and will not listen, you may in the end need to leave quietly for a faithful church, for your own sake and your family’s. But do not leave in a spirit of pride, and do not stop loving the people you leave.

On a Tuesday. If you are tolerating a sin because confronting it would be uncomfortable, Christ calls you to repent, and he calls as the one whose blood has already paid for what you bring him. Later in this chapter a false prophetess is given time to repent and refuses it (2:21). The door that stands open in this verse is open now.

verseByVerse.quote: He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. To the one who conquers I will give some of the hidden manna, and I will give him a white stone, with a new name written on the stone that no one knows except the one who receives it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Manna was the bread from heaven that fed Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 16), and a jar of it was kept in the ark of the covenant (Exodus 16:33–34; Hebrews 9:4). Jewish tradition said that Jeremiah hid the ark before the Babylonians destroyed the temple (2 Maccabees 2:4–8), and some writers expected manna to fall again in the days of the Messiah.

Three promises against the guild. Every one of the three promises of them is the reverse of something the compromisers in Pergamum were arguing for. They wanted the guild dinner; Christ offers hidden manna. They wanted the token of admission; Christ offers a white stone. They wanted to keep their standing in the city; Christ offers a new name.

The hidden manna. The jar of manna in the ark was hidden in the sense that it lay behind the veil, where only the high priest went, once a year. Set that against the issue in the letter and the promise lands exactly. The argument in Pergamum was about meat: eat what the temple provides, or lose your income. Christ answers with a different menu. Israel in the desert was fed by God alone, daily, for four decades, in a place with no fields and no guilds, and nobody starved. And the Lord who says this once said of himself, in a synagogue argument about manna, I am the bread of life (John 6:35, 48–51). Those who refuse to eat food offered to idols will eat the bread of heaven: Christ himself, and the feast of eternal life with him, the marriage supper of the Lamb (19:9). What is hidden now is a Person, and the hiddenness is temporary.

A white stone. This one is genuinely uncertain, and several proposals have been made by careful readers. A juror in a Greek court dropped a white pebble (psēphon leukēn) for acquittal and a black one for condemnation. A victor at the games could be given a token that admitted him to the celebration banquet. A guest at a feast received an inscribed ticket, and inscribed stones were also worn as amulets. Given the banquet in this verse, a likely meaning is a ticket of admission to the messianic feast, combined with the sense of acquittal: the white stone of the verdict not guilty. If acquittal is in view, the stone is justification in a picture: God the Judge declaring a guilty person not guilty, not because the charge was false but because Christ has borne the sentence (Romans 8:33–34). Those shut out of the guilds’ feasts are admitted to Christ’s. What all the proposals share matters more than deciding between them: the stone is small, personal, handed to one individual, and it is the thing that gets him in.

A new name. A new name (onoma kainon) in Scripture marks a changed identity and relationship conferred by God: Abram became Abraham, Jacob became Israel, Simon became Peter. Isaiah 62:2 and 65:15 promise God’s people a new name. Whose name is it? Possibly the believer’s new name, given by Christ, a personal and intimate sign of belonging; or Christ’s own name, which only those who know him truly understand (3:12; 19:12). Either way, the striking clause is the privacy of it. Nobody else knows it. Whatever else it means, it means that the knowledge Christ has of each of his people is particular and not generic. He is not handing out identical certificates to a crowd.

What the city takes and Christ gives. A tradesman in Pergamum who refuses the guild dinner loses, in order: his contracts, his standing, and eventually the way the city refers to him. He becomes the awkward one, the man who could not be reasonable. That is a real cost and this letter does not pretend otherwise. What it says is that a name is being kept for him which the city could not have given and cannot take, written on a stone, known to Christ and to him and to nobody else in the world.

What it does not mean. Nothing here supports secret knowledge for spiritual elites, as later Gnostic groups taught. The new name is known by the one who receives it, and every conquering believer receives one.

Does God really know me personally, or just love his people in general? He knows you personally, and this verse is the answer, deliberately intimate. For anyone who has ever felt that God’s love is a general policy rather than something addressed to them, that he saves crowds and might not have noticed one particular obscure believer in one particular unglamorous town, here is a private name, on a stone, in his hand, for you. The Good Shepherd calls his own sheep by name (John 10:3), and he knew you before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4). You are not lost in the crowd of the redeemed.

Will I lose my own identity in heaven? No. A new name in Scripture does not erase the person; it fulfils him. Abraham was still the man from Ur, and Peter was still the fisherman from Galilee, but each became more truly himself under the name God gave. In the new creation you will be you, healed, completed and free from sin, not dissolved into a crowd or turned into someone else. What will be gone is everything false that sin attached to your name: the shame, the labels, the reputation the world gave you. What remains is the person Christ redeemed and named.

For worship. The manna in the ark lay behind a curtain no ordinary Israelite could pass, and the true Bread from heaven opened the way through that curtain by giving his own flesh for the life of the world (John 6:51; Hebrews 10:19–20). What was hidden in the holiest place he now gives, himself, to tradesmen shut out of every dinner in the city. And he who has a name written that no one knows but himself (19:12) writes a name for each of his people, so that the Lord and each guest at his table share a secret the whole world cannot read.
verseByVerse.note: The meaning of the white stone is uncertain; white stones were used as tokens of acquittal and as tickets of admission to feasts.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–29 — To the Church in Thyatira
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Thyatira, the least distinguished of the seven towns and full of trade guilds, receives the longest letter. Christ comes as the Son of God, with eyes like a flame of fire (v. 18), and commends a church growing in love, faith, service and endurance (v. 19). But it tolerates a self-styled prophetess he calls Jezebel, who teaches Balaam’s programme again and has refused the time given her to repent (vv. 20–21). Her judgement is announced, with the door of repentance still open to those she has drawn in (vv. 22–23). The faithful remnant are given no other burden than to hold fast until he comes (vv. 24–25), and are promised a share in his rule and the morning star, who is Christ himself (vv. 26–29).
verseByVerse.theology:
Warm but Undiscerning

Thyatira grew in love, faith, service and endurance, yet tolerated a self-appointed prophetess teaching compromise. Christ gave her time to repent; to the faithful he lays no other burden than to hold fast until he comes.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In a guild town, her teaching offered relief with a spiritual justification.

Now: The faithful in a compromised church are not asked to fix it, only to hold on, and they are promised the morning star.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to the angel of the church in Thyatira write: 'The words of the Son of God, who has eyes like a flame of fire, and whose feet are like burnished bronze. "'I know your works, your love and faith and service and patient endurance, and that your latter works exceed the first.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Thyatira, about 40 miles (65 kilometres) southeast of Pergamum, was probably the least important of the seven cities. It had no great temple, no governor, no wonder of the world, and it sat in a valley with no natural defences. It was a centre of manufacturing and trade, and inscriptions show an unusual number of trade guilds there: wool, linen, dyeing, leather, pottery, slave trading and, especially, bronze-working. Lydia, the seller of purple cloth whom Paul met in Philippi, came from Thyatira (Acts 16:14). Each guild had a patron god and held feasts in the god’s honour, and membership was almost necessary for anyone who wanted to work. The city’s chief god was Apollo, worshipped as son of Zeus, and the emperor was honoured as son of god too.

The words of the Son of God. This is the only time this title (ho huios tou theou) appears in Revelation. In a city that honoured Apollo and the emperor as sons of Zeus, Christ declares himself the true Son of God. The title echoes Psalm 2, which is quoted in vv. 26–27: the LORD’s anointed, his Son, will rule the nations. And this least celebrated, most commercial town receives the longest of the seven letters, from the highest title in the book.

Eyes like a flame of fire. From John’s first vision (1:14): eyes that see through every disguise, chosen for this church because Thyatira’s problem is hidden inside a congregation that looks healthy from outside. He will search minds and hearts (v. 23).

Feet like burnished bronze. In a town of metalworkers, this is an image they would know exactly: refined bronze coming out of the furnace, shining, hard, and not to be argued with. Feet that stand firm and trample evil.

Love and faith and service and patient endurance. Then the commendation, and it is among the warmest given to any of the seven. Four qualities are named and they are paired. Love (agapēn) and faith (pistin, or faithfulness): the inward dispositions. Service (diakonian, practical ministry to people who need it) and patient endurance (hypomonēn): the outward expressions. The order is not accidental: love produces service; faith produces endurance. Read that against Ephesus and the contrast is almost surgical. The very things Ephesus lacked, Thyatira had in abundance.

Your latter works exceed the first. Unlike Ephesus, which had declined from its first love, Thyatira was growing.

Two churches, each rebuked where the other excelled. This sets up the hardest lesson in the chapter, and it should be said before the criticism arrives so that it is not mistaken for a technicality. A congregation can be growing in love, growing in practical care, more useful this decade than last, warm, generous and well thought of, and be in serious danger. Warmth is not a substitute for discernment any more than discernment was a substitute for warmth at Ephesus.

Which is more dangerous, cold orthodoxy or warm tolerance? Both, and that is the point. Most Christians have a settled instinct here: some are sure the peril is cold orthodoxy, others are sure it is loose tolerance, and each is quietly confident that the failing they can see in others is the serious one. Chapter 2 rebukes both, in adjacent letters, in the same voice, from the same eyes of fire. Whichever of the two you find it easy to condemn is probably not the letter written to you. The goal is not a midpoint between truth and love but the fullness of both, as in Christ, who came full of grace and truth (John 1:14).
verseByVerse.note: Thyatira was a town of trade guilds, whose feasts honoured pagan gods. Lydia came from there.

verseByVerse.quote: But I have this against you, that you tolerate that woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess and is teaching and seducing my servants to practice sexual immorality and to eat food sacrificed to idols. I gave her time to repent, but she refuses to repent of her sexual immorality.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Jezebel was the Phoenician wife of King Ahab of Israel (1 Kings 16:31). She promoted the worship of Baal, killed the LORD’s prophets, supported hundreds of prophets of Baal and Asherah at her own table, arranged a judicial murder to get a man’s vineyard, and led Israel into idolatry, which Scripture calls whoredom and sorcery (1 Kings 18:4, 19; 21:1–16; 2 Kings 9:22). She was the Old Testament’s great example of a powerful person leading God’s people into false worship, and she operated from inside the institution.

You tolerate that woman Jezebel. The verb aimed at the church is tolerate (apheis, let alone, permit). Nobody in Thyatira is accused of believing what she taught. They are accused of letting her go on teaching it. And Jezebel is almost certainly a symbolic name, comparing this woman to Ahab’s queen, the way we might call someone a Judas. Every hearer in Thyatira would have caught it instantly. She was a real person in the church, possibly an influential and well-connected woman, and her teaching was having the same effect as the old Jezebel’s.

Who calls herself a prophetess. “Calls herself” (hē legousa heautēn): the claim is self-issued, and the church has apparently not tested it, which is precisely what Ephesus did do and was commended for (v. 2). She claimed to speak for God, which gave her teaching authority and made it hard to challenge.

Seducing my servants. Seducing (plana, leading astray) is the word used of Satan, who deceives the whole world (12:9). And see whom she seduces: my servants, Christ’s own people.

Balaam’s programme again. These are the same two things named in verse 14, now with a prophetic authority claimed behind it. Probably she taught that Christians could join in the guild feasts with their idolatry and immorality, perhaps claiming that God had revealed this freedom to her, or that experiencing the deep things of Satan could not harm a truly spiritual person (v. 24).

The prophet who did not call himself. Set beside her the one who is speaking. Jezebel’s credentials were self-issued. Christ is the true Prophet, the one Moses said God would raise up (Deuteronomy 18:15; Acts 3:22), and he said of his teaching that it was not his own but the Father’s who sent him, and that the one who speaks on his own authority seeks his own glory (John 7:16–18). She offered a freedom that left people in their sins; he gives the freedom of the Son, who sets people free indeed (John 8:36). And she was seducing his servants, people he had freed by his blood (1:5). The anger in this letter is the anger of a Redeemer watching what he bought being stolen.

Why nobody confronted her. The reason is not hard to reconstruct in a guild town: her doctrine solved a real problem. If the sacrificed meat is nothing and the temple evening is a formality, then a dyer can keep his membership and his contracts. She was not offering vice. She was offering relief, with a spiritual justification attached, a way to keep one’s job and status without suffering. And it is very difficult to confront somebody who is telling frightened people what they urgently want to be true.

Time to repent. Time (chronon): Christ had been patient, perhaps through warnings from the church or simply by his own forbearance (Romans 2:4). The delay was not indifference. The years in which the church did nothing and the false teaching flourished were years the Lord was holding open. What looked to the faithful remnant like God ignoring an outrage was God waiting for a woman to turn. But the verb in the second half is present and continuous: she refuses (ou thelei, does not want to). Her problem was not ignorance but an unwilling heart. She has been given room, she knows what it is for, and she is going on saying no. Mercy that is refused for long enough does not become permanent tolerance. It runs out, and the next verse is what that looks like.

Delay is not always absence. Hold on to that when a wrong goes unpunished for a long time and heaven appears to have no opinion. Peter wrote to churches in these same provinces that the Lord is not slow to fulfil his promise as some count slowness, but is patient, not wishing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:9). Sometimes the silence a believer finds unbearable is mercy being extended to somebody he has already written off. Sometimes it is being extended to him.

Where Christians differ: does this passage forbid women from teaching? Some use it to argue against women preaching; others say it shows women prophesied and taught in the church, and the problem was only false teaching. This commentary’s view: Jezebel is rebuked for false teaching and immorality, not for being a woman who spoke. Scripture recognises women who prophesied (Acts 21:9; 1 Corinthians 11:5). This passage does not settle questions of church office; those are taught elsewhere. This commentary holds the complementarian view that the office of elder and the authoritative teaching of the gathered church are given to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7), because Paul grounds it in creation rather than in local custom (1 Timothy 2:13), while women serve in many vital ministries; many faithful Christians read those passages differently, and they are brothers and sisters. The lesson here is for every church and every teacher, male or female: no claim to speak for God gives anyone the right to teach what contradicts his word. The same teaching was condemned at Pergamum six verses earlier with no reference to anyone’s sex, and the parallel Christ draws there is with Balaam, a man.

Are there prophets like this today, and how should I treat someone who claims a word from God? The apostles and prophets laid the foundation of the church once for all (Ephesians 2:20), and with the canon of Scripture complete, this commentary holds, charitably, that the revelatory gift of prophecy has ceased; many sincere believers disagree, and they are brothers and sisters. Either way, the test is the same. Anyone who claims a word from God must be tested by the written word (1 Thessalonians 5:20–21; 1 John 4:1). If the supposed message makes sin acceptable, contradicts Scripture, or adds a requirement or a freedom the Bible does not give, it is not from God, however confident or impressive the speaker. You do not need to be unkind; you do need to say no. Many continuationist believers (those who hold that the gift continues) would agree that any prophecy today must be tested by Scripture and can never add to it.

On a Tuesday. If you find yourself drawn to a teacher mainly because he or she tells you what you want to hear about your money, your body or your comfort, take that as a warning sign rather than a confirmation.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I will throw her onto a sickbed, and those who commit adultery with her I will throw into great tribulation, unless they repent of her works, and I will strike her children dead. And all the churches will know that I am he who searches mind and heart, and I will give to each of you according to your works.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. The old Jezebel’s end was terrible (2 Kings 9:30–37), and her family was destroyed (2 Kings 10). Christ’s judgement here is proportionate and fitting. These are the hardest two verses in the seven letters, but almost every clause contains a distinction that a quick reading loses.

A sickbed. The Greek is a deliberate irony that the English cannot fully carry. The word for bed (klinēn) is the word used for the couch on which the guild banquets were eaten and the sin committed. The bed she chose becomes the bed she cannot leave. Compare 1 Corinthians 11:30, where abuse of the Lord’s Supper brought sickness and death. And the verb is throw, the same verb used of the devil throwing believers into prison at Smyrna in verse 10. Different hand, different purpose, and the reader is meant to feel the symmetry.

Unless they repent. Those who commit adultery with her (moicheuontas) are those who follow her teaching, whether literally sleeping with her or joining in her spiritual unfaithfulness. And there it is: the door, standing open in the middle of the sentence of judgement. The threat is conditional for everyone except the woman who has already spent her allotted time refusing. Even at this point, with the verdict being pronounced, anyone who will turn may turn. Judgement in Scripture almost always arrives with that clause attached, and it is not decoration. Christ’s warnings are meant to bring people back.

Strike her children dead. This is the sentence that makes readers flinch, and it should not be waved away. Two things need saying. First, her children (ta tekna autēs) in the Old Testament idiom that Christ is using means her spiritual offspring, her followers, those who have taken her teaching so far into themselves that they now reproduce it, rather than her literal children. The verse has just distinguished two groups: those who commit adultery with her, who may still repent, and the children, who are hers. The wording marks a difference between people who have been drawn in and people who have become her. Strike dead (apoktenō en thanatō, literally kill with death) is probably a Hebrew way of saying kill with pestilence or plague: a severe judgement on those who refuse to turn. Second, this is what Scripture consistently says the end of persistent, chosen rebellion is, and it says it plainly rather than leaving the reader to discover it later. Christ is not more severe here than the New Testament is elsewhere; he is simply less indirect.

He who searches mind and heart. Searches (eraunōn) means examines, investigates. Mind and heart is literally kidneys and hearts (nephrous kai kardias). In Hebrew thinking, the kidneys, the organs furthest inside a body, were the seat of the deepest emotions, and the heart the seat of thought and will. And it is a clear echo of the Old Testament’s claim about God alone: I the LORD search the heart and test the mind, to give every man according to his ways (Jeremiah 17:10; compare Psalm 7:9). Christ takes the LORD’s own role. The claim is not that Christ is well informed. It is that he sees the part of a person that the person himself cannot get at, whatever outward show of spirituality people make, and this is said in a letter to a church that could not tell a prophetess from a fraud.

According to your works. A principle of judgement throughout Scripture (Psalm 62:12; Romans 2:6; 2 Corinthians 5:10). A reader who has grasped that salvation is by grace through faith alone will stop at that sentence, and the question deserves a straight answer. Scripture says both things without embarrassment: no one is justified by works of the law (Galatians 2:16), and each will be repaid according to what he has done. They are not in tension once the question each is answering is clear. Nobody is admitted on the strength of his works; the works are the evidence of whose he is, and they are the measure of what is given afterwards. A tree is not made alive by its fruit, and is identified by nothing else.

Each of you. The pronoun shifts at the end, and it changes who is being addressed. Verses 20 to 23 have been about her and them. The last clause turns and says each of you. The letter has been discussing a faction, and it ends the discussion by putting the whole congregation, one by one, in front of the eyes of fire.

Does God still send sickness as judgement today? He can, and Scripture records it (Acts 5:1–11; 1 Corinthians 11:30), but we are never given the right to read it into another person’s illness. Most sickness is simply part of living in a fallen world, and the godliest believers suffer it (2 Corinthians 12:7–9; 1 Timothy 5:23). If you are ill and your conscience is troubled about a specific, unrepented sin, confess it to God and put it right, and receive his forgiveness (James 5:15–16). If your conscience is clear, do not let anyone burden you with the idea that your illness is punishment. For those in Christ, even discipline is a Father’s love, never condemnation (Hebrews 12:6; Romans 8:1).

On a Tuesday. Being searched to the heart is frightening only for as long as we are hiding something. For anyone who has been drawn into sin by a persuasive voice, there is relief in being fully known by the one whose sentence still contains the words unless they repent. Turning to him today is easier than tomorrow.

verseByVerse.quote: But to the rest of you in Thyatira, who do not hold this teaching, who have not learned what some call the deep things of Satan, to you I say, I do not lay on you any other burden. Only hold fast what you have until I come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Gnostic groups in the second century boasted of knowing the deep things, secret spiritual knowledge reserved for the initiated. Some taught that the truly spiritual person could indulge the body without harm, or even should experience evil in order to master it. Jezebel’s teaching seems to have been an early form of this.

The rest of you in Thyatira. The tone changes completely. In a church whose besetting fault was tolerance, there were people who had quietly refused, and Christ addresses them directly and separately, which is itself a kindness. He knows exactly who in that congregation had said no.

The deep things of Satan. The phrasing, what some call, suggests Christ is repeating the faction’s own slogan back at them with one word changed. They were very likely advertising the deep things (ta bathea) of God (1 Corinthians 2:10): a mature, advanced spirituality for people who had got beyond scruples, an inner freedom that let a believer walk through the guild feast untouched because he understood what the ordinary members did not. Christ calls it by its real name: the deep things of Satan. Alternatively, they claimed that to know Satan’s depths, to explore sin from the inside, was a mark of spiritual maturity. Either way, the supposed higher knowledge was demonic. Every generation produces some version of that offer, and it always flatters. Christ substitutes one noun and the whole thing collapses.

No other burden. This sentence is for anyone who is tired. Burden (baros) means weight, and it echoes the Jerusalem council’s letter, which said it laid no greater burden on Gentile believers than to abstain from idol food and sexual immorality (Acts 15:28–29). Christ adds no new requirements, no secret knowledge. He does not tell the faithful remnant to launch a campaign, purge the membership, or fix the church. He has already said what he will do about Jezebel and he will do it himself. To the people who have been holding on in a compromised congregation, the risen Christ says: nothing further is required of you.

The weight put where it belongs. That is an extraordinary pastoral moment, and it is aimed at a recognisable kind of exhaustion. There are believers in difficult churches who carry the whole thing on their shoulders, who feel personally answerable for every error nobody else is confronting, and who are being slowly ground down by a responsibility they were never actually given. The letter puts the weight where it belongs: on the one with the eyes of fire.

Hold fast until I come. That is the one thing. Not advance, not achieve, not reform: hold. Hold fast (kratēsate) is the verb used of Pergamum in verse 13, a word for gripping something in a wind, and what is to be held is what they already have: the apostolic gospel. And the time limit is stated: until I come (achris hou an hēxō), until his return. Holding on is not asked of anyone with no end in view, and this is the first clear mention in the letters of his final coming. There is an end point. A believer is not being asked to grip in the dark for ever with no prospect of relief; he is being asked to grip until a specific person arrives, and that person has set out.

Should I stay in a church where error is tolerated, or leave? Christ did not tell the faithful in Thyatira to leave; he told them to hold fast, and said he would deal with Jezebel himself. So do not leave lightly, and do not make yourself responsible for fixing everything. Speak the truth where you have the opportunity, keep your own faith clean, pray for the church and wait. But if the church’s leaders themselves deny the gospel or require you to accept sin, and will not listen, it may become right to go to a faithful church, especially for the sake of your children. Thyatira still had a true congregation within it; not every building with a cross on it does.

How do I recognise a deep things offer today? It usually comes with three marks. It promises insight that ordinary Christians lack, available through a special teacher, technique, experience or method. It quietly makes the plain commands of Scripture seem childish or optional for the mature. And it flatters you: you are more advanced, freer, more enlightened than the people still worried about holiness. Real Christian growth looks different. It is deeper humility, simpler trust in Christ, greater love, and more obedience to the plain things, not less. If something new makes the old gospel seem small, it is not from God.

verseByVerse.quote: The one who conquers and who keeps my works until the end, to him I will give authority over the nations, and he will rule them with a rod of iron, as when earthen pots are broken in pieces, even as I myself have received authority from my Father. And I will give him the morning star. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Psalm 2 describes the nations raging against the LORD and his anointed king, his Son. God says he will give the nations to his Son, who will break them with a rod of iron and dash them in pieces like a potter’s vessel (Psalm 2:8–9).

Keeps my works until the end. Keeps my works (ho tērōn achri telous ta erga mou): these stand over against Jezebel’s works in verse 22. They are the works Christ commands and produces, and the two sets of works are the two ways of getting through life in a guild town. The letter has now named both. Until the end: perseverance to the last. Conquering, in this book, is not a single dramatic act; it is defined by duration.

Authority over the nations. The promise to Thyatira is the longest of the seven and the strangest, and it is given to the church in the least important town on the road. Authority (exousian): Christians in Thyatira had no power at all; some of them had lost their guild membership and could not get work in a town where everything was guild work. They had just been told that their whole assignment was to hold on. To these people, Christ promises that they will share his rule over the nations. Believers will reign with Christ (3:21; 20:4–6; 22:5; 1 Corinthians 6:2–3).

A rod of iron. The wording of verses 26 and 27 is a direct quotation of Psalm 2, the great coronation psalm in which the nations rage and God installs his King on Zion and says to him: Ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage (Psalm 2:8). Rule (poimanei) is literally shepherd: the Greek Old Testament translated Psalm 2:9 with that word, though in this context the shepherd’s rod is used in judgement. Rod of iron: unbreakable authority. Earthen pots: Thyatira’s potters knew that unfired clay can be reshaped but a fired pot can only be broken, and broken pots cannot be repaired. Opposition to Christ will be utterly broken.

In the flow. This promise gathers up threads from the whole book. In 1:6 Christ had already made his people a kingdom; here the conqueror is promised a share in his rule. The rod of iron is used again of Christ himself, the male child who is to rule the nations (12:5) and the rider whose sword strikes them (19:15), so the church’s authority is never its own; it is his, shared. Thyatira, holding on in the smallest town on the road, is given a share in the ending of the whole story.

Received from my Father. That psalm is about the Messiah. Christ quotes it, and then does something startling with it: he hands it over. Christ received this authority from the Father (Matthew 28:18). The authority the Father gave him, he gives to the ones who conquer, as the Son of God shares his inheritance with the sons of God (Romans 8:17).

The morning star. Every other promise in the seven letters is a thing: a tree, a crown, a stone, a name, a pillar, a throne. This one is a person. The morning star (ton astera ton prōinon) is the planet Venus, which shines brightly before dawn, announcing the coming day, and the book says plainly who it is in its final chapter: I am the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star (22:16). Behind it stands Balaam’s own prophecy, which is a fine irony in a letter about Balaam’s teaching: a star shall come out of Jacob, and a sceptre shall rise out of Israel (Numbers 24:17). Christ is that royal star. Roman generals are said to have honoured Venus as the star of victory, but Christ is the true sign of triumph.

The star that means the sun is coming. The morning star shines brightest in the last hour of the night, before any light shows in the east, and it does not announce more night. It means the sun is coming. So the last word to Thyatira is not authority after all. Authority is promised, and then something better is added on top of it, and the something better is himself. To a congregation being urged to hold on until he comes, the final promise is that when he comes he will give them himself. Every other reward in these letters is something from his hand. This one is the hand.

Where Christians differ: when do believers rule the nations? Premillennialists, dispensational Christians among them, see this fulfilled in a future thousand-year reign on earth after Christ returns, reading Revelation 20 as following chapter 19 in time; many godly believers hold this view. This commentary is amillennial: it reads the thousand years as a picture of the present age, because Revelation often retells the same age from different angles, and elsewhere the New Testament places the resurrection and judgement of all together at Christ’s one return (John 5:28–29). This commentary’s view: believers already share Christ’s reign in a hidden way, as a kingdom of priests (1:6), and those who die in Christ reign with him now in heaven (20:4–6), which this commentary reads as the present age between Christ’s comings. The rule over the nations is completed at Christ’s return, when his enemies are judged (19:15) and his people reign with him for ever in the new creation (22:5). There is no separate future millennium on earth, though those who expect one share the hope that matters most: Christ will return in person and reign.

What it does not mean. Ruling with a rod of iron does not mean Christians now seek political power to impose the faith. Christ breaks his enemies by his word and at his coming. Our part now is faithful witness.

What does reigning with Christ look like now, in an ordinary life? Mostly it looks like what it looked like in Thyatira: faithfulness without power. Believers are already seated with Christ in the heavenly places (Ephesians 2:6), and they share his rule as his word goes out and the nations are discipled (Matthew 28:18–20). In practice that means praying with authority for the world, refusing to bow to the idols of the market, standing for truth, serving others as Christ served, and overcoming evil with good (Romans 12:21). It does not look like dominance. The authority is real, but for now it wears the shape of the cross, and it will be seen openly when he comes.

Will the saints really judge and rule? Yes. Scripture says the saints will judge the world and even angels (1 Corinthians 6:2–3), and will reign with Christ for ever (22:5). We do not know all that this will involve, but it means that the weak and despised of this age will be honoured with responsibility in the age to come, under Christ and in perfect agreement with his justice. It is not revenge. It is the restoration of humanity to the dominion God gave Adam at the beginning (Genesis 1:28; Psalm 8:6), now held in Christ, the true and better Adam.

On a Tuesday. If you feel powerless, holding on in a small place, keep doing the plain obedient things his Spirit is working in you. And when the night feels darkest, look for the morning star: he rose while it was still dark, and the day is coming.

For worship. The King of Psalm 2 did not take the nations by breaking them first. He let himself be broken, and the Father gave him the nations as the reward of his obedience to death (Philippians 2:8–9). Now he shares that inheritance with dyers and potters who lost their guild places for his name, and above the inheritance he gives the one gift that makes it worth having. The star Balaam saw far off, which rose over an empty tomb, will rise over every faithful church at the end of its night, and it will not set.

2.text: <sup>1</sup>“To the angel of the church in Ephesus write: ‘The words of him who holds the seven stars in his right hand, who walks among the seven golden lampstands.<sup>2</sup>”‘I know your works, your toil and your patient endurance, and how you cannot bear with those who are evil, but have tested those who call themselves apostles and are not, and found them to be false.<sup>3</sup>I know you are enduring patiently and bearing up for my name’s sake, and you have not grown weary.<sup>4</sup>But I have this against you, that you have abandoned the love you had at first.<sup>5</sup>Remember therefore from where you have fallen; repent, and do the works you did at first. If not, I will come to you and remove your lampstand from its place, unless you repent.<sup>6</sup>Yet this you have: you hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate.<sup>7</sup>He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. To the one who conquers I will grant to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God.’<sup>8</sup>“And to the angel of the church in Smyrna write: ‘The words of the first and the last, who died and came to life.<sup>9</sup>”‘I know your tribulation and your poverty (but you are rich) and the slander of those who say that they are Jews and are not, but are a synagogue of Satan.<sup>10</sup>Do not fear what you are about to suffer. Behold, the devil is about to throw some of you into prison, that you may be tested, and for ten days you will have tribulation. Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life.<sup>11</sup>He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. The one who conquers will not be hurt by the second death.’<sup>12</sup>“And to the angel of the church in Pergamum write: ‘The words of him who has the sharp two-edged sword.<sup>13</sup>”‘I know where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is. Yet you hold fast my name, and you did not deny my faith even in the days of Antipas my faithful witness, who was killed among you, where Satan dwells.<sup>14</sup>But I have a few things against you: you have some there who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before the sons of Israel, so that they might eat food sacrificed to idols and practice sexual immorality.<sup>15</sup>So also you have some who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans.<sup>16</sup>Therefore repent. If not, I will come to you soon and war against them with the sword of my mouth.<sup>17</sup>He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. To the one who conquers I will give some of the hidden manna, and I will give him a white stone, with a new name written on the stone that no one knows except the one who receives it.’<sup>18</sup>“And to the angel of the church in Thyatira write: ‘The words of the Son of God, who has eyes like a flame of fire, and whose feet are like burnished bronze.<sup>19</sup>”‘I know your works, your love and faith and service and patient endurance, and that your latter works exceed the first.<sup>20</sup>But I have this against you, that you tolerate that woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess and is teaching and seducing my servants to practice sexual immorality and to eat food sacrificed to idols.<sup>21</sup>I gave her time to repent, but she refuses to repent of her sexual immorality.<sup>22</sup>Behold, I will throw her onto a sickbed, and those who commit adultery with her I will throw into great tribulation, unless they repent of her works,<sup>23</sup>and I will strike her children dead. And all the churches will know that I am he who searches mind and heart, and I will give to each of you according to your works.<sup>24</sup>But to the rest of you in Thyatira, who do not hold this teaching, who have not learned what some call the deep things of Satan, to you I say, I do not lay on you any other burden.<sup>25</sup>Only hold fast what you have until I come.<sup>26</sup>The one who conquers and who keeps my works until the end, to him I will give authority over the nations,<sup>27</sup>and he will rule them with a rod of iron, as when earthen pots are broken in pieces, even as I myself have received authority from my Father.<sup>28</sup>And I will give him the morning star.<sup>29</sup>He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.’

3.title: Letters to Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea
3.overview:
The last three of the seven letters complete Christ’s diagnosis of his churches. Sardis has a reputation for life but is dead. Philadelphia is small and weak, yet receives no rebuke and some of the richest promises. Laodicea is wealthy and self-satisfied, and receives the sharpest rebuke of all.

Taken together, the seven letters are a mirror in which any church, and any believer, can find itself; seven, the number of completeness, makes them a portrait of the church in every age, not only in first-century Asia.

The chapter ends with Christ standing at the door and knocking. The one who will come with the clouds (1:7) is the same one who knocks at Laodicea’s door (3:20): the book holds the cosmic and the personal together.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — To the Church in Sardis
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sardis, once the capital of Lydia, was by John’s day a comfortable town living on a great past. Christ, who holds the seven spirits of God and the seven stars, gives it the bluntest verdict in the letters: it has a name for being alive, but it is dead (v. 1). No heresy and no persecution are mentioned. He calls it to wake up, strengthen what remains, remember the gospel it received, keep it and repent, or he will come like a thief, as attackers twice took the city by climbing the unwatched cliff (vv. 2–3). Yet a few in Sardis have not soiled their garments, and they are promised white clothing, a name never blotted out of the book of life, and Christ’s confession of their name before his Father (vv. 4–6).
verseByVerse.theology:
A Name for Being Alive

Sardis had a reputation for life and was dead. Christ calls it to wake up, strengthen what remains, remember and repent, and he counts the few who have not soiled their garments.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The city had twice fallen to a night climb while the guards slept.

Now: Ask whether the reasons you would give for your church’s health are reasons Sardis could have given.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to the angel of the church in Sardis write: 'The words of him who has the seven spirits of God and the seven stars. "I know your works. You have the reputation of being alive, but you are dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Revelation 3 contains the last three of Christ’s seven letters. Sardis has a name for being alive but is dead; Christ calls it to wake up, strengthen what remains, remember the gospel and repent, yet promises that the faithful few will walk with him in white, never be blotted out of the book of life, and be acknowledged before the Father (vv. 1–6). Philadelphia has little strength but has kept his word; he who holds the key of David sets before it an open door no one can shut and will keep it in the hour of trial (vv. 7–13). Laodicea is lukewarm and thinks itself rich; Christ counsels it to buy from him gold, white clothes and eye salve, stands at the door knocking, and promises the conqueror a seat on his throne (vv. 14–22). Each time Christ’s verdict overturns the church’s reputation: the church that looked alive was dead, the weak church was strong in faithfulness, and the rich church was poor.

The setting. Sardis, about 30 miles (50 kilometres) southeast of Thyatira, had been the capital of Lydia, whose king Croesus was proverbial for his wealth; the earliest known coins were struck in Lydia, very probably at Sardis. Its acropolis was thought impregnable, yet it fell twice by surprise (see v. 3). Destroyed by an earthquake in AD 17 and rebuilt with help from the emperor Tiberius, by John’s day it was prosperous but living on its past glory. It had a large and wealthy Jewish community, and a great temple of Artemis.

The seven spirits and the seven stars. Both phrases have been used already, the sevenfold Spirit at 1:4 and the stars at 1:16, 20, and putting them together says something precise to a dying church. Seven in this book is the number of completeness, so the seven spirits are the one Holy Spirit in all his fullness, who gives life; a dead church needs nothing so much as the life-giving Spirit, and Christ has him to give. The seven stars are the churches held in his hand: this church is still his. Everything a church needs in order to come alive is in the hands of the person writing the letter. Jesus said that an hour was coming, and was already here, when the dead would hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear would live (John 5:25). This letter is that voice, spoken into a congregation with a name and no pulse.

A name for being alive. This is the bluntest assessment in the seven letters. The word for reputation is onoma, a name, and it is not gossip or misunderstanding; it means the congregation is genuinely well regarded, perhaps busy, respected and admired by other churches, and that the regard is based on something observable. Something is going on at Sardis that reads, from outside, as life. Yet it is dead (nekros): spiritually lifeless. And nothing in the letter suggests heresy. There is no false teacher here, no Jezebel, no Balaam, no persecution, and that last absence tells its own story, because Sardis is one of only two churches with no enemies mentioned at all. Perhaps nobody troubled them because there was nothing worth attacking. Paul describes people who have the appearance of godliness but deny its power (2 Timothy 3:5).

A full building. Dead church has become a phrase people throw at congregations they dislike, so consider what the diagnosis means. Christ is not describing an empty building but a full one: services, a name, enough activity to sustain a reputation across a whole province, and nothing inside it. A body can be laid out with its clothes arranged and its hands folded and look, from the doorway, very much like a man asleep.

Living inside the reputation. The gap between the two verdicts is the whole letter. Nobody in that room thought they were dead; they had the reviews to prove otherwise. Of all seven churches this is the hardest to diagnose from inside, because the evidence a member would reach for, our history and what people say about us, is the very thing being contradicted. The eyes of flame (1:14) do not read reviews. Reputation is one of the heart’s favourite substitutes for God: it lets a person, or a congregation, feel alive on other people’s good opinion. The cure is not to despise what others think but to care more about what Christ sees.

How can I tell whether a church, or my own faith, is alive? Not by activity or reputation, which is exactly what Sardis had. Look instead for the marks the Spirit produces. Is Christ himself loved and spoken of, or only the church’s programmes and history? Is the word of God believed, preached and obeyed? Is there real repentance when sin is exposed, rather than management of appearances? Is there prayer that expects God to act? Is there love that costs something, and are people being brought to faith and growing? None of these is measured on a single Sunday. But if they are absent for years, the name is outliving the life.

For worship. The one who writes to a dead church has been dead himself. He lay in a sealed tomb, and on the third day he walked out of it with the keys of Death and Hades in his hand (1:18), and the Spirit of life is his to give. Sardis had a famous name and a quiet grave; he has the name above every name and an empty one. No congregation is so far gone that his voice cannot reach it, and the Lord of the seven stars has never yet spoken to the dead without raising those he came to raise.
verseByVerse.note: Sardis had been a great royal city. Its seemingly impregnable citadel was taken by surprise more than once in its history.

verseByVerse.quote: Wake up, and strengthen what remains and is about to die, for I have not found your works complete in the sight of my God. Remember, then, what you received and heard. Keep it, and repent. If you will not wake up, I will come like a thief, and you will not know at what hour I will come against you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Jesus had warned his disciples to stay awake because the thief comes when no one expects him (Matthew 24:42–44), and Paul used the same image (1 Thessalonians 5:2–6).

Wake up. Five commands come in a rush, and the first one governs the rest. “Wake up” (ginou grēgorōn) is literally become watchful, keep on being alert: a present imperative, a summons to a state, not a single act. And it is an odd thing to say to a corpse, which is the first hint that the death of verse 1 is a verdict on the congregation as a body rather than on every individual in it. Verse 4 will confirm it: a few names in Sardis are still very much alive.

Strengthen what remains. There is something left: good news in the middle of the worst assessment in the chapter. Strengthen (stērison) means to make firm, to brace. Christ does not tell Sardis to start something new; he tells it to put its weight under what is still standing. There are embers that can be fanned into flame: a handful who still pray, a half-abandoned practice, a doctrine still confessed without conviction.

Not complete in the sight of my God. Not wrong. Not false. Incomplete: peplērōmena means filled up, brought to fullness. Their works are outwardly correct but inwardly empty. And the phrase in the sight of my God is the whole difficulty in six words. In the sight of the province of Asia, the works of Sardis were finished enough to build a reputation on. Two audiences, two verdicts, and only one of them is looking at the part that counts.

The one whose works were complete. The man giving this verdict speaks of my God, as he did on the cross (Matthew 27:46) and on the morning he rose (John 20:17), and he alone has ever stood before that God with works filled to the brim. He finished the work the Father gave him to do (John 17:4), and with his last breath he said that it was finished (John 19:30). That is why the remedy in the next sentence is memory, not effort. What Sardis received and heard was the news of that finished work: Christ died for our sins, was buried and was raised (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). A church with half-done works is not cured by doing more of them, but by going back to the one whose work needs nothing added, and being made alive by it again. His finished obedience is counted to all who trust him (Romans 5:19; Philippians 3:9), so that even their unfinished works are accepted for his sake.

Remember what you received and heard. The remedy at Ephesus was also memory (2:5), and here as there it points backwards to something specific. Received (eilēphas) and heard (ēkousas) are the standard vocabulary for the apostolic gospel handed on from person to person (1 Corinthians 15:1–3): the gospel they were first taught, and the grace they were given. Sardis does not need a new message. It needs the old one to mean something again.

Keep it, and repent. Hold on to it (tērei, keep on keeping), and turn round (metanoēson, a decisive turning). The verbs together describe a church that still possesses the truth and has stopped being changed by it. Repentance here is not the abandonment of a false position but the recovery of a true one that had gone quietly inert.

If you will not wake up. For anyone who knew the city, this was local history used as a weapon. Sardis stood on a spur of rock with sheer cliffs and was thought impregnable, yet it fell twice in the same way. In 546 BC, so the historian Herodotus tells, a soldier of Cyrus watched a defender climb down the rock face to retrieve a dropped helmet, noted the route and led a party up it; in 214 BC a Cretan climber did much the same for Antiochus III at night. Twice Sardis lost everything because nobody was watching the one place that did not seem to need watching. Christ is telling a church in that particular town that its besetting civic sin has become its spiritual one.

Like a thief. Unexpectedly, without warning. This may refer to a judgement on Sardis in history, or to Christ’s final return, which will be a disaster for those found asleep (16:15). And note the object of the coming: I will come against you. Elsewhere in these letters his coming is the church’s hope, the thing worth holding on for (2:25; 3:11). Here the same arrival is a threat. It is the same event; what differs is which side of the wall you are on when it happens. For the watchful, the thief image is no threat at all (1 Thessalonians 5:4).

What it does not mean. Coming like a thief does not mean Christ’s return will be secret or invisible. It means unexpected. Many earnest Christians, especially in dispensational churches, have been taught to expect a secret rapture before a time of tribulation, and they love his appearing; but where the New Testament uses the thief picture it describes the one visible return (1 Thessalonians 5:2–4; 2 Peter 3:10), which Paul says will be preceded by events he names (2 Thessalonians 2:1–3). Every eye will see him (1:7); but those who are not watching will be caught unprepared, as Sardis was by its enemies.

What does staying awake look like in an ordinary week? It is not anxious date-setting or constant emotional intensity. It is the steady habits of someone who expects his Lord. Pray regularly, and include his coming in your prayers (22:20). Keep listening to God’s word, privately and with his people. Deal with sin while it is small, before it hardens into habit. Watch where comfort is making you careless. And stay among believers who will tell you the truth about yourself (Hebrews 3:13). Spiritual sleep rarely starts with a decision to stop believing. It starts with a hundred small neglects that each seemed harmless.

What if I have already drifted asleep? Then this letter is for you, and it begins with hope: something remains, and Christ is speaking to you because he means to wake you. Do not wait to feel alive before you act. Do what he says, in his order. Remember the gospel you first received: that Christ died for your sins and rose again. Hold on to it, and turn back to him in plain repentance, naming what put you to sleep. Then strengthen what is left: go back to church, open the Bible again, pray even briefly, and tell a mature Christian where you are. Sleepers are woken one call at a time.

On a Tuesday. Ask where your unguarded cliff is: the one area of your life you have assumed needs no watching.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet you have still a few names in Sardis, people who have not soiled their garments, and they will walk with me in white, for they are worthy. The one who conquers will be clothed thus in white garments, and I will never blot his name out of the book of life. I will confess his name before my Father and before his angels. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Sardis was famous for its wool and dyeing industry. White garments were worn at festivals, at victories and by citizens on special occasions, and in the ancient world a soiled robe could disqualify a worshipper from entering a temple. Ancient cities kept registers of citizens, and a name was erased when a citizen died or was disgraced. The idea of God’s book goes back to Exodus 32:32–33, Psalm 69:28 and Daniel 12:1, where those whose names are written in the book will be delivered.

A few names in Sardis. Not a few people: a few names (onomata), which is the same word used in verse 1 of the church’s reputation. The congregation has a name for being alive and is dead; a handful of individuals have no name at all in the province and are alive. Christ knows them individually, and the shepherd who calls his own sheep by name (John 10:3) is counting them one at a time in a church he has just pronounced dead.

People who have not soiled their garments. Soiled (emolynan) means stained, defiled. Clothing in Scripture often pictures a person’s life and conduct (Jude 23; Zechariah 3:3–5). These few had not been stained by compromise with the culture’s sin and idolatry. What exactly they refused is not stated, and the silence should be respected. No heresy is named in this letter and no persecution; whatever kept these few clean was probably unremarkable and certainly unrewarded. Their reward, three times over, is that somebody was watching.

Walk with me in white. Three promises follow, and each one answers something the letter has already raised. The first is fellowship and white garments. Walk with me: they will share the company of Christ. White: purity, victory and festival joy. Throughout this book white clothing is the dress of heaven: the martyrs under the altar (6:11), the great multitude (7:9), the armies that follow him (19:14). Worthy (axioi) should not be read as a claim about merit. Four chapters later the same book will say that the white robes were washed and made white in the blood of the Lamb (7:14), which is a deliberately impossible image and settles where the whiteness comes from. Their worthiness is that their lives fit the gift, not that they earned it. Even the fine linen of 19:8, the righteous deeds of the saints, is something granted to the bride to wear, not something she wove for herself. And the one who conquers will be clothed thus: every conqueror, not only the few in Sardis, wears the robe of righteousness that Christ gives (Isaiah 61:10).

Never blot his name out. The second promise, with the strongest negative in Greek (ou mē). The book of life (biblou tēs zōēs) is God’s register of those who belong to him and will have eternal life, and Revelation says these names were written before the foundation of the world (13:8; 17:8). Every hearer in Sardis knew what an erased name on a city register meant. And the promise is given precisely to people whose names carried no weight in the town at all. The register that matters is not kept in Sardis, and there is no scribe anywhere with authority to reach it.

I will confess his name. The third promise, and the best. Confess (homologēsō) means acknowledge openly, literally say the same thing. This is a direct echo of what Jesus said in Galilee: everyone who acknowledges me before men, I also will acknowledge before my Father who is in heaven (Matthew 10:32; Luke 12:8). So a believer in an unimportant town, whose faithfulness nobody recorded and whose congregation had ceased to notice him, will one day hear his name said aloud by Jesus Christ in front of the Father and the assembled angels.

Names that matter. That is the whole answer to a church living on reputation. Sardis had a name and no life; these few had life and no name. And the one with the eyes of flame, who misses nothing done in the dark, will speak their names in the only place where a name is worth having. He is not ashamed to call them brothers (Hebrews 2:11).

Where Christians differ: can a name be blotted out of the book of life? Arminian Christians (who hold that a true believer can finally fall away), many of them earnest and godly, read this verse as implying that believers who fail to persevere can have their names erased and lose their salvation, and they point to texts that speak of blotting out (Exodus 32:33; Psalm 69:28) and to the warning of Revelation 22:19. This commentary’s view: the verse is a promise, not a threat. Christ never says he blots anyone out; he says he will never do it. Names in the Lamb’s book were written before the foundation of the world (13:8; 17:8), so those who belong to Christ cannot be removed. Those who never persevere show that they were never truly written (1 John 2:19). The warnings in these letters are the means God uses to keep his people persevering; the promises assure them that he will.

How can I know my name is written in the book of life? You cannot read the book, but you can see its fruit. Names were written by God’s free choice before the world began (Ephesians 1:4), and the evidence that yours is there is that you have come to Christ: you trust him alone for forgiveness, you love him, however weakly, and you want to follow him (John 6:37; 2 Peter 1:10). Do not look for assurance in a feeling or a past decision alone; look at Christ, and at whether you are looking at him. Jesus told his disciples to rejoice that their names are written in heaven (Luke 10:20). That joy is meant for ordinary believers.

What if I have been ashamed of Christ in the past? Then remember Peter. He denied Jesus three times with oaths, and Jesus restored him three times by a charcoal fire (John 21:15–19), and he went on to confess Christ before the council and, at the last, in his death. The promise of being acknowledged before the Father is not for those who have never failed, but for those who come back and keep confessing him. If you have kept quiet about Christ out of fear, confess that to him; he forgives it. Then take the next opportunity to own him, gently and plainly. Your past silence does not cancel his present welcome.

For worship. The Lamb whose book it is let his own name be dragged through the courts and written up among criminals. He was numbered with the transgressors (Luke 22:37) and cut off from the land of the living (Isaiah 53:8), so that the names in his book would never be cut off. The white he gives was bought with red. And the register he keeps is not a draft he might revise, but the roll of those he died for, written before the world began and guarded by the one who rose to keep it. Not one name in it will be missing on the day he reads it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — To the Church in Philadelphia
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Philadelphia was the youngest of the seven cities, on a gateway road and on a fault line; after the earthquake of AD 17 its people camped outside the walls for years. Christ comes as the holy and true one who holds the key of David (v. 7). He sets before this church of little power an open door no one can shut, because it has kept his word and not denied his name (v. 8). Its accusers will learn that he has loved it (v. 9), and he will keep it in the hour of trial coming on the whole world (v. 10); the readings of that promise are set out at the verse. It is to hold fast what it has (v. 11), and the conqueror will be a pillar in God’s temple, never to go out, bearing the names of God, of the new Jerusalem and of Christ himself (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.theology:
Little Power, No Rebuke

Christ holds the key of David and sets an open door before a weak church that has kept his word. Its accusers will learn that he has loved it; the faithful will be pillars in the temple of God and bear his names.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A small congregation in an earthquake town had been told it had no share in the promises.

Now: Christ measures a church by faithfulness, not size.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to the angel of the church in Philadelphia write: 'The words of the holy one, the true one, who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut, who shuts and no one opens. "I know your works. Behold, I have set before you an open door, which no one is able to shut. I know that you have but little power, and yet you have kept my word and have not denied my name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Philadelphia, about 28 miles (45 kilometres) southeast of Sardis, was the youngest of the seven cities, founded in the second century BC by the kings of Pergamum and named after Attalus II, whose loyalty to his brother King Eumenes II earned him the nickname Philadelphus, brother-lover. It stood at the gateway to the high plateau of Phrygia, on an important road, and is often said to have been founded to spread Greek culture eastward: a city with an open door. Badly damaged in the earthquake of AD 17, with aftershocks for years that drove many residents to live outside the city, it was rebuilt with help from Tiberius and renamed Neocaesarea, New Caesar. Like Smyrna, the church faced hostility from the local synagogue.

The words of the holy one, the true one. Christ introduces himself with descriptions that, unlike most of the letters, are not drawn from the vision of chapter 1. The holy one (ho hagios) is in the Old Testament the title of God himself: to whom then will you compare me, says the Holy One (Isaiah 40:25). The true one (ho alēthinos) means not merely truthful, but genuine, real as against counterfeit, faithful. To a congregation being told by the synagogue across the street that it was not the real people of God, the sender identifies himself as the Real One. And it should make us catch our breath that he takes the title of the Holy One of Israel, the name Isaiah gives to God again and again (Isaiah 1:4; 43:3). The one who opens the door to this weak church is not a kindly doorkeeper but holiness itself, and that is exactly why no one can shut what he has opened.

The key of David. This is quoted almost word for word from Isaiah 22, where a steward named Shebna is stripped of office and the key of the house of David is laid on the shoulder of Eliakim (Isaiah 22:22). The key is the steward’s badge of office: authority over who is admitted to the king’s house. Christ, David’s greater son, has authority over the house and kingdom of David, and he decides who enters. In chapter 1 he held the keys of Death and Hades; here he holds the key of admission to the kingdom. Whoever else in Philadelphia claimed the right to decide who was in and who was out, the decision was being made elsewhere.

An open door. Two meanings fit, and both are defensible. First, the door into the kingdom (thyran ēneōgmenēn), guaranteed by Christ, held open for a congregation being told by its neighbours that it had no right of entry. Second, a door of opportunity for the gospel, as Paul used the phrase, a door for the word (1 Corinthians 16:9; 2 Corinthians 2:12; Colossians 4:3), which fits a city founded to spread Greek culture eastward and sitting on the road inland. The two are not in competition: the church put out of the synagogue has been given a door nobody in that synagogue can close, and a door out into the world besides.

But little power. Small in numbers, influence and resources (mikran dynamin). Christ does not rebuke them for this, and he does not tell them to grow. He names the weakness as a simple fact. Weakness is not failure.

And yet you have kept my word. Small, and faithful: they held on to the truth and did not disown Christ under pressure. Of the two churches he finds nothing to criticise in, one was poor and hunted and the other was small and weak.

Is a small church a failing church? No. That sentence of Christ’s belongs to a very large number of believers and congregations. There are churches of thirty people in places nobody has heard of, holding on, keeping the word, not denying the name, and quietly convinced that whatever God is doing in the world is happening somewhere else with more resources. Philadelphia is the letter written to them, and it contains no rebuke of any kind. Size is not the measure Christ uses. A small church should still pray for growth and walk through the doors God opens, but it should not despise itself. Christ does not.

How do I know which door God has opened for me? Usually by looking at the people and opportunities already in front of you, rather than waiting for a dramatic sign. Paul saw open doors in places where people were ready to listen, even when there were many adversaries (1 Corinthians 16:9). Ask: who in my life is asking questions, going through a hard time, or open to friendship? Where do I have a natural reason to be and speak? Pray for opportunities (Colossians 4:3), then take the small ones: an invitation, an honest answer, an offer of help in Christ’s name. If one door closes, it was not the only door. Christ holds the key, and he does not run out of doors.
verseByVerse.note: Philadelphia was a small city often shaken by earthquakes.

parallels.desc: he shall open, and none shall shut

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I will make those of the synagogue of Satan who say that they are Jews and are not, but lie—behold, I will make them come and bow down before your feet, and they will learn that I have loved you. Because you have kept my word about patient endurance, I will keep you from the hour of trial that is coming on the whole world, to try those who dwell on the earth. I am coming soon. Hold fast what you have, so that no one may seize your crown.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Isaiah prophesied that the nations who had oppressed Israel would come and bow down at Israel’s feet, acknowledging that the LORD had loved his people (Isaiah 45:14; 49:23; 60:14). Here the roles are startlingly reversed: Jewish persecutors will bow before a church that was probably mostly Gentile, acknowledging that Christ has loved it.

The synagogue of Satan. As at Smyrna (2:9), and the phrase needs the same guard: this is not a statement about Jewish people. The writer and his Lord were Jews, and Paul longed and prayed for the salvation of his Jewish kinsmen (Romans 9:1–5; 10:1). Satan means adversary, and the charge is functional: a particular group in one town was denouncing its Christian neighbours and telling them they had no share in the promises. By rejecting the Messiah and persecuting his people, they had forfeited the right to the name of God’s people. Lie (pseudontai): their claim is false.

Bow down before your feet. What makes this verse remarkable is where the imagery comes from. The Old Testament repeatedly promises that the nations will come and bow down before Israel. Christ takes that promise and applies it to a small congregation of Gentile and Jewish believers in Philadelphia, with the roles the other way round. He is not abolishing the promise; he is saying who the true Israel turns out to be, the same argument Paul makes at length in Romans 9 to 11, where he also holds out hope for ethnic Israel (Romans 11:25–29); Christians differ over what that hope involves. Bow down (proskynēsousin, prostrate themselves) is not worship of the church, but acknowledgement that the church is God’s true people. This may happen through their conversion, as Paul hoped (Romans 11:11–14), or at the final judgement, when every knee bows (Philippians 2:10–11).

They will learn that I have loved you. The point of the bowing is not humiliation. The sentence does not end with before your feet; it ends with this. Loved (ēgapēsa, I loved) points to a love already shown in a deed, and this book has named the deed: to him who loves us and has freed us from our sins by his blood (1:5). It also echoes Isaiah 43:4, where the LORD says to Israel that they are precious in his eyes and he loves them. The love once claimed exclusively by the synagogue belongs to the despised church. The vindication being promised is not that its opponents will be crushed. It is that they will find out the truth, and the truth they will find out is not that Philadelphia was right, but that Philadelphia was loved.

My word about patient endurance. The Greek reads literally the word of my endurance (ton logon tēs hypomonēs mou): either the command to endure as Christ endured, or the message of his own endurance, and the second deserves its weight. Before he asked any church to endure, he endured. He set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51), endured hostility from sinners, and for the joy set before him endured the cross, despising the shame (Hebrews 12:2–3). When he was dared to come down from the cross, he stayed on it (Matthew 27:40–42). Paul prays that believers’ hearts may be directed to the steadfastness of Christ (2 Thessalonians 3:5). Philadelphia’s endurance is not a private virtue it supplies; it is a share in his. That is why the promise that follows rests on his keeping, not theirs.

I will keep you from the hour of trial. Keep from (tērēsō ek) means keep out of, guard from. There is a play on words: because you have kept my word, I will keep you. The hour of trial (tēs hōras tou peirasmou) is a time of testing coming on the whole world, which the rest of Revelation describes in the seals, trumpets and bowls. And the ground of the promise is not in dispute: Philadelphia is kept because it kept his word, and the keeping is his doing.

Those who dwell on the earth. Throughout Revelation this phrase (tous katoikountas epi tēs gēs) means unbelievers, the world in rebellion against God (6:10; 13:8; 17:8). The trial is aimed at them, not at the church.

In the flow. Here the letter to Philadelphia looks ahead to the rest of the book. The hour of trial coming on the whole world is what the seals, trumpets and bowls of chapters 6 to 16 will show, and the keeping promised here is pictured at 7:3, where God’s servants are sealed on their foreheads before the winds of judgement are let loose. So these verses are a small preview of Revelation’s whole message: the world will be shaken, the church’s enemies will have to acknowledge whom Christ has loved, and the church is kept through it all, not taken out of it.

Where Christians differ: is this a promise of a pre-tribulation rapture? Dispensationalists (who see distinct purposes of God for Israel and the church) read “keep you from the hour of trial” as a promise that the church will be removed from the earth before a final seven-year tribulation. Teachers such as John Walvoord and Charles Ryrie argued it with care, and the argument has real force: the promise is deliverance from an hour, not merely from harm within it, and the trial is explicitly worldwide. This commentary’s view: the same words appear in John 17:15, where Jesus prays not that the Father would take his disciples out of the world, but that he would keep them from the evil one. To keep from is to protect within, not to remove from. Revelation consistently shows God’s people sealed and protected in the midst of the judgements (7:3; 9:4; 12:6, 14), while they still suffer at the hands of the beast. The promise was made to a church in the first century, which was never raptured; it was preserved. God protects his people from his wrath and from losing their faith, not from all suffering. There is one visible return of Christ, not a secret rapture.

So that no one may seize your crown. First comes the promise that sustains endurance: I am coming soon (tachy, quickly), the words repeated three times in the book’s last chapter (22:7, 12, 20). Then the instruction to the weakest church is the same as to the compromised one at Thyatira: hold on. Not achieve, not expand: hold (kratei, grip). And the danger named is not that the crown will be lost by failure but that someone may seize it (labē, take), the language of an athlete’s wreath (stephanon) being taken by a rival. The crown is already theirs in promise and is worth guarding.

If Christ keeps his people in the hour of trial, why do Christians still suffer? Because the keeping is not exemption from all pain but protection from the things that would destroy them. The believers in Revelation are sealed so that God’s judgements do not fall on them (7:3; 9:4), yet they are hated and sometimes killed by the beast (13:7). What Christ guarantees is that no suffering will separate them from his love (Romans 8:35–39), that their faith will not finally fail (Luke 22:32), and that they will never face God’s wrath (1 Thessalonians 5:9). So if you are suffering, you have not been left out of the promise. You are being kept inside the storm, as the disciples were kept in the boat.

Could someone really take my crown? Not by force against Christ’s will, since no one can snatch his sheep out of his hand (John 10:28–29). The warning works the way a parent’s warning works: it is one of the means by which Christ keeps his people holding on. A crown can be seized only by letting go of the one who gives it, which is what false teachers, persecutors and the lure of an easier life invite us to do. The true believer hears the warning and grips harder, and that gripping is itself the evidence of the grace that keeps him. So take the warning seriously, and take the promise more seriously still.

On a Tuesday. If you are opposed for your faith, do not strike back; pray that your opponents will learn that Christ loves you by coming to love him too. And when a hard season comes, ask him not to remove you from it but to keep you in it, and he will.

For worship. There was an hour from which the Son would not ask to be kept. Father, glorify your name, he said, and walked into it (John 12:27–28): betrayed, condemned, forsaken, crowned with thorns instead of a victor’s wreath. Because he was not spared his hour, his people are kept in theirs. The crown he holds out to a church with little power was won under a crown of thorns, and the one who wore that crown will not let anyone take theirs.

verseByVerse.quote: The one who conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God. Never shall he go out of it, and I will write on him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem, which comes down from my God out of heaven, and my own new name. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. In a city shaken by earthquakes, where buildings collapsed and people fled outside the walls, a pillar was the part of a building that stood firm.
