Columns often remained standing in ruined temples. Cities sometimes honoured a distinguished citizen or priest by setting up a pillar inscribed with his name in a temple. And Philadelphia had twice been renamed after emperors (Neocaesarea and Flavia); Christ gives a greater name.

A pillar in the temple of my God. A reader who knows what Philadelphia had lived through can watch the promises land one after another. A pillar (stylon, column) speaks of permanence, stability and honour. This is spoken to people whose city had been shaken flat in AD 17, whose aftershocks went on for years, and who had spent seasons living in the fields outside the walls because no roof could be trusted. Those with little power and shut out of the synagogue will be pillars in God’s own temple. Paul called church leaders pillars (Galatians 2:9); here every conqueror is one.

Not architecture but presence. The image needs one clarification, because it can be read as though a person becomes masonry. The last chapters of this book say plainly that the new Jerusalem has no temple building in it, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb (21:22). So the promise is not a job in a building. To be a pillar there is to belong permanently in God’s presence: a place in what does not shake.

Never shall he go out of it. This is the clause that would have stopped the room: certainly never again (ou mē … eti). No more running into the fields at three in the morning. No more coming back to see what is left standing. Eternal security means that once Christ has brought a person into God’s presence, that person will never be put out again: whoever comes to me I will never cast out, Jesus said (John 6:37).

The name of my God. Then three names, written on him. A name marks ownership. The high priest wore the name of the LORD on his forehead, on a gold plate engraved Holy to the LORD (Exodus 28:36–38). Believers bear God’s name, as his servants (14:1; 22:4), in contrast to those who bear the beast’s mark (13:16–17). In the ancient world a slave might be branded and a soldier marked; here the mark is not degradation but belonging to God himself.

The new Jerusalem. The new Jerusalem is the city of God, the bride of the Lamb, coming down from heaven in the new creation (21:2, 10). This is citizenship, given to a congregation put out of its synagogue and told it had no home. Believers are citizens of that city (Philippians 3:20; Hebrews 12:22), whatever earthly citizenship they lose. And Philadelphia had twice taken a new civic name to flatter an emperor, and the names faded when the dynasties did; this one is written on the person, not on a milestone.

My own new name. Last and least expected. Not a name for the believer this time, but Christ’s own (19:12, 16), expressing his full revelation and victory at his return. Whatever it is, it is not yet fully disclosed; the book will say at 19:12 that he has a name written that no one knows but himself. There is more of Christ still to be revealed than has yet been revealed, and believers will share in his glory. The ones who will bear it include a handful of people with little power in a town on a fault line.

My God, four times. Read the verse again and count: the temple of my God, the name of my God, the city of my God, coming down from my God. The risen Christ cannot describe the believer’s reward without naming his Father as his own, and that is the reward. On the morning he rose he sent word to his disciples that he was ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God (John 20:17). Everything promised here belongs first to the Son and is shared with those who belong to him: his Father’s house, his Father’s name, his Father’s city, and at last his own name. The weak are made pillars in that temple because the Son has brought them into his own place there.

Is the new Jerusalem a place, or the people of God? Both, and Revelation holds them together. The city is described as the bride, the wife of the Lamb (21:9–10), so it pictures the redeemed people themselves in their final glory. But it is also the home where God dwells with his people on a renewed earth (21:1–3), a real place in a real new creation, not a cloud or a mood. To bear the city’s name now means you already belong to that people and are on your way to that home. Your citizenship is held in heaven even while your passport says something else (Philippians 3:20).

On a Tuesday. When the ground moves under you this week, a diagnosis, a redundancy, a family upheaval, remember the promise made to a city that knew earthquakes: you have a place in God’s presence that no aftershock can reach.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–22 — To the Church in Laodicea
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Laodicea was the richest town on the circuit, a banking centre known for black wool and an eye ointment, and it had rebuilt itself after the earthquake of AD 60 without Rome’s help. Christ comes as the Amen, the faithful and true witness, and the source of God’s creation (v. 14). Like its piped water, neither hot like the healing springs of Hierapolis nor cold like the water of Colossae, the church is useless, and he is about to spit it out (vv. 15–16). It says it needs nothing, not knowing that it is poor, blind and naked, and he counsels it to buy from him gold, white garments and eye salve (vv. 17–18). His rebuke is love (v. 19); he stands at the door and knocks, offering to eat with anyone who opens (v. 20), and promises the conqueror a seat with him on his throne, grounded on his own finished victory (vv. 21–22).
verseByVerse.theology:
Useless, Not Merely Lukewarm

Laodicea’s water was neither hot nor cold and good for nothing, and so was its church. Rich and self-sufficient, it did not know it was poor, blind and naked. Christ counsels it to buy from him, disciplines because he loves, and knocks at the door.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A city that refused imperial relief produced a church that said, “I need nothing.”

Now: Ask who in your town is helped because your church exists, and open the door to him.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to the angel of the church in Laodicea write: 'The words of the Amen, the faithful and true witness, the beginning of God's creation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Laodicea, about 40 miles (65 kilometres) southeast of Philadelphia, stood in the Lycus valley at the junction of three trade roads, about 10 miles (16 kilometres) from Colossae and 6 miles (10 kilometres) from Hierapolis. It was the richest town on the circuit: a banking centre, famous for a glossy black wool, and home to a medical school, which ancient writers connect with a Phrygian eye powder. When an earthquake devastated it in AD 60, it rebuilt itself from its own wealth, without help from Rome, as the historian Tacitus records, and much of this letter is written against that pride. Its weakness was water, piped in through an aqueduct. Paul mentions the church in Colossians 2:1 and 4:13–16 and asked the Colossians to share letters with it; it was probably founded by Epaphras.

The Amen. Christ introduces himself with three titles, and every one of them is a rebuke before a word of criticism is spoken. The first is a strange thing to call a person. Amēn is the Hebrew word for it is firm, it is so, the word a congregation says at the end of a prayer to put its weight behind what has been said. Isaiah 65:16 speaks of the God of truth, literally the God of Amen: the one who can be relied on absolutely. And Paul says that all the promises of God find their Yes in Christ, and that is why it is through him that we utter our Amen (2 Corinthians 1:20). To a church that will shortly be described as neither one thing nor the other, the sender identifies himself as the one who is definitively, unwaveringly what he is.

The faithful and true witness. Faithful was already his title at 1:5, and here true is added. A witness who is faithful will not lie; a witness who is true reports what is actually there. And this is being said immediately before the most unflattering assessment given to any of the seven churches, addressed to a congregation whose own opinion of itself is about to be quoted back at it. If the testimony that follows is unwelcome, the credentials of the witness have been stated in advance.

The beginning of God’s creation. The Greek is archē: origin, source, ruler, the root inside our word architect, the one from whom a thing begins. Colossians, a letter Laodicea had heard read (Colossians 4:16), says that by Christ all things were created, that he is before all things, and that he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead (Colossians 1:15–18). He is the origin and ruler of everything God made, including Laodicea’s banks, its wool and its medicine.

Where Christians differ: does this mean Christ was created? The ancient Arians (fourth-century followers of the teacher Arius), and Jehovah’s Witnesses today, read “the beginning of God’s creation” as meaning that Christ was the first being God created. This commentary’s view: the word archē can mean the beginning in the sense of the source or ruler, and that is its meaning here. Revelation gives Christ the titles of God: the first and the last (1:17), the Alpha and the Omega and the beginning and the end (22:13), worshipped with the Father (5:13). John’s Gospel says all things were made through the Word, and without him nothing was made (John 1:1–3); so he cannot himself be a made thing. Christ is the uncreated source of creation, not its first product.

The one thing with weight. So before the letter says anything at all about lukewarmness, it has set three immovable things in front of a church that has drifted: the Amen, the true witness, and the source of everything that exists. Laodicea’s problem is that nothing in its life has any weight. The remedy begins by naming the one thing that does.

How do I answer someone at my door who says this verse proves Jesus was created? Gently, and from the Bible they are holding. Show that archē means source or ruler as well as first in a series, just as we speak of the principal of a school. Then turn to the same book: the Lord God is the Alpha and the Omega in 1:8, and Jesus takes that very title, with the beginning and the end, in 22:13. If the Father is the beginning without being created, so is the Son. Add John 1:3: everything that was made was made through him, so he cannot be among the things made. Then, more important than winning, speak of why it matters: only God can save, and the one who died for us is God the Son.

On a Tuesday. When you end a prayer this week, remember that your Amen is not a full stop but your weight leaning on the one who is God’s Yes to every promise.
verseByVerse.note: Laodicea, about ten miles from Colossae, was a wealthy banking and textile city. Rebuilt without imperial aid after an earthquake in AD 60, it prided itself on needing nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: "I know your works: you are neither cold nor hot. Would that you were either cold or hot! So, because you are lukewarm, and neither hot nor cold, I will spit you out of my mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Nearby Hierapolis, six miles north, had famous hot springs, used for healing; the white terraces they left behind are visible from Laodicea across the valley. Colossae, ten miles east, is usually said to have had cold, refreshing water. Laodicea’s water was piped in from a distance, arriving tepid and full of minerals; the remains of its pipes show thick deposits of calcium carbonate. It was probably unpleasant to drink, the kind of water that makes people want to spit it out.

Neither cold nor hot. This is the verse everyone remembers and one of the most often misread, and the local geography probably explains it. Cold (psychros) and hot (zestos, boiling): the image comes from the local water, not from a scale of spiritual temperature. Hot water heals and cold water refreshes, and the two neighbouring towns were known for exactly those two services. Both are useful. Lukewarm water is useless.

Would that you were either cold or hot! Christ is not saying that it would be better to be against him (cold) than half-hearted. In the light of the water image, both cold and hot are good: either healing like Hierapolis or refreshing like Colossae. The complaint is not that the church is half-hearted on a scale from zero to ten, but that it is useless: a city with everything, supplying nothing. He would rather have anything than this, and of all the conditions in these seven letters, the one hardest to do anything with is the one doing no harm and no good.

A more searching charge. That reading is far more searching than the usual one, and much harder to escape. A congregation examining itself for lukewarmness in the popular sense asks about the temperature of its feelings, and any honest person will find some warmth somewhere and take comfort. The question this verse actually asks is different: what is your church for? Who in your town is helped because you exist? If the doors closed on Sunday and the building were sold, who outside the membership would notice, and what exactly would they miss?

Water from the spring. What Christ wants from Laodicea is what he himself has always been. He healed the sick who were brought to him at evening, and he called the weary to come to him for rest (Matthew 11:28). He promised that whoever believes in him would have rivers of living water flowing from his heart, and John explains that he meant the Spirit (John 7:37–39). A church joined to him is meant to carry that water to others: healing for the wounded and refreshment for the tired. Laodicea’s works were tepid because they were its own, drawn through a city’s pipes rather than from the spring. The cure is not to work harder at the right temperature but to go back to the source.

I will spit you out. Lukewarm (chliaros) is tepid. The verb (emesai) is to vomit, to spew. Most English versions soften it, and the softening loses the picture: this is the involuntary reaction of a body to something it cannot keep down. Nobody decides to do it. It is the reaction of a man handed a cup of Laodicean tap water. Yet the wording, literally I am about to spit (mellō, I am on the point of), leaves time for repentance (v. 19).

Where Christians differ: what do hot and cold mean? The common reading takes hot as spiritually zealous, cold as openly hostile, and lukewarm as half-hearted; on that reading Christ would prefer open hostility to half-heartedness. This commentary’s view: the local water explains the image better. Both hot and cold water are good; lukewarm water is useless and sickening. Christ does not want anyone to be cold toward him. He wants his church to be useful, either healing or refreshing, by real faith and love. Laodicea’s self-satisfied religion did no good to anyone.

What it does not mean. Being spat out does not mean that true believers lose their salvation. Christ is warning a church as a whole, much of which, like Sardis, may never have been truly converted. The response he wants is repentance (v. 19).

Am I lukewarm? One thing should be said plainly, because this verse frightens sensitive readers and hardly troubles the people it was written for, which is itself the pattern the letter describes. A Christian who reads verse 16 and is alarmed by it is, by that reaction, showing that it is probably not describing him. Lukewarmness is not a state that worries about itself. Laodicea was entirely comfortable. So the better questions are these: is my faith doing anyone any good? Does anyone find healing or refreshment because of my prayers, my words, my time, my money? Have I come to feel that I need nothing from Christ? If the honest answer troubles you, do what verse 19 says, and you will not stay lukewarm.
verseByVerse.note: Often explained from local water: hot springs at nearby Hierapolis and cold water at Colossae, while Laodicea’s piped-in water arrived tepid. Both hot and cold are useful; lukewarm is not.

verseByVerse.quote: For you say, "I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing," not realizing that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked. I counsel you to buy from me gold refined by fire, so that you may be rich, and white garments so that you may clothe yourself and the shame of your nakedness may not be seen, and salve to anoint your eyes, so that you may see.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Each part of Christ’s counsel aims at one of Laodicea’s sources of pride: its banks and gold, its famous black wool, and its eye medicine. The proud city that rebuilt without Rome’s help after the earthquake had a church with the same attitude toward God.

For you say. Christ quotes the church’s own sentence back at it, and it is the only place in the seven letters where a congregation is allowed to speak. It echoes Hosea 12:8, where Ephraim boasts that it is rich and has found wealth, and no one can find sin in it. Three clauses, and the third is the fatal one. Being rich is not a sin. Having prospered is not a sin. Needing nothing is the end of the Christian life, because the whole of it runs on asking.

The town seeps through the walls. They had grounds for the boast. Laodicea had rebuilt itself after the earthquake out of its own reserves, without an emperor’s relief. It is very hard to be a self-sufficient city for a generation without becoming a self-sufficient church, and nobody in the congregation would have felt a decision being made. Self-sufficiency may be the most respectable idol there is, because from outside it looks like good management. Its quiet creed is that I can look after myself, and the gospel offends it for the simplest of reasons: grace is only for people who admit that they cannot.

Wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked. Five words, and the first two are the diagnosis of the other three. Wretched (talaipōros) is the word Paul uses of himself in Romans 7:24. Pitiable (eleeinos) means fit to be pitied, and Laodicea, which pitied nobody and needed nothing, is the object of pity in the only court that matters. Then the three that answer the three industries: poor (ptōchos, a beggar) to the banking town, blind (typhlos) to the town with the eye clinic, naked (gymnos, shamefully exposed) to the town that clothed the empire in black wool. The richest church was spiritually a naked blind beggar.

You do not know. And the governing phrase (ouk oidas, you do not know) is the whole tragedy of the letter. Christ says, I know your works (v. 15); they do not know their own condition. Laodicea is a church that has read its own accounts and concluded that everything is fine. Smyrna was poor and rich; Laodicea is rich and poor (2:9).

I counsel you to buy from me. Then verse 18, and its tone lands before its content does. Counsel (symbouleuō) means advise. Not I command. To the church he has just threatened to spit out, Christ offers advice, as a friend, like a merchant approaching a buyer. There is even a trace of humour in it: a church in the wealthiest town on the circuit is being invited to go shopping. Buy from me echoes Isaiah 55:1, where the LORD invites those who have no money to come, buy and eat, without money and without price. They must come to Christ for what they need, admitting they have nothing to pay with.

Gold refined by fire. The bank has no money. What is offered is gold that has been through the furnace (pepyrōmenon ek pyros): purified gold, the true riches of faith tested by trials, exactly the image Peter used (1 Peter 1:7), and the treasure of Christ himself.

White garments. White, in a town whose fortune was built on glossy black. The white garments are the righteousness Christ gives (3:4–5; 19:8). In Scripture, nakedness is a picture of shame and judgement (Ezekiel 16:37), and from the first garden only God could cover it (Genesis 3:7, 21). The one thing Laodicea could not manufacture is the one thing it needed to wear.

Salve to anoint your eyes. Salve (kollourion) is eye ointment. Laodicea’s medical school is thought to have made a compound for weak eyes, sold across the province. Laodicea could sell sight to strangers and could not see itself. They need spiritual sight, which only Christ’s Spirit can give, to see their real condition and his glory (Ephesians 1:18). Whatever the remedy, it is applied by him and not compounded locally, and its first effect would be that the congregation finally reads verse 17 as a description of itself.

What the merchant paid. Each thing Christ offers he obtained at his own cost. Though he was rich, for our sake he became poor, so that by his poverty we might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). The soldiers stripped him and divided his clothes at the cross (John 19:23–24), and he hung there exposed so that sinners might be clothed. He opened the eyes of a man born blind and said that he had come so that those who do not see may see (John 9:39). The banker’s gold, the weaver’s cloth and the doctor’s salve cannot be bought in Laodicea because they are not merchandise. They are what Christ is and what he gives, and the price was paid on his side of the counter.

Three purchases, one first move. Every one of them requires the same thing: coming to him with empty hands and asking. That is what I need nothing makes impossible, and it is why this is perhaps the most dangerous condition of the seven.

How should a well-off Christian live in the light of this letter? Gratefully, generously and watchfully. Paul tells the rich not to be haughty or to set their hopes on uncertain riches, but on God, who richly provides everything to enjoy, and to be rich in good works, generous and ready to share (1 Timothy 6:17–19). In practice: give regularly and sacrificially, not just from what is left over; use your home and resources for others; keep praying daily for what you seem not to need, because you do; and watch for the moment comfort makes you feel that church, prayer or Scripture are optional. Wealth is a trust, not a verdict. The poorest believer and the richest come to Christ the same way: as beggars.

verseByVerse.quote: Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline, so be zealous and repent. Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Proverbs 3:12 says that the LORD reproves the one he loves, as a father the son in whom he delights, a verse also quoted in Hebrews 12:5–6. In the Song of Songs 5:2, the beloved knocks at the door, saying, open to me. In the ancient world, eating together was a sign of friendship and acceptance.

Those whom I love. After everything that has been said, this. The verb for love here is not the usual agapaō but philō, the warmer word for affection between friends, the word used of the Father’s love for the Son and of Jesus’ love for Lazarus (John 5:20; 11:36). To the worst church on the road, Christ uses the fondest word in the chapter. Reprove (elenchō) means expose, convict. Discipline (paideuō) means train, correct, as a parent trains a child. Christ’s harsh words are the wounds of a friend (Proverbs 27:6).

The rebuke explained. The sentence comes from Proverbs, the same text Hebrews takes up at length to explain why hard providences are not evidence of rejection (Hebrews 12:5–11). And it reverses the entire meaning of the letter’s severity. The threat to spit them out was not the sound of Christ washing his hands of Laodicea. It was the sound of him refusing to leave it alone. The rebuke came first and the declaration of love came after, and the second explains the first rather than softening it. The churches that received no rebuke were not the better loved. Indifference does not bother to correct.

So be zealous and repent. Two commands, and the first is present and continuous: keep on being zealous (zēleue, be earnest, burn with zeal), a word from the same family as the word for hot, zestos, in verse 15. To the lukewarm church, the cure for tepid is not warm. It is boiling. The second command is a single decisive act: repent (metanoēson), once, now. Neither is worked up from within; both answer the love just declared.

I stand at the door and knock. Then the best-known sentence in the seven letters, and it is almost always quoted out of position. Stand (hestēka) is I have taken my stand and remain standing; knock (krouō) is keep knocking. Christ is standing outside a church: the congregation that thinks it needs nothing, and has managed the remarkable feat of conducting its life with its Lord on the wrong side of the door. He is not far off. He is on the step, and he is knocking, which means he intends to be heard. And the church inside is in session, and busy, and has no idea.

If anyone. It is singular (ean tis, if anyone). The letter has been addressed to a congregation throughout, and at the decisive moment it narrows to one person. A whole church may be lukewarm; the door is opened by individuals. Nobody in Laodicea had to wait for a majority.

Eat with him. What he offers on the other side of the door is not a rebuke but a meal. The word (deipnēsō) is the evening meal, the unhurried one at the end of the day, not food snatched standing up but the table where a household sits and talks. In the ancient world, eating with someone was the public sign of accepting them; it is what got Jesus into trouble repeatedly (Luke 15:2), and he shared meals with his disciples after rising (Luke 24:30; John 21:12). To the church he has just called wretched, pitiable, poor, blind and naked, the offer is dinner. And he with me: the reciprocity is the last touch. Christ does not come in as an inspector who eats and leaves. He comes as a guest and stays as the host, and this book will end with a wedding supper (19:9).

Where Christians differ: an invitation to unbelievers? This verse is often used in evangelism, as Christ knocking at the door of an unbeliever’s heart, waiting to be invited in. This commentary’s view: in context it is addressed to a church, calling professing believers to repent and restore fellowship with Christ. It can rightly be applied to unbelievers, since the gospel calls everyone to turn to Christ, and many professing members of Laodicea were probably not truly converted. But the verse does not mean that Christ is helpless until a sinner decides to let him in. Scripture teaches that the dead sinner can respond only because God first gives new life (John 6:44; Ephesians 2:1–5). When Christ knocks, his voice is powerful: it opens deaf ears, and his sheep hear his voice (John 10:27). The free invitation and God’s sovereign grace stand together.

Is the hardship in my life God’s discipline? It may be, and if you belong to Christ, it is never his rejection. Discipline in Scripture is broader than punishment: it is training, the way a father shapes a son, and it can come through rebuke, through the consequences of sin, or through hardships that have no link to any particular sin (Hebrews 12:7–11). You do not need to identify the exact reason for every trial. Ask instead what God may be teaching you, confess any sin you know of, and trust that he is treating you as a beloved child. The evidence of his love is not the absence of correction but the cross, and the promise that it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness.

What does opening the door look like for a believer? Hearing his voice in his word and doing what it says. In practice: admit, in plain words to him, that you have been carrying on without him; repent of the specific things that crowded him out, whether busyness, comfort, a habit or a grudge; and make room for him again, in unhurried prayer, in reading Scripture to meet him rather than to tick a box, and in gathering at his table with his people. He has not been waiting with folded arms. He has been knocking, and he is eager to come in.

On a Tuesday. Listen for the knock this week: in the passage that unsettles you, the sermon that names your comfort, the friend who asks a hard question. And at the Lord’s Supper, remember that Christ invites himself to eat with his people.

For worship. He who stands outside the door of his church once suffered outside the gate of his city (Hebrews 13:12), shut out so that sinners could be brought in. He has borne exclusion before, and he is not put off by it now. The love that rebukes is the love that bled, and the meal he offers is already paid for: he is both the guest who asks to come in and the host who has laid the table with his own body and blood. The day is coming when the knocking will be over, and the whole household will sit down with him at the marriage supper of the Lamb.

verseByVerse.quote: The one who conquers, I will grant him to sit with me on my throne, as I also conquered and sat down with my Father on his throne. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. The final promise of the seven letters is the highest of all, and it is given to the worst church. It leads directly into chapters 4–5, where John sees God’s throne and the Lamb who conquered.

As I also conquered. Read the second half of the sentence first, because it is the ground of the first. Christ conquered (enikēsa, past tense: a finished victory), and the word is the same one used of the believer throughout these letters. He conquered by his death and resurrection (5:5–6), and then he sat down at the Father’s right hand (Hebrews 1:3; 12:2). The victory is not pending. The seat is not empty. Every promise made to the seven churches rests on a conquest that is finished and a throne that is occupied. And Christ’s throne and the Father’s throne are one (22:1, 3).

To sit with me on my throne. Then the astonishing clause. Grant (dōsō) is give: a gift, not an earned right. The conqueror is to sit with me on my throne. Not near it. Not in front of it. On it, sharing Christ’s royal rule. In the next chapter John will see that throne, with twenty-four elders casting their crowns before it, and this verse says that ordinary Christians will be seated on it with Christ. Jesus promised the Twelve that they would sit on thrones (Matthew 19:28), and believers will reign with him (2:26–27; 20:4; 22:5; 2 Timothy 2:12). Paul said the same thing in a flat sentence that most readers hurry past: God raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places (Ephesians 2:6).

What conquering has meant. Consider how the word conquer has been defined by these two chapters, because it decides who this promise is for. It has not once meant achievement. At Ephesus it meant recovering a love that had been put down. At Smyrna it meant not denying him in a cell. At Pergamum it meant refusing a dinner invitation. At Thyatira it meant holding on. At Sardis it meant keeping a garment clean when nobody was looking. At Philadelphia it meant keeping his word with very little strength. And here at Laodicea it means getting up and opening a door. The throne of the universe is promised to people whose great victory was answering a knock.

The seven promises together. The seven letters are finished, and the pattern of the promises is complete: the tree of life, escape from the second death, hidden manna and a new name, authority over the nations and the morning star, white garments and a name confessed before the Father, a pillar in the temple that never shakes, and now a seat on the throne. Every single one is given to the same people: ordinary believers in seven unremarkable towns, most of whose names nobody wrote down. And every one is, in the end, Christ himself and life with him.

Let him hear. The final call, for the seventh time, to every church since. The next words in the book are after this, and a door opens in heaven.

What it does not mean. Sharing Christ’s throne does not mean believers become gods or share his divine nature. It means they share in his reign as redeemed human beings, kings and priests under him (1:6; 5:10).

I am so weak; how can I conquer? By trusting the one who already has. The promise is grounded in his victory, not yours: I conquered. Your conquering is joined to his, the way a soldier shares the triumph of a general who has already won the war. It looks like the small things these letters have named: coming back to Christ when you have drifted, saying no to compromise, holding on, opening the door. Philadelphia had little power and received no rebuke at all. And he does not leave you to do it alone; he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6). Weakness is not disqualification. It is the place where his strength is seen (2 Corinthians 12:9).

For worship. He conquered. That is the sentence the rest of the book will spend nineteen chapters unfolding, and it is already in the past tense. The Lamb who was slain has sat down beside his Father on the throne of heaven, and there is nothing left to be won that he has not already won. The dragon is coming, and the beast, and the harlot city, and the long ranks of the martyrs, and every one of them arrives after this verse, on the far side of a finished victory. And the Victor has made room on his throne for those who answered his knock.

4.title: Holy, Holy, Holy: The Throne Room of Heaven
4.overview:
After the letters to the seven churches, John is called up through an open door in heaven and stands before the throne of God. Before any seal is opened or any judgement falls, the church is shown what governs history: this throne, this God, and the worship that surrounds him.

Chapters 4 and 5 belong together and stand at the centre of the book. Chapter 4 shows who God is: the Creator of all things, holy beyond measure, worshipped without ceasing. Chapter 5 shows how he rules and redeems: through the Lamb who was slain and has conquered. Everything that follows in Revelation comes from this room.

Some read the call Come up here (v. 1) as a picture of the church raptured before a tribulation. This commentary reads it as John’s own summons to receive the vision; the reasons, and respect for the other view, are given at the verse.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Throne Room of Heaven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John sees a door open in heaven and is summoned in the Spirit to the throne, and the first thing he sees is that it is occupied (vv. 1–2). The one seated on it is described only by light in precious stones, encircled by a rainbow, the covenant sign (v. 3). Around the throne sit twenty-four elders in white with golden crowns; from it come Sinai’s lightning and thunder; before it burn seven torches, the Spirit of God, and lies a sea like crystal (vv. 4–6a). Four living creatures, drawn from Ezekiel’s cherubim and Isaiah’s seraphim, never cease to sing Holy, holy, holy (vv. 6b–8). Whenever they give glory, the elders fall down, cast their crowns before the throne and praise God as the Creator by whose will all things exist (vv. 9–11).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Throne Comes First

Before any seal is opened, John is shown an occupied throne, ringed by a rainbow and surrounded by unceasing worship: holy, holy, holy. The Creator of all things is worthy.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Domitian liked to be called “our Lord and God”; the elders give those words to the true throne.

Now: Lay down every crown you were given before the one who gave it.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I looked, and behold, a door standing open in heaven! And the first voice, which I had heard speaking to me like a trumpet, said, "Come up here, and I will show you what must take place after this." At once I was in the Spirit, and behold, a throne stood in heaven, with one seated on the throne.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Revelation 4 takes John, and the reader, into the throne room of heaven before any judgement or beast appears. Through a door standing open in heaven John is called up to see what must happen (v. 1). At the centre is a throne, and one seated on it, shining like precious stones and encircled by an emerald rainbow (vv. 2–3). Around it sit twenty-four elders in white with golden crowns; lightning and thunder come from it; seven torches, the Spirit of God, burn before it, and before it spreads a sea like crystal (vv. 4–6a). Four living creatures, full of eyes, like a lion, an ox, a man and an eagle, never stop crying Holy, holy, holy (vv. 6b–8), and the elders cast their crowns before the throne, praising God as the Creator of all things (vv. 9–11). Before John sees anything of the world’s chaos, he sees that the universe has a centre, and it is a throne that is occupied.

The setting. The vision draws on the great throne visions of the Old Testament: Isaiah 6, where the Lord sits on a high throne and the seraphim cry Holy, holy, holy; Ezekiel 1, with its four living creatures, wheels, rainbow and crystal expanse; Daniel 7, where thrones are set and the Ancient of Days sits in judgement; and 1 Kings 22:19, where Micaiah sees the LORD on his throne with the host of heaven. For readers living under the emperor, whose court ceremonies were grand and whose subjects were expected to hail him as lord and god, this chapter declares who truly sits on the throne of the universe.

A door standing open in heaven. The letters are finished, and the view rises from the road in Asia to the room where the world is governed. “After this” (meta tauta) means after John saw these things, not necessarily after the events of chapters 2 and 3 in history. It marks a new vision, as it will again (7:1, 9; 15:5; 18:1). What follows is not the next instalment of a timetable; it is the next thing shown to him. And the door has been opened and stands open (thyra ēneōgmenē). Philadelphia was promised an open door that no one could shut (3:8); Laodicea had Christ knocking at a closed one (3:20). Now heaven’s own door stands open.

The first voice. This is the voice of the risen Christ, the one like a son of man of the first vision (1:10–13), and he has just told Laodicea that he conquered and sat down with his Father on his throne (3:21). He does not invite John into a room he has never entered. He is the forerunner who has gone ahead of his people into the presence behind the curtain (Hebrews 6:19–20), and in the next chapter John will see him standing at the very centre of this throne as a Lamb (5:6). The door stands open because the one who holds the key of David has opened it (3:7).

Come up here. John is summoned, in vision, into heaven, to see earth’s history from heaven’s point of view. “Must” (dei) is God’s sure plan, as in 1:1. Nothing that John is about to see is improvised.

At once I was in the Spirit. The second of four times the phrase marks a new stage of the book (1:10; 4:2; 17:3; 21:10). He is not describing a technique. Something is being done to him.

A throne stood in heaven. Then the sentence the whole book turns on. Nothing else is described first. Not the walls, not the light, not the attendants. A throne (thronos), and somebody on it. The word occurs about forty-seven times in Revelation, far more than in all the rest of the New Testament together, and it is the book’s central symbol: God rules. Rome’s throne, and Satan’s throne (2:13), are rivals that will fall. And its position here is deliberate. Before one seal is opened, before a single horseman rides, before the dragon appears or the beast rises out of the sea, John is shown a throne that is occupied.

With one seated on the throne. Seated (kathēmenos): God is not anxious or pacing; he sits, at rest, in sovereign control. John does not describe God himself in human form, only his radiance (v. 3), in reverent restraint. He is called, throughout the book, simply the one seated on the throne.

Where Christians differ: is John’s ascent the rapture of the church? Dispensationalists often read “Come up here” as a picture of the church raptured before the tribulation, noting that the word “church” does not appear on earth from chapter 4 until 22:16. That observation is a real feature of the text, and the reading is held by many believers who love this book. This commentary’s view: the call is to John alone, to receive a vision; nothing suggests the whole church is taken up. Ezekiel was lifted up by the Spirit in vision in much the same way (Ezekiel 8:3; 11:1). The church appears throughout chapters 4–22 under other names: servants of God (7:3), saints (13:7), those who keep God’s commandments and hold the testimony of Jesus (12:17), the bride (19:7). The saints are under the altar (6:9), sealed (7:3) and conquering by the blood of the Lamb (12:11). The word church is absent because the visions use symbolic language, not because the church has gone. There is one visible return of Christ, not a secret rapture.

Is this where believers who have died are now? In a real sense, yes. The throne room is the presence of God, and Scripture says that to be absent from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23). Revelation shows the souls of the martyrs before the throne (6:9–11) and a great multitude serving God day and night in his temple (7:15). So when a believer dies, he goes to be with Christ in this presence, conscious and at rest, awaiting the resurrection of the body and the new creation (21:1–4). The symbols are not a map, but the reality behind them is where your believing loved ones are.

How does a throne in heaven help me when my life is falling apart? It does not explain your trouble, and it was not meant to. It tells you who is in charge of it. The churches hearing this were facing prison and death, and the first thing God showed them was not a way out but a throne that was occupied. Nothing in your life is outside his rule: not the diagnosis, the betrayal, the loss, or the news. He is not pacing; he is seated. When you pray, begin there, as the Lord’s Prayer does: Our Father in heaven. The ground under you may shake. The throne does not.

On a Tuesday. John saw the throne before he saw any of the troubles, and a morning can have the same order: the one who is seated before the headlines.

verseByVerse.quote: And he who sat there had the appearance of jasper and carnelian, and around the throne was a rainbow that had the appearance of an emerald.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Ezekiel saw a rainbow-like brightness around the throne of God (Ezekiel 1:28). The rainbow first appeared after the flood, as the sign of God’s covenant never again to destroy the earth by water (Genesis 9:12–17). In the foundations of the new Jerusalem jasper is the first stone and carnelian the sixth (21:19–20), and the city has the glory of God, its radiance like jasper, clear as crystal (21:11).

Jasper and carnelian. John has been given a sight no living man has had, and when he comes to describe the one seated on the throne he describes no face, no form, no figure, no size. He gives three colours and stops, describing God only by comparison with dazzling light through gems. Jasper (iaspidi) in the ancient world was a name for various precious stones, not only the opaque stone the modern name suggests; 21:11 describes it as clear as crystal, which points to something like a diamond: brilliant, colourless, throwing light in every direction. Carnelian (sardiō) is a fiery red stone, probably named after Sardis: deep and burning, perhaps God’s blazing holiness, even his wrath. Blazing white light and blood-red fire, and no shape between them.

The first and the last of his people’s stones. The two stones may well not be chosen at random. On the high priest’s breastpiece, where the names of Israel’s tribes were carried before God, carnelian was the first of the twelve stones and jasper the last (Exodus 28:17–20). The one on the throne is bounded, as it were, by the first and the last of the stones that bore his people’s names before him, and the first and the last is exactly what Christ called himself in 1:17. The God of this throne has always carried his people on the heart of their high priest, and that high priest has now come: Jesus, who holds his priesthood permanently and always lives to intercede for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:24–25).

Why no face? Not because there was nothing to see. Scripture is consistent that no one may look on God and live (Exodus 33:20). God is light, dwelling in unapproachable light, whom no one has ever seen or can see (1 Timothy 6:16). Every prophet who came close reported the same difficulty. Ezekiel piles up qualifiers until the grammar buckles: the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD (Ezekiel 1:28). Isaiah described the train of a robe and the smoke (Isaiah 6:1–4). Even here, the two most searching words in the verse are the appearance of, and John uses them twice.

The mercy of restraint. That restraint is itself a mercy, and there is a warning inside it for anyone who wants a picture. Every attempt to draw God ends in something smaller than God, which is the reason the second commandment exists. What the vision gives instead is what light does when it strikes a stone: a description of an effect, because the cause cannot be looked at.

A rainbow like an emerald. Then the third colour, and it changes everything: emerald green (smaragdinō), encircling the throne completely, so that no one can approach from any direction without coming through it. The rainbow entered Scripture at the end of the flood, when God set his bow in the cloud and called it the sign of a covenant. The picture there is often understood as a warrior hanging up his weapon, the bow turned away from the earth: When the bow is in the clouds, I will see it and remember the everlasting covenant (Genesis 9:16). It was a promise given after judgement had fallen, to a world that deserved it and had just seen what God can do.

The order is the theology. So set the three colours together in the order John gives them. Blazing holiness. Burning judgement. And around the whole throne, without a gap, a covenant promise. The throne of judgement is surrounded by grace. A covenant, in Scripture, is a binding promise by which God pledges himself to a people and then keeps his word whatever it costs him. The rainbow says that the one on this throne has bound himself in that way, and he will not violate his covenant (Psalm 89:34). Chapters of trumpets and bowls and plagues are about to be poured out from this room, and every one of them will come out from inside a rainbow.

Will we ever see God’s face? Yes, in Christ. The last chapter of this book promises that his servants will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads (22:4). Jesus said the pure in heart will see God (Matthew 5:8), and John wrote that when Christ appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). Even now, God’s glory is seen in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6): whoever has seen him has seen the Father (John 14:9). What sinful eyes cannot bear now, glorified eyes will see with joy. That sight, theologians have long said, is the highest happiness of heaven.

Why does the rainbow matter if God is about to judge the world? Because it tells you what kind of judge he is. The rainbow does not mean there will be no judgement; Revelation is full of it. It means God’s judgements come from a throne bound by covenant faithfulness. He keeps his promises to his people even while he judges a rebellious world, and every judgement serves his purpose of rescuing and renewing. For a believer, the rainbow says: the storm you see coming out of the throne will not touch the promise around it. God has bound himself to you, in Christ, at his own initiative, and he cannot go back on it.

For worship. Holy beyond describing and terrible beyond looking at, the one on the throne has wrapped his majesty in a promise, and he has never let it slip. The covenant he made with Noah after the waters he has crowned with a better one, made in the blood of his Son (Luke 22:20), in whom every promise of God finds its Yes. So the light no eye can bear and the fire no sinner can survive are encircled on every side by faithfulness, and there is no direction from which his people come to him that does not pass through the green.

verseByVerse.quote: Around the throne were twenty-four thrones, and seated on the thrones were twenty-four elders, clothed in white garments, with golden crowns on their heads. From the throne came flashes of lightning, and rumblings and peals of thunder, and before the throne were burning seven torches of fire, which are the seven spirits of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. King David divided the temple priests into twenty-four divisions (1 Chronicles 24:3–19), and the temple musicians into twenty-four groups (1 Chronicles 25). At Sinai, God’s presence came with thunder, lightning and a thick cloud (Exodus 19:16). Daniel saw thrones set in place around the Ancient of Days (Daniel 7:9).

Twenty-four elders. Elders (presbyterous): they sit on thrones, so they share in God’s rule. They wear white, so they are pure. They wear golden crowns (stephanous, victors’ wreaths), so they have conquered.

Where Christians differ: who are the twenty-four elders? Some see them as an order of angels, a heavenly council around God (Psalm 89:7), since they appear alongside the living creatures and are distinguished from the redeemed multitude of 7:9. Others see them as representing the whole people of God, Old Testament and New: the twelve tribes of Israel and the twelve apostles. A third reading notes that David divided the priests into twenty-four courses, so that twenty-four could stand for the whole priesthood. This commentary’s view: the second view is the most likely. The new Jerusalem bears the names of the twelve tribes on its gates and the twelve apostles on its foundations (21:12–14), a clear twelve plus twelve. The elders receive what the seven letters promise to conquering believers: white robes, crowns and thrones. They represent the one people of God, redeemed from both covenants, already worshipping in heaven. The church on earth is represented before the throne.

White garments and golden crowns. White garments: exactly what was promised to the conquerors at Sardis (3:5). Golden crowns: the victor’s wreath promised at Smyrna (2:10). Thrones of their own: the promise made to Laodicea at the end of the letters (3:21). Every reward held out to the seven churches is already visible in the throne room, being worn, before the first seal is opened. Each was promised in Christ’s own voice, and each rests on what he did: the robes are white because they were washed in his blood (7:14), and the thrones are shared because he conquered and sat down on his (3:21). The promises are not aspirations. They are furniture.

Lightning and thunder. This is Sinai. When God came down on the mountain there were thunders and lightnings and a thick cloud and a very loud trumpet blast, and the people trembled (Exodus 19:16–19). The same sequence of lightning, rumblings and thunder appears at the climax of each series of judgements (8:5; 11:19; 16:18), each time intensified, linking them to this throne: God is about to act.

Not a quiet room. Whatever the peace of heaven is, it is not the peace of a library; there is a storm coming out of the middle of the room. It is the peace of people standing perfectly still in the presence of something that could level a mountain.

Sinai with a mediator. Hebrews sets this same thunder beside the gospel. Believers have not come to a mountain burning with fire, darkness and storm, where even Moses said that he trembled with fear; they have come to the city of the living God, to innumerable angels, to the assembly of the firstborn, to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood (Hebrews 12:18–24). The thunder has not been turned down. What has changed is who stands between it and the people. At Sinai the people were kept at the foot of the mountain; in this room the elders sit on thrones within reach of the lightning, because a mediator has come.

Seven torches of fire. John interprets the symbol himself, as he did at 1:20, and the sevenfold Spirit has already been named at 1:4 and 3:1. Zechariah’s lampstand stands behind the image again (Zechariah 4:2–6): the Holy Spirit in his fullness. Fire speaks of holiness, light and purifying power. And see where the Spirit is: before the throne, ready to be sent out into all the earth (5:6). The Spirit at work in seven struggling congregations on a road in Asia is the Spirit blazing in front of the throne of God, and he is not two Spirits.

If lightning comes from the throne, how can I approach it with confidence? Through the High Priest who sits at its right hand. Hebrews says that because we have a great high priest who sympathises with our weakness, we may draw near to the throne of grace with confidence, to receive mercy and find grace in time of need (Hebrews 4:14–16). The lightning is real: God is holy, and no sinner can stand before him on his own merits. But the elders sit there in white, near the storm, unafraid, because their robes have been washed in the blood of the Lamb (7:14). You come the same way. Not cautiously hoping to be tolerated, but welcomed for Christ’s sake.

For worship. The God who thunders from the throne has filled the seats around it with forgiven sinners, and he did it without turning the storm down. The holiness that kept a nation at the foot of a mountain was satisfied on a hill outside Jerusalem, and those for whom it was satisfied now sit in white within reach of the throne, at peace. And the fire that blazes before him is not kept there. The risen Christ has poured out that Spirit on his people (Acts 2:33), so that the weakest believer carries in his heart a flame from the throne room of God.
verseByVerse.note: Twenty-four may combine the twelve tribes and the twelve apostles — the whole people of God.

verseByVerse.quote: and before the throne there was as it were a sea of glass, like crystal. And around the throne, on each side of the throne, are four living creatures, full of eyes in front and behind: the first living creature like a lion, the second living creature like an ox, the third living creature with the face of a man, and the fourth living creature like an eagle in flight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. In Ezekiel 1:5–22, four living creatures, each with four faces (man, lion, ox and eagle), carry God’s throne-chariot, with wheels full of eyes, beneath an expanse like awesome crystal; Ezekiel later identifies them as cherubim (Ezekiel 10:20). In Isaiah 6:2, seraphim with six wings stand above God’s throne.

A sea of glass. Two qualifiers in a few words, as it were and like, and they are the marks of a man describing something for which no word exists. A floor before the throne, flat and shining and utterly still. The sea of glass (thalassa hyalinē) would have struck the first hearers, because ancient glass was usually cloudy, so glass as clear as crystal was rare and precious.

What stands behind the sea. Several things stand behind the image. When the elders of Israel went up Sinai and saw the God of Israel, there was under his feet as it were a pavement of sapphire stone, like the very heaven for clearness (Exodus 24:10), the same doubled hesitation. In Solomon’s temple a huge bronze basin called the Sea stood in the courtyard for washing before the priests could serve; the way to God always ran past water. And in the ancient imagination the sea was chaos itself, restless and dangerous and full of what could not be tamed, which is why the beast will come up out of it in chapter 13, and why the new creation is announced with the words and the sea was no more (21:1).

The chaos is a floor. Here the sea is glass. Still, transparent, with the light going straight through it. Whatever threatens the church in the chapters ahead is in this room already, and it lies still at his feet. In 15:2, the conquerors stand beside the sea of glass mingled with fire, like Israel beside the Red Sea after the exodus, singing.

Four living creatures. Living creatures (zōa, living beings) are not beasts; that is a different word, thēria, used for the evil beasts of chapter 13. They are high angelic beings, combining features of Ezekiel’s cherubim and Isaiah’s seraphim: John’s creatures have Ezekiel’s faces and Isaiah’s wings and song. They are nearest of all, nearer than the elders. Four is the number of the earth (four corners, four winds, 7:1). They seem to represent the whole of creation, worshipping its Creator.

Full of eyes. Eyes speak of ceaseless watchfulness and knowledge: nothing escapes their sight, nor God’s.

Lion, ox, man and eagle. Each represents the highest of a kind of creature: the lion, the noblest of wild animals; the ox, the strongest of domestic animals; man, the wisest of all; the eagle, the swiftest of birds. Ancient rabbis said much the same. Together they show all creation, at its best, worshipping God. In Ezekiel each creature had all four faces; here each has one.

Adoration, not administration. The nearest beings to the throne of God are not administrators. They are worshippers covered in eyes, whose entire function is to see and to say what they see. Nearness to God does not produce mere activity; it produces adoration. That is the direction the whole book is travelling, and the church is being shown its destination before it is shown its road.

In the flow. These four creatures do not stay in the background of the book. In the next chapter they fall before the Lamb and say the Amen to the song of all creation (5:8, 14). When the first four seals are broken, it is one of them each time who calls Come, and a horseman rides out (6:1–7); later one of them hands the seven angels the bowls of God’s wrath (15:7). The beings who never stop praising God’s holiness are the ones who summon his judgements on the earth. Praise and judgement come out of the same room because both come from the same holy God.

The cherubim and the Lamb. These are cherubim, and Israel knew where cherubim belonged. Two of them were beaten out of gold on the lid of the ark, wings spread over the mercy seat, facing the place where the high priest sprinkled blood once a year (Exodus 25:18–22; Hebrews 9:5). Paul uses hilastērion, the Greek Old Testament’s word for that lid, when he says that God put Christ forward as a propitiation by his blood (Romans 3:25). A propitiation is an offering that satisfies God’s just anger at sin, because the one offered takes that anger on himself in the sinner’s place (1 John 4:10). So it is fitting that in the next chapter the Lamb stands between the throne and these four creatures, and that they fall down before him (5:6, 8). The beings whose images guarded the place of atonement for centuries bow before the one whose blood made atonement.

What it does not mean. The four creatures were later linked by church tradition with the four Gospels. Irenaeus first made the link in the second century; the pairing that stuck (Matthew the man, Mark the lion, Luke the ox, John the eagle) is Jerome’s. It is a memorable devotional association, but it is not what the text means. The creatures represent creation worshipping God. The instinct behind the tradition is sound, all the same: creation and the gospel both come from this room.

Does all creation really worship God? Yes, in its own way. The heavens declare the glory of God (Psalm 19:1), and the psalmist calls sea creatures, fire, hail, mountains, trees, beasts and birds to praise the LORD (Psalm 148:7–10). They do it by being what he made them to be, displaying his wisdom and power. In the next chapter every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea joins the song (5:13). Creation now groans under the curse, waiting for the freedom of God’s children (Romans 8:19–22), but it was made for praise and will be renewed for it. When you look at a hawk or a field of cattle, you are looking at worshippers. Humans are the ones who were made to put that praise into words.

For worship. The sea that terrified the ancient world lies before his throne as still as glass, and once, on a night in Galilee, the same stillness came down on a real sea at the word of a man who had been asleep in the boat. Who then is this, his disciples asked, that even the wind and the sea obey him (Mark 4:41)? This room is the answer. The fiercest, the strongest, the wisest and the swiftest of God’s creatures stand nearest his glory, covered in eyes, and they have never seen anything in him that made them want to stop praising; and the one who said Peace, be still shares the throne they surround.

verseByVerse.quote: And the four living creatures, each of them with six wings, are full of eyes all around and within, and day and night they never cease to say, "Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. In Isaiah 6:2–3, the seraphim, each with six wings, cover their faces and feet and call to one another: Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory. Isaiah, seeing it, cried out, Woe is me! For I am lost. He heard it in the year King Uzziah died, at the end of a reign of some fifty years that had given his lifetime its stability (Isaiah 6:1).

Six wings. Six wings, like the seraphim: two to cover their faces, in reverence; two to cover their feet, in humility; two to fly, in service (Isaiah 6:2). And they are full of eyes all around and within: ceaseless awareness of God and of all his works, seeing everything, inside and out.

They never cease. Literally they have no rest (anapausin ouk echousin). Their worship is ceaseless because God’s holiness is inexhaustible. In contrast, those who worship the beast have no rest day or night in torment (14:11). The same phrase describes the two destinies of creatures: endless joy in worshipping God, or endless restlessness in refusing him.

Holy, holy, holy. Isaiah heard this song some eight hundred years earlier. It is the same three words, and the fact that they have not changed in eight centuries, or in the centuries since, is part of the point. Holy is hagios, in Hebrew qadosh: set apart, utterly other, pure. Hebrew often intensifies a word by repeating it, and three times is the superlative: holy beyond all measure. And there is only one attribute of God that Scripture ever trebles like this. Nobody sings loving, loving, loving or mighty, mighty, mighty. God is love and God is almighty and both are said plainly, but the word said three times before the throne, day and night, without ceasing, is holy. Christians have long seen in the threefold Holy a hint of the Trinity, Father, Son and Spirit, though the main point is God’s infinite holiness.

What holiness means. Holy is a word about distance before it is a moral word. God is not a larger version of us, not the best example of anything on our scale; he is in a category with one member, and because he is wholly other, he is wholly pure. Teachers such as R. C. Sproul spent a lifetime on this one word, and rightly: get it wrong and every other doctrine sags, because sin stops being an outrage and grace stops being a miracle.

Whose glory Isaiah saw. John’s Gospel adds a sentence that changes how this song is heard. After quoting Isaiah, John says that Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him (John 12:41), and the him is Jesus. The Lord high and lifted up in the year Uzziah died, before whom the seraphim cried holy, is the one whose glory John saw full of grace and truth (John 1:14). The holiness the seraphim could not look at is not a holiness Christ merely reports from a distance; it is his own, the glory he had with the Father before the world existed (John 17:5).

The Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come. Almighty (pantokratōr, ruler of all) is the title of 1:8. And the three tenses are those of 1:4, 8, with the order changed. There it was who is and who was and who is to come, beginning with the present. Here it begins with the past. Seen from the throne room rather than from a struggling church in Asia, the titles run in the ordinary order of time, past, present and future: God’s eternity, and his coming to judge and renew. And the middle term is the one being sung over: he is.

Is God vain to want endless praise? No, and the question deserves a straight answer. First, praise is not something God lacks and needs topping up. He was not lonely or unadmired before there was a universe; Father, Son and Spirit have delighted in one another from eternity, and nothing was made to fill a gap. Second, praise is what happens when anything true is seen clearly. Nobody watching a sunrise over water has to be commanded to say something; the praise is not a tax levied on the viewer but the completion of the seeing. To ask people who are looking at God to stop praising him would be to ask them to look at him and not notice. What is happening in this room is not flattery. It is accuracy. And it is for our good: we were made to find our joy in him.

Won’t heaven be boring if it is endless worship? Not if worship is what this chapter shows. Boredom is what happens when a thing is exhausted, when you have seen all there is and the eye has nowhere further to go. The creatures nearest the throne are covered in eyes, have been looking without pause, day and night, and have not yet come to the end of the first word. It is not that they must keep saying it. It is that they cannot stop. Worship in heaven is not a never-ending church service as we know it; it is the whole of life, work, fellowship and joy, lived in the open presence of the God who is infinitely worth knowing (22:3–5). The only way it could bore us would be for God to be smaller than he is.

On a Tuesday. When you next confess your sin, start where Isaiah started, with God’s holiness, and you will find your sin is more serious and his grace more astonishing than you had thought.

verseByVerse.quote: And whenever the living creatures give glory and honor and thanks to him who is seated on the throne, who lives forever and ever, the twenty-four elders fall down before him who is seated on the throne and worship him who lives forever and ever. They cast their crowns before the throne, saying, "Worthy are you, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. When a king was defeated or became a client of Rome, he might lay his crown before the conqueror as a sign of submission; the historian Tacitus describes Tiridates of Armenia taking the royal diadem from his head and laying it at the foot of the emperor Nero’s statue.

Whenever the living creatures give glory. The chapter ends with a movement, and it is one of the most eloquent gestures in the book. Glory (doxan), honour (timēn), thanks (eucharistian): creation praises God for who he is and gives thanks for what he has done. And the word whenever makes it a pattern rather than a single event. Every time the creatures begin, the elders go down.

Who lives forever and ever. In contrast to emperors who live and die. If John wrote, as most scholars think, about AD 95 (some, preterist interpreters especially, date the book before AD 70), Domitian was dead within a year or two of this book, murdered in his own palace in AD 96. The one on this throne has no successor.

The elders fall down. Two things happen: they fall, and they throw. Worship (proskynēsousin, prostrate themselves) involves the body, and falling is what people do in the presence of God: Ezekiel, Daniel, John himself in chapter 1.

They cast their crowns before the throne. Throwing the crown is different. That is a decision about what to do with a reward. These crowns were given. Nobody in that room manufactured one. They are the victor’s wreaths promised to the conquerors of Smyrna and Philadelphia, handed over by Christ himself, and the elders will not keep them on in front of the throne. Whatever honour God gives his people, they give back to him. Their victory was his.

Worthy are you, our Lord and God. Worthy (axios) means deserving. The word is said to have been used in acclaiming the emperor at his arrival. Only God is worthy. And a first-century hearer would have flinched at the next phrase. Our Lord and God (ho kyrios kai ho theos hēmōn) was precisely the title Domitian liked to hear, as the Roman historian Suetonius reports (dominus et deus noster). The congregations hearing this letter were under pressure to say those words to a man in Rome. John gives them the same words to say, and a different throne.

For you created all things. The ground of the worthiness is stated: by your will (dia to thelēma sou). God is worthy of worship because he is the Creator. Not merely because he is strong, and not merely because he will win, but because everything that exists does so at his pleasure and would stop existing if he stopped willing it. And take the order seriously: they existed comes before and were created. Perhaps they existed in his purpose and then came into being; or they exist now because they were created. Either way, the intention preceded the act. Nothing in the universe is an accident or an afterthought, including the small congregation in Thyatira and the person reading this sentence.

Through whom all things were made. The elders sing to the Creator, and the New Testament names the one through whom the creating was done. All things were made through the Word, and without him was not any thing made that was made (John 1:3); by the Son all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions (Colossians 1:16). The Creator praised here did not make the world without his Son. So the one who takes the scroll in the next chapter is the one through whom the world was made. The one who made all things is the one who comes forward to redeem them.

A song deliberately incomplete. That is where chapter 4 stops, and it is deliberately incomplete. The song here is about creation, and creation alone is not enough to save anybody; the world he made is the world in rebellion against him. In the next chapter a scroll will appear that nobody in heaven or earth is able to open, and John will weep. The answer to that will be a new song, and the new song will not be about creation but about redemption, sung to the Lamb who was slain.

What crowns do I have to cast down now? Anything you are tempted to wear as though you earned it. There is a very practical question in the elders’ gesture for anybody who has ever done anything well. What are you holding that was given to you and is being worn as though it were your own achievement? A capacity, a competence, an upbringing, a marriage, a body that still works, thirty years of faithful service in a church, a ministry others admire. None of it was self-generated (1 Corinthians 4:7). Cast it down by thanking God for it specifically, by using it for others rather than for your reputation, and by refusing to compare yourself with those who seem to have less. What is worn in this life is thrown down in the next, and the sooner a person starts throwing, the less it will cost him at the end.

If God made everything by his will, where did evil come from? Not from God’s creating. Everything he made was very good (Genesis 1:31). Evil entered through the rebellion of creatures, angelic and human, who turned from him (Genesis 3; Jude 6). God is not the author of sin, yet nothing escapes his sovereign rule, and he governs even evil for his good purposes, as he did supremely at the cross (Acts 2:23; 4:27–28). Scripture does not explain everything about this, and we should not pretend it does. But it shows us what God has done about evil: the Creator entered his creation to bear its curse, and the next chapter shows him on the throne as the Lamb who was slain.

On a Tuesday. When you are asked this week, in whatever form, to give to someone or something else the loyalty that belongs to God alone, say the elders’ words under your breath: our Lord and God. There is only one throne that title belongs to.

And the first voice, which I had heard speaking to me like a trumpet, said, “Come up here, and I will show you what must take place after this.”<sup>2</sup>At once I was in the Spirit, and behold, a throne stood in heaven, with one seated on the throne.<sup>3</sup>And he who sat there had the appearance of jasper and carnelian, and around the throne was a rainbow that had the appearance of an emerald.<sup>4</sup>Around the throne were twenty-four thrones, and seated on the thrones were twenty-four elders, clothed in white garments, with golden crowns on their heads.<sup>5</sup>From the throne came flashes of lightning, and rumblings and peals of thunder, and before the throne were burning seven torches of fire, which are the seven spirits of God,<sup>6</sup>and before the throne there was as it were a sea of glass, like crystal. And around the throne, on each side of the throne, are four living creatures, full of eyes in front and behind:<sup>7</sup>the first living creature like a lion, the second living creature like an ox, the third living creature with the face of a man, and the fourth living creature like an eagle in flight.<sup>8</sup>And the four living creatures, each of them with six wings, are full of eyes all around and within, and day and night they never cease to say, “Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!”<sup>9</sup>And whenever the living creatures give glory and honor and thanks to him who is seated on the throne, who lives forever and ever,<sup>10</sup>the twenty-four elders fall down before him who is seated on the throne and worship him who lives forever and ever. 5.title: The Scroll and the Lamb
5.overview:
Chapter 5 moves from crisis to worship. A scroll sealed with seven seals lies in the hand of the one on the throne, and no one anywhere is worthy to open it, so John weeps. Then an elder announces that the Lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered, and when John looks, he sees a Lamb standing as though it had been slain.

The scroll holds God’s plan to judge evil and redeem his creation, and opening it means carrying that plan out; the seals, trumpets and bowls that follow are the Lamb opening it.

The Lion who is the Lamb is the heart of the chapter. Christ conquered by dying: the one with the right to open history is the one who gave himself as its sacrifice. The crucified one reigns, and heaven and earth worship him with the Father.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Scroll and the Lamb
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A scroll written on both sides and sealed with seven seals is held in God’s right hand, and a mighty angel asks who is worthy to open it (vv. 1–2). No one in heaven, on earth or under the earth is found worthy, and John weeps loudly (vv. 3–4). An elder stops his tears with an announcement: the Lion of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered (v. 5). John looks and sees a Lamb standing as though slain, with seven horns and seven eyes, and the Lamb takes the scroll (vv. 6–7). The living creatures and elders fall before him with the prayers of the saints and sing a new song: he is worthy because by his blood he ransomed people for God from every nation and made them a kingdom and priests (vv. 8–10). Myriads of angels join in (vv. 11–12), and at last every creature praises the one on the throne and the Lamb together (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lion Is the Lamb

No one is worthy to open the sealed scroll of God’s purpose until the Lion of Judah is announced, and John sees a Lamb standing, as though slain. He takes the scroll, and heaven and earth worship him who ransomed a people by his blood.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: John wept at a world with no resolution; his tears were answered by a person, not an argument.

Now: No prayer offered in faith is lost; the prayers of the saints are held in golden bowls before the throne.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw in the right hand of him who was seated on the throne a scroll written within and on the back, sealed with seven seals. And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming with a loud voice, "Who is worthy to open the scroll and break its seals?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Revelation 5 continues the throne-room vision of chapter 4 and introduces the Lamb. In God’s right hand is a scroll sealed with seven seals, and a mighty angel asks who is worthy to open it (vv. 1–2). No one in all creation is able, and John weeps (vv. 3–4). An elder tells him to stop: the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered and can open it (v. 5). John looks and sees not a lion but a Lamb standing as though it had been slain, and the Lamb takes the scroll (vv. 6–7). The living creatures and elders sing a new song: the Lamb is worthy, because by his blood he ransomed people for God from every tribe, language, people and nation and made them a kingdom and priests (vv. 8–10). Countless angels join in (vv. 11–12), and finally every creature praises the one on the throne and the Lamb together (vv. 13–14). Only the crucified and risen Christ, who conquered by dying, can carry God’s plan for history to its end.

The setting. In the ancient world important documents such as wills, contracts and title deeds were written on scrolls, rolled up and sealed. Under Roman law a will was commonly sealed by seven witnesses, each with his own seal, and after the testator’s death it was opened formally, once the seals had been checked. A sealed book was also a familiar prophetic picture. Ezekiel was handed a scroll written on the front and the back, full of lamentation and mourning and woe (Ezekiel 2:9–10). Daniel was told to shut up the words and seal the book until the time of the end (Daniel 12:4, 9). John’s vision is built out of both.

A scroll in his right hand. John is still in the throne room, still looking at the Creator before whom the elders have just cast their crowns, and the whole chapter turns on what he now notices in that hand. The right hand is the hand of power, authority and action in Scripture: your right hand, O LORD, shatters the enemy (Exodus 15:6). The scroll (biblion) is not lying on a table in the corner of heaven waiting to be consulted. It is held, gripped, in the hand of the God who made all things.

Written within and on the back. Ancient scrolls were normally written on one side only, because the papyrus fibres on the reverse ran the wrong way and caught the pen. A document written on both sides, what scholars call an opisthograph, was unusual, and here it pictures contents that are complete, with no room for anything further. Nothing can be added to this plan. God is not drafting history as he goes, waiting to see how things turn out before he writes the next chapter. It is written, front and back, to the edges.

Sealed with seven seals. Sealed up tight (katesphragismenon). The seals do not mean the plan is uncertain. They mean it is closed: it exists, it is finished, it is in God’s hand, and it is shut. In the vision the plan of God for the world is complete, and yet nothing in it moves until someone worthy opens it.

And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming with a loud voice, Who is worthy to open the scroll and break its seals? The verb for proclaiming is the herald’s word, and the voice is loud enough to reach, as the next verse shows, heaven and earth and under the earth. This is a summons to the entire creation, and it asks one question.
