Which question is asked. Not who is strong enough, and not who is clever enough. Who is worthy? The word (axios) means deserving, qualified. The issue is not capability but standing. Anyone can break a seal; a seal is wax. What the moment requires is somebody with the right to break it: the future of the world waits not on power but on the moral qualification of a person. Heaven’s herald is asking for someone whose worth can bear the weight of the world’s future, and when the answer comes it will be a Lamb, worthy because he was slain (5:9).

What is the scroll? Many suggestions have been made: the Old Testament, the book of life, a title deed to the world waiting for its heir, a last will and testament with the inheritance of the saints. The text itself only shows what happens when it is opened, and what happens is the sweep of history from the cross to the new creation. The best answer is that it contains God’s plan to judge evil and redeem his creation, his purpose for history from the cross to the end. Opening it means not only revealing that plan but carrying it out. As the seals are broken in chapter 6, events happen on earth.

Is the scroll the same as the book of life? Probably not, though they are related. The book of life (3:5; 13:8; 20:12) is the register of those who belong to the Lamb, and it is never described as sealed. This scroll is the unfolding of God’s purpose in history, judgement and salvation together. But the two are bound up with each other, because the purpose that the scroll carries out is the bringing home of every name written in that other book. The plan of history and the list of the redeemed are in the same hands.

verseByVerse.quote: And no one in heaven or on earth or under the earth was able to open the scroll or to look into it, and I began to weep loudly because no one was found worthy to open the scroll or to look into it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one in heaven or on earth or under the earth. The three-tier phrase is the ancient way of saying everywhere: heaven, with its angels and powers; earth, with the living; and under the earth, the realm of the dead. It is a complete search of the universe, and it returns nothing.

Able to open the scroll. Consider who was in the room while that search was conducted. Twenty-four elders. Four living creatures who have never taken their eyes off God. Presently, myriads of myriads of angels. Not one of them was worthy. On earth, the whole roll of human greatness, every philosopher, reformer, general and king, and not one. And under the earth, the dead, including every saint who had died in faith. Abraham was not worthy. Moses was not worthy. David, the sweet psalmist of Israel, was not worthy. Not even to look inside. That is hard news for anyone hoping that a good record will be enough to stand before God: if Abraham and David could not be found worthy, neither can we. It is also the best news there is, because the worthiness heaven required was never going to be ours. It was going to be our Saviour’s.

I began to weep loudly. The verb (eklaion) is emphatic and continuous: John did not become quietly emotional; he broke down and sobbed, and the tense suggests he kept on doing it until somebody stopped him. These are the only tears shed in the throne room anywhere in this book, and two chapters from the end God himself will wipe away every tear from every eye (21:4).

Why so extreme a reaction? Because John has grasped what the closed scroll means. If nobody opens it, the plan stays shut. The martyrs under the altar are never answered (6:10). Rome goes on for ever. The seven churches keep meeting in borrowed rooms until they die out one by one, and nothing in the sealed purposes of God ever comes to anything. An unopened scroll is a world with no resolution: evil never judged, suffering never ended, God’s promises never fulfilled, the persecuted church never vindicated, and history simply running down like a clock nobody winds. His tears are the right response to a world without a redeemer.

No one was found worthy. All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23). The search fails, not because the universe is short of strength, but because it is short of righteousness.

The one the search could not find. The failed search describes the redeemer before he appears. He must belong to the race that fell, or he cannot stand in for it; so the Son had to be made like his brothers in every respect (Hebrews 2:17). He must be without sin, or he needs redeeming himself; so he was tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). And he must have a worth no creature has; so he is the Word who was with God and was God, and who became flesh (John 1:1, 14). Every one of those requirements is met in one person, and in no other. No angel and no saint could be found worthy, because the only one who was is not merely a creature.

That grief is not exotic. Any honest believer has felt a version of it. It is what settles on a person reading the news for the fortieth year and noticing that the same things keep happening. It is what a woman feels standing in a cemetery in a country where nobody was ever tried for what was done. It is the specific despair of suspecting that the world is not going anywhere: that there is no scroll, or that if there is one, it will never be opened.

What John does not do. He does not tell himself that it will probably work out. He does not console himself with the throne he has just seen, though the throne is still there in front of him. He weeps, in heaven, in the presence of God, and Scripture records it without embarrassment and without rebuking him. And the weeping is answered, but not by an argument. Nobody in the following verse tells John he was overreacting.

If the plan was always going to be carried out, why make John weep at all? Because God wants us to know what the answer is worth. A rescue is only understood by someone who has looked at the drop. If John had seen the Lamb first, he would have admired him; having seen the empty universe first, he worships him. The same is true for us. The gospel is not meant to be received as pleasant extra information by people who were managing quite well. It is meant to land on people who have seen, for one honest moment, that without Christ there is no one, anywhere, who can put the world right, or put them right.

Is it wrong for me to feel this despair? No. To feel the weight of a world that has not been put right is to see it truly, and Scripture is full of believers who cried out how long (Psalm 13:1; Habakkuk 1:2; Revelation 6:10). What would be wrong is to stay there as though the elder had never spoken. Weep, and then listen. The Christian is not the person who never feels the darkness, but the person who has been told who walked into it.

verseByVerse.quote: And one of the elders said to me, "Weep no more; behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so that he can open the scroll and its seven seals."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Two great messianic titles from the Old Testament stand behind this verse. Dying Jacob calls Judah a lion’s cub and says the sceptre shall not depart from Judah until tribute comes to him, and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples (Genesis 49:9–10). Isaiah promises a shoot from the stump of Jesse, David’s father, on whom the Spirit of the LORD would rest, who would judge the poor with righteousness and strike the earth with the rod of his mouth; the root of Jesse would stand as a signal for the peoples (Isaiah 11:1–4, 10). Some Jewish writings of the time used both images for a warrior Messiah who would destroy Israel’s enemies.

Weep no more. Literally stop weeping (mē klaie). Not you were wrong to weep. Not compose yourself. The tears are not criticised; they are ended, and they are ended by an announcement about a person, not by advice. That is the shape of every real Christian comfort. Nobody is talked out of grief by being told that things are not so bad. Grief stops when somebody walks into the room.

The Lion of the tribe of Judah. The lion (leōn) is royal, powerful and conquering. Jesus was born of the tribe of Judah (Hebrews 7:14), the tribe of kings, and he is the King promised to Judah on Jacob’s deathbed nearly two thousand years before. Between them these two titles carry the whole hope of Israel: the royal lion, and the living root of a dynasty that had been cut down to a stump.

The Root of David. The word is rhiza, root. Not only David’s descendant but David’s root, his source (22:16). Jesus once asked the Pharisees how, if David calls the Messiah Lord, he can be his son (Matthew 22:41–45). Here is the answer: he is both David’s offspring and David’s Lord, the branch that grew from the family tree and the root from which the whole tree drew its life. A stump looks dead. This root was never dead.

Has conquered. The verb is enikēsen, the same word that ends every one of the seven letters as a promise to the one who conquers (2:7, 11, 17, 26; 3:5, 12, 21). Whatever the churches of Asia are being asked to do, he has already done. The tense is past: not he is conquering, not he will conquer, but he conquered, and the matter is closed. Christ conquered first, and his people conquer through him, by his blood (3:21; 12:11).

So that he can open the scroll. He can open the scroll because he has conquered. The right to unroll the purposes of God was not given to him as a courtesy of rank. It was won. Somewhere in history a battle was fought, and the outcome of it is the reason anything at all is about to happen in this book.

Conquered whom, and when? Christ conquered sin, death and Satan at the cross and in his resurrection. At the cross he disarmed the rulers and authorities and triumphed over them (Colossians 2:15); through death he destroyed the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil (Hebrews 2:14); and he rose as the firstborn of the dead (1:5). The battle that decides history is not still to be fought at the end of the age. It was fought outside Jerusalem around AD 30, and everything in Revelation from here on is the outworking of a victory already won.

If Christ has already conquered, why is the world still so dark? Because a war can be decided before it is over. The decisive battle has been won, the enemy’s doom is sealed, and the remaining fighting is real but cannot change the outcome. That is exactly what the rest of this book shows: seals, trumpets and bowls of real suffering, a dragon who is furious because he knows that his time is short (12:12), and through it all the Lamb holding the scroll. The darkness is not a sign that the victory failed. It is the last struggle of an enemy who has already lost.

On a Tuesday. When grief over the world or over your own life comes, do not wait for an argument to make it lift. Turn to Christ and say his titles to him: Lion of Judah, Root of David, the one who has conquered. The one who won the war is the one opening the scroll of your days.

For worship. The King promised to Judah on a deathbed in Egypt grew up before God like a root out of dry ground, with no beauty that anyone desired (Isaiah 53:2), and the house of David looked finished. Then he was cut off out of the land of the living (Isaiah 53:8), and on the third day he rose, and the stump of Jesse had a living King again. The Lion of Judah is the Lord of David, and his victory needs no sequel. John’s tears stopped at his name, and every tear on earth will stop at his face (21:4).

verseByVerse.quote: And between the throne and the four living creatures and among the elders I saw a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain, with seven horns and with seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth. And he went and took the scroll from the right hand of him who was seated on the throne.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. The Passover lamb was killed and its blood put on the doorposts, so that the LORD passed over Israel when he judged Egypt (Exodus 12). Isaiah describes the Servant of the LORD led like a lamb to the slaughter, bearing the sin of many (Isaiah 53:7, 12). John the Baptist pointed to Jesus as the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29). In Jewish apocalyptic writing a horned ram sometimes represented a conquering leader (Daniel 8:3; 1 Enoch 90). Zechariah speaks of the seven eyes of the LORD, which range through the whole earth (Zechariah 4:10).

I saw a Lamb. He was told a Lion. He sees a Lamb. That single substitution is a key to the whole book, and everything that follows must be read through it. Revelation will go on speaking the language of conquest, warfare, thrones and armies for seventeen more chapters, and this verse has just defined what every one of those words means. The Lion conquers as a Lamb. Power has been redefined by sacrifice. In plain terms: Christ did not win by crushing his enemies but by dying for his people, and the cross, which looked like his defeat, was the very act that disarmed sin, death and the devil (Colossians 2:15; Hebrews 2:14). This is the heart of Revelation, and of the gospel.

The Lamb’s name. The word John uses is arnion. It is not the term amnos used of Christ elsewhere (John 1:29; Acts 8:32); arnion is diminutive in form, though by John’s day it usually meant simply a lamb. John uses it twenty-eight times of Christ in this book, and it becomes his main name for him. In the most violent, cosmic, thunderous book in the Bible, the name of the conqueror is the plain word for a young sheep.

At the centre. See where he stands: between the throne and the four living creatures, among the elders. That is the very centre of heaven. The Lamb does not appear on the edge of the throne room as a guest or petitioner. He is in the middle, and later John will speak of the Lamb in the midst of the throne (7:17) and of the throne of God and of the Lamb (22:1). He shares God’s throne.

Standing, as though it had been slain. Two impossible things in one clause. “Standing” (hestēkos) is alive, risen, upright. And the word behind slain is esphagmenon, from a verb used for cutting a sacrificial animal’s throat: butchered, not merely killed. It is a perfect participle, a past action whose result is still in force: the wounds are not a memory. This Lamb is standing, which is resurrection and life, and is at the same time visibly, permanently, a slaughtered animal.

The marks are the credential. It is the centre of the Christian faith rendered as a picture. The one thing that will never be erased from the new creation is the evidence of what it cost. When Thomas needed proof, the risen Christ did not produce a restored body but a scarred one: put out your hand, and place it in my side (John 20:27). Heaven’s throne room is not a place where the crucifixion has been tidied away and forgotten. His death is not a past event he has moved beyond; it is the permanent ground of his authority and of our salvation, and the whole company falls down in front of it.

Does Jesus still suffer in heaven? No. The perfect tense means the effect of his death remains, not that the dying goes on. Christ died once for all (Hebrews 9:26–28; Romans 6:9–10), and his sacrifice is finished (John 19:30). He is standing, not lying on an altar. The marks are like the scar on a soldier who has come home: they are no longer pain, they are proof. And this is why the Lord’s Supper is a remembrance and not a repetition. We do not offer Christ again; we feed on a sacrifice that was completed, and whose marks he carries into eternity.

With seven horns. A horn in the Old Testament is strength (Deuteronomy 33:17; Psalm 18:2), the weapon of a strong animal and the emblem of a king. Seven of them is complete power. The Lamb is not weak. All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him (Matthew 28:18).

Seven eyes. Seven eyes is complete knowledge, seeing everything; the phrase is quarried from Zechariah, where the seven eyes of the LORD range through the whole earth (Zechariah 4:10). The seven spirits are the Holy Spirit in his fullness (1:4). And see whose eyes they are: the Spirit is the Spirit of the Lamb, sent out by him into all the earth (John 15:26; 16:7; Acts 2:33). The Lamb is all-powerful, all-knowing, and present everywhere by his Spirit: fully God. The picture is deliberately impossible to draw. It is meant to be believed.

He took the scroll. The sentence is flat, almost domestic, and the room has been holding its breath for six verses. “Took” (eilēphen) is perfect tense again, a decisive act with lasting result. Nobody stops him. He walks up and takes it, and the reaching out of that hand is the moment the future of the world is unlocked. It echoes Daniel 7:13–14, where one like a son of man comes to the Ancient of Days and is given dominion and glory and a kingdom. The Lamb receives authority to carry out God’s whole plan for history.

What it does not mean. The Lamb’s gentleness does not cancel his justice; the same book speaks of the wrath of the Lamb (6:16). Revelation’s Christ is the slain Lamb who conquers, and the conquering Lamb who was slain.

Why does the Lamb take the scroll from the Father, rather than having it already? Because the picture is of the Son receiving, as the risen Messiah, the authority he won. As God the Son he shares the Father’s rule eternally. As the incarnate Son who obeyed to the point of death, he is given the name above every name (Philippians 2:8–11) and all authority in heaven and on earth (Matthew 28:18). There is no rivalry here. The Father gives and the Son takes, in perfect agreement, and the plan of the Father is carried out by the hand of the Son.

So is the Lamb a picture of how Christians should live? Yes, and that is one of the most practical things in the book. The Lamb’s way of victory, through sacrifice, truth-telling and faithful suffering rather than force, is the way he calls his people to walk. The saints conquer the accuser by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death (12:11). That does not make Christians doormats, and it does not forbid lawful government its sword (Romans 13:4). It means the church never advances Christ’s kingdom by coercion, manipulation or worldly power, and that faithfulness which looks like losing is often how the Lamb wins.

On a Tuesday. In the meeting where you could win by bending the truth, in the family argument where you could crush by being cleverer, in the moment when you are wronged and could get even, ask what the Lamb would look like here. His seven eyes, the Spirit sent out into all the earth, go with you. It will often look like losing. So did the cross. And where you fail, he walked this way perfectly in your place, and his blood answers for the rest.
verseByVerse.note: The Lion of v. 5 turns out to be a slain Lamb. Horns stand for power and eyes for knowledge.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had taken the scroll, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb, each holding a harp, and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints. And they sang a new song, saying, "Worthy are you to take the scroll and to open its seals, for you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation, and you have made them a kingdom and priests to our God, and they shall reign on the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Harps, or lyres, were used in temple worship (1 Chronicles 25:1; Psalm 33:2). Incense was burned twice a day on the golden altar in front of the veil, and its smoke was a picture of prayer rising to God: let my prayer be counted as incense before you (Psalm 141:2). The Psalms and prophets often call for a new song, celebrating a new act of salvation (Psalm 96:1; 98:1; Isaiah 42:10).

They fell down before the Lamb. The response to the taking of the scroll is immediate and total. The same posture given to the one on the throne in chapter 4 (4:10) is given here to the Lamb, without a word of explanation and without anyone objecting. And in this book angels twice refuse worship outright, telling John to worship God (19:10; 22:8–9). No creature may receive it. The Lamb receives it in the presence of God the Father, and the room approves: Jesus is God.

Golden bowls of incense. They are holding two things. The harp is for the song about to be sung. “Saints” (hagiōn, holy ones) means all believers, not a special class of the especially devout. The prayers of ordinary Christians are in golden bowls in the throne room of the universe, held by the highest beings in creation, at the moment the scroll is opened.

None of them evaporated. Take that as concretely as it is meant. Every desperate prayer prayed by a believer in Smyrna the night before a hearing. Every prayer of a slave in Laodicea that nobody else in the household knew about. Every muttered, distracted, badly worded prayer said by anyone reading this at the kitchen table before work: the ones that felt as though they hit the ceiling and slid down the wall. None of them evaporated. They were collected. They are in golden bowls, and the bowls are full, and an elder is holding them in front of the throne.

And some of it was explosive. There is more in the picture. At 8:3–5 those same prayers, mixed with incense, are offered on the golden altar, and then fire from the altar is thrown onto the earth, and there are peals of thunder, lightning and an earthquake. The persecuted church’s cries for justice (6:10) are heard, and prayers that seemed to accomplish nothing come down again as the opening act of God’s judgement on the world that ignored them. Nothing prayed in faith is wasted, and some of it turns out to have been explosive.

What about prayers that were never answered? Two things are true together. First, God does not always give what we ask, because he is wiser than our requests; Paul asked three times for his thorn to be removed and was given grace instead (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). Second, no prayer of faith is lost. It is kept before God and woven into his purposes in ways we often cannot see in this life. A mother who prayed for thirty years for a son who was converted after her funeral did not pray in vain; her prayers were in the bowl the whole time. Keep asking. The bowls are not yet full, and nothing put into them is thrown away.

Does this mean the elders pray for us, or that we should pray to saints in heaven? No. The elders present the prayers; they do not produce them or receive them as the ones prayed to. The prayers are the saints’ own prayers, offered to God. Scripture nowhere invites believers to address their prayers to departed saints or angels, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). Pray directly to the Father, through the Son, by the Spirit. What this verse adds is not a new channel for prayer but an assurance about where every prayer arrives.

A new song. New (kainēn) in kind, not merely recent: a new act of redemption, greater than the exodus, calls for a new song. Chapter 4 ended with a song about creation. This one has a different subject.

For you were slain. There is the answer to the herald’s question in verse 2: who is worthy? You are. The ground of the worthiness is not his power, though he has seven horns, nor his knowledge, though he has seven eyes. It is his death. Heaven’s argument for the Lamb is a wound.

By your blood you ransomed people. “Ransomed” (ēgorasas) is the ordinary word for buying in the market, used also of buying slaves: here, to buy a person out of ownership by paying the price. The price is named in the same clause. This is substitutionary atonement. Substitutionary means in our place: the penalty our sins deserved fell on him instead of on us (Isaiah 53:5–6; 1 Peter 2:24), and atonement means the making right of what sin had broken between us and God. Christ paid the price that set us free. You were bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:20), ransomed not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Peter 1:18–19).

From every tribe. Four terms, the number of the whole earth. John uses this fourfold phrase some seven times in this book, each time in a slightly different order, as if to stop anyone turning it into a fixed list. The church is gloriously multinational, and this fulfils God’s promise to Abraham that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3). Nobody is outside the reach of it. And nobody is ransomed as a nation or a category: the purchase is of people, out of every group there is.

A kingdom and priests. The same phrase as 1:6, and both are lifted from Sinai (Exodus 19:6). The tense matters: you have made, already done, not pending. A kingdom means they belong to the King and share his rule. Priests means they have direct access to God and serve him in worship, intercession and witness. What Israel was called to be at Sinai, the ransomed of every nation now are in Christ.

They shall reign on the earth. The redeemed share in Christ’s rule, and their rule is on the earth: the renewed earth of the new creation (21:1; 22:5). Whatever a reader concludes about the thousand years of 20:1–6, the destination of the redeemed in this book is not an escape from the material world into a spiritual one. Salvation is not escape from creation but the renewal of it.

Where Christians differ: did Christ die for every person, or for his people? Many Christians hold that Christ died equally for every person, making salvation possible for all, so that it becomes actual when people believe; they hold it from a deep conviction that God loves the whole world (John 3:16; 1 John 2:2), and they are brothers and sisters in the same gospel. This commentary’s view: the song says that Christ’s blood actually ransomed people for God, not that it made a ransom possible. And it ransomed people from every tribe, language, people and nation, not every person in every nation. This is definite atonement: Christ died with the intention of actually saving those the Father gave him (John 10:11, 15; Ephesians 5:25), and his death secures their salvation. Its value is infinite, sufficient for all, and the gospel is to be offered freely to everyone. But its design is to save a people chosen from every nation, and it does not fail.

Can I then tell anyone that Christ died for them? You can tell every person, without hesitation, that Christ died for sinners, that he is able and willing to save all who come to him, and that whoever believes in him will not perish (John 3:16; 6:37). That is the gospel the apostles preached, and it is a sincere offer, because the sacrifice is of infinite worth and the invitation is God’s own. What definite atonement adds is not a limit on the offer but a certainty about the result: the Lamb’s blood did not merely make salvation available and then wait to see who would take it. It bought a people, and the Spirit will bring every one of them home. That is why missionaries can go to the hardest places with confidence.

Is a faith that sings about blood not primitive? It can sound so to modern ears, but the song is not celebrating violence. Blood in Scripture stands for a life given up in death (Leviticus 17:11). To sing that the Lamb ransomed people by his blood is to sing that he gave his own life to set others free, the very opposite of the strong crushing the weak. Every culture honours the soldier who dies for his comrades or the father who runs back into the burning house. The cross is that, raised to its height: the innocent Son of God giving himself for the guilty, so that their real debt is really paid. What would be primitive is a god who shrugged at evil, or one who made someone else pay for it against his will. This God pays himself, in his Son, freely.

Textual note. Some manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “redeemed us” and “made us kings and priests, and we shall reign”, making the elders sing about themselves. The best manuscripts read “ransomed people” (or simply ransomed for God from every tribe) and “made them … they shall reign”. Some manuscripts also read they reign (present tense) rather than they shall reign. Both are true: believers reign now with Christ in a hidden way (1:6), and will reign fully in the new creation.

What it does not mean. Reigning on the earth does not mean, in this commentary’s amillennial reading, a future thousand-year political reign before the final state, though premillennial brothers expect one. Revelation’s closing picture places the reign of the saints in the new creation, and so the promise is fulfilled in the new heaven and new earth, where God’s servants will reign for ever and ever (22:5).

How do I reign now, when my life feels so small? Not by holding office or winning arguments, but by belonging to the King and sharing his victory. You reign when sin no longer has dominion over you (Romans 6:14), when you pray and heaven’s purposes move, when you refuse to be ruled by fear, money or the opinion of others, and when you suffer faithfully rather than giving in. The reign is hidden now, as Christ’s own reign was hidden on the cross, but it is real; and one day it will be revealed on a renewed earth. The widow praying in a care home is not less a royal priest than the preacher on a platform.

On a Tuesday. Look around your church on Sunday. If there are people there whose language, background or skin is not yours, you are looking at what the Lamb bought. Make a point of learning one of their names, and praying for one place in the world where the gospel has not yet reached a tribe or language.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I looked, and I heard around the throne and the living creatures and the elders the voice of many angels, numbering myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands, saying with a loud voice, "Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Daniel describes the Ancient of Days with a thousand thousands serving him and ten thousand times ten thousand standing before him (Daniel 7:10). At Jesus’ birth, a multitude of the heavenly host appeared with the shepherds, praising God (Luke 2:13–14).

The voice of many angels. The circle of worship widens: first the living creatures and elders, now countless angels. The singing has been going on out there the whole time John was weeping.

Myriads of myriads. A myriad (myrias) is ten thousand, the largest number Greek had a single word for. Ten thousand times ten thousand is a hundred million, but myriads of myriads is not a count; it is the language running out. Daniel used much the same expression of the throne of the Ancient of Days, and John has been quarrying Daniel 7 since chapter 1. The point is not arithmetic. It is that the ring of worshippers extends beyond the range of counting.

Worthy is the Lamb who was slain. The angels speak of the Lamb rather than to him. Perhaps that is because he did not die for them, though they join in praising what he did. And there is something the angels are doing here that they cannot do in the fullest sense. The song of verse 9 is sung by those ransomed by his blood; the angels in verse 12 sing about a redemption they have watched but not received. Peter writes that the angels long to look into the sufferings of Christ and the glories that follow them (1 Peter 1:11–12). Whatever the honour of an unfallen angel, it does not include being bought. The forgiven sinner in the back row of an ordinary congregation has a line in this song that Gabriel cannot sing.

Two songs, one throne. Set the two songs side by side, because the difference between them is the gospel. In chapter 4 the elders sang worthy are you, our Lord and God, and the ground was creation: you created all things (4:11). Here the angels sing worthy is the Lamb, and the ground is the cross: he was slain. Two songs, one throne, and the second could not have been sung by anyone before Calvary.

Seven gifts. Seven qualities, the complete set. In Greek a single article governs all seven, joining them as one whole. Everything there is to give is given, and it is given to a slaughtered lamb.

Every currency of Rome. The seven are every currency the Roman world traded in, everything that kings and emperors claimed. A congregation that had been shut out of the guilds, fined, boycotted and in some places killed is being told where all seven actually belong. And wealth is in the list. The one who though he was rich, yet for your sake became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9), who was laid in a borrowed tomb, is worthy of all the riches of the universe.

Why do the angels worship, if Christ did not die for them? Because they love God’s glory, and in the cross they have seen it more clearly than in anything else. Through the church the manifold wisdom of God is made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places (Ephesians 3:10). The angels watched the Son of God make worlds; they watched him leave heaven, sleep in a manger, pray in anguish in Gethsemane and die. They had never seen holiness and love meet like that. Their worship is a rebuke to any believer who finds the cross dull. If beings who were never lost cannot stop singing about it, how much more should those who were.

On a Tuesday. When you sit down in a small church on a wet Sunday with a thin congregation and an out-of-tune piano, remember that you are not the whole choir. You are joining a song that has been going on around the throne beyond counting, and your voice is wanted in it.

For worship. Every one of the seven was refused him once. He had nowhere to lay his head (Matthew 8:20). His wisdom was called madness, his power hung helpless on a beam, and the only honour men paid him was a robe of mockery and a reed for a sceptre. His glory was hidden in darkness at noon, and in place of blessing he heard the taunts of those who passed by (Matthew 27:39). Now ten thousand times ten thousand voices give all seven back at once, and they give them to the Lamb precisely because he was slain. Nothing in heaven is worth more than the one earth thought worthless.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea, and all that is in them, saying, "To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and might forever and ever!" And the four living creatures said, "Amen!" and the elders fell down and worshiped.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Paul says that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:10–11).

Every creature. The circle widens one last time, and this time it takes in everything that exists (pan ktisma): the same three regions searched in verse 3, with the sea added. There, the search found nobody worthy; here, the whole of it is singing. What began with a silence that made a man weep ends with every created thing, the living, the dead, the powers above, and whatever is in the deep, making one sound. John sees ahead to the end, when all creation acknowledges God and the Lamb.

To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb. The climax: one doxology, two recipients, no distinction between them. Chapter 4 praised God as Creator; chapter 5 has praised the Lamb as Redeemer; now both are worshipped together in a single sentence, in exactly the same words, and nobody in the room regards that as a problem. The doctrine of the Trinity is not argued anywhere in Revelation. It is simply what worship in heaven looks like. This is the clearest picture in the book of the Son’s full equality with the Father.

Blessing first. Four attributes here rather than seven, and the first of them is blessing, which is not something a creature can add to God. To bless God is to speak well of him, to say back to him what he is. That is the last thing all creation does in this vision, and it is the only thing it can do that God has not already got.

Amen. So be it, it is true. The beings nearest the throne, who have been singing holy, holy, holy without pause, do not add anything; they agree. Then the elders fall down and worship. The worship ends where it began, with the living creatures and elders, and the last movement in the chapter is a silence: twenty-four figures on their faces with their crowns already on the floor.

Look back at where this chapter started. A sealed scroll, a challenge nobody could answer, and a man weeping loudly in the middle of heaven because it looked as though the world would never be put right. By verse 14 the same man is listening to every creature in existence say the same thing at once. Nothing changed in between except that a Lamb walked forward and took a scroll.

Where Christians differ: will every creature be saved? Universalists, some of them sincerely longing for God’s mercy to reach everyone, read this verse, with Philippians 2:10–11, as meaning that all creatures, including those now in rebellion, will finally be reconciled and saved. This commentary’s view: universal acknowledgement is not universal salvation. Revelation clearly teaches that some will be thrown into the lake of fire for ever (14:9–11; 20:10, 15; 21:8). Every creature will confess that God and the Lamb are worthy; for the redeemed it is joyful worship, and for the lost it is the forced admission of a truth they rejected. God’s glory will be acknowledged everywhere, in mercy and in justice.

What it does not mean. Worshipping the Lamb with the Father does not mean there are two Gods. Revelation is strictly monotheistic. The Father and the Son share one throne (22:1, 3) and receive one worship.

How can creatures in the sea and under the earth praise God? In the way the heavens declare the glory of God (Psalm 19:1) and the trees of the field clap their hands (Isaiah 55:12): by being what God made them to be, under his rule, and showing his glory. John sees the whole created order brought into harmony with its Maker, the creation that now groans (Romans 8:19–22) set free and giving voice to praise. For rational creatures it is conscious praise; for the rest of creation it is the praise of a world put right. Nothing God made is left out of the song.

What comes next. The seven seals are about to be broken, and the four horsemen are behind the first four of them. Conquest, war, famine and death are coming, and after them the souls under the altar and the sky rolling up like a scroll. Every one of those seals is opened by the Lamb’s own hand. Whatever rides out of this scroll rides at the word of the Lamb who was slain, and it goes no further than he permits. That is the comfort a reader must carry into chapter 6.

For worship. The sound at the end of this chapter is the sound the world was made for. Sea and sky and the dark places under the earth, which have groaned together under the curse, find their voice, and the first word they say is blessing. They say it to the Father and to the Son in one breath, because the Son has done what the Father sent him to do, making peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20). The silence that once made a man weep in heaven has become a single chord, and it is held for ever.

5.text: <sup>1</sup>Then I saw in the right hand of him who was seated on the throne a scroll written within and on the back, sealed with seven seals.<sup>2</sup>And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming with a loud voice, “Who is worthy to open the scroll and break its seals?”<sup>3</sup>And no one in heaven or on earth or under the earth was able to open the scroll or to look into it,<sup>4</sup>and I began to weep loudly because no one was found worthy to open the scroll or to look into it.<sup>5</sup>And one of the elders said to me, “Weep no more; behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so that he can open the scroll and its seven seals.”<sup>6</sup>And between the throne and the four living creatures and among the elders I saw a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain, with seven horns and with seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth.<sup>7</sup>And he went and took the scroll from the right hand of him who was seated on the throne.<sup>8</sup>And when he had taken the scroll, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb, each holding a harp, and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints.<sup>9</sup>And they sang a new song, saying, “Worthy are you to take the scroll and to open its seals, for you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation,<sup>10</sup>and you have made them a kingdom and priests to our God, and they shall reign on the earth.”<sup>11</sup>Then I looked, and I heard around the throne and the living creatures and the elders the voice of many angels, numbering myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands,<sup>12</sup>saying with a loud voice, “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing!”<sup>13</sup>And I heard every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea, and all that is in them, saying, “To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and might forever and ever!”<sup>14</sup>And the four living creatures said, “Amen!” and the elders fell down and worshiped.

6.title: The Opening of the Seals
6.overview:
The Lamb begins to open the seven seals. The first four release the four horsemen: conquest, war, famine and death. The fifth shows the souls of the martyrs under the heavenly altar, crying “How long?” The sixth shakes the whole created order, and the people of the earth hide from the face of God and the wrath of the Lamb. The seventh seal, with its silence in heaven, is held back until chapter 8.

Reading the seals. Some read the seals, trumpets and bowls as three successive series of future events; this commentary reads them as parallel passes over the same stretch of history, each ending at the last day. The main reason is that the sixth seal already brings the great day of wrath (vv. 12–17), and yet the book goes on. The other view is noted with respect at the verses.

So the horsemen are not four events in a future timeline only. They are the troubles that have marked a fallen world in every age, ridden out under the Lamb’s hand and within his limits. And the martyrs’ question, How long?, is one the church has asked since Abel’s blood cried from the ground.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–8: four horsemen ride out at the Lamb’s word. The white horse brings conquest, the red horse takes peace from the earth so that people kill one another, the black horse brings famine prices while the oil and wine are spared, and the pale horse is Death, with Hades following, given authority over a fourth of the earth. Each is given or permitted what it does.

Verses 9–11: under the altar the martyrs cry How long?, and are given white robes and told to rest until the number of their fellow servants is complete.

Verses 12–17: the sixth seal moves every fixed point in creation, and everyone from kings to slaves hides from the face of God and the wrath of the Lamb. The chapter ends on a question: who can stand?
verseByVerse.theology:
The Seals in the Lamb’s Hand

Conquest, war, famine and death ride out only when the Lamb opens the seals, and every one of them is given or permitted within a limit. The martyrs cry “How long?” and are robed and told to rest; the sixth seal removes every fixed point but the throne.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The churches met the red horse and the pale one without being told why.

Now: Crying out for justice is not unbelief; handing vengeance to God is obedience. And who can stand? Those washed in the Lamb’s blood.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I watched when the Lamb opened one of the seven seals, and I heard one of the four living creatures say with a voice like thunder, "Come!" And I looked, and behold, a white horse! And its rider had a bow, and a crown was given to him, and he came out conquering, and to conquer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Revelation 6 shows the Lamb opening the first six seals of the scroll, and what happens on earth as he does. At the summons of the four living creatures four horsemen ride out: a white horse whose rider conquers, a red horse that takes peace from the earth, a black horse bringing famine and high prices, and a pale horse named Death, followed by Hades, killing a quarter of the earth (vv. 1–8). At the fifth seal the souls of martyrs under the altar cry out, How long?, and are given white robes and told to wait until the number of their fellow martyrs is complete (vv. 9–11). At the sixth, the universe comes apart, and everyone from kings to slaves begs the mountains to hide them from the face of God and the wrath of the Lamb, for the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand (vv. 12–17)? The wars, famines and deaths of history are not out of control: they are released by the Lamb, limited by God, and leading to the final day of judgement.

The setting. Zechariah saw horses of different colours, red, black, white and dappled, sent out to patrol the earth (Zechariah 1:8–11; 6:1–8). Jesus, in his teaching about the end, spoke of wars and rumours of wars, nation against nation, famines and earthquakes as the beginning of the birth pains, followed by persecution, and then the sun darkened, the moon not giving its light, and the stars falling from heaven (Matthew 24:6–29; Luke 21:9–26). The seals follow the same order. In the first century Rome feared the Parthians, an empire to the east whose mounted archers had defeated Roman armies and who were famous for their skill with the bow.

The Lamb opens a seal. History begins to move, and three things about the mechanics of this chapter govern how everything after it is read. First, who is doing it. Every horror in this chapter is released by the hand that was pierced, and the reader who has just watched chapter 5 knows exactly whose hand that is. The disasters are not outside his control; they are part of his plan.

Come! Second, the summons. The word is a command to the horseman, calling him out. One of the beings nearest the throne speaks, and the horseman comes. Heaven speaks first; earth responds. The living creatures represent creation in its fullness, and they summon the judgements that must come before creation is set free and renewed.

Third, the grammar. Watch for the passive verbs through the next seven verses: a crown was given, the rider was permitted, he was given a great sword, they were given authority. Four times. “Was given” (edothē) is a phrase that recurs through Revelation for God’s permission. Even evil powers act only as God allows. Nothing here takes itself.

How the seals fit the rest of the book. The seals are the first of three sevens, followed by trumpets (8–11) and bowls (15–16), and how a reader relates them shapes the whole book. On the reading followed in this commentary, held in various forms by Augustine, William Hendriksen, G. K. Beale and the amillennial tradition generally (amillennial: the view that the thousand years of chapter 20 picture the present age between Christ’s two comings), the three series are not one long timeline but parallel passes over the same stretch of history, each running from the cross to the last day, each more intense than the last. What favours it is that all three series end at the same place: the sixth seal brings the sky rolling up and the kings hiding (6:12–17); the seventh trumpet announces that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord (11:15); the seventh bowl is followed by a voice saying It is done (16:17). Futurist readers, such as John Walvoord, take the sevens as consecutive events in a future tribulation, many of them within a premillennial or dispensational scheme; preterist readers see much of the book fulfilled in the first century, in the fall of Jerusalem and the persecuting empire. These are faithful Christians reading the same Bible with the same reverence, and each reading guards something true. The point of this chapter is the same either way: whatever these riders are, the Lamb sends them.

A white horse. The bow was the weapon of the Parthian cavalry who haunted Rome’s eastern frontier. The crown (stephanos) is the victor’s wreath, not a king’s diadem. And it was given to him: even the conqueror rides on a permission.

Conquering, and to conquer. Military conquest, invasion, empire-building. He is not content with one victory; he rides out to win the next one too. Every empire in history has had this horseman at its head.

Where Christians differ: who is the rider on the white horse? Some, from the early church onward, identify him with Christ, since Christ rides a white horse in 19:11, and they read the first seal as the gospel going out and conquering; white is the colour of holiness elsewhere in the book, and the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations (Mark 13:10). Others see him as the antichrist or false messiahs, imitating Christ. Others take him as military conquest in general. This commentary’s view: the rider is conquering war, aggression and empire, like the other three horsemen, who all bring disaster. The four belong together as a set of judgements, following Jesus’ teaching (wars, then famines and death). Christ in chapter 19 has many crowns and a sword from his mouth, not a bow; and Christ is the one opening the seals, not one released by them. The white colour may suggest a deceptive imitation of Christ, as conquerors always promise peace and glory, or the white horses of victorious generals.

Textual note. Some manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “Come and see”, as if the living creature were speaking to John. The best manuscripts read simply “Come!”, addressed to the horseman.

What it does not mean. The four horsemen are not one-time future events only. They describe what happens throughout the age between Christ’s comings, and they were as real in John’s day as they are in ours. Nor does God’s permission make him the author of human evil: he limits it, uses it and will judge it.

Should I try to match the horsemen to current events? No. Every generation has done it, and every generation that named this war or that dictator as the fulfilment has been wrong, because the seals are not a coded timetable of one decade but a description of the whole age. That is a relief, not a disappointment. It means you do not need to decode the news to understand it. When armies invade, you already know three things: this was foretold, it is under the Lamb’s authority, and it is not the end of the story. Read the newspaper with Revelation 6 open, not to calculate dates, but to remember whose hand is on the seal.

Why would a loving God release such things at all? Because the world is in rebellion against him, and judgement on sin is part of his goodness, not an exception to it. A God who let evil run on for ever unchecked and unpunished would not be loving. But see how these first judgements work: they are partial, limited and early, and their purpose is stated plainly later: they did not repent (9:20–21). They are warnings loud enough to be heard, given while there is still time to turn. The God who sends the horsemen is the same God who, in the previous chapter, sent his Son to die for people from every nation.

For worship. The first thing heaven wants the suffering church to know about the troubles of history is the identity of the one who opens them. Not chance, not Caesar, not the devil: the Lamb who was slain. Every crown the conquerors wear was given, and can be taken back. The kingdoms rise and fall, and the Lamb is not shaken, because he holds the scroll by right of the blood he shed (5:9).
verseByVerse.note: The four horsemen draw on Zechariah’s visions. Some take the white rider to be Christ (compare 19:11); many see him as conquest, the first of four judgments.

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature say, "Come!" And out came another horse, bright red. Its rider was permitted to take peace from the earth, so that people should slay one another, and he was given a great sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. In John’s day the empire boasted of the Pax Romana, the peace of Rome, kept by its legions. Yet the first century saw civil war in AD 68–69, the year of the four emperors, the Jewish war that destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70, and endless bloodshed on the frontiers.

Bright red. Fiery red, the colour of fire and blood, and its association is unmistakable in a chapter about slaughter. What follows conquest is not peace.

To take peace from the earth. Two things in that clause. The rider does not bring war; he takes peace away, which assumes that peace was there and was a gift. Ordinary quiet, a town where the shops open, a night without sirens, children walking to school, is not the natural state of things that occasionally breaks down. It is a mercy being extended, and it can be withdrawn.

The peace the rider cannot reach. One peace is missing from this rider’s list. In the upper room, with soldiers already on their way, Jesus told his disciples that he was leaving them his own peace, not as the world gives (John 14:27), and within hours he went to the cross to make it. Paul says that he himself is our peace, having broken down the dividing wall of hostility (Ephesians 2:14). The red horse can take away the peace of streets and nations. It cannot touch peace with God, because that peace was not made on earth by treaty but by the Lamb, and it is kept in heaven, where no horse rides.

On a leash. The permission comes twice in this verse, and the whole vision turns on it. Nothing here is out of control. That is a hard comfort rather than an easy one, and it should be given as it stands: Scripture does not say that God is doing his best against forces he cannot restrain. It says that even the horse of war rides on a permission, and therefore on a leash.

Slay one another. Then the specific horror. The Greek is reciprocal, one another, mutual killing. This is civil war, the neighbour with the knife, the country that turns on itself. And the twentieth century, which by most estimates killed more people in war and massacre than any century before it, did much of its killing exactly that way: not chiefly invaders against defenders but citizens against their own, in Rwanda, in Cambodia, in the Soviet countryside, in the Balkans. The verb for slay is the same one used for the Lamb who was slain (5:6). Human sin, released and allowed to run, destroys itself, and it does to people what it did to the Son of God.

A great sword. The word means the short blade a Roman soldier actually carried for close combat, and the word used for the sword of the state’s authority in Romans 13:4. It is not the long broadsword of the battlefield charge. It is the instrument of ordinary official violence, and here it has been handed to a horseman whose only business is that men should kill each other.

If God permits this, is he responsible for it? Scripture holds two things together without flinching and refuses to release either. God is never the author of evil, and no man who takes up a sword can plead that heaven made him do it. And nothing happens outside God’s governance, including this. Joseph said both in one sentence about the worst thing his brothers ever did: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). The brothers were guilty. God was not idle. Both clauses stand (the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, both at 5.4).

Why the difference matters. A believer watching the news from a war can believe one of two things. Either the world has slipped its moorings and God is somewhere off-stage hoping for the best, in which case there is nothing to pray for and no reason to expect an end. Or the red horse rides on a permission granted in the throne room by a Lamb with the marks still on him. The second is far harder to look at, and it is the only one with any hope in it.

Does this mean Christians may never serve as soldiers? No. The sword here is wielded for slaughter, but Scripture also says the governing authority does not bear the sword in vain and is God’s servant to punish wrongdoing (Romans 13:4). John the Baptist told soldiers to be honest and content, not to leave the army (Luke 3:14), and the first Gentile convert was a centurion (Acts 10). The historic Reformed view is that Christians may lawfully wage war upon just and necessary occasions (Westminster 23.2; 1689 24.2). Many Christians in good conscience hold otherwise, and should be honoured. What this verse forbids is not the defence of the innocent but the lust for blood, and it warns that even just wars are fought in a world where the red horse rides.

On a Tuesday. You already hold the peace the rider cannot reach, so be a peacemaker (Matthew 5:9) in the small wars nearest you, at home, at work and in church, where the sin that fuels the red horse works on a smaller scale, and point people to the Prince of Peace.

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature say, "Come!" And I looked, and behold, a black horse! And its rider had a pair of scales in his hand. And I heard what seemed to be a voice in the midst of the four living creatures, saying, "A quart of wheat for a denarius, and three quarts of barley for a denarius, and do not harm the oil and wine!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. A denarius was a day’s wage for a labourer (Matthew 20:2). A quart (a choinix, about a litre) of wheat was roughly one person’s daily ration. Normally a denarius would buy eight to sixteen times as much. Around AD 92, during a grain shortage, the emperor Domitian ordered that no new vines be planted in Italy and that half the vineyards in the provinces be cut down to grow more grain; protest, especially from Asia, led him to drop the order.

A black horse! War has ridden through; now comes what always follows an army. Fields trampled, men conscripted off the land, granaries emptied, roads unsafe for carts. Famine is not usually a separate disaster. It is the second half of a war. Black is the colour of mourning, hunger and death; Lamentations speaks of faces blacker than soot and skin hot as an oven with the burning heat of famine (Lamentations 4:8; 5:10).

A pair of scales. The scales are the point. Grain sold by weight rather than by the sackful is grain being rationed, and the prophets used exactly this image: when I break your supply of bread, ten women shall bake your bread in a single oven and shall dole out your bread again by weight (Leviticus 26:26); they shall eat bread by weight and with anxiety (Ezekiel 4:16). A man watching his food weighed out in front of him knows precisely how bad things have become.

A voice in the midst. It comes from the very centre of heaven, the place where the Lamb was standing a chapter earlier, between the throne and the four living creatures (5:6). Whether the voice is the Lamb’s or the Father’s, it comes from where he stands, and it draws the limit of the famine. The one who measures out this hunger is the one who had compassion on a crowd because they had nothing to eat (Mark 8:2), and who taught his disciples to ask for bread one day at a time (Matthew 6:11). Famine in this world does not happen behind his back. The boundary around it was drawn in the throne room.

A quart of wheat for a denarius. Famine prices: roughly ten times the normal cost. Do the arithmetic the way a first-century hearer would have done it instantly. A man works from dawn to dusk and earns enough to feed himself, and nothing for his wife or his children. If he switches to barley, coarse and cheap, the food of the poor and of animals, he gets three days’ worth, and the family eats badly and is still hungry. This is not a picture of mass starvation with bodies in the street. It is something more familiar and more grinding: a working man in full employment who cannot feed his household, and who knows there is nothing further he can do about it.

Do not harm the oil and wine! Olive trees and vines have deep roots and survive drought better than grain. The judgement is limited: severe, but not total. It is a warning, not yet the end.

The cellar and the street. But there is also irony in the line. Oil and wine were the produce of estates rather than smallholdings, the goods of the comfortable. What the prohibition describes is the specific injustice of every food crisis in history: the price of bread soars and the luxury trade goes on undisturbed. The rich man’s cellar is untouched while a labourer counts out grain by weight in the street outside. Famines are rarely a simple absence of food; they are ordinarily a failure of access, and the people who die are the people who cannot pay.

What it does not mean. The scales here are not the scales of justice but of scarcity: food weighed out because there is not enough of it.

What should a Christian do when prices soar and money is tight? Three things. Trust, first: your Father knows what you need, and he feeds the birds who neither sow nor reap (Matthew 6:25–33). That does not promise luxury, but it does promise that you are not forgotten. Then share: the early church met famine by sending relief to believers in need (Acts 11:28–30), and those with oil and wine in the cellar are called to open it. And be honest about which side of the street you are on. If the rise in the price of bread is an inconvenience rather than a crisis for you, this verse is asking you what you are doing for the person for whom it is a crisis.
verseByVerse.note: A denarius was a day’s wage; a quart of wheat was about one person’s daily ration — famine prices.

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth living creature say, "Come!" And I looked, and behold, a pale horse! And its rider's name was Death, and Hades followed him. And they were given authority over a fourth of the earth, to kill with sword and with famine and with pestilence and by wild beasts of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. In Ezekiel, God speaks of sending his four disastrous acts of judgement on Jerusalem: sword, famine, wild beasts and pestilence (Ezekiel 14:21). The fourth horseman brings all four. John is not inventing a scenario. He is using the standing vocabulary of covenant judgement that every reader of the prophets already knew.

A pale horse! The word is chlōros, pale green, greenish-grey, the root of our words chlorine and chlorophyll. Elsewhere in the New Testament it means the green of grass (8:7; Mark 6:39). Used of a body, it is the colour of a corpse, of sickness and decay. Here it means the green of a face.

Death, and Hades. This rider is the only one of the four who is named. The first three were anonymous forces; this one has a name, Death (ho Thanatos), personified, and behind him walks a second figure. Hades (ho Hadēs) is the realm of the dead, the place that receives what Death takes. One kills, and the other collects.

Whose keys? A reader of this book has heard both words before, and John expects him to remember. In the first chapter the risen Christ said: I have the keys of Death and Hades (1:18). The two figures riding out at the fourth seal are the two whose keys are on the belt of the one who opened the seal. They ride only at his word, and the man who holds their keys is the man who let them out. And at 20:14 the same two are thrown into the lake of fire.

A fourth of the earth. The fourth divine passive of the chapter, and this time an explicit fraction. A fourth. Not half, not all. Every rider so far has been permitted, and now the permission is quantified. Death is given a portion and not the whole. Later in the book the trumpets will touch a third (8:7–12), and only with the bowls does anything become total (16:1). The judgements in Revelation escalate, and they escalate because they are being measured out by somebody, in stages, with a purpose.

Pestilence and wild beasts. “Pestilence” is literally death, a common word in the Greek Old Testament for plague. The fourth horseman sums up the first three and adds disease and wild animals. These are the great killers of human history.

The four are complete. What has been shown is not a coded map of the twenty-first century but the ordinary, terrible furniture of human history: empires that conquer, nations that turn on themselves, hunger that follows the armies, and death that gathers what is left, all riding out at the word of the Lamb, within a fraction, in front of a throne. Jesus called wars and famines only the beginning of the birth pains (Matthew 24:8), which supports reading the seals as troubles that mark the whole age before the end.

The hand on the seal. That is not a comfortable doctrine, but the only alternative is that these things ride at nobody’s word at all. The churches in Asia were about to meet the red horse and the pale one personally. What they were given was not an explanation of why. It was the identity of the hand on the seal.

If Christians die in the same plagues, what difference does faith make? All the difference, though not always the difference we would choose. The same disease may strike a believer and an unbeliever, but it does not do the same thing to them. For the one who is not in Christ, death is the end of every opportunity and the entrance to judgement. For the believer, Death and Hades ride under the authority of his own Saviour, who has already been through death and come out holding its keys. Death can take his body; it cannot keep it. It can end his life here; it delivers him to Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23). The pale horse is a thief to the world and, for the Christian, only a servant opening a door.

Was a pandemic God’s judgement? In the broad sense, yes: every plague belongs to a world under the curse, and every one is a summons to repent, as Jesus said of a tower that fell on eighteen people (Luke 13:4–5). In the narrow sense, we are not told which specific sins of which specific people a particular disaster answers, and anyone who claims to know is speaking beyond Scripture. The right response to a plague is not to point at others, but to examine ourselves, care for the sick at cost as Christians have done since the plagues of the Roman empire, and remember how short life is.

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God and for the witness they had borne. They cried out with a loud voice, "O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Leviticus says the life of the flesh is in the blood (Leviticus 17:11), and Paul spoke of his coming death as being poured out like a drink offering (2 Timothy 4:6; Philippians 2:17). The cry How long? is the cry of suffering believers throughout the Psalms (Psalm 13:1–2; 79:5–10; 94:3) and the prophets (Habakkuk 1:2; Zechariah 1:12).

Under the altar. This seal breaks the pattern: there is no horse, no rider, no thundered Come! The camera turns away from the earth, and what John sees is a congregation. The altar (thysiastērion) is the place of sacrifice. Why under the altar? In the temple the blood of a sacrifice was poured out at its base (Leviticus 4:7), so the place where the life of every offering collected was the foot of the altar. These people are lying exactly where the blood of the offerings went. Their deaths were not waste; they were an offering, and heaven has put them where an offering belongs. What looked like defeat was worship.

The souls. “Souls” means persons, lives. They have died, but they are alive and conscious in God’s presence, waiting for the resurrection. And the word for slain is the same word used of the Lamb at 5:6. What was done to Christ has been done to them, and Scripture says so with a single deliberate word. They share his death.

For the word of God. As John himself was on Patmos on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus (1:9). They died because they would not stop believing and confessing Christ. Antipas of Pergamum, the faithful witness who was killed where Satan dwells (2:13), would be among them.

Where are they now? The verse settles, in passing, a question asked at every funeral. Between death and resurrection, believers are conscious, recognisable, in the presence of God, capable of speech, and not yet finished, because the body is still in the ground and the resurrection has not happened. Paul says the same: my desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better (Philippians 1:23). Not unconscious. Not yet complete. With him.

O Sovereign Lord. Then they speak, and what they say is startling. “Sovereign Lord” is the word for an absolute master over a household, a title chosen because their complaint is precisely that he has the power to act and has not. Holy and true: because God is holy and true, he must judge evil. Their prayer appeals to his character. Holy means utterly set apart from evil, so pure that he cannot look on wrong with approval (Habakkuk 1:13); true means he keeps every word he has spoken. A holy God cannot leave murder unanswered for ever, and a true God cannot forget his promise to vindicate his people.

How long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth? “How long” (heōs pote) is literally until when. This is the cry of the psalms of complaint, in substance word for word: how long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever (Psalm 13:1)? Laments of this kind, honest complaints poured out to God, are often reckoned to make up about a third of the Psalter. “Judge” (krineis) and “avenge” (ekdikeis, vindicate, see justice done). “Those who dwell on the earth” is, in Revelation, a standing name for unbelievers in rebellion against God (3:10). They do not ask for personal revenge, but for God to act as judge and put things right publicly. It is a prayer for justice, which God promises to answer: will not God give justice to his elect, who cry to him day and night? (Luke 18:7–8; Romans 12:19).

In the flow. The chapter turns on the fifth seal. The first four seals showed what the whole world suffers; the fifth shows what the church suffers, and that heaven has not forgotten it. And the martyrs’ question, How long?, drives much of the rest of the book. It is answered in part at the sixth seal, when the great day of wrath arrives (6:17); again when the prayers of all the saints rise with the incense and fire is thrown on the earth (8:3–5); and finally when heaven praises God for avenging the blood of his servants on the great prostitute (19:2). Revelation is, among other things, God’s long answer to this prayer.

Blood that speaks. The cry is old: the blood of Abel cried to God from the ground (Genesis 4:10), and the martyrs’ blood cries the same way. But Hebrews says that believers have come to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel (Hebrews 12:24). Abel’s blood asks for justice. Christ’s blood speaks of forgiveness, and obtains it. These martyrs can cry for judgement in God’s presence without fear for themselves only because a better blood has already spoken for them.

Should believers pray for vengeance? A careful Christian will raise it, and it deserves a real answer rather than a nervous one. Did not Christ tell us to love our enemies and pray for those who persecute us (Matthew 5:44), and did not Stephen die asking that the sin not be held against them (Acts 7:60)? Four things settle it. First, they are not asking to do anything; they are asking God to do it. Vengeance belongs to him and nobody else: never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God (Romans 12:19), and that command is a command to hand the matter over, not to pretend the matter does not exist. Second, they do not name individuals or ask for a particular punishment. They ask the judge to judge. Third, what they are asking for is not private satisfaction but justice, which God has promised and the world urgently needs. A universe in which murder is finally shrugged at is not a kind universe. Fourth, the two prayers are not rivals: Christ prayed for his executioners’ forgiveness (Luke 23:34) and also promised that every hidden thing would be brought into the open (Luke 12:2–3). The one who repents is forgiven. The one who does not is judged. Praying for both is not confusion; it is the whole gospel with nothing left out.

The second burden lifted. That frees a believer from something needless. Anyone who has been genuinely wronged, assaulted, defrauded, lied about, bereaved by somebody who was never charged, often carries a double burden: the injury itself, and the guilt of still minding about it. This verse takes the second one away. The holiest company in Scripture, standing in the immediate presence of God, wearing the marks of martyrdom, are asking out loud how long justice is going to take. Nobody tells them to stop.

Where Christians differ: do the dead sleep until the resurrection? Some groups, such as Seventh-day Adventists and Jehovah’s Witnesses, teach soul sleep: that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection, or that the soul does not exist apart from the body. This commentary’s view: the martyrs are conscious, speaking, praying and comforted, while their bodies are in the grave. Scripture teaches an intermediate state in which believers are with Christ at once when they die (Luke 23:43; Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8). They are not yet in their final state, which comes at the resurrection, but they are with the Lord, at rest (v. 11). Nor is there any purgatory (the Roman Catholic teaching that the saved are cleansed by suffering after death); they are under the altar, in God’s presence, not being purified.

Do the dead in Christ know what is happening on earth? This verse shows they know enough to know that justice has not yet been done, and that is as far as Scripture takes us. It does not teach that departed loved ones watch over us, hear our words, or can be spoken to, and we should not try. What it does teach is better: they are with Christ, at rest, conscious, and joined with us in longing for his coming. The communion of saints is real, but it runs through Christ, not around him. You can thank God for them and look forward to seeing them; you do not need to talk to them.

How do I pray this prayer without becoming bitter? Pray it to God, out loud, in the words of the Psalms if you need them, rather than rehearsing it privately against the person. Tell him exactly what was done and that it was wrong. Then leave the verdict with him, and ask him for the grace to bless the person if they repent. Bitterness is justice held in your own hands too long. The martyrs’ prayer is justice handed over to the only Judge who will get it exactly right, and that is why it can be prayed by someone who also forgives.

For worship. The martyrs cry with a loud voice, and they cry to a God who has heard a loud cry before. In the days of his flesh his own Son offered up prayers with loud cries and tears to the one who could save him from death, and was heard (Hebrews 5:7), and on the third day the answer walked out of the tomb. Every saint who died for his name is already alive in his presence, and not one drop of their blood is forgotten. The Judge of all the earth will do right (Genesis 18:25), and his delay is not deafness. He heard his Son, and he hears them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they were each given a white robe and told to rest a little longer, until the number of their fellow servants and their brothers should be complete, who were to be killed as they themselves had been.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A white robe. They asked how long, and the answer comes in two parts, neither of them what the question asked for: a garment and a word. Before anything is explained, something is handed over. The white robe means purity, victory, vindication. It is the promise made to the conquerors in Sardis (3:4–5), worn by the elders (4:4) and by the great multitude (7:9), and 7:14 will say where the whiteness comes from: they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb. The image is deliberately impossible, and it settles that the robe is not a reward for dying well. It is the verdict of the court delivered in advance. Paul’s word for this is justification: God pronouncing a person righteous on the ground of what Christ has done for him, not of what he has done himself (Romans 5:1, 9). The martyrs’ deaths did not earn the robe; the Lamb’s death did, and their faithfulness to death showed whose they were. Whatever the world’s courts said about these people, and many of them were executed as criminals by lawful courts, heaven has dressed them in the colour of innocence. And note the word each: not a general amnesty issued to a category, but a robe apiece, handed to individuals by the God who counts a few names in Sardis one at a time (3:4).

To rest a little longer. The first thing in the word is rest. The verb means to cease from labour, to stop. It is not a command to be patient in the sense of gritting the teeth; it is permission to stop working. Their part is finished. Whatever is still to be done about the injustice done to them is not their assignment any more. Their rest contrasts with the restless torment of those who worship the beast, who have no rest, day or night (14:11). Blessed indeed are the dead who die in the Lord, that they may rest from their labours (14:13). And it is a little longer: there is an end, and God calls the wait short. That is time measured in heaven, where a thousand years are as one day (2 Peter 3:8), not in a prison cell, where one day can feel like a thousand years.

Until the number should be complete. “Complete” means filled up. God has a set number of martyrs, as he has a set number of the elect, the fullness of the Gentiles coming in (Romans 11:25). The end will come when his purposes are complete, not before. History moves on God’s timetable. And the number is not a casualty estimate but a roll. Nobody in it is an accident, and nobody outside it will be taken by mistake. It does not mean God takes pleasure in their deaths: precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints (Psalm 116:15).

To be killed as they had been. This is the third thing in the sentence, and it is very hard. More martyrdoms are coming. The church was not promised escape from suffering. The delay in judgement is not administrative. God is waiting because there are more still to come, and they will die in the same way. The answer to how long until you avenge our blood is: until the rest of your brothers have shed theirs.

The patience that produced Paul. But consider what the delay is doing on the other side of the ledger. God is patient, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance (2 Peter 3:9), and his plan includes the faithful witness of the church through suffering.
