Every year the judgement is postponed is a year in which somebody who is currently an enemy of God can be brought in. The man who wrote most of the New Testament’s letters about grace had held the coats at the first martyrdom (Acts 7:58; 8:1). Paul was in the number of the persecutors before he was in the number of the persecuted, and he said that he received mercy so that in him, the foremost of sinners, Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who were to believe (1 Timothy 1:16). The patience the martyrs are being asked to accept is the patience that produced Paul.

Should I expect to be martyred? Most Christians in history have not been, and most readers of this page will not be. But every Christian is called to be ready, and in parts of the world today the number is still being filled. What this verse forbids is the assumption that faithfulness will be safe. Jesus said that if they persecuted him they would persecute his followers (John 15:20), and the costs in the West are usually smaller: a lost promotion, a broken friendship, mockery. Prepare for those now, because the courage to die for Christ is ordinarily built from a thousand small refusals to be ashamed of him. And when you have been ashamed of him, as Peter was, remember that Christ made the good confession before Pilate perfectly in your place (1 Timothy 6:13), that his faithfulness is counted as yours, and that his Spirit gives the words when the hour comes (Matthew 10:19–20).

If God has fixed the number, why pray or evangelise? Because God fixes the ends and the means together. The same God who knows the full number of his people has appointed that they be gathered through preaching, prayer and the witness of the church, often at the cost of suffering. A fixed number does not make the work pointless; it makes it certain. Paul kept preaching in Corinth because the Lord told him, I have many in this city who are my people (Acts 18:10). The roll is full of names not yet called, and your witness may be how one of them is.

So the fifth seal is honest. It does not answer the question of timing at all, and it does not pretend it has. It gives three things instead: a verdict delivered early, an end that is fixed, and a reason for the wait that is not indifference. For a congregation in Smyrna expecting arrests, that was the whole of the comfort available, and it turned out to be enough for sixty generations.

On a Tuesday. If you are waiting on God for something that has not come, a healing, a justice, a prodigal’s return, his answer to the martyrs was not an explanation but a robe and rest. Those are offered to you first: his verdict over you in Christ, and leave to put down what he has told you to stop carrying. And pray this week for a persecuted church: it may yet see its persecutors become like Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the sixth seal, I looked, and behold, there was a great earthquake, and the sun became black as sackcloth, the full moon became like blood, and the stars of the sky fell to the earth as the fig tree sheds its winter fruit when shaken by a gale. The sky vanished like a scroll that is being rolled up, and every mountain and island was removed from its place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. The Old Testament prophets described the Day of the LORD in terms of cosmic collapse: the sun and moon darkened, the stars falling, the heavens rolled up like a scroll, the mountains shaking (Isaiah 13:10; 34:4; Joel 2:10, 31; Haggai 2:6). Jesus used the same language for his coming (Matthew 24:29–30). Sometimes this language described the fall of earthly empires: Isaiah 13 is about Babylon, Ezekiel 32:7–8 about Egypt, Isaiah 34 about Edom. But here its universal scope points to the end of the age.

A great earthquake. The sixth seal is opened, and the whole stage is struck, from the ground upward. In Scripture, earthquakes accompany God’s coming in power: the whole mountain trembled greatly at Sinai (Exodus 19:18), and yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heavens (Hebrews 12:26–27). Asia was earthquake country. Sardis and Philadelphia had been flattened in AD 17, and every reader would have understood the terror.

Black as sackcloth. Sackcloth was coarse cloth woven from black goat hair and worn in mourning, so the comparison is exact and not merely poetic. The sun itself puts on mourning.

Like blood. As in Joel 2:31: the sun shall be turned to darkness, and the moon to blood, before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes. Peter quoted it at Pentecost (Acts 2:20).

Winter fruit. Isaiah had already compared the falling host of heaven to leaves falling from the fig tree (Isaiah 34:4), and John sharpens the picture to the fruit. Late figs that never ripened hang on through the winter, hard and green and useless, and the first real storm brings them down in a shower. The homely image reduces the stars to windfall. The lights that sailors steered by and astrologers consulted and emperors stamped on their coins come down like unripe fruit off a tree in a gale, and the tree does not notice.

Like a scroll. “Vanished” means split apart, removed. Isaiah says the skies roll up like a scroll (Isaiah 34:4). The created order as we know it passes away: the heavens will pass away with a roar (2 Peter 3:10), and from the presence of him who sits on the great white throne earth and sky flee away (20:11). Even the mountains and islands are moved, and nothing is left to hide behind.

The fixed points removed. That is the actual argument of these three verses, and it is aimed at people under pressure from something that looks immovable. Everything humanity has ever used as a fixed reference point is in this list: the ground that does not move, the sun that always rises, the stars that guide you home, the mountains that define permanence. Every one of them, in three verses, gone. And the throne is not in the list. Chapter 4 established where the one fixed point is, and chapter 6 now removes every rival. When the sky is rolled up like a scroll there will be one thing left standing in the universe, and it will be the thing that was described first.

The one who rolls up the sky. Hebrews takes a psalm about the end of the heavens and says it was spoken to the Son: you, Lord, laid the foundation of the earth in the beginning, and the heavens are the work of your hands; they will perish, but you remain; like a robe you will roll them up, but you are the same (Hebrews 1:10–12). The hand that rolls up the sky in this seal is the hand that opened the seal. And Jesus said that when the sun is darkened and the stars fall, all the tribes of the earth will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory (Matthew 24:29–30). The fixed points are taken away so that he may be seen.

Where Christians differ: is this the end, or a stage on the way? Many futurist readers, including premillennial and dispensational Christians, place the sixth seal early in a future tribulation, with many more judgements to follow in a strict sequence; they take seriously that the book has an order, and they are brothers and sisters, not opponents. This commentary’s view: the sixth seal describes the final day of judgement itself, when Christ returns. The language is the language Jesus used for his coming, and the people cry that the great day of wrath has come (v. 17). This shows that Revelation is not one long timeline but a series of parallel visions, each ending at or near the end. The seals take us to the end; the trumpets and bowls go over the same ground again from other angles, with growing intensity. This is called recapitulation (the same period told again), and it fits the amillennial reading of the book, which takes the thousand years of chapter 20 as the present age.

What it does not mean. The cosmic language is not a scientific description of astronomical events. It is the prophets’ way of describing the shaking and passing away of the whole created order at God’s coming. It may be literal in part, and it is certainly real; but its main point is that nothing in creation can stand before its Creator.

Will the world really end, or be renewed? Both, in the biblical sense. The present order, scarred by sin, will pass away; but God does not throw his creation away and start from nothing. He makes all things new (21:5). As the flood purged the old world without abolishing the earth (2 Peter 3:6–7), so the fire of the last day will purify and transform creation, which waits with eager longing to be set free from its bondage to corruption (Romans 8:19–21). The sky rolling up is not the end of everything God made. It is the end of everything that stood between creation and its glory.

Should I be afraid of the end of the world? If you are in Christ, no. For the believer, the day the sky is rolled up is the day of his redemption: when these things begin to take place, straighten up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near (Luke 21:28). The fear that grips people over world events, war, climate, economic collapse, is answered not by pretending nothing will be shaken, but by knowing the one who cannot be. Christians should care for the world, work for the good of their neighbours and take real dangers seriously. But they do not need to panic, because the end of the world is in the same hands as its beginning.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the kings of the earth and the great ones and the generals and the rich and the powerful, and everyone, slave and free, hid themselves in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains, calling to the mountains and rocks, "Fall on us and hide us from the face of him who is seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb, for the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Isaiah describes people fleeing into the caves of the rocks and the holes of the ground from before the terror of the LORD, when he rises to terrify the earth (Isaiah 2:19–21). Hosea says they shall say to the mountains, Cover us, and to the hills, Fall on us (Hosea 10:8). Jesus quoted Hosea on his way to the cross (Luke 23:30). Malachi asks who can endure the day of his coming, and who can stand when he appears (Malachi 3:2), and Nahum asks who can stand before his indignation (Nahum 1:6).

The kings of the earth. The last three verses of the chapter turn from the sky to people, and they are the most searching in it. Seven classes of people, which in this book means the complete list, the whole of humanity, and five of them are the top of the pyramid. The kings are the same kings of the earth over whom Christ is ruler (1:5); the great ones are nobles and top officials; the generals commanded a thousand men each. Those who seemed untouchable, who persecuted the church, are the first to flee.

Slave and free. The two words that in the Roman world divided the whole human race take in everybody, and the order starts at the top. Every category that ordinarily protects a person is named first and named uselessly. A king has an army. A general has the army itself. A rich man can buy his way out of most things and a powerful one can arrange them. On this day the list of people who cannot help themselves runs from the throne down to the labour gang, and the emperor and the man he owns end up behind the same rock. Every one of those protections is something people quietly trust instead of God, and the day shows what such trust was worth: the army, the money and the influence cannot even hide them.

Fall on us. The mountains have just been moved (v. 14), and there is nowhere to hide. This is the terrible part. They are asking mountains to crush them. Given the choice between being buried alive and being looked at, they choose the burial. Not repentance, but terror. They do not ask for mercy; they ask to be hidden.

From the face. What they are hiding from is not fire and not an army. It is the face. Moses asked to see God’s glory and was told that no one could see his face and live (Exodus 33:18–20). The great blessing of Israel was that the LORD would make his face shine upon you (Numbers 6:25). The whole hope of this book is that his servants will see his face (22:4). The same face that the redeemed long to see is what the lost cannot bear, and here men are begging geology to spare them from it.

The wrath of the Lamb. “Wrath” is settled, righteous anger. Put the two words side by side and they should not fit. Lambs do not have wrath. That is the point, and it is the exact counterpart of 5:5–6: there John was told a Lion and shown a Lamb, and here the Lamb turns out to be what men flee from. This is not a mild Christ who has finally lost his temper. It is the same Lamb, with the same wounds, and the wrath is the other face of the love that bore them. The Lamb is gentle, but he is not soft. Those who reject the Lamb’s sacrifice will face the Lamb’s anger. The one who died for sinners will judge those who refuse him (John 5:22, 27; Acts 17:31). Nothing is more terrible than mercy that has been refused for long enough, and the only thing left to meet is the one who offered it.

For the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand? “The great day” (hē hēmera hē megalē) is the Day of the LORD, the final judgement (Joel 2:11, 31; Zephaniah 1:14). “Their wrath” is the wrath of God and the Lamb, one wrath. “Who can stand” (tis dynatai stathēnai): who is able to stand firm, survive and be acquitted? The question is the last word of the chapter, and it is left hanging deliberately. It is not rhetorical despair; it is a real question, and the whole of the next chapter is the answer. Before the seventh seal is opened, John will be shown a hundred and forty-four thousand sealed on the forehead and a multitude nobody can count, standing before the throne and before the Lamb (7:9). Standing: the very thing this verse asks who can do.

Is an angry God less loving than a calm one? No, the opposite. If someone you love is being destroyed by a drug or by an abuser, love does not shrug; it is angry, and the more you love, the angrier you are. There is nothing childish or sudden in his anger: it is his holy love set firmly against whatever destroys the world and the creatures he made. A God who felt nothing about cruelty, lies and murder would not be kinder; he would be indifferent. And the wonder of the gospel is that this God bore his own wrath in the Lamb, so that it need not fall on us (Romans 5:9).

Two places to stand. So the honest question this chapter leaves with a reader is not whether the world is going to be shaken. It says plainly that it is, and that the shaking has been going on since the first horse rode out. The question is where a person will be standing when the last of the fixed points goes, and there are only two options in the text: behind a rock, or in front of the throne in a white robe. What separates them is not courage or achievement but the blood of the Lamb (7:14): the wrath they are spared is the Lamb’s, and so is the blood that spares them.

Will people get another chance on that day? No. These people know exactly who they are hiding from, and they still do not repent; they ask to be hidden, not forgiven. That is the frightening thing: seeing God does not by itself change a heart that has refused him. Scripture holds out no second chance after death or after his coming. It is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgement (Hebrews 9:27). That is why the invitation is so urgent now: behold, now is the favourable time; behold, now is the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2). The only time to run to the Lamb is before the day of his wrath.

How can I be sure I will stand? Not by examining your courage or your record, but by looking where the multitude in chapter 7 looked: to the blood of the Lamb. If you have turned from your sin and trusted Christ, his death has already borne the wrath you deserved, and there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). Your assurance rests on his finished work, confirmed by the Spirit’s witness that you are God’s child (Romans 8:16) and by the fruit of a changed life. If your faith is weak, it is still faith in a strong Saviour. Those he has sealed will stand, not because they are strong, but because he holds them.

On a Tuesday. People hide now in quieter ways, behind busyness, wealth, cleverness or simply never thinking about it, and some of them sit beside us at work. While it is still called today, the shelter is open, for them and for us.

For worship. The wrath of the Lamb is real, and the Lamb is the one who drank it. On the cross the face of the Father was turned away from his Son, so that the face which the kings of the earth cannot bear could shine on sinners in peace. He bore the darkness so that the redeemed might see his face; he was crushed so that they need never ask the mountains to fall. Who can stand? Only those who stand in him. And everyone who stands in him will stand for ever, robed in white, before the throne and before the Lamb.

And its rider’s name was Death, and Hades followed him. And they were given authority over a fourth of the earth, to kill with sword and with famine and with pestilence and by wild beasts of the earth.<sup>9</sup>When he opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God and for the witness they had borne.<sup>10</sup>They cried out with a loud voice, “O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?”<sup>11</sup>Then they were each given a white robe and told to rest a little longer, until the number of their fellow servants and their brothers should be complete, who were to be killed as they themselves had been.<sup>12</sup>When he opened the sixth seal, I looked, and behold, there was a great earthquake, and the sun became black as sackcloth, the full moon became like blood,<sup>13</sup>and the stars of the sky fell to the earth as the fig tree sheds its winter fruit when shaken by a gale.<sup>14</sup>The sky vanished like a scroll that is being rolled up, and every mountain and island was removed from its place.<sup>15</sup>Then the kings of the earth and the great ones and the generals and the rich and the powerful, and everyone, slave and free, hid themselves in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains,<sup>16</sup>calling to the mountains and rocks, “Fall on us and hide us from the face of him who is seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb,<sup>17</sup>for the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand?”

7.title: The Sealed and the Standing: God's People in the Storm
7.overview:
Chapter 7 is a pause between the sixth and seventh seals, and it answers the question that ended chapter 6: “Who can stand?” It shows the whole people of God twice. First the 144,000 sealed from the twelve tribes of Israel (vv. 1–8): the church on earth, complete and protected in the middle of judgement. Then the great multitude from every nation (vv. 9–17): the same church before the throne, standing where the kings of the earth could not.

Christians read the 144,000 in different ways. Some take them as literal Jewish believers in a future tribulation. This commentary takes them as the whole church, God’s true Israel, for reasons set out at verse 4: the tribe list matches no Old Testament register (Judah first, Dan missing, Levi counted), the number 12 × 12 × 1,000 is plainly symbolic, and John hears a number and then sees a crowd no one could count, as in 5:5–6 he heard of a Lion and saw a Lamb.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The seventh seal is not opened until 8:1, and this section sits in the gap. Four angels hold back the four winds of judgement, and a fifth angel, rising from the east with the seal of the living God, orders them to wait until God’s servants are sealed on their foreheads (vv. 1–3). The picture behind it is Ezekiel 9:4, where those who grieve over Jerusalem’s sins are marked and spared. Judgement is not cancelled; it is delayed until God’s people are marked.

Verses 4–8 give the number of the sealed, 144,000, twelve thousand from each of twelve tribes, in a list that matches no tribal register in the Old Testament. Who they are is set out at verse 4.
verseByVerse.theology:
Sealed Before the Storm

The winds of judgement are held back until God’s servants are sealed on their foreheads, as in Ezekiel 9. The 144,000 are the whole people of God, counted to the last person; God knows the number exactly.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The seal did not exempt them from the tribulation; it marked them as God’s within it.

Now: The text caps nobody’s hope: the next scene is a multitude no one could number.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth, holding back the four winds of the earth, that no wind might blow on earth or sea or against any tree. Then I saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun, with the seal of the living God, and he called with a loud voice to the four angels who had been given power to harm earth and sea, saying, "Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees, until we have sealed the servants of our God on their foreheads."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Revelation 7 is a pause between the sixth and seventh seals, and it answers the question that ended chapter 6: who can stand? Four angels hold back the winds of judgement until God’s servants are sealed on their foreheads (vv. 1–3). John hears the number of the sealed, 144,000 from the twelve tribes of Israel (vv. 4–8), and then sees a multitude no one could count, from every nation, standing before the throne and the Lamb in white robes, crying that salvation belongs to God and to the Lamb, while all the angels fall down and worship (vv. 9–12). These have come out of the great tribulation and washed their robes in the Lamb’s blood; so God shelters them, the Lamb shepherds them to springs of living water, and God wipes away every tear (vv. 13–17). The chapter shows the church twice: sealed on earth as God’s true Israel before the storm, and safe in heaven for ever after it.

The setting. In Ezekiel 9:4–6, before Jerusalem was judged, God told a man with a writing case to put a mark on the foreheads of those who sigh and groan over the abominations committed in the city, so that the executioners would spare them. At the first Passover the blood on the doorposts marked the houses God would pass over (Exodus 12:13). In the ancient world a seal on a document or object marked ownership and protection; slaves and soldiers were sometimes branded with their master’s or general’s mark.

Holding back the four winds. Four angels, four corners, four winds: four is the number of the created world in this book, its compass points and its extent (Jeremiah 49:36). The winds are destructive forces of judgement, perhaps the four horsemen of chapter 6 under another image, since Zechariah links the horses and the four winds of heaven (Zechariah 6:1–5). “Holding back” means gripping firmly. Judgement is restrained by God’s angels until his purpose is done.

That no wind might blow. Anyone who has stood outside before a storm knows that stillness. The air stops. The leaves do not move. Nothing has happened yet, and everything is about to. That is the atmosphere of the first three verses, and the reader is meant to feel it: all creation waits. The winds have not been cancelled. They are being held.

From the rising of the sun. That is the east, the direction of dawn and, in Ezekiel, the direction from which the glory of God returns to his temple (Ezekiel 43:2). Hope comes before judgement. And this fifth angel outranks the four, because he gives them orders.

With the seal of the living God. The seal is a signet ring, a stamp, and it is the seal of the living God, in contrast to idols that are dead. A seal marked ownership, gave protection, since tampering with a sealed item was an offence against the owner, and guaranteed authenticity. All three are in play here.

Until we have sealed. That is the shape of the whole chapter. The judgement is not cancelled; it is delayed, and it is delayed for one reason: God’s people are not marked yet. Every year of history since is an instance of the same arrangement, and the reason is stated elsewhere in one line: the Lord is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:9).

Sealed in him. The seal marks God’s ownership and guarantees his protection, and the New Testament says where it is found. Believers are sealed with the Holy Spirit (2 Corinthians 1:22; Ephesians 4:30), and Paul says they are sealed in Christ, at the moment they believe in him (Ephesians 1:13). The seal is given to people joined to Jesus, and he bore it first: on him God the Father has set his seal (John 6:27). When this company appears again, the mark on their foreheads is a name, the Lamb’s name and his Father’s name (14:1). So the sealing is not a second scheme running alongside the cross. The Lamb who set the judgements of chapter 6 in motion is the Lamb whose name his people carry through them. The hand that releases the winds belongs to the one who owns the people they cannot destroy.

Whose name is on you? One more thing, and the whole book turns on it later. The mark goes on their foreheads. In chapter 13 another power will demand a mark on the right hand or the forehead, and nobody will be able to buy or sell without it (13:16–17). Everyone alive is marked by somebody. The only question in this book is whose name is on you, and the sealing happens first, six chapters before the counterfeit is even offered.

What it does not mean. Sealing does not protect believers from all suffering or from death; many will be martyred (6:11; 13:7), and the very next scene shows this same company coming out of the great tribulation, which means they went through it. The seal is a mark of ownership that suffering cannot remove. It protects them from the wrath of God that falls on unbelievers (9:4), and above all from losing their faith and their place in God’s kingdom. What is guaranteed is not an easy passage but a safe arrival.

How do I know whether I am sealed? The seal is the Holy Spirit himself, given to everyone who believes: in him you also, when you heard the word of truth and believed in him, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit (Ephesians 1:13). So the question is not whether you have had a special experience but whether you have trusted Christ. The Spirit’s presence shows itself in a faith that keeps looking to Jesus, in a growing hatred of sin and love of holiness, in love for other believers, and in his inward witness that you are a child of God (Romans 8:15–16). These may be faint at times. The seal does not depend on your feeling it.

Can the seal be broken? No. God seals his own for the day of redemption (Ephesians 4:30), and no one can snatch them out of the Father’s hand (John 10:28–29). A believer may grieve the Spirit, fall into serious sin, and lose for a time the joy of his salvation, but he cannot lose the Spirit’s seal. This is the doctrine of perseverance: those God has truly called he keeps to the end (Philippians 1:6). It is not a licence for carelessness, because a person who is happy to live in sin has reason to ask whether he was ever sealed at all. It is a comfort for the weak, who fear that their grip will fail. Your grip is not what holds you.

On a Tuesday. Whatever comes this week, the diagnosis, the redundancy, the slander, God has marked you as his own, and he does not lose what he owns. And remember who was marked in Ezekiel: those who grieved over sin around them. If the evils of your culture and of your own heart grieve you, even feebly, that grief is not a sign that you are unmarked. It is one of the Spirit’s fingerprints.

For worship. What patience, to hold back the storm of the ages for people who could never have held it back themselves. And what tenderness, that the name pressed on their foreheads is the name of the Lamb who was slain for them, so that the mark of his ownership is also the mark of his love. The living God has written himself on his people, and no wind, no beast and no grave can rub it out. We are his.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard the number of the sealed, 144,000, sealed from every tribe of the sons of Israel: 12,000 from the tribe of Judah were sealed, 12,000 from the tribe of Reuben, 12,000 from the tribe of Gad, 12,000 from the tribe of Asher, 12,000 from the tribe of Naphtali, 12,000 from the tribe of Manasseh, 12,000 from the tribe of Simeon, 12,000 from the tribe of Levi, 12,000 from the tribe of Issachar, 12,000 from the tribe of Zebulun, 12,000 from the tribe of Joseph, 12,000 from the tribe of Benjamin were sealed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Israel was made up of twelve tribes descended from the sons of Jacob. The Old Testament lists them about twenty times, in many different orders. By John’s day ten of the tribes had been scattered since the Assyrian conquest in 722 BC, and Jews looked forward to God gathering all twelve tribes in the last days (Isaiah 11:12; Ezekiel 37:15–28). Before a war, Israel took a census of the tribes to count its fighting men (Numbers 1). Jesus chose twelve apostles, who would sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes (Matthew 19:28), signalling that he was reconstituting Israel around himself.

The number of the sealed. The twelve tribes are named one after another with a deliberateness that slows the reading right down. 144,000 is 12 × 12 × 1,000: twelve (the tribes of Israel) times twelve (the apostles), times a thousand (a vast, complete number). In a book where seven means fullness and myriads of myriads means beyond counting, that is how numbers work. It is a symbolic number for the complete people of God, the whole of God’s true Israel. What does true Israel mean? Israel was always meant to be the people who belong to God by his promise, and Paul says that not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel (Romans 9:6–8). Those who belong to the Messiah, Jew or Gentile, are the Israel the promises were made to. So the numbered army and the uncountable multitude of verse 9 are one company seen from two sides: as God counts them, complete with nobody missing, and as they appear, beyond counting.

From every tribe. Organised like an army, counted by tribes as in the census of Numbers 1. In 14:1–4 the 144,000 stand with the Lamb on Mount Zion, follow him wherever he goes, and are called firstfruits for God and the Lamb, redeemed from mankind. They are God’s army, which conquers not by fighting but by following the Lamb.

From the tribe of Judah. The list is strange in four ways at once, which is strong evidence of what it means. Judah is first, though Reuben was the firstborn, because the Messiah, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, has just been introduced (5:5). Dan is missing altogether, and Dan was the tribe that set up an idol and became a byword for apostasy (Judges 18:30–31; 1 Kings 12:29–30). Levi, which received no land and is often left out of lists of the tribes counted for war and territory, is counted as a tribe, perhaps because all God’s people are now priests (1:6). And Joseph is listed alongside Manasseh, Joseph’s own son, while Ephraim disappears. The result is a list that matches no tribal register in the Old Testament. It is twelve names arranged theologically rather than genealogically: the new Israel, gathered around the Messiah.

Where Christians differ: who are the 144,000? Dispensationalists (who see God as working with Israel and the church along two distinct tracks) usually see them as literal ethnic Jews, converted during a future tribulation after the church has been raptured, that is, caught up to Christ before it begins, who then evangelise the world; what favours this in their eyes is that the text names the tribes one by one, which is a great deal of trouble to go to for a symbol, and many devout believers hold it because they take God’s promises to Israel seriously. Jehovah’s Witnesses teach that exactly 144,000 people form a heavenly class, while other believers live on earth. Others take them as Jewish Christians in the church, distinct from Gentile believers. This commentary’s view: the 144,000 are the whole church, the true Israel of God, Jew and Gentile together, seen on earth, sealed and protected. Four reasons. First, John hears a number (v. 4) and then sees a countless multitude from every nation (v. 9), just as in 5:5–6 he heard of a Lion and saw a Lamb: the two are the same reality, described first in Old Testament terms and then in its fulfilment. Second, the sealing is for all God’s servants (v. 3), and in 9:4 everyone without the seal is harmed, so the sealed must be all believers. Third, the New Testament calls the church, on the most likely reading, the Israel of God (Galatians 6:16), the twelve tribes in the dispersion (James 1:1), and Abraham’s offspring (Galatians 3:29). Fourth, the tribe list itself has been deliberately altered, which signals a symbolic, not a literal, Israel. Nothing in the text supports a special class of 144,000 with a different destiny.

If the 144,000 are the church, what of God’s future for the Jewish people? The two do not conflict. The 144,000 picture the whole people of God, sealed and counted, and the great multitude of v. 9 is the same people seen as they are, from every nation. Paul’s hope for Israel (Romans 11:25–26), however it is read, is part of that people being gathered; the elect of Israel are included in God’s complete number, not set apart from it. Christians differ over how and when that turning will come, and whether it is a great end-time conversion or the steady gathering of the Jewish remnant through the age, but all agree that it will be by faith in Jesus the Messiah, into the one olive tree.

What do I say when someone at the door says only 144,000 go to heaven? Point gently to the next verse. The teaching that only 144,000 people go to heaven while the rest of the saved live for ever on earth cannot be got out of this chapter. In the same vision John sees a multitude that no one could number, standing before the throne in white robes, and later they are said to serve God in his temple (v. 15). Whatever one thinks of the 144,000, the text does not cap the number of the redeemed. It does the opposite: it names a number and then immediately shows a crowd too large to count. Then turn to the deeper question, who Jesus is, because that is where the real difference lies.

Do I need to know which tribe I belong to? No. The chapter never asks anyone to work out his tribe. What it says about the sealed is that they are the servants of our God (v. 3), and what it says about the multitude is that they washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb (v. 14). Those are the two descriptions given, and neither of them is a bloodline. If you belong to Christ, you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise (Galatians 3:29). Your place in God’s Israel is secured by faith, not by ancestry.

Why is Dan left out, and does that mean Danites are lost? No individual is excluded from salvation by his ancestry. The omission is a warning, not a verdict on bloodlines: the tribe that led Israel into idolatry stands as a picture of what idolatry does, in a book that calls Christians again and again to refuse the idols of their age. Some early writers speculated that the antichrist would come from Dan, but the text says nothing of that. The lesson for us is simpler: no heritage, however privileged, protects a person who turns to idols, and no heritage, however compromised, keeps out a person who turns to Christ.
verseByVerse.note: The tribe list is unusual: Judah comes first, Dan is missing, and both Joseph and his son Manasseh appear.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–17 — A Great Multitude from Every Nation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 9–12: John sees a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, standing before the throne in white robes with palm branches, and crying that salvation belongs to God and to the Lamb. All the angels fall on their faces and add a sevenfold praise, opened and closed with Amen.

Verses 13–17: an elder asks who they are, and gives the answer himself. They are coming out of the great tribulation, and they have washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb. Therefore they serve before the throne, God spreads his tent over them, and the promises of Isaiah 49:10 are kept: no more hunger, thirst or scorching heat, the Lamb as their shepherd leading them to springs of living water, and God wiping away every tear.
verseByVerse.theology:
Washed in the Blood of the Lamb

A multitude from every nation stands before the throne and sings that salvation belongs to God and to the Lamb. They came out of the great tribulation, washed their robes in the Lamb’s blood, and are sheltered by God’s presence.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Hunger, thirst and scorching heat were the daily lot of many first hearers.

Now: God himself will wipe away every tear, every one, by name.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I looked, and behold, a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palm branches in their hands, and crying out with a loud voice, "Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. God promised Abraham that his offspring would be as numerous as the stars of heaven, too many to count (Genesis 15:5; 22:17). At the Feast of Tabernacles Israel waved palm branches and lived in booths, remembering how God had sheltered them in the wilderness (Leviticus 23:40–43). When Jesus entered Jerusalem, the crowds waved palm branches and shouted Hosanna, which means save us (John 12:13). Palm branches were also used to celebrate military victories (1 Maccabees 13:51).

A great multitude that no one could number. A moment ago there was a precise figure and a list of twelve names. Now there is a crowd nobody can count, and the phrase takes the reader back to a promise made to a childless old man standing outside his tent at night: look toward heaven, and number the stars, if you are able to number them; so shall your offspring be (Genesis 15:5). That promise has been kept, and this is what it looks like when it is. Heaven will not be thinly populated.

From every nation. Four terms, as in 5:9: all humanity. The Lamb’s blood ransomed people from every group, and here they are. This chapter is the receipt for that transaction. The purchase was made in chapter 5; here are the purchased, standing in the room.

Standing. This answers the question of 6:17: who can stand? These can, because the Lamb stands for them. While kings and generals crawled into caves, here is the answer, and it is not a class of person anyone would have picked: a crowd with no rank, no army and no leverage, drawn from every obscure corner of the world, upright before the throne while the great ones of the earth are face down under the rocks.

Clothed in white robes. Purity, victory, washed in the Lamb’s blood (v. 14). The robes have been promised since 3:5 and given since 6:11.

Palm branches. They mean victory and joyful celebration, like a heavenly Feast of Tabernacles. That was the week each autumn when Israel moved out of its houses and lived in booths made of branches to remember the wilderness, a festival of harvest home, of a journey finished. God will shelter them (v. 15), and the wilderness journey is over. And palms were what the crowd waved on the road into Jerusalem, shouting save us.

Salvation belongs to our God! That makes the cry the answer to the shout on that road. They asked save now; they are here saying that salvation belongs to him. It is his, it comes from him, it is his to give and nobody else’s to supply. They give all the credit to God and the Lamb. Salvation is entirely his work: planned by the Father, accomplished by the Son. As Jonah said from the belly of the fish, salvation belongs to the LORD (Jonah 2:9).

Not one syllable about themselves. Everything in the Christian life depends on the word belongs. The multitude has come out of the great tribulation. Some of them died under torture. Every one of them held on when it would have been easier not to. And when they open their mouths in front of the throne, not one syllable of the song is about what they did. They do not sing we endured. They sing that salvation belongs to God and to the Lamb, and there is no second clause. That is the test of whether a person has understood the gospel: if everything you are were explained out loud in front of the throne, whose name would the account turn on?

Will we keep our nations and languages in heaven? It seems so. John does not see a crowd in which every distinction has been erased, but people still recognisable as from every nation, tribe, people and language. At the end of the book the kings of the earth bring the glory and honour of the nations into the new Jerusalem (21:24–26). The gospel does not flatten cultures into one; it redeems people within them and gathers them around one throne. What will be gone is everything sinful in our cultures: the pride, the hostility, the walls. What remains is a unity so rich that it needs every tongue to sing it.

Does no one could number mean that most people will be saved? Scripture does not tell us the proportion, and Jesus warned that the gate is narrow and few find it (Matthew 7:13–14). But neither should we imagine heaven as a tiny remnant huddled in a corner. From the perspective of the end, gathered from every age and nation, the redeemed are a countless multitude. Both truths matter. The narrowness of the gate makes us urgent about our own soul and our neighbours’; the size of the crowd makes us confident that the gospel will not fail. God is not saving a few survivors from a lost world. He is gathering a world.

On a Tuesday. When a Christian tells how he came to faith, the story often drifts into being about himself: what he decided, what he gave up. The multitude tells it the other way round, and so may we. And the believer from another country at the back of your church is someone you are going to stand beside for ever.
verseByVerse.note: John hears a number (v. 4) but sees a multitude no one can count — likely the same people seen from two angles.

verseByVerse.quote: And all the angels were standing around the throne and around the elders and the four living creatures, and they fell on their faces before the throne and worshiped God, saying, "Amen! Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving and honor and power and might be to our God forever and ever! Amen."
verseByVerse.commentary:
All the angels. John gives the seating plan carefully. In the middle, the throne. Around it, the living creatures and the elders. And in the outer ring, all the angels, the myriads of myriads from 5:11. But the multitude of verse 9 is described as before the throne and before the Lamb, which seems to put the redeemed nearer than the angelic host. John does not press the point, and we should not build on it, but the picture is striking: ransomed sinners stand before the throne, and the beings who never fell stand in the outer ring.

They fell on their faces. They have been standing throughout; now they go down. What has prompted it? The multitude sang. Jesus said there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents (Luke 15:10); here is joy over a countless multitude.

Amen! They agree with the multitude’s cry. The word means it is firm, it is so, and the whole doxology begins and ends with it.

Seven ascriptions. As in 5:12, this is complete praise, everything there is to give, given. Every item has the definite article in Greek: the blessing, the glory, all of it, belongs to God. And the list is almost the same as the sevenfold ascription to the Lamb in 5:12, with thanksgiving here in place of wealth. The change is probably not accidental. Wealth is what a conqueror receives; thanksgiving is what a redeemed people offer.

The redeemed sing, and heaven agrees. The song that sets the whole company of angels on their faces was started by people who had been slaves, shopkeepers, soldiers, prostitutes and thieves, out of every language on earth. Peter wrote that angels long to look into the salvation preached to us (1 Peter 1:12). Here, at last, they are looking at it close up, and this is what looking does to them. They can only confirm a song they cannot sing on their own account, because nobody has ever ransomed an angel.

In the flow. The worship of chapters 4 and 5 returns here. There the creatures, the elders and the angels praised the Creator and the Lamb who was slain; here the same company praises God for what the Lamb’s death has produced, a people from every nation standing before the throne. The interlude of chapter 7 began with the question of 6:17, who can stand?, and it reaches its height in worship. And the next sound heaven makes after this Amen, when the seventh seal is opened, is silence (8:1).

The Amen on the throne. There is a reason the angels’ word is Amen. In this book it is one of Christ’s own names: the words of the Amen, the faithful and true witness (3:14). Paul puts it plainly: all the promises of God find their Yes in him, and so it is through him that we say our Amen to God (2 Corinthians 1:20). What does that mean? Every promise God ever made, to rescue, forgive, gather and bring home, was made good in Jesus, and the crowd in white is the proof standing in the room. When heaven says Amen to salvation belonging to God and to the Lamb, it is agreeing with a fact the Lamb himself established. The angels can only confirm the song. He is the reason it is true.

Do we worship with the angels now? Yes. When the church gathers, it comes not only to a building but to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, to innumerable angels in festal gathering, and to the assembly of the firstborn (Hebrews 12:22–23). That does not mean we pray to angels or seek their presence; they are fellow servants who point away from themselves (19:10). It means that the smallest gathering of believers on a Sunday morning is joined to a worship far larger than itself. Your Amen at the end of a prayer is the same word the angels say here, and it belongs in the same song.

For worship. He was on that throne when the seals were breaking and the horses were riding and the winds were straining against four angels’ hands, and he is on it still. Wisdom that planned a ransom no angel could have imagined, power that raised the slain Lamb, might that will bring every one of his people home: all of it is his, and heaven has nothing to add but its Amen. The oldest servants of God bow lowest at the newest song, and he is worthy of every word they say.

verseByVerse.quote: Then one of the elders addressed me, saying, "Who are these, clothed in white robes, and from where have they come?" I said to him, "Sir, you know." And he said to me, "These are the ones coming out of the great tribulation. They have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Daniel speaks of a time of trouble such as never has been, and at that time God’s people will be delivered, everyone whose name shall be found written in the book (Daniel 12:1). Jesus spoke of great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world (Matthew 24:21). When God asked Ezekiel whether the dry bones could live, the prophet answered, O Lord GOD, you know (Ezekiel 37:3).

Then one of the elders addressed me, saying, Who are these, clothed in white robes, and from where have they come? An elder turns to John and asks him a question he cannot possibly answer. It is a teacher’s question, asked to give the answer rather than to get one, and John knows it. The elder wants John, and us, to understand.

Sir, you know. This is not evasion; it is the honest reply of a man who has been asked something beyond him and does not intend to guess. Ezekiel gave the same answer standing in a valley full of dry bones. Some ignorance is itself a form of faith, and Scripture records both men practising it. And Revelation interprets itself here: the elder, not John, supplies the answer.

Coming out of the great tribulation. The answer comes in two halves, and each half settles something. First, the tense: a present participle, the ones who keep coming. Not a single group arriving at once, but a steady stream of believers coming out of tribulation, as each one dies or as the age ends. Second, the article: the great tribulation. John has already called himself their partner in the tribulation in the first chapter (1:9), using the same word of his own present situation, and Jesus said plainly that in the world you will have tribulation (John 16:33).

Where Christians differ: what is the great tribulation? Dispensationalists understand it as a specific seven-year period at the end of history, after the church has been raptured (caught up to Christ beforehand), and see this multitude as those converted during that time. They read promises such as 3:10 and 1 Thessalonians 4:17 as promises of removal, and they love the Lord’s appearing as much as anyone; this commentary reads those verses as promises of keeping and of meeting the Lord at his one visible coming. This commentary’s view: the great tribulation describes the suffering of God’s people throughout the whole age between Christ’s comings, which John and his readers were already in (1:9; 2:9–10; Acts 14:22). In the Olivet discourse (his teaching on the Mount of Olives about the end) Jesus spoke of it first in the siege of Jerusalem in AD 70 (as preterist readers rightly stress), and that siege also pictures the tribulation of the whole age (Matthew 24:21–22); Scripture expects a final intensification before the end (2 Thessalonians 2:3–4), and no secret rapture removes the church from it. The multitude is the whole number of the redeemed, from every nation, coming out of that tribulation through all history. The present tense, “coming out”, suits a continuing stream. The church is not removed from tribulation; it is brought through it.

So will Christians go through the tribulation? Yes, and we are in it now. Scripture nowhere promises a secret removal of the church before trouble comes. In his prayer in John 17, Jesus asked the Father not to take his people out of the world but to keep them from the evil one (John 17:15). Paul told new converts that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God (Acts 14:22). For most believers in history, and many today, that has meant prison, poverty or death; for others it means quieter pressures. Christ will return once, visibly, to gather his people and judge the world (Matthew 24:30–31; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). Until then, the promise is not escape but keeping.

Made them white in the blood. This is the sentence the whole chapter has been walking toward, and it is an impossible sentence on purpose. Blood does not whiten cloth; anyone who has tried to get blood out of a shirt knows what it does. There is one blood in the universe that does what no other can, and its effect is not a stain but a whiteness nothing else produces. The blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7); though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow (Isaiah 1:18). Israel washed their garments to meet God at Sinai (Exodus 19:10, 14); these have washed theirs in something better.

Their action, his detergent. And the verb is active: they washed. There is something a person must do, and the whole book is an appeal to repent, hold fast and come. But the sentence contains its own safeguard: they washed in the blood of the Lamb. The action is theirs; the detergent is entirely his. Nobody in that multitude contributed a drop of what makes them white, and their sufferings did not whiten them either. They washed their robes by trusting in his blood.

From where have they come? That is the answer to the elder’s second question, and it is the more important one. He asked not only who are these but from where have they come. They came from every nation on earth, and out of the great tribulation, and from under the executioner’s sword in some cases, and none of that is the answer. They came from the blood of the Lamb. Every person in a crowd nobody can count arrived there by the same road, and there is no second road, and no one of them can tell a better story about the journey than the person next to him.

Is it not narrow to say there is only one road? Every view of salvation has a narrow door somewhere. The moralist says only the good get in; the modern sceptic says only the open-minded do. The gospel’s door is narrow in a different way: the only qualification is to admit you have none, and to come to the Lamb. That is why the crowd that comes through it is the widest in history, from every nation, tribe, people and language (v. 9). A salvation won by goodness would be open only to the decent. A salvation given by blood is open to the thief, the persecutor and the respectable sinner alike.

How do I wash my robe in the Lamb’s blood? By coming to Christ as a sinner and trusting that his death was for you. That is how it begins: you admit that your own robe is stained beyond your power to clean, and you rest your whole weight on his sacrifice. And it continues, because the Christian keeps coming back to the same fountain: if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9). So when you sin this week, do not try to scrub the stain out yourself with good resolutions before you dare approach God. Go straight to the blood. It is the only thing that has ever made anyone white.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore they are before the throne of God, and serve him day and night in his temple; and he who sits on the throne will shelter them with his presence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. In the wilderness God’s glory dwelt in the tabernacle, a tent among his people, and he sheltered them with the pillar of cloud by day and fire by night (Exodus 40:34–38). Isaiah promised that the LORD would create a cloud by day and fire by night over Zion as a canopy and a shelter (Isaiah 4:5–6). John’s Gospel says the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, literally pitched his tent among us (John 1:14).

Therefore. The word carries the entire logic of the gospel. Not because they endured, though they did. Not because they were faithful under torture, though many were. Therefore: because of the washing in the previous verse, and because of nothing else, they are standing where they are standing.

Serve him in his temple. “Serve” is not general helpfulness but the service of worship, the word used of priests ministering in the sanctuary (Hebrews 8:5). In the temple in Jerusalem only priests entered the holy place, and only one man went behind the veil, once a year, with blood, having washed. Here a crowd from every nation on earth is inside, permanently, doing priestly work, in the inner shrine where God dwells. The promise of 1:6 has arrived: he made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father. In the new Jerusalem, God and the Lamb are the temple (21:22).

Day and night. It is the phrase used of the living creatures who never cease (4:8). But there is no night in the city at the end of this book (21:25; 22:5), so the expression is not measuring hours. It means without interruption: no fatigue, no distraction, no sin, no need to stop and earn a living, no Monday. Heaven’s service is not exhausting; it is perfect freedom and delight.

Shelter them with his presence. The English can only half carry this clause. The Greek is skēnōsei ep’ autous: literally, he will spread his tent over them. It is the word for the tabernacle, the tent God pitched in the middle of Israel’s camp so that he could live among them in the wilderness (Exodus 25:8; 40:34), the same word John used in the first chapter of his Gospel, and the word of 21:3, when the dwelling place of God is with man, and he will dwell with them.

Proximity, not distance. So the picture is not chiefly of protection from something. It is of nearness. God puts his tent over these people, the way a father pulls a blanket over a child, the way the cloud stood over the tabernacle in the desert. They are not being kept at a safe distance from the throne and defended; they are being covered by the one on it. The people who were driven out by persecution, who perhaps had no home, are given God himself as their home.

The same throne, two companies. Set that beside where the previous chapter ended. In 6:16 the great ones of the earth begged the mountains to fall on them and hide them from the face of him who is seated on the throne. Here, the same throne, the same one seated on it, and a crowd with no rank at all is being sheltered under him. The identical presence is the thing one company cannot bear to look at and the thing the other company lives inside. And the difference between the two, once again, is not in the people. It is in verse 14.

Will heaven be boring? Only to someone who imagines it as an endless church service he did not enjoy on earth. The service here is the joyful activity of people made perfect, in the presence of the most interesting being there is, God himself, whose glory is inexhaustible. Elsewhere Revelation speaks of reigning (22:5), of the glory of the nations brought in (21:26), and of a city with streets and a river. Service in Scripture includes worship, but it also includes work: Adam was put in the garden to work it (Genesis 2:15). Whatever heaven holds, it will not be less than the best of this life. Boredom is a symptom of a fallen heart, and it will not be there.

verseByVerse.quote: They shall hunger no more, neither thirst anymore; the sun shall not strike them, nor any scorching heat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. The words come almost directly from Isaiah 49:10, God’s promise to the exiles returning home. John takes the promise made to a people in exile and gives it to a multitude out of every nation. He sees the final fulfilment of the promise of a new exodus.

Hunger no more. The list is specific and bodily: hunger, thirst, sunstroke. These are not spiritual metaphors to the people first hearing them. The black horse rode out with a pair of scales in chapter 6 (6:5–6), and believers in Smyrna were poor in the beggar’s sense (2:9), very probably in part because of their faith. Hunger and thirst, the daily fears of the poor and the punishments of persecution, are over for ever. Jesus promised that whoever comes to him shall not hunger, and whoever believes in him shall never thirst (John 6:35), and believers taste it already in him.

Scorching heat. A slave working a field in Asia Minor in August knew precisely what scorching heat does to a man who cannot stop. The Psalm promises that the sun shall not strike you by day (Psalm 121:6), and in 16:8–9 the fourth bowl scorches the wicked with fire from the sun; the redeemed are spared.

Deliverance of the body. That plainness is doing theological work, and it cuts against an instinct most Christians have absorbed without noticing. Ask a congregation what heaven will be like and the answers come back weightless: light, peace, spirits, somewhere else. The Bible almost never talks that way. It promises a body that works, food, water, shade, a city with streets in it, and a Lamb who has to lead people to springs, which means there is somewhere to walk and something to arrive at. Many Greek thinkers wanted deliverance from the body. Scripture promises deliverance of it.

The one who hungered and thirsted. These promises can be made only because someone bore what they remove. Hunger, thirst and the sun on a labourer’s back belong to the ground God cursed after Adam’s sin: by the sweat of your face you shall eat bread (Genesis 3:17–19). Jesus walked into that curse. He was hungry in the wilderness (Matthew 4:2), weary at a well at noon and asking for a drink (John 4:6–7), and on the cross he said, I thirst (John 19:28). Christ became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), and that is why this book can say that one day nothing accursed will remain (22:3). Behind the words never again stands not a better climate but a substitute, who went without so that his people never will.

Why negatives? There is a reason the promises are stated as negatives: no hunger, no thirst, no striking sun. A negative is the only honest way to describe a condition nobody alive has experienced. No one can picture a body that never tires, because everybody reading this has been tired every day of his life. What can be pictured is the absence of a specific misery, and that is what John gives: not an abstraction, but the removal, one by one, of things the reader could name from this week.

Your own line in the verse. Take whatever is wearing you down: the diagnosis managed daily, the arithmetic at the end of the month that never quite works, the exhaustion that sleep no longer touches. Each is a hunger of some kind, and each has its own line in this verse. The promise is not that you will stop minding about them. It is that they will not be there.

Will we eat and drink in heaven? Scripture gives good reason to think so in the resurrection. The risen Jesus ate fish in front of his disciples (Luke 24:42–43), he spoke of drinking the fruit of the vine new in his Father’s kingdom (Matthew 26:29), and the end of the age is pictured as a feast, the marriage supper of the Lamb (19:9; Isaiah 25:6). We should not press details we are not given. But the hope of the Christian is not to become a ghost. It is to be raised in a body like Christ’s, on a renewed earth, where eating will be joy and not survival, and hunger will never come again.

On a Tuesday. A meal carried to a neighbour is a foretaste of the promise. Care for those who are hungry and thirsty now (Matthew 25:35), because the King counts what you do for the least of his brothers as done for him.

For worship. The God of this promise has pity on his people. He knows the empty stomach of the poor, the dry throat of the traveller and the heat on the labourer’s back, and he has sworn that none of it will follow them home. Every line of the verse names something taken away, because what takes its place is beyond our words: it is himself.

verseByVerse.quote: For the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be their shepherd, and he will guide them to springs of living water, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Psalm 23 begins, The LORD is my shepherd. Ezekiel promised that God himself would search for his sheep, and would set over them one shepherd, his servant David (Ezekiel 34:11–16, 23). Jesus said, I am the good shepherd; the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11). Isaiah promised that God will swallow up death for ever, and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces (Isaiah 25:8).

The Lamb will be their shepherd. The last verse of the chapter contains three promises, and the first of them is a sentence no one but John would have dared write. In the midst of the throne means at the centre, sharing God’s throne. Lambs are shepherded; they do not shepherd.

The third reversal. This is the third of the great reversals in this book: the Lion who is a Lamb (5:5–6), the Lamb who has wrath (6:16), and now the Lamb who is a Shepherd. Every one of them works the same way: the image that ought to be weak turns out to be the strong one, and the strength is of a kind nobody was looking for.

And the shepherd is one of us. Psalm 23, Ezekiel’s promise and the good shepherd all arrive at once here: the shepherd who leads this flock is the one who was himself led like a lamb to the slaughter (Isaiah 53:7). He knows what they have suffered because he suffered it. He is not directing the flock from a height; he is walking in front of it, and he has scars.

Springs of living water. Literally springs of waters of life: not a cistern, not a well that has to be drawn from, but water coming up out of the ground under its own pressure and not stopping. It is eternal life flowing from God himself, the fountain of living waters (Jeremiah 2:13), the offer he made to a woman at a well at noon (John 4:14) and cried out on the last day of the feast (John 7:37–39), and it is where this book will finish, with the river of the water of life flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb (22:1).

Every tear. Think about what that sentence requires. It requires that there be tears in the first place: the promise is not that nothing bad happened but that something is done about it afterwards. It requires that God knows which ones and whose: every tear, not the general average of human sorrow. And it requires that he does it himself. Not an angel with a cloth. Not time healing it. God, personally, close enough to touch a face, as a parent dries a child’s eyes. It is repeated in 21:4: death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore.

Take it as it is written. Anyone who has sat with somebody dying, or stood at a small grave, or gone on getting up in the morning after the worst thing, should take this verse exactly as it is written and not one degree weaker. The tears were real, and they were counted, and every one of them will be dealt with by the hand of God on a human face. And the hand doing it belongs to the Lamb who was slaughtered, who is the shepherd, who has come through death itself.

Will I remember my sorrows in heaven? Scripture does not say that our memories will be erased, and the Lamb’s own wounds suggest that the past is not simply deleted. But it will be transformed. The sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed (Romans 8:18), and what was once only pain will be seen as part of a story that ended in God’s glory and our joy. Joseph could say of his worst years that God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). In heaven every believer will be able to say that of everything, and say it without a tear.

What about loved ones who did not believe? This is the hardest question a grieving Christian asks, and Scripture does not answer every part of it. What it does promise is that God will wipe away every tear, which means that nothing, not even this, will spoil the joy of the redeemed. We will see then with perfect clarity the holiness and justice of God, and we will be wholly at one with him. Until then, do not presume to know the final state of anyone whose last hours you did not see, since God can save to the last breath, and do not let the question keep you from trusting his goodness. The Judge of all the earth will do right (Genesis 18:25).

The answer complete. The question at the end of chapter 6 was who can stand? Here is the answer, and it has taken seventeen verses: a crowd nobody can count, from every nation and tribe and people and language, sealed before the winds were let loose, washed in blood that makes cloth white, standing before the throne with palm branches, sheltered under the tent of God, led by a Lamb to water that never runs dry, with a Father wiping their faces. They can stand. And there is nothing in the list that any of them did.

On a Tuesday. Read this verse to someone who is grieving this week, slowly, without explaining it away. And if you are the one weeping, do not be ashamed of the tears. They are not a failure of faith; they are the very thing God has promised personally to deal with. Let the Lamb shepherd you now, through his word, his people and his table, to the springs he has already opened.

7.text: <sup>1</sup>After this I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth, holding back the four winds of the earth, that no wind might blow on earth or sea or against any tree.<sup>2</sup>Then I saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun, with the seal of the living God, and he called with a loud voice to the four angels who had been given power to harm earth and sea,<sup>3</sup>saying, “Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees, until we have sealed the servants of our God on their foreheads.”<sup>4</sup>And I heard the number of the sealed, 144,000, sealed from every tribe of the sons of Israel:<sup>5</sup>12,000 from the tribe of Judah were sealed, 12,000 from the tribe of Reuben, 12,000 from the tribe of Gad,<sup>6</sup>12,000 from the tribe of Asher, 12,000 from the tribe of Naphtali, 12,000 from the tribe of Manasseh,<sup>7</sup>12,000 from the tribe of Simeon, 12,000 from the tribe of Levi, 12,000 from the tribe of Issachar,<sup>8</sup>12,000 from the tribe of Zebulun, 12,000 from the tribe of Joseph, 12,000 from the tribe of Benjamin were sealed.<sup>9</sup>After this I looked, and behold, a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palm branches in their hands,<sup>10</sup>and crying out with a loud voice, “Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!”<sup>11</sup>And all the angels were standing around the throne and around the elders and the four living creatures, and they fell on their faces before the throne and worshiped God,<sup>12</sup>saying, “Amen! Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving and honor and power and might be to our God forever and ever! Amen.”<sup>13</sup>Then one of the elders addressed me, saying, “Who are these, clothed in white robes, and from where have they come?”<sup>14</sup>I said to him, “Sir, you know.” And he said to me, “These are the ones coming out of the great tribulation. They have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.<sup>15</sup>Therefore they are before the throne of God, and serve him day and night in his temple; and he who sits on the throne will shelter them with his presence.<sup>16</sup>They shall hunger no more, neither thirst anymore; the sun shall not strike them, nor any scorching heat.<sup>17</sup>For the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be their shepherd, and he will guide them to springs of living water, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.”

8.title: The Seventh Seal and the First Four Trumpets
8.overview:
The seventh seal releases no horseman and no catastrophe. It releases silence: heaven, after four chapters of unbroken praise, holds its breath for about half an hour, because God is about to act.

Out of the silence, seven trumpets are given to seven angels. Before they sound, another angel offers incense with the prayers of all the saints, and then throws fire from the same altar on the earth. This is the answer to the martyrs’ cry of 6:10: the prayers of God’s people are not lost, and the trumpets are part of how he answers them.

The first four trumpets echo the plagues on Egypt (hail and fire, water turned to blood, darkness), each limited to a third. As then, God judges an oppressing world to expose its false gods and to bring his people out; these judgements are warnings, not the end.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The Seventh Seal and the Golden Censer
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1: the last seal is opened, and heaven falls silent for about half an hour, the hush Scripture commands before God acts (Habakkuk 2:20; Zephaniah 1:7). Verse 2: seven angels who stand before God are given seven trumpets, the second of the book’s three sevens.

Verses 3–5: before a trumpet sounds, another angel offers much incense with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar, and the smoke rises before God. Then he fills the same censer with fire from the altar and throws it on the earth, with thunder, lightning and an earthquake. The trumpets are the answer to the church’s praying.
verseByVerse.theology:
Prayer and the Censer

Heaven falls silent, and the prayers of all the saints rise with much incense given at the altar. Then the same censer is filled with fire and thrown to the earth: the trumpets are God’s answer to his people’s prayers.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The martyrs’ “How long?” is being answered.

Now: Prayers that seem to do nothing are gathered, perfected, and answered in God’s time.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Lamb opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Revelation 8 opens the seventh seal and begins the seven trumpets. When the last seal is broken, heaven falls silent for half an hour (v. 1). Seven angels receive seven trumpets, and another angel offers incense with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar (vv. 2–4); then he throws fire from the altar on the earth, with thunder, lightning and earthquake: the saints’ prayers are being answered in judgement (v. 5). The first four trumpets strike a third of creation: the land, the sea, the fresh water through a star called Wormwood, and the sun, moon and stars (vv. 6–12). An eagle cries woe, woe, woe because of the three trumpets still to come (v. 13). The trumpets echo the plagues on Egypt: partial warnings, so that people may repent, sent in answer to the prayers of God’s suffering people.

The setting. Trumpets in the Old Testament announced God’s presence at Sinai (Exodus 19:16), summoned Israel to worship and war (Numbers 10:1–10), brought down the walls of Jericho (Joshua 6:16–20), and warned of coming judgement (Joel 2:1; Ezekiel 33:3–6). The trumpets of Revelation recall the ten plagues on Egypt: hail and fire, water turned to blood, darkness, locusts. As the plagues judged Pharaoh’s Egypt and freed Israel, so the trumpets judge the world that persecutes God’s people, while his sealed servants are protected (9:4).

The seventh seal. The scroll is now fully open. Everything in this book has been building to the opening of the last seal, and what happens first is nothing. No rider, no voice, no announcement. Heaven stops. What does the scroll contain? The seventh seal seems to unfold into the seven trumpets, as the seventh trumpet unfolds into the seven bowls. Each series ends at the final judgement, and then the next goes over the same ground with greater intensity.

Silence in heaven. The four living creatures have been saying holy, holy, holy day and night without ceasing (4:8). Myriads of myriads of angels have been crying Worthy is the Lamb (5:12). A multitude nobody could number has been shouting that salvation belongs to God (7:10). All of it goes quiet, and John has nothing to write down.

Why the silence? Three explanations fit together. Awe, first, and this is the most probable: it is the silence Scripture repeatedly commands before God acts in judgement. The LORD is in his holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before him (Habakkuk 2:20). Be silent before the Lord GOD, for the day of the LORD is near (Zephaniah 1:7). Be silent, all flesh, before the LORD, for he has roused himself from his holy dwelling (Zechariah 2:13). In all three the silence is the hush before a verdict, and in all three what follows is God rising to act. Prayer, second: in the temple, incense was offered while the people prayed outside, the whole multitude praying at the hour of incense (Luke 1:10), and what happens immediately after this silence is an angel offering incense with the prayers of all the saints. On that reading heaven falls silent so that the prayers of the church can be heard (vv. 3–4). And third, the stillness before a storm: judgement is about to fall. Either way, the silence is not empty. It is loaded. And here God’s holiness is felt rather than defined: the God who is about to judge is so pure and so great that even sinless creatures, who have praised him without a pause, stop and say nothing at all.

About half an hour. The vagueness of about in a book of exact numbers is striking; John is describing what it felt like. Half an hour of silence in a room is close to unbearable, far longer than the pauses of almost any human ceremony. Whatever is coming, heaven considers it worth stopping everything for.

The hand on the last seal. In chapter 5 no one in heaven or on earth could open the scroll, and John wept, until the Lamb who had been slain took it (5:9). Every seal since has been broken by that hand, and so is this one. The silence is not the hush before some unknown force. It is heaven holding its breath while the crucified Lamb carries God’s purpose for the world into its next stage, so the history about to unfold in the trumpets is not out of control.

What do I do when God is silent to my prayers? There is something here for the believer who has been on the other end of a silence: who has prayed for a year about the same thing and heard nothing back, and drawn the natural conclusion. This verse does not explain that experience away, but it does say something about the nature of heaven’s quiet. The silence here is not absence and it is not indifference. It is the pause of a court before sentence, and it comes immediately before the prayers of the saints are carried up and then answered. God being quiet and God being idle are not the same thing, and this half hour is the proof. So keep praying through the silence. Tell him honestly that he seems silent, as the Psalms do (Psalm 22:2). And hold on to what he has said, in his word, while you wait for what he has not yet said.

Should our worship include silence? It is wise and biblical to make room for it. Be still, and know that I am God (Psalm 46:10). Much modern worship, and much modern life, is afraid of quiet, filling every gap with music or words. A pause after the reading of Scripture, or before confession, or at the Lord’s Table, is not dead time. It is a way of saying with the whole of heaven that God is about to speak or act, and that we have stopped to listen. Silence is not a form of worship that needs special techniques; it is simply reverence with the noise turned off.

For worship. Heaven’s praise has never stopped for lack of things to say about him, and here it stops because nothing said would be enough. He needs none of our noise to be glorious. He is the Judge who has heard every prayer and is rising to answer, and the half hour of heaven’s quiet is full of him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw the seven angels who stand before God, and seven trumpets were given to them. And another angel came and stood at the altar with a golden censer, and he was given much incense to offer with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar before the throne, and the smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the saints, rose before God from the hand of the angel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. In the tabernacle and temple a golden altar of incense stood in the Holy Place, before the curtain of the Most Holy Place (Exodus 30:1–10). Every morning and evening a priest burned incense on it (Exodus 30:7–8), while the people prayed outside (Luke 1:8–10). The rising smoke pictured prayer going up to God: let my prayer be counted as incense before you (Psalm 141:2). Jewish tradition named seven archangels who stand before God, among them Gabriel, who said, I am Gabriel, who stand in the presence of God (Luke 1:19).
