The seven angels who stand before God. The definite article suggests a particular known order, angels of the highest rank, ready to serve. The trumpets were given: they come from God. They are the second of the book’s three sevens.

What a trumpet meant. Beyond Sinai, Jericho and the alarm of war, a trumpet announced the year of Jubilee, when debts were cancelled and slaves went free (Leviticus 25:9), and it will sound at the end, when the dead are raised (1 Corinthians 15:52; 1 Thessalonians 4:16). A trumpet means: attention, something is about to happen, and you cannot sleep through it.

A golden censer. But before a single trumpet is blown, the vision stops and does something else entirely. The censer is a firepan for carrying burning coals and incense. This is the fulfilment of 5:8, where the elders held golden bowls of incense which John explained were the prayers of the saints. Now the incense is being burned.

The prayers of all the saints. Three details matter. The first is all the saints: every believer, not only the martyrs, not only the prayers that were well phrased or persevered in longest. All of them, which includes prayers prayed by people who did not know how to pray, in the dark, badly, and then forgot about.

Much incense, given. The second detail is that the incense is given to him. The prayers do not go up on their own account. Something is added to them at the altar, from the other side, making them acceptable and fragrant before God. Honest prayers are not impressive; the mind wanders and the words run out. This verse says they are not offered as they left the mouth.

The golden altar. In heaven the altar is right before the throne. In the earthly temple the altar of incense stood outside the curtain, and only the high priest went beyond it once a year. Here there is no curtain. The prayers of God’s people go straight into his presence.

Rose before God. The third detail is the direction. They arrive. The prayers of persecuted believers in small churches across Asia rise to the throne of the universe, not as a general principle but as a thing happening in front of a man’s eyes. Not one is lost, and the cry of the martyrs, How long? (6:10), is among them.

Something has occurred. Consider what that does to the ordinary experience of praying. A believer kneels by a bed at eleven at night, says something short and inadequate about a son who is not speaking to him, and gets up feeling that nothing has occurred. On the evidence of this verse, something has occurred. The words went up. They were mixed with much incense from the hand of another, and they stood before God, and God is not deaf and does not mislay things.

Where Christians differ: should we pray to angels or saints, or through them? Roman Catholic and Orthodox traditions have used passages like this to support asking angels and departed saints to present our prayers to God. This commentary’s view: the angel serves as part of the heavenly worship, offering the prayers before God, but he is not prayed to, and the saints on earth do not address him. Scripture teaches that there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5), and that believers may come boldly to the throne of grace through him (Hebrews 4:14–16). The incense that makes our prayers acceptable is the intercession and merit of Christ, our great High Priest, who always lives to intercede for us (Hebrews 7:25). Pray to God alone, through Christ alone.

Is this angel Christ? Some have taken him so, since he does a high priest’s work. But John calls him simply another angel, and Revelation never calls Christ an angel; elsewhere in the book Christ is the Lamb on the throne, receiving worship, not a servant at the altar. The more likely reading is that he is an angelic servant in the heavenly worship, showing that the saints’ prayers rise before God and are answered in his judgements. Yet the reality the picture points to is Christ’s own intercession: it is because of him that any prayer of ours is accepted at all.

Why do my prayers need incense? Because even our best prayers are mixed with sin, distraction and self-interest, and a holy God could not receive them on their own merits. That is not a reason to stop praying; it is the reason Christ prays for us. Whatever you ask in my name, Jesus said, this I will do (John 14:13). To pray in his name is not to add a formula at the end, but to come trusting that he has made you welcome and that his perfect intercession covers your imperfect words. The Spirit, too, helps us in our weakness, interceding with groanings too deep for words (Romans 8:26). Your prayer does not have to be good to be heard. It has to be offered through him.

On a Tuesday. Do not wait until you can pray well. Pray the short, tired prayer at the end of the day, especially for persecuted believers, and believe that it arrived. If it helps, keep a simple list of what you have asked, and look back at it in six months: many of the prayers you forgot, God has remembered.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar and threw it on the earth, and there were peals of thunder, rumblings, flashes of lightning, and an earthquake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. In Ezekiel a man clothed in linen is told to fill his hands with burning coals from between the cherubim and scatter them over Jerusalem in judgement (Ezekiel 10:2). The coal from the altar that touched Isaiah’s lips brought cleansing (Isaiah 6:6–7); here fire from the altar brings judgement.

Fire from the altar. And then the verse turns, and it is a surprise. The censer that a moment ago was carrying the prayers of all the saints up to God is now filled with fire from that same altar. The same altar is the source of both.

Threw it on the earth. What went up as incense comes back as fire. The trumpets that follow are the answer to the church’s praying, and the answer arrives in the form of judgement on the world that made the praying necessary. The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working (James 5:16).

How long is answered. Under the altar in chapter 6, the martyrs asked how long before God would judge and avenge their blood (6:10). They were told to rest a little longer, and this is the little longer coming to an end: the seven trumpets are the answer.

Operating the levers from their knees. Prayer, in this book, is one of the means by which the judgements of God are set in motion. The most powerless people in the Roman empire, slaves, widows, boycotted tradesmen, prisoners awaiting a hearing, were moving history from their knees the whole time, without seeing a single result. The commonest objection a Christian raises against his own prayer life is that it appears to do nothing, and this verse answers it with a picture rather than an argument. The prayer that seemed to evaporate went into a golden bowl. The bowl went to an altar. The altar had fire on it. And the fire came back down.

Thunder, lightning and earthquake. These are the Sinai signs from 4:5, where they came out of the throne, the signs of God’s throne and presence, now with an earthquake added. John uses the list twice more, each time more intensely, at 11:19 and 16:18–21, and each series of judgements ends with it, showing that each reaches the final judgement. The earthquake is his standing signal that God has begun to act.

The kingdom of his Christ. And what are the trumpets answering? Not private grudges. The souls under the altar had been slain for the word of God and for the witness they had borne (6:9), the testimony of Jesus for which John himself was on Patmos (1:9), and the prayer the church has prayed since its Lord taught it is your kingdom come. So the fire thrown on the earth is God taking the side of those who took Christ’s side. The trumpets are heading somewhere, and the seventh will say where: the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever (11:15). Every prayer in the censer was in the end a prayer for that, and every one is answered when it comes.

What it does not mean. This does not mean Christians should pray for the destruction of their enemies. We pray for God’s kingdom to come, which includes the defeat of evil, and we pray for our enemies’ repentance. God decides how to answer, and his judgements are always just.

If God is sovereign, why does he need our prayers? He does not need them in the sense of being unable to act without them. But he has chosen to work through them, as he works through preaching and through all the means he appoints. The God who decreed the end also decreed the prayers that would lead to it, and he gives his people the dignity of taking part. That is why Elijah prayed for rain after God had promised it (1 Kings 18:1, 41–45; James 5:17–18). Sovereignty does not make prayer pointless; it makes it effective, because we are asking the one who actually governs the world, not a God who is hoping things work out.

What should I pray for, then? Begin where Jesus taught us: hallowed be your name, your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven (Matthew 6:9–10). Those three petitions contain everything in this verse, the defeat of evil, the vindication of God’s people and the coming of his reign. Then pray for particular persecuted believers you have heard about, for the salvation of the lost, including those who oppose the gospel, and for justice where it has been denied. Bring your own needs too; he cares about them. But let the big prayers have a place, because they are the ones the golden bowls are full of.

On a Tuesday. History is shaped not only by governments and armies but by the prayers of God’s people. The midweek prayer meeting can look small and pointless from the inside. Remember the censer. Ten tired people in a church hall praying for the persecuted church are doing something that echoes in thunder.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 6–12: the first four trumpets strike the created order, each within a limit of a third. Hail and fire mixed with blood burn the land; something like a burning mountain turns the sea to blood and wrecks the ships; a star called Wormwood makes the fresh water bitter, and many die; and the sun, moon and stars are partly darkened. The pattern is the plagues on Egypt.

Verse 13: an eagle flying overhead cries woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth, one woe for each trumpet still to come. The remaining three will fall on people.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Trumpets Are the Plagues of Egypt

Hail and fire, water turned to blood, bitterness and darkness strike earth, sea, fresh water and sky, each limited to a third. As in Egypt, the aim is to expose false gods and bring God’s people out.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: For coastal churches, a stricken sea meant a stricken economy.

Now: Do not decode these as headlines; see in them the failure of every false security, and the warning to repent.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the seven angels who had the seven trumpets prepared to blow them. The first angel blew his trumpet, and there followed hail and fire, mixed with blood, and these were thrown upon the earth. And a third of the earth was burned up, and a third of the trees were burned up, and all green grass was burned up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. The seventh plague on Egypt was hail mixed with fire, which struck down every plant and broke every tree of the field (Exodus 9:23–25). Joel speaks of blood and fire and columns of smoke before the day of the LORD (Joel 2:30).

Prepared to blow them. One verse of pure anticipation. Everything is ordered and deliberate. And then the first sounds, and what follows is the plagues of Egypt happening again on a larger stage.

The plagues of Egypt again. That parallel governs the whole trumpet sequence. The first trumpet brings hail and fire, the seventh plague (Exodus 9:23–25). The second turns a third of the sea to blood, the first plague (Exodus 7:20–21). The fourth darkens the lights, the ninth plague (Exodus 10:21–23). The fifth trumpet will bring locusts (Exodus 10:12–15), and the sixth will end with people refusing to repent, exactly as Pharaoh did.

Why Egypt? The point of the parallel is not decoration. The plagues on Egypt were not random cruelty; they had two purposes, both stated in Exodus. They were aimed at the gods of Egypt: on all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgements (Exodus 12:12), and many have seen in the plagues blows at the Nile, the sun and other things Egypt worshipped. And they were aimed at getting a people out: let my people go. So when John dresses the trumpets in the clothes of the exodus, he is telling seven small congregations that the empire grinding them is Egypt, that the God who broke Egypt is not retired, and that the purpose of what is coming is the same as then: to expose the gods that cannot save, and to bring his people out.

This time the Lamb comes first. In Egypt the plagues fell first, and the lamb came at the end, on the night its blood marked the doors. In Revelation the order is reversed. Before a single trumpet sounds, John has seen the Lamb standing as though slain, and heard heaven sing that by his blood he ransomed a people and made them a kingdom and priests (5:6, 9–10), the echo of what God said to Israel at Sinai after the exodus (Exodus 19:6). Paul says it outright: Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7). So the trumpets fall on a world in which the decisive deliverance has already happened. The new exodus does not wait on the plagues. It was won at the cross, and it ends with the redeemed standing beside a sea of glass, singing the song of Moses and the song of the Lamb (15:2–3).

Hail and fire, mixed with blood. Like the plague on Egypt, but worse: blood is added. And they were thrown, a divine passive (the Bible’s way of saying God acts without naming him): God throws them.

A third. The seals struck a quarter (6:8); the trumpets strike a third; the bowls will strike everything (16). Ezekiel spoke of judgement on Jerusalem by thirds (Ezekiel 5:2, 12). The judgements escalate in stages, and the escalation is the argument: these are not the end. They are warnings that get louder because they are not being heard, and chapter 9 will say so in as many words: the rest of mankind did not repent (9:20). All green grass perhaps means all the grass in the third that is burned.

A fraction is a mercy. Two thirds of the earth is not burned. Somebody is holding the line at a third, and the same hand that holds it wrote the number down. Judgement that stops short is a warning that is still waiting for an answer.

Where Christians differ: are the trumpets literal events? Some read the trumpets as literal future events, perhaps nuclear war or asteroid strikes, and they rightly insist that God’s judgements are real and not mere ideas. Preterists see them in the Jewish war of AD 66 to 70. Historicists match each trumpet to an event in church history (invasions of the Roman Empire by Goths, Vandals and others). This commentary’s view: the trumpets are symbolic pictures of God’s judgements on a rebellious world throughout the age between Christ’s comings, drawn from the plagues of Egypt. They include natural disasters and ecological catastrophes, which are real and recur through history, as warnings to repent. Their purpose is stated in 9:20–21: to call people to turn from idols. They are not a timeline to be decoded, but they are real, and they may also intensify before the end.

Not from the newspaper. Generation after generation has matched these verses to its own headlines, often with great confidence, and so far always wrongly. The images are quarried from Exodus, not from the newspaper. What is permanent is the argument: the created order turns against a humanity in rebellion against its Maker, the things people depend on fail them, and none of it happens outside the throne room.

If God burns the earth in judgement, should Christians care for the environment? Yes. The earth is the LORD’s (Psalm 24:1), and Adam was set in the garden to work it and keep it (Genesis 2:15). That mandate has never been withdrawn. The fact that God judges creation because of human sin is not permission for us to abuse it; if anything, it shows how seriously God takes what happens to his world. Christians care for creation not because they think they can save the planet, but because it belongs to God and he means to renew it. Look after it as a steward looks after his master’s estate, knowing the master is coming back.

When a wildfire or a storm destroys a town, is that a trumpet? In the broad sense, yes: every disaster in a fallen world is a trumpet blast, a warning that the world is not as it should be and that life is short. Jesus said so when a tower fell on eighteen people: unless you repent, you will all likewise perish (Luke 13:4–5). But we are not told which disaster answers which sin, and Christians suffer them too. The right response is to grieve with the bereaved, help generously and practically, examine our own hearts, and point people to the only shelter that no fire can reach.
verseByVerse.note: The trumpet plagues echo the plagues on Egypt, but each strikes only a third — judgment still held back.

verseByVerse.quote: The second angel blew his trumpet, and something like a great mountain, burning with fire, was thrown into the sea, and a third of the sea became blood. A third of the living creatures in the sea died, and a third of the ships were destroyed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. The first plague on Egypt turned the Nile to blood, so that the fish died (Exodus 7:20–21). Jeremiah calls Babylon a destroying mountain, which God will roll down from the crags and make a burnt mountain (Jeremiah 51:25). In AD 79 the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in Italy buried Pompeii, and stories of a burning mountain and the sea would still have been remembered by John’s readers.

Something like a great mountain. The wording hesitates: John is describing what he has no vocabulary for, and he says so rather than pretending. The image may suggest a volcanic eruption, or a falling empire like Babylon, since a mountain in prophetic language is often a kingdom: immovable, dominating the landscape, permanent. It is not a prediction of a particular volcano or meteor. And the sea becomes blood, as the Nile did, on a greater scale.

A third of the ships. For the seven churches on the coast of Asia the sea was not scenery. It was the economy: trade, food, transport. Ephesus and Smyrna were harbours. Rome’s grain came from Egypt by ship, and nearly every luxury on the list that chapter 18 will read out over the fall of Babylon came by sea. A third of the ships destroyed is a commercial collapse, and the merchants of the earth, who in chapter 18 will weep because no one buys their cargo any more (18:11, 17–19), discover that the system they trusted was never load-bearing.

The sea in this book. And the sea carries a further weight. It is where the beast comes from (13:1). It is the ancient image of chaos, restless and untameable, which is why the throne room has a sea of glass, like crystal, still and calm before God (4:6), and why the new creation is announced with the words and the sea was no more (21:1). The second trumpet strikes the thing the world sails on and the thing the beast rises out of, and does it with a measured third.

Another mountain. In the prophets a mountain is a kingdom, and this one burns and goes down into the sea. But Scripture has another mountain. Daniel saw a stone cut out by no human hand strike the great image of the world’s empires and become a great mountain that filled the whole earth, the kingdom the God of heaven sets up that shall never be destroyed (Daniel 2:34–35, 44). Jesus spoke of himself as that stone (Luke 20:17–18), and this book shows where his mountain stands: the Lamb on Mount Zion with his people (14:1). What does that mean for a believer watching powers fall? Every empire the world builds is a mountain that can be thrown into the sea. The kingdom of Christ is the one mountain that grows, and the people on it are not going under.

What has any of this to do with me? A working reader will ask it, and it should be answered rather than avoided. The answer is in what gets hit. The trumpets do not fall on temples and armies. They fall on the earth a man farms, the sea a man trades on, the water a man drinks and the light a man works by. God’s judgements in this chapter land on the ordinary infrastructure of confidence: the things that make it possible to believe that tomorrow will be much like today. Anyone who has watched a business fail, or a pension shrink in a crash he did not cause, has met the second trumpet in miniature. The point is not that such an event is a punishment aimed at that person; Scripture is careful about that (Luke 13:4–5). The point is what it reveals. Every one of these systems is holding up somebody’s confidence, and every one of them can be taken down by a third in a single afternoon. The only thing this book has shown that cannot be taken down is the throne, and it was shown first, on purpose, before any of this began.

Is it wrong, then, to save, invest or run a business? No. Scripture commends work, diligence and wise provision (Proverbs 6:6–8; 1 Timothy 5:8), and trade is part of the ordinary good life God gives. What this trumpet warns against is trust: as for the rich in this present age, charge them not to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17). Use money; do not lean on it. Be generous with it, because generosity is the surest sign that your heart is not anchored to the ships.

For worship. He made the sea and set its bounds. The ancient world feared it as the home of chaos, and the God of this verse is not afraid of it at all. In the flesh he walked on its waves, and with a rebuke he made its storm lie down, and told his terrified friends, take heart; it is I. The ships of every empire can go down together. The one who stood in that boat cannot be moved, and no one he holds will sink.

verseByVerse.quote: The third angel blew his trumpet, and a great star fell from heaven, blazing like a torch, and it fell on a third of the rivers and on the springs of water. The name of the star is Wormwood. A third of the waters became wormwood, and many people died from the water, because it had been made bitter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Wormwood is a shrub of the Middle East with an intensely bitter taste, related to the plant used to make absinthe. In the Old Testament it pictures bitterness, sorrow and God’s judgement: I will feed this people with bitter food, and give them poisonous water to drink (Jeremiah 9:15; 23:15; Lamentations 3:15, 19). Amos accuses those who turn justice to wormwood and cast down righteousness to the earth (Amos 5:7). At Marah God made bitter water sweet for Israel (Exodus 15:23–25); here, sweet water is made bitter. Isaiah describes the king of Babylon as a day star fallen from heaven (Isaiah 14:12).

A great star. In Revelation stars can represent angels (1:20; 9:1). This may be an angel carrying out God’s judgement, or simply a burning, meteor-like object. It falls on fresh water this time, rivers and springs, the thing no settlement can exist without.

Wormwood. The name tells us its meaning: bitterness. Those who turn away from the living water of God, and drink the poisoned waters of idolatry, find life bitter. My people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water (Jeremiah 2:13; 9:13–15).

Many people died. This is the first trumpet where the text says plainly that people died. Wormwood is not normally deadly; the image is intensified. The waters of life become the waters of death.

The judgement matches the crime. That line in Amos is the key to the trumpet. In Amos, men make justice bitter, and here God makes their water bitter. A society that has poisoned what should have refreshed people finds its own wells undrinkable. This is the shape of divine judgement throughout Scripture: not an arbitrary penalty attached to an offence, but the offence itself, served back.

Springs of living water. Set this trumpet beside the chapter before it. There the Lamb at the centre of the throne leads his people to springs of living water (7:17); here a third of the springs of the earth are made bitter. The contrast is the book’s own. People who forsake the fountain, as Jeremiah put it, end with wells that poison them, and the fountain is offered again in a person: on the last day of the feast Jesus stood up and cried out, If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink (John 7:37). What does that mean? Water stands for life, the thing no one can do without, and the world’s own springs, its pleasures, systems and hopes, can turn bitter overnight. The life Christ gives does not come from the world’s springs at all, so no star falling on them can touch it.

What it does not mean. Wormwood is not a code word for a specific modern disaster, such as the Chernobyl nuclear accident. It has been widely repeated that Chernobyl is the Ukrainian word for wormwood and that the 1986 disaster is therefore this verse. The linguistic claim is roughly right, since the name relates to a variety of the plant, and the interpretation is not: on that logic the verse would have nothing to say to the churches John actually wrote to, or to any generation between them and 1986. Revelation’s symbols draw on the Old Testament, not on modern place names.

What if I am the one who has been made bitter? There is a plain application here for anyone in that condition. A person can live for decades on water that has been made bitter, by an injustice never put right, by a marriage that went wrong, by a betrayal nobody was ever called to account for, and go on functioning, and never taste anything sweet again. Scripture takes that condition seriously enough to name a trumpet after it, and warns that a root of bitterness springs up and causes trouble, and by it many become defiled (Hebrews 12:15). The way out is not to pretend the wrong did not happen, but to hand it to God the Judge, as the martyrs did (6:10), and to drink from a different spring. The God who made the waters of Marah sweet can do the same in a soul. It is often slow, and it usually begins with honest prayer about the very thing that poisoned the well.
verseByVerse.note: Wormwood is a bitter plant, used by the prophets as a picture of bitter judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: The fourth angel blew his trumpet, and a third of the sun was struck, and a third of the moon, and a third of the stars, so that a third of their light might be darkened, and a third of the day might be kept from shining, and likewise a third of the night. Then I looked, and I heard an eagle crying with a loud voice as it flew directly overhead, "Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth, at the blasts of the other trumpets that the three angels are about to blow!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. The ninth plague on Egypt was darkness that could be felt over the land for three days, so that no one rose from his place, though the people of Israel had light where they lived (Exodus 10:21–23). God created the sun, moon and stars on the fourth day, to give light and to mark times (Genesis 1:14–18). The Egyptians worshipped the sun god, so the darkness was a judgement on their gods. Hosea says, set the trumpet to your lips, for one like a vulture (or eagle) is over the house of the LORD (Hosea 8:1).

A third of the sun was struck. The word for struck shares its root with the word for plague. God strikes the lights he created, and the world that worships created things instead of the Creator (Romans 1:25) loses part of the light it takes for granted.

A third of their light. The word third occurs five times in one verse. The repetition is not clumsy writing; it is the drumbeat of the whole sequence, and somebody is counting. As the first four seals form a set, so do the first four trumpets, and they strike the natural world: land, sea, fresh water, sky.

The sun god cannot keep his lamp lit. The gods being judged in the ninth plague were unmistakable: Egypt worshipped the sun. Ra was the head of the pantheon, and Pharaoh was his son. To darken the sun over Egypt was to demonstrate publicly that the chief god of the empire could not keep his own lamp lit. The same argument runs in the province of Asia. The emperor was often associated with the sun; Nero had himself portrayed with rays around his head. And the heavenly bodies were what the ancient world steered by, planted by and read its fortunes by. The fourth trumpet strikes the calendar, the compass and the horoscope in a single stroke.

Reliable light. What is being taken away is not light in general but reliable light: the confidence that the day will behave as days have always behaved. Total darkness announces itself as a catastrophe. A partial failure of the light is worse in its way, because it says that the machinery is not as fixed as everyone assumed. That strikes at one of the heart’s favourite idols, control. The steady round of day and night was always God’s promise (Genesis 8:22), never humanity’s achievement, and the fourth trumpet reminds a self-sufficient world whose gift it was.

Darkness at noon. Darkening the day was the prophets’ sign of the day of the LORD: I will make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in broad daylight (Amos 8:9). Once in history it happened at noon, while one man hung on a hill outside Jerusalem. From the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land until the ninth hour (Matthew 27:45), while Jesus hung on the cross and cried out that God had forsaken him. The darkness of God’s judgement fell, in full, on his Son, in the place of everyone who trusts him. The fourth trumpet’s darkness is partial and a warning. The darkness at the cross was the real thing, and it was borne once by the Son so that it need never fall on those who belong to him.

An eagle crying. The chapter ends with a warning nobody could sleep through. The Greek word covers both the eagle and the vulture, and both associations are working: the eagle was the standard of the Roman legions, and the vulture is the bird of prey circling over what is about to die. Jesus used the same ambiguity: wherever the corpse is, there the vultures will gather (Matthew 24:28). Directly overhead is mid-heaven, the highest point of the sky, where everyone on the ground can see and hear.

Woe, woe, woe. A cry of grief and doom: three woes, one for each of the three trumpets still to come (9:12; 11:14). And the phrase the eagle uses becomes a technical term in this book: those who dwell on the earth. It occurs about ten times, and it almost never means simply everyone alive. It means unbelievers in rebellion against God, people with no other citizenship who want none (6:10; 13:8). The saints in this book live on the earth too. They are never called earth-dwellers.

The other trumpets. The last three will be worse, and the escalation is explicit. Four trumpets have struck the whole created order. The remaining three will fall on people directly, with demonic torment and death, and chapter 9 opens the shaft of the bottomless pit.

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “an angel flying” instead of “an eagle flying”. The two Greek words (angelou and aetou) look somewhat alike. The best manuscripts read “eagle”.

A mercy in the shape of a threat. So the eagle’s cry is announced in advance, in daylight, at the top of the sky, in a loud voice, to people who still have time to do something about it. Every warning in Revelation is an act of patience, and the God who sends an eagle across the sky before the fifth trumpet is not a God who wants anybody caught unawares.

Can a Christian be an earth-dweller? Not in John’s sense, because the phrase describes where a person’s heart lives, not where his feet stand. But Christians can drift toward it, living as though this world were all there is, anxious about what earth-dwellers are anxious about and hoping for what they hope for. The test is simple and searching: if everything in this chapter happened, the land, the sea, the water and the light, what would you have left? If that question frightens you, the fear itself is a sign that your heart is already turning homeward, and Christ casts out no one who comes to him (John 6:37). Our citizenship is in heaven, and from it we await a Saviour (Philippians 3:20). Live here fully, love your neighbours, work hard; but keep your passport in the right place.

Are we near the last trumpets? On the reading followed here, the trumpets sound throughout the age between Christ’s comings, and they may grow louder as the end approaches; so in one sense every generation hears them. We are not told the date of the end, and Jesus said that no one knows the day or the hour (Matthew 24:36). What we are told is that the end is always near enough to matter. The right question is not how close the last trumpet is, but whether you are ready if it sounded tonight.

On a Tuesday. There is usually someone we have meant to talk to about Christ for years. The eagle shouts in daylight so that no one is caught by surprise. Someone once warned us, and Christ brought us in; now his Spirit gives his church power to do the same, with tears (Acts 1:8).

For worship. He made the sun and moon and stars on the fourth day, and he can dim them with a word, while the gods men worship go dark with them. He alone is the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change (James 1:17): the sun may falter, and he never does. In the city to come there is no need of sun or moon, for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb (21:23).

8.text: <sup>1</sup>When the Lamb opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.<sup>2</sup>Then I saw the seven angels who stand before God, and seven trumpets were given to them.<sup>3</sup>And another angel came and stood at the altar with a golden censer, and he was given much incense to offer with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar before the throne,<sup>4</sup>and the smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the saints, rose before God from the hand of the angel.<sup>5</sup>Then the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar and threw it on the earth, and there were peals of thunder, rumblings, flashes of lightning, and an earthquake.<sup>6</sup>Now the seven angels who had the seven trumpets prepared to blow them.<sup>7</sup>The first angel blew his trumpet, and there followed hail and fire, mixed with blood, and these were thrown upon the earth. And a third of the earth was burned up, and a third of the trees were burned up, and all green grass was burned up.<sup>8</sup>The second angel blew his trumpet, and something like a great mountain, burning with fire, was thrown into the sea, and a third of the sea became blood.<sup>9</sup>A third of the living creatures in the sea died, and a third of the ships were destroyed.<sup>10</sup>The third angel blew his trumpet, and a great star fell from heaven, blazing like a torch, and it fell on a third of the rivers and on the springs of water.<sup>11</sup>The name of the star is Wormwood. A third of the waters became wormwood, and many people died from the water, because it had been made bitter.<sup>12</sup>The fourth angel blew his trumpet, and a third of the sun was struck, and a third of the moon, and a third of the stars, so that a third of their light might be darkened, and a third of the day might be kept from shining, and likewise a third of the night.<sup>13</sup>Then I looked, and I heard an eagle crying with a loud voice as it flew directly overhead, “Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth, at the blasts of the other trumpets that the three angels are about to blow!”

9.title: The Fifth and Sixth Trumpets: The Demonic and the Deadly
9.overview:
Chapter 9 gives the fifth and sixth trumpets, the first two of the three woes, and judgement now falls on people rather than on nature. The fifth trumpet opens the abyss, and demonic locusts, drawn from Joel’s locust army, torment for five months those who do not have God’s seal; their king is Abaddon, Apollyon, the Destroyer. The sixth releases four angels bound at the Euphrates, the frontier from which Israel’s ancient enemies had come, and a vast cavalry kills a third of mankind.

The chapter ends on its most sobering verse: the rest of mankind did not repent. Like the plagues on Egypt, the trumpets were warnings, and like Pharaoh, the survivors hardened their hearts. Judgement by itself does not change a heart; only grace does.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Fifth Trumpet: The Locusts from the Abyss
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–6: a fallen star is given the key to the bottomless pit, smoke darkens the sun, and locusts with the power of scorpions come out. They may not touch the grass, only those without the seal of God, and they may torment for five months but not kill, so that people long to die and cannot.

Verses 7–12: John describes them in a string of likenesses drawn from Joel: war horses, what looked like crowns, human faces, lions’ teeth, iron breastplates, the roar of chariots, and stings in their tails. Their king is the angel of the abyss, Abaddon in Hebrew and Apollyon in Greek, the Destroyer. Then a line of bookkeeping: the first woe has passed.
verseByVerse.theology:
On a Permission

A fallen star is given the key to the abyss; the locusts are told whom they may not touch and allowed five months. Their king is Abaddon, Apollyon, the destroyer: a creature on a leash, not God’s rival.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The torment fell on those without God’s seal, and it ended when the season ended.

Now: If you have longed to die, you are in the company of Job, Moses and Elijah, not under condemnation. Tell another believer.

verseByVerse.quote: And the fifth angel blew his trumpet, and I saw a star fallen from heaven to earth, and he was given the key to the shaft of the bottomless pit. He opened the shaft of the bottomless pit, and from the shaft rose smoke like the smoke of a great furnace, and the sun and the air were darkened with the smoke from the shaft.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Revelation 9 describes the fifth and sixth trumpets, the first two woes, in which judgement moves from nature to people, and from natural forces to demonic ones. At the fifth trumpet a fallen star opens the bottomless pit, and out of its smoke come locusts with scorpions’ stings, allowed to torment, but not kill, those without God’s seal for five months, so that people long to die (vv. 1–6). They look like monstrous war horses with human faces, and their king is the angel of the pit, Abaddon or Apollyon, the Destroyer (vv. 7–12). At the sixth trumpet a voice from the altar releases four angels bound at the Euphrates, prepared for this very hour, and an army of two hundred million fire-breathing cavalry kills a third of mankind (vv. 13–19). Yet the rest still do not repent of their demons and idols, murders, sorceries, immorality and thefts (vv. 20–21). The chapter shows a world given over to the demonic powers it has chosen, God’s protection of his sealed people, and the terrible hardness of the human heart.

The setting. The eighth plague on Egypt was locusts, which covered the land and darkened it (Exodus 10:12–15). The prophet Joel described a locust plague as an invading army: like horses, with a sound like chariots, with teeth like a lion’s, darkening the sun and moon, a picture of the Day of the LORD (Joel 1:4–7; 2:1–11). In the ancient Near East a locust swarm could strip a whole region bare in hours. In Jewish thought the abyss was the prison of evil spirits (Luke 8:31; 2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6).

A star fallen from heaven. The grammar does half the work. John does not say he saw a star fall; he saw a star fallen, a completed event whose result is still standing. The falling happened, and this is the aftermath. And the star is at once treated as a person: he is given a key and he opens the shaft, which no lump of burning rock could do. A star in Revelation can represent an angel (1:20).

Who is the fallen star? Many take him to be Satan, and the case is strong. Jesus said, I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven (Luke 10:18); Isaiah’s taunt against the king of Babylon, how you are fallen from heaven, O Day Star, son of Dawn (Isaiah 14:12), has been read that way since the early church; and in 12:9 this book will describe the dragon being thrown down to the earth. Others take him to be one of God’s angels on commission, since 20:1 shows an angel coming down from heaven with the key of the bottomless pit and a great chain, and that one is plainly no enemy. This is probably a fallen angel, possibly Satan himself. The text does not settle it, and on the point that matters it does not need to.

He was given the key. Permission from God again. Whoever holds the key received it, and there is only one place in this book where keys are kept: Christ said, I have the keys of Death and Hades (1:18). Any other key is borrowed. Even the opening of the abyss is a delegated act, and every detail that follows says the same: the locusts were given power, told what to harm, and allowed only five months.

The abyss. In the Greek Old Testament the word is used for the primeval deep of Genesis 1:2 and for the waters under the earth. In the New Testament it is where demons are kept and where they do not want to go: the legion in the Gerasene man begged Jesus not to command them to depart into the abyss (Luke 8:31). Peter and Jude both describe rebel angels kept in chains of gloomy darkness until the judgement (2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6). The beast rises from it (11:7; 17:8) and Satan will be bound in it (20:1–3). And it has a shaft, a narrow neck, which means it has a mouth that can be shut, and it is opened only by permission.

Smoke like the smoke of a great furnace. The reader is meant to hear Sodom, where Abraham saw the smoke of the land going up like the smoke of a furnace (Genesis 19:28), and Sinai, wrapped in smoke like the smoke of a kiln (Exodus 19:18). Hell’s darkness is rising into the world.

The sun and the air were darkened. Before anything comes out, the light goes, and that is exactly right as a description of what evil does. It does not usually arrive arguing. It arrives as a haze: things that were clear stop being clear, and after a while nobody can see far enough to be sure of anything. The god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, to keep them from seeing the light of the gospel (2 Corinthians 4:4). The fourth trumpet darkened the sun by direct judgement; the fifth darkens it by pollution from below.

Is the devil real, or only a symbol of evil? Real. Revelation uses symbols to describe him, a star, a dragon, a serpent, but the symbols point to a personal being, a fallen angel who deceives the whole world (12:9). Jesus spoke to him in the wilderness and named him a murderer and a liar (John 8:44). C. S. Lewis warned that people go wrong about devils in two opposite directions: some laugh them off as a myth, and others cannot stop staring at them. Scripture avoids both. It takes Satan seriously and never makes him the centre. He is real, he is hostile, and he is on a chain held by Christ.

On a Tuesday. A Christian has no need to be fascinated by the demonic, whether in the occult, in entertainment that glamorises it, or in curiosity that wants to look into the pit, and no need to fear it either, because the one who holds all the keys is his. When your thinking goes hazy about right and wrong, when things that were plain start to look complicated, suspect smoke, and go back to the light of God’s word.

verseByVerse.quote: Then from the smoke came locusts on the earth, and they were given power like the power of scorpions of the earth. They were told not to harm the grass of the earth or any green plant or any tree, but only those people who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Locusts. They were the standard ancient image of total devastation, and Joel built a whole prophecy on them: an army that leaves a garden of Eden looking like a desert behind it (Joel 2:3). There is nothing to fight. They come as a shadow on the horizon, and when they lift there is nothing green left standing.

Wrong in every particular. But these locusts are wrong in every particular, and the wrongness is the point. They come out of the abyss rather than off the fields. They are given the power of scorpions, which locusts do not have. And the next clause tells them not to touch a single blade of grass, which is the one thing locusts exist to do. Whatever John is describing, it is not an infestation. They are demonic powers, pictured as a locust plague: what comes up when the pit is opened, wearing the shape of the most feared plague in the ancient world.

The power of scorpions. A scorpion’s sting is rarely fatal to a healthy adult, and it is agonising. Rehoboam threatened Israel with it as an image of intensified cruelty (1 Kings 12:11), and Jesus linked scorpions with the power of the enemy (Luke 10:19). This is a judgement that does not kill, and it is not therefore a lesser judgement.

Not to harm the grass. They were told: the divine passive again (the Bible’s way of saying God acts without naming him), which has governed every judgement since chapter 6. There is a fence around the vegetation. Ordinary locusts eat plants; these are forbidden to. Their target is people.

Those who do not have the seal. And there is a fence around people, drawn along one line: the seal of God. This is the first time the sealing of 7:3 is cashed out. God’s people are protected from this demonic torment, as Israel in Goshen was protected from the plagues on Egypt (Exodus 8:22; 9:4, 26; 10:23). When the destroyer went through at the Passover, the doorposts of the sealed households were marked with blood. The seal on the forehead is the doorpost of Exodus, moved from the house to the person. And this protection covers all who have God’s seal, which confirms that the 144,000 sealed in chapter 7 are all believers.

What the seal does. It does not exempt anybody from the great tribulation (7:14), and it did not spare the martyrs under the altar. What it does is set a limit on what can be done to a sealed person and by whom, and the boundary was drawn before the shaft was opened. The evil one does not touch him who is born of God (1 John 5:18).

Nothing shall hurt you. Jesus had already drawn this scene in miniature. When the seventy-two (seventy in some manuscripts, followed by the KJV) came back rejoicing that even the demons were subject to them, he said, I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven. Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall hurt you (Luke 10:18–19). A fallen star, scorpions, and a people the enemy cannot harm: the fifth trumpet is that promise worked out across history. And he added what matters most: rejoice not that the spirits obey you, but that your names are written in heaven (Luke 10:20). The sealed are safe for the same reason. Their safety is not their own strength against the pit. It is Christ’s authority over it, and their names in the Lamb’s book of life (21:27).

What does the seal actually protect, when Christians still suffer? This is where a believer’s honest fear should be answered rather than flattered. The seal is not a promise that nothing will happen to you. Christians get cancer, lose jobs, are lied about, go to prison, and die. What the seal guarantees is that nothing can reach past it to touch what you actually are: your union with Christ, your adoption, your inheritance. There are torments in this chapter that go on for five months and cannot be escaped, the torment of a soul handed over to the darkness it chose, and a marked person is not on the list. And the reason is not his courage. It is the name on his forehead.

Can a Christian be troubled by demons? Troubled, yes; owned, no. Believers are told to resist the devil (James 4:7) and to put on the whole armour of God against the schemes of the devil (Ephesians 6:11), which only makes sense if he attacks them. He tempts, accuses, deceives and stirs up persecution. But a Christian is the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19), and the house cannot be possessed by another master. If you are a believer in spiritual distress, you do not need a special ritual. You need what every Christian has: the word of God, prayer in Jesus’ name, the fellowship and oversight of your church, and confidence that he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4).

On a Tuesday. When you feel spiritually attacked, by an accusing thought that will not leave, a temptation that feels unusually strong, a darkness in your mind, do not panic, and do not fight it in your own strength. Remind yourself whose name is on your forehead. Then do the ordinary things the devil hates most: pray, read the word, tell a Christian friend, and get some sleep.

verseByVerse.quote: They were allowed to torment them for five months, but not to kill them, and their torment was like the torment of a scorpion when it stings someone. And in those days people will seek death and will not find it. They will long to die, but death will flee from them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. In the Near East the locust season ran roughly from spring to late summer. Job speaks of those who long for death, but it comes not, and dig for it more than for hidden treasures (Job 3:21). Jeremiah said the survivors of a judged nation would prefer death to life (Jeremiah 8:3).

Five months, but not to kill. Permission again, and two boundaries: a duration and a limit. They may torment; they may not kill. Five months, and not a day more.

Why five months? The most likely answer is the plainest one: the life of a locust swarm, from hatching to death, is often said to be about five months, roughly May to September. The number is not a code. It means one locust season: a real, bounded, recognisable stretch of time with a beginning and an end that everybody in an agricultural society could measure. It will feel endless while it lasts. It is not endless. God limits the time, and he does not allow them to kill. The purpose of the torment is to bring people to repentance (v. 20).

Like the torment of a scorpion. Agonising but not fatal. What might this torment be? Perhaps the spiritual and psychological misery of life under demonic deception: despair, emptiness, fear, addiction, the inner torment of a life without God that has given itself to the powers of darkness.

Death will flee from them. This is the condition in which existence itself has become the punishment, and the one exit a person would take has been closed. And still they do not turn to God.

A state worse than dying. The horror of the verse, rightly read, is not that God is cruel. It is that there is a state worse than dying, and that human beings can arrive at it by their own steady choosing. The most merciful thing in the passage is that it has a five-month fence around it, and that the fence was put there by God.

Is this verse about me, if I have wished I would not wake up? Some readers will read it from the outside as a description of a future horror. Others will read it and recognise the country. There are Christians who have lain awake and wished quite specifically not to wake up. If that is you, this verse is not describing your condemnation, and it should not be allowed to sound as though it is. Wanting to die is not the same as being abandoned by God, and Scripture proves it by the company: Job wanted it, Moses asked God to kill him (Numbers 11:15), Elijah sat under a tree and asked to die soon after the greatest victory of his life (1 Kings 19:4), and Jonah asked twice. God did not reject one of them for it. He fed Elijah and let him sleep. And look at who is in this verse and who is not: the torment falls expressly on those who do not have the seal of God (v. 4).

What should I do if I am in that dark place? Tell someone, this week, out loud: a pastor, a Christian friend, your doctor. If you are in immediate danger, contact emergency services or a crisis line today. That is not weakness or lack of faith; it is what the body of Christ, and the ordinary means of medicine God gives, are for. Despair says the darkness is permanent and there is no door. This whole book is the announcement that there is a door, that it has been opened from the other side at enormous cost, and that the one who opened it personally holds the keys of Death and Hades (1:18). Your life is in his hands, and he has not finished with it.
verseByVerse.note: Five months is roughly the life span of a locust, or the season in which they swarm.

verseByVerse.quote: In appearance the locusts were like horses prepared for battle: on their heads were what looked like crowns of gold; their faces were like human faces, their hair like women's hair, and their teeth like lions' teeth; they had breastplates like breastplates of iron, and the noise of their wings was like the noise of many chariots with horses rushing into battle. They have tails and stings like scorpions, and their power to hurt people for five months is in their tails.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Joel says the locusts look like horses and run like war horses, with a noise like chariots (Joel 2:4–5). A locust’s head does look rather like a horse’s; the Italian word for a grasshopper, cavalletta, means little horse, and the German Heupferd means hay horse. Joel says the invader has the teeth of a lion (Joel 1:6). The Parthians, Rome’s feared eastern enemy, were famous mounted archers who wore their hair long.

Like horses prepared for battle. The description is deliberately impossible to draw: John piles up comparisons in four verses, nearly every one introduced by like. He is not filing a report on a species but telling a congregation what it felt like to look at. The crowns are only what looked like crowns, a counterfeit authority; everything in this book that is genuinely crowned is crowned by God. The human faces are the worst detail, because whatever this is, it has intelligence and intention, and it looks back at you. The long hair suggests a locust’s streaming antennae and perhaps the long-haired Parthian riders; the lions’ teeth are Joel’s; the iron breastplates mean there is no attacking them. And the noise of their wings is like chariots rushing into battle (Joel 2:5): a swarm is often heard before it is seen, a dry roar that fills the sky.

Stings in their tails. The sting is in the back end, and the sixth trumpet will repeat it (v. 19). Twice in one chapter the injury comes from behind, after the thing has apparently passed, and that is how a great deal of evil works: the damage is done afterwards, by what was left in the wound.

Every category slips. Taken whole, the portrait does exactly what John intends. It has a man’s face and a lion’s teeth. It wears armour and a crown that is not a crown. It is a locust that will not eat grass and a horse that is not a horse. Every category the mind reaches for slips. That is what comes up out of the abyss.

The true crown and the true face. Set the portrait beside the one this book began with. The locusts wear what only looked like crowns of gold and have faces like human faces, and nothing about them is human. Later John sees one like a son of man, with a golden crown on his head (14:14), and from the first chapter his face has been like the sun shining in full strength (1:16). His is the real face of a real man, and the real crown, and he did not seize it: he was crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death (Hebrews 2:9). What the abyss counterfeits, Christ actually is. Evil can imitate authority and wear a borrowed humanity. It cannot be what he is, a man who is also Lord, and who wears his crown because he died.

Where Christians differ: what are the locusts? Some popular writers have identified them with modern weapons, such as attack helicopters with rotor blades, tail guns and armoured cockpits. Historicists have identified them with the Muslim Arab armies of the seventh century. Others take them as literal demonic creatures to be unleashed in a future tribulation. This commentary’s view: the locusts are demonic powers, released by God’s permission to torment those who have rejected him, pictured with images drawn from Joel’s locust army. John uses “like” again and again, signalling symbols, not technical descriptions. Reading modern technology into them ignores how the first readers would have understood the book. The locusts describe demonic torment, real and terrible, wherever people give themselves over to evil, throughout the age and especially toward its end.

Left behind by the next generation. Every attempt to identify these creatures with a weapon has been overtaken by the next generation’s equally confident guess. What is permanent is the anatomy of spiritual evil: intelligent, armoured, crowned with an authority it did not earn, deafening, and stinging from behind. A congregation in Pergamum living under the shadow of Satan’s throne (2:13) did not need the picture decoded. They needed to be told that it comes up on a permission and goes down on a timetable.

What does this look like in ordinary life? Usually not monsters. It looks like something that seems glorious and wears a crown: an ideology that promises liberation, a pleasure that promises freedom, a habit that looks harmless in the first year. It has a human face, so it seems reasonable. It is armoured, so argument bounces off it. And it stings from behind: the pornography that seemed private and later poisons a marriage, the gambling that was fun until the debts arrived, the bitterness nursed for years that finally isolates a man from everyone. The way to resist is not to study the creature but to stay near Christ, who has already disarmed the powers (Colossians 2:15).

verseByVerse.quote: They have as king over them the angel of the bottomless pit. His name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in Greek he is called Apollyon. The first woe has passed; behold, two woes are still to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Proverbs says that the locusts have no king, yet all of them march in rank (Proverbs 30:27). These locusts do have a king. In the Old Testament Abaddon (Hebrew for destruction) is a name for the place of the dead, linked with Sheol and death: Sheol is naked before God, and Abaddon has no covering (Job 26:6; 28:22; Psalm 88:11; Proverbs 15:11). The locust was, it seems, among the emblems of the Greek god Apollo, and emperors since Augustus had linked themselves with Apollo; Domitian, by some accounts, was among them.

A king over them. That is what makes the line unnerving: Proverbs says locusts have no king, and these do. The chaos is organised, and it has a commander. The angel of the abyss is either Satan himself or a high-ranking demonic spirit under him.

Abaddon and Apollyon. John gives the name twice so that neither half of his congregation misses it. Abaddon means destruction; Apollyon means the destroyer. The two names say the same thing in two languages, which is John’s way of saying that this figure is not a local problem. The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy; Christ came that they may have life and have it abundantly (John 10:10).

A barb in the name. There is probably a barb in the Greek name. Apollo, whose emblems included the locust, was a god the emperors liked to be linked with, so a Christian in Ephesus hearing Apollyon read out would have made the connection without being told: the god the empire boasts in has a name very like destroyer, and the thing he actually rules is a pit.

His only competence. And that is the only thing this figure can do. Not create, not build, not make anything at all. His entire competence is destruction, and his name is his job description. Set that beside the one seated on the throne, whose song in chapter 4 is you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created (4:11), and the asymmetry is total. One of these two makes things out of nothing. The other unmakes what somebody else made, and can be shut in a shaft.

The destroyer destroyed. And the Destroyer has met the one person he could not unmake. The Son of God appeared in order to destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3:8), and he did it by dying: through death he destroyed the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil (Hebrews 2:14). Satan’s hold on people was their guilt and their fear of death. At the cross Jesus paid the guilt, and on the third day he walked out of the grave, so the weapon has been taken out of the destroyer’s hand. Apollyon still rules a pit. Christ holds the keys of Death and Hades (1:18).

The first woe has passed. A single verse of bookkeeping, and it does two things. It confirms that the eagle’s three woes in 8:13 map onto the fifth, sixth and seventh trumpets: worse is coming. And it says has passed. Whatever came up out of that shaft went back down, and John is already speaking of it in the past tense. Every affliction in this book is announced, measured, and then reported finished, and the one who keeps the register has never once lost count.

Are God and Satan two equal powers fighting it out? No, and this fear troubles thoughtful Christians more than they usually admit: the sense that good and evil are two roughly matched forces wrestling for the world, with the outcome genuinely uncertain. Revelation never allows it. The destroyer is a subject in a passive sentence: he is given a key, he is allowed five months, he is told what he may not touch. He is not the opposite number of God. He is a creature with a leash and a name. His true opposite, if he has one, is an archangel like Michael (12:7), not the Creator. God has no rival.

Is this the Apollyon of The Pilgrim’s Progress? Yes. John Bunyan took the name from this verse for the monster that meets Christian in the Valley of Humiliation, claiming him as his subject and trying to frighten him back. Christian is wounded, thrown down, and loses his sword; then he recovers it and, with a word of Scripture on his lips, gives Apollyon a thrust that sends him flying away. It is a fine picture of the point of this verse. The destroyer is real and fierce, and he claims what is not his; but the believer resists him with the word of God and the promise of victory, and he flees (James 4:7).

On a Tuesday. When a temptation comes dressed up as freedom, success or pleasure, ask what it builds and what it destroys. And if you are in the middle of something hard, say the bookkeeping verse to yourself: this, too, will be reported as passed.

For worship. The king of the pit rules a hole in the ground; the King of kings rules heaven and earth from a throne before which the elders cast their crowns. He does not only outlast the ruin. He reverses it, beginning with ruined sinners, whom he builds again into sons. Abaddon’s name means destruction. Jesus means the LORD saves.
verseByVerse.note: Abaddon means “destruction” and Apollyon “destroyer.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — The Sixth Trumpet: The Army from the Euphrates
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 13–16: at the sixth trumpet a voice from the horns of the golden altar, where the saints’ prayers were offered (8:3–5), orders the release of four angels bound at the Euphrates. They were prepared for a fixed hour, and they are released to kill a third of mankind with a cavalry numbered at twice ten thousand times ten thousand.

Verses 17–19: the horses breathe fire, smoke and sulphur, the substance of Sodom and of the lake of fire, and their tails are like serpents.

Verses 20–21: the survivors did not repent of their idols, which cannot see or hear or walk, or of their murders, sorceries, sexual immorality and thefts.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Order Comes from the Altar

The voice that releases the four angels comes from the altar where the saints’ prayers are offered. They were prepared for the hour, day, month and year. Yet the survivors did not repent of their idols, sorceries and sins.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Beyond the Euphrates lay the invader every Roman province feared.

Now: Judgement alone does not change hearts; we become like what we worship.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the sixth angel blew his trumpet, and I heard a voice from the four horns of the golden altar before God, saying to the sixth angel who had the trumpet, "Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. The Euphrates was the north-eastern boundary of the land promised to Abraham (Genesis 15:18). In John’s day it was the eastern frontier of the Roman Empire, beyond which lay the Parthians, whose cavalry had destroyed a Roman army at Carrhae in 53 BC. The altar of incense had a horn at each corner (Exodus 30:2–3).

A voice from the golden altar. Of all the places a command could come from, this is the one that matters. In 8:3–4 an angel offered much incense at this altar with the prayers of all the saints, and in 8:5 its fire was thrown on the earth. Now a voice speaks out of its four horns and releases the sixth trumpet. That is the third time in two chapters the connection has been made: the judgements of God are the answer to the praying of his people, issued from the place where that praying is received.

The horns of the altar. The horns were the four projections at the altar’s corners, and they were the part a man grasped when he fled to the sanctuary claiming protection (1 Kings 1:50–51). Blood was put on them at the great atoning sacrifices (Leviticus 4:7, 18). They were the place of refuge and the place of blood, and both pointed to Christ. The blood on those horns could not take away sins (Hebrews 10:4); his blood, shed once for all, secured an eternal redemption (Hebrews 9:12). What does that mean? Anyone who runs to him and takes hold of him by faith is safe from the judgement this voice releases, because the sacrifice for his sins has already been made. Those who reject that atonement face judgement from the same altar.

Where the prayers went. A congregation that has prayed for years about wickedness that nobody seems to be doing anything about is being told where its prayers went and what they are doing.

Release the four angels. They are bound, and have been for a long time, since somebody had to bind them. These are evil angels, held in check by God until now (Jude 6; 2 Peter 2:4). And they are released by an order, from an altar, at a specified moment. Nothing hostile in this universe moves except on a permission, and every permission is issued from the throne room.

The direction the end comes from. To say the Euphrates to a first-century reader was to say what the border says in any country that has been invaded across one: Assyria and Babylon had come from beyond it, and Parthia, the one power Rome had never subdued, waited there. In Revelation place names often carry symbolic meaning (Babylon, Sodom, Egypt), and the river stands for the frontier from which invasion comes. This verse says something specific about every invasion in history: the horde crossing the border was on a rope, and the rope was in God’s hand, and the hand let go at a moment of its own choosing.

Textual note. Some important manuscripts read “a voice from the horns of the golden altar”, without the word “four”. The meaning is unchanged.

What holds evil back now? God does, through means he has appointed. Paul speaks of something that restrains lawlessness until the appointed time (2 Thessalonians 2:6–7), and Christians have usually understood that to include the ordinary restraints God gives in his common grace: lawful government, which bears the sword against evil (Romans 13:4), conscience, the family, the presence and prayers of the church, salt in a decaying world (Matthew 5:13). Common grace means the kindness God shows to all people, believers or not: he sends rain on the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45), and he holds back the worst of human evil so that ordinary life can go on. We rarely see how much is being held back. Every peaceful year, every war that did not happen, every evil plan that failed, is the four angels still bound. That is why we pray for those in authority, that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life (1 Timothy 2:1–2).
verseByVerse.note: The Euphrates was the eastern frontier of the Roman world, beyond which lay the feared Parthians.

verseByVerse.quote: So the four angels, who had been prepared for the hour, the day, the month, and the year, were released to kill a third of mankind. The number of mounted troops was twice ten thousand times ten thousand; I heard their number.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Prepared for the hour. The Greek has a single article governing all four units of time, which makes them one appointed moment rather than a span: the hour, which falls on the day, in the month, of the year. This is a diary entry. God has appointed the exact moment.

A steadying sentence. The catastrophe that appears to prove that nobody is steering has a time stamp on it, applied in advance. That is not the same as saying the catastrophe is good, and Scripture never says so: God has no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11). It is saying that history is not a series of accidents interrupted occasionally by providence.

His hour, and ours. The Gospels show what living under a fixed hour looked like in a human life. Men tried to arrest Jesus, and no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come (John 7:30). He walked through hostility untouched until the appointed time, and when it came he did not run from it, but said that for this purpose he had come to this hour (John 12:27). The same Father who fixed the hour of the cross fixes the hour of every judgement in this chapter. What does that mean for a believer? Nothing in your story comes early or late by accident. You are kept by the same timetable that kept him.

A third of mankind. The fraction moves again. The horsemen had a fourth (6:8); the first four trumpets took a third of the earth, the sea, the water and the light; now a third of mankind. Under the fifth trumpet they longed for death; now it comes. Still two thirds are untouched, and the reason will be stated with brutal clarity in verse 20.

Twice ten thousand times ten thousand. Two hundred million, if it is arithmetic. It is almost certainly not. A myriad, ten thousand, was the largest number Greek had a single word for, so a myriad of myriads is the language reaching its ceiling, and John has used it already of the angels around the throne (5:11), as Daniel did before him (Daniel 7:10). Doubling it is not a census; it is a way of saying, and then twice that again. The whole Roman army had perhaps three hundred thousand soldiers.

I heard their number. John did not count them. He was told, exactly as with the 144,000: I heard the number of the sealed (7:4). A reader who takes one as a figure of overwhelming completeness should take the other the same way: God’s army, sealed and counted, and the demonic army, vast and destructive.

A matter of proportion. The church in Asia was a few thousand people in seven towns, meeting in houses, with no standing whatever. The forces arrayed against them are described in a figure that runs off the end of the counting system. And the whole of that host was on the wrong side of a river, tied up, waiting for a word from an altar.

Where Christians differ: is this a literal army of two hundred million? Some popular writers have identified it with a future Chinese army, after a report in the 1960s that China could field a militia of two hundred million. This commentary’s view: the number is symbolic of an overwhelming, uncountable host, a demonic army more than a human one, as the description of the horses that follows makes clear. Its point is the terror of war and destruction let loose, not a prediction about any particular nation. Readings that tie it to modern nations have repeatedly had to be revised as world politics changed.

Should I be afraid of dying in some catastrophe? If you belong to Christ, your hour is fixed too, and it is fixed by your Father. My times are in your hand (Psalm 31:15). No bomb, virus, accident or army can take you a moment before he calls you home, and none can keep you a moment after. That does not make Christians careless; we take sensible precautions, because God works through means. But it does free us from the dread that hangs over people who think their lives are at the mercy of chance. Whether death comes in old age or in a catastrophe, for the believer it comes on an appointment kept by a Saviour.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is how I saw the horses in my vision and those who rode them: they wore breastplates the color of fire and of sapphire and of sulfur, and the heads of the horses were like lions' heads, and fire and smoke and sulfur came out of their mouths. By these three plagues a third of mankind was killed, by the fire and smoke and sulfur coming out of their mouths. For the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails, for their tails are like serpents with heads, and by means of them they wound.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Fire and sulphur (brimstone) rained down on Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:24). In Revelation they are the elements of the lake of fire (14:10; 19:20; 20:10; 21:8). The Parthian cavalry were famous for shooting arrows backwards over the horse’s rump as they rode away, so that their power seemed to be in their tails.

In my vision. John reminds the reader, in the middle of the description, that this is a vision, not cavalry seen through a telescope.

Fire, sapphire and sulphur. Red, dark blue like smoke, and the sickly yellow of brimstone: the colours of the three things that come out of the horses’ mouths. The riders are wearing what the horses breathe.

Fire and smoke and sulphur. Lions’ heads speak of ferocity. Sulphur is the smell of Sodom (see the setting), the smell of judgement. What comes out of these mouths is the substance of hell itself breaking out into the world.

By these three plagues. The Exodus vocabulary again. And the killing is done by what proceeds out of a mouth, which in this book is never accidental: the weapon of Christ is the sharp sword that comes from his mouth (1:16; 19:15). What comes out of a mouth kills or saves.

Tails like serpents. Twice now the tail has been the dangerous end, and here the tails are given heads of their own. It is a grotesque image and a precise one: these horses kill from the front and wound from behind.

John has signed the picture. The word for serpents in this book has a single owner: the great dragon is that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan (12:9; 20:2). Whatever historical shape this army takes, and the Parthian archers shooting backwards would have come to mind at once for any reader in Asia, the tail that stings from behind belongs to the serpent.

Evil does its worst work with its back turned. That is how ruin often arrives in a life. The moment of the encounter is rarely the moment of the damage. The affair ended years ago; the consequences are only now walking through the door. The drink was put down; the liver was not consulted. The words were said in one bad evening; the son has not called since. The person it wounds usually thought the danger had passed.

Is there hope when I am living with the sting of my own past sin? Yes. The consequences of sin may remain for a time, and God does not always remove them; David was forgiven, and still his household suffered (2 Samuel 12:13–14). But the guilt is gone the moment you confess it, and the serpent’s sting has been drawn at the cross: the sting of death is sin, but thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 15:56–57). Do the repairing you can do: apologise, make restitution, keep faith with those you hurt. Then refuse to let the accuser keep stinging you with what God has forgiven. God is able to bring good even out of the wreckage (Romans 8:28), and he often does it slowly.

How do I pray against spiritual powers without becoming obsessed with them? By keeping your eyes on Christ rather than on the enemy. Paul tells us that we wrestle not against flesh and blood but against the spiritual forces of evil (Ephesians 6:12), and then the armour he describes is almost entirely ordinary: truth, righteousness, the gospel, faith, salvation, the word of God, and prayer at all times in the Spirit. You do not need to name or map demons, or address them in prayer. Pray to the Father, in the name of the Son who has already triumphed over them (Colossians 2:15), for his kingdom to come and for deliverance from evil. That is how Jesus taught us to pray (Matthew 6:13).

For worship. From the first pages of the Bible the serpent’s end was promised: the offspring of the woman would bruise his head, though his own heel would be bruised in doing it (Genesis 3:15). The bruise was the cross, and the crushing began there. The serpent still bites, but he bites as a beaten enemy, and the one who took his deadliest strike in his own body will have the last word over every lie the serpent has ever told.

verseByVerse.quote: The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent of the works of their hands nor give up worshiping demons and idols of gold and silver and bronze and stone and wood, which cannot see or hear or walk, nor did they repent of their murders or their sorceries or their sexual immorality or their thefts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Pharaoh hardened his heart again and again under the plagues on Egypt (Exodus 8:15, 32; 9:34). The Old Testament mocks idols that have mouths but do not speak, eyes but do not see, ears but do not hear (Psalm 115:4–7; 135:15–17; Daniel 5:23). Paul taught that behind idols are demons (1 Corinthians 10:20).

Did not repent. This is the sentence the whole trumpet sequence has been building toward. Start with the rest. Two thirds of mankind survived. Every fraction in the last four chapters existed for the sake of the people who were left, and this verse says what the survivors did with the mercy of being alive. The trumpets were warnings, calling people to repent, and they did not. The same words return in 16:9, 11.

Suffering does not automatically produce repentance. That answers a question many people carry unspoken: surely if God sent something undeniable, the world would turn. Revelation says it has been tried. The sky has gone dark, the water has turned bitter, a third of the human race has died, and the survivors go back to what they were doing. Suffering by itself does not change the heart. It hardens as often as it softens, and Pharaoh, whose plagues these are, is the standing proof: after plague after plague he hardened his heart, and the last thing he did was drive into a sea that had opened.

Which cannot see or hear or walk. What they will not give up comes in two lists, and the order is not accidental.
