First the idols, described with contempt, as in the Psalms: they have mouths, but do not speak; eyes, but do not see; those who make them become like them (Psalm 115:4–8). The last clause of that psalm is the sting. You become like what you worship, and worship something blind and deaf, and in the end you cannot see or hear either, which is exactly what this chapter has just described. Gold, silver, bronze, stone, wood: idols for the rich and the poor alike.

Behind the idols, demons. Idolatry is not harmless. What pagans sacrifice they offer to demons and not to God (1 Corinthians 10:20). The statue is wood; what is being served through it is not nothing. And the very powers that tormented them in this chapter are the ones they keep worshipping. Idols include anything people trust and serve in place of God: money, power, pleasure, status; covetousness, which is idolatry (Colossians 3:5).

Eyes like a flame of fire. Set the idols beside the one who walks through this book. They cannot see; the risen Christ has eyes like a flame of fire and says to each church, I know your works (2:18–19). They cannot walk; he walks among the seven golden lampstands (2:1). And the psalm’s rule runs in his direction too. We become like what we worship, and those who behold the glory of the Lord are being transformed into the same image (2 Corinthians 3:18). What does that mean? A person who keeps looking at Christ, in his word, slowly comes to see as he sees and love what he loves. Idols make their worshippers blind and deaf. Christ makes his worshippers like himself.

Murders, sorceries, immorality, thefts. The second list is startlingly ordinary: the commandments of the second table (the commandments about our neighbour), murder, adultery, theft. Sorceries (pharmakeia, from which our word pharmacy comes) means drugs and potions used in magic and the occult: the attempt to control life, luck, love and death by technique rather than by trusting God.

Root and fruit. Set the two lists together and the diagnosis is complete. Idolatry, breaking the first table of the law (the commandments about God himself), always leads to breaking the second (Romans 1:21–32). Idolatry is the root; murder, manipulation, immorality and theft are the fruit. A person who has replaced God will end up destroying his neighbour’s life, body, marriage or property, because there is nothing left to stop him. And none of these four is exotic. Every one of them is available on an ordinary Tuesday.

Where Christians differ: can people repent whenever they choose? Many Christians, especially in the Arminian tradition, hold that God gives grace to all that restores to every person the ability to repent and believe if they choose to; they hold it out of a deep concern for human responsibility and God’s love for the world, and they are our brothers and sisters. This commentary’s view: this verse shows the terrible bondage of the human will apart from grace. Even under overwhelming judgement, people do not repent, because their hearts are enslaved to sin and they love darkness (John 3:19). Scripture teaches that sinners are dead in sin (Ephesians 2:1) and unable to come to Christ unless the Father draws them (John 6:44). Repentance is God’s gift (Acts 11:18; 2 Timothy 2:25). This does not excuse unbelievers; they are responsible for refusing. But it shows why we pray for God to give new hearts, and why we preach the gospel, which is God’s power to save (Romans 1:16).

Did not, not could not. The distinction matters, because the whole chapter is finally about a door that stayed open and was not used. The judgements were fractional so there would be somebody left to turn. The trumpets were warnings and not the end. An eagle flew overhead in daylight shouting three woes before the first of them landed. God went to extraordinary lengths to be heard, and the last word of the chapter is that they did not repent. The bondage of the will is real, and it is a bondage they love; the refusal is theirs, and so is the guilt. A sceptic will ask how anyone can be blamed for what he cannot do without grace. But this inability is not that of a paralysed man who longs to walk and cannot. It is that of a man who will not leave the woman who is ruining him, because he loves her. What holds them is what they want (John 3:19), and no one is excused for wanting evil.

In the flow. The sixth trumpet ends here, and the book does not move straight on to the seventh. As between the sixth and seventh seals, an interlude follows (10:1–11:14), and it answers the problem this verse leaves. If judgement alone does not bring people to repentance, what will? Chapters 10 and 11 answer: the witness of the church. John is told to prophesy again about many peoples and nations (10:11), the two witnesses testify in sackcloth, and after their death and vindication the rest are terrified and give glory to the God of heaven (11:13). The trumpets warn; the gospel, carried by a suffering church, is what God uses to turn hearts.

Verse 20 in a life. An idol is whatever you would be unable to give up. Take the thing you have already been warned about, by your body, by your bank, by your husband or wife, by a friend who took a risk in saying it, and see how expertly the warning has been explained away. That is verse 20 happening in a life, at a scale where it can still be repented of. And if seeing it grieves you, that grief is not hardness. It is the Spirit’s work, and the one who sent the warning is the one who forgives.

Is my unbelieving friend beyond hope, if even disasters do not move people? No. What disasters cannot do, God can. The same Paul who was dead in sin was turned around in a moment on the Damascus road. Hardness of heart is a reason to stop relying on arguments and circumstances to do the work, and to rely instead on the Spirit, who gives new hearts (Ezekiel 36:26). So keep praying for them, one by one, keep loving them, and keep telling them the gospel plainly when the door opens. God often uses suffering as the occasion of conversion, but it is always grace, not the suffering, that saves.

Are horoscopes, tarot and crystals harmless fun? Scripture treats them as anything but. They belong to the family of sorceries named here: attempts to know or control the future and the self apart from God. Israel was forbidden every form of divination (Deuteronomy 18:10–12), and the new believers in Ephesus burned their magic books publicly at great cost (Acts 19:19). Even when they are meant lightly, they train the heart to look for guidance and security somewhere other than the Lord. A Christian has no need of them. Your future is not in the stars; it is in the hands of the one who made them.

Does pharmakeia mean Christians should avoid medicine? No. The word here is about magic and the occult, not about medicine, and reading it that way is a misuse. Scripture treats medical care as a good gift: Paul told Timothy to take a little wine for his stomach (1 Timothy 5:23), Luke was a physician (Colossians 4:14), and Jesus said that those who are sick need a doctor (Luke 5:31). Taking prescribed medication, including for mental illness, is not a lack of faith. What is condemned is using substances to manipulate spiritual powers, or to escape into darkness, rather than receiving God’s gifts with thanksgiving.

On a Tuesday. Name the warning you have been explaining away, and do one concrete thing about it before the week is out: delete the app, make the phone call, confess the sin. Repentance is a turning, not a feeling, and you do not turn alone: the Spirit who gives new hearts gives the strength for it. You will never turn perfectly, but Christ obeyed perfectly in your place and his obedience is counted as yours (Romans 5:19), so even a halting repentance is welcomed for his sake.

For worship. The God of this chapter measures his judgements, sends warnings in daylight and holds back the hosts of the abyss to leave room for repentance. And when the human heart still refuses, he does what no trumpet can do: he gives a new heart, and puts his Spirit within, and turns the rebel into a son. Salvation belongs to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb, for even our repentance was his gift.

They will long to die, but death will flee from them.<sup>7</sup>In appearance the locusts were like horses prepared for battle: on their heads were what looked like crowns of gold; their faces were like human faces,<sup>8</sup>their hair like women’s hair, and their teeth like lions’ teeth;<sup>9</sup>they had breastplates like breastplates of iron, and the noise of their wings was like the noise of many chariots with horses rushing into battle.<sup>10</sup>They have tails and stings like scorpions, and their power to hurt people for five months is in their tails.<sup>11</sup>They have as king over them the angel of the bottomless pit. His name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in Greek he is called Apollyon.<sup>12</sup>The first woe has passed; behold, two woes are still to come.<sup>13</sup>Then the sixth angel blew his trumpet, and I heard a voice from the four horns of the golden altar before God,<sup>14</sup>saying to the sixth angel who had the trumpet, “Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates.”<sup>15</sup>So the four angels, who had been prepared for the hour, the day, the month, and the year, were released to kill a third of mankind.<sup>16</sup>The number of mounted troops was twice ten thousand times ten thousand; I heard their number.<sup>17</sup>And this is how I saw the horses in my vision and those who rode them: they wore breastplates the color of fire and of sapphire and of sulfur, and the heads of the horses were like lions’ heads, and fire and smoke and sulfur came out of their mouths.<sup>18</sup>By these three plagues a third of mankind was killed, by the fire and smoke and sulfur coming out of their mouths.<sup>19</sup>For the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails, for their tails are like serpents with heads, and by means of them they wound.<sup>20</sup>The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent of the works of their hands nor give up worshiping demons and idols of gold and silver and bronze and stone and wood, which cannot see or hear or walk,<sup>21</sup>nor did they repent of their murders or their sorceries or their sexual immorality or their thefts.

10.title: The Angel and the Little Scroll
10.overview:
Chapter 10 is a pause between the sixth and seventh trumpets, as chapter 7 was between the sixth and seventh seals. Before the last trumpet sounds, the vision turns to the church’s commission: John is given a little scroll to eat and sent to prophesy again.

A mighty angel comes down clothed in Christ’s reflected glory, plants his feet on sea and land, and roars like a lion. Seven thunders speak, and John is told not to write what they said: the one sealed message in an unsealed book. The angel swears by the Creator that there will be no more delay, and that at the seventh trumpet the mystery of God will be finished.

The little scroll is sweet in John’s mouth and bitter in his stomach, as Ezekiel’s was. God’s word is sweet to receive, because it is the good news of grace, and bitter to carry, because it brings judgement as well as salvation and costs those who speak it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Angel and the Little Scroll
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: a mighty angel comes down wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head and a face like the sun, holding a little open scroll, and sets his feet on sea and land. Verses 3–4: he roars like a lion, the seven thunders sound, and John, about to write, is told to seal up what they said.

Verses 5–7: the angel raises his hand and swears by the one who made heaven, earth and sea that there will be no more delay, and that at the seventh trumpet the mystery of God will be fulfilled, as he announced to the prophets.

Verses 8–11: John takes the scroll and eats it, sweet in his mouth and bitter in his stomach, and is told that he must again prophesy about many peoples and nations and languages and kings.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sealed Thunders and the Swallowed Scroll

A mighty angel in his master’s glory stands on sea and land. What the seven thunders said is sealed, the one sealed sentence in an unsealed book. The angel swears there will be no more delay, and John must eat the little scroll: sweet in the mouth, bitter in the stomach.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: An exiled old man was recommissioned to prophesy to peoples, nations and kings.

Now: Do not claim to know what God has withheld; and expect the gospel to be sweet to receive and costly to carry.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw another mighty angel coming down from heaven, wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, and his face was like the sun, and his legs like pillars of fire. He had a little scroll open in his hand. And he set his right foot on the sea, and his left foot on the land,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Revelation 10 is a pause between the sixth and seventh trumpets, as chapter 7 was between the sixth and seventh seals. A mighty angel comes down from heaven, robed in cloud, crowned with a rainbow, with a little open scroll in his hand, and plants his feet on sea and land (vv. 1–2). He roars like a lion; seven thunders speak, but John is told to seal up what they said (vv. 3–4). The angel swears by the eternal Creator that there will be no more delay: when the seventh trumpet sounds, the mystery of God announced by the prophets will be fulfilled (vv. 5–7). John eats the little scroll, sweet as honey in his mouth and bitter in his stomach, and is told he must prophesy again about many peoples, nations, languages and kings (vv. 8–11). The chapter renews John’s commission, like Ezekiel’s: God’s word is sweet to receive and bitter to carry, because it brings both salvation and judgement and its bearers must suffer. Over it all stands the Creator, who has sworn that his plan will be finished exactly as he promised.

The setting. In Ezekiel 2:8–3:3, God gives Ezekiel a scroll written on front and back with lamentation, mourning and woe, and tells him to eat it; it is sweet as honey in his mouth, and then he is sent to prophesy to Israel. In Daniel 12:4–9, Daniel is told to seal up his vision until the end, and a man clothed in linen raises both hands to heaven and swears by him who lives for ever that it will be for a time, times and half a time. Revelation 10 echoes both.

John does not rush his sevens. The seventh trumpet does not sound until 11:15, and the repetition of an interlude is itself an argument. Twice now, at the very point where a reader is braced for the end, the vision stops and turns to look at the church. God does not hurry past his people on the way to the finish. Before the last trumpet, he shows them where they stand and what they are for.

Another mighty angel. Every detail of this figure is one the reader has already met, and that is what has made him controversial. The cloud is what God travels in and what Christ returns on (1:7). The rainbow was around the throne in 4:3, the sign of God’s covenant faithfulness since the days of Noah. His face like the sun is how the risen Christ was described in 1:16. His legs like pillars of fire recall the feet like burnished bronze in 1:15, and the pillar of fire that led Israel through the wilderness by night (Exodus 13:21). Some serious readers have concluded that this is Christ himself.

Where Christians differ: is the mighty angel Christ? Some identify him with Christ himself, because of the cloud, the rainbow, the sun-like face and the fiery legs. Three things tell against it, and they should be given plainly. The word is allos: another mighty angel, another of the same kind as the mighty angel of 5:2, which puts him in a category with the angels. In verse 6 he swears by the one who lives for ever and ever, and swearing by a higher authority is not something Christ does or needs to do; when God made a promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself (Hebrews 6:13). And Revelation never once calls Christ an angel, though it gives him many other names; he is the one the angels worship (5:11–12). This commentary’s view: he is most likely a powerful angel who reflects Christ’s glory and represents him. Angels who come from God’s presence share something of his glory, as Moses’ face shone after he had been with God (Exodus 34:29).

A herald in his master’s livery. That reading explains the borrowed glory. When an ambassador arrives wearing the king’s colours, the point is not that he is the king but whose message he is carrying. Every ray of light on this angel’s face is reflected light, and the more glorious a servant of God appears, the more firmly he sends worship on to God (19:10; 22:9).

A little scroll open in his hand. Two things about it. It is little, a different word from the great sealed scroll of chapter 5. And it is open. Nobody in heaven or on earth could break the seals of that scroll until the Lamb who was slain took it. This one is already unrolled, lying open in an angel’s hand, and in a few verses John will be told to take it. It is probably closely connected with the scroll of chapter 5: God’s revealed purpose, now handed to a man to proclaim. Whether it is a portion of the great scroll or a separate commission is not stated. What the Lamb alone could open, the Lamb now gives away.

His right foot on the sea. The posture is a claim. Land and sea are the ancient way of saying everywhere, and planting a foot on something is what a conqueror does to territory: every place that the sole of your foot will tread upon I have given to you (Joshua 1:3). He is standing on the world because his message concerns the whole of it. And he has one foot on the element the beast will rise out of (13:1) and one on the element the second beast will rise out of (13:11).

Before the beasts appear. Hold that picture when the next chapters grow dark. Before the dragon or either beast comes up, a messenger from heaven has been shown standing on the places they come from, with a covenant rainbow over his head. The order of the visions is itself a comfort. Evil will rise out of the sea and out of the earth, and it will look for a time as though it owns them. But God has already shown his church whose feet are on that ground.

What is the rainbow doing here, in a chapter about judgement? It is a reminder of what God has promised, worn over the head of the one bringing his message. After the flood God set his bow in the cloud as a sign that he would never again destroy the earth by water (Genesis 9:13–16), and in Revelation the same bow encircles his throne (4:3). So even the heralds of judgement come with mercy over their heads. The judgements of Revelation are real and terrible, but they are not the outbursts of a God who has forgotten his covenant. They are the acts of a faithful God clearing the ground for a new creation, and keeping every promise to his people while he does it.

verseByVerse.quote: and called out with a loud voice, like a lion roaring. When he called out, the seven thunders sounded. And when the seven thunders had sounded, I was about to write, but I heard a voice from heaven saying, "Seal up what the seven thunders have said, and do not write it down."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Amos 3:8 says the lion has roared; who will not fear? The Lord GOD has spoken; who can but prophesy? Hosea 11:10 says the LORD will roar like a lion, and Joel 3:16 that the LORD roars from Zion. Psalm 29 describes the voice of the LORD seven times as thunder over the waters. Paul was caught up into paradise and heard things that cannot be told, which man may not utter (2 Corinthians 12:4).

Like a lion roaring. A lion’s roar is not a warning shot. It can be heard for miles, and its purpose is to announce possession of territory. Amos, Hosea and Joel used it of God speaking. And in this book there is one Lion, of the tribe of Judah, who turned out to be a Lamb (5:5–6). The angel standing on sea and land roars with his master’s voice, and the roar says: this ground is claimed.

The seven thunders. The definite article is odd and deliberate, as though John expects his readers to know which ones. The likeliest background is Psalm 29, where the voice of the LORD sounds over the waters seven times, breaking the cedars, flashing forth flames of fire, shaking the wilderness, and ending with the whole temple crying Glory! So this is a further series of seven: seven seals, seven trumpets, seven thunders. A full sequence of divine speech has just been uttered.

They spoke words. John hears them, and he understands them. That is clear from what follows, since a man does not reach for a pen to write down noise. Whatever the thunders said, it was articulate, it was complete, and it came from the same source as everything else in this book.

Do not write it down. This is the reverse of every other word John receives about writing. He has been told to write from the beginning (1:11, 19), and at the end he will be told, write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true (21:5). Once he is told not to, and the pen is already in his hand. The prohibition arrives mid-action, and what he heard is taken from every reader since.

The one sealed sentence. Daniel was told to seal his book until the time of the end (Daniel 12:4, 9). At the close of this book John is told not to seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near (22:10). Revelation is the unsealed book. There is exactly one sealed message in it, and we do not have it.

Why were the thunders sealed? Several answers have been offered. Perhaps they were further judgements that God has chosen to cancel or cut short, so that the end comes without more warnings, and the very next verse says there will be no more delay. Perhaps they are held back to show that the warnings already given are enough. Or perhaps they are sealed simply to teach that God has not told us everything. None of the first answers can be proved, and the honest position is that nobody knows, because the whole point of the verse is that we were not told. What is certain is the last lesson: the secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever, that we may do all the words of this law (Deuteronomy 29:29).

A boundary God has set. Note what the revealed things are for in Moses’ sentence: not so that we may know, but so that we may do. There is an appetite, not always a healthy one, for more than has been given: the date, the identity, the name behind the number. This verse says that the appetite has a limit and that God set it.

What it does not mean. The sealed thunders do not invite speculation. Some groups have claimed that their founders revealed what the seven thunders said, and anybody who claims it is claiming something John himself was forbidden to give. What God has sealed, no one may unseal, and the canon is closed (22:18–19). We have everything we need for life and godliness in what is written (2 Peter 1:3; 2 Timothy 3:16–17).

Does this mean the Bible is incomplete? No. It means the Bible is complete for its purpose, which is not the same as exhaustive. God has not told us everything he knows; he has told us everything we need, to know him, to be saved, and to live for him until Christ returns. A father does not tell a child everything about the family finances, and the child is not the poorer for it; he is told what he needs, by someone who loves him and knows the rest. The sealed thunders are a reminder that Scripture’s silences are as deliberate as its words, and that a believer who keeps to what is written is not missing anything God meant him to have.

When God does not answer my question. There is a gentler application here too, for a believer who has spent years asking God something that has never been answered. Why did that happen? Why was there no child? Why did the prayer of a good man seem to come to nothing? This verse does not say the answer does not exist. The thunders spoke; there was content; John understood it. It says the answer exists and has not been given, and that the withholding is deliberate and comes from heaven in a voice. Being told no by God about a piece of information is not the same as there being nothing there. And the God who withholds it is the same God who did not withhold his own Son (Romans 8:32). He can be trusted with what he keeps.

On a Tuesday. When a book, a video or a preacher offers you the hidden key to the end times, the date or the name or the sequence the rest of the church has missed, remember that an apostle with the pen in his hand was told to stop. And when your own unanswered question returns in the night, put beside it the things God has plainly said: that he works all things together for good for those who love him, that nothing can separate you from his love, and that he will wipe away every tear. Those are revealed, and they are yours.

For worship. The God of glory thunders, and he speaks in sevens and is never exhausted. He says more than any man could write, keeps back what he chooses, and owes no one an explanation. Yet he has not spoken in riddles about the one thing that matters: in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2). The thunders were sealed; the Son was sent. In Christ he has given us his last and clearest word, and with it himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel whom I saw standing on the sea and on the land raised his right hand to heaven and swore by him who lives forever and ever, who created heaven and what is in it, the earth and what is in it, and the sea and what is in it, that there would be no more delay, but that in the days of the trumpet call to be sounded by the seventh angel, the mystery of God would be fulfilled, just as he announced to his servants the prophets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. In Daniel 12:7, a man clothed in linen raised his hands to heaven and swore by him who lives for ever that it would be for a time, times and half a time, and that when the shattering of the power of the holy people came to an end, all these things would be finished. Raising the hand was the gesture of a solemn oath (Genesis 14:22; Deuteronomy 32:40). The martyrs had asked, How long? (6:10), and were told to rest a little longer (6:11).

He swore. The gesture is a formal oath, and the whole scene is quarried from Daniel 12. Men swear by something greater than themselves, and in oaths the final confirmation ends every argument (Hebrews 6:16). This angel swears by the greatest there is.

Who created heaven, earth and sea. The angel is standing on the sea and the land, and he swears by the one who made them. Whatever the beasts about to come out of them may claim, the ground under this oath belongs to somebody else. And because God made it all, he has both the right and the power to bring it to its end. A maker may finish what he began.

No more delay. This is the answer to the question asked by the souls under the altar, how long (6:10)? They were told to rest a little longer. Here, under oath, standing on the whole world, an angel announces that the little longer has run out. Turned the other way round, that is urgent good news for today: every day before the trumpet is a day on which a rebel may still come home. When it sounds, the door will be shut, as the door of the ark was shut and the door to the wedding feast was shut (Genesis 7:16; Matthew 25:10).

Textual note. The King James Version translates “that there should be time no longer”, which some have taken to mean the end of time itself. The Greek word chronos can mean delay, and the context, answering the martyrs’ How long?, shows that this is the meaning here.

The hardest thing is the waiting. Often the hardest thing in the Christian life is not the suffering itself so much as its open-endedness: not knowing whether it goes on for another month or another forty years. This verse does not tell the church when. It tells the church that the when has been fixed and sworn to by the Creator of everything. A prisoner who knows the date of his release can bear a great deal. A believer who knows that the date has been sworn to by God can bear more. Whatever you are waiting on God for, you may still have to wait, but you do not have to wait wondering whether he means it.

But if there is no more delay, why has it been two thousand years? Because the oath concerns what happens when the seventh trumpet sounds, not a stopwatch started in John’s day. Revelation shows the whole age between Christ’s first and second comings from several angles, and each cycle of sevens ends at the edge of the last judgement. This oath says that when God’s moment arrives there will be no further postponement, no last extension, no second thoughts. Peter answers the same question directly: the Lord is not slow to fulfil his promise as some count slowness, but is patient, not wishing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:8–9). Every year that passes is not God forgetting. It is God gathering the last of his elect, and the day he has fixed will not move.

The mystery of God would be fulfilled. Mystery in the New Testament never means a puzzle nobody can solve. It means something once hidden that has now been disclosed: a secret told. It is God’s plan of salvation in Christ, including the gathering of Gentiles with Jews into one people (Ephesians 3:3–6; Colossians 1:26–27), and its completion when all things are united in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth (Ephesians 1:9–10). The seventh trumpet will announce it: the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ (11:15). And the verb means completed, brought to its goal, the same family of words as the cry from the cross: it is finished. What the seventh trumpet completes on the stage of the whole world is what Christ finished at the cross, brought at last to its full and visible end.

Just as he announced to the prophets. Nothing new is being introduced. What the seventh trumpet will complete is the programme God published through Isaiah and Daniel and Amos and the rest; for the Lord GOD does nothing without revealing his secret to his servants the prophets (Amos 3:7). And the word for announced is the verb behind gospel and evangelise. God’s final victory is not a threat he has kept up his sleeve. It is good news, and he has been telling it for centuries.

In the flow. The oath stands where it does for a reason. The sixth trumpet ended with the survivors refusing to repent of their idols, murders, sorceries, sexual immorality and thefts (9:20–21): warning after warning had been given, and the world had hardened. So before the last trumpet God has it sworn that the time of warnings is nearly over. The oath reaches back to the martyrs’ cry in 6:10 and forward to 11:15–18, where the seventh trumpet sounds and the elders give thanks that the time has come to judge the dead. Between the two, chapters 10 and 11 show what the church does with the time that is left: it takes the word and speaks it.

How should this change the way I read the news? It should make you sober without making you frantic. The headlines are not the whole story, and they are not the last word. The world will not drift on for ever, nor collapse by accident, nor end when men decide; it will be brought to its goal by the God who made it, at a moment he has fixed and sworn to. So you do not need to decode current events to know where history is going. You need to know who is finishing it. That frees you to grieve real evils without despair, to work for good without imagining that everything depends on you, and to pray, as the church always has, Come, Lord Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the voice that I had heard from heaven spoke to me again, saying, "Go, take the scroll that is open in the hand of the angel who is standing on the sea and on the land." So I went to the angel and told him to give me the little scroll. And he said to me, "Take and eat it; it will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey." And I took the little scroll from the hand of the angel and ate it. It was sweet as honey in my mouth, but when I had eaten it my stomach was made bitter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Ezekiel ate a scroll full of lamentation and woe, and it was sweet as honey in his mouth (Ezekiel 3:1–3); afterwards he went in bitterness, in the heat of his spirit, and sat among the exiles seven days, overwhelmed (Ezekiel 3:14–15). Jeremiah said, your words were found, and I ate them, and your words became to me a joy and the delight of my heart (Jeremiah 15:16), and yet his ministry brought him great suffering. Psalm 19:10 and 119:103 call God’s words sweeter than honey.

Go, take the scroll. The voice that told him not to write now tells him to move. God’s word must be received personally. John does not snatch the scroll. He walks across and asks, and a mighty angel with his feet on the world hands a book to an old man who asked for it.

Take and eat it. The verb is strong: devour it, eat it up. Ezekiel was given this exact commission some seven hundred years earlier (see the setting), and John expects it to be recognised.

Why eating? Eating is the picture, and it is chosen carefully. A messenger could be handed a script and read it out; that is what a herald does. This is not that. Nobody delivers a message by digesting it. What eating does is make a thing part of you, slowly, internally, irreversibly. To eat a scroll means to take God’s word inside, to absorb it and make it part of oneself, before speaking it to others. God’s word is not first material to be transmitted. It is food to be taken into a person until it is in his blood, and only then does he speak. A prophet cannot pass on what he has not first taken in. Our Lord lived this himself: hungry in the wilderness, he answered the tempter from Deuteronomy, man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God (Matthew 4:4; Deuteronomy 8:3).

Sweet as honey. Both tastes are true of the gospel at once. Why sweet? Because it is the word of God, sweeter also than honey and drippings of the honeycomb (Psalm 19:10), full of grace, telling of his victory and the salvation of his people.

Why bitter? Because of what is in it. It brings judgement on the unrepentant, and those who proclaim it will suffer, as chapter 11 is about to show. John is about to be shown two witnesses killed in the street, a dragon hunting a woman, a beast making war on the saints and conquering them, and a city drunk on the blood of the martyrs. A man cannot take that in and feel nothing. Ezekiel left his commission in bitterness and sat stunned among the exiles for a week. The word that saves is also the word that judges, and nobody who loves people can carry the second half of that sentence lightly.

Sweet first, bitter after. John reports it in the order he experienced it. The angel had warned him in the reverse order, bitter then sweet, as though preparing him for the sting; the experience arrived the other way round.

The order of the two tastes. It describes something every honest Christian eventually recognises. The gospel is sweet on the way in and costly on the way down. People are not usually won by being told first what it will require; they are won by being told they are loved and forgiven, and it is honey. The bitterness comes later, and it is not a sign that something has gone wrong. It is the taste of a truth being taken in by a person who now has to live in a world that does not want it.

The taste of ministry. And it is specifically the taste of bearing witness. Anyone who has had to say a true thing that would cost him a friendship knows the exact sequence: the delight of knowing it, and then the churning at two in the morning before the conversation. Much of that churning is the fear of losing someone’s good opinion, and it shows how much we have leaned on being liked. But the one who carries God’s word is already approved where it matters most, by the God who sent it, and that frees him to risk a friend’s displeasure for the friend’s good (Galatians 1:10). A preacher who finds Scripture only bitter has forgotten why he started. The prophet gets both, in that order, from the same scroll.

Where their Lord was crucified. The little scroll is probably bound up with the scroll the Lamb took and opened (5:5–9), so what John swallows is the purpose the Lamb has unsealed, and its sweetness is the Lamb’s victory. The bitterness has the Lamb’s shape too. The very next chapter shows two witnesses lying dead in the street of the great city where their Lord was crucified (11:8). That is the road of the scroll’s bearers: they follow the Lamb wherever he goes (14:4), and he went by a cross. What does that mean? The cost of carrying God’s word is not a sign that the message has failed. It is the mark of belonging to the one whose own witness ended at a cross, and then at an empty tomb.

Why is Revelation so hard to read? This verse is the honest answer. Partly because it was never meant to be a comfortable read. It is sweet as honey: the Lamb reigns, the martyrs are vindicated, God wipes away every tear. And it is bitter, because the road to those things runs through everything in chapters 11 to 20. John was given both, and he was made to swallow before he was allowed to speak. If you find parts of this book troubling, you are reading it as its first reader did. Keep reading to the end. The bitterness is real, but it is not the last taste.

What does eating the word look like for an ordinary Christian? It is the difference between reading the Bible and taking it in. Read a passage slowly, more than once. Ask what it shows you of God, what it says to you, and what it asks of you. Turn it into prayer before you put it down. Carry one verse with you through the day and come back to it at odd moments, the way you return to a conversation that mattered. Memorise some of it, because what is in you cannot be taken away. You will not do this perfectly, and your standing does not hang on it: Christ kept his Father’s word perfectly in your place. But a short passage chewed is worth more than a long one swallowed whole and forgotten by lunch.

What if the Bible has only felt bitter to me lately? Then you may be in exactly the place this verse describes, and it is not a sign that God has left you. Sometimes the bitterness is the cost of obeying, or the grief of seeing sin and judgement clearly, and that is the word doing its work. Sometimes it is that you have been reading the commands without the promises, the law without the gospel. Go back to the honey: read a Gospel, a psalm of trust, Romans 8, Isaiah 53, and look at Christ for yourself, not only at your duty. The scroll is sweet first. Ask God to let you taste that again, and he will.

For worship. The word of the Lord is sweeter than honey, and he feeds his servants with it before he sends them. And the bitterness, too, he knows from the inside. At Golgotha, before they crucified him, they offered him wine mixed with gall, and when he tasted it he would not drink (Matthew 27:34): he would not dull one moment of what he had come to bear. He took the full bitterness of judgement that his people had earned, so that the bitterness left for them is only the cost of witness, never the taste of condemnation. He tasted death for everyone (Hebrews 2:9), and he gives them honey from the rock.
verseByVerse.note: Like Ezekiel, John eats God’s message: sweet to receive, bitter because it announces judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: And I was told, "You must again prophesy about many peoples and nations and languages and kings."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You must again prophesy. Very probably an old man, on a bare island under Roman banishment, with no congregation, no pulpit and no way home, who has already written the seven letters and seen the throne, the seals and the trumpets. By any ordinary reckoning his work is behind him. The word must is the same word used in 1:1 of the things that must soon take place, and the word Jesus used of his own suffering. This is not an invitation and it is not a career step. It is a commission, renewed: he has already prophesied, and now he must go on, with the second half of the book.

Many peoples and kings. The fourfold phrase is the one John has used since 5:9 and 7:9 for the whole human race, with kings substituted for tribes, because from chapter 11 onward the book turns to the powers of the earth. A prisoner with no legal standing has just been given a preaching commission covering every nation on earth and their rulers, and the only equipment he is issued is a small scroll he has eaten.

The Lamb’s nations. These are the very peoples the Lamb bought: by his blood he ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation (5:9). And the kings in the list will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings (17:14). So John is not sent to announce an open contest. He is sent to tell the nations who owns them, and to call them to the one who died for people among them.

About, or against. The preposition can bear either. Prophecy in Scripture is very rarely prediction for its own sake. It is God’s verdict on the present, delivered out loud, usually to people who did not ask for it. Emperors who thought themselves gods are about to hear what heaven thinks of them, from a man they had exiled, and through his book, and the church that takes up his commission (11:3–6), they still do.

Are there prophets like John today? Not in John’s sense. John received new revelation directly from God, and what he received is now written down as the last book of the Bible, with a warning against adding to it or taking from it (22:18–19). That kind of prophecy has ceased, because the canon is complete. Many Christians in Pentecostal and charismatic churches believe God still gives prophetic words today, though most of them agree that no such word equals Scripture or adds to it; this commentary holds that the gifts of new revelation have ceased (the view called cessationism, from the word cease), and honours them as brothers and sisters who love the same Word. But the prophetic task of the church goes on. Every faithful preacher who opens this book, and every believer who tells a neighbour what God has said in Scripture, is declaring God’s word to peoples and nations and kings. We do not receive new thunders. We carry the scroll that has already been opened, and it is enough.

When my useful years seem over. There is something here for any Christian who has concluded that his work for God is finished, because of age, or illness, or a job that ended, or a church that no longer asks. John’s circumstances were worse than most: exiled, elderly, isolated, and, by long tradition, already the author of a Gospel and three letters. Heaven’s assessment was again. The most extraordinary assignment of his life arrived after everything that looked like his ministry had been taken away from him. The work may look different now: prayer instead of travel, a letter instead of a sermon, faithfulness in a small room instead of influence in a large one. But no one who belongs to Christ is ever discharged from his service while he still has breath.

The shape of the chapter. A messenger in his master’s glory plants his feet on the world; the thunders are sealed; the Creator’s oath is sworn; and a scroll is handed to a man, who eats it and is sent back to work. That is the pattern of every real commission God has ever given. He does not hand out information to be relayed. He feeds a person with his own word until it is inside him, and then sends him out to say it, and the sweetness and the bitterness both come from the same source, and neither of them is a mistake.

On a Tuesday. Pray for kings and all who are in high positions (1 Timothy 2:1–2). Then bring it closer: who in your own small world needs to hear what God has said, and has no one else to tell them? You do not need John’s visions to do it. You need the scroll he ate, which is open on your table, and the Spirit who once made frightened disciples speak the word with boldness (Acts 4:31), and who lives in you.

It was sweet as honey in my mouth, but when I had eaten it my stomach was made bitter.<sup>11</sup>And I was told, “You must again prophesy about many peoples and nations and languages and kings.”

11.title: The Two Witnesses and the Seventh Trumpet
11.overview:
Chapter 11 shows the whole church age from two angles: the measuring of the temple (the church’s preservation), the ministry of the two witnesses (the church’s prophetic witness), their death and resurrection (the church’s apparent defeat and vindication), and the seventh trumpet (the kingdom declared). It is also one of the most debated chapters in the book.

Dispensationalists read the measuring of the temple in vv. 1–2 as a prophecy of a rebuilt temple in Jerusalem. This commentary reads the temple as the church, as Paul regularly uses temple language for God’s people (1 Corinthians 3:16; 2 Corinthians 6:16; Ephesians 2:21): its inner life is kept safe while its outward life is exposed to the world for a limited time.

The two witnesses of vv. 3–13 have been identified as Moses and Elijah, as Enoch and Elijah, or, as most Reformed readers hold, as the whole witnessing church. Two is the number of legal testimony (Deuteronomy 19:15), and their powers are the powers of the prophetic word, which both judges and saves.

The seventh trumpet of vv. 15–19 releases no new plague. It announces that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ: the answer to the prayer “Your kingdom come”, declared as already done, with the rest of the book still to unfold it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: John measures the temple, the altar and the worshippers, but not the outer court, which is given over to the nations for forty-two months. Something is claimed and something is deliberately left out, and both are God’s decision.

Verses 3–6: two witnesses in sackcloth, the olive trees and lampstands of Zechariah 4, prophesy for 1,260 days with the powers of Elijah and Moses.

Verses 7–10: when their testimony is finished, the beast kills them; their bodies lie unburied in the great city where their Lord was crucified, and the world celebrates.

Verses 11–14: God breathes life into them, calls them up in a cloud while their enemies watch, and after an earthquake the survivors give glory to the God of heaven. The second woe has passed.
verseByVerse.theology:
Measured, Trampled, Raised

God measures his temple and leaves the outer court to be trampled for a bounded time. His two witnesses prophesy in sackcloth, are killed when their testimony is finished, lie unburied while the world celebrates, and are raised and called up in their enemies’ sight.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Plagues had not moved the world; the witnesses’ death and vindication did.

Now: No faithful witness is cut off before his testimony is finished, and a witness that troubles nobody may not be one.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I was given a measuring rod like a staff, and I was told, "Rise and measure the temple of God and the altar and those who worship there, but do not measure the court outside the temple; leave that out, for it is given over to the nations, and they will trample the holy city for forty-two months.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Revelation 11 shows the church’s life and witness in this age, and then the seventh trumpet. John measures God’s temple, its altar and its worshippers, but leaves out the outer court, given to the nations to trample for forty-two months (vv. 1–2): God’s people are safe in their inner life and exposed outwardly. Two witnesses in sackcloth prophesy for 1,260 days with the powers of Moses and Elijah (vv. 3–6). The beast kills them, and their bodies lie in the great city where their Lord was crucified while the world celebrates (vv. 7–10). After three and a half days God raises them and calls them up to heaven in a cloud, and an earthquake brings the survivors to give glory to God (vv. 11–14). Then the seventh trumpet sounds: the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and God’s temple in heaven opens to show the ark of the covenant (vv. 15–19). It is the story of the Lord Jesus told again in the lives of his people: witness, death, resurrection, ascension, and a kingdom that cannot be shaken.

The setting. Measuring in the Old Testament can mean protecting what belongs to God, as when Ezekiel watches a new temple measured (Ezekiel 40–48) and Zechariah sees Jerusalem measured, with the LORD as a wall of fire around her (Zechariah 2:1–5); or it can mean marking out for judgement (2 Kings 21:13; Lamentations 2:8). Daniel spoke of a time, times and half a time (three and a half years) during which a hostile king would persecute God’s holy people (Daniel 7:25; 12:7). Jesus said that Jerusalem would be trampled underfoot by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled (Luke 21:24).

A measuring rod. The rod is a reed, a measuring stick; Ezekiel’s was about three metres long (Ezekiel 40:5). Here measuring is not surveying but the act of a legal owner marking out what is his and what he intends to protect. To be measured is to be claimed.

Those who worship there. The word for temple, naos, is the sanctuary, the inner shrine, not the whole complex of courts. The third item on the list is the surprise. You can measure a building and an altar with a reed. You cannot measure worshippers with one, unless the temple is made of them. In the New Testament the temple of God is the church, God’s people in whom he dwells: do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you (1 Corinthians 3:16–17; 2 Corinthians 6:16; Ephesians 2:19–22; 1 Peter 2:5)? Measuring the temple means God marks out his people as his own and guarantees their protection, as the sealing of God’s servants on their foreheads did in chapter 7: one truth in two figures.

The temple of his body. The church can be called God’s temple only because of someone else. When Jesus said, destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up, John explains that he was speaking about the temple of his body (John 2:19–21). He is the true sanctuary, the place where God and man meet, and believers become living stones only by coming to him, the living stone rejected by men but chosen and precious in the sight of God (1 Peter 2:4–5). That is why the worshippers can be measured with the temple: they are built into him. What John measures is the people who are in Christ, and to be in him is to be counted.

Leave that out. The phrase is literally throw it outside. The outer court was where Gentiles could come in Herod’s temple. Here it stands for the church’s outward, visible life in the world, which is exposed to attack. Something is measured, and something is deliberately left unmeasured, and both are God’s decision. The trampling is permitted, and the permission comes from him, for a set time; he has not abandoned his people or lost control.

Protected and exposed. The church is not promised that nothing can be trampled. It is promised that what the trampling can reach is not the temple. Buildings burn, reputations are ruined, denominations collapse, believers are imprisoned and killed; none of that touches the sanctuary, the altar or the worshippers, and God has drawn the line himself. A Christian who expects only protection will be bewildered by the exposure.

Forty-two months. The holy city is God’s people, the church, the new Jerusalem in the making (21:2). This is the first appearance of a period the book names again and again, in three interchangeable forms: forty-two months (11:2; 13:5), 1,260 days (11:3; 12:6), and a time, and times, and half a time (12:14). All three are three and a half years. They come from Daniel, where the little horn wears out the saints for a time, times, and half a time (Daniel 7:25; 12:7), and they recall the three and a half years of drought in Elijah’s day (Luke 4:25; James 5:17).

Half of seven. In a book where seven is the number of completeness, half of seven is the number of a period that is real, severe, and definitely not complete: broken off before it can run its course. On the reading this commentary follows, it is the whole period between Christ’s first and second comings, when the church witnesses and suffers. Its message is the reason John keeps repeating it: this is a bounded time. Somebody has already written down when it stops.

Where Christians differ: is this a literal temple in Jerusalem? Dispensationalists (who keep God’s plans for Israel and the church distinct and expect a future seven-year tribulation) hold that a third temple will be rebuilt in Jerusalem before Christ returns, with sacrifices restored, and that this passage describes it during a literal three-and-a-half-year period. This view has the merit of wanting to take the words plainly, and those who hold it love the Scriptures. Preterists (who read much of Revelation as fulfilled in the first century) date the book before AD 70 and see here the Jerusalem temple about to fall to Rome, and Jesus’ words in Luke 21:24 give that view real weight. But on the usual dating John wrote around AD 95, a quarter of a century after the temple was destroyed, so a literal reading requires a temple that does not yet exist. This commentary’s view: the temple is the church, the people of God. The New Testament never anticipates a rebuilt temple with renewed sacrifices; Hebrews teaches that Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice has made the temple and its sacrifices obsolete (Hebrews 8:13; 10:11–18). Revelation itself shows no temple in the new Jerusalem, because God and the Lamb are its temple (21:22). The worshippers are measured with the temple, showing that people are in view. And the number forty-two months is drawn from Daniel’s symbolic times, used in Revelation for the whole church age.

If I am measured and protected, why do Christians still suffer and die? Because the protection promised here is not protection from all harm but protection of what you truly are in God. The outer court is trampled, and that is real: believers lose jobs, health, property and sometimes life. What cannot be touched is your belonging to God, your access to him, and your final salvation. Jesus said the same in one breath: some of you they will put to death, yet not a hair of your head will perish (Luke 21:16–18). Both are true. The world can reach your body and your circumstances. It cannot reach the place where God has measured you as his own, and it cannot keep you there beyond the time he has fixed.

On a Tuesday. When your reputation is attacked for following Christ, or the church you love is shrinking, or the culture treats your faith as a joke, do not conclude that the sanctuary has fallen. Go to the altar. Pray. Worship with God’s people on the Lord’s day. That is the measured ground, and nothing outside it can take it from you.

For worship. The Lord knows those who are his, and he has measured them with his own rod. Not one worshipper is missing from his count; not one is left in the outer court by oversight. Let the nations trample what they are permitted to trample for the days he has numbered. The sanctuary is his, the altar is his, the worshippers are his, and the Lamb who was slain has written down the day the trampling ends.
verseByVerse.note: Forty-two months, 1,260 days (v. 3) and “a time, and times, and half a time” (12:14) are all three and a half years — Daniel’s limited time of trouble.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will grant authority to my two witnesses, and they will prophesy for 1,260 days, clothed in sackcloth." These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. In Zechariah 4, the prophet sees a golden lampstand with two olive trees beside it, supplying oil; they are the two anointed ones who stand by the Lord of the whole earth, Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest, a king and a priest who rebuilt the temple, not by might nor by power, but by God’s Spirit. In the law, two witnesses were required to establish a matter (Deuteronomy 19:15). Jesus sent his disciples out two by two (Luke 10:1). Sackcloth was worn in mourning and repentance, as by the prophets (Isaiah 20:2; Jonah 3:5–6).

My two witnesses. Witness is the church’s calling throughout Revelation (1:2, 9; 2:13; 6:9; 12:11, 17), and the Greek word would in time give us our word martyr, because so many who bore witness died for it. Two is the legal number for valid testimony (Deuteronomy 19:15). Their whole activity in this chapter is testimony, and it is true, and it will stand in God’s court. And the authority is granted. They do not take it, earn it or vote it to themselves. It is given by the one who calls them my witnesses.

For 1,260 days. This is forty-two months, the same period as the trampling of the holy city (v. 2). The trampling and the testimony run side by side for exactly the same length of time, which means there is never a day when the church is being trampled and has nothing to say.

Clothed in sackcloth. Coarse black goat hair, the dress of mourning and repentance, worn by Jacob for a son he thought was dead and by the whole city of Nineveh at Jonah’s preaching. Their message is a call to repentance, and they grieve over the world’s sin. That sets the tone of the church’s testimony in this age: not swagger, but mourning. The witnesses do not gloat over the world they warn; they weep over it, as their Lord wept over Jerusalem.

Two olive trees and two lampstands. The image is lifted whole from Zechariah 4, where two olive trees beside a lampstand feed oil directly into the lamps. In 1:20, the lampstands are the churches. So the two witnesses are the church, in its role of witness, and its witness depends on the Spirit, not on might or power. In Zechariah there is one lampstand; here there are two, perhaps for the two witnesses required by law, or for the church drawn from Jews and Gentiles.

The Anointed One behind the olive trees. In Zechariah the two olive trees are the two anointed ones, a governor of David’s line and a high priest. In Jesus the two offices meet in one person. He is the Christ, the Anointed, the Son of David, and he is a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek, who was both king of Salem and priest of God Most High (Psalm 110:1–4; Hebrews 7:1–3). He is also the faithful witness (1:5), who made the good confession before Pontius Pilate and was put to death (1 Timothy 6:13). The witnesses’ authority is his, and so is their oil, for he has made his people a kingdom, priests to his God and Father (1:6). The church holds up, in mourning clothes, the light of the one who is both her King and her Priest.

Not by might, nor by power. The Zechariah vision turns on the word spoken to Zerubbabel in the middle of it (Zechariah 4:6). A lampstand cannot make light or oil; it holds up what is poured into it. The church testifying in sackcloth for 1,260 days is not running on its own reserves, and never was. That answers the sense that the church is too small, too tired and too compromised to be heard. The witnesses are two, in mourning dress, in a city that will kill them. They are also connected to an inexhaustible supply, and the authority they have was granted.

In the flow. Chapter 10 ended with John told that he must prophesy again about many peoples, nations, languages and kings (10:11). These verses show what that prophesying looks like when the whole church takes it up. The measuring of verses 1–2 showed that God’s people are safe; now we learn what they are kept safe for. They are not hidden away to wait for the end but sent out to speak until it comes.

Where Christians differ: who are the two witnesses? Many futurists (who expect most of Revelation to be fulfilled just before Christ returns) see them as two individual prophets in a future tribulation, often Moses and Elijah returned, because the powers described in the next verses are precisely theirs and because those two stood with Christ on the mount of transfiguration (Matthew 17:3); or Enoch and Elijah, the two men in Scripture who did not die (Genesis 5:24; 2 Kings 2:11). Others suggest Peter and Paul, martyred in Rome. These readings take the Moses and Elijah details seriously, and they deserve a respectful hearing. This commentary’s view: the two witnesses symbolise the witnessing church throughout this age. Revelation tells us the lampstands are churches (1:20). Their ministry lasts for the same period as the church’s trampling, the whole age. The whole world sees their deaths (v. 9), which suits a worldwide church better than two individuals. And the beast makes war on them (v. 7), as it makes war on the saints (13:7). They are pictured with the powers of Moses and Elijah, the law and the prophets, because the church carries on the prophetic witness of the Old Testament, in the power of the Spirit. On any reading the substance of the passage is unchanged: God has witnesses, they are given authority, they speak for a bounded time, they are killed, and they are raised.

Are the 1,260 days a literal three and a half years? Futurist readers take them as the second half of a future seven-year tribulation. But John uses the three forms interchangeably for the same period (11:2–3; 12:6, 14; 13:5), drawn from Daniel, during which the church witnesses, is nourished in the wilderness and is persecuted by the beast. The more likely reading is that they describe the whole age between Christ’s comings: a limited time, cut short, under God’s control. That means you are living in the 1,260 days now. This chapter is not about someone else at the end of history. It is about the church you belong to, this week.

Is the witness of these verses only for preachers? No. The two witnesses are two lampstands (v. 4), and the lampstands are churches (1:20), so the calling belongs to every believer. A witness is simply someone who tells what he knows to be true. You know that Christ died for sinners, that he rose, and that he has forgiven you. You bear witness when you live honestly at work, when you speak of God without embarrassment in ordinary conversation, when you explain why you hope, when you invite a friend to church, when you refuse to join in what dishonours Christ, and when you suffer patiently. Most witness is not a sermon. It is a life lived in the open with a reason for it, and the reason given gently and respectfully when someone asks (1 Peter 3:15). The Spirit supplies the oil. You hold up the lamp, and a lampstand is not meant to be impressive, only to hold the light where it can be seen.

For worship. The oil in the lamps was poured first on him. The Father gave his Son the Spirit without measure (John 3:34), and the risen Christ, having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, poured him out on his people (Acts 2:33). So frail lamps that could never light themselves burn on through every century of trampling, because the supply is in heaven and it is his. He is the Lord of the lampstands, who walks among his churches, who grants authority to weak people in mourning clothes, and whose light the darkness has never overcome.

verseByVerse.quote: And if anyone would harm them, fire pours from their mouth and consumes their foes. If anyone would harm them, this is how he is doomed to be killed. They have the power to shut the sky, that no rain may fall during the days of their prophesying, and they have power over the waters to turn them into blood and to strike the earth with every kind of plague, as often as they desire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Elijah called down fire from heaven on soldiers sent to arrest him (2 Kings 1:10–12), and announced a drought that lasted three and a half years (1 Kings 17:1; James 5:17). Moses turned the Nile into blood and struck Egypt with plagues (Exodus 7–11). God told Jeremiah, I am making my words in your mouth a fire, and this people wood, and the fire shall consume them (Jeremiah 5:14).

Fire from their mouth. Not from heaven, as in Elijah’s case, and not from the hand, but from the mouth. In this book that is a settled image: the sharp two-edged sword comes from the mouth of Christ (1:16; 19:15). The weapon is the word. What these witnesses do is speak. The word of judgement they proclaim will finally consume those who reject it.

This is how he is doomed. The sentence is stated twice, which is unusual and deliberate. It reads like a standing legal rule rather than a description of a single event: harm them, and this is what follows. “Doomed” is dei, must, the word of divine necessity. Those who oppose God’s witnesses are opposing God, and will be judged by the word they rejected: the word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day (John 12:48). The witnesses are not the executioners. They speak; the judgement falls from somewhere else.

Power to shut the sky. That is Elijah exactly (1 Kings 17:1; Luke 4:25). Luke and James both give Elijah’s drought this very length (1 Kings 18:1 says only that the rain returned in the third year): the number of this chapter, arriving in the source material. The church’s prayers and witness have real power in the world: the prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working, and James makes the point with Elijah, a man with a nature like ours (James 5:16–18).

Waters into blood. That is Moses in Egypt (Exodus 7:17–20). The plagues of the trumpets are linked to the church’s witness and prayers (8:3–5): the prayers of the saints rise before God, and fire from the altar is thrown on the earth. The witnesses’ word announces God’s judgements, and their prayers call them down.

Moses and Elijah, and Jesus only. Moses and Elijah stand behind the two witnesses, and the pairing is not random. They are the law and the prophets, the two halves of the Old Testament, and they are the two who appeared with Christ on the mountain and spoke with him about his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:30–31). Then the cloud came, and the Father said, This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him, and when the voice had spoken, Jesus was found alone (Luke 9:35–36). That is where the witnesses’ power comes from. The law and the prophets point to him, and the church speaks with the authority of Moses and Elijah only because it speaks the word of the Son they pointed to, standing before every Pharaoh and every Ahab to say the true thing about him.

As often as they desire. The phrase is startling and should not be softened: God does not ration his witnesses’ authority. But hold it beside verse 7, where they are killed in the street. These are people with power to shut the sky, and they are about to be overpowered, and both are true at once. That is the experience of the church in every century: the word of God in the mouth of believers has real, world-altering force, and the people who carry it are frequently humiliated and killed. John gives both, two verses apart.

Where Christians differ: should the church expect such miracles today? Some read these verses as promising that end-time believers will perform Elijah-like and Moses-like miracles, and some charismatic groups expect such signs as normal. This commentary’s view: the images are symbolic of the power of the church’s witness, which comes through the word of God and prayer. The miraculous signs of Moses, Elijah and the apostles served to confirm new revelation at key moments in redemptive history (Hebrews 2:3–4; 2 Corinthians 12:12). This commentary holds that such sign gifts ceased once the apostles’ foundational work and the canon of Scripture were complete (Ephesians 2:20). Many faithful believers, continuationists who hold that all the gifts continue today, weigh the evidence differently, and they are brothers and sisters to be honoured, not dismissed. God still answers prayer powerfully, and still judges the world; but the church’s fire is the word it speaks, not miracles performed at will.

What it does not mean. This does not authorise Christians to call down judgement on their enemies. When James and John wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village, Jesus rebuked them (Luke 9:54–55). The fire is God’s, through the word; we preach and pray, and leave judgement to God.

So how should I pray about evil in the world? Pray boldly, because the prayers of the saints are taken up into the purposes of God (8:3–5), and pray as Jesus taught, first for God’s name, his kingdom and his will. Ask God to stop the wicked, to defend the oppressed, to bring down unjust rulers and to bring justice for the persecuted, as the psalms do. But pray also for the conversion of those who do evil, as Stephen did for the men stoning him, and as Christ did from the cross (Luke 23:34, a prayer missing from some early manuscripts but widely judged genuine). Leave the manner and the timing of judgement to God. The witnesses’ fire is a word spoken, not a grudge nursed. Your part is to speak truly and to pray; his part is to judge rightly, and he will.
verseByVerse.note: Their powers recall Elijah (fire, drought) and Moses (water to blood, plagues).

verseByVerse.quote: And when they have finished their testimony, the beast that rises from the bottomless pit will make war on them and conquer them and kill them, and their dead bodies will lie in the street of the great city that symbolically is called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. In Daniel 7:21, the horn of the fourth beast made war with the saints and prevailed over them. To leave a body unburied was the greatest dishonour in the ancient world (Psalm 79:2–3). Sodom was the Old Testament’s symbol of wickedness (Genesis 19; Isaiah 1:10); Egypt was the land of slavery and oppression of God’s people.

When they have finished. The first words change everything. The beast does not interrupt them; until the testimony is complete, nothing could harm them. God’s witnesses are immortal until their work is done, and only when God allows it can the beast touch them.

A promise you can put weight on. It is not the promise most people want. It does not say the witness will be protected. It says the witness will be finished. Nobody in God’s service is cut off mid-sentence by accident, and the man who dies at forty with half his work apparently undone has, on the testimony of this verse, completed it. The missionary who dies in her first year on the field, the young pastor buried before his church was built, the mother who did not live to see her children grown: each was given a testimony to bear, and each was allowed to finish it. The length was God’s decision, and so was the completion. God measures a life by whether it carried the testimony he gave, and by that measure no faithful life is cut short.

The beast from the bottomless pit. The word is a wild animal. He appears here for the first time, introduced with the definite article as if already known from Daniel 7, two chapters before he is described in full in chapter 13. He represents the power of the state, or of any human system, when it sets itself against God and persecutes his people. And he rises from the abyss, a pit that had to be unlocked with a key that somebody was given (9:1–2): he is not a rival power from somewhere outside God’s rule.

Conquer them. Here is the word that ought to stop a reader. “Conquer” is the verb of the promise to the faithful in every one of the seven letters, the verb used of Christ himself in 5:5. Here it is used of the beast, against the saints, successfully, and it will be used that way again at 13:7. Revelation will not pretend the church always wins its battles. It says plainly that the church loses, visibly, in public, at the hands of a power that is permitted to defeat it.

Same verb, opposite direction. And the whole book exists to redefine what that defeat means, because the definitive instance of somebody conquering by being killed is the Lamb standing in the middle of the throne, looking as though it had been slain (5:6). The beast conquers by killing witnesses. The Lamb conquered by being killed. The church conquers by being faithful unto death, as the Lamb did: they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death (12:11). Apparent defeat is real victory.

The great city. Everywhere else in Revelation, the great city is Babylon (16:19; 17:18; 18:10), the world system opposed to God, and the whole book is a tale of two cities, this one and the holy city (v. 2). Their bodies lie in the street: not in a prison or a tomb, but in the open, where the traffic goes. Whatever public humiliation looks like in a given century, that is what is described.

Symbolically Sodom and Egypt. John supplies the key himself. “Symbolically” is literally spiritually, in the manner the Spirit speaks: these names are not addresses. It is Sodom in its wickedness, Egypt in its oppression of God’s people.

Where their Lord was crucified. This points to Jerusalem, where Jesus died, which in rejecting him became like Sodom and Egypt, as Isaiah had warned her long before when he called her rulers rulers of Sodom (Isaiah 1:9–10). And the great city is wherever the world rejects Christ and persecutes his witnesses. Piling four identities onto one city is the point: wherever the people of God are opposed, that place becomes Sodom and Egypt and Babylon and the city that killed the Lord. It is one city under many names, and it has a branch in every generation. As their Lord was treated, so are they: if they persecuted me, they will also persecute you (John 15:18–20).

If the beast can conquer the church, how is Christ winning? He is winning the way he won at the cross: by what looks like defeat. The beast has power over bodies, but not over souls (Matthew 10:28). He can kill the witnesses only after their testimony is finished, only in the place and time God permits, and only to send them where their Lord has gone. Every martyr’s death is a testimony completed, not a testimony stopped. And the story does not end in the street. Read on two verses: breath from God, a voice from heaven, a cloud. The beast’s victories are real, temporary and already reversed in the counsel of God. Christ’s victory is real, permanent and already won.

On a Tuesday. Do not live as though your life were fragile in God’s hands. It is fragile in the world’s hands, and secure in his. Do today what he has given you to do, leave the length of your days to him, and pray for Christians in places where the beast is openly making war: they are not losing; they are finishing their testimony.

For worship. He who holds the keys of death and Hades decides when each witness has finished, and he knows what finishing costs. He completed the work his Father gave him to do (John 17:4), and on the cross he said, It is finished, and bowed his head and gave up his spirit (John 19:30). The street where the bodies lay is the street where he was led out to die, and he went that way first, so that no witness of his would ever walk it alone. The beast is a creature on a leash, let up from a pit that is not his own.

verseByVerse.quote: For three and a half days some from the peoples and tribes and languages and nations will gaze at their dead bodies and refuse to let them be placed in a tomb, and those who dwell on the earth will rejoice over them and make merry and exchange presents, because these two prophets had been a torment to those who dwell on the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For three and a half days. Three and a half days against the three and a half years of their witness, and the proportion is the message: the humiliation is real and it is brief.

Peoples and tribes and languages. The four terms are the ones used for all humanity (5:9; 7:9), and in 5:9 they described the ransomed multitude. Now they describe the spectators: the same world that the Lamb bought is standing in the street looking at the bodies. And the verb is to look at, to watch: a public appetite that any generation which has watched a humiliation circulate for days will recognise exactly.

No tomb. In the ancient world burial was owed even to an enemy; refusing it was a way of saying that a person did not count as human. The psalmist’s lament over Jerusalem was exactly this: they have given the bodies of your servants to the birds of the heavens for food, and there was no one to bury them (Psalm 79:2–3).

Exchange presents. Sending gifts is the language of a festival, as at Purim (Esther 9:19, 22): a grotesque parody of a holiday, held because two preachers are dead. Every other celebration in these chapters is in heaven; this one is on the earth. Compare the joy of heaven when Babylon falls (18:20; 19:1–3): the book has two parties in it, held by different people for opposite reasons. And those who dwell on the earth, twice in this verse, is John’s technical term (8:13) for people whose home and hope and heart are nowhere else. Every Christian lives on the earth; none is called an earth-dweller.

The people stood by, watching. This verse has already been lived once, in the city where their Lord was crucified. At the cross too the crowds came to look: the people stood by, watching, and the rulers scoffed (Luke 23:35), and the multitudes had assembled for the spectacle (Luke 23:48). Herod and Pilate, enemies until then, became friends that very day (Luke 23:12). But the likeness breaks at the tomb. His body was not left in the street: Joseph of Arimathea laid it in his own new tomb (Matthew 27:57–60), and on the third day the tomb was empty. The witnesses’ disgrace is the disgrace he bore first, and it will end the way his ended.

A torment. The word used of the locusts tormenting people in 9:5. The witnesses had no army and no legal standing; what they had was a message, and the message was intolerable. Calling people to repent, and warning them of judgement, tormented the consciences of the world. People hate the light, because it exposes their deeds (John 3:20). Ahab said it to Elijah’s face: is it you, you troubler of Israel (1 Kings 18:17)?

A warning and a comfort in one sentence. The warning: if the world is entirely comfortable with what your congregation says, it is not saying what these two were saying. A witness that troubles nobody is probably not a witness. The comfort: when Christians find themselves treated as a problem to be removed rather than an opinion to be debated, that is not evidence that something has gone wrong. It is the treatment the two witnesses received, and the treatment their Lord received in the same city.

Should I try to be offensive, then, so that I know I am faithful? No. The torment comes from the truth, not from the manner. The witnesses are in sackcloth, not armour; they mourn over the world, they do not sneer at it. Peter tells Christians to make sure that if they suffer, it is for doing good and for the name of Christ, not for being meddlers or for doing wrong (1 Peter 4:15–16), and to give their reasons with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15).
