A Christian who is rude and is resented for it has not been persecuted; he has been rude. Aim to be kind, honest and clear, and let any offence be the offence of the cross.

On a Tuesday. When you see a Christian publicly humiliated, whether justly for a real fall or unjustly for faithfulness, refuse to join the crowd that gazes: your Lord was once its spectacle, and he did not leave you in your own disgrace. Do not pass the story on for the pleasure of it. Pray, and if the person belongs to Christ, stand with them.

verseByVerse.quote: But after the three and a half days a breath of life from God entered them, and they stood up on their feet, and great fear fell on those who saw them. Then they heard a loud voice from heaven saying to them, "Come up here!" And they went up to heaven in a cloud, and their enemies watched them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. In Ezekiel 37:5, 10, God says to the dry bones that he will cause breath to enter them and they will live, and breath came into them, and they lived and stood on their feet, an exceedingly great army. Elijah was taken up to heaven in a whirlwind (2 Kings 2:11). Jesus ascended in a cloud while his disciples watched (Acts 1:9).

A breath of life from God. The wording is Ezekiel’s, and any reader who knows the valley of dry bones will hear it at once. The same word means breath and spirit, in the Hebrew of Ezekiel as in the Greek here. As in Ezekiel 37 and Genesis 2:7, God gives life by his breath. The witnesses are raised by God, as their Lord was. What a public that had refused them burial declared finished stands up in the street.

Great fear fell. The party stops mid-sentence. Three and a half days of gazing at corpses, and then the corpses stand up. The resurrection of God’s people is their vindication, and their enemies’ dismay.

Come up here. It is the call John himself heard in 4:1, and it summons them into God’s presence.

In a cloud. That is how Christ ascended, a cloud taking him out of the disciples’ sight (Acts 1:9), and how he will return (1:7). The witnesses are given their Lord’s death, in his city, and then their Lord’s resurrection and his ascension, in that order. And the last clause is not decoration. When Jesus rose, the world did not see it; the guards saw an angel roll back the stone, became like dead men, and were afterwards paid to say something else (Matthew 28:2–4, 11–15), and the risen Christ appeared to chosen witnesses, not to all the people (Acts 10:40–41). Here the vindication is public, and the people who arranged the deaths are standing in the street with their gifts still in their hands.

What the witnesses do not do. They do not argue, retaliate, or explain. They stand up, and they are called, and they go. Vindication in Scripture is almost never something a person achieves; it is something done to him by somebody else, usually later than he would have chosen. Peter told the churches of Asia Minor exactly that: humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you (1 Peter 5:6).

Where Christians differ: is this the rapture? Some read this as a rapture, a catching up of believers to heaven, in the middle of a future seven-year tribulation, whether of two individual prophets or of the church. Many who expect such a rapture learned it from teachers they rightly love, and they long for Christ as truly as anyone. This commentary’s view: if the two witnesses are the church, their resurrection and ascension picture the resurrection of believers at Christ’s return, when the dead in Christ rise and the church is caught up to meet the Lord in the clouds (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). It is public, seen by their enemies, not secret. It follows the church’s whole period of witness and suffering, and it is followed at once by the final judgement and the seventh trumpet (v. 15), which Paul also links with the last trumpet (1 Corinthians 15:52). There is one visible return, with one resurrection of the righteous and the gathering of the church at that time. That return may be near, but it will not be secret, and Scripture names events that come before it (2 Thessalonians 2:1–4).

Will my body really be raised? Yes. The breath of God that entered the witnesses is the picture of a real promise: the same Spirit who raised Jesus from the dead will give life to your mortal body (Romans 8:11). The Christian hope is not that the soul escapes the body for ever, but that the body itself is raised, changed and glorified, like Christ’s own body (Philippians 3:21). When a believer dies, his soul goes at once to be with Christ (Philippians 1:23), and his body rests in the grave, still united to Christ, until the last trumpet. Then the dead in Christ will rise, and those alive will be changed, and together they will meet the Lord, in full view of the world that buried them.

On a Tuesday. Whatever happens to you for Christ’s sake, God will have the last word, and it will be resurrection. So you do not have to win every argument, clear your name in every circle, or have the last word yourself. Tell the truth, do what is right, and leave your reputation with God.

For worship. The breath that moved over the waters at creation, that filled Adam’s nostrils and swept through the valley of dry bones, is the breath that raised the Lord Jesus from the tomb, and it will raise every one of his people. He who was called up into the cloud before the eyes of his disciples will call his church up in the same way, before the eyes of the whole world. The grave cannot keep what he has claimed, and the Lord who called Come up here has not lost the address.

verseByVerse.quote: And at that hour there was a great earthquake, and a tenth of the city fell. Seven thousand people were killed in the earthquake, and the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven. The second woe has passed; behold, the third woe is soon to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. In Elijah’s day, God kept seven thousand in Israel who had not bowed the knee to Baal (1 Kings 19:18). In the Old Testament, giving glory to God sometimes means confessing the truth and turning to him in repentance (Joshua 7:19; Jeremiah 13:16).

A great earthquake. Earthquakes accompany God’s coming in judgement (6:12; 8:5; 16:18). At that hour: the vindication of the witnesses and the shaking of the city are one event. Heaven does not let the ascension pass without the earth feeling it.

And a tenth of the city fell. The proportions run the opposite way from everything in the book so far. In chapter 6 a fourth of the earth was struck; in chapters 8 and 9 a third, repeatedly. Here it is a tenth: still partial, and much smaller. A tithe, perhaps: a portion given up in judgement, while the rest is spared to repent.

Seven thousand. Literally, seven thousand names of men; seven speaks of completeness. And the number carries an echo of Elijah, who stands behind these witnesses: there seven thousand were the remnant preserved. Here seven thousand fall and the great majority are spared. The arithmetic of grace has been turned the other way up.

Gave glory to the God of heaven. Set that against 9:20, two chapters earlier: the rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent. The same kind of survivors, and the opposite outcome. Two witnesses prophesied in sackcloth, were killed, and were raised, and nine tenths of a city gave glory to God. What judgements alone could not do, the church’s witness, death and vindication achieve.

Where Christians differ: is this genuine repentance? Some careful interpreters take “gave glory” as a terrified, forced acknowledgement of God, not true conversion. This commentary’s view: the phrase in Revelation is used for true worship and repentance: in 14:7 the angel calls the nations to fear God and give him glory, and in 16:9 those who did not repent refused to give him glory. Here, unlike 9:20–21, the response is positive. It points to the fruit of the church’s faithful witness: many from the nations turning to God. This fits the great multitude from every nation (7:9) and the nations walking by the light of the new Jerusalem (21:24).

The grain that dies. If that reading is right, the chapter has made an argument about how the world is reached, and it is not the argument most churches would have made. Plagues did not do it, nor a third of mankind dying. What did it was two witnesses in mourning dress, refusing to stop speaking, being killed for it, and being raised. It is the pattern of their Lord. Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, Jesus said, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit, and he added that his servants must follow him on the same road (John 12:24–26). His death and resurrection began the gathering of the nations; theirs, joined to his, carries it on. Tertullian put it in a line the church has never forgotten: the blood of Christians is seed.

The second woe has passed. The bookkeeping verse again, matching 9:12. The eagle’s three woes of 8:13 are the fifth, sixth and seventh trumpets. The third woe, the seventh trumpet, is announced as soon, and the very next verse sounds the seventh trumpet, which turns out to contain no plague that John describes, only the announcement of a kingdom.

Then why do disasters not bring people to God? Sometimes they do, for a while; churches fill after a catastrophe and empty again within months. This chapter explains why that is not enough. Fear of judgement by itself hardens as often as it humbles (9:20–21; 16:9). What turns hearts is the word of God, carried by witnesses whose lives and deaths make it credible, and applied by the Spirit. That is why the church must not wait for a crisis to do its evangelism for it. Crises shake people. Christ, preached by people who love him more than their own lives, saves them.

On a Tuesday. Perhaps there is someone you have prayed for and spoken to for years without visible result. This chapter does not promise you will see the harvest, but it does tell you how harvests come: through faithful, patient, costly witness that does not stop. Keep speaking and praying: the breath of God that raised the witnesses is the Spirit who gives your words life, and the seed is in the ground.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 15–17: the seventh trumpet brings no plague, only an announcement that the kingdom of the world has changed hands, and the elders leave their thrones to give thanks to the God who has taken his great power and begun to reign.

Verses 18–19: the nations’ rage is answered with judgement and reward, small and great alike, and the temple in heaven opens to show the ark of his covenant.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Kingdom Has Come

The seventh trumpet announces that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ. God is now praised as the one who is and who was, for the one to come has come, and the ark of his covenant is seen in his temple.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The outcome was declared with eleven chapters still to run.

Now: Believers live inside a victory already won and not yet seen; small and great alike will be rewarded.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the seventh angel blew his trumpet, and there were loud voices in heaven, saying, "The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever." And the twenty-four elders who sit on their thrones before God fell on their faces and worshiped God, saying, "We give thanks to you, Lord God Almighty, who is and who was, for you have taken your great power and begun to reign.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Psalm 2:2 speaks of the kings of the earth setting themselves against the LORD and against his Anointed. Daniel 2:44 and 7:14, 27 foretell a kingdom that God will set up that will never be destroyed, given to the Son of Man and to the saints of the Most High, an everlasting kingdom. Exodus 15:18, the song of Moses, ends: The LORD will reign forever and ever.

The seventh trumpet. The last trumpet, the third woe (11:14), announced in 10:7 as the moment when the mystery of God would be fulfilled. Paul speaks of the last trumpet at which the dead are raised (1 Corinthians 15:52; 1 Thessalonians 4:16). Six trumpets brought hail, blood, wormwood, darkness, locusts and cavalry. The seventh does not describe new plagues. It brings an announcement, and it is the sentence the whole book has been climbing towards.

The kingdom of the world. The phrase is singular; later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read the kingdoms, but the earliest have the singular. There is one worldly kingdom under many governments: the whole world system, under the rule of Satan and the beast, and it has changed hands. “Christ” is the Anointed One, as in Psalm 2: the King whom God set on Zion while the nations raged.

Has become. The verb is past tense, a completed act, and that is what makes the sentence extraordinary. Heaven does not announce that the kingdom of the world will become God’s. It announces a transfer so certain that it is described as done: a herald reading out a result, not a forecast.

The result announced at half-time. And it is announced at the seventh trumpet, with eleven chapters of the book still to run. The dragon has not appeared yet, the beast has not been described, and Babylon has not fallen. The outcome is declared before the conflict is described, and that is a key to how the whole book is built. It is the account of a war whose result was announced at the halfway point, and before that at an empty tomb.

What it meant to the first hearers. They were being read a document that told them the empire would get worse, that a beast would be given authority over every tribe and people, that they would be conquered and killed. And in the middle of it, loud voices in heaven saying that the kingdom of the world has already changed owner. They were not being asked to hope for a victory. They were being asked to live inside one that had not yet been made visible.

He shall reign. “He” is singular. God and his Christ reign as one; the Father and the Son do not have two thrones but one (22:1, 3). The reign is eternal: no thousand-year limit, no end. The song of Moses at the Red Sea ended with the same words (Exodus 15:18).

The twenty-four elders. Twenty-four figures who have thrones of their own get off them and put their faces on the floor. Their response is not analysis. It is adoration.

Who is and who was. Here a small detail carries a great deal. The divine title in this book has been threefold from the first chapter: who is and who was and who is to come (1:4, 8; 4:8). Here it is twofold. Who is and who was, and the third term is gone. It is not an oversight. The one who is to come has come. The title had a future tense in it for as long as there was a future to wait for, and at the seventh trumpet the future tense drops out of the name of God.

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add “and art to come” after “who is and who was”. The best manuscripts do not have it, and its absence is deliberate: at this point in the vision, God has come.

Taken your great power. Decisively taken: not been given, taken. God did not lack power before; he has always been sovereign, but now his reign is openly established over all opposition. That is what the title Almighty has meant all along: the ruler of all, in whose hand even his enemies have always been. What was hidden is revealed; what was contested is settled.

Where Christians differ: does Christ’s kingdom come gradually or suddenly? Postmillennialists believe that the gospel will gradually transform the world until most of humanity is Christian, and then Christ will return. Premillennialists believe Christ will return to set up a thousand-year earthly kingdom (20:4–6), and dispensationalists add a distinct future for national Israel in that kingdom; both take the promise of a renewed earth with welcome seriousness. This commentary’s view: Christ already reigns now, at the Father’s right hand (1:5; Ephesians 1:20–22), and his kingdom grows through the gospel. But the kingdom of the world becomes the kingdom of Christ in full only at his return, at the last trumpet, when he judges the living and the dead. There is no thousand-year interval between the last trumpet and the eternal reign; he will reign for ever and ever from the moment of his return. This is the amillennial view: it expects no future thousand-year reign on earth and reads the thousand years of chapter 20 as Christ’s present reign. It rests on passages like this one, where the last trumpet brings in the eternal kingdom at once. Many godly Christians read chapter 20 otherwise, and they love his appearing as much as anyone.

If Christ reigns now, why does the world look the way it does? Because his reign is real now but not yet visible to all. He sits at the Father’s right hand with all authority in heaven and on earth (Matthew 28:18), and he is gathering his people through the gospel and restraining evil within limits he has set. But he is patient, and he allows the outer court to be trampled for the appointed time. Hebrews says it exactly: at present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him. But we see him, crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death (Hebrews 2:8–9). We live by what we see in him, not by what we see in the headlines. At the last trumpet the two will match.

On a Tuesday. When the news makes it look as though the kingdom of the world belongs to whoever is loudest or cruellest, say to yourself the sentence heaven has already said: it has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ. That does not make you careless about the world; it makes you unafraid in it. Give thanks, as the elders did, before you see it, because the thanksgiving of the faithful is always ahead of the evidence.

For worship. Hallelujah, for the Lord our God the Almighty reigns. The last time the kingdom of the world stood face to face with the Christ, it was in a Roman governor’s hall, and it held all the power in the room. My kingdom is not of this world, Jesus said; his servants did not fight, and the soldiers crowned him with thorns and crucified him under a notice that called him King (John 18:36; 19:2, 19). Now the kingdom of the world has become his, not seized by the sword but announced by the trumpet, and twenty-four thrones stand empty because their occupants are on their faces. The song of Moses at the sea and the chorus of the elders end on the same words: for ever and ever.

verseByVerse.quote: The nations raged, but your wrath came, and the time for the dead to be judged, and for rewarding your servants, the prophets and saints, and those who fear your name, both small and great, and for destroying the destroyers of the earth." Then God's temple in heaven was opened, and the ark of his covenant was seen within his temple. There were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, an earthquake, and heavy hail.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Psalm 2:1, 5 says the nations rage, but God speaks to them in his wrath. The ark of the covenant, the gold-covered chest that held the tablets of the law, stood in the Most Holy Place, the place of God’s throne on earth, where the high priest sprinkled atoning blood once a year (Exodus 25:10–22; Leviticus 16). It is never heard of after Babylon destroyed the temple in 586 BC. Jewish tradition said Jeremiah hid it, and it would reappear when God gathered his people again (2 Maccabees 2:4–8).

The nations raged. The words are from Psalm 2, which Revelation has been quoting since 2:27. Here it reports the raging in the past tense: it is over, and it was answered. And the two words share a root, raged (were angry) and wrath. The nations’ anger against God is met by God’s anger against them. Their rage is futile; his is just and final.

The time for the dead. “Time” is the appointed moment. The final judgement of all the dead (20:11–15). Everyone, without exception, including everyone who died believing the matter was closed. Nothing has been filed away.

Both small and great. This is the longest clause in the verse, and its generosity is the point. “Rewarding” is literally giving the wages. Three overlapping groups, prophets, saints, and simply those who fear your name, and then a phrase that refuses to let anybody be ranked out of it: both small and great. There is no tier system at this reward. No one is too insignificant to be noticed and rewarded; not even a cup of cold water given to one of these little ones will lose its reward (Matthew 10:42). The two witnesses who shut the sky and the widow who kept praying and never told anybody are in the same sentence.

Reward and grace. God intends to give things to people for what they did, and the New Testament is entirely unembarrassed about that (Matthew 6:4; 1 Corinthians 3:14; Hebrews 11:6). But the reward Christ brings with him (22:12) is grace, not wages in the strict sense. The servants were bought before they ever served; their works were prepared by God beforehand (Ephesians 2:10); and when he rewards them he is crowning his own gifts. Grace is not the abolition of reward. It is the reason a reward is possible at all.

Destroying the destroyers. The word is ruining, corrupting, and the same root is used twice, which the English preserves. A fitting justice: those who ruin the earth, morally and physically, by violence, idolatry and corruption, will be ruined. Babylon is said to have corrupted the earth (19:2). Nothing arbitrary is happening: the sentence is the crime, said back. God made the earth good, and he will judge those who destroy it, and renew it.

The ark of his covenant. For a Jewish reader this may have been the most astonishing sentence in the chapter. The ark stood in the Most Holy Place, behind the veil, and only the high priest saw it, once a year. It vanished from history when Babylon destroyed the temple, if not before; Jeremiah had said the day would come when people would no longer say the ark of the covenant of the LORD, nor miss it (Jeremiah 3:16). For centuries the holiest object in Israel’s worship had simply been gone. Here it is. In the temple in heaven, in plain view, with the doors open.

What the ark means. The ark was the chest that held the covenant, the tablets of the law, under a lid where blood was sprinkled once a year. To see it standing there is to be told that the covenant was never lost when the building fell, that God has kept his side of it, and that the place where blood was applied for a nation’s sin is still in the room. And the New Testament names what that lid always pointed to. The word for it, the mercy seat (Hebrews 9:5), is the word Paul uses of Christ: God put him forward as a propitiation by his blood (Romans 3:25). The word describes a sacrifice that absorbs the judgement the sinner deserved, so that God’s anger is spent and turned aside, and it fits this verse exactly: the wrath announced here against the nations was borne by Christ for everyone who comes to him. The law lay in the box, and the blood on the lid covered the sins of those who had broken it; Christ kept that law in full, and his blood covers for ever. The Most Holy Place, once closed to all but the high priest, is opened, and the chapter that began by measuring a temple and leaving part of it to be trampled ends by opening the real one.

Lightning, thunder and hail. John’s standing signal that God has acted, used at 4:5 with three elements, at 8:5 with four, and here with five; the same sign, intensified again, ends the bowls (16:18–21). The nations raged; his wrath came; the covenant stands open in the light; and the last sound in the chapter is thunder over an ark that nobody had seen for centuries.

What it does not mean. The seventh trumpet does not end the book because Revelation is not a straight timeline. Chapter 12 will go back to the birth of Christ and show the same age again, from the angle of the spiritual war behind it.

Does the open temple mean I can come to God now, or only at the end? Now. The vision shows what is true in heaven at all times and will be visible to all at the end. When Christ died, the curtain of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom (Matthew 27:51), and Hebrews says we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us (Hebrews 10:19–22). You do not need a priest, a pilgrimage or a special state of feeling. You come through Christ, in prayer, at any hour, and you are welcome. The ark in heaven is the guarantee that the covenant under which you come will never be broken.

How can a God of love be angry? Because love that is never angry at evil is not love but indifference. A father who shrugs at the man beating his child does not love the child. His anger does not flare and cool like ours; it is his holiness standing steadily against everything that wrecks what he made, and this verse calls such people the destroyers of the earth. And the astonishing thing is where that wrath went for those who trust Christ: it fell on him, so that they are saved from it (Isaiah 53:5–6; Romans 5:9). The cross that shows how seriously God takes evil also shows how far he will go to save the people who did it.

On a Tuesday. If you are one of the small, unnoticed servants, the one who visits, prays, sets out the chairs, cares for an elderly parent, and is never thanked, this verse is for you: both small and great. God has seen it, and he intends to reward it.

11.text: <sup>1</sup>Then I was given a measuring rod like a staff, and I was told, “Rise and measure the temple of God and the altar and those who worship there,<sup>2</sup>but do not measure the court outside the temple; leave that out, for it is given over to the nations, and they will trample the holy city for forty-two months.<sup>3</sup>And I will grant authority to my two witnesses, and they will prophesy for 1,260 days, clothed in sackcloth.”<sup>4</sup>These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth.<sup>5</sup>And if anyone would harm them, fire pours from their mouth and consumes their foes. If anyone would harm them, this is how he is doomed to be killed.<sup>6</sup>They have the power to shut the sky, that no rain may fall during the days of their prophesying, and they have power over the waters to turn them into blood and to strike the earth with every kind of plague, as often as they desire.<sup>7</sup>And when they have finished their testimony, the beast that rises from the bottomless pit will make war on them and conquer them and kill them,<sup>8</sup>and their dead bodies will lie in the street of the great city that symbolically is called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified.<sup>9</sup>For three and a half days some from the peoples and tribes and languages and nations will gaze at their dead bodies and refuse to let them be placed in a tomb,<sup>10</sup>and those who dwell on the earth will rejoice over them and make merry and exchange presents, because these two prophets had been a torment to those who dwell on the earth.<sup>11</sup>But after the three and a half days a breath of life from God entered them, and they stood up on their feet, and great fear fell on those who saw them.<sup>12</sup>Then they heard a loud voice from heaven saying to them, “Come up here!” And they went up to heaven in a cloud, and their enemies watched them.<sup>13</sup>And at that hour there was a great earthquake, and a tenth of the city fell. Seven thousand people were killed in the earthquake, and the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven.<sup>14</sup>The second woe has passed; behold, the third woe is soon to come.<sup>15</sup>Then the seventh angel blew his trumpet, and there were loud voices in heaven, saying, “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever.”<sup>16</sup>And the twenty-four elders who sit on their thrones before God fell on their faces and worshiped God,<sup>17</sup>saying, “We give thanks to you, Lord God Almighty, who is and who was, for you have taken your great power and begun to reign.<sup>18</sup>The nations raged, but your wrath came, and the time for the dead to be judged, and for rewarding your servants, the prophets and saints, and those who fear your name, both small and great, and for destroying the destroyers of the earth.”<sup>19</sup>Then God’s temple in heaven was opened, and the ark of his covenant was seen within his temple. There were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, an earthquake, and heavy hail.

12.title: The Woman, the Dragon, and the War in Heaven
12.overview:
Chapter 12 goes behind the scenes. Much of what comes before (the seals, the trumpets, the witnesses) and what follows (the beasts, the bowls, Babylon’s fall) is explained here: the dragon’s war against the woman, the birth of the child who will rule the nations, the war in heaven that casts Satan down, and the dragon’s fury against the woman’s other children. This is why the church is persecuted: having failed to destroy the child, the dragon turns on those who hold to the testimony of Jesus.

The woman clothed with the sun draws on Joseph’s dream (Genesis 37:9) and on the prophets’ picture of Zion as a mother in labour. She is not Mary, though the birth of Jesus is in view. She is the people of God: Israel, who gave birth to the Messiah, and the church, which continues that people.

The great red dragon is Satan, as verse 9 says plainly, and his seven heads and ten horns anticipate the beast of chapter 13, his instrument. In the war of vv. 7–12 Michael throws the dragon down, but the song that follows says where the victory was really won: the saints conquered him by the blood of the Lamb. The dragon is thrown down because the Lamb was slain.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Woman and the Dragon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–4: two signs in heaven. A woman clothed with the sun, crowned with twelve stars and in labour, is the covenant people from whom the Messiah comes. A great red dragon with seven royal crowns stands before her, waiting to devour her child.

Verses 5–6: she bears the Messiah-King of Psalm 2, and he is caught up to God’s throne untouched. The woman flees into the wilderness, to a place God has prepared, where she is fed for 1,260 days: the position of the church between the ascension and the end.
verseByVerse.theology:
The War Behind the War

The woman, the covenant people, Israel and the church, bears the Messiah, while the dragon waits to devour the child. The child is caught up to God’s throne, and the woman is kept and fed in the wilderness for a measured time.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Every attack on the promised line, from Pharaoh to Herod, was the dragon at the woman’s feet.

Now: The church’s wilderness is hard, but it is a place prepared by God.

verseByVerse.quote: And a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars. She was pregnant and was crying out in birth pains and the agony of giving birth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Revelation 12 goes behind the scenes of history to show the spiritual war that explains why the church suffers. A woman clothed with the sun cries out in labour, and a great red dragon waits to devour her child (vv. 1–4). She bears a son who will rule the nations with a rod of iron; he is caught up to God’s throne, and she flees to the wilderness, where God nourishes her for 1,260 days (vv. 5–6). Michael and his angels throw the dragon, the ancient serpent, the devil and Satan, down to earth, and heaven rejoices that the accuser is gone and that believers have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony, loving not their lives even unto death (vv. 7–12). The furious dragon pursues the woman, who is carried to safety on eagle’s wings, and then makes war on the rest of her offspring, who keep God’s commandments and hold to the testimony of Jesus (vv. 13–17). Satan is a defeated enemy, beaten at the cross, enraged because his time is short, and the people he rages against are protected by God and conquer him through Christ’s blood and their faithful witness.

The setting. In Joseph’s dream, the sun, moon and eleven stars bowed down to him, representing his father, mother and brothers, the family of Israel (Genesis 37:9–10). The prophets picture Israel, or Zion, as a woman in labour, longing for deliverance (Isaiah 26:17–18; 66:7–9; Micah 4:10; 5:3). In Genesis 3:15, God told the serpent that the offspring of the woman would bruise his head, and that he would bruise his heel. Ancient myths told similar stories: in the Greek myth, the dragon Python pursued the goddess Leto, pregnant with Apollo, who later killed the dragon. Some emperors, Augustus and Nero among them, liked to be associated with Apollo. Revelation tells the true story behind the myths: the real child is Christ, and the real dragon is Satan.

The war behind the war. The book turns here. Chapters 1 to 11 have shown what happens on earth and in heaven as the scroll is opened; chapter 12 pulls the curtain back further and shows why. From here to chapter 20 the reader is looking at the dragon, his two beasts and their city, and this chapter introduces all of it. And it begins, not with the dragon, but with a woman and a child. Before we are shown the enemy, we are shown the one he cannot defeat.

A great sign. A sign is something that stands for something else. It is the first time Revelation uses the word, and John says so before he describes anything, which is his standing courtesy to the reader. This is a sign; read it as one.

A woman clothed with the sun. Who is she? The imagery answers it. In Joseph’s dream the sun, the moon and the stars were his father, mother and brothers; add Joseph, and you have twelve. The sun, the moon and twelve stars is Israel, the covenant people from whom the Messiah comes. The twelve stars are the twelve tribes of Israel, and also, as the book will show at the end, the twelve apostles (21:12–14). She is the people of God, the messianic community from which the Messiah comes and which continues as the church.

Birth pains. This is the suffering of God’s people in the Old Testament as they waited for the Messiah: the long years of Israel’s history, under oppression, longing for the promised offspring. John does not soften it.

Glory and agony at once. She is clothed in glory and she is in agony, both at once, and that combination is the whole doctrine of the people of God in one picture. Seen from heaven, the church is clothed with the sun and crowned with stars. Seen from the street, she is a woman in labour, crying out, with something enormous waiting for her. Both are accurate.

Pain with an outcome. Birth pain in Scripture is usually suffering with an outcome. Isaiah confessed that Israel’s labour had brought forth only wind, and then heard God promise that the dead would rise (Isaiah 26:17–19); Jesus used it of the troubles before the end: all these are but the beginning of the birth pains (Matthew 24:8); Paul used it of the whole creation groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now (Romans 8:22). In God’s hands the pain of his people is real, it is severe, and it is going somewhere. And if you have known a labour that ended in loss, this picture does not mock your grief: the Lord who wept at a grave is near to the broken-hearted, and he has promised that the dead will rise.

Born of woman. The labour has one child in view. When the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman (Galatians 4:4), and the promise made at the gate of Eden became a baby in Bethlehem. Every groan of Israel’s long history was waiting for him. And Jesus used this very picture of his own death and rising. On the night before the cross he told his disciples that a woman in labour has sorrow, but when the child is born she no longer remembers the anguish, for joy that a human being has been born into the world; so their sorrow at his death would turn to joy when they saw him again (John 16:20–22). The pains of God’s people are the pains of a birth, because the one they wait for has already come out of the grave.

Where Christians differ: is the woman Mary? Roman Catholic tradition has long identified the woman with the Virgin Mary, and has used this passage in support of Marian devotion and of her bodily assumption into heaven. Its love for the mother of the Lord is not wrong in itself. This commentary’s view: the woman is the people of God, Israel and then the church. There is a secondary allusion to Mary, who literally gave birth to the Messiah, and she belongs to the people of God. But the woman’s experiences cannot be Mary’s: she is persecuted in the wilderness for 1,260 days after her child ascends (v. 6), and she has other offspring who keep God’s commandments and hold the testimony of Jesus (v. 17), who are believers. The twelve stars point to the twelve tribes. Nothing here supports praying to Mary, or her being given a special role in salvation.

How should Protestants think of Mary, then? With great honour, and without worship. She was a real woman of faith, chosen by grace to bear the Son of God, and she called herself the Lord’s servant and God her Saviour (Luke 1:38, 47). All generations call her blessed, and rightly. But she was a sinner saved by her Son like everyone else, and Scripture never asks us to pray to her or through her. Paul says there is only one go-between who stands between God and humanity, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all (1 Timothy 2:5–6). The best way to honour Mary is to do what she said at Cana: whatever he says to you, do it (John 2:5).

On a Tuesday. When the church seems weak and noisy and in distress, and your own Christian life feels more like labour than glory, remember that heaven sees her clothed with the sun. Your pain, borne in faith, is not wasted. It is going somewhere.
verseByVerse.note: The sun, moon and twelve stars recall Joseph’s dream of Israel’s family. The woman seems to be the people of God, from whom the Messiah came.

verseByVerse.quote: And another sign appeared in heaven: behold, a great red dragon, with seven heads and ten horns, and on his heads seven diadems. His tail swept down a third of the stars of heaven and cast them to the earth. And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that when she bore her child he might devour it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. In the Old Testament, the sea monster or dragon (Leviathan, Rahab) is a symbol of chaos and of evil powers opposed to God, and of empires such as Egypt (Isaiah 27:1; 51:9; Psalm 74:13–14; Ezekiel 29:3). Daniel 7 describes four beasts, the fourth with ten horns, representing world empires. Daniel 8:10 describes a horn that grew great and threw down some of the stars to the ground and trampled them. At Christ’s birth, King Herod tried to kill him by slaughtering the infants of Bethlehem (Matthew 2:13–18).

A great red dragon. A sign again, and John says so again. This is not what Satan looks like; it is what Satan is, rendered in a picture. The dragon is a great serpent, identified in verse 9 as the devil, Satan, and in the Old Testament the chaos monster of the deep that God alone can master. “Red” is fiery red, the colour of bloodshed, like the second horseman (6:4). He was a murderer from the beginning (John 8:44).

Seven heads and ten horns. Every detail is a counterfeit of something already seen in this book. Seven heads: seven is God’s number of completeness, and the dragon wears it, a picture of complete cunning or power. Ten horns: horns are power, and ten is fullness of a lesser kind, great strength, as in Daniel’s fourth beast. And the sharpest detail is the diadems, royal crowns, not victors’ wreaths. The woman wears a victor’s crown of stars; the dragon wears seven royal crowns. Satan claims royal authority over the world (Luke 4:5–6; John 12:31). He is claiming a sovereignty he does not hold; his crowns are claims, not rights. The beast of chapter 13 will look like him, because the beast is his agent.

Who the crowns belong to. The rider on the white horse will come with many diadems on his head (19:12), and the Gospels tell how he came by them. The first crown anyone put on Jesus was twisted out of thorns by soldiers who knelt before him in mockery (Matthew 27:29). The usurper grasps at royalty; the true King accepted shame, and that is why Hebrews can say we see him crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death (Hebrews 2:9). The dragon’s crowns were seized. Christ’s were given him by his Father, on the far side of a cross.

A third of the stars. Stars can represent angels (1:20; 9:1). This probably refers to the angels who fell with Satan, the demons (v. 9). Or it pictures his destructive power and his attack on God’s people, like the horn in Daniel 8:10. A third is the same fraction that ran through the trumpets. Even in the account of his greatest success the dragon gets a limited portion. Two thirds stayed.

That he might devour it. That single sentence is the plot of the Old Testament. Immediately after the fall God promised that the woman’s offspring would crush the serpent’s head (Genesis 3:15). Everything after that is the serpent trying to get to the child first. Cain kills Abel. Pharaoh orders every Hebrew boy thrown into the Nile (Exodus 1). Athaliah destroys the whole royal family of Judah and misses one baby hidden in a bedroom (2 Kings 11:1–3). Haman obtains a decree to destroy every Jew in the empire (Esther 3). When the child is finally born, Herod sends soldiers to Bethlehem to kill every boy under two (Matthew 2:16). And finally there is the cross. Every one of those is the dragon standing in front of the woman with his mouth open. Matthew reports Herod’s massacre as history; John shows what was underneath it.

The second layer. Few parts of Scripture show it as directly as this chapter, though Job 1–2 and Daniel 10 draw back the same curtain. The events are real, a real decree, a real sword, real children, and there is something behind them that is also real, and hostile, and personal, and has been at this for a very long time. Paul said the same thing without the picture: we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness (Ephesians 6:12).

How little he does. In the next verse the child is taken to the throne of God, and the dragon does not lay a finger on him.

Is the devil a real person, or a symbol for evil? He is real. The dragon is a picture, but it is a picture of someone, as the lion is a picture of Christ. Jesus spoke to him in the wilderness, named him a liar and a murderer, and spoke of his fall (Matthew 4:1–11; John 8:44; Luke 10:18). He is a created spirit, a fallen angel, not God’s equal and not everywhere at once. He has intelligence, a will and a strategy. That is why Scripture tells us to be sober and watchful (1 Peter 5:8). But it never tells us to be fascinated by him or terrified of him. Resist him, firm in your faith (1 Peter 5:9), and he will flee from you (James 4:7).

Does every bad thing happen because of Satan? No. Scripture names three enemies: the world, the flesh and the devil (Ephesians 2:1–3). Much evil comes from our own sinful desires (James 1:14), and much suffering comes simply from living in a fallen world. Blaming the devil for every sin can become a way of avoiding repentance. But this chapter does warn us not to be naive. Behind the great persecutions and the great lies of history, and sometimes behind the attacks on a single believer’s faith, there is a personal enemy. Take sin seriously as your own, and take the devil seriously as real, and keep your eyes on the child who went past him to the throne.

On a Tuesday. When you read of persecution, of children harmed, of attempts to silence the church, recognise the old pattern. Pray against it, act against it where you can, and remember that the dragon has stood with his mouth open many times before and gone away hungry.

verseByVerse.quote: She gave birth to a male child, one who is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron, but her child was caught up to God and to his throne, and the woman fled into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, in which she is to be nourished for 1,260 days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Psalm 2:9 says that God’s Son, his anointed King, will break the nations with a rod of iron. After the exodus, God led Israel into the wilderness, where he fed them with manna and protected them for forty years (Exodus 16; Deuteronomy 8:2–4). Elijah fled into the wilderness and was fed by ravens and an angel (1 Kings 17:2–6; 19:4–8). The holy family fled into Egypt to escape Herod (Matthew 2:13–15).

A male child. The phrase is literally a son, a male, echoing Isaiah 66:7, where Zion gives birth to a son before her labour pains. The identification is settled by the quotation. It is Psalm 2:9, the coronation psalm of the Messiah, which this book has already applied to Christ and to those who conquer (2:27) and will apply again at 19:15. The child is Christ, the Messiah-King.

From birth to throne. Here the story is compressed almost to nothing. Between the birth and the throne there is nothing. No childhood, no Galilee, no Sermon on the Mount, no miracles, no cross, no empty tomb. More than thirty years, the whole Gospel story of his ministry, death and resurrection, pass in a comma.

Why the compression? Because of what this chapter is showing. It is not telling the story of Jesus; it is telling the story of the dragon’s attempt on him, and the point being made is that the attempt failed completely. From the dragon’s side there is nothing to report between the birth and the throne except a total defeat. He stood there with his mouth open and the child went straight past him to the seat of God. Christ was not devoured; he was exalted to God’s throne.

Caught up. The verb means snatched, seized with force. It is the word Paul uses of the man caught up to the third heaven (2 Corinthians 12:2) and of believers caught up to meet the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:17). Whatever the dragon intended, the child was snatched out of his reach.

The cross was not avoided. Be clear about what the compression does and does not mean, because it can mislead. It does not mean the cross was skipped. The cross is in this book everywhere: the Lamb standing as though slain is the central image of the whole vision, and in this same chapter the saints conquer the dragon by the blood of the Lamb (12:11). It means the cross, which seemed to be Satan’s victory, led to Christ’s enthronement. He devoured nothing. The child he was waiting for went to the throne, and the route ran through a grave that could not hold him.

Into the wilderness. The child is safe on the throne; the mother is in the desert. That is the position of the church between the ascension and the end. In Scripture the wilderness is a place of testing but also of God’s protection and provision, where a nation was fed for forty years by bread that arrived each morning. It is a hard address, and it is not abandonment.

A place prepared. “Prepared by God” uses the same verb as the place Christ has gone to prepare for his people (John 14:2). The desert was not an accident of flight; the accommodation was booked. The church lives as pilgrims and exiles (1 Peter 1:1; 2:11): not hidden from the world, not yet in the promised land, but protected and provided for by God.

Nourished for 1,260 days. “Nourished” is fed, sustained, and the Greek says literally that they feed her, without naming who they are. As God fed Israel with manna, he sustains his church by his word and Spirit. 1,260 days is the same period as the witnesses’ prophesying and the trampling of the holy city (11:2–3): the whole age between Christ’s ascension and return. The church in this age is a woman in a desert, fed by an unseen hand, for a period that has already been measured.

How does God feed his church in the wilderness? By the ordinary means he has appointed. He feeds us through his word, read and preached; through prayer; through the Lord’s Supper and baptism; and through the fellowship of believers who bear one another’s burdens. That is our manna, and like manna it comes daily and must be gathered daily; yesterday’s portion will not do for today. So if you are feeling starved, ask first whether you have been at the table. The church that neglects the word and gathered worship is not being left hungry by God. It has stopped coming to where he lays the food.

On a Tuesday. If you are in a dry stretch of life, with no prospects, no company and no visible progress, this verse tells you what that place is. It is not where God loses track of his people. It is where he feeds them himself, with the bread that comes down from heaven.

For worship. The Child is on the throne. He who was born in weakness was caught up in power; he who was laid in a manger sits at the right hand of the Majesty on high, and the nations are his inheritance. And the God who seated him there has not forgotten the mother. He prepared her place before she fled; he numbered her days before they began; he feeds her every morning in a land where nothing grows. The Shepherd of Israel, who rained down manna and set a table in the wilderness, is the Shepherd of his church, and she shall not want.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Satan Thrown Down to Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 7–9: Michael and his angels defeat the dragon, and he loses his place in heaven. He is named four ways, the great dragon, the ancient serpent, the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world, and is thrown down to the earth.

Verses 10–12: a voice in heaven explains it as a court case. The accuser of the brothers has lost his standing, and they conquer him by the blood of the Lamb, by their testimony, and by not loving their lives even to death. Heaven rejoices; the earth is warned, because the devil is furious and his time is short.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Accuser Thrown Down

Satan, the accuser who stood as prosecutor before God, is thrown down. The saints conquer him by the blood of the Lamb, by the word of their testimony, and by not loving their lives even to death.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Congregations that had buried martyrs were told those deaths were victories.

Now: The voice reciting your record has lost its standing, because the charges were paid. His fury is the fury of one whose time is short.

verseByVerse.quote: Now war arose in heaven, Michael and his angels fighting against the dragon. And the dragon and his angels fought back, but he was defeated, and there was no longer any place for them in heaven. And the great dragon was thrown down, that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world—he was thrown down to the earth, and his angels were thrown down with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. In Daniel 10:13, 21 and 12:1, Michael is the great prince who has charge of God’s people. In Jude 9 he is called the archangel. In Job 1–2 and Zechariah 3:1, Satan appears before God to accuse God’s people. Jesus said, when the seventy-two returned from their mission, I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven (Luke 10:18), and, as the cross approached, now will the ruler of this world be cast out (John 12:31).

War in heaven. Michael’s name is Hebrew for who is like God? He is named in Scripture only in Daniel, Jude and here: the protector of God’s people, and an archangel who, disputing with the devil about the body of Moses, did not presume to pronounce a blasphemous judgement but said, the Lord rebuke you (Jude 9). He is a creature, and a careful one. And it is Michael, not God or Christ, who fights the dragon. Satan is not God’s equal rival but a creature defeated by another creature. The real victory has already been won by the Lamb (v. 11); Michael’s victory in heaven reflects Christ’s victory on earth. The dragon was defeated, literally he was not strong enough: powerful, but not powerful enough, and that phrase is the whole of his career.

No longer any place. What was Satan doing in heaven at all? The Old Testament answers it plainly, and the answer is the key to the whole chapter. In Job he presents himself among the sons of God and accuses a righteous man to God’s face: does Job fear God for no reason (Job 1:9)? In Zechariah he stands at the right hand of the high priest to accuse him, and the priest is wearing filthy garments, and the accusation is true (Zechariah 3:1–4). Satan’s place in heaven was never a throne. It was a prosecutor’s bench, and he has lost it (v. 10).

That ancient serpent. Four names in two verses, and each one is a job description. The great dragon: the chaos monster, raw destructive power. That ancient serpent: and the adjective is doing work. This is the same one, the serpent of Eden who deceived Eve (Genesis 3:1), the one whose head the woman’s offspring would crush (Genesis 3:15).

The devil and Satan. “Devil” is Greek for slanderer, accuser; “Satan” is Hebrew for adversary, accuser. Two of the four names mean the same thing, and the next verse will make that the point.

The deceiver of the whole world. The deceiver is the one who leads astray. That is his method, and it has not changed since the first conversation in the garden, which was not a threat but a question: did God actually say? Deception is his main weapon, from Eden onwards: the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, and he disguises himself as an angel of light (2 Corinthians 4:4; 11:3, 14). He deceives the nations through the beast and false prophet (13:14; 20:3, 8). He is not mainly described in this book as a torturer or even a tempter. He is a liar with a legal practice.

Thrown down. Three times in one verse. He did not withdraw; he was removed, by force. His sphere is now the earth, where he rages against the church (v. 12).

Where Christians differ: when was Satan thrown down? Some place this at Satan’s original fall before creation, linking it with Isaiah 14 and Ezekiel 28; others, many futurists among them, at a future point in the last days, at the midpoint of a seven-year tribulation. Both readings take Satan’s defeat with real seriousness. This commentary’s view: the context places it at Christ’s death, resurrection and ascension. The child has just been caught up to God’s throne (v. 5), and the voice in heaven says that salvation and the kingdom have now come, because the accuser has been thrown down, and that believers conquered him by the blood of the Lamb (vv. 10–11). The cross is where Satan was defeated (John 12:31–32; Colossians 2:15; Hebrews 2:14). His original rebellion lies behind this, and his final destruction lies ahead (20:10), but his decisive defeat happened at Calvary.

If Satan was defeated at the cross, why is he still so active? Because a defeated enemy is not yet a removed enemy. Think of a war in which the decisive battle has been won, but fighting goes on in the provinces until the final surrender. The outcome is settled; the danger is real. Satan has lost his place as accuser and, on the reading of chapter 20 this commentary follows, his hold on the nations (20:2–3), so that the gospel now goes freely to every people. But he can still tempt, deceive and persecute, within limits God sets. That is why Peter calls him a roaring lion and in the same breath tells you to resist him, firm in your faith (1 Peter 5:8–9). You fight a real enemy from the side that has already won.

On a Tuesday. When you face temptation or accusation, remember that the devil is a defeated enemy. He lies, and his greatest lie is that he is winning. Learn to recognise his voice: it usually sounds like a question about God’s goodness (did God really say? does God really care?) or a verdict on your worth (you will never change; you are not really his). Answer it with what God has actually said. Jesus met every temptation in the wilderness with it is written.

For worship. Who is like God? Not the dragon, with all his heads and crowns; he was not strong enough. Not even Michael, whose very name is a confession that there is none like the Lord. The Lord Jesus disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, triumphing over them in the cross. He saw Satan fall like lightning, and he has the final word over him.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard a loud voice in heaven, saying, "Now the salvation and the power and the kingdom of our God and the authority of his Christ have come, for the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them day and night before our God. And they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death. Therefore, rejoice, O heavens and you who dwell in them! But woe to you, O earth and sea, for the devil has come down to you in great wrath, because he knows that his time is short!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. In Zechariah 3:1–5, Satan stands at the right hand of Joshua the high priest to accuse him; the LORD rebukes Satan and removes Joshua’s filthy garments, clothing him in pure clothes. Paul asks who shall bring any charge against God’s elect. It is God who justifies; who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died, and who intercedes for us (Romans 8:33–34).

Now the salvation. “Now” is at this moment. Heaven explains what has just happened. It is not only future: it arrived at the cross and resurrection, and Christ now has all authority in heaven and on earth (Matthew 28:18).

The accuser of our brothers. The explanation is entirely about a court case. The dragon is not called the tempter here, or the destroyer, or the ruler of this world. He is the prosecutor, and the verb is continuous. Satan accuses believers before God, pointing to their sins and arguing that they deserve condemnation. And he accuses them in their own consciences.

The file is accurate. Take that as literally as it is written, because it explains something a great many Christians experience and cannot name. There has been, in the presence of God, a voice reciting a list. And it was not inventing the charges; that is the terrible part. The prosecutor’s file in Zechariah 3 was accurate, and the high priest really was standing there in filthy clothes. The accusations against you are, on the whole, true. And they were being read out, day and night, for as long as the accuser had standing in the room. He has been thrown out. Not because the charges were false, and not because God stopped listening. He has lost his case because Christ has paid for every sin, and there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). Justification is the Bible’s name for it: the Judge pronouncing guilty people righteous, not by pretending the charges are false, but because Christ bore them and his righteousness is counted to everyone who trusts him (Romans 4:5; 2 Corinthians 5:21). It is hard news for the religious person who hopes to answer the accuser with a better record. The record is the problem; only the blood answers him.

By the blood of the Lamb. This is the definition of the book’s central verb, promised in every one of the seven letters. Here is what it consists of, in three clauses. First, by the blood of the Lamb, and it is the ground of the other two. The accuser was not defeated by an argument, and certainly not by the saints’ record. He was defeated because the charges were paid. As John wrote to the churches, the blood of Jesus goes on cleansing those who walk in the light from every sin (1 John 1:7). A prosecutor whose every allegation has already been settled by somebody else has nothing to do in the room. That is why he is outside: there is no case left to bring.

The word of their testimony. Second, and it follows from the first. Testimony is witness: holding to and speaking the truth about Jesus. What they said, not what they achieved. They say the true thing about Christ in front of people who do not want to hear it, and that saying is a weapon. The deceiver is defeated when the truth is told.

They loved not their lives. Third, and it is the cost. This does not mean they hated living. It means that when it came to a choice between their lives and their testimony, the testimony won. Some of them died for it. Satan’s last weapon is the threat of death, and it has no power over those who do not cling to their lives (Hebrews 2:14–15). A person who is not holding on to his own life has nothing left that can be threatened. Jesus said that whoever loses his life for his sake will find it (Matthew 16:25).

The shape of Christian courage. Read those three clauses in order and the shape of Christian courage appears. It does not begin with bravery. It begins with a verdict already delivered in blood, produces speech, and only then costs something. Nobody in this verse is asked to be fearless first. You are asked to stand on the blood, to open your mouth, and to trust God with what it costs.

Rejoice, O heavens. “You who dwell” is literally you who pitch your tent there. Heaven rejoices because the accuser is gone, and believers, whose real home is in heaven, share this joy. Contrast those who dwell on the earth elsewhere in the book: God’s people, even while they walk the earth, are counted among those whose tent is pitched in heaven.

Woe to you, O earth. His defeat makes him more furious, not less. The same event produces opposite reactions in the two places, and John holds both. Heaven celebrates; earth is warned.

His time is short. Literally a little time: the whole age between Christ’s ascension and return, the same as the 1,260 days. He knows he is doomed, and the persecution of the church is the rage of a defeated enemy. The pressure a believer feels is not the pressure of an advancing army; it is the fury of one who has been thrown out of the courtroom and has read the timetable. A cornered animal is dangerous precisely because it is cornered. And short here is short as heaven measures it, which is not always short as a suffering church measures it, and is short nonetheless.

What it does not mean. Conquering by the blood of the Lamb does not mean using the phrase as a magic formula, as in some deliverance practices. It means trusting in Christ’s finished work as the answer to every accusation.

What do I say when my conscience accuses me? First, be honest: if the accusation is true, do not argue with it. Confess the sin to God plainly, and where needed put it right with the person you wronged. Then answer the accusation with Christ. Not, it was not so bad; but, it was worse than that, and Jesus died for it. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins (1 John 1:9), and Christ himself is our advocate with the Father (1 John 2:1). Learn the difference between the Spirit’s conviction, which is specific and leads you to Christ, and the accuser’s condemnation, which is vague, endless and drives you away from him. The first is a mercy. The second has been thrown out of court.

Does loving not my life mean I must be ready to die? Yes, in principle every Christian is called to love Christ more than life itself (Luke 14:26), and in some places that is a daily reality. But for most believers it is lived out in smaller deaths first: not loving your comfort, your reputation, your career or your safety more than your testimony. The man who will not risk a colleague’s scorn is not yet ready for a lion. Do not try to manufacture courage for a martyrdom that may never come. Be faithful in today’s small cost, and trust God to give you dying grace if he ever asks you to die.

For worship. The accuser stood before the throne day and night with a true list of our sins, and the Lamb did not dispute a line of it. He paid it. The prosecutor’s bench is empty because the Judge’s own Son took the sentence, and the blood that now speaks in that room speaks a better word than the blood of Abel (Hebrews 12:24).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — The Dragon Pursues the Woman
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 13–16: thrown down and unable to reach the child, the dragon pursues the woman. She is given eagle’s wings, as Israel was carried out of Egypt (Exodus 19:4), and is fed in the wilderness for a time, and times, and half a time. The flood he pours from his mouth is swallowed by the earth.

Verse 17: he turns to make war on the rest of her offspring, marked by two things: they keep God’s commandments and hold to the testimony of Jesus. The chapter ends with the dragon standing on the shore.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Complete Exodus

Thrown down, the dragon pursues the woman, but she is given eagle’s wings and carried to the wilderness to be fed. The flood from his mouth is swallowed by the earth, and he turns on her children, those who keep God’s commandments and hold to the testimony of Jesus.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The church under Rome was living inside the story of Exodus, and knew how it ended.

Now: Persecution is the rage of a defeated accuser, and the wilderness is where God feeds his people.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the dragon saw that he had been thrown down to the earth, he pursued the woman who had given birth to the male child. But the woman was given the two wings of the great eagle so that she might fly from the serpent into the wilderness, to the place where she is to be nourished for a time, and times, and half a time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. God told Israel at Sinai, you have seen how I bore you on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself (Exodus 19:4). Deuteronomy 32:11 pictures God as an eagle that stirs up its nest and carries its young on its pinions. Isaiah 40:31 says those who wait for the LORD shall mount up with wings like eagles. Daniel 7:25 speaks of the saints given into the hand of the persecuting king for a time, times and half a time.

He pursued the woman. Catch the logic of the verse. He goes after the woman because he has been thrown down. He cannot reach the child, who is on the throne. He cannot go back to the courtroom. So he turns on the mother, the child’s people, the church. Persecution of the church is Satan’s revenge on Christ.

What persecution means. That does not make the persecution less real. What it does is settle what persecution means. It is not evidence that the dragon is gaining ground. It is evidence that he has lost the only ground that mattered and has nowhere else to go. Jesus said it on the Damascus road: Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me (Acts 9:4)? To strike the church is to aim at Christ, and to miss.

The two wings of the great eagle. She does not grow the wings or buy them; they are given. The image is the exodus (Exodus 19:4): as God carried Israel out of Egypt, he carries his church through the wilderness of this age, and the desert is where the dragon cannot follow and the food arrives anyway.

The exodus all over again. The chapter now has a complete exodus in it: a tyrant trying to kill the children, a child rescued, a flight, a wilderness, a place prepared, food from an unseen hand, eagles’ wings, and in the next verses a flood that the enemy intended for the woman and the ground swallowing it. This is not decoration. John is telling seven congregations under Roman pressure that they are living in the book of Exodus, and that they already know how it ends. And the church walks the exodus road because her Lord walked it first. Matthew saw it in the child’s own life: carried into Egypt out of Herod’s reach and called out again, to fulfil the word, Out of Egypt I called my son (Matthew 2:15). Christ is our Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7), and his people’s flight through the desert is a share in his.

For a time, and times, and half a time. From Daniel 7:25 and 12:7: one year, two years and half a year, three and a half years. The same period as 1,260 days (v. 6) and forty-two months (11:2): the whole church age, a time of persecution limited by God. John uses all three forms interchangeably within two chapters, a strong argument that he means one thing by them.

In the flow. The woman’s flight has been told once already (v. 6). Then the story stopped for the war in heaven and the song of victory (vv. 7–12), and now it takes up her flight again and tells it more fully, with the same period of time. Before we see the dragon chase the church, we are shown why: he has lost in heaven, and the earth is all he has left. Verses 13–14 are not a second flight but the first one, now with its cause explained.

If the church is protected, why do some churches die out? Because the promise is to the church of Christ as a whole, not to every congregation or denomination. The seven churches of chapters 2 and 3 have long since disappeared from most of their cities, and Jesus warned Ephesus that he would remove its lampstand if it did not repent (2:5). Churches can lose the gospel and die. But the people of God has never died out, and never will: when the church declined in one land, it grew in another, and today it is found in nearly every nation on earth. Pray for your own church to be faithful. Rest in the promise that Christ’s church cannot fail.

On a Tuesday. When you have no strength left, remember who gives the wings. Waiting on the Lord is not passive. It is turning to him in prayer and in his word when you would rather give up, and finding, again and again, that he carries you.

verseByVerse.quote: The serpent poured water like a river out of his mouth after the woman, to sweep her away with a flood. But the earth came to the help of the woman, and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed the river that the dragon had poured from his mouth. Then the dragon became furious with the woman and went off to make war on the rest of her offspring, on those who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus. And he stood on the sand of the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. In the Psalms, floods and many waters picture overwhelming danger and the attacks of enemies (Psalm 18:4, 16; 32:6; 124:4–5). At the Red Sea, God opened a path through the waters for Israel, and the waters swept away Pharaoh’s army (Exodus 14–15). When Korah rebelled against Moses, the earth opened its mouth and swallowed the rebels (Numbers 16:30–32). In the song of Moses, Israel sang, you stretched out your right hand; the earth swallowed them (Exodus 15:12).

Water like a river. Two mouths, and the whole passage turns on them. The dragon’s mouth pours out a river; the earth’s mouth swallows it. What comes out of the dragon’s mouth is what has always come out of it. In verse 9 he was called the deceiver of the whole world, and his one method is speech. The flood is lies, deception, false teaching, slander and propaganda. As the witnesses’ fire is their word (11:5), so Satan’s flood is his. He tries to drown the church in falsehood.

A flood of words. In the Psalms, overwhelming waters are the standard image for hostile speech and danger: save me, O God, for the waters have come up to my neck (Psalm 69:1–2). A flood is how a reputation is destroyed or a truth buried: not one accusation, which can be answered, but a volume of it arriving faster than anybody can respond, until the truth is simply under water.

The earth came to the help of the woman. The rescue comes from the least likely quarter. The earth in this book is usually where the trouble is: the earth-dwellers, the beast from the earth, the outer court given over to be trampled. Here it swallows a river, as the ground swallowed Korah (Numbers 16:32). God is not restricted to the instruments a believer would have expected. He has used a pagan king’s decree, a famine, a shipwreck and an earthquake in a prison to protect his people, and here he uses the ground.

The rest of her offspring. Frustrated at the mother, he turns on the children. The phrase, literally the rest of her seed, reaches straight back to Genesis 3:15 and the enmity between the serpent’s offspring and the woman’s. Christ is her first offspring, the one who crushed the serpent’s head at the cost of his own heel; believers are her other children, his brothers and sisters, whom he is not ashamed to call his own (Romans 8:29; Hebrews 2:11–13). That is why they are hunted, and why the hunt cannot succeed. Paul applies the old promise to an ordinary congregation: the God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet (Romans 16:20). If the church as a whole is protected, individual believers are still attacked, but they are attacked as people already on the winning side of Genesis 3:15.

Commandments and testimony. John pauses to define them, and there are only two marks. They keep the commandments of God: obedience, ordinary and unglamorous, in the things God has actually commanded rather than the things a person would prefer to be judged on. None keeps them perfectly. They are the people who conquered by the blood (v. 11), and their standing rests on the Son who kept his Father’s commandments in their place (John 15:10; Romans 5:19); their obedience is the fruit of that blood, not its price. And they hold to the testimony of Jesus: confession; they have not let go of what they say about him. This is the definition of a true believer in Revelation, obedience to God and loyalty to Jesus (14:12), and these are Satan’s targets.

How short the list is. There is a quiet challenge in it. Not those who understand this book. Not those who identified the beast correctly. Not those who never suffered. Obedience and confession, held on to. That is what the dragon goes to war against, and that is all it takes to be on his list.

And he stood on the sand of the sea. The chapter ends quietly and ominously. The dragon takes his stand at the shoreline, looking out at the water, and the very next sentence in the book is: and I saw a beast rising out of the sea. Satan works through human agents and systems, and the last image of chapter 12 and the first of chapter 13 are a single movement.

Textual note. The last sentence is numbered 12:18 in some Bibles and 13:1 in others. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “I stood on the sand of the sea”, making John the subject. The best manuscripts read “he stood”, referring to the dragon.

Watching without panic. The reader now has all he needs to face what comes next. The child is on the throne. The accuser has been thrown out and has no case to bring. The woman is fed in a place prepared for her. The saints conquer by blood already shed and words already spoken. And the dragon standing on that beach, about to summon the worst thing in the book, is a defeated prosecutor with a short time, doing the only thing left to him.

How do I keep from being swept away by the flood of lies? Know the truth well enough to recognise the counterfeit. Bank clerks learn to spot forged notes by handling real ones. So read the whole Bible regularly, sit under faithful preaching, and learn the great truths of the faith, perhaps through a good confession or catechism. Be slow to believe what you hear about fellow Christians, and test every teaching by Scripture, as the Bereans did (Acts 17:11). Notice which voices make God seem less good, sin less serious or Christ less necessary, and turn them off. And stay close to the church: a flood sweeps away the one standing alone far more easily than a people holding on together.

On a Tuesday. Where does the flood reach you most this week, through a screen, a conversation, a fear? Put God’s word in its place. Obey him in the plain things today, in the strength of the Spirit Christ has given you, and when you fail, go back to the blood that silenced the accuser: it answers today’s failures too.

For worship. The Lord sits enthroned over the flood; the Lord sits enthroned as king for ever. The dragon poured out a river of lies, and the God who split the Red Sea and opened the ground under Korah made the earth itself swallow it. He commands sea and land and every creature to serve his people. And the children the dragon hunts belong to the Son, and no one will snatch them out of his hand (John 10:28). The dragon stands on the sand. The Lamb stands on Mount Zion, and the next time the curtain opens, his people are standing with him.

12.text: <sup>1</sup>And a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars.<sup>2</sup>She was pregnant and was crying out in birth pains and the agony of giving birth.<sup>3</sup>And another sign appeared in heaven: behold, a great red dragon, with seven heads and ten horns, and on his heads seven diadems.<sup>4</sup>His tail swept down a third of the stars of heaven and cast them to the earth. And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that when she bore her child he might devour it.<sup>5</sup>She gave birth to a male child, one who is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron, but her child was caught up to God and to his throne,<sup>6</sup>and the woman fled into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, in which she is to be nourished for 1,260 days.<sup>7</sup>Now war arose in heaven, Michael and his angels fighting against the dragon. And the dragon and his angels fought back,<sup>8</sup>but he was defeated, and there was no longer any place for them in heaven.<sup>9</sup>And the great dragon was thrown down, that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world—he was thrown down to the earth, and his angels were thrown down with him.<sup>10</sup>And I heard a loud voice in heaven, saying, “Now the salvation and the power and the kingdom of our God and the authority of his Christ have come, for the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them day and night before our God.<sup>11</sup>And they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death.<sup>12</sup>Therefore, rejoice, O heavens and you who dwell in them! But woe to you, O earth and sea, for the devil has come down to you in great wrath, because he knows that his time is short!”<sup>13</sup>And when the dragon saw that he had been thrown down to the earth, he pursued the woman who had given birth to the male child.<sup>14</sup>But the woman was given the two wings of the great eagle so that she might fly from the serpent into the wilderness, to the place where she is to be nourished for a time, and times, and half a time.<sup>15</sup>The serpent poured water like a river out of his mouth after the woman, to sweep her away with a flood.<sup>16</sup>But the earth came to the help of the woman, and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed the river that the dragon had poured from his mouth.<sup>17</sup>Then the dragon became furious with the woman and went off to make war on the rest of her offspring, on those who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus. And he stood on the sand of the sea.

13.title: The Two Beasts: The Dragon's Earthly Instruments
13.overview:
Chapter 13 shows how Satan works through human power. The dragon, standing on the seashore, calls up two beasts, one from the sea and one from the land, and hands them his authority.
