Together they imitate the Holy Trinity: the dragon gives his authority as the Father gives all things to the Son; the beast from the sea has a counterfeit death and resurrection; and the beast from the land points away from itself to the first beast, as the Spirit glorifies the Son. It is the pattern of every power, political and religious, that demands the allegiance belonging to God alone.

Who is the beast from the sea? Preterists identify it with Nero and Rome, and the healed wound with the rumour after Nero’s death in AD 68 that he would return from the east. Historicists have identified it with later powers, including the papacy. Futurists see a single world ruler at the end of history. This commentary reads the beast as the persecuting power that claims divine authority in every age: Rome and its emperor cult first, many later forms after it, and a final form before Christ returns.

What is 666? Three readings are common, and each sheds some light. Nero Caesar written in Hebrew letters adds up to 666 (spelled without the final n, 616, the reading of some early manuscripts). Six falls one short of seven, the number of completeness, so 666 pictures a power that keeps falling short of God. And six is the number of humanity, created on the sixth day: the beast is human power at its grandest, and still only human.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–4: a beast rises from the sea with the dragon’s own features, blasphemous names on its heads and the marks of Daniel’s four beasts combined in one. The dragon gives it his power and throne. A mortal wound that is healed makes the whole earth marvel, and the world worships the dragon and the beast because nobody seems able to fight it.

Verses 5–8: it is given a blaspheming mouth, forty-two months of authority, and permission to make war on the saints and conquer them. All the earth-dwellers worship it, except those whose names are written in the Lamb’s book of life.

Verses 9–10 turn to the reader: the saints meet the beast not with the sword but with endurance and faith.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Beast from the Sea

The dragon gives the beast his power, throne and authority. It mimics the Lamb’s death and resurrection, wins the world’s worship because it seems unbeatable, and is allowed to speak blasphemies and make war on the saints for forty-two months.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Rome’s emperors bore divine titles on coins and inscriptions.

Now: Worship of power begins as a calculation that resistance is pointless. The saints’ calling is endurance and faith; their names are in the Lamb’s book.

verseByVerse.quote: And I saw a beast rising out of the sea, with ten horns and seven heads, with ten diadems on its horns and blasphemous names on its heads. And the beast that I saw was like a leopard; its feet were like a bear's, and its mouth was like a lion's mouth. And to it the dragon gave his power and his throne and great authority.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Revelation 13 introduces the dragon’s two allies, the instruments through which Satan makes war on the saints. A beast rises from the sea, with the dragon’s seven heads and ten horns and the features of Daniel’s four beasts, and the dragon gives it his power, throne and authority (vv. 1–2). One of its heads seems mortally wounded but is healed, and the whole world worships the dragon and the beast: who is like the beast? (vv. 3–4). For forty-two months it blasphemes God and conquers the saints, and everyone whose name is not written in the Lamb’s book of life worships it (vv. 5–8). The saints are called to endurance and faith, not the sword (vv. 9–10). A second beast rises from the earth, with horns like a lamb but speaking like a dragon; it promotes the first beast’s worship with deceptive signs and a speaking image, has those who refuse killed, and makes everyone take a mark on the right hand or forehead, without which no one can buy or sell (vv. 11–17). The beast’s number is 666, the number of a man (v. 18). In John’s day the beast was Rome and its emperor cult; through the age it takes many forms; and it will reach a final climax before Christ returns. And under every boast runs a quiet refrain: it was given, it was allowed. The throne above the dragon has not moved.

The setting. In Daniel 7, four beasts rise from the sea: a lion, a bear, a leopard and a terrifying fourth beast with ten horns, representing four world empires, usually understood as Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece and Rome. For John’s readers, Rome came from across the sea, and Roman governors arrived in Asia by ship. The emperors claimed divine titles: the coins called Augustus son of god, and Domitian liked to be addressed as lord and god.

A beast rising out of the sea. At the end of chapter 12 the dragon stood on the seashore; this is what he calls up. The sea in this book is the ancient image of chaos and of the unmanageable, the realm of evil (Daniel 7:2–3) and of the abyss (11:7). That is why the throne room has it lying still as glass (4:6), and why the new creation is announced with the words and the sea was no more (21:1). Empires come up out of the churn. And to a congregation on the coast of Asia, the sea was also the direction Rome arrived from.

Ten horns and seven heads. Count the features against the dragon of 12:3, because the correspondence is close and deliberate: seven heads, ten horns, and royal crowns. The beast is the dragon’s image. What comes out of the water is what the dragon looks like when he takes a form that can hold public office. In 17:9–12 the seven heads are seven mountains and seven kings, and the ten horns ten kings.

Ten diadems and blasphemous names. Two differences from the dragon, and both are pointed. The dragon wore seven diadems on his heads; the beast wears ten on its horns: more crowns, and worn on the instruments of force rather than on the seat of thought. And the blasphemous names are titles that belong only to God. To a first-century reader that was not a metaphor: coins, inscriptions and court flattery gave the emperors titles such as divine, son of god, saviour of the world, and even lord and god.

Leopard, bear and lion. This is Daniel 7: four beasts from the sea, four kingdoms. John names three of them in reverse order and gives their features to one animal. What Daniel saw as a succession of empires, John sees gathered into a single creature.

One beast in many costumes. The point is not chronology. There has only ever been one beast, wearing different national costumes: Babylon, Persia, Greece and Rome are not four different problems but four appearances of the same thing, and it appears again in every century, the spirit of every empire that sets itself against God. Any reader who has decided the beast is one particular regime should notice that John has just merged four of them.

The dragon gave. The beast’s power comes from Satan, a grim parody of how the Father gives authority to the Son (2:27). Three nouns, and they answer an offer Christ was made in a desert. The devil showed him all the kingdoms of the world and said, to you I will give all this authority and their glory, for it has been delivered to me (Luke 4:6). Christ refused. The beast accepts. And that is the whole difference between the two kingdoms in this book: one of them takes a throne from the dragon, and the other takes a cross from his Father.

Where Christians differ: who is the beast? Preterists, who read the book as fulfilled mainly in the first century, identify the beast with the Roman Empire and the emperor Nero. Historicists, who read it as a map of church history, including many Reformers, identified it with the papacy. Futurists, who expect most of the book to be fulfilled just before Christ returns, see a single future world dictator, the Antichrist, at the end of history. This commentary’s view: the beast is the persecuting power of the state, or any human system, that claims divine authority and demands worship, empowered by Satan. In John’s day it was clearly the Roman Empire and its emperor cult; through history it has reappeared in many forms, whenever a power demands the total loyalty that belongs to God alone; and Scripture expects a final, intensified manifestation before Christ returns, the man of lawlessness (2 Thessalonians 2:3–10). Many Reformers were right to see beastly features in the persecuting medieval church, but the beast is wider than any one institution. This combined view gathers what is true in each of the others: it honours the first readers, every generation, and the end.

How do I tell when a government has become beastly? Look for the marks this chapter gives. A beastly power claims what belongs to God: titles of divinity, final authority over conscience, the right to define good and evil without reference to him. It demands worship, not merely obedience: total loyalty, public affirmation, the bowing of the mind. And it punishes those who will not give it, by exclusion or by force. A government can be unjust, corrupt or foolish without being the beast; governing authorities are instituted by God (Romans 13:1–7), and Christians must still honour it and obey it in everything lawful (1 Peter 2:13–17). But when it commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands, we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29).

On a Tuesday. Pay your taxes, keep the law, speak honourably of rulers, and name them, local and national, in your prayers. And keep one thing back that no government may have: your worship, your conscience and your confession that Jesus is Lord.

For worship. The beast came up out of the sea wearing titles stolen from heaven: son of god, saviour of the world, lord and god. Every one of them already had an owner. A Samaritan town said of Jesus that this is indeed the Saviour of the world (John 4:42), and a doubting disciple, shown the wounds, answered him, My Lord and my God (John 20:28). The beast borrows its throne from a dragon who has no throne of his own; the Lamb is in the midst of the throne of God for ever. The King wears by right every name the beast can only forge.
verseByVerse.note: This beast combines the four beasts of Daniel 7 — leopard, bear, lion and the ten-horned beast.

verseByVerse.quote: One of its heads seemed to have a mortal wound, but its mortal wound was healed, and the whole earth marveled as they followed the beast. And they worshiped the dragon, for he had given his authority to the beast, and they worshiped the beast, saying, "Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. After Nero’s suicide in AD 68 the empire fell into civil war and seemed about to collapse, until Vespasian restored order. In the Old Testament, Who is like you, O LORD? is a cry of praise to God (Exodus 15:11; Psalm 35:10; Micah 7:18); the name Michael means Who is like God?

A mortal wound. The phrase is literally slain to death, and the word is the same one that describes the Lamb standing, as though it had been slain, at 5:6. John does not use that word loosely. The beast imitates Christ’s death.

Its mortal wound was healed. A parody of Christ’s resurrection: a figure bearing a death wound and alive anyway, demanding the worship that belongs to the one who really died and really rose. The beast’s power seems to be destroyed, then revives. Godless powers often seem to fall, only to reappear in new forms.

Satan invents nothing. That is the key to this chapter and the two that follow. Everything the dragon produces is an imitation. A beast with a resurrection. A second beast with horns like a lamb. A mark on the forehead. An image that breathes. A city called great. Satan creates nothing; he copies, and the copies are close enough to be mistaken for the original by people who have not looked carefully. Which is why the best protection against the counterfeit is close acquaintance with the real thing, and the real thing is a person. The beast’s wound heals and it goes on as before, demanding to be worshipped. The Lamb kept his wounds, and showed them to Thomas in his hands and side (John 20:27); he laid down his life and took it up again (John 10:18), and he rose to give life, not to take it. A counterfeit resurrection needs worship to keep itself going. The true one was given so that we might live.

What the wound refers to. What the wound refers to historically is disputed. Some point to Nero, whom many in the eastern provinces refused to believe was dead, expecting him to return from beyond the Euphrates with a Parthian army (the Nero redivivus myth), a rumour that produced several impostors. Some point to the empire itself, which came close to disintegrating in the civil wars of AD 68 to 69, when four emperors ruled in a single year, and then recovered completely under Vespasian. Some hold it is still future. What is not disputed is the effect. The wound is what makes the beast credible.

The whole earth marveled. “Followed” is literally went after, as disciples follow a master. The world follows the beast as the church follows the Lamb wherever he goes (14:4). Everyone is following someone.

They worshiped the dragon. Worshipping the beast is really worshipping Satan. All idolatry has a demonic source: what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons and not to God (1 Corinthians 10:20). People who would never knowingly kneel to the devil kneel to him anyway, through the thing he has dressed up for them.

And they worshiped the beast, saying, Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it? Two things about that chant, and both would have landed hard on a Jewish ear. First, it is a parody of the song of the exodus. When Israel came through the sea, Moses and the people sang, who is like you, O LORD, among the gods? Who is like you, majestic in holiness (Exodus 15:11)? The world’s worship uses the same sentence with a different object. Second, the name Michael, who threw the dragon out of heaven in the previous chapter, means who is like God? The beast’s worshippers are chanting the archangel’s name at the wrong address. And the answer to their question has already been given: Michael, Who is like God, has already defeated the dragon (12:7–9), and the Lamb will conquer the beast, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings (17:14).

The first act of worship is a calculation. The second half of the chant is the more revealing: who can fight against it? Nobody claims the beast is kind, or just, or true. Very few people consciously decide to worship a tyrant. They conclude that resistance is pointless and that a sensible person accommodates himself to the thing, and that quiet conclusion, reached without ceremony, is what the verse describes. It happens in a nation, and in an office, a school, a family: the moment someone decides that the strongest voice in the room must be obeyed because it is the strongest.

What it does not mean. The healed wound is not a prediction that a particular leader will be assassinated and then come back to life. It is a parody of Christ’s death and resurrection, showing that the beast is a counterfeit Christ, and that evil powers revive after apparent defeat.

When evil seems to have been beaten and then comes back, what should I think? That this is exactly what Revelation told you to expect. Godless powers rise, fall and revive in new forms throughout this age, because the beast has a healed head. Do not put your final hope in any political victory, as though one election or one revolution could finish evil off; and do not despair when the old evil returns in new clothes. Only one death and resurrection is final, and it is not the beast’s. The Lamb was really slain and really lives, and he alone will bring evil to its end, at his coming.

On a Tuesday. Watch what amazes you, and ask where in your own life you have quietly decided that something is too big to oppose, a habit, an expectation at work, a voice in the culture, and that going along is simply realism. Then ask who you are following, and whether that is the one you would call Lord out loud.

verseByVerse.quote: And the beast was given a mouth uttering haughty and blasphemous words, and it was allowed to exercise authority for forty-two months. It opened its mouth to utter blasphemies against God, blaspheming his name and his dwelling, that is, those who dwell in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. In Daniel 7:8, 11, 20, 25, the little horn has a mouth speaking great things, and speaks words against the Most High. Antiochus IV Epiphanes, the Greek king who persecuted the Jews in 167–164 BC, called himself God manifest, desecrated the temple, and is often seen as a forerunner of the antichrist (Daniel 11:36; 1 Maccabees 1).

A mouth was given. “Was given” comes four times in verses 5 to 7. The beast did not acquire its mouth; it was given one. It does nothing except by permission. God sets its limits. “Haughty” is literally great things, arrogant boasts, the very phrase of Daniel’s little horn. The chain of permission runs upward past the dragon to the throne of God. These divine passives, verbs that say something was given without naming the giver, because the giver is God, are the reason a Christian can read this chapter without despair.

Forty-two months. It did not seize its term of office; it was allowed one. Whatever authority it exercises is on licence, and the licence has an expiry date printed on it. Forty-two months is the same period as the trampling of the holy city (11:2), the witnesses’ prophesying (11:3), and the woman’s protection in the wilderness (12:6, 14): the whole church age, between Christ’s comings. The same clock governs the persecution and the preserving.

His name and his dwelling. Three objects, and the third repays attention. It blasphemes his name, his character, who God is. It blasphemes his dwelling, his tabernacle, and then John adds his own explanation in case anybody imagines a building: that is, those who dwell in heaven. God’s dwelling is with his people (21:3), and those who dwell in heaven are believers, whose citizenship is there and who are seated with Christ in the heavenly places (12:12; Ephesians 2:6). So the beast mocks and slanders the church.

To slander the church is to slander God. John states it as a simple equivalence. That is the logic of the voice on the Damascus road: not, why do you persecute my followers, but Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me (Acts 9:4)? What is done to the body is done to the head. A believer who is mocked for Christ is not alone in being mocked.

The beast’s chief weapon is its mouth. It has ten horns, the authority of the dragon and a healed mortal wound, and yet the verses describing what it does are entirely about its mouth. It talks. It utters. It blasphemes. The great opposition to the church in this book is not chiefly a police force; it is a story about reality, repeated with enormous confidence and reach, in which God is small, his people are contemptible and the beast is the only realistic option. Christians braced for a knock at the door are sometimes worn down instead by years of being told, pleasantly, that what they believe is ridiculous.

Against a mouth, a mouth. And against a mouth, the church has been issued a mouth. That is its whole armament: the word of their testimony (12:11), and behind it the sharp sword that comes from the mouth of Christ (1:16; 19:15). The beast’s words are loud. Christ’s word is true, and it will have the last say.

The one condemned for blasphemy. Behind this mouth stands Daniel’s little horn, speaking great things against the Most High until the Ancient of Days takes away its dominion and gives an everlasting dominion to one like a son of man (Daniel 7:8–14). At his trial Jesus claimed that vision as his own: you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven. The high priest tore his garments, and the council condemned him for blasphemy (Mark 14:62–64). So the Son was condemned as a blasphemer for telling the truth about himself, while the beast, which blasphemes in earnest, is worshipped. The verdicts will be reversed. The beast’s mouth runs for forty-two months; the Son of Man’s dominion is everlasting.

How do I stay steady when everything around me mocks my faith? Expect it, so it does not unsettle you; this chapter told you it would come. Then keep your mind full of the truth, because constant mockery works by slow erosion more than by argument. Spend more time with God’s voice than with the voices that belittle him: in Scripture, in worship, in the company of believers. Remember that the mockery is aimed at God first, and he is not threatened by it. And refuse to answer contempt with contempt. A gentle, unashamed, cheerful faith is itself a reply the beast’s mouth cannot answer.

verseByVerse.quote: Also it was allowed to make war on the saints and to conquer them. And authority was given it over every tribe and people and language and nation, and all who dwell on earth will worship it, everyone whose name has not been written from the foundation of the world in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Daniel 7:21 says the horn made war with the saints and prevailed over them, until the Ancient of Days came and judgement was given for the saints.

Allowed to conquer them. It is one of the hardest sentences in the book, and it should not be hurried past. The beast is permitted to make war on Christians, and permitted to win. The verb is the one promised to the conqueror in each of the seven letters; here, as at 11:7, the beast is its subject and the saints its victims. Revelation will not tell the church that faithfulness guarantees survival. Congregations are overrun. Believers are imprisoned and executed.

Two kinds of victory. Hold that beside 12:11 and the two sentences interpret each other. There, the saints conquered the dragon by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death. The people are the same and so is the verb; only the outcome is reversed, and the resolution is in the last clause: in Revelation those killed for their faith are the true conquerors (12:11; 15:2). The beast wins the battle of bodies; the saints win the battle of faithfulness, and only one of those victories is visible from the street.

Every tribe and people. The fourfold phrase from 5:9, a parody of the Lamb’s redeemed from every tribe, language, people and nation. The beast’s rule seems universal. It is given, and it covers exactly the territory that has already been bought by somebody else.

All who dwell on earth. Those who dwell on the earth is John’s technical term, established at 8:13, for the unbelieving world, people whose whole account is settled here. It is not a geographical description; the saints live on the earth too and are never called earth-dwellers. Everyone worships something. Those who do not worship God will worship the beast.

The book of life of the Lamb. Then the safeguard, and it is the comfort of the chapter. There is a register. “Written” is perfect tense: it has been written and stands written, from the foundation of the world, before anybody had done anything to deserve entry or exclusion. The only ones who resist the beast are those written in the Lamb’s book, by God’s eternal choice. Their perseverance rests not on their own strength but on God’s election; yet no one’s idolatry is excused by it, and faithful endurance is its fruit.

Where Christians differ: what does “from the foundation of the world” go with? The Greek word order allows “the Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world” (as in the King James Version) or “written from the foundation of the world in the book of life” (as in the ESV). This commentary’s view: the second is more likely, because 17:8 uses the same phrase clearly of names written in the book of life from the foundation of the world. Both truths are biblical: Christ was foreknown as the sacrifice before the foundation of the world (1 Peter 1:20), and God chose his people in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4). The verse teaches unconditional election: God wrote the names of his people in the Lamb’s book before they were born, not because of anything they would do, and he keeps them from worshipping the beast. Christians in the Arminian tradition (who hold that God chose those he foresaw would believe) read such verses differently, and they too rejoice in the Lamb’s book; this commentary holds that a choice made before anyone had done anything fits this verse and Ephesians 1:4–5 best.

Is it fair for God to write some names and not others? No one in this verse is treated unjustly. The people outside the book are not dragged to the beast against their will; they marvel at it, follow it and worship it gladly, and they are judged for what they chose (14:9–11). The people inside it did not earn their place; every name was written before its owner had done anything. So no one receives less than justice, and some receive mercy instead. Paul met the same objection and answered first by bowing before God’s right to have mercy (Romans 9:14–20). The wonder is not that some names are missing. It is that any are there at all, and that whoever comes to the Lamb finds his name among them.

Could I be deceived into worshipping the beast without realising it? The verse says the opposite. The people who worship are those whose names are not written; the ones whose names are written are kept. That is not a promise that a believer will never be frightened, never waver and never fail: Peter denied Christ three times in a courtyard, and was restored. It is a promise about who does the holding. Jesus said it without symbols: no one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28). And the book that decides it is the book of the Lamb who was slain. The register is not a list of the people who held out. It is the property of the one with the wounds, and the entries were made before the world existed.

How can I know my name is written there? Not by trying to read the book, which God has not opened to us, but by looking to the Lamb whose book it is. The names written there are the names of those who come to him; Jesus said all that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37). If you are trusting Christ alone for your salvation, turning from sin, and holding to him, that is the evidence that you were chosen. Election is not a locked door to worry at. It is the foundation under the feet of everyone who has already come in.

On a Tuesday. If you are anxious about whether you would stand firm under pressure, take your eyes off your own strength and put them on the Lamb’s book. You are not kept by your courage; you are kept by his grip. That does not make you careless. It makes you grateful, and gratitude is a far stronger defence against idolatry than fear.

For worship. Before the mountains were brought forth, the Father wrote the names of his children, and he wrote them in a book that bears the title of a wound: the book of life of the Lamb who was slain. The register was opened in eternity and paid for at Calvary. The beast may conquer bodies, but it cannot erase a single line, and the Son will lose nothing of all that he has been given, but raise it up on the last day.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone has an ear, let him hear: If anyone is to be taken captive, to captivity he goes; if anyone is to be slain with the sword, with the sword must he be slain. Here is a call for the endurance and faith of the saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Jeremiah 15:2 and 43:11 say: those who are for pestilence, to pestilence, and those who are for the sword, to the sword, and those who are for captivity, to captivity. When Peter drew his sword to defend Jesus, Jesus said, put your sword back into its place, for all who take the sword will perish by the sword (Matthew 26:52).

If anyone has an ear, let him hear. The call of the seven letters (2:7), a direct application to the church. But there is a difference here, and it is easy to miss. In chapters 2 and 3 it always ran on: let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. Here the words about the churches are gone. This call is addressed to whoever is listening, and John, having just described a beast conquering the saints, turns and says: this part is for you personally.

To captivity he goes. The saying comes from Jeremiah, and it is the language of a sentence already passed. Some believers will be imprisoned, within God’s sovereign plan. That is not fatalism, and the last sentence of the verse rules it out. It means that a Christian facing the beast should not spend his strength looking for an escape route at the cost of his faith, and should not conclude when arrest comes that something has gone wrong with God’s arrangements.

With the sword must he be slain. Some will be executed, and this too is within God’s purpose. That sounds bleak until it is set beside the alternative: a Christianity that promises deliverance from every hard thing, and so leaves a believer, when the door actually opens, concluding that God has failed. This verse takes that conclusion away in advance. Nothing that happens to a Christian at the hands of the beast is outside what was appointed, or a surprise to the one who holds the keys.

Textual note. The manuscripts differ on the second line. Some read “if anyone kills with the sword, with the sword he must be killed”, a warning against taking up the sword, as in Matthew 26:52 and the King James Version. Others read “if anyone is to be killed with the sword, with the sword he must be killed”, a call to accept martyrdom. Either way, the lesson is the same: believers must not resist the beast by violence, but endure in faith.

The endurance and faith of the saints. That is the point of the whole passage. “Endurance” is staying power, holding a position under weight. “Faith” is faith and faithfulness; the Greek covers both, and both fit. The church’s response to the beast is not rebellion, revolution or violence, but patient endurance and faithful trust. This is how the saints conquer.

The Lamb who would not draw the sword. The endurance asked here is the way the Lamb himself went. In the garden Peter drew his sword, and Jesus told him to put it back; he could have appealed to his Father for more than twelve legions of angels, but then how should the Scriptures be fulfilled (Matthew 26:52–54)? So he was taken captive and put to death under Roman authority, like a lamb led to the slaughter, silent before its shearers (Isaiah 53:7). Peter, who had swung that sword, learned the lesson and passed it on: Christ suffered for you, leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his steps; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly (1 Peter 2:21–23). The saints face the beast the way the Lamb faced Rome.

What is not on the list. Not violent resistance. Not clever manoeuvring, not political leverage, not withdrawal into a compound. The beast has ten horns, the authority of the dragon and the worship of the whole earth, and the instruction to the church facing it is: stay where you are and keep trusting him. Most of what the New Testament asks of believers in trouble is not spectacular. It is the refusal to move, and that is not passivity. It is trust in the one who holds the keys, and it is some of the hardest work a believer ever does. And a like phrase returns at 14:12, so that at the two darkest points of the book the reader is told that what is asked of him is endurance and faith.

In the flow. These two verses break into the vision like a hand on the reader’s shoulder. John has just described the first beast conquering the saints (v. 7), and he is about to describe a second beast that makes the whole earth worship the first (vv. 11–17). Between the two he stops and tells the church what to do, as the loud voice in heaven did in the middle of chapter 12 (12:10–12). The chapter is given not to satisfy curiosity about the future but so that believers will stand firm in the present.

What it does not mean. This does not mean Christians may never defend themselves or others, or that believers should seek martyrdom. It means that the church does not advance its cause by force, and that when persecution comes because of faith, believers accept suffering rather than deny Christ or take up arms for the gospel.

May a Christian flee persecution, or must he stay? He may flee, if he can do so without denying Christ. Jesus said, when they persecute you in one town, flee to the next (Matthew 10:23), and Paul escaped Damascus in a basket. What this verse forbids is escape by compromise: buying safety with a denial, a pinch of incense, a lie. If the way out is open and clean, a believer may take it. If the only way out runs through unfaithfulness, then captivity is the appointed road, and Christ walks it with him.

On a Tuesday. Endurance is learned in small things before it is needed in great ones: in keeping your word when it costs you, in staying kind to someone who mocks you, in going on praying when prayer seems unanswered. The Spirit of the Lamb who would not draw the sword grows it in you. You will still flinch and fail; the Lamb never did, and his perfect obedience is counted as yours (Romans 5:19), so failure sends you back to him, not out of his company.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 11–15: a second beast, later called the false prophet, rises from the land. It looks like a lamb and speaks like the dragon, and its whole task is to make the world worship the first beast: it works signs, even fire from heaven, sets up a speaking image, and has those who will not worship it killed, as in Daniel 3.

Verses 16–18: it marks everyone, small and great, on the right hand or the forehead, so that no one can buy or sell without the beast’s name or number. The number, 666, calls for wisdom: it is the number of a man.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Beast from the Land

A second beast with horns like a lamb and a voice like a dragon makes the world worship the first. It works signs, gives the image a voice, and requires a mark, the beast’s name, without which no one can buy or sell. Its number, 666, is the number of a man.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Local notables ran the imperial cult, and refusing it cost a tradesman his living.

Now: The mark is an allegiance, not a device; nobody takes it by accident. Test teachers by what they say, not by how familiar they look.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw another beast rising out of the earth. It had two horns like a lamb and it spoke like a dragon. It exercises all the authority of the first beast in its presence, and makes the earth and its inhabitants worship the first beast, whose mortal wound was healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Jesus warned of false prophets who come in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves (Matthew 7:15), and of false christs and false prophets who would perform great signs to deceive, if possible, even the elect (Matthew 24:24). In the province of Asia, the emperor cult was promoted by local elites: priests of the imperial temples, city councils and the provincial council, who organised festivals, sacrifices and games in the emperor’s honour.

Another beast out of the earth. A second beast, from the opposite element: the first came out of the sea, from far away; this one comes from the land, local and familiar. Between them the dragon has the whole world covered, which is exactly what the angel of 10:2 was answering when he planted one foot on the sea and one on the land. This beast is later called the false prophet (16:13; 19:20; 20:10).

Two horns like a lamb. It looks harmless, even Christlike: a parody of the Lamb who stands at the centre of this whole book. But the true Lamb has seven horns, the fullness of power (5:6), and he holds that power because he was slain; this one has two, and it has never bled for anyone. Religious deception often looks gentle and attractive.

And it spoke like a dragon. Then it opens its mouth, and what comes out is the dragon. Its message is Satan’s. It looks like a lamb but sounds like the serpent, deceiving as he did in Eden. Paul said Satan disguises himself as an angel of light, so it is no surprise if his servants also disguise themselves as servants of righteousness (2 Corinthians 11:14–15). The consistent New Testament warning about deception is not that it will look frightening. It is that it will look familiar, and that the test is not appearance but speech.

A usable test. Which gives an ordinary believer something to work with. The question to ask of a teacher, a movement or a message is not whether it feels Christian, looks Christian or uses Christian vocabulary; the horns are convincing. The question is what it actually says when it speaks at length, and whether that is what the dragon says: that God is not to be taken at his word, that his commands are a cage, that sin is not so serious, that Christ is one way among many, that safety lies in accommodation.

All the authority of the first beast. The second beast is not a rival; it is a department. Many readers call dragon, beast and false prophet an unholy trinity, a counterfeit of Father, Son and Spirit. The dragon gives his authority to the beast, as the Father gives all things to the Son. The beast bears a death wound and lives, and receives worship. And the false prophet does not draw attention to himself at all: his entire function is to make the world worship the beast, which is precisely what the Holy Spirit does for Christ. He will glorify me, Jesus said (John 16:14). The imitation is close.

Worship the first beast. The false prophet’s role is religious: to promote the worship of the political power. In every age that means whatever religion, philosophy, media or education persuades people to give a human power the devotion that belongs to God. In the province of Asia the priests of the imperial cult were not Romans sent from abroad but leading men of the cities: neighbours, patrons, people the church knew. The pressure to worship did not arrive only from the sea. It came up out of the local ground.

Can the false prophet be inside the church? Yes, and that is the most sobering point here. The second beast looks like a lamb, and the most effective deceivers have always spoken from within Christian circles. The letters to Pergamum and Thyatira warned of Balaam and Jezebel, teachers inside the congregations who taught believers to compromise with idolatry (2:14, 20). Whenever a church leader tells Christians that faithfulness to Christ can wait, that the culture’s demands must be accommodated, or that the gospel needs updating to suit the powers of the day, the lamb’s horns are showing. Test teachers by Scripture, however gentle their manner (1 John 4:1).

For worship. There is only one Lamb, and he never flattered, never deceived, and never asked anyone to worship any but God. And there is only one Spirit of truth, who does not speak on his own authority, but takes what is Christ’s and declares it, so that the Son is glorified. The unholy trinity can only imitate what the holy Trinity is. The Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are one God, whose glory no counterfeit can steal and whose voice his sheep know.
verseByVerse.note: This second beast is later called “the false prophet.”

verseByVerse.quote: It performs great signs, even making fire come down from heaven to earth in front of people, and by the signs that it is allowed to work in the presence of the beast it deceives those who dwell on earth, telling them to make an image for the beast that was wounded by the sword and yet lived. And it was allowed to give breath to the image of the beast, so that the image of the beast might even speak and might cause those who would not worship the image of the beast to be slain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. In Daniel 3, King Nebuchadnezzar set up a golden image and commanded everyone to worship it, on pain of death; Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego refused. Elijah called down fire from heaven to prove that the LORD is God (1 Kings 18:38). Pharaoh’s magicians copied some of Moses’ miracles (Exodus 7:11, 22). In the ancient world, statues in temples were sometimes made to appear to speak or move by priests using hidden devices or ventriloquism. In the province of Asia, statues of the emperor stood in temples and public squares, and Christians were sometimes required to offer incense before them to prove their loyalty, as Pliny reported from neighbouring Bithynia around AD 112.

Great signs. “Signs” is the same word John uses throughout his Gospel for the miracles of Jesus. These are counterfeit miracles, imitating Elijah and the two witnesses (11:5). It will not do to dismiss them as mere stagecraft. Scripture is consistent that supernatural power is not by itself proof of anything. Moses warned Israel that a prophet might give a sign that actually came to pass and still be leading them to other gods, and that God was testing them by it (Deuteronomy 13:1–3). Paul warned that the coming of the lawless one would be with all power and false signs and wonders (2 Thessalonians 2:9).

Fire from heaven. And fire from heaven is a pointed choice. That is Elijah’s sign on Carmel, the great moment in the Old Testament when fire falling from the sky settled who the true God was in front of a watching nation. The false prophet reproduces the credential of Israel’s great prophet, and the two witnesses of chapter 11 had Elijah’s powers too. Both sides in this book have fire. Only one of them has the truth.

Signs that point to him. John chose the word signs carefully. In his Gospel the signs of Jesus, water made wine, a blind man’s eyes opened, Lazarus called out of the tomb, were written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name (John 20:30–31). Every true sign is a signpost to him, and it gives life. The beast’s signs point to an image, and they end in a death sentence for anyone who will not bow. And Jesus would not perform wonders on demand: to those who asked for a sign he promised only the sign of Jonah, his own death and resurrection (Matthew 12:38–40). The deceiver performs in order to be worshipped. The Son of God went to the cross, and that is the sign by which his people know him.

It deceives. Deception is its main weapon, as it is Satan’s (12:9). “Allowed”: again, God’s permission and limits. Even the deceiving miracles run on a licence. The phrase in the presence of can also mean on behalf of, and both are true: the false prophet works in the beast’s presence and for its benefit.

An image for the beast. Idolatry of the state, of its leader or of its ideology. Behind it stands Daniel 3, and the parallel is close enough that a first-century reader would have felt it: an image set up on a plain, an order that everyone bow at a signal, and a furnace for anyone who would not.

Breath to the image. The word is spirit, breath: a parody of God giving breath to the witnesses (11:11). The Old Testament’s standing mockery of idols is that they cannot speak: they have mouths, but do not speak; eyes, but do not see (Psalm 115:5), and John used that psalm himself at 9:20. Here the mockery seems to be answered. This idol talks back, and what it says is a death sentence. Whether the mechanism is a priest behind a wall or something genuinely uncanny changes nothing about the demand, which is the same demand made on the plain of Dura: bow, or be killed.

Those who would not worship. As in Daniel 3, the demand for worship is enforced with death. Three young men said no on the plain of Dura, and said the thing that ought to be carved over this chapter: our God whom we serve is able to deliver us, and he will deliver us out of your hand, O king. But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods (Daniel 3:17–18). But if not. That is the endurance of the saints in three words.

Force and plausibility. This is the sequence the chapter has been building. The first beast supplies the force. The second supplies the plausibility: the signs, the wonders, the reasons, the respectable local men who will explain that this is only a formality. Raw power alone has never been able to command worship for long. It needs somebody with lamb’s horns to make the case.

What are the images that demand worship today? Few modern people bow to statues, but the pattern is the same wherever a human power or idea is set up to be honoured as ultimate and refusal is punished. It may be a leader whose portrait must hang in every home, an ideology that requires public affirmation of what God calls sin, or a national or tribal cause placed above Christ. Often the punishment is not death but loss: of job, standing, reputation or access. The question to ask is simple: am I being required to say or do what amounts to confessing that something other than Christ is Lord? If so, then, like the three young men, the Christian answers: we will not serve your gods.

On a Tuesday. When something spectacular is offered as proof that a teacher or movement is from God, ask what it is leading you to worship. And practise the three words now, in small matters, so they are ready in large ones: God is able to deliver me. But if not, I will still not bow.

verseByVerse.quote: Also it causes all, both small and great, both rich and poor, both free and slave, to be marked on the right hand or the forehead, so that no one can buy or sell unless he has the mark, that is, the name of the beast or the number of its name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. In Deuteronomy 6:8, Israel was told to bind God’s commandments as a sign on their hand and as frontlets between their eyes, so that their actions and thoughts would be shaped by his word. In the ancient world, slaves were sometimes branded or tattooed with their owner’s mark, and soldiers with their general’s name. Trade guilds in the cities of Asia required members to honour patron gods and the emperor; refusing could exclude a Christian from work and trade (2:9, 14, 20). Roman coins bore the emperor’s image and divine titles.

Small and great, rich and poor. Three pairs, covering every social division there was: status, wealth and legal condition. Nobody is exempt by being important and nobody is overlooked for being insignificant; the demand reaches the senator and the slave in the same sentence.

Marked on the right hand or the forehead. “Mark” is a stamp, a brand, the impression of a seal on a document or coin. It is a counterfeit, and the original has already been shown. In 7:3 the servants of God were sealed on their foreheads before the winds were released, and in 14:1 the 144,000 have the Lamb’s name and his Father’s name written on their foreheads. Everyone in this book is marked, with God’s name or the beast’s; there is no unmarked category, and the only question the book ever asks is whose name is on you.

Hand and forehead. In Deuteronomy 6:8 these are what you do and what you think. The beast demands exactly what God demanded, in the same two places, which is what makes it a parody rather than merely an atrocity. The mark means belonging to the beast and serving it, in thought and deed.

The marks of Jesus. The New Testament has its own answer to the beast’s brand. Paul, beaten and stoned for his Lord, wrote, I bear on my body the marks of Jesus (Galatians 6:17), using the word for the brand a master burned into a slave. He belonged to someone, and did not mind who saw it. But the deepest mark is not on the servant. It is on the Master. The Lamb carries in his hands and side the wounds by which he bought his people (John 20:27), and the name he writes on their foreheads (14:1) is the name of one who was marked for them first. The beast stamps its people to own them. Christ was pierced to redeem them, with his own precious blood (1 Peter 1:18–19).

No one can buy or sell. This is where the chapter stops being theoretical for most readers. The pressure is not only a threat of death. It is a threat to trade. You may keep your convictions and lose your livelihood, or you may make one small formal gesture and go on feeding your family. In John’s day, Christians who refused guild idolatry could lose their livelihood, and that may lie behind Smyrna’s poverty (2:9). Later, under the emperor Decius in the third century, citizens had to obtain a certificate stating that they had sacrificed to the gods, and papyrus copies of such certificates survive. A piece of paper was the difference between a working life and ruin.

The name of the beast. To bear someone’s name is to belong to them. The text itself defines the mark here: not a device but a name, an identity, a declaration of who owns you and whose name you will confess.

Where Christians differ: what is the mark of the beast? Over the centuries, many things have been identified as the mark: barcodes, credit cards, identity cards, microchips implanted in the hand, even vaccines. Every generation since printing has identified it with its own newest technology, and so far every generation has been wrong. Those who worried were usually sincere believers afraid of betraying Christ, and that fear deserves a gentle answer. This commentary’s view: the mark is not a physical device that someone might take by accident. It is a symbol of allegiance, the counterpart of God’s seal, which is also invisible (God’s name, 14:1, and his Spirit, Ephesians 1:13). To receive the mark is to give one’s worship and loyalty to the beast: to think and act as its servant. No one receives it without choosing to worship the beast (14:9–11). Christians should not live in fear of new technologies as though they might accidentally take the mark. They should watch their loyalty, and refuse to compromise their worship of Christ, whatever the economic cost.

What if I take the mark by accident? Nobody in this chapter takes it by accident. It is the visible sign of a worship already given, on people who have already marvelled, already worshipped and already decided that nobody can fight against the beast. A person does not stumble into it. And the ones whose names are in the Lamb’s book, written from the foundation of the world, are not the ones at that counter. If you are afraid of having the mark, that fear is itself evidence that your heart belongs to Christ. Those who bear the beast’s mark are not worried about it; they are proud of it.

What does this look like at work? It looks like the moment when keeping your job, winning the contract or being promoted requires you to do what Christ forbids: to lie on a report, to affirm what God calls evil, to join in a ritual of loyalty to something other than him, or to stay silent about your faith when silence would be a denial. Most working days involve no such choice, and a Christian should work hard and well for ordinary employers (Colossians 3:23). But when the choice comes, the issue is not the money. It is whose name is on your hand. Settle the answer before the day arrives, and trust the God who feeds the birds to provide for you if obedience costs you your income.

On a Tuesday. If you know a believer who has lost work for refusing to compromise, help them. The church that shares its bread makes the beast’s economic threat far weaker.

verseByVerse.quote: This calls for wisdom: let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and his number is 666.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. In Hebrew and Greek, letters of the alphabet also served as numbers, so every name had a numerical value. The practice of adding up the letters of a name was called gematria. A graffito at Pompeii reads: I love her whose number is 545. Nero Caesar, written in Hebrew letters (nrwn qsr), adds up to 666. Spelled without the final n, as in the Latin form Nero, it adds up to 616, and some manuscripts of Revelation read 616.

This calls for wisdom. Wisdom here is not cleverness, but spiritual discernment, to recognise the beast for what it is (17:9). Few verses in the Bible have been used more irresponsibly, so it is best to begin with what it actually says.

Calculate the number. The verb is count up, reckon, from the word for a pebble used in counting. John is not forbidding the exercise; he is setting a puzzle for people who had the key. Number puzzles of this kind were familiar in the first century, and many who heard this letter read aloud probably recognised what John was asking.

The number of a man. Literally of a human being. It may mean a particular man, or a human number, the number of humanity. Both are grammatically possible. The beast, for all its claims to divinity, is merely human.

His number is 666. Six is one short of seven, the number of completeness and perfection. Three sixes: falling short again and again, a counterfeit trinity that never reaches the divine. Jesus’ name in Greek adds up to 888, as some early Christians noticed, and they linked eight, one beyond seven, with the eighth day, the day of resurrection and new creation. The beast is the ultimate human pretender to deity, always falling short. The number also very likely pointed John’s first readers to Nero, the persecuting emperor, as the model of the beast.

A portrait, not only a cipher. Whatever the beast is, and whichever century it appears in, it is a magnificent, terrifying, world-conquering almost. It has seven heads it did not earn, ten crowns it was given, a resurrection it counterfeited, and it cannot reach seven. On this reading 666 is not merely a cipher hiding an identity; it is a portrait of every human power that reaches for God’s place and falls short. Set beside it the one man who did not reach. Christ Jesus, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself and became obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross; therefore God highly exalted him (Philippians 2:6–9). The beast grasps at deity and stays a six. The Son, who is God, stooped to become a man, and God lifted him up.

Textual note. A few early manuscripts read 616 instead of 666, as the early church father Irenaeus noted around AD 180. He defended 666 as the original, which the best manuscripts support. The variant may have arisen because 616 matches the Latin spelling of Nero Caesar, which shows that early readers connected the number with Nero. A variant that changes the number by exactly the value of one dropped letter is hard to explain as coincidence.

Where Christians differ: who is 666? The number has been applied to countless figures: popes, Muhammad, Napoleon, Hitler, various modern politicians, and titles such as the papal title Vicarius Filii Dei. This commentary’s view: the number pointed first to Nero, the emperor who began Rome’s persecution of Christians in AD 64 and became the pattern of the persecuting beast; and its symbolism, six falling short of seven, describes every human power that claims to be divine. Attempts to fit it to later figures, often made by earnest believers under real pressure, have repeatedly failed and brought discredit on the church. The right response is not number-crunching names in the news, but the wisdom to recognise and resist any power that demands worship.

What it does not mean. The number 666 is not unlucky or dangerous in itself. Christians need not fear house numbers, phone numbers or dates containing it. Its meaning lies in what it symbolises.

In the flow. The number closes the darkest chapter in the book, and the very next words open on light: John looks, and there is the Lamb standing on Mount Zion with the 144,000, who have his name and his Father’s name written on their foreheads (14:1). The sequence is deliberate. A human number on the beast’s people is answered at once by a divine name on the Lamb’s. Chapters 12 and 13 have shown the dragon and his two beasts at full strength; chapter 14 shows who is still standing.

So what am I meant to take from this chapter, if not a name? A recognition. The beast is whatever demands the allegiance that belongs to God, backed by force, made plausible by religion, and enforced through the ability to buy and sell. It has worn many costumes and it will wear more, until its final form before Christ returns. Every one of them is a six: gigantic, apparently unbeatable, worshipped by the whole earth, and one short of the number that belongs to the Lamb. So learn to recognise its marks, refuse its worship, endure its pressure, and keep your eyes on the one whose name is above every name.

On a Tuesday. The next time a book, a sermon or a viral post claims to have identified the beast in today’s headlines, smile, close it, and open the Gospel instead. You do not need to know the beast’s name to resist him. You need to know the Lamb’s.
verseByVerse.note: Letters also served as numbers. Many think 666 spells “Neron Caesar” (the Greek form) in Hebrew letters; some manuscripts read 616, which fits the Latin spelling of the name. Others see 666 as falling short of seven again and again.

13.text: <sup>1</sup>And I saw a beast rising out of the sea, with ten horns and seven heads, with ten diadems on its horns and blasphemous names on its heads.<sup>2</sup>And the beast that I saw was like a leopard; its feet were like a bear’s, and its mouth was like a lion’s mouth. And to it the dragon gave his power and his throne and great authority.<sup>3</sup>One of its heads seemed to have a mortal wound, but its mortal wound was healed, and the whole earth marveled as they followed the beast.<sup>4</sup>And they worshiped the dragon, for he had given his authority to the beast, and they worshiped the beast, saying, “Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it?”<sup>5</sup>And the beast was given a mouth uttering haughty and blasphemous words, and it was allowed to exercise authority for forty-two months.<sup>6</sup>It opened its mouth to utter blasphemies against God, blaspheming his name and his dwelling, that is, those who dwell in heaven.<sup>7</sup>Also it was allowed to make war on the saints and to conquer them. And authority was given it over every tribe and people and language and nation,<sup>8</sup>and all who dwell on earth will worship it, everyone whose name has not been written from the foundation of the world in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain.<sup>9</sup>If anyone has an ear, let him hear:<sup>10</sup>If anyone is to be taken captive, to captivity he goes; if anyone is to be slain with the sword, with the sword must he be slain. Here is a call for the endurance and faith of the saints.<sup>11</sup>Then I saw another beast rising out of the earth. It had two horns like a lamb and it spoke like a dragon.<sup>12</sup>It exercises all the authority of the first beast in its presence, and makes the earth and its inhabitants worship the first beast, whose mortal wound was healed.<sup>13</sup>It performs great signs, even making fire come down from heaven to earth in front of people,<sup>14</sup>and by the signs that it is allowed to work in the presence of the beast it deceives those who dwell on earth, telling them to make an image for the beast that was wounded by the sword and yet lived.<sup>15</sup>And it was allowed to give breath to the image of the beast, so that the image of the beast might even speak and might cause those who would not worship the image of the beast to be slain.<sup>16</sup>Also it causes all, both small and great, both rich and poor, both free and slave, to be marked on the right hand or the forehead,<sup>17</sup>so that no one can buy or sell unless he has the mark, that is, the name of the beast or the number of its name.<sup>18</sup>This calls for wisdom: let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and his number is 666.

14.title: The Lamb, the Harvest, and the Three Angels
14.overview:
Chapter 14 answers the terror of chapter 13 with three visions. First, the Lamb on Mount Zion with the 144,000, the whole people of God, standing where the beast could not reach them. Second, three angels flying overhead with the gospel, the fall of Babylon, and a warning. Third, the harvest of the earth: the grain harvest of the redeemed and the grape harvest of the wicked, the two outcomes of the last day.

Coming between the seals and trumpets and the bowls, Babylon’s fall and the new creation, the chapter tells the end in advance: the Lamb is on Mount Zion, the harvest is coming, and the one who endures to the end will be saved.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The Lamb and the 144,000 on Mount Zion
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–3: chapter 13 ended with a mark on the forehead; chapter 14 opens with a different name in the same place. The Lamb stands on Mount Zion with the 144,000, complete, bearing his name and his Father’s, and they sing a new song that only the redeemed can learn.

Verses 4–5: they have kept themselves from the beast’s idolatry, they follow the Lamb wherever he goes, they are firstfruits for God, and no lie is found in their mouth.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lamb on Mount Zion

Against the beast’s mark stand the 144,000 with the Lamb’s name on their foreheads, singing a new song only the redeemed can learn. They follow the Lamb wherever he goes, and are blameless because they were bought.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Not one of those sealed in chapter 7 is missing.

Now: The song of the cross is learned by coming to the Lamb, and no one who comes is turned away.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I looked, and behold, on Mount Zion stood the Lamb, and with him 144,000 who had his name and his Father's name written on their foreheads. And I heard a voice from heaven like the roar of many waters and like the sound of loud thunder. The voice I heard was like the sound of harpists playing on their harps, and they were singing a new song before the throne and before the four living creatures and before the elders. No one could learn that song except the 144,000 who had been redeemed from the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Revelation 14 answers the terror of chapter 13 with visions of hope and judgement. The Lamb stands on Mount Zion with the 144,000, who bear his and his Father’s name, not the beast’s mark, and sing a new song only the redeemed can learn; they follow the Lamb wherever he goes (vv. 1–5). Three angels then fly overhead: an eternal gospel to every nation, the fall of Babylon, and a warning that the beast’s worshippers will drink God’s wrath for ever (vv. 6–11). The saints are called to endure, and those who die in the Lord are blessed (vv. 12–13). Last come two harvests: one like a son of man reaps the earth, and the grapes are thrown into the winepress of God’s wrath (vv. 14–20). The chapter sets the two destinies side by side and calls everyone to choose now whom they will worship.

The setting. Mount Zion was the hill of Jerusalem where David’s city and the temple stood, and it became a name for God’s dwelling and his people. Psalm 2:6 says God has set his King on Zion, his holy hill. Joel 2:32 says that in Mount Zion there shall be those who escape, and among the survivors those whom the LORD calls. Hebrews 12:22 tells believers that they have come to Mount Zion, the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem.

A different forehead and a different name. Chapter 13 ended with a mark on the right hand or the forehead, and a number. Chapter 14 opens with a different forehead and a different name: not an unmarked crowd, but a marked one, wearing another name in the same place.

On Mount Zion stood the Lamb. Firm and victorious, in contrast to the dragon standing on the sand of the sea (12:17). The beasts rose from the sea and the earth; the Lamb stands on Zion, the place of God’s King, where God installs him in the teeth of the raging nations (Psalm 2:6). Zion here is the heavenly Zion, where the church already belongs (Hebrews 12:22). In 5:6 the Lamb was standing as though slain. Here he is simply standing, and the company with him is counted and complete.

His Father’s name on their foreheads. Not one is missing: after all the beast’s war on the saints, the full number sealed in 7:4 stands with the Lamb. And their seal is now revealed: the name of the Lamb and the Father, in contrast to the beast’s name on its followers (13:17).

Who are the 144,000? They are the same as in chapter 7: the complete people of God, redeemed and sealed with the name of the Lamb and his Father. They are not a literal number from ethnic Israel, and not the special class of “anointed” taught by Jehovah’s Witnesses. Many dispensational readers, who rightly take God’s promises to Israel seriously, see them as Jewish believers of the last days; this commentary reads them as the whole church because in chapter 7 John hears a counted number and then sees a multitude no one could number, from every nation (7:4, 9). The number is twelve times twelve times a thousand: the twelve tribes and the twelve apostles, the whole people of God of both covenants, multiplied to fullness. If you belong to Christ, you are in this number. Not one of his people is left out of the count, and none is counted twice.

Many waters and loud thunder. Three comparisons follow, and they should not be flattened into one. The roar of many waters is how the voice of the risen Christ was described at 1:15, and how Ezekiel described the sound of the glory of God returning to the temple (Ezekiel 43:2). Thunder is the voice of God at Sinai.

Like harpists. And then, in the same breath, harps, one of the gentlest sounds of the ancient world. Powerful and also beautiful, overwhelming and tender at the same volume. Human music can hardly do both; a waterfall is not tender, and a harp cannot be heard over one. This is what the worship of heaven sounds like.

A new song. A new song is sung in Scripture when God has done something unprecedented (Psalm 96:1; 98:1), and it was sung once before in this book, when the elders sang of the Lamb who by his blood ransomed people for God (5:9). That is the subject of this song too.

No one could learn that song. Only the redeemed can sing the song of redemption, because only they have experienced it. Not because the words are difficult; a song about being ransomed by blood can be printed and read by anyone. It cannot be learned, in the sense of being sung truly, by a person who has not been ransomed. Angels can praise God for salvation (7:11–12), but they cannot sing as those who have been bought with the Lamb’s blood. Peter says angels long to look into these things (1 Peter 1:12).

What if I cannot sing, or worship feels dry? The new song is not a matter of musical ability or of feeling a certain way on a Sunday. It is the confession of a redeemed heart: I was bought by the blood of the Lamb, and I belong to him. You can sing it in a quavering voice, or say it silently in a hospital bed, and heaven hears it as part of the great chorus. Dry seasons come to every believer. When they do, keep gathering with God’s people, keep singing the true words even when your feelings lag behind, and look again at the cross that the song is about. The feelings usually follow the looking.

On a Tuesday. When you are tempted to compromise to keep your place, your income or your friends, say to yourself: I belong to the Lamb, and his Father’s name is on me. And next Sunday, when the church sings of the blood that bought you, sing it as your own story.

For worship. Worthy is the Lamb who stands on Zion. The raging of the nations did not move him from the hill where God set his King, and the war of the beast did not strike one name from his company. He bought them, every one, with his own blood, and wrote his Father’s name where the world could see it. The song they sing he taught them by redeeming them, and every line of it is about him: slain, and yet standing; the price paid, and the purchase complete. Waters and thunder and harps at once: it is the sound of a Redeemer who has lost none of those he bought.

verseByVerse.quote: It is these who have not defiled themselves with women, for they are virgins. It is these who follow the Lamb wherever he goes. These have been redeemed from mankind as firstfruits for God and the Lamb, and in their mouth no lie was found, for they are blameless.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Israel’s soldiers abstained from sexual relations during holy war (Deuteronomy 23:9–10; 1 Samuel 21:5), and firstfruits were the first of the harvest, offered to God (Exodus 23:19; Leviticus 23:10). The prophets picture God’s people as his virgin bride (Jeremiah 18:13; 31:4), and idolatry as adultery or prostitution (Hosea 1–3; Ezekiel 16). Paul told the Corinthians he had betrothed them to Christ, to present them as a pure virgin (2 Corinthians 11:2). Zephaniah 3:13 says that the remnant of Israel shall speak no lies, nor shall there be found in their mouth a deceitful tongue.

They are virgins. This is one of the hardest sentences in the book to read well. “Virgins” is a word that can be used of men as well as women. In the context of Revelation, where Babylon is the great prostitute (17:1–5) and idolatry is spiritual immorality (2:14, 20), this means they kept themselves pure from the idolatry of the beast. They are the faithful bride of the Lamb (19:7–8; 21:2).

Spiritual faithfulness. This book is about to spend two chapters on a prostitute called Babylon who made all nations drink the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality (v. 8), and it ends with a Bride. In that setting, virgins means those who did not go to bed with the beast. They kept themselves for one Lord in a world offering many.

Holy warriors. They are also like holy warriors, set apart for the Lamb’s war. The number 144,000 came out of a tribal muster in chapter 7, twelve thousand from each tribe, which is how Israel counted an army. Soldiers under a holy-war vow kept from sexual relations for the campaign, as Uriah would not go home to his wife while the ark and the army were in tents (2 Samuel 11:11). On this reading John is describing consecrated troops on active service, and the language is ceremonial rather than a judgement on marriage or on women: the company includes every believing woman, and the picture is drawn from the army camp. The two pictures say one thing together: this company has kept itself wholly for the Lamb.

Where Christians differ: does this praise celibacy? Some, from the early church onwards, have read this verse as praising literal virginity and celibacy as a higher form of Christian life, and used it to support celibate monks, nuns and clergy. Many who choose celibacy do so out of real devotion to Christ, and that devotion deserves honour. This commentary’s view: the virginity here is spiritual purity from idolatry, the faithfulness of the Lamb’s bride. Scripture honours marriage (Hebrews 13:4; Genesis 2:24), calls forbidding marriage a teaching of demons (1 Timothy 4:1–3), and says that marriage is not defiling. Celibacy is a good gift for some (1 Corinthians 7:7–8), but it is not a higher state of holiness. The 144,000 are the whole church, married and single, who refused to commit spiritual adultery with the beast.

They follow the Lamb. “Follow” is the word for discipleship. That is the simplest definition of a Christian in the whole book, and after two chapters of dragons and beasts and numbers it is startlingly plain. Following was the first thing Jesus asked of anybody, follow me, said to fishermen at their nets, and it is the last thing he says to Peter at the end of John’s Gospel, twice (John 21:19, 22). In contrast, the world follows the beast (13:3).

Wherever. The weight is in that word. Following is easy while the road is going somewhere a person would have chosen. This book has shown where the Lamb actually goes: to a cross, and through death, and in the meantime among lampstands in difficult towns. Wherever he goes includes suffering and death. To follow him wherever is to have surrendered the veto in advance, and it is what distinguishes a disciple from an admirer.

Firstfruits. The firstfruit is the first sheaf of a harvest, brought to God before the rest was gathered. A firstfruit belongs wholly to God, and it guarantees that more is coming. That suggests that the harvest of verse 15 is the gathering of the redeemed. James calls believers a kind of firstfruits of God’s creatures (James 1:18), and Paul calls Christ himself the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Corinthians 15:20). Here the whole church is the firstfruits offered from all humanity, the pledge of a renewed creation.

No lie was found. The phrase echoes the Servant of Isaiah 53:9, in whose mouth there was no deceit, and the remnant of Zephaniah. In a book whose villain is the deceiver of the whole world (12:9) and whose second beast deceives by signs (13:14), truthfulness is not a minor virtue. It is the mark of the other side. The Lamb’s people tell the truth. They did not say Caesar is Lord, and they did not deny Christ.

Blameless. The word is without blemish, the technical word for a sacrificial animal without defect. It is what Peter says of Christ, the lamb without blemish or spot (1 Peter 1:19). Nobody in this company achieved it. Verse 3 has already said they were redeemed, which means bought, which means the blamelessness was purchased and given. Their blamelessness comes from his blood, in which they washed their robes and made them white (7:14), and it shows in their faithful lives. Here is how it was given: God counts the Lamb’s perfect record as theirs, because on the cross he counted their sins as his (2 Corinthians 5:21). Scripture’s word for it is justification, a judge’s verdict that the guilty now stand in the right for Christ’s sake. It is not sinless perfection in this life. Over a lifetime he begins to make them in fact what he has declared them to be.

I have not kept myself pure. Is there a place for me here? Yes, if you come to the Lamb. Not one of the 144,000 was pure by nature; every one was redeemed, bought out of a defiled humanity. The Corinthian church Paul wanted to present as a pure virgin to Christ included former idolaters, adulterers and thieves, and he says to them: such were some of you, but you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified (1 Corinthians 6:11). Sexual sin and spiritual unfaithfulness in your past are real, and must be confessed and turned from. But they do not bar you from the Lamb’s company. His blood makes the defiled clean, and from now on you follow him.

Does following the Lamb wherever he goes mean I must give up everything? It means you give him the right to ask for anything. Most days he asks for ordinary things: honesty, kindness, a clean conscience, faithfulness in your work and family, time with him and his people. Some days he asks for something costly: a relationship you must end, a career move you must refuse, a reputation you must lose for his sake. The disciple does not decide in advance which roads he will take with Christ and which he will not. And he is never asked to go anywhere the Lamb has not gone first.

On a Tuesday. The Lamb bought you and counts you blameless, so speak the truth, even when a lie would be easier. Think of the small lies told to smooth a day: the excuse at work, the exaggeration, the pretended agreement. The people of the Lamb are known by their mouths.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 6–7: an angel flies overhead, where all can see, with an eternal gospel for every nation: fear God, give him glory, and worship the Creator, for the hour of his judgment has come.

Verse 8: a second angel announces Babylon fallen, three chapters before she is described.

Verses 9–11: a third warns that those who worship the beast will drink God’s wrath unmixed, for ever.

Verses 12–13: the saints are called to endure, and heaven has John write that the dead who die in the Lord are blessed; the Spirit adds that they rest, and their deeds follow them.
verseByVerse.theology:
Gospel, Fall, and Warning

An angel flies overhead with an eternal gospel: fear God and worship the Creator. A second announces Babylon fallen. A third warns that worshippers of the beast will drink God’s wrath unmixed. Then: blessed are the dead who die in the Lord.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The empire was at its height when its fall was announced in the past tense.

Now: Fear God rather than the beast; the warning is given so that the saints endure, and their deeds follow them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw another angel flying directly overhead, with an eternal gospel to proclaim to those who dwell on earth, to every nation and tribe and language and people. And he said with a loud voice, "Fear God and give him glory, because the hour of his judgment has come, and worship him who made heaven and earth, the sea and the springs of water."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. The eagle flew overhead crying woe (8:13); now an angel flies overhead with good news. Paul preached to pagans at Lystra and Athens that they should turn from vain things to the living God who made heaven and earth and the sea (Acts 14:15; 17:24–31), and that God has fixed a day on which he will judge the world. Jesus said that this gospel of the kingdom will be proclaimed throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come (Matthew 24:14).

Three angels, three announcements. Three angels follow one another through these verses with three announcements, and they arrive in the order the gospel usually arrives: an appeal, a warning about the world, and a warning about the alternative. God does not judge without first calling.

Directly overhead. Literally in mid-heaven, at the zenith, the position of the eagle in 8:13: where all can see and hear at once. Nobody will be able to say the message was hard to come by.

An eternal gospel. It is the only time Revelation uses the noun gospel. It is eternal because it never changes and its effects last for ever. Even in the midst of judgement, God proclaims good news. Some have questioned whether what follows is the gospel at all, since it contains no mention of the cross. But this is a book in which the announcement of the cross has already been made at great length; the whole of chapter 5 is the gospel, and the Lamb who was slain has been at the centre of every scene since. And to people under a beast, the news that the true God is still calling them to himself is good news of the most concrete kind.

To those who dwell on earth. The audience is those who dwell on earth, John’s standing term for the people who have settled for this world. To the same people who worship the beast (13:8), God offers the gospel. The good news is proclaimed to precisely the group that has been refusing it for chapters.

Fear God and give him glory. To give him glory is to worship him and repent (11:13; 16:9). And the first command is the one modern readers find hardest. Fear God does not mean cringing terror, and it does not mean a mild respect either. It means taking God seriously as what he actually is: the settled, awed recognition that there is someone there of a different order altogether. Proverbs calls it the beginning of knowledge (Proverbs 1:7).

Fearing the right thing. It is aimed at people who have spent the whole book being terrified of a beast. The remedy for fearing the wrong thing is not fearlessness.
