It is fearing the right thing, which turns out to set a person free from everything else. Jesus said it plainly: do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell (Matthew 10:28). The one who fears God need fear no one else.

The hour of his judgment. The good news includes the warning. Judgement is near, so turn now. Good news that ignored the judgement would not be good; it would be a lie told to people walking towards a cliff.

By a man whom he has appointed. The hour of judgement the angel announces has a face. When Paul made this same appeal to the Athenians, turn to the God who made the world, he ended it with a person: God has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed, and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead (Acts 17:31). The Father has given all judgement to the Son (John 5:22). That is why the first angel’s message is good news and not only warning. The one who will judge is the one who died for sinners, and the call to fear God and give him glory is a call to come to the Judge while he still stands as Saviour. A few verses later he appears on a white cloud with a sickle in his hand (v. 14).

Him who made heaven and earth. The Creator, who alone deserves worship (4:11), echoing the fourth commandment (Exodus 20:11). And the list is deliberate: heaven, earth, sea and fresh water are the four realms struck by the first four trumpets (8:7–12). The one who made them all is the one to worship, not the beast who rose from the sea and earth. This is the argument Paul made to pagans who had no Bible: where there is no shared Scripture there is still a shared sky.

Is the angel’s call to give God glory a kind of vanity? In anyone else it would be. When a human being demands praise, he is asking for more than he is worth, and we rightly call it vanity. But God is the one being of whom all praise is simply true, and he commands it because it is good for us. Everybody worships something; the angel is speaking to people who have been bowing to a beast. To be told to give glory to the God who made heaven and earth is to be told to stop handing your heart to things that cannot bear it: a career, a reputation, a nation, another person. Every lesser god takes from its worshippers. This God gave his own Son for his (Romans 8:32). And worship is where a creature finds his joy, for in God’s presence there is fullness of joy (Psalm 16:11).

Where Christians differ: is this a last chance after death, or a different gospel? Some have read the eternal gospel as a final chance for salvation given after the church’s age, or even as a gospel different from that of Christ, without the cross. This commentary’s view: the eternal gospel is the same gospel of Jesus Christ preached throughout this age, summed up here in the call to turn from idols to the living God, which was the first step of the apostles’ preaching to pagans (1 Thessalonians 1:9–10). Paul says there is no other gospel (Galatians 1:6–9). It is proclaimed to the living, before the hour of judgement, not after death (Hebrews 9:27). The angel pictures the worldwide preaching of the gospel by the church before the end.

How do I share the gospel with someone who does not believe the Bible? Start where the angel starts and where Paul started: with the God who made them. Every person lives in a world they did not make, with a conscience they did not invent, and a longing for meaning and justice they cannot explain away. Talk about the Creator who gave them life, the sin that has turned us from him, the judgement that is coming, and the Saviour he has sent. Do not hide the cross, because it is the heart of the message; but you need not begin with a debate about the Bible. Begin with the shared sky, and let the word of God do its own work as you open it.

On a Tuesday. Who, of everyone you know, seems furthest from God? The gospel is for that person too. Make them your daily prayer, and look for one natural opening to speak of the God who made us and the Christ who saves us.

verseByVerse.quote: Another angel, a second, followed, saying, "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, she who made all nations drink the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Babylon was the great empire that destroyed Jerusalem and the temple in 586 BC and took God’s people into exile. It became the Bible’s symbol of human pride and rebellion against God, from the tower of Babel (Genesis 11) onwards. Isaiah 21:9 cries, fallen, fallen is Babylon; and all the carved images of her gods he has shattered to the ground. Jeremiah 51:7–8 says Babylon was a golden cup in the LORD’s hand, making all the earth drunken; the nations drank her wine, therefore they went mad; suddenly Babylon has fallen. Peter almost certainly means Rome when he writes from Babylon (1 Peter 5:13).

Fallen, fallen. Babylon appears here for the first time, in a single verse, announced as already finished. Chapters 17 and 18 will describe her at length; this is the headline running ahead of the story. The words are Isaiah’s (Isaiah 21:9). The doubling is the sound of a herald, the way news of a great collapse actually gets shouted in the streets.

The grammar of certainty. “Fallen” is past tense, twice. The angel announces the collapse of an empire that is, at the moment of speaking, at the height of its power. What God has decided is reported as though it had already happened, because from his side it has. Scholars call it the prophetic perfect, and it is exactly what a Christian in Ephesus needed. The empire in front of him was not wobbling. It was collecting his taxes, running his courts and threatening his trade. And the message read out in his congregation used the past tense.

Why the past tense is safe. The angel can speak of Babylon’s fall as finished because the decisive battle is already behind him. On the eve of the cross Jesus said, now is the judgement of this world; now will the ruler of this world be cast out (John 12:31). Paul says that at the cross Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, triumphing over them (Colossians 2:15). Babylon still glitters, but the power behind her was broken on a hill outside Jerusalem. Her fall is in the past tense because his victory is.

Who is Babylon? The historical Babylon had been a ruin for centuries when John wrote, so the name is being used as Sodom and Egypt were at 11:8, as a type. In John’s day, Babylon was Rome, the great city built on seven hills (17:9, 18), the city that had destroyed the temple, as Babylon had; and Peter sends greetings from she who is at Babylon (1 Peter 5:13). But the name is older than Rome and outlives it. Babylon in Scripture begins at a tower built so that a people could make a name for themselves (Genesis 11:4), and that project has never closed. It stands for every proud human civilisation organised without God: its economics, culture, pleasures and power, however good its roads are.

The wine of her passion. “Passion” can mean passion or wrath, and the double sense is deliberate. Babylon seduces the nations into idolatry and immorality, like a prostitute offering wine to intoxicate her clients. Two things in the image. It is seduction, not conquest: the nations were not forced; they were poured a drink. And it is intoxication: the loss of judgement, the inability to see straight, the cheerful certainty that everything is fine. The same wine she makes them drink becomes the wine of God’s wrath (v. 10; 16:19). Those who drink her passion will drink God’s anger.

The sword and the glass. That is how the world’s system actually recruits, and it is why the church has so often failed to notice. The beast comes with a sword and is obvious. Babylon comes with a glass, and is charming, and pays well, and does not appear to be asking for anything at all. Probably more Christians have been lost to Babylon’s wine than to the beast’s sword. And she does not recruit only the irreligious. A churchgoer can refuse the beast’s mark on Sunday and still be drunk on Babylon’s wine all week, measuring his life by the same success, comfort and reputation as everyone else.

How do I live in Babylon without drinking her wine? The way the exiles did in the first Babylon: seek the welfare of the city where God has sent you, and pray for it (Jeremiah 29:7), while refusing its gods. Daniel served the king faithfully and would not eat his food or stop praying. So work hard, be a good neighbour, enjoy God’s good gifts with thanks. But watch what intoxicates you: the pull of money, status, comfort, entertainment and approval that slowly dulls your love for Christ. A useful question is what you could not give up without bitterness. Whatever that is, hold it more loosely, and hold Christ more tightly.

On a Tuesday. When the advertisements, the ambitions and the anxieties of the day press in on you, say quietly to yourself what the angel said: fallen, fallen. It will help you see straight. You are not obliged to admire, envy or fear a city whose ruin God has already announced.

For worship. The Lord has spoken, and Babylon is fallen. Nineveh is dust, the old Babylon is a mound in the desert, and the Rome that killed the apostles lies in ruins for tourists to walk through, while the church of the Lamb is gathered from every nation under heaven. Every proud city has its date already written; only one city has foundations, whose designer and builder is God (Hebrews 11:10). The past tense of God is the future of the world.

verseByVerse.quote: And another angel, a third, followed them, saying with a loud voice, "If anyone worships the beast and its image and receives a mark on his forehead or on his hand, he also will drink the wine of God's wrath, poured full strength into the cup of his anger, and he will be tormented with fire and sulfur in the presence of the holy angels and in the presence of the Lamb. And the smoke of their torment goes up forever and ever, and they have no rest, day or night, these worshipers of the beast and its image, and whoever receives the mark of its name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. In the Old Testament, the cup of God’s wrath is a picture of judgement (Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15–16). Wine in the ancient world was usually mixed with water; to pour it full strength, unmixed, was to make it at its most powerful. Fire and sulphur destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:24), and the smoke of the land went up like the smoke of a furnace (Genesis 19:28). Isaiah 34:9–10 describes Edom’s judgement: its smoke shall go up for ever.

If anyone worships the beast. This is one of the most terrible warnings in the New Testament, and it should be read exactly as it stands, without softening and without relish. The warning is aimed at those who choose to worship the beast; no one takes the mark by accident. And the order of the angels is the mercy of the passage: nobody arrives at verse 11 without having been flown over by verse 6. The first of these three was an eternal gospel at the height of heaven where every nation could see it.

Full strength. The image answers the previous verse precisely. Babylon poured a drink; so does God. Those who drank hers will drink his. And the detail is exact: unmixed, undiluted. The cup of God’s wrath is an Old Testament image (Psalm 75:8); here John says plainly that nothing has been added to dilute it.

The water left out. The judgements of the seals and trumpets were mixed with mercy, partial and limited: a fourth, a third, a tenth, forty-two months, a limit on the locusts, a restraint on the winds. That was the mixing. This verse is what the cup is like when the water is left out: God’s wrath unmixed, with no mercy left.

Fire and sulfur. Fire and sulphur is Sodom, and it is the lake of fire (19:20; 20:10; 21:8).

In the presence of the Lamb. Not that the angels and the Lamb watch with pleasure, but that the judgement is carried out under their authority, and is just. The one who refused the Lamb’s mercy faces the Lamb as judge. Whatever else hell is, it is not a place God has forgotten. Holy means utterly pure and set apart from all evil, and that is what makes this presence unbearable. The same holiness that is the joy of heaven is a consuming fire to anyone who stands before it uncovered (Isaiah 33:14; Hebrews 12:29). And the one present is the Lamb: the one who was slaughtered, who wept at a tomb, who prayed for the men who crucified him (Luke 23:34; some early manuscripts lack that prayer, though many scholars judge it genuine). Nobody who is finally lost will be able to say that the Judge did not offer himself first.

Forever and ever. Literally to the ages of the ages, the same phrase used for God’s eternal life (4:9; 15:7) and for the saints’ reign (22:5). The smoke going up for ever is Isaiah’s picture of Edom. The torment does not end.

No rest, day or night. In contrast with the living creatures, who have no rest from praise (4:8), and with the dead in the Lord, who rest from their labours (v. 13). Two eternities are set side by side, and the difference is what a person is doing in them. And the verse says twice who it falls on: the beast’s worshippers. Not people who were unlucky, or confused, or never called.

Where Christians differ: is hell eternal conscious punishment? Annihilationists (or conditionalists) believe the wicked are punished and then cease to exist, and read “the smoke goes up forever” as the lasting result of a destruction that is complete. Some who hold this love the Bible and are trying to be faithful to it. Universalists believe all will finally be saved. This commentary’s view: this passage teaches eternal, conscious punishment. The wicked are tormented, they have no rest day or night, and this continues for ever and ever. Revelation 20:10 uses the same language of the devil, beast and false prophet: tormented day and night for ever and ever, which plainly cannot mean annihilation. Jesus spoke of eternal punishment in the same breath as eternal life (Matthew 25:46). This is terrible, and it should be spoken of with tears, not glee. But it is what Scripture says, and it shows both the seriousness of sin against an infinitely holy God and the greatness of Christ’s love in bearing God’s wrath for all who trust in him.

What it does not mean. This warning is not meant to make Christians afraid that they might lose their salvation. It is meant to make them refuse the beast at any cost, and to warn the world.

The cup in Gethsemane. Set this verse beside the garden. On the night before he died, the Son of God fell on his face and prayed, my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will (Matthew 26:39). This was the cup. He drank it, full strength, on the cross, when the darkness came down and he cried out that God had forsaken him. Everyone who trusts in him has had their portion drunk already. The wrath that falls on the beast’s worshippers has no claim left on Christ’s people, because it fell on him.

How can the smoke of their torment rise for ever if God is love? Because his love is holy, and sin against him is infinitely serious. We measure the guilt of a crime partly by the dignity of the one wronged; to rebel against the infinitely good God who made us is no small matter. Hell is also God giving people, in the end, what they have chosen: life without him, who is the source of all light, rest and joy. And those in hell do not repent there; this book shows the lost cursing God rather than turning to him (16:9, 11). Verse 10 sets it in the presence of the holy angels and of the Lamb: nothing about it is hidden from the one who loved most, because nothing about it is unjust. Above all, remember who is the Judge. It is the Lamb, who bore this wrath himself so that it need not fall on anyone who comes to him. No one is in hell who wanted the mercy offered.

What about someone I love who has died without Christ, as far as I know? Scripture does not tell us the destination of any individual, and it never invites us to pronounce on the dead. You did not see every moment of their last days or the whole of their heart, and God is merciful beyond our knowledge. What you can do is leave them in the hands of the Judge of all the earth, who will do right (Genesis 18:25), and grieve honestly. And for those still alive, Scripture tells us that the Judge is the Lamb, that the gospel is still being flown overhead, and that intercession is the very work you were made a priest to do (1:6). Pray, and keep praying. Saul of Tarsus stood guarding the coats at Stephen’s death.

On a Tuesday. Let this verse make you more urgent, not more harsh: more willing to speak of Christ to a friend, more earnest in prayer for the lost, and more grateful every time you take the cup of blessing at the Lord’s table, knowing whose cup made it possible.

verseByVerse.quote: Here is a call for the endurance of the saints, those who keep the commandments of God and their faith in Jesus. And I heard a voice from heaven saying, "Write this: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on." "Blessed indeed," says the Spirit, "that they may rest from their labors, for their deeds follow them!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. This is the second of Revelation’s seven beatitudes (1:3). Isaiah 57:1–2 says the righteous man perishes, and no one lays it to heart, but he enters into peace; they rest in their beds who walk in their uprightness. Hebrews 4:9–11 speaks of a Sabbath rest that remains for the people of God.

The endurance of the saints. A like sentence appeared at 13:10, and it appears both times immediately after the darkest material in the book: there after the beast conquering the saints, here after the cup of undiluted wrath. Twice John writes something almost unbearable and then turns to the reader and says: this is what it is for. The response sought is not panic, and not a campaign, but endurance. Because the stakes are eternal, believers must endure, refusing the beast, whatever it costs; and the warning of verses 9 to 11 is a reason to stay faithful for people whose cup the Lamb has already drunk.

Commandments and faith. “Faith in Jesus” can mean faith in Jesus, or the faithfulness of Jesus. As in 12:17, obedience and faith together mark the true believer, and nothing has been added to them. Either reading of the phrase lands on the same ground. No saint keeps the commandments perfectly (James 3:2), but Jesus was faithful to the end, and his obedience is counted to all who trust him (Romans 5:19). Their endurance rests on his.

Blessed are the dead. This is one of the few sentences in the book that John is specifically commanded to write down (compare 19:9; 21:5). Not blessed are the strong, or the victorious, or those who escape. To a congregation that had buried people and expected to bury more, at the exact point in the book where the beast is killing anyone who will not take the mark, God stops the vision to dictate a sentence about the ones who did not survive.

In the Lord. The phrase means united to Christ by faith, and the qualifier carries everything. Death is not blessed in itself; Paul calls it the last enemy (1 Corinthians 15:26), and this book throws it into the lake of fire (20:14). What is blessed is dying in him, the same phrase Paul uses of the dead in Christ whom he expects to rise (1 Thessalonians 4:16). “From now on” means from this point in history, as persecution intensifies, or from the moment of death. Those who die faithful, perhaps as martyrs, are not to be pitied: the world calls them losers; heaven calls them blessed. What does in the Lord actually mean? It means the believer is joined to Christ, so that what happened to Christ counts for him: Christ died, and his death is the believer’s; Christ rose, and his rising is the pledge of the believer’s (Romans 6:5). A Christian does not die alone, or as a stranger to God. He dies as a member of the one who has already come out the other side.

Why death in the Lord is blessed. Death can be called blessed only because the Lord himself went into it. Christ shared our flesh and blood so that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, the devil, and deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery (Hebrews 2:14–15). In the first chapter of this book he says, I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades (1:18). A believer’s death is therefore not a door into the dark but a door whose key is in the hand of the one who loved him. The Lord went through it first, and came back holding it open.

Says the Spirit. Apart from the seven letters, the Spirit speaks in his own voice only here and at 22:17. “Indeed” is yes: the Spirit adds his confirmation. “Labors” is toil, hard work, the exhaustion of service and suffering. It is the rest the martyrs under the altar were told to take in 6:11. Whatever heaven is, it is first described here as the end of being tired. In contrast with the restless torment of the beast’s worshippers (v. 11), the dead in Christ rest.

Their deeds follow them. Not go before them as a credential, and not stay behind as a legacy. They follow, like servants walking behind their master into a house. Their faithful works are not lost; they go with them into God’s presence, as evidence of their faith and as the basis of their reward (22:12). Nothing done for Christ is wasted; your labour is not in vain in the Lord (1 Corinthians 15:58). The visits nobody recorded, the giving that cost something, the years of raising children in the faith, the prayers said in an empty kitchen: all of it walks in behind the person who did it.

Where Christians differ: do believers go to purgatory, or rest? Roman Catholic teaching holds that many who die in God’s grace must still be purified in purgatory before entering heaven. Others hold that the soul sleeps until the resurrection. Catholic friends hold purgatory out of a real sense of God’s holiness, and that concern is right; the question is what Christ’s blood has already done. This commentary’s view: the dead in the Lord are blessed from the moment of death, and they rest. There is no purging of sin after death; Christ’s blood has cleansed them completely (1 John 1:7; Hebrews 10:14), and to be absent from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). Their rest is conscious enjoyment of Christ (6:9–11), not unconscious sleep. They wait for the resurrection of the body, but they are already with him.

What it does not mean. Their deeds following them does not mean they are saved by their works. Their works follow them; they do not go before them to buy them entry.

What should I say at the funeral of a believer? Say this verse. It was written down at heaven’s express command for exactly that moment. Grieve, because death is an enemy and the loss is real; Jesus wept at Lazarus’s tomb. But grieve as those who have hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). The one you loved is not lost, not sleeping in the dark, not being purged somewhere. They are with Christ, resting, conscious, at home. Their work is finished and none of it is forgotten. And one day their body, laid in the ground, will be raised in glory. Say that to the widow, the orphan, the friend. It is the truest comfort there is.

What if I feel my life has accomplished very little for Christ? Then this verse is for you. The deeds that follow the dead in the Lord are not only the public ones. They include every hidden kindness, every faithful year in a small place, every prayer for a child, every temptation resisted that nobody saw. God sees what no one records, and he forgets nothing done in his name, not even a cup of cold water. You are not asked to be impressive. You are asked to be faithful, and the Lord who works in you to will and to work for his good pleasure will see that what he has done through you follows you home.

For worship. God gives his weary servants rest, and he does a stranger kindness still: he lets their works follow them in, though every good thing they did was his own work in them, prepared beforehand that they should walk in it (Ephesians 2:10). He crowns his own gifts and calls them theirs. The Spirit says yes to it. And the Lord in whom they died, who saw every labour nobody recorded, receives them home and says to each, well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your master (Matthew 25:21).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–20 — The Harvest of the Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 14–16: one like a son of man, crowned and seated on a white cloud, reaps the ripe harvest of the earth at the hour the Father has set.

Verses 17–20: at the word of the angel from the altar, the grapes of the vine of the earth are gathered and trodden in the winepress of God’s wrath outside the city. The blood and the 1,600 stadia (four times four times a hundred, four being the number of the earth) mean a judgement covering the whole world.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Harvest of the Earth

One like a son of man reaps the ripe harvest, and the vintage of the earth is trodden in the winepress of God’s wrath outside the city. The timing is set by the one who has watched the field.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The order for the vintage came from the altar where the martyrs’ prayers were received.

Now: The delay was never indifference but patience; the judge who reaps is the one who was trodden outside the city for us.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I looked, and behold, a white cloud, and seated on the cloud one like a son of man, with a golden crown on his head, and a sharp sickle in his hand. And another angel came out of the temple, calling with a loud voice to him who sat on the cloud, "Put in your sickle, and reap, for the hour to reap has come, for the harvest of the earth is fully ripe." So he who sat on the cloud swung his sickle across the earth, and the earth was reaped.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Joel 3:13 says: put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe; go in, tread, for the winepress is full. The vats overflow, for their evil is great. Daniel 7:13 shows one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven. Jesus told parables of harvest at the end of the age: the wheat gathered into the barn and the weeds burned (Matthew 13:24–30, 36–43), and the angels sent to gather his elect from the four winds (Matthew 24:31). He said the harvest is plentiful (Matthew 9:37–38), and that the fields are white for harvest (John 4:35).

One like a son of man. One like a son of man coming with the clouds is Daniel 7:13, and it is the phrase this book used of the risen Christ in its first chapter (1:13). This is Christ, coming on the clouds (1:7).

A golden crown and a sharp sickle. The crown is the victor’s: he has conquered. And in his hand, instead of a sword or a sceptre, a farm implement, the curved blade for harvesting grain.

Put in your sickle. Some have taken the figure on the cloud as an angel, on the grounds that here an angel tells him to start reaping, which seems an odd thing for a creature to say to the Son of God. The objection is fair and should be stated. But the angel brings the message from God’s presence, the temple: the Father has fixed the hour. Christ himself said that of that day or that hour no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father (Mark 13:32; Acts 1:7). The angel does not command Christ; he conveys the Father’s timing. A message from the sanctuary saying the hour has come is exactly what the Son said he was waiting for.

Fully ripe. The timing is stated twice. The word means has become dry, over-ready: grain that has stood in the field until it is at the point of being lost. Anyone who has waited on a crop knows there is a right day. Cut too early and the grain is green and worthless; wait too long and it shatters on the ground and the season’s work is gone. The point of the image is not the violence of reaping. It is that a decision about timing is being made by someone who has been watching the field.

The answer to how long. This answers the question that has run through this book since 6:10. The delay was never indifference and never a failure of nerve. It was a harvest not yet ready, and Peter says exactly what was ripening: the Lord is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance (2 Peter 3:9).

The earth was reaped. After chapters of seals, trumpets, beasts and dragons, the end arrives in a single sentence with no resistance recorded: no battle, no dialogue. The instrument that finishes the age is a sickle swung once by a man on a cloud.

In the flow. Chapter 13 showed the beast at the height of its power, and chapter 14 answers it by telling the end of the story in advance, closing with the harvest that ends the age. The bowls of chapters 15 and 16 will cover the same ground again, and chapters 17 to 19 open up Babylon’s fall and Christ’s coming at length. That is how Revelation works: it tells the story of this age more than once, and each telling arrives at the same single return of Christ (19:11–16).

Where Christians differ: is the grain harvest salvation or judgement? Some see both harvests in vv. 14–20 as judgement, following Joel 3:13. Others see the grain harvest as the gathering of the redeemed and the grape harvest as the judgement of the wicked. This commentary’s view: the grain harvest is most likely the gathering of God’s people at Christ’s return. Christ himself reaps it, as he sends his angels to gather his elect (Matthew 24:31); in the Gospels, the grain harvest is regularly the harvest of salvation (Matthew 9:37–38; 13:30; John 4:35–38); and the 144,000 have just been called firstfruits (v. 4), the beginning of this harvest. Nothing is said about destroying the grain. The grape harvest, by contrast, is explicitly thrown into the winepress of God’s wrath. Together they picture the two outcomes of the last day.

Is this the rapture? It is the one gathering of God’s people at Christ’s visible return, which is what the New Testament means by our being caught up to meet the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). There is no hint here of a secret removal of the church years before the end. Many believers were taught a secret rapture by teachers they love, and they share this same longing for the Lord; this commentary differs because the gathering of the church in the New Testament comes with his visible appearing, after events Scripture names (Matthew 24:29–31; 2 Thessalonians 2:1–4). The Son of Man comes on a white cloud, in the sight of the world, at the hour the Father has set, and reaps the whole earth at once. That is the hope of every believer: not escape from history halfway through, but the Lord himself coming at its end to gather his harvest home.

On a Tuesday. If you are tired of waiting for the Lord to come, remember why he waits: there is grain still ripening, perhaps in your own family. Use the time, and pray the Lord of the harvest to send out labourers. And if you are anxious about the end, look at who holds the sickle: the Son of Man who loved you and gave himself for you.

verseByVerse.quote: Then another angel came out of the temple in heaven, and he too had a sharp sickle. And another angel came out from the altar, the angel who has authority over the fire, and he called with a loud voice to the one who had the sharp sickle, "Put in your sickle and gather the clusters from the vine of the earth, for its grapes are ripe." So the angel swung his sickle across the earth and gathered the grape harvest of the earth and threw it into the great winepress of the wrath of God. And the winepress was trodden outside the city, and blood flowed from the winepress, as high as a horse's bridle, for 1,600 stadia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Grapes were trodden in a winepress, a stone vat in which people trampled the grapes, and the juice ran down a channel into a lower vat. The red juice looked like blood. Isaiah 63:1–6 shows the LORD coming from Edom with garments stained crimson, saying, I have trodden the winepress alone; I trod them in my anger, and their lifeblood spattered on my garments. Joel 3:13 says, tread, for the winepress is full. Executions were carried out outside the city (Leviticus 24:14; Hebrews 13:12). A stadion was about 185 metres (607 feet), so 1,600 stadia is about 300 kilometres (184 miles), roughly the length of the land of Israel from north to south.

Another sickle. This time an angel holds the sickle, carrying out the judgement. The second harvest begins, and the order to begin it comes from an unexpected address.

From the altar. That altar is where the prayers of all the saints were offered with incense (8:3–4). It is where the fire came from that was thrown down on the earth (8:5). And beneath it are the souls of the martyrs who cried, How long? (6:9–10). So the command to begin the vintage of God’s wrath is issued by the angel in charge of the fire at the altar where the church’s prayers have been going up for the whole book. The martyrs asked; this is the answer arriving, and it comes out of the place where the asking was received.

The vine of the earth. In contrast with Christ, the true vine (John 15:1), and Israel, God’s vine, which yielded wild grapes (Isaiah 5:1–7). The earth’s vine is humanity in rebellion, ripe in its sin.

The winepress of God’s wrath. The judgement is described in terms of the crushing of grapes. John is quoting Isaiah and Joel at once. And Christ himself treads the winepress in 19:15.

Outside the city. “The city” is probably God’s city, the holy city where his people are (20:9). Judgement falls outside, where his enemies are. And this is the detail that ought to stop a Christian reader. Outside the city is where the sin offering was burned under the law, and it is where Jesus died: so Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood (Hebrews 13:12).

Two treadings outside the city. Say that plainly, because it is the mercy hidden inside one of the most violent verses in the book. There are two treadings of that press outside that city. At the first, one man went in alone and the blood was his own. Everyone at the second will have refused the first.

As high as a horse’s bridle. Horrific, deliberately exaggerated imagery. The measurements are symbolic and the arithmetic is not hidden. 1,600 is four times four times a hundred (or forty times forty): four, the number of the earth with its four corners and four winds, squared and multiplied. A judgement covering the whole earth, completely. Jewish writings used similar language: 1 Enoch 100:3 says the horse will walk up to its chest in the blood of sinners. Blood as high as a horse’s bridle across the length of a country is not a forecast of casualties. It is a statement of scale, and of horror, in the only register that can carry it.

What it does not mean. This is not a literal river of blood to be measured. Nor does it portray God as cruel. It is the just answer to the blood of the martyrs (6:10; 16:6; 19:2), and it falls only on those who refused his eternal gospel (v. 6).

Two harvests, one day. The chapter ends there, without comment. Revelation does not make judgement palatable and it does not apologise for it. The same chapter contains one of the gentlest sentences in the book, blessed are the dead who die in the Lord, and one of the most terrible. The grain harvest and the grape harvest are two sides of the one final coming: the harvest is the end of the age, and the reapers are angels (Matthew 13:39).

Should I be glad about the judgement of the wicked? Glad that God will put every wrong right, yes; the martyrs pray for it, and heaven rejoices at the justice of God (19:1–2). It would be a strange love that did not long for evil to end and the oppressed to be vindicated. But never glad in a cold or gloating way, and never as though you deserved to be on the other side of the city wall. God himself takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but rather that they turn and live (Ezekiel 33:11). Hold together justice and tears, as Jesus did when he wept over Jerusalem. And let it drive you to pray and to speak while the gospel is still flying overhead.

On a Tuesday. When you hear of great evil and wonder whether anyone will ever answer for it, remember this winepress: no injustice will be overlooked. And when you are tempted to think your own sin small, remember the first treading, where the blood was his.

For worship. Holy is the Judge who forgets no drop of his people’s blood, and answers from the altar the prayers that rose from it. The vine of the earth is ripe, and its end will be just. But there is another vine, and the Father is its vinedresser. Its branches are pruned, never trodden; they are cut only to bear more fruit, and their fruit remains (John 15:1–2, 16). Every one of them once belonged to the vine of the earth, and was joined to the true Vine by grace, and lives by his life.
verseByVerse.note: The 1,600 stadia (v. 20) are about 184 miles; a stadion was about 607 feet — roughly the length of the land of Israel.

14.text: <sup>1</sup>Then I looked, and behold, on Mount Zion stood the Lamb, and with him 144,000 who had his name and his Father’s name written on their foreheads.<sup>2</sup>And I heard a voice from heaven like the roar of many waters and like the sound of loud thunder. The voice I heard was like the sound of harpists playing on their harps,<sup>3</sup>and they were singing a new song before the throne and before the four living creatures and before the elders. No one could learn that song except the 144,000 who had been redeemed from the earth.<sup>4</sup>It is these who have not defiled themselves with women, for they are virgins. It is these who follow the Lamb wherever he goes. These have been redeemed from mankind as firstfruits for God and the Lamb,<sup>5</sup>and in their mouth no lie was found, for they are blameless.<sup>6</sup>Then I saw another angel flying directly overhead, with an eternal gospel to proclaim to those who dwell on earth, to every nation and tribe and language and people.<sup>7</sup>And he said with a loud voice, “Fear God and give him glory, because the hour of his judgment has come, and worship him who made heaven and earth, the sea and the springs of water.”<sup>8</sup>Another angel, a second, followed, saying, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, she who made all nations drink the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality.”<sup>9</sup>And another angel, a third, followed them, saying with a loud voice, “If anyone worships the beast and its image and receives a mark on his forehead or on his hand,<sup>10</sup>he also will drink the wine of God’s wrath, poured full strength into the cup of his anger, and he will be tormented with fire and sulfur in the presence of the holy angels and in the presence of the Lamb.<sup>11</sup>And the smoke of their torment goes up forever and ever, and they have no rest, day or night, these worshipers of the beast and its image, and whoever receives the mark of its name.”<sup>12</sup>Here is a call for the endurance of the saints, those who keep the commandments of God and their faith in Jesus.<sup>13</sup>And I heard a voice from heaven saying, “Write this: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on.” “Blessed indeed,” says the Spirit, “that they may rest from their labors, for their deeds follow them!”<sup>14</sup>Then I looked, and behold, a white cloud, and seated on the cloud one like a son of man, with a golden crown on his head, and a sharp sickle in his hand.<sup>15</sup>And another angel came out of the temple, calling with a loud voice to him who sat on the cloud, “Put in your sickle, and reap, for the hour to reap has come, for the harvest of the earth is fully ripe.”<sup>16</sup>So he who sat on the cloud swung his sickle across the earth, and the earth was reaped.<sup>17</sup>Then another angel came out of the temple in heaven, and he too had a sharp sickle.<sup>18</sup>And another angel came out from the altar, the angel who has authority over the fire, and he called with a loud voice to the one who had the sharp sickle, “Put in your sickle and gather the clusters from the vine of the earth, for its grapes are ripe.”<sup>19</sup>So the angel swung his sickle across the earth and gathered the grape harvest of the earth and threw it into the great winepress of the wrath of God.<sup>20</sup>And the winepress was trodden outside the city, and blood flowed from the winepress, as high as a horse’s bridle, for 1,600 stadia.

21.title: All Things New: The New Heaven, New Earth, and New Jerusalem
21.overview:
Chapter 21 is where the whole of Revelation has been heading. The sealed scroll, the trumpets, the suffering saints and the martyrs’ cry of ‘How long?’ all move toward the voice from the throne that announces a new creation. It is not a consolation prize for a plan that nearly failed; it is the goal for which the whole story was told.

The chapter has two movements. Verses 1–8 show the new heaven and new earth from a distance: the city coming down, God living with his people, the end of tears and death, and who will inherit and who will not. Verses 9–27 come close: an angel shows John the new Jerusalem in detail, its gates and foundations, its size, its materials and its light.

The key is what the city is. It is a people before it is a place: the bride of the Lamb, the people of God made perfect and living in his presence, with God and the Lamb at the centre.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The New Heaven and the New Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1–8 give the new creation in a few strokes. Verses 1–2: this world renewed rather than replaced, and the holy city coming down from God as a bride. Verses 3–4: God living with his people, and the end of death and tears. Verses 5–6: God himself speaks, and gives the water of life free to the thirsty. Verses 7–8: the last promise to the one who conquers, and the warning of the second death.
verseByVerse.theology:
All Things New

A new heaven and earth, renewed rather than replaced, and the holy city coming down as a bride. God dwells with his people and wipes away every tear; death, mourning, crying and pain are gone. He gives the water of life freely to the thirsty.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: John, cut off by the sea from his churches, hears that the sea will be no more.

Now: God answers grief not by explanation but by removal, with his own hand on the face.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea was no more. And I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Revelation 21 shows the goal of all history: God living with his people for ever in a new creation. John sees a new heaven and a new earth, with no more sea, and the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God like a bride (vv. 1–2). God’s dwelling is now with humanity: he wipes away every tear and ends death, mourning, crying and pain (vv. 3–4). He says, I am making all things new, and gives the water of life freely to the thirsty; the one who conquers will be his son, but the cowardly, faithless and wicked will have their part in the lake of fire (vv. 5–8). An angel then shows John the bride, which is the city: its gates bear the names of Israel’s twelve tribes and its foundations the names of the twelve apostles (vv. 9–14); it is a perfect cube, twelve thousand stadia each way (vv. 15–17), of jasper and pure gold, with jewelled foundations and gates of pearl (vv. 18–21). It has no temple, for God and the Lamb are its temple, and no sun, for the Lamb is its lamp; its gates never shut, and nothing unclean enters, only those written in the Lamb’s book of life (vv. 22–27). Babylon has fallen and the bride has come, and at the centre of it all is not a place but a Person: God himself with his people, and the Lamb as the lamp of the city.

The setting. Isaiah 65:17–25 and 66:22 promise new heavens and a new earth, where the former things shall not be remembered, and there will be no more weeping. Isaiah 54:11–12 promises a city built with sapphires, rubies and jewels. Ezekiel 40–48 describes a restored city and temple, ending with the name of the city: The LORD is there (Ezekiel 48:35). Abraham looked forward to the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God (Hebrews 11:10). Peter says we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells (2 Peter 3:13).

A new heaven and a new earth. The whole Bible has been travelling toward this sentence. It opened with In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth (Genesis 1:1), and it now says it again with one word changed. “New” (kainon) usually stresses newness of quality rather than mere recency: new in kind, fresh, renewed. John uses the same word here, in verse 5, and of the new Jerusalem, the new name and the new song. So God is not scrapping his creation but renewing it, not putting a different world in place of this one, but making this world new.

The pattern of the resurrection body. The risen body of Jesus is the pattern. It was the same body that was laid in the tomb, transformed and glorified, with the wounds still in the hands. So a Christian’s hope is not that he will escape the material world into something vague and vaporous. It is that this world, soil, water, weather, bodies, work, cities, will be put right. God does not abandon what he made. He never has.

Passed away. “Passed away” (apēlthan, gone away). The first creation, under the curse of sin, has gone (20:11). What passes away is the first form of things, the fallen form, not the handiwork of God itself.

No more sea. This troubles people who love the sea, but John is not making a statement about oceanography. In this book the sea has a settled meaning. It is the ancient image of chaos, which is why the throne room has it lying flat as glass under God’s feet (4:6); it is where the beast comes up from (13:1); it is what swallowed the dead who had no graves (20:13). And there is a personal edge to it that John’s first readers would have felt at once. He is writing from an island, and the sea was very likely the thing keeping him from his churches. The promise is not that there will be no water; the next chapter has a river. It is that there will be nothing left that separates, threatens or devours: no more chaos, danger, evil or separation.

Coming down. “New Jerusalem”: the fulfilment of all God’s promises to Zion. “Coming down” (katabainousan): it is God’s gift, not human achievement. Watch the direction, because almost every popular picture of the Christian hope gets it backwards. The city comes down. In this vision nobody is going up. Believers will rise to meet the Lord at his coming (1 Thessalonians 4:17), but to welcome him on his way down, not to leave the earth behind. Babel tried to build up to heaven (Genesis 11:4); the new Jerusalem comes down from heaven. The last movement in the Bible is not humanity being evacuated to the sky; it is heaven arriving on a renewed earth, which is what Christians have always prayed for without noticing: your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven (Matthew 6:10).

A bride adorned. “Prepared” (hētoimasmenēn). “Adorned” (kekosmēmenēn, beautifully dressed; our word cosmetics comes from it). The city is not a bride’s residence: the city and the bride are the same thing, as verse 9 makes plain when an angel offers to show John the Bride and then shows him a city. The new Jerusalem is not only a place; it is a people, God’s people in their perfected community, in contrast to Babylon the prostitute. Two women, two cities, and the book has been asking since chapter 17 which one a reader has been dressing for.

The husband is the Lamb. A bride is adorned for someone, and verse 9 names him: the Bride, the wife of the Lamb. The city is beautiful because of what her husband has done for her, not because of what she did for herself. Even the fine linen she wears was granted to her (19:8). So the last picture of the people of God in Scripture is not a people who finally made themselves worthy. It is a people whom a crucified and risen Husband has washed and dressed for himself.

Where Christians differ: will this earth be destroyed and replaced, or renewed? Some Christians, reading 2 Peter 3:10, where the KJV says the earth and the works on it will be burned up, believe the present creation will be annihilated and replaced with something entirely new. The earliest manuscripts there read that the earth will be exposed, or laid bare, and most modern Bibles follow them. Others think of eternity as a purely spiritual existence in heaven. Faithful Christians have held each of these views, and all of them expect the same Lord. This commentary’s view: Scripture teaches that this creation will be renewed and transformed, not discarded. Paul says creation will be set free from bondage (Romans 8:21); Jesus speaks of the renewal of all things (Matthew 19:28); Peter speaks of the restoration of all things (Acts 3:21). The fire of 2 Peter 3 purifies, as metal is refined, and the earth is laid bare to judgement. Just as our bodies will be raised and transformed, not replaced, so creation will be raised and transformed. The final hope of believers is not disembodied existence but resurrection life on a new earth, with God.

Is heaven now the same as the new earth? Not yet. When a believer dies, he goes to be with Christ in heaven, conscious and at rest (Philippians 1:23), and that is far better than this life. But it is not the end of the story. The end is the resurrection of the body at Christ’s return and life with God on the new earth. So there are two stages of the Christian hope: with Christ in heaven at death, and with Christ in the new creation, bodily, for ever. When Christians speak of going to heaven, they are speaking truly of the first. This chapter is about the second, and it is better still.

Will we be ourselves, and will we know each other? Yes. Resurrection means the same person raised, not a stranger. The disciples recognised the risen Jesus, and Moses and Elijah were known on the mountain (Matthew 17:3). Paul says we shall know fully, even as we have been fully known (1 Corinthians 13:12). Jesus does say that in the resurrection people neither marry nor are given in marriage (Matthew 22:30), probably because the marriage every human marriage pointed to, Christ and his bride, has arrived. But nothing good in the love between husband and wife, parents and children, friends in Christ, will be lost. It will be taken up into something larger, not cancelled.

On a Tuesday. Your future is not an endless cloud but a renewed earth. The garden you tend, the work you do well, the body you look after, the city you seek the good of: these are not meaningless because this world is passing. They are the first form of things God intends to make new. And if you are weary of a broken world, a broken body, a broken family, look up. What is coming is not an escape from all that God made, but all that God made, mended.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying, "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. The heart of God’s covenant promise throughout Scripture is: I will be your God, and you shall be my people, and I will dwell among you (Leviticus 26:11–12; Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 37:27). Isaiah 35:10 and 65:19 promise that sorrow and sighing shall flee away, and no more shall be heard the sound of weeping.

The dwelling place of God. “Dwelling place” (hē skēnē, tent, tabernacle). God’s tabernacle, his presence, is now permanently with humanity. What Eden had, and sin lost, is restored and surpassed.

He will dwell with them. The verb is the tent word again, as in 7:15: God will pitch his tent with them. Follow that one word through the Bible and the whole story is on a single thread. God walked with the man and the woman in a garden in the cool of the day, and they were sent out. He told Moses, let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst (Exodus 25:8), and a tent was pitched in the middle of the camp. Solomon built a house and the glory filled it, and Ezekiel watched that glory leave. Then the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, pitched his tent among us, and John, who is writing this, is the man who wrote that sentence (John 1:14). Then the Spirit came and made a temple out of ordinary people (1 Corinthians 3:16). And here is the end of it: no tent in a camp, no house on a hill, no veil, no exclusions. God with man, permanently, in the open.

His people. “People” (laoi, plural, peoples, in many of the earliest manuscripts; others have the singular, which most English Bibles follow). The many nations of the redeemed, now one people of God. The promise once made to Israel now includes all nations. And the covenant formula that runs through the whole Old Testament arrives complete. It was said to Abraham, to Israel at Sinai, through Jeremiah and Ezekiel, always as a promise. Here it is reported as a fact.

God himself. “God himself” (autos ho theos). Not an angel, not a representative, not glory at a safe distance, not merely his gifts, but God himself: Immanuel, God with us, in full. The thing the whole Bible has been arranging is not improved circumstances for human beings. It is his presence.

Every tear. The promise is made twice in this book (7:17), and both times it says that God does it himself, with his hand, on a face. Not an angel with a cloth. Not time healing it. Isaiah promised it first: he will swallow up death forever; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces (Isaiah 25:8).

No more death. Four abolitions follow, each to be taken on its own. Death first: the thing that has taken everyone a reader has ever loved, and will take him. Gone, and 20:14 has already shown how: thrown into the lake of fire. The last enemy destroyed (1 Corinthians 15:26).

Mourning, crying, pain. Mourning (penthos) is grief itself, the heaviness that settles on a house after a death. Crying (kraugē) is the outcry that grief makes, at a graveside or alone in a car. Pain covers both the body’s pain and the labour that wears a person out, which takes the reader back to the curse in Genesis 3 and undoes it. And every one of them is answered by removal, not by explanation. Nobody in this verse is told why it happened. The promise is not that the tears will finally make sense. It is that they will be wiped off a face by God, and that the thing that caused them will be dead.

The former things. “The former things” (ta prōta, the first things). This is the verse to hold when the reason for a grief has never arrived and probably never will. God does not, in the end, argue with a bereaved person. He comes over and attends to the face.

Will we remember those we loved who are lost? Scripture does not explain how, and we should not claim to know more than it says. But it does say that we will be ourselves, known and knowing (1 Corinthians 13:12), and that God himself will wipe away every tear. We will see as God sees, and share his perfect justice and his perfect love. Whatever we remember, nothing will spoil the joy he gives. And that is a reason now to pray and to speak to those we love while there is time.

Is it wrong to grieve now, if this is coming? No. Jesus wept at the grave of Lazarus, shortly before he raised him (John 11:35), so tears and hope can stand side by side in the same heart. Paul does not tell the Thessalonians not to grieve, but not to grieve as others do who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Grief is love that has lost its object for a while; this verse does not shame it, it promises it an end. So weep honestly, at the graveside and in the car. Then bring the tears to the God who has promised to wipe them away himself, and let him be the one who comforts you.

On a Tuesday. These are verses for funerals and hospital corridors, worth having by heart before the phone rings. When you sit with someone who is mourning, you do not need to explain their loss; simply be present, as God will be present, and if the moment is right, read them these two verses. And when your own pain comes, chronic illness, an empty chair at the table, the child who will not speak to you, say to yourself: this is one of the former things, and the former things are passing away.

verseByVerse.quote: And he who was seated on the throne said, "Behold, I am making all things new." Also he said, "Write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true." And he said to me, "It is done! I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end. To the thirsty I will give from the spring of the water of life without payment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. This is one of the very few places in Revelation where the One on the throne is plainly the speaker; the last was 1:8. Isaiah 43:19 says, behold, I am doing a new thing. Isaiah 55:1 calls: come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and he who has no money, come, buy and eat; buy wine and milk without money and without price.

Making all things new. At 1:8 God said who he is; here he says what he does, and the two sentences bracket the dragon, the beast, the bowls and the burning city. “I am making” (poiō) is present tense: it is happening, not merely scheduled. All things, with nothing excepted. And the object is not what most people assume. He does not say I am making all new things. He says I am making all things new: renewal, not replacement. The same things, this world, these people, the bodies in the ground, are being made new. God’s work of renewal has already begun in Christ, in whom anyone is a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17), and it will be completed.

Trustworthy and true. “Trustworthy” (pistoi, faithful) and “true” (alēthinoi): the new creation is certain. This is the third and last time John is told to write a particular sentence. At 14:13: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord. At 19:9: Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb. And here: I am making all things new. Every one of the three is a promise a suffering church would find nearly impossible to believe, and every one of them is given its own command to record it and its own guarantee of truthfulness.

It is done. “It is done” (gegonan, they have happened), the same verb as at the seventh bowl (16:17), where it stood in the singular. The whole plan of God is complete. And it echoes, in thought though not in the same Greek word, the cry from the cross, It is finished (John 19:30). The finished work on the cross made the final victory certain, and the same voice now says it over a finished world.

Alpha and Omega. The title from 1:8, and it has waited twenty chapters to be used again. God began everything and brings everything to its goal. He was the first letter when there was nothing yet to write, and he is the last one now that everything has been written. Nothing in history has slipped out from between those two letters.

Without payment. And here, at the summit of the book, after the great white throne and the lake of fire, comes an offer. Not a reward, not a wage: a drink, given away. “Water of life”: eternal life, God himself. “Without payment” (dōrean): as a gift, freely, for nothing, the same word Paul uses of being justified by his grace as a gift (Romans 3:24). And note the only qualification named: the thirsty. Not the deserving, not the improved, not the people who worked it out. The single requirement for the water of life is wanting it, knowing that you need it, and the book will make the same offer one last time in its final chapter with the doors held open (22:17).

The spring has a face. The One on the throne makes the offer, and the Gospel John wrote shows who carries it out. At a well in Samaria a tired man asked a woman for a drink and then offered her living water, so that whoever drinks it will never be thirsty again (John 4:10–14). At the feast he stood and cried out, if anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink (John 7:37). In this book it is the Lamb who guides his people to springs of living water (7:17), and in the next chapter the river flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb (22:1). The water of life is not a substance handed over a counter. It is life with God, and it comes to us through his Son.

What if I do not feel thirsty? Then ask God to make you thirsty, and notice that you are already asking. Thirst is not a strong religious feeling; it is need, and need is there whether you feel it or not. The restless dissatisfaction that no achievement fills, the guilt you cannot shake off, the fear of death, the longing for something you cannot name: these are thirst. Many come to Christ not burning with desire but simply tired of drinking from wells that do not satisfy (Jeremiah 2:13). Come as you are. The offer is to the thirsty, and the Spirit who makes people thirsty is the same Spirit who brings them to the spring.

On a Tuesday. Notice where you go when you are dry: the screen, the shopping, the drink, the approval of others. Each of them is a well that runs out. Bring that thirst to Christ in prayer instead, and drink from his word before you drink from anything else. And when someone tells you their life is empty, do not lecture them. Tell them where the spring is, and that it costs nothing.

For worship. The One who sits on the throne, who spoke the first word of creation and will speak the last, uses his voice at the end of all things to say, I am making all things new. He is the Alpha, before the first star, and the Omega, after the last tear. And this God, who owes no one anything, ends history by giving a drink away. It is free to us because it was not free to him: the Son who offers it hung on a cross and said, I thirst (John 19:28), and went without, so that all who come to him might drink and live.

verseByVerse.quote: The one who conquers will have this heritage, and I will be his God and he will be my son. But as for the cowardly, the faithless, the detestable, as for murderers, the sexually immoral, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars, their portion will be in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur, which is the second death."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. The seven letters each ended with a promise to the one who conquers (chapters 2–3); here is the sum of them all. Paul takes God’s promise about David’s son, I will be to him a father, and applies it to all believers: I will be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me (2 Corinthians 6:18).

This heritage. “Heritage” (klēronomēsei, will inherit). The last of the promises to the conqueror, and the reader should hear the whole series close. Seven times in chapters 2 and 3 something was promised to the one who conquers: the tree of life, escape from the second death, hidden manna and a white stone, authority over the nations and the morning star, white garments and a name confessed before the Father, a pillar in the temple, a seat on the throne. Here is the final one, and it is not a thing at all. The meek shall inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5). Believers are heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17).

My son. “Son” (huios): an heir, with full rights. That sentence was said in the Old Testament about one man’s heir: God said it to David about the son who would sit on his throne. It is the promise that made the royal line, and it was fulfilled in Christ. And here it is handed, without qualification, to anyone who conquers, which chapter 12 defined as anyone who holds on to Christ at cost: they conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony (12:11). Through Christ, the Son, believers become sons and daughters of God by adoption (Galatians 4:4–7). In adoption God brings into his family those who by nature were children of wrath, as Paul says (Ephesians 2:3), and makes them his own: his name, his love, his house and his inheritance, with no probation and no second-class rank. It is not a feeling but an act of God, the right to become his children given to all who receive Christ (John 1:12), and he does not undo it. Which means the final reward of this book is not real estate. It is adoption. Everything else on the list, the tree, the crown, the stone, the throne, turns out to have been describing what belongs to a son in his father’s house.

The cowardly. “Cowardly” (deilois, timid, fearful). Eight kinds of people, and the first will stop any honest reader: the cowardly, listed ahead of the murderers and the idolaters, in a book written to people who had every reason to be frightened. Heading the list are those who, out of fear, deny Christ under persecution.

Fear and cowardice. That has to be handled carefully, because it will land on the wrong person if it is not. The word does not mean a Christian who is afraid. If fear disqualified, the list would include Elijah under a broom tree, Peter in a courtyard, and every one of the apostles on the night of the arrest. Christ said, fear not, to John in the first chapter of this book precisely because John was on his face and terrified (1:17). What the word names, in this setting, is the person whose fear made the decision: who denied the name, took the mark, said the words about Caesar and went home safe, and never came back. Cowardice here is not an emotion; it is apostasy carried out for the sake of safety. So a believer who reads verse 8, trembles, and runs to Christ is, by that very reaction, showing that it is not describing him. And Peter, who denied Christ three times with oaths, was given breakfast on a beach and a commission (John 21).

The faithless and the detestable. “Faithless” (apistois, unbelieving, unfaithful): those who refuse to trust and obey Christ. “Detestable” (ebdelygmenois, polluted with abominations): those who share Babylon’s abominations (17:4).

All liars. The sins of Babylon and the beast’s worshippers (9:21; 22:15). “All liars”: those who belong to the father of lies (John 8:44) and the false prophet. And the last item on the list closes a loop that has run through the whole book. The dragon is the deceiver of the whole world; the second beast deceives by signs; Babylon deceived the nations by her sorcery. And of the redeemed on Mount Zion John wrote, in their mouth no lie was found (14:5). Two companies, and one of the things that finally separates them is whether they belong to the truth.

Their portion. “Portion” (meros, share, part), as in 20:14–15. The heritage of the conqueror and the portion of the faithless stand side by side in two verses: an inheritance in the Father’s house, or a share in the lake. There is no third place.

What it does not mean. This list does not mean that anyone who has ever committed these sins is beyond salvation. Paul lists similar sins and then says, and such were some of you, but you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 6:9–11). The list describes those who persist in these sins without repentance, refusing the free water of life (v. 6). Even a murderer or an idolater who comes thirsty to Christ will be given the water of life.

Does all liars mean that any lie damns, so that a Christian who has lied is lost? No. The list describes the settled character of those who belong to the lie and reject the truth (22:15), not believers who have sinned and repented. Every believer has lied; the blood of Jesus cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7). The warning is for those who make falsehood their way of life, and a call to everyone to come to Christ.

How can the God who wipes away every tear also have a lake of fire? Because the God who wipes away tears takes seriously what caused them. A judge who shrugged at murder, cruelty and lies would not be kind; he would be indifferent to their victims, and the tears of verse 4 would never truly be dried. Hell is not God losing his temper. It is a holy God giving sinners, at the last, the just reward of their sin and what they have insisted on all along: life without him (2 Thessalonians 1:9). And look at the order of the chapter. The offer of free water (v. 6) comes before the warning (v. 8). No one in the lake is there because the spring was closed to him.

Do I have to be a hero to be one who conquers? No. In Revelation conquering is not winning a battle by strength but holding on to Christ when it costs you, and the Lamb is the model: he conquered by being slain (5:5–6). The one who conquers is the ordinary believer who keeps trusting Christ through illness, mockery, temptation and loss, who falls and gets up, and who does not give Christ up. It is the persevering faith that God himself works in his people and keeps alive to the end (Philippians 1:6; 1 Peter 1:5). If you are still clinging to him today, however weakly, you are among the conquerors, and the inheritance is yours.

On a Tuesday. Be watchful over the two sins on this list that sound smallest: cowardice and lying. Where are you tempted this week to keep quiet about Christ to stay safe, or to shade the truth to look better? Say the true thing, kindly. You have not received a spirit of fear but the Spirit of adoption (Romans 8:15), and he makes timid children bold to own the Christ who first owned them.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 9–27 show the bride as a city, set deliberately against the prostitute Babylon of chapter 17. Verses 9–14: the city’s glory, its gates named for Israel’s tribes and its foundations for the Lamb’s apostles. Verses 15–21: its measurements, a perfect cube like the Most Holy Place, and its jasper, gold and pearl. Verses 22–27: no temple, no sun and no night, because God and the Lamb are there, and no one enters but those written in the Lamb’s book of life.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Bride, the City

The Bride is shown as a city coming down from God, bearing the names of the twelve tribes and the twelve apostles. It is a cube, the Most Holy Place enlarged, with no temple, for its temple is God and the Lamb; no sun, for the Lamb is its lamp; gates that never shut; and only those written in the Lamb’s book inside.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: What the high priest carried over his heart once a year is now the city’s foundation, and every gate is a pearl.

Now: Nobody will be nearer to God than anybody else, and there will be no night.

verseByVerse.quote: Then came one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls full of the seven last plagues and spoke to me, saying, "Come, I will show you the Bride, the wife of the Lamb." And he carried me away in the Spirit to a great, high mountain, and showed me the holy city Jerusalem coming down out of heaven from God, having the glory of God, its radiance like a most rare jewel, like a jasper, clear as crystal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the flow. Verses 1–8 announced the new creation in a few strokes; from here to 22:5 John is shown the city in detail. The section is built as the twin of 17:1–19:10: the same kind of angel, the same invitation, the same journey in the Spirit, but a bride instead of a prostitute. So the book’s long contrast between two cities reaches its last turn, and only one city is left standing. Everything that follows, the wall, the gates, the cube and the river, describes the bride announced in verse 2.

One of the seven angels. John describes the angel at length because he wants the reader to make a connection. At 17:1 it was one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls who said, Come, I will show you the judgement of the great prostitute. The same rank, the same opening word, and a different woman. Those who carried out judgement now reveal glory. The hands that poured out the bowls of wrath are the hands that draw back the curtain on the bride.

The Bride, the wife of the Lamb. “Bride” (nymphē) and “wife” (gynaika). The marriage of 19:7 has happened. The church is now the Lamb’s wife. Every wedding in the Bible, from Adam waking to find Eve, to the wedding at Cana where the wine ran out, has been a rehearsal for this.

A great, high mountain. The fourth “in the Spirit” of the book (1:10; 4:2; 17:3). And the locations answer each other. To see the prostitute, John was carried into a wilderness (17:3). To see the Bride, he is carried to a great, high mountain, the place of revelation and of God’s dwelling, which is where Ezekiel was taken to be shown a city (Ezekiel 40:2). One woman is seen in a desert; the other from a height. Many readers also hear a contrast with another mountain: the devil once took Jesus up a very high mountain to show him the kingdoms of the world and their glory. Jesus refused that glory, went to the cross instead, and here is what the Father gives him.

The holy city. He promised a Bride and produced a city, and John does not treat that as a change of subject. The people are the place, as the New Testament says everywhere: the church is a building, a temple, a body, a household, a bride. And for the second time in nine verses the city comes down. Every proud human city since Babel has tried to build itself up and make a name for itself; this one is lowered into place, finished, by Someone else.

Having the glory of God. “Glory” (doxan). The first thing said about the city is not its size or its gates. It is that it has the glory of God: the weight of God’s presence, the glory later Jewish teachers called the shekinah, God’s dwelling presence, which filled the tabernacle so that Moses could not enter, and the temple so that the priests could not stand to minister (Exodus 40:34–35; 1 Kings 8:11; Ezekiel 43:2–5). God’s presence makes the city what it is. The thing that had to be curtained off is now the city’s ordinary lighting.

Like a jasper. “Radiance” (phōstēr, light, brilliance). “Jasper”: as in 4:3, where it describes the appearance of the one seated on the throne. The city looks like him. “Clear as crystal”: pure, transparent, nothing hidden. A bride wearing her husband’s likeness is not a bad definition of what the church is finally for, and it is what Paul meant by being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another (2 Corinthians 3:18).

How can the church I know be this bride? The church you know is quarrelsome, slow, sometimes hypocritical, and you are part of the problem. Christ knows that better than you do, and he loves her anyway. He gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her, and present her to himself in splendour, without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:25–27). The bride is not beautiful because she made herself so; she shines with the glory of God. What you see now is the bride on the way to the wedding, dusty from the road. Do not despise what Christ is making beautiful. Stay in her, serve her, and pray for her.

On a Tuesday. Christ gave himself up for the church, you included, and loves her as she is. Before you criticise your congregation this week, pray for it person by person: the elders, the struggling family, the difficult member. Then do one quiet thing to serve it.

verseByVerse.quote: It had a great, high wall, with twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and on the gates the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel were inscribed— on the east three gates, on the north three gates, on the south three gates, and on the west three gates. And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and on them were the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It had a great, high wall. Start with the wall, named first and the strangest thing here. A wall in the ancient world had one purpose: to keep an army out. This city has no army to fear; the last enemy was thrown into the lake of fire a chapter ago (20:10, 14), and its gates are never shut anyway (v. 25). The wall is not there out of fear. It says that this place has an inside, and verse 27 states the boundary plainly: nothing unclean will ever enter it.

A good thing that cannot be spoiled. Measure that against everything you have ever loved. Every good thing you have known could be got at: the marriage, the friendship, the church, the health, the work of a lifetime. Something always found a way in and spoiled it, and usually from the inside. Here at last is a good thing with a boundary that holds. The wall is not the anxiety of a city under siege. It is the settled fact of a city that will never be spoiled again.

Twelve angels. “Gates” (pylōnas). The first time heavenly guards are posted anywhere in the Bible, they are cherubim outside a garden with a flaming sword, and their work is to keep people out (Genesis 3:24). Here twelve of them stand at twelve gates that never close (v. 25). Nothing about the posting has changed except what it is for. The sentries are still at their stations, and there is nothing left for them to do but watch the nations walk in.

The names of the twelve tribes. Old Testament Israel is part of the city, and God’s promises to Israel are fulfilled. Twelve gates, three on each side, is the layout of the camp of Israel in the wilderness, where three tribes camped on each side of the tabernacle (Numbers 2), and it is the plan of Ezekiel’s city, which ends with twelve gates named for the twelve tribes (Ezekiel 48:30–35). Every believer who enters the city enters through a gate with an Israelite name over it, because salvation is from the Jews (John 4:22).

From every side. People will come from east and west, and from north and south, and recline at table in the kingdom of God (Luke 13:29). A city with gates on one side has a preferred approach and a back door. This one can be entered from anywhere: from the east where the exiles went, from the north where the invasions came, from the south where Egypt was, from the west where Rome was. Nobody arrives at the wrong side.

Twelve foundations. Twelve tribes on the gates and twelve apostles in the foundations: Israel and the church, built into one structure, and neither of them is an extension bolted on to the other. Together they form one city, the one people of God across both covenants. It is also one reason many readers take the twenty-four elders (4:4) as Israel and the church together, twelve and twelve. Paul said the same thing without the architecture: the household of God, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:19–20).

Names in the foundations. There is something quietly astonishing about names in foundations. Twelve men are named in the stonework of the eternal city, and every reader knows what those twelve were like: fishermen, a tax collector, a zealot, a man who denied Christ with oaths, and a man who would not believe the resurrection without putting his hand in the wound. Their names are cut into the foundations of the new creation. Set that beside the city they are being contrasted with. Babylon’s great ones were her merchants (18:23).
