This city’s great ones are twelve provincial nobodies, who suffered for saying that a crucified man had come back, and many of whom, as the early church remembered, died for it. Grace builds with unlikely stones.

Apostles of the Lamb. John does not simply say the twelve apostles; he says the twelve apostles of the Lamb, and those words carry the weight. These men are in the foundations for one reason: they were with him, they saw him die and rise, and they told what they had seen (Acts 1:21–22; 1 John 1:1–3). Their names are cut into the stone because their witness to him is what the city stands on. And the gates bear Israel’s names because all the promises made to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob find their yes in him (2 Corinthians 1:20). He is the son of Abraham and the son of David, Israel’s Messiah, and every Gentile who walks in comes as a guest of Israel’s King. Tribes on the gates, apostles below, and the Lamb holding the whole city together.

What it does not mean. Israel’s names on the gates and the apostles’ names on the foundations do not mean there are two peoples of God, one Jewish and one Christian, with different destinies. There is one city, one bride, one people, built on Christ.

Then does God still have a purpose for the Jewish people? Christians differ on the details, and the question deserves care. Many Reformed readers, from the Puritans onward, have understood Romans 11:25–29 to promise a future turning of many Jews to Christ before the end, because the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable; others read all Israel there as the whole elect people of God, Jew and Gentile. Both agree with this chapter: whatever God does for Israel, he does through faith in Jesus the Messiah, and into the one city. So pray for Jewish people to know their Messiah, honour the people through whom the Scriptures and the Saviour came, and reject every form of contempt for them.

On a Tuesday. You belong to a city built on the apostles’ witness. Their teaching, written in the New Testament, is the ground on which the church stands, and nothing newer replaces it. So read the apostles this week as men who were there, and build on what they saw.

verseByVerse.quote: And the one who spoke with me had a measuring rod of gold to measure the city and its gates and walls. The city lies foursquare, its length the same as its width. And he measured the city with his rod, 12,000 stadia. Its length and width and height are equal. He also measured its wall, 144 cubits by human measurement, which is also an angel's measurement.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Ezekiel saw an angel measuring the new temple and city (Ezekiel 40–48). A stadion was about 185 metres (607 feet), so 12,000 stadia is about 2,220 kilometres (1,380 miles), roughly the distance from London to Athens. A cubit was about 45 centimetres (18 inches), so 144 cubits is about 65 metres (216 feet).

A measuring rod of gold. Measuring, in this book, means claiming and protecting. John was given a rod at 11:1 and told to measure the temple, the altar and the worshippers, and expressly not the outer court, which was given over to be trampled. The measuring there was partial, and it was a mercy. This one is total: the city, its gates and its walls, all of it, with a rod of gold, fitting for a golden city. Measuring shows that the city is complete, secure and belongs to God.

Foursquare. “Foursquare” (tetragōnos, square): perfect, complete, with nothing lopsided, unfinished or left over. The size first: a city some 2,200 kilometres across, and that in every direction, including up. Nobody is meant to picture this. What the figure does is answer a fear few Christians like to admit: whether there will be room. 12,000 is 12 × 1,000, the people of God (twelve) in fullness (a thousand): room for the great multitude no one can count. Then the shape, the detail everything in the chapter has been building toward: the city is a perfect cube.

There is one cube in the Bible. In Solomon’s temple, the inner sanctuary, the Most Holy Place, was twenty cubits long, twenty wide and twenty high (1 Kings 6:20). It was the place where the ark stood behind the veil, which one man entered once a year with blood, having washed, and did not linger in. The new Jerusalem is that room, expanded to the size of a continent, with everybody living inside it. The whole city is the Most Holy Place: God’s presence fills it all, and all God’s people dwell where once only the high priest could go. That is the key to the city, and it explains verse 22 in advance: there is no temple in the city because the city is the temple, and there is no veil because there is nothing left to keep anyone out.

The forerunner behind the curtain. How can a whole people live in a room once closed to all but one man? Hebrews answers. Christ entered once for all into the holy places, not with the blood of goats and calves but with his own blood, and secured an eternal redemption (Hebrews 9:12). And he did not go in to come out again alone. He went behind the curtain as a forerunner on our behalf (Hebrews 6:19–20), the first of a great company. The cube is where that forerunner was always heading, with his people behind him. Every believer in the city stands where Christ has gone first, welcomed because he is welcomed.

144 cubits. 144 is 12 × 12, the number of God’s people, as in the 144,000 (7:4). The angel uses ordinary human units, not some heavenly currency that would come out differently, but their meaning is symbolic, and the proportions are deliberately impossible. A wall of about 65 metres (John does not say whether that is its height or its thickness) around a city over two thousand kilometres high would not keep anything out and could not be seen from most of the city. Which is the point. The wall, compared with the city, is small: protection is no longer needed. It is a boundary, marking what is inside as holy, and its gates never close.

If the numbers are symbols, is the new creation real? Yes, entirely. Symbols in Scripture are not a way of saying less than the truth but more than plain words can carry. The cube tells you something no floor plan could: that every one of God’s people will live in the immediate presence of God, as near as the high priest ever was, and nearer. The new creation is as real as the risen body of Jesus, which could be touched and ate fish (Luke 24:39–43). What the symbols do is stop us shrinking it to the size of our imagination. Whatever it is like, it is not less than this.

On a Tuesday. Worship now as one who will one day dwell in the Most Holy Place. When you pray, you are not shouting through a closed door; through Christ you already have access to the Father (Hebrews 10:19–22). Come in boldly, and come often. And if you have feared that there will be no room for you, because of your past, your weakness or your failures, look at the size of the city. God did not build it small.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes give 12,000 stadia as about 1,380 miles; 144 cubits is about 216 feet. The city is a perfect cube, like the Most Holy Place in Solomon’s temple.

verseByVerse.quote: The wall was built of jasper, while the city was pure gold, like clear glass. The foundations of the wall of the city were adorned with every kind of jewel. The first was jasper, the second sapphire, the third agate, the fourth emerald, the fifth onyx, the sixth carnelian, the seventh chrysolite, the eighth beryl, the ninth topaz, the tenth chrysoprase, the eleventh jacinth, the twelfth amethyst. And the twelve gates were twelve pearls, each of the gates made of a single pearl, and the street of the city was pure gold, like transparent glass.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Isaiah 54:11–12 promises Jerusalem foundations of sapphires, battlements of agate, gates of carbuncles and walls of precious stones. The king of Tyre, in Eden, was covered with every precious stone (Ezekiel 28:13). The prostitute Babylon was adorned with gold, jewels and pearls (17:4).

Jasper and pure gold. Jasper is the appearance of the One on the throne (4:3), so the wall reflects his glory. “Pure gold” (chrysion katharon) recalls the gold-covered Most Holy Place (1 Kings 6:20), but this is gold that light goes through, a kind unknown on earth, and John says the same of the street: purity and glory together. Whatever this city is made of, its most precious substance has stopped being opaque. Nothing in it casts a shadow or hides what is behind it.

Every kind of jewel. Twelve stones on twelve foundations recall the high priest’s breastplate. The high priest of Israel wore a breastpiece set with twelve stones in four rows, one for each tribe, and he bore the names of the sons of Israel on his heart when he went into the Holy Place, as a memorial before the LORD (Exodus 28:29). About eight of John’s twelve names also appear in the Greek translation of the breastplate list, and the others may well be other names for similar stones. So the foundations of the city are the high priest’s breastpiece, laid out flat and built into the ground. What one man carried over his heart into the holy place is now the foundation everybody walks on. The whole people of God, precious to him, now in his presence for ever.

Twelve stones. John takes a verse and a half to list twelve stones one by one, and the slowness is the effect: a man walking along a wall naming colours, clear, blue, green, red, golden, purple. The exact identity of ancient gem names is uncertain. The point is overwhelming beauty and variety, reflecting God’s glory in many colours, like the many nations of the redeemed. And jasper and carnelian, the first and sixth stones here, are the two John used of the one seated on the throne, and emerald, the fourth, was the colour of the rainbow round it (4:3).

Gates of pearl. Pearls were among the most valuable things in the ancient world, and gates each made of a single pearl are beyond imagination; this is the source of the phrase pearly gates. And unlike gold and gems, a pearl is not mined or cut. It is made by an oyster, slowly, around an irritant it cannot expel, usually a tiny parasite rather than the grain of grit of popular telling, covered over layer by layer for years. Jesus told a parable about a merchant in search of fine pearls who found one of great value and sold all that he had to buy it. The gates into the eternal city are pearls, every one a single stone: the costliest entrance imaginable, and never shut (v. 25). Revelation itself says who may walk through them: blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may enter the city by the gates (22:14), and the robes are made white in the blood of the Lamb (7:14). The gates are priceless; the way through them was paid for by him.

The street. “Street” (plateia, main street, broad way). The most valuable substance the ancient world knew, used for the surface people walk on. Babylon’s cargo list began with gold and silver and jewels and pearls (18:12), and merchants wept when they could no longer sell it. Here the same materials are paving. It is a statement about proportion. Everything the world killed for turns out, in the only city that lasts, to be pavement, and a reader who has spent a lifetime arranging his affairs around such things is being shown what they are for.

Does this mean God wants me rich now? No. This is the opposite of a prosperity gospel. The gold is in the street, under feet, precisely so that no one in the city will ever want it again. Jesus warned that a man’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions (Luke 12:15), and Paul that the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils (1 Timothy 6:10). God gives some of his people wealth to steward, and many of his people poverty to bear, and he loves both the same. What this verse promises is that the poorest believer will one day walk on what the richest unbeliever spent his life chasing.

On a Tuesday. Hold the things of this world loosely: Christ, though he was rich, became poor for your sake (2 Corinthians 8:9), and in his city gold is pavement. Look at one purchase you are planning, or one financial worry that keeps you awake, and ask how it looks from a street paved with gold. Then give something away this week, generously and quietly, as a person who knows where real wealth is stored (Matthew 6:19–21).
verseByVerse.note: The twelve jewels recall the stones on the high priest’s breastpiece, engraved with the names of the tribes.

verseByVerse.quote: And I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. For Israel, the temple was the centre of life: the place where God dwelt and where sacrifices were offered. Ezekiel’s vision of the restored city centred on a new temple (Ezekiel 40–48). Jesus told the Samaritan woman that the hour was coming when true worshippers would worship the Father in spirit and truth, not on a particular mountain (John 4:21–24). The temple in Jerusalem had been destroyed by the Romans in AD 70, and many Jews hoped it would be rebuilt.

No temple. “Temple” (naon, sanctuary). A Jewish reader would expect the new Jerusalem to have a glorious temple, and Ezekiel spent nine chapters on one. But there is none. Consider what a temple is. Most ancient peoples built them, and in their different ways they answered one problem: God is holy and people are not, so there must be a designated place, a mediating class, a set of rules for approach, and a barrier between the god and the worshipper. Israel’s, given by God himself, was carefully ordered. There was a court the nations could enter, a court beyond that for Israel, a court beyond that for men, a court beyond that for priests, and behind a curtain a room one man entered once a year with blood in his hands.

Its temple is the Lord God. There is no temple, not because worship has ended, but because the arrangement a temple exists to manage has ended. The problem a temple solves, how sinful people can be near a holy God without being destroyed, has been solved somewhere else, by Someone, and the verse names him. Now God’s presence fills the whole city, and nothing separates his people from him. God and the Lamb together are the temple: the Son shares the Father’s presence and glory.

There is no temple because there is a Lamb. The last two words are the answer. When Jesus died, the curtain of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom (Matthew 27:51): from the top, by Someone reaching down. This verse is that tearing carried to its conclusion. He is not merely the priest and not merely the sacrifice. He is the building. There is no outer court, no restricted section, no closer and further; nobody is nearer to God than anybody else, and nobody is waiting outside for a priest to come back and tell him it went well.

What it does not mean. No temple does not mean no worship. The whole city is a temple, and all of life is worship. It also confirms that there will be no rebuilt temple with renewed sacrifices in God’s final plan; Christ’s sacrifice has fulfilled them all. Some Christians, especially dispensationalists (who expect a thousand-year reign of Christ on earth with a rebuilt temple in Jerusalem), read the prophets differently, and they are brothers who love the same Christ. This commentary reads the thousand years of chapter 20 as Christ’s present reign (the view called amillennial) and expects no temple, because Hebrews says Christ’s one offering has made the old system obsolete (Hebrews 8:13; 10:12–14).

Then do church buildings and Sunday worship matter now? Yes, but not as temples. A church building is a meeting place, not a holy house where God lives and elsewhere he does not; the temple of God now is his people (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21–22), and the Lord meets them wherever two or three gather in his name (Matthew 18:20). Gathering with God’s people matters greatly, because God tells us not to neglect it (Hebrews 10:24–25), and the Lord’s Day is the church’s glad day for it. It is also a rehearsal for the city: his people together before his face. But no place, priest or ritual stands between you and God. Through Christ you may draw near anywhere, at any hour, and on that day there will be nowhere that is not his presence.

Nearness no one earns. Every Christian who has ever felt that God is available in certain places and at certain times, that some people have better access, that the holy is somewhere he visits rather than somewhere he lives: this verse is the end of all of it. And it ends every scheme for earning a place near him. Plenty of people, churchgoers and sceptics both, assume that nearness to God is earned by ceremony, by effort or by being decent. In this city nobody is nearer for having tried harder, because there was only ever one way in, and it was a Lamb.

For worship. In the temple courts Jesus said, Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up, and he was speaking about the temple of his body (John 2:19–21). They destroyed it on a hill outside the city wall, and on the third day God raised it, and the true temple has stood ever since, alive for evermore. In the city to come no house of stone is needed, because the Temple has a face, and his people live in its light with nothing between. The temple was always him. Praise to the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb, the temple, the priest and the sacrifice, in whose presence we shall dwell for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: And the city has no need of sun or moon to shine on it, for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb. By its light will the nations walk, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it, and its gates will never be shut by day—and there will be no night there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Isaiah 60 lies behind these verses: nations coming to Zion’s light, gates open continually, and the LORD as Zion’s everlasting light. In ancient cities, gates were shut at night for protection.

No need of sun or moon. The second thing missing, after the temple: the sun. Genesis 1 gives two great lights on the fourth day, and Isaiah promised a day when the sun would no longer be the light by day, nor the moon give brightness, but the LORD would be an everlasting light (Isaiah 60:19). The sun will be as unneeded as a candle at noon. The sun and moon have been doing a job on loan for the whole of history, and the owner has arrived.

Its lamp is the Lamb. “Lamp” (lychnos) is a household lamp, the small clay dish with a wick that lit a single room after dark. God’s glory is the light, and the Lamb is the lamp through which it shines. That is precisely what he has been since the first chapter, where his face was like the sun shining in full strength (1:16), and precisely what he said of himself: I am the light of the world. We see the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). No one in the city will ever see God’s glory except through the Lamb; and no one will ever need to see it any other way.

The nations. The redeemed from every nation, living in God’s light. Their national and cultural diversity is preserved in the new creation. This is Isaiah 60 again: nations shall come to your light. Babel scattered the nations in confusion; the Lamb gathers them, not into one language and one culture, but into one light.

The kings of the earth. “Kings of the earth”: the same phrase used of those who committed immorality with Babylon (17:2; 18:9). It is startling in a book where the kings of the earth have gathered to make war on the Lamb (16:14; 19:19). What John is describing is not an amnesty for Babylon but the redemption of the nations as nations. Some kings, who once rebelled, are redeemed. The good things of human culture, its achievements, beauty and treasures, cleansed of sin, are brought into the new creation.

What is their glory? The text does not list it, and guessing is a poor substitute for reading. But the phrase does imply that what the peoples of the earth have made and been is not simply erased. Something is carried in. That is a real word to anyone who has wondered whether ordinary human work has any future: whether the making of music, the building of things, the raising of crops and children and languages and cities is all going into a fire. This verse says the gates are open, and something is being brought in through them.

No night there. Every walled city in the ancient world closed its gates at sundown, and that was the moment the day’s safety ended: after dark, whatever was outside stayed outside, and anybody who had not got home was not getting home. This city has gates that never shut, and John gives the reason: there will be no night there. The two clauses are one thought. The gates stay open because the hour at which a gate is shut never comes: perfect safety and perfect welcome. Anyone who has lain awake at three in the morning knows what is being taken away. Night in Scripture is not simply darkness; it is when the thief comes, when the enemy moves, when a person is alone with what he has done, when the sick get worse and the frightened get more frightened. There is none of it, ever again.

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “the nations of them which are saved shall walk in the light of it”, adding “of them which are saved”. The best manuscripts simply read “the nations”. The addition explains correctly who the nations are.

Where Christians differ: does this mean the nations outside are finally saved? Some read the nations and kings coming into the city as unbelievers being saved after the final judgement, so that all will eventually enter. The hope behind that reading, that all might be saved, is a tender one. This commentary’s view: the nations here are the redeemed nations, the great multitude from every nation (7:9), who come into the city because their names are written in the Lamb’s book (v. 27). The lake of fire is final (20:15; 21:8), and outside the city are those who practise wickedness (22:15). The passage shows that the redeemed include people from every nation, and that the best of human culture is brought in, purified. It does not teach a second chance after death.

Will there still be different nations and cultures? It seems so. John sees nations walking by the light, and earlier a multitude from every nation, tribe, people and language (7:9). The new creation is not a grey sameness in which every trace of who we were is dissolved. Just as each believer will be himself, made perfect, so the peoples of the earth seem to be there as themselves, cleansed of pride and hostility, every tongue confessing that Jesus Christ is Lord (Philippians 2:11). So love believers whose culture is not yours. You will be living with them for ever, and their way of praising the Lamb will be part of the glory.

Will we be busy, or bored? Neither tired nor bored. Scripture pictures the age to come not as endless idleness but as reigning, serving and worshipping (22:3, 5), with bodies that do not wear out and hearts that do not drift. Boredom is the soul running out of interest, and in the presence of an infinite God that can never happen; there will always be more of him to know and enjoy. If the thought of worship for ever sounds dull, that is because our worship now is so thin. Ask God this week to give you a taste of it, and read Revelation 4–5 aloud.

On a Tuesday. When night comes, literally or in your soul, the sleepless hour, the dark diagnosis, remember that night has an end, and the city is coming where the Lamb is the lamp and the gates are never shut.

For worship. The Light of the world hung on a cross at noon while darkness covered the whole land, and on the third day he rose before the sun was up. Now the glory of God shines through him like a flame through a lamp, and no shadow falls anywhere in the city. The nations he bought walk by his light, the kings who once made war on him come in carrying gifts, and the gates stand open at what would have been midnight. Glory to the Lamb, the lamp of the city, in whose light we shall see light.

verseByVerse.quote: They will bring into it the glory and the honor of the nations. But nothing unclean will ever enter it, nor anyone who does what is detestable or false, but only those who are written in the Lamb's book of life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Isaiah 52:1 says that the uncircumcised and the unclean shall no more come into Jerusalem. Isaiah 60:5, 11 says the wealth of the nations shall come to Zion. Haggai 2:7 says the treasures of all nations shall come in and God will fill his house with glory.

The glory and the honour. The two verses have to be held together, because each guards the other. Verse 26 is the widest sentence in the chapter: the glory and the honour of the nations, not of one nation, and not of the church only. All that is good and beautiful in the world’s peoples is gathered into God’s city. The multitude of chapter 7 came from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, and they do not arrive empty-handed.

Nothing unclean. “Unclean” (koinon, common, defiled, profane). Verse 27 immediately shuts the door on any sentimentality about verse 26. The gates are always open, and they are not unguarded. This is not a city where everything is welcome; it is a city where everything that is welcome has been made clean. Unclean is the ceremonial word, what could not come into the sanctuary, and it fits a city that is all sanctuary. This is not fussiness on God’s part; it is what holiness is. God is light, and in him is no darkness at all (1 John 1:5), and a city that is all his dwelling can no more hold uncleanness than noon can hold midnight.

Detestable or false. These are the sins of Babylon and the beast. Detestable is the word used all through the Old Testament of idolatry, and it was written on the prostitute’s forehead in 17:5. False is the last word of the list, and fittingly so in a book where the dragon, the false prophet and Babylon all ruled by deceit: the city of the One who is true has no room for a lie.

The Lamb’s book of life. Look at how the sentence actually ends, because the criterion is not a moral audit. The one qualification for entry: belonging to the Lamb. Not good works, not nationality, not religious heritage, but the Lamb’s choice and the Lamb’s blood. Those whose names were written before the foundation of the world (13:8; 17:8). At 13:8 the KJV joins from the foundation of the world to the Lamb slain instead; the Greek can be read either way, and 17:8 favours the reading given here. That is the last mention of the book of life in Revelation (the KJV has one more at 22:19, where the Greek manuscripts read tree of life), and it lands exactly where it did at the great white throne (20:12, 15): not on what a person achieved but on whether his name is in a register belonging to a Lamb who was slain.

How the unclean become clean. The two halves of these verses are not in tension at all. Nothing unclean enters, and the whole book has been showing how the unclean become clean, in the most impossible image it could find: they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb (7:14). Nobody walks in on his own record. Everybody who walks in has had something done to him first.

In the flow. Chapter 21 ends here, but the vision does not: the chapter break is a later convenience, and John goes straight on to the river and the tree (22:1–5). The two verses also gather up the chapter. Verse 8 said who has no part in the new creation, and verse 27 says who has no way through its gates; verse 6 offered water without payment, and the Lamb’s book of life names those who drink it. And they prepare the book’s last beatitude, where the same gates open to those who wash their robes (22:14).

Will I still sin there? No. The struggle every believer knows, wanting to do right and finding sin still close at hand (Romans 7:21), will be over. Those who enter are not only forgiven but made perfect in holiness (Hebrews 12:23), and when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). Nothing unclean will ever enter, and that includes the remnants of sin in you. This is one of the sweetest promises in the chapter for a tired Christian: not only no more sorrow, but no more sinning. You will love God as you have always wanted to, without anything dragging you back.

How can I be sure my name is written? Not by searching for it in a secret register, but by looking to the Lamb whose book it is. The names written there are the names of those who trust him, and Jesus said, whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37). If you are resting on Christ alone, and not on your record, you may be sure. Assurance grows as you see the Spirit’s fruit in you, as you walk in obedience, and as the Spirit bears witness with your spirit that you are a child of God (Romans 8:16). If you are not sure, do not try harder to feel sure. Come to him again.

On a Tuesday. If your name is written in the Lamb’s book, the gates of pearl are open to you. Live clean in the light of that day. Is there anything you are doing in secret that would not belong inside that city? Put it out of your life this week; confess it, and ask for help from a trusted brother or sister if you need it. Not to earn your entry: the Lamb paid for it, his perfect obedience is counted as yours, and your faltering obedience is accepted for his sake. Do it because you are going to live in a city of light, and the Spirit who will make you perfect there is already at work in you here.

For worship. Before there was a world to fall, the Lamb had a book, and names were written in it; he set his love on people who would one day be unclean, and in time he went to the cross to wash them. Now the gates stand open, and every name in the book walks through, and not one is missing. God himself is with them: no temple, because he is there; no sun, because he is there; no night, because he is there. To him who loves us and has freed us from our sins by his blood be glory and dominion for ever and ever.

21.text: <sup>1</sup>Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea was no more.<sup>2</sup>And I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.<sup>3</sup>And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying, “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God.<sup>4</sup>He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away.”<sup>5</sup>And he who was seated on the throne said, “Behold, I am making all things new.” Also he said, “Write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true.”<sup>6</sup>And he said to me, “It is done! I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end. To the thirsty I will give from the spring of the water of life without payment.<sup>7</sup>The one who conquers will have this heritage, and I will be his God and he will be my son.<sup>8</sup>But as for the cowardly, the faithless, the detestable, as for murderers, the sexually immoral, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars, their portion will be in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur, which is the second death.”<sup>9</sup>Then came one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls full of the seven last plagues and spoke to me, saying, “Come, I will show you the Bride, the wife of the Lamb.”<sup>10</sup>And he carried me away in the Spirit to a great, high mountain, and showed me the holy city Jerusalem coming down out of heaven from God,<sup>11</sup>having the glory of God, its radiance like a most rare jewel, like a jasper, clear as crystal.<sup>12</sup>It had a great, high wall, with twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and on the gates the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel were inscribed—<sup>13</sup>on the east three gates, on the north three gates, on the south three gates, and on the west three gates.<sup>14</sup>And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and on them were the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.<sup>15</sup>And the one who spoke with me had a measuring rod of gold to measure the city and its gates and walls.<sup>16</sup>The city lies foursquare, its length the same as its width. And he measured the city with his rod, 12,000 stadia. Its length and width and height are equal.<sup>17</sup>He also measured its wall, 144 cubits by human measurement, which is also an angel’s measurement.<sup>18</sup>The wall was built of jasper, while the city was pure gold, like clear glass.<sup>19</sup>The foundations of the wall of the city were adorned with every kind of jewel. The first was jasper, the second sapphire, the third agate, the fourth emerald,<sup>20</sup>the fifth onyx, the sixth carnelian, the seventh chrysolite, the eighth beryl, the ninth topaz, the tenth chrysoprase, the eleventh jacinth, the twelfth amethyst.<sup>21</sup>And the twelve gates were twelve pearls, each of the gates made of a single pearl, and the street of the city was pure gold, like transparent glass.<sup>22</sup>And I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb.<sup>23</sup>And the city has no need of sun or moon to shine on it, for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb.<sup>24</sup>By its light will the nations walk, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it,<sup>25</sup>and its gates will never be shut by day—and there will be no night there.<sup>26</sup>They will bring into it the glory and the honor of the nations.<sup>27</sup>But nothing unclean will ever enter it, nor anyone who does what is detestable or false, but only those who are written in the Lamb’s book of life.

22.title: Come, Lord Jesus: The River, the Tree, and the Final Invitation
22.overview:
The last chapter of Revelation, and of the Bible, gathers up the threads of the whole story. The river of the water of life, the tree of life, God’s servants seeing his face and bearing his name, and no more night. Then Christ says three times that he is coming soon, and the church answers, Come, Lord Jesus.

The chapter has two parts. Verses 1–5 finish the vision of the city, and they return to Eden, but to something greater: the river now flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, and the tree once guarded by cherubim stands open on both banks of the street. Verses 6–21 close the book: the angel’s guarantee, Jesus speaking in his own voice, the Spirit and the Bride inviting the thirsty, a warning not to tamper with the book, and a last word of grace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The River and the Tree of Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1–5 complete the description of the city. Verses 1–2: the river and the tree of life, the way to which has been closed since Genesis 3, now open to all, with leaves for the healing of the nations. Verses 3–5: the curse lifted, the throne of God and of the Lamb in the city, and the promise that his servants will see his face and reign for ever.
verseByVerse.theology:
The River and the Tree

The river of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, and the tree of life stands open with fruit every month and leaves for the healing of the nations. The curse is gone, and his servants will see his face.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The way to the tree, guarded since Eden, stands open in the middle of the street.

Now: Heaven is not first a place but a face, seen at last and lived by.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the angel showed me the river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb through the middle of the street of the city; also, on either side of the river, the tree of life with its twelve kinds of fruit, yielding its fruit each month. The leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Revelation 22 finishes the vision of the new creation and closes the book, and the whole Bible. The river of the water of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, and the tree of life grows on both banks, with leaves for the healing of the nations (vv. 1–2). The curse is gone; God’s servants will worship him, see his face, bear his name and reign for ever (vv. 3–5). Then the epilogue. Christ says three times, I am coming soon (vv. 7, 12, 20), blesses the one who keeps this book (v. 7), and brings his reward as the Alpha and the Omega (vv. 12–13). John is told again to worship God, not the angel (vv. 8–9), and not to seal the book, for the time is near (vv. 10–11). Those who wash their robes may enter the city; outside are the wicked (vv. 14–15). Jesus names himself the root and descendant of David, the bright morning star (v. 16). The Spirit and the bride say, Come, and the thirsty may take the water of life freely (v. 17). No one may add to or take away from the book (vv. 18–19). The Bible that began in a garden with a tree of life ends in a garden-city with the tree of life, God’s people seeing his face, and the church praying, Come, Lord Jesus. And its last word, after all the thunder of this book, is grace (vv. 20–21).

The setting. Behind these verses stand Genesis 2–3; Ezekiel 47:1–12, with its river flowing from the temple and its trees of healing; and Zechariah 14:8, which promises living waters flowing out from Jerusalem.

A river and a tree. The Bible has been away from these two things for more than eleven hundred chapters, and here they are again. Genesis 2 has a river flowing out of Eden to water the garden, and the tree of life in the midst of the garden. Genesis 3 ends with the man and the woman put out, and cherubim with a flaming sword set to guard the way to the tree of life (Genesis 3:24). From that verse to this one, nobody eats from it. The whole of Scripture happens in the interval between a tree being fenced off and a tree being handed back.

The river of the water of life. Eternal life, abundant and flowing, pure and shining. The promise of 7:17 and 21:6 fulfilled: the Lamb will guide them to springs of living water, and the thirsty will drink without payment. What was a cup offered in the last chapter is a river here.

From the throne. One throne, two names, and John does not pause to explain how. Life flows from God’s rule; the source of all life is God himself, through the Lamb, by the Spirit (John 7:39). And what flows out of the throne is not judgement but water. Ezekiel saw the same thing: water trickling from under the threshold of the temple, deepening as it went until it was a river nobody could cross, with trees on both banks whose leaves would not wither (Ezekiel 47:1–12). In this book thunder and lightning came from the throne (4:5); at the end, a river does.

Down the street. Life is at the centre of the city’s life. Babylon’s streets were full of merchants and their cargoes; this street carries the water of life past every door.

The tree of life. “Tree of life” (xylon zōēs). What Adam and Eve lost is restored, as promised to the first of the seven churches: To the one who conquers I will grant to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God (2:7). Ephesus was told that in a letter. Here is the tree. “On either side”: perhaps a whole avenue of trees of life, or one tree spanning the river. It is impossible to draw and easy to understand: wherever a person walks, it is on both sides of him. The word for tree (xylon, wood) is also used of the cross (Acts 5:30; 1 Peter 2:24); by the tree on which Christ died, we have access to the tree of life.

Not simply Eden reopened. The differences are the point. Eden was a garden; this is a garden inside a city, with the river running through the middle of the street, so that all the work and culture of humanity is gathered around the tree rather than exiled from it. Eden had one tree of life; here it lines both banks. Eden could be lost; this cannot. God does not restore his people to the place they started. He takes them somewhere better than the place they started, and the road ran through a cross.

Fruit each month. Constant abundance. Twelve: the number of God’s people. Fruit every month: no more seasons of want or scarcity. Ezekiel 47:12 says its fruit will not fail. Anyone who has grown anything knows that fruit trees rest; there are months with nothing on them. This one does not stop.

The healing of the nations. “Healing” (therapeian; our word therapy comes from it). The phrase puzzles readers, and rightly: the previous chapter has just abolished pain. Ezekiel is the source again: their fruit will be for food, and their leaves for healing (Ezekiel 47:12). The word can mean care and tending as much as cure: the leaves sustain the full health of the nations, so that the life of the city is continually supplied, not merely started. And nations has been a hostile word for most of this book: the nations raged, the nations drank Babylon’s wine, the beast had authority over every nation. Here the nations are the ones being tended. The long wound in human history, peoples divided at a tower, scattered and at each other’s throats ever since, has leaves growing for it.

Could we ever lose the tree of life again? No. Adam stood on probation, able to fall, and fell. The redeemed stand in Christ, who has already passed every test for them and cannot fail. The curse is gone (v. 3), the serpent is in the lake of fire (20:10), and those who enter the city are made perfect in holiness, confirmed in a love for God that will never cool. The tree that was guarded by a sword is now given as a right (v. 14), and what Christ gives by right he never takes back. There will be no second fall, because there will be no second serpent and no unrenewed heart.

What about the wars and hatreds between peoples now? This verse is God’s answer, and it should shape how Christians live meanwhile. The divisions of race, nation and tribe that have caused so much blood are not permanent; they are among the things the leaves of the tree will heal. So the church is meant to be a foretaste of that healing now: Jew and Gentile, rich and poor, one in Christ (Galatians 3:28; Ephesians 2:14–16). If there is someone of another background in your church you avoid, or a people you have been taught to despise, this verse says you will spend eternity with the redeemed of them. Begin now.

On a Tuesday. You are not waiting for the river to start: Jesus said that rivers of living water would flow from within whoever believes in him, by the Spirit (John 7:38–39). So drink today, in prayer and in his word, before you go to anything else. And let what flows to you flow on: forgive the person who wronged you, and bring some healing where you can.
verseByVerse.note: Eden’s river and tree of life return, now in a city.

verseByVerse.quote: No longer will there be anything accursed, but the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants will worship him. They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads. And night will be no more. They will need no light of lamp or sun, for the Lord God will be their light, and they will reign forever and ever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Zechariah 14:11 promises that there shall never again be a decree of utter destruction (curse) on Jerusalem. Jesus said, blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God (Matthew 5:8).

No longer will there be anything accursed. “Accursed” (katathema, curse, anything under a curse). One clause, and it reaches back to the third chapter of the Bible. When the man and the woman were sent out, God said the ground was cursed because of the man; in pain he would eat of it, thorns and thistles would come up, and the man would return to the dust (Genesis 3:17–19). Everything hard about human existence, the labour that exhausts, the ground that resists, the body that fails, has stood under that sentence. And it is lifted. Not managed, not compensated for, not explained: removed. Everything that sin brought, death, pain, toil, decay, enmity, is gone.

Two trees. The removal was accomplished by Someone becoming a curse for us, for it is written, cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree (Galatians 3:13). There are two trees at the end of this book. On one of them the curse was absorbed; from the other the fruit is handed out twelve times a year.

The throne of God and of the Lamb. God reigns at the centre of the new creation. His rule is the source of its life and peace. The throne has been the fixed point of the vision since chapter 4, and it has always been in heaven. Now it is in the city, on the renewed earth, at the end of the street with the river running out of it.

His servants will worship him. “Worship” (latreusousin, serve as priests, worship). “Him” is singular: God and the Lamb together as one. Eternal life is worship and service, freely and joyfully given. John has spent the book watching heaven worship; now the redeemed on the new earth join in for ever.

They will see his face. This is the summit of the promise: the beatific vision, the blessed sight, as the church has called it, seeing God face to face. Moses, who spoke with God as a man speaks to his friend, asked for exactly this one thing, and was told no man could see God’s face and live. He was put in a cleft of the rock and covered with a hand and shown God’s back (Exodus 33:18–23). The high priest went behind the veil, and even then a cloud of incense had to cover the mercy seat so that he would not die (Leviticus 16:13). Isaiah saw the train of a robe and cried out that he was undone. In chapter 6 of this book, kings and generals begged mountains to fall on them and hide them from the face of him who is seated on the throne (6:16). And here, without ceremony, in a short clause: they will see his face. Ordinary people, a slave from Laodicea, a widow from Thyatira, a man who once denied Christ in a courtyard, looking directly at God, and living. To see his face is to know him fully, be fully known, and be fully accepted (1 Corinthians 13:12).

That is what heaven is. Not a location with good weather; not a reunion, though there will be one; not the end of trouble, though trouble ends. It is a face. John wrote the same promise in a letter, and admitted he could not fill it in: what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). Everything else in these two chapters, the gold, the jewels, the river, the open gates, is furniture in a room where that is happening.

His name on their foreheads. The last of the marked foreheads in this book (3:12; 7:3; 14:1), and the counterfeit, the beast’s mark (13:16), is gone. Everyone is labelled, and these are labelled with him: they belong to him completely, publicly and for ever. Like the high priest, who wore Holy to the LORD on a gold plate on his forehead (Exodus 28:36–38), all God’s people are priests in his presence.

They will reign. “Reign” (basileusousin). Not for a thousand years only, but for ever and ever. The promise of Daniel 7:18, 27 that the saints of the Most High will possess the kingdom for ever. Adam was made to rule over creation under God (Genesis 1:26–28); redeemed humanity will finally fulfil that calling. And the last word of the description is reign: the promise made to Laodicea, the weakest church on the road, that the one who conquers would sit with Christ on his throne (3:21), arriving in full.

How can we see the face of God, who is spirit? Scripture does not explain the mechanics, and we should not pretend to. But two things are clear. First, we will see God in Christ. Jesus said, whoever has seen me has seen the Father (John 14:9), and the glory of God shines in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). The risen Lord, in his glorified body, will be before our eyes. Second, the seeing will be more than sight: knowing God directly, with nothing between, in a way we cannot now imagine. What Moses could not survive, we will be able to bear, because we will have been made like him.

Will there be work in the new creation? Yes, but not toil. His servants will serve him, and they will reign; serving and reigning are active words. The curse made work painful and frustrating, thorns, sweat, futility, but work itself came before the fall (Genesis 2:15). What is lifted is the curse, not the calling. Imagine work that never fails, never wearies you, never goes to waste, and is done entirely for the joy of God. That is not boredom. That is what you were made for, and what every good day of work now is a faint taste of.

On a Tuesday. If seeing God’s face is the goal of everything, then the most important thing you can do is seek his face now (Psalm 27:8), in his word and in prayer. Ask what in your life is competing with that longing: ambition, comfort, a relationship, a grievance. And when the curse bites, the aching back, the job that frustrates, the illness that does not lift, remember that it is one of the last things on its way out. You will one day work without thorns and rest without fear, and look up into his face.

For worship. The face that Moses was not allowed to see once came close enough to touch. It was the face of a baby in Bethlehem, a face set toward Jerusalem (Luke 9:51), a face that men spat on and covered and struck (Mark 14:65), so that the face of God might be turned toward sinners in blessing for ever. The LORD make his face to shine upon you, the priests prayed, and at last the prayer is answered without limit. Forgiven sinners will look on him, and they will not die of it; they will live by it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 6–16 begin the epilogue, which closes the book by matching its opening (1:1–8). Verses 6–7: the angel’s guarantee, Christ’s first I am coming soon, and the blessing on the one who keeps the book. Verses 8–9: John falls before the angel a second time and is told, Worship God. Verses 10–11: the book is left unsealed, unlike Daniel’s, and lives are fixed in the way they are going. Verses 12–13: Christ comes bringing his reward, and claims the titles of God. Verses 14–15: the last beatitude, for those who wash their robes, and those left outside. Verse 16: Jesus names himself, the root and descendant of David, the bright morning star.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Testimony of Jesus

The book closes as it opened: blessed is the one who keeps its words. The angel refuses John’s worship again: Worship God. The book is left unsealed, for the time is near. Jesus, the Alpha and Omega, root and descendant of David, the bright morning star, is coming soon; blessed are those who wash their robes.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The whole vision was given for the churches, to be read aloud in small rooms.

Now: While the door is open, ask which way your life is already heading.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to me, "These words are trustworthy and true. And the Lord, the God of the spirits of the prophets, has sent his angel to show his servants what must soon take place." "And behold, I am coming soon. Blessed is the one who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Trustworthy and true. As in 21:5: the whole book is guaranteed. The vision is over, and the book closes by going back to its first sentence (1:1): the same chain of revelation, the same angel, the same servants, the same things that must soon take place. John is signing off by matching the letterhead.

The God of the spirits of the prophets. The title says that the same God who spoke through Isaiah and Ezekiel and Daniel, whose words have been echoed on nearly every page of this book, is the one who has spoken here. God, who inspired the prophets, has inspired this book. Revelation stands in the line of the Old Testament prophets, with their authority (2 Peter 1:21). It is not a new departure. It is the last chapter of a document that has been in progress for some fifteen centuries.

His servants. As in 1:1. The revelation is for all God’s servants, not a spiritual elite. It was meant to be read aloud in ordinary congregations, by ordinary believers, and understood well enough to be obeyed.

I am coming soon. The speaker changes without warning: the angel has been talking, and suddenly it is Christ himself. He will say this three times in this chapter (vv. 7, 12, 20), and it is the drumbeat the book ends on. And the great hope of the church is not an event, a date or a programme, but a Person arriving. It is the same Jesus who said in the upper room, I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also (John 14:3), and of whom the angels said at the ascension that he would come in the same way as they had seen him go (Acts 1:11). The one who is coming is the one who was pierced (1:7), and he is coming for his own.

The one who keeps. The sixth beatitude, almost word for word the first one (1:3). “Keeps” (tērōn, obeys, holds fast). The book opens and closes with a blessing on the same person: not the one who understands every symbol, or charts it, or identifies the beast, but the one who keeps it. Revelation is to be obeyed, not merely studied. Whatever else a reader takes from it, that is the bracket he is being asked to live inside.

Soon, after two thousand years? The honest answer has three parts. First, the word stresses that his coming is the next great event in God’s plan, sure and sudden, not that it will come within a set number of years; it is always near and could be soon, though Scripture does name things that will come before it, such as the great rebellion and the man of lawlessness (2 Thessalonians 2:3), so the church is to watch, not to set dates. Second, the New Testament dates the last days from the resurrection (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2): we have been living at the edge of the end ever since. Third, Peter answered this very objection while it was fresh: with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and he is not slow to fulfil his promise as some count slowness, but patient (2 Peter 3:8–9). The delay is not indifference. It is mercy, and somebody is being brought in during it, perhaps someone you love.

How do I keep a book so full of symbols? You keep what it plainly asks, which is a great deal and not hard to see. Worship God alone, and refuse every rival, whether Caesar, money or comfort. Hold to Jesus when it costs you. Do not compromise with the sins the letters to the churches name. Endure suffering without giving up the faith. Tell the truth. Long for Christ’s coming, and invite others to come to him. You do not need to settle every question about the seals and the beast to obey that, and many believers who never solved a single symbol have kept this book faithfully.

On a Tuesday. If arguments about the end times have made you anxious or proud, lay them down for a while. Read the book again for its commands and its comfort, and let Christ’s promise, I am coming soon, be the thing that shapes your week.

verseByVerse.quote: I, John, am the one who heard and saw these things. And when I heard and saw them, I fell down to worship at the feet of the angel who showed them to me, but he said to me, "You must not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers the prophets, and with those who keep the words of this book. Worship God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. In ancient law a matter was established by eyewitness testimony (Deuteronomy 19:15), and John’s Gospel and first letter stress it: we have heard, we have seen with our eyes, we have touched (John 19:35; 21:24; 1 John 1:1–3).

Heard and saw. John signs his testimony as an eyewitness. He did not invent these visions; he received them. The early church, from the second century on, believed that this John was the apostle, the man who leaned on Jesus at the Last Supper and stood at the foot of the cross; some scholars think he was another John, but either way he signs as a witness.

I fell down to worship. A second time. He did it at 19:10, was stopped in almost these words, and here, with the correction already in his own manuscript three chapters earlier, he goes down again. That is not flattering to John, and he wrote it down anyway, honestly, to warn us. It matters when it happens. Not in the middle of the terror, not at the dragon or the beast or the lake of fire, but immediately after the river and the tree and the face. It is the beauty that undoes him. The instinct is right; only the direction is wrong. A man overwhelmed by glory reaches for the nearest thing that is holding it.

A comfort in a repeated fault. It should be a comfort to anyone who has repeated a sin he had already repented of: one of the last things the apostle who wrote this book records about himself is a mistake he had made before. God did not withdraw the revelation. The angel corrected him and the book went on. Repeated failure is a reason to be humble and watchful, not a sign that God has given up on you.

You must not do that! The same urgent warning as in 19:10. There is no pause, no softening, no acceptance of the honour for a moment before declining it.

A fellow servant. Angels, prophets and all obedient believers are fellow servants of God. No created being deserves worship. And look at how the angel describes himself, because the list is longer than it was at 19:10. He is a fellow servant with John, with the prophets, and, this is new, with those who keep the words of this book. That last group is the reader. An angel of God has just put himself in the same category as an ordinary Christian who reads Revelation and does what it says.

Worship God. Two words, among the shortest complete instructions in Scripture. Twenty-two chapters of visions, and this is the summary. Throughout Revelation, the choice has been whom to worship: God and the Lamb, or the dragon and the beast. This also says something about the Lamb. All through the book the Lamb has been worshipped with the same worship as God, by angels who would never accept it themselves (5:8–14). The angel refuses worship because he is a creature; the Lamb receives it because he is not.

Is it wrong, then, to pray to angels or saints? Yes. If the angel who showed John the new Jerusalem would not accept even a bow of worship, no angel or departed saint may be prayed to or venerated. Scripture gives us one Mediator, Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5), and through him we come straight to the Father (Hebrews 4:14–16). We may thank God for the saints and follow their faith (Hebrews 13:7). But we pray only to God, through Christ, by the Spirit. Anything else, however well meant, gives a servant what belongs to the Master.

On a Tuesday. The permanent danger in the church is that the people through whom God speaks, preachers, writers, movements, worship leaders, receive what belongs to God, and the danger is greatest when what they bring is genuinely glorious. The remedy is not to think less of the messenger. It is two words: worship God. It is worth asking whom you quote most, whose approval you most want, what spiritual experience you chase. Thank God for them. Then look past them to him.

For worship. The mighty angel who showed John the city of gold will not accept a single bow. He stands beside an old man on an island as a fellow servant and turns him round to face the throne. Every glory John has seen, the river, the tree, the gates of pearl, was only ever a window, and the One beyond it is worthy of everything a creature can give. He made all things, and he redeemed his people with the blood of his Son. Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God Almighty, and to him and to the Lamb be blessing and honour and glory for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to me, "Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near. Let the evildoer still do evil, and the filthy still be filthy, and the righteous still do right, and the holy still be holy."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Daniel was told to shut up the words and seal the book until the time of the end, because his visions concerned the distant future (Daniel 8:26; 12:4, 9). Daniel 12:10 says many shall purify themselves, but the wicked shall act wickedly, and none of the wicked shall understand. Ezekiel 3:27 says, he who will hear, let him hear; and he who will refuse to hear, let him refuse.

Do not seal. The exact reverse of what Daniel was told. Daniel’s vision was for the far future; John’s is for now. The last days have begun. The book must be open, read and obeyed by the churches. And it is the reverse of what John himself was told at 10:4, when the seven thunders spoke and he was reaching for his pen: seal up what the seven thunders have said. There is exactly one sealed message in Revelation, and we do not have it. Everything else in the book is open, on purpose, by instruction. So it is not a locked document awaiting a key, and it never was. Its blessing falls on the person who keeps it rather than the person who cracks it.

The Lamb has broken the seals. Why can John’s book stay open when Daniel’s was shut? Revelation has already answered. In chapter 5 there was a scroll sealed with seven seals, no one in heaven or on earth was able to open it, and John wept. Then the Lamb who had been slain took the scroll, because by his blood he had ransomed a people for God (5:4–9). The time is near because he has come, died, risen and taken his throne; what Daniel waited for has begun. A sealed book belongs to an age still waiting for its Lord. An open book belongs to the age in which the Lamb has already conquered.

Still do evil. This is the hardest verse in the chapter, and it must not be softened. Read carelessly it sounds like God shrugging, a permission slip for wickedness. It is not a command to keep sinning, but a solemn warning: time is short, and character is being fixed. Those who persistently refuse God’s call harden themselves, and when Christ comes there will be no more opportunity to change.

Three things settle what it means. First, its position: between the time is near and I am coming soon, bracketed by urgency on both sides, which is the opposite of fatalism. Second, its form. It is a prophetic announcement, like the word given to Ezekiel when Israel had stopped listening (Ezekiel 3:27). What it says is that a moment arrives after which character is fixed, that there is a point beyond which a person’s direction of travel becomes his destination. Everyone knows this is true of habits within a lifetime; the verse says it is finally true of lives. Third, and most importantly, what it does to the reader, placed in front of him as the book is nearly finished. It asks: which of these four descriptions fits the direction you are already going? The door is open now, and the invitation is six verses away, but it will not be open for ever. And if a reader trembles here because he fears he has already hardened, the fear itself is the sign that he has not: the hardened do not worry about hardening, and the invitation of verse 17 is for him.

The righteous still do right. An encouragement: keep on in righteousness and holiness. Do not give up because the end seems delayed or the world seems to win. Holiness, too, is a direction that becomes a destiny, and it is God’s work in them before it is theirs (Philippians 2:13): the righteous who keep on will find that what they practised in weakness here is what they will be in glory.

Is it too late for someone I love? While a person is alive, the invitation stands, and you must not treat anyone as beyond reach. The thief on the cross turned in his last hours; Manasseh, one of the worst kings Judah ever had, repented after decades of evil (2 Chronicles 33:12–13). Paul called himself the foremost of sinners, saved as an example of Christ’s patience (1 Timothy 1:15–16). This verse warns that the door will close at Christ’s coming or at death, not that it has already closed on your son or your friend. So keep praying for them, keep loving them, and keep telling them the truth. It is the very urgency of this verse that makes your prayers matter.

On a Tuesday. Your daily choices are shaping who you will be for ever. The small kindness, the resisted temptation, the honest answer, the hour in prayer: by the Spirit at work in you, these are not lost; they are the grain of the person you are becoming. And if you know a direction in your life is wrong, do not wait for a better moment to turn. Turn today.
verseByVerse.note: Daniel was told to seal his book until the end; John is told not to, because the time is near.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, I am coming soon, bringing my recompense with me, to repay each one for what he has done. I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Jesus said the Son of Man will come with his angels in the glory of his Father, and then he will repay each person according to what he has done (Matthew 16:27).

My recompense with me. The second of the chapter’s three announcements, and this one has the reward already in his hand. “Recompense” (misthos, wages, reward). Bringing it with him: not sent for afterwards, not calculated on arrival. Isaiah said it first of the coming of God: his reward is with him (Isaiah 40:10). Christ brings with him the reward of his people and the judgement of the wicked.

Each one. “What he has done” (to ergon, his work). Singular: the whole pattern of a life. As in 20:12–13. The book has raised this before, to Thyatira at 2:23 and at the great white throne, and the answer has not moved. A record has never yet admitted anybody into the city, for no record is clean but Christ’s, and his perfect obedience is counted as his people’s (Romans 5:19). Yet it never fails to show whose a person is, and their flawed works, accepted for his sake, are the measure of what he gives afterwards. And hold on to each one. In a scene involving every human being who has ever lived, nothing is averaged. The visits nobody recorded, the giving that hurt, the cup of cold water: each one, by name.

Alpha and Omega, first and last. All three titles together. God said Alpha and Omega in 1:8 and 21:6. Christ said first and last in 1:17 and 2:8, and it is Isaiah’s exclusive divine self-identification: I am the first and I am the last; besides me there is no god (Isaiah 44:6). Now Christ claims all of them: the clearest statement in Revelation that Jesus shares the identity of the one God. Jesus, then, is not a lesser god, a great angel or the best of the prophets. He is the one God of Israel, with the Father, equal in being, glory and worship, who became man without ceasing to be God (John 1:1, 14). The titles move between the Father and the Son through this book without a seam and without an explanation, and that is not carelessness. Revelation never argues for the deity of Christ; it simply speaks as though the question could not arise. The one who began all things will end them.

But what if I have nothing to bring? There is a fear on the other side of this verse, and it keeps quiet Christians awake. A man converted at sixty, or a woman who has spent twenty years ill in a back bedroom, reads repay each one for what he has done and thinks: there is nothing of mine to bring. Two things answer him. The first is that what gets rewarded is not what he achieved but what Christ produced in him, and Christ does not fail to produce: the vine bears the fruit and the branch only carries it (John 15:5). Patient suffering, quiet prayer and faithfulness in small things are works too. The second is the parable Christ told about precisely this complaint: the men hired at the eleventh hour were paid the same as those who had borne the burden of the day, and the owner wronged nobody (Matthew 20:1–16). Nobody will stand in that scene feeling short-changed, and nobody will stand in it thinking he earned what he is holding.

Will some in heaven be happier than others? Scripture does teach rewards that differ: the servant with ten minas and the one with five are given different charges (Luke 19:16–19), and some works survive the fire while others are burned up (1 Corinthians 3:12–15). But no one in the city will be unhappy, envious or lacking. An old picture helps: a thimble and a bucket can both be full. Every vessel will be filled to the brim with God, and every redeemed person will rejoice in the honour given to the others. And every crown will be cast at the feet of the One who earned them all (4:10).

On a Tuesday. Live as someone whose Lord is bringing his reward with him. Do the unseen faithful thing, the visit, the gift, the patient answer to a difficult child, without needing anyone to notice; he notices.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life and that they may enter the city by the gates. Outside are the dogs and sorcerers and the sexually immoral and murderers and idolaters, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed are those who wash their robes. The seventh and last beatitude of Revelation, and it lands on the one act the whole book has been describing. Not blessed are those who understood it. Not blessed are those who suffered, though many did. Blessed are those who wash their robes, and 7:14 has already said in what: they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb. “Wash” (plynontes, present tense: keep washing). The one who trusts in Christ’s blood for cleansing, continually.

The right to the tree of life. “Right” (exousia, authority, right of access). The tree guarded by cherubim with a flaming sword since the fall is now available by right rather than by trespass. A right here does not mean something they earned. It is a standing Christ won and gives, as John wrote in his Gospel: to all who received him he gave the right to become children of God (John 1:12).

By the gates. Through the pearly gates, always open (21:25). A strangely ordinary phrase: not carried in, not admitted by a side door, but walking through the front gates like a citizen coming home.

Outside. “Outside” (exō), as in 21:8: those who persist in sin without repentance are excluded. Dogs were unclean scavengers in the street, and the law used the word of what was excluded from the sanctuary (Deuteronomy 23:18). Paul used it of men who insisted on adding requirements to the gospel (Philippians 3:2). “Loves and practices falsehood”: the followers of the father of lies, and the first verb is the sharper. Not merely tells lies: loves them. The dragon has been the deceiver of the whole world since 12:9, and the redeemed on Mount Zion were described in one clause: in their mouth no lie was found (14:5). At the very end, the line between the two companies runs through whether a person loved the truth. This does not mean they are just beyond the walls in the new creation; it means they are shut out of God’s presence, in the lake of fire (21:8).

In the flow. This last beatitude gathers the whole vision of 21:1–22:5 into one contrast. Inside are those who have washed, with the tree and the gates; outside is much the same list that 21:8 gave. The book has been showing since chapter 7 how a person passes from the second company to the first, and here it says it for the last time in a single verb: wash. Two verses later comes the invitation that tells anyone who will how to do it: come and take the water of life without price (v. 17).

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “Blessed are they that do his commandments” (poiountes tas entolas autou) instead of “Blessed are those who wash their robes” (plynontes tas stolas autōn). The two phrases look similar in Greek capital letters, and a tired copyist could slip from one to the other. The best and earliest manuscripts read “wash their robes”, and this fits 7:14 exactly. The difference is significant: access to the tree of life comes by cleansing in Christ’s blood, not by law-keeping. One reading makes the entrance depend on obedience; the other makes it depend on being washed. The manuscripts favour the second, and so does the book’s steady teaching that the Lamb’s blood is what makes people clean (1:5; 5:9; 7:14).

What it does not mean. The sins listed are not beyond forgiveness: anyone who washes their robes in the Lamb’s blood, whatever their past, may enter.

What does it mean to keep washing my robes? It means living by daily repentance and faith. You were washed once for all when you first trusted Christ: justified, forgiven, declared clean (1 Corinthians 6:11). But you still sin, and Jesus told Peter that one who has bathed needs only to wash his feet (John 13:10). So each day you bring your fresh sins to him, name them honestly, and trust his blood again, not to be saved again but to walk in the joy of being saved. John promises that when we confess our sins, God, faithful and just, forgives them and washes us clean of all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9).

On a Tuesday. End each day by naming before God where you failed, and thanking him by name for the blood that covers it. And love the truth, in what you say, what you watch and what you believe: the people of the city loved the truth because they loved the One who is the Truth.

For worship. Adam went out of the garden with nothing in his hands, and his children come back through open gates in robes washed white, to the tree he lost. Sinners from every list in this book, sorcerers, the immoral, liars, idolaters, have walked through those gates, because they washed in the fountain opened for sin and uncleanness (Zechariah 13:1), and the fountain is the Lamb’s own blood. Blessed be the Lamb, who makes the filthy clean and gives the outcast the right to come home.
verseByVerse.note: The last of the seven “blessed” sayings in Revelation. Some manuscripts read “do his commandments” for “wash their robes” (ESV note) — the reading of the King James Version.

verseByVerse.quote: "I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify to you about these things for the churches. I am the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Isaiah 11:1, 10 promises a shoot from the stump of Jesse, the root of Jesse, who will stand as a banner for the peoples. Numbers 24:17 says a star shall come out of Jacob, and a sceptre shall rise out of Israel. Peter speaks of the morning star rising in our hearts (2 Peter 1:19).

I, Jesus. The name at last. It is the only place in Revelation where Jesus names himself this way, and it comes after twenty-one chapters of titles: the Lamb, the faithful witness, the first and the last, the Word of God, King of kings. At the end he uses the name his mother used, the human name given to a carpenter’s son in a village. He personally guarantees the whole book. “To you” is plural: Revelation is a letter for every congregation in every age. This enormous vision, thrones and dragons and bowls and a city two thousand kilometres high, was produced for congregations, to be read aloud in rooms. So the close returns to 1:11 and its seven small assemblies on a road in Asia.

The root and the descendant of David. As in 5:5, both at once, and the pairing is deliberate. To be David’s descendant is to come after him, the promised son of the royal line, born in David’s town. To be David’s root is to be what David grew out of; a root is not produced by the tree, it produces the tree. Jesus once set that riddle himself, in the temple, and nobody could answer it: if David calls the Christ Lord, how is he his son? (Matthew 22:41–45). This verse is the answer, given by the man who asked the question. He is David’s son by birth and David’s Lord by nature, and the two belong to one person.

The bright morning star. The morning star is Venus, the planet the ancients counted among the stars, the brightest light in the sky before dawn, heralding the new day. Christ is the sign that the long night of this age is nearly over and the day of the new creation is about to dawn. As promised to Thyatira (2:28), the conqueror receives Christ himself. That promise, made to a church in what is often called the least important town of the seven, was never explained. Here it is: the morning star is himself. Behind it, very likely, stands the prophecy of Balaam, of all people: a star shall come out of Jacob. And the morning star rises when the sky is at its darkest and the night has gone on longest. It does not announce more night. It means the sun is on its way. Which is what this book has been saying to frightened congregations from its first page. It never promises that the dark will be short. It promises who is standing in it.

What it does not mean. The morning star title does not link Christ with Lucifer, the day star of Isaiah 14:12. The confusion is understandable, because the KJV’s Lucifer is simply the Latin word for the morning star, used there of a proud king’s fall. Christ is the true light; the fallen king of Babylon was a false one.

Why does it matter that he is both David’s root and son? Because only such a Saviour could save us. If Jesus were only David’s son, a good man of the royal line, he could not bear the infinite weight of our sin or give eternal life. If he were only David’s Lord, God but not man, he could not stand in our place, die our death or sympathise with our weakness. He is both, one person, true God and true man, as the Westminster Confession (8.2) and the 1689 London Baptist Confession (8.2) both confess. That is why he can be the Lamb who was slain and the Alpha and the Omega in the same chapter, and why you can trust him with everything.

On a Tuesday. When your night feels long, a grief that will not lift, a prayer still unanswered, a church in decline, look for the morning star. Christ does not promise that the dark is short; he promises that he is in it, and that he is the sign of the coming day. Say his name this week in the hard moment: Jesus. It is the name he chose to sign this book with, and it means the LORD saves.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 17–21 are the Bible’s last words. Verse 17: the last invitation, to the thirsty and to whoever desires, free of charge. Verses 18–19: a solemn warning against adding to or taking from the book (compare Deuteronomy 4:2). Verses 20–21: Christ’s final promise to come soon, the church’s answering prayer, and a closing blessing of grace.
verseByVerse.theology:
Come

The Spirit and the Bride say, “Come”; whoever hears is to say it too; whoever is thirsty may take the water of life without price. The book is not to be added to or taken from. Jesus says, “Surely I am coming soon,” and the church answers, “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!”
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The earliest church prayed Marana tha: Our Lord, come.

Now: A book full of judgement ends with grace, and the invitation is open to all.

verseByVerse.quote: The Spirit and the Bride say, "Come." And let the one who hears say, "Come." And let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Isaiah 55:1 invites: come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and he who has no money, come, buy and eat. Jesus stood up at the Feast of Booths and cried out, if anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink (John 7:37). He said, come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matthew 11:28).
