The last invitation. This is the last invitation in the Bible, the widest sentence in what many readers find the most frightening book in Scripture. After the dragon and the beast and the lake of fire and the great white throne, one of the last things God says to the human race is, come and have a drink. Four movements, built like a chain.

The Spirit and the Bride. “Come” (erchou). The Holy Spirit and the church speak together, with one verb between them. They pray to Christ, Come (as in v. 20), longing for his return. And they invite the world to come to Christ. The church, filled with the Spirit, both prays for Christ’s coming and calls sinners to come to him. That is the entire mission of the church in a few words, and it settles the relationship: the church does not invite people on its own authority, and the Spirit does not work around the church. They say it together.

The one who hears. Everyone who hears this book read in church (1:3) is to join the prayer and the invitation. The invitation is handed on. Anyone who has heard it becomes one of the people saying it, and there is no interval and no qualification: not the one who has matured, not the one who has been trained. The person who has just heard is immediately in the chorus.

The one who is thirsty. Now the direction reverses. The first two clauses were the church calling out; this one is somebody walking in. The invitation is to anyone who knows their need. Thirst is the only qualification: not worthiness, not understanding, not improvement.

Without price. The last clause takes away even the word thirsty, which might sound like a condition, and replaces it with whoever desires: whoever wishes, whoever will. Then the price is stated, in the same word as at 21:6: as a free gift. The last offer in the Bible is free grace. Isaiah shouted it seven centuries before Christ; Jesus shouted it on the last and greatest day of the feast; and he said it quietly to one woman at a well at noon (John 4:14).

The water comes from the Lamb. The invitation is to a Person, not to a principle. Five verses earlier the river of the water of life was flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb (22:1), and in the Gospel John wrote, Jesus says, whoever believes in me shall never thirst (John 6:35). To come is to come to him; to take is to trust him. The Lamb who was slain is the one holding out the cup.

Where the verse is placed. Two verses earlier the dogs and sorcerers and murderers were outside the gate. One verse later comes a solemn warning about tampering with the book. And in between, unfenced, is the freest offer in Scripture. That is not carelessness. It is the last word on the character of the God who has been running this entire book: the One whose judgements have filled most of the book ends by holding out a cup and asking nothing for it. So the answer to the question raised at 20:15, whether a name is written in the book of life, is not, have I done enough? Nobody has. It is whether a person is thirsty, and whether he will come and take what is being handed to him for nothing.

Where Christians differ: if salvation depends on God’s choice, is this invitation sincere? Some argue that if God has chosen who will be saved, a universal invitation is meaningless; others argue that the invitation proves people have free will to come in their own power. Both sides want to protect something true: God’s sovereignty, and the sincerity of his offer. This commentary’s view: the gospel invitation is sincere and is to be offered freely to everyone without exception. Whoever wants to may come, and no one who comes will be turned away (John 6:37). At the same time, no one comes unless the Father draws them (John 6:44), and those who come are those whose names were written in the Lamb’s book (13:8). God’s sovereign grace does not make the invitation less real; it makes it effective. The Spirit who says Come is the Spirit who gives the thirst and the will to come.

What if I am not sure I am chosen? Then come anyway, because the invitation is not addressed to the chosen; it is addressed to the thirsty, and to whoever desires. You do not need to read the Lamb’s book before you drink. You learn that your name is written there by coming, not before coming. No one has ever come to Christ and been told, sorry, you were not on the list. Jesus promised the opposite: whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37). Election is a comfort to those who have come, not a barrier for those still thinking about it. If you want the water, take it.

How do I actually invite someone? Simply, honestly and personally, as one thirsty person telling another where the water is (22:17). Pray for that person first, and ask God for an opening. Live in a way that raises questions. When the moment comes, speak of Christ himself, not only of church: who he is, what he did on the cross, and that the water of life is free. Ask, would you like to read one of the Gospels with me? or, can I tell you why I trust Jesus? Invite them to hear the word preached. And leave the results with the Spirit, who says Come alongside you.

verseByVerse.quote: I warn everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book: if anyone adds to them, God will add to him the plagues described in this book, and if anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God will take away his share in the tree of life and in the holy city, which are described in this book.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Moses warned Israel: you shall not add to the word that I command you, nor take from it (Deuteronomy 4:2; 12:32). Proverbs 30:6 says, do not add to his words, lest he rebuke you and you be found a liar. In the ancient world, authors sometimes added curses to their writings to prevent tampering, and treaties between kings could carry similar clauses.

I warn everyone. The verb means to testify, to declare solemnly. It is probably Jesus himself speaking (v. 20: he who testifies to these things), and the warning reaches every congregation and every reader. It is severe but not unprecedented: John is doing what a careful author did when the text was finished, sealing it against tampering.

The testimony of Jesus. The book being guarded is not a loose collection of predictions. Its first words name it: the revelation of Jesus Christ (1:1). Its last verses name the one who stands behind it: he who testifies to these things (v. 20), the faithful and true witness (3:14). To add to it is to put words in his mouth; to take away from it is to silence him. And the share that can be lost, in the tree of life and the holy city, is a share in him, for the tree grows by the river that flows from his throne and the city’s lamp is the Lamb. The warning is severe because what it guards is Christ’s own voice speaking to his churches.

If anyone adds. Adding to God’s word means claiming new revelation, new teaching with divine authority, or twisting the book with false prophecy: supplying what God did not say, the date, the identity, the extra requirement, the private revelation that completes what Scripture left open.

If anyone takes away. Taking away means removing, denying or ignoring parts of God’s word: its warnings, its judgements, its demands or its promises, quietly setting aside the judgement, or the exclusivity, or the return, because it is unpopular or uncomfortable. The penalty is the loss of eternal life itself. Such a person shows they never truly belonged to the Lamb. And the penalties fit the offences exactly, as everything in this book does. Add to the words, and what is added to you is the plagues; take away from the words, and what is taken from you is the tree and the city. In each case a person receives the operation he performed.

Textual note. Where modern Bibles read his share in the tree of life, the KJV reads his part out of the book of life. Almost all Greek manuscripts have tree, and book seems to have entered the printed Greek text from the Latin, so modern Bibles follow the manuscripts; the meaning is much the same.

Where Christians differ: does this verse close the whole canon of Scripture? Strictly, the warning applies to the book of Revelation. Some therefore argue it says nothing about the rest of the Bible. Others give a later voice authority beside Scripture: Roman Catholic teaching sets sacred Tradition, as interpreted by the church, alongside the Bible, and groups such as the Latter-day Saints add new scriptures like the Book of Mormon. Most Christians who believe God still gives prophetic words today make no such claim, and agree that nothing may be added to Scripture. This commentary’s view: the direct reference is to Revelation, but it applies the principle of Deuteronomy 4:2 to the final book of the New Testament, written, as the early church believed, by the last surviving apostle, and it fittingly closes the whole canon. With the death of the apostles, the foundation was laid (Ephesians 2:20), and the faith was once for all delivered to the saints (Jude 3). God has spoken his final word in his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2). Scripture is complete and sufficient (2 Timothy 3:16–17). No later revelation, vision, tradition or book may be added to it with equal authority, and no part of it may be removed. This commentary holds that the canon is closed and Scripture alone is our final authority.

What it does not mean. The warning does not condemn faithful copying, translation or teaching of the Bible. It condemns deliberately adding false teaching to it or cutting out what we do not like. Comparing manuscripts to establish what John actually wrote is the opposite of tampering with what John wrote: it is the effort to make sure nothing has been added or lost. The textual notes in this commentary are that work being done honestly and in the open.

Can a true believer lose his salvation by taking away from this book? No. The warning describes those who falsify God’s word, and shows that such people never truly belonged to Christ: they went out from us, but they were not of us (1 John 2:19). Christ’s sheep will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of his hand (John 10:28). For believers the warning is a solemn reason to handle Scripture with reverence, and one of the means God uses to keep them faithful. A Christian who misunderstands a verse, or struggles to believe a hard one, is not what this describes. It describes the person who sets himself above the word and edits God.

What about Christians who hear words from God today? This commentary holds, charitably, that the gifts of new revelation ceased with the apostles, because the foundation has been laid and Scripture is complete. Many dear brothers and sisters believe God still gives prophetic words, and most of them would agree that no such word can add to Scripture, bind the conscience or carry its authority. That agreement is what matters most here. Test every impression, dream or prophecy by the written word (1 Thessalonians 5:20–21; 1 John 4:1). If anything claims to add a new doctrine, a new requirement or a new date, this verse says: do not receive it. The Bible is enough.

What about the extra books in some Bibles? The books called the Apocrypha, found in Roman Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, were not part of the Hebrew Scriptures that Jesus and the apostles received, and they are never quoted in the New Testament as Scripture. The Reformed confessions say they are not inspired, and are no part of the canon, though they may be read as human writings with some historical value (the Westminster Confession 1.3; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.3). The sixty-six books of the Old and New Testaments are the whole of God’s written word. This is not the church deciding what God said, but the church recognising the books God gave.

On a Tuesday. Few readers will ever publish an edition of Revelation, but many are tempted to do privately what the verse forbids: to add a chart the text does not authorise, or to skip the parts that are hard to hear. Which passages do you avoid? Read one of them this week, slowly, and ask God to make you willing to receive it.

verseByVerse.quote: He who testifies to these things says, "Surely I am coming soon." Amen. Come, Lord Jesus! The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Paul ended his letters with a grace blessing, and Revelation ends as a letter, as it began (1:4).

Surely I am coming soon. He who testifies is Jesus, the faithful witness (1:5), and surely means yes, truly. The third and final I am coming soon in this chapter, the last recorded words of Jesus Christ in the Bible. Not a command, not a warning, not a doctrine. A promise about arriving. Everything he is has been unfolded across twenty-two chapters: the one who walks among the lampstands, the Lamb who was slaughtered and is standing, the rider with a sword out of his mouth, the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star. And the last thing he says is that he is on his way and will not be long. John answers for the church with Amen, so be it. It is the only fitting reply, and it is barely a word: an agreement.

Come, Lord Jesus! The church answers Christ’s promise with a request, the Greek form of Maranatha. In Aramaic, the language of the first believers in Jerusalem, it was a single short phrase: Marana tha, Our Lord, come. Paul dropped it untranslated into a letter to Corinth (1 Corinthians 16:22), and it appears in the early church manual called the Didache (10:6), which suggests it was already a prayer people said without needing it explained. The final prayer of the Bible: the prayer of a bride for her bridegroom, of a persecuted church for its deliverer, of a groaning creation for its renewal (Romans 8:22–23). Not fear, but longing: that is the state of the church between the two comings, and it is the answer to everything the book has shown. Not a strategy. Not a timetable. A prayer that Someone would come, said by people who cannot make him come and are certain he will.

A gentle test. It is a fair test of a Christian’s actual condition, gently applied. A person who says Come, Lord Jesus and means it is a person who has nothing here he would be unwilling to have interrupted. That is not a rebuke to anybody who finds the prayer harder than he expected; it is simply what the prayer measures. And Revelation was written to people who could say it because they had already lost most of what a person might have wanted to keep. If the test finds you wanting, you are not lost: the wish to want him more is already his Spirit at work in you, and he teaches this prayer to anyone who asks.

Grace. The last verse of the Bible is a benediction. Four horsemen. A third of mankind dead. A dragon waiting to devour a child. A beast given authority over every tribe and people and language and nation. Bowls of wrath. A city drunk on the blood of the saints, burned in a single hour. A great white throne with the books opened and no place found for earth or sky. It is among the most terrifying documents ever written. And the last word is grace. Not a warning, though there have been many, and not instructions for a final generation, but the same word Paul ended every one of his letters with: unearned favour given to people who have nothing to bring. Everything in it, from the first word to the last, rests on the grace of the Lord Jesus. And then the last word of the Bible, Amen: it is firm; it is so.

Textual note. The manuscripts differ on the last line. Some read “with all”; others, “with all the saints” (followed, for example, by the RSV); others, followed by the King James Version, “with you all”. The meaning is essentially the same: grace for all God’s people. Some manuscripts omit the final Amen.

What it does not mean. “With all” does not mean that grace will save everyone regardless of faith. The blessing is for those who hear and keep the words of this book (1:3), the church to which it is addressed.

So the Bible closes. It opened with a garden, a river and a tree, and a man and a woman walking with God in the cool of the day; and it closes with a city, a river and a tree, and a countless multitude out of every nation looking directly at his face. Between the two a curse fell on the ground and was carried away on a cross, and the whole of human history ran its course; and at the centre of it stands a Lamb, looking as though it had been slaughtered, who took a scroll nobody else was worthy to open, and opened it.

What if I find it hard to pray Come, Lord Jesus? Nothing need be wrong with you; you are being honest, and honesty is where prayer starts. Many believers love this world’s good gifts, a marriage, children, a calling, and fear losing them, or fear the judgement itself. Bring both to God. Remember that his coming does not take away any good thing; it gives every good thing back, perfected, with him at the centre. Remember that the Judge is your Saviour, so you need not fear condemnation. And ask him to make you long for him more than his gifts. Pray the prayer even when it is small; desire grows by being exercised, and he is pleased with the smallest true longing.

How should I live while I wait? Watchfully, not anxiously; busily, not idly. Jesus told parables of servants who were found working when the master came (Matthew 24:45–46), and Paul rebuked those who stopped working to wait for the end (2 Thessalonians 3:10–12). So do your work well, love your family, serve your church, tell others about Christ, and keep your hope fixed on his coming (Titus 2:13). Do not try to set dates; do not let the delay make you careless. Live every day as one of his servants who may be called to give account tonight, and who would be glad of it.

Is longing for Christ’s return just a way of escaping the world? No, the reverse. Escapism wants to get away from the world and leave it as it is. This prayer asks the Lord to come to the world and put it right: to lift the curse, judge the oppressor, dry the tears and make all things new (21:4–5; 22:3). That is why the hope makes believers more useful here, not less. Those who know that their labour in the Lord is not in vain can give themselves to it fully (1 Corinthians 15:58), and those who know the Judge is coming can leave vengeance to him and love their enemies now (Romans 12:19–21). The prayer is not a retreat. It is the church asking for the one thing that will finally make every good work complete.

On a Tuesday. Make this your prayer every day: Come, Lord Jesus. Say it in the morning before you look at your phone, at night when you lie down, at the graveside and when the news is bad. You do not have to hold yourself together until he comes; his grace is with you, and it will be enough for every day between now and then.

For worship. He is the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end. He was dead, and behold, he is alive for evermore, and he has the keys of Death and Hades. He walks among his churches, he holds the stars in his right hand, he opened the scroll no one else could open, and he is coming soon. The last thing he says to his people is a promise, and the last thing he leaves with them, after everything, is grace. To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honour and glory and might for ever and ever. Amen. Come, Lord Jesus.
verseByVerse.note: “Come, Lord Jesus” matches the Aramaic prayer Maranatha that Paul quotes.

The leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations.<sup>3</sup>No longer will there be anything accursed, but the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants will worship him.<sup>4</sup>They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads.<sup>5</sup>And night will be no more. They will need no light of lamp or sun, for the Lord God will be their light, and they will reign forever and ever.<sup>6</sup>And he said to me, “These words are trustworthy and true. And the Lord, the God of the spirits of the prophets, has sent his angel to show his servants what must soon take place.”<sup>7</sup>“And behold, I am coming soon. Blessed is the one who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book.”<sup>8</sup>I, John, am the one who heard and saw these things. And when I heard and saw them, I fell down to worship at the feet of the angel who showed them to me,<sup>9</sup>but he said to me, “You must not do that! Worship God.”<sup>10</sup>And he said to me, “Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near.<sup>11</sup>Let the evildoer still do evil, and the filthy still be filthy, and the righteous still do right, and the holy still be holy.”<sup>12</sup>“Behold, I am coming soon, bringing my recompense with me, to repay each one for what he has done.<sup>13</sup>I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end.”<sup>14</sup>Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life and that they may enter the city by the gates.<sup>15</sup>Outside are the dogs and sorcerers and the sexually immoral and murderers and idolaters, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood.<sup>16</sup>“I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify to you about these things for the churches. Come, Lord Jesus!<sup>21</sup>The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all. Amen.

15.title: The Song of Moses and the Lamb
15.overview:
Chapter 15, eight verses long, prepares for the seven bowls of chapter 16, as chapters 4–5 prepared for the seals and 8:1–5 for the trumpets: before a single bowl is poured, the coming judgements are set inside the worship and rule of God. Heaven sings before it acts.

There are two scenes. In vv. 1–4 those who conquered the beast stand beside the sea of glass with harps and sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb. In vv. 5–8 seven angels come out of the heavenly sanctuary, receive seven golden bowls, and the sanctuary fills with God’s glory so that no one can enter until the plagues are finished. The song comes first so that the judgements are not misread.

The song joins God’s two great saving acts, the exodus and the cross: the God who opened the Red Sea is the God who opened the tomb. Its words are drawn almost entirely from the Psalms, Jeremiah and Deuteronomy.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The Song of the Victorious
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1: the third and last sign in heaven, after the woman and the dragon of chapter 12: seven angels with the last plagues, in which the wrath of God is finished.

Verses 2–4: beside the sea of glass, now mingled with fire, stand those who conquered the beast, like Israel on the far shore of the Red Sea. They sing one song of Moses and the Lamb, made of Scripture and entirely about God: his deeds, his ways, his name and his righteous acts.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Song of Moses and the Lamb

Seven angels hold the last plagues, and with them God’s wrath is finished: it has an end, as his mercy does not. Beside the sea of glass, those who conquered the beast sing one song of Moses and the Lamb, made of Scripture and entirely about God.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Those the beast conquered in the street are standing on the far shore with harps.

Now: Faithfulness that consists in refusing to bow still counts as conquering.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw another sign in heaven, great and amazing, seven angels with seven plagues, which are the last, for with them the wrath of God is finished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Revelation 15 is the shortest chapter in the book, and it gets the reader ready for the seven bowls of chapter 16, the last plagues, which complete God’s wrath (v. 1). Before they fall, John sees those who conquered the beast standing beside a sea of glass mixed with fire, holding harps (v. 2). Like Israel beside the Red Sea, they sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb: God’s deeds are great, his ways just and true, and all nations will worship him (vv. 3–4). Then the heavenly sanctuary, the tent of witness, opens; seven angels dressed as priests come out and receive seven golden bowls full of God’s wrath, and smoke from his glory fills the sanctuary so that no one can enter until the plagues are finished (vv. 5–8). The judgements are set inside worship: before a single drop falls, heaven has already sung that every one of God’s ways is just and true.

The setting. The bowl judgements follow the pattern of the plagues on Egypt even more closely than the trumpets did: sores, water turned to blood, darkness, frogs, hail. And the scene by the sea of glass recalls Israel singing beside the Red Sea after God destroyed Pharaoh’s army (Exodus 15). The new exodus is complete. John’s first readers, small congregations in Asia under the shadow of Rome, would have heard the whole story of their own deliverance in the shape of the one their Bible began with: a tyrant who would not let God’s people go, plagues that broke his power, a sea, a far shore, and a song.

Another sign in heaven. John has used it of signs in heaven twice before, both times in chapter 12: the woman clothed with the sun (12:1) and the great red dragon (12:3). This is the third and last. A woman, a dragon, and seven angels with the last plagues: the mother, the enemy, and the end. This sign announces the book’s final movement.

Great and amazing. It is an odd pair of words for a plague, and John will use them again in two verses about God’s deeds. What is being described is not merely dreadful but astonishing. The plagues are not the collapse of God’s plan. They are one of his works, and heaven looks at them the way it looks at creation and redemption: with wonder.

The last plagues. The word for plagues means blows, strokes. And they are the last: the final series. The seals struck a quarter of the earth (6:8), the trumpets a third (8:7–12); the bowls strike everything. Each series has been wider than the one before: first a warning, then a louder warning, and now the end.

The wrath of God is finished. This is the clause that governs the whole of chapter 16. The verb means to complete, to carry to its goal, the same root as the word Jesus spoke from the cross: it is finished (John 19:30). Something is being brought to its appointed completion, and the sentence says so before a single bowl is lifted.

The wrath of God has an end. That is a strange and necessary thing to be told at this point in the book, to readers who might fear that it is a reservoir with no bottom. God’s wrath in history has a goal, and there is a last plague after which there are no more.

His mercy has no last plague. And that is not true of his mercy, which is the point of the contrast. Scripture says again and again that his steadfast love endures for ever, and it never once says that of his anger. His anger is for a moment and his favour for a lifetime (Psalm 30:5). He does not keep his anger for ever, because he delights in steadfast love (Micah 7:18). His judgements in history always have a stopping point written into them. His grace has none.

Two places where wrath is finished. There is one more thing in the word finished. If the wrath of God against sin is a thing that can be completed, the question worth asking is where it was completed for a Christian, and the answer is the cross, where John’s Gospel uses the same verb, and where, as the rest of the New Testament teaches, the same wrath fell (Romans 3:25; Galatians 3:13; 1 John 4:10). There, God’s wrath against his people’s sin was finished, borne in full by Christ in their place. Here, his wrath against the unrepentant world is completed. There are two places in John’s writings where the wrath of God is brought to its end. One of them is a hill outside Jerusalem, and for everyone who trusts in Christ it happened before any of this began.

What it does not mean. “Last” does not necessarily mean the bowls happen after the seals and trumpets in strict time. They are the last in John’s sequence of visions and in their intensity, describing the final outpouring of God’s judgement, which the earlier series also reached in their own way (6:12–17; 11:15–19).

Does finished mean the wicked stop being punished? No. The wrath of God is finished in the sense that his judgements on this present age reach their goal: the plagues stop, history is wound up, and Christ returns. But Revelation is plain that the punishment of those who refuse him is conscious and without end (14:10–11; 20:10, 15). What is finished in chapter 16 is the series of warning blows in history, the last chances given to a rebellious world. After that comes not a pause and a fresh start but the final judgement. That is exactly why the word finished is such good news for a Christian and such a solemn one for anyone else.

How can a God of love have wrath at all? Because a love that could watch the beloved destroyed and feel nothing would not be love at all. There is nothing petulant or unbalanced in God’s wrath. It is the same holiness that makes him faithful and kind, turned against evil, and a God who stayed calm while his children were harmed would not be more loving for it. The conquerors by the sea in the next verses do not apologise for his judgements; they sing that his ways are just and true (15:3). And the gospel does not say that God set his wrath aside to love us. It says that he loved us so much that he bore his own wrath in his Son (Romans 3:25–26; 1 John 4:10). The cross is where love and wrath meet, and neither is diminished.

On a Tuesday. When the news is full of disaster, remember that nothing in it is beyond God’s measuring: even his judgements are counted, seven, and the last. And when you think of friends who do not know Christ, let the word last move you. The blows will not go on for ever, and the time to turn is now.

For worship. Great and amazing is the God who measures even his anger. He counted the blows, seven and the last, and set a boundary to his wrath as he set one to the sea: thus far shall you come, and no farther (Job 38:11). His steadfast love was given no such boundary; it is from everlasting to everlasting on those who fear him (Psalm 103:17).

verseByVerse.quote: And I saw what appeared to be a sea of glass mingled with fire—and also those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name, standing beside the sea of glass with harps of God in their hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Israel crossed the Red Sea and stood on the far shore, safe, while the waters closed over Pharaoh’s army (Exodus 14:26–31). Then Moses and Israel sang (Exodus 15:1–18), and Miriam led the women with tambourines (Exodus 15:20–21). The sea of glass first appeared before God’s throne in 4:6, flat and still and clear as crystal.

A sea of glass mingled with fire. In chapter 4 the sea of glass was stretched out in front of the throne, calm and transparent: the sea, which in the Bible stands for chaos and the place the beast came up from (13:1), still as crystal and lying subdued under God’s feet. Now there is fire in it. Something has changed in the eleven chapters between, and the fire is judgement: the same fire that was taken from the altar and thrown down on the earth (8:5), or the reflection of God’s blazing holiness. The floor of heaven has begun to glow.

Those who had conquered. The verb seems to contradict something the reader was told two chapters ago. At 13:7 the beast was allowed to conquer the saints. Here the same people are the conquering ones. One verb tells the same encounter both ways.

Both statements are true. Holding them together is one of the main things this book asks of a suffering Christian. From the street, the beast won: the believers were arrested, tried and killed. From the sea of glass, they won: they are standing, with instruments in their hands, and the beast is not in the room. And 12:11 has already explained how a defeat becomes a victory: by the Lamb’s blood and the word of testimony, held even to death. The winning was not survival. It was refusing to let go, and the losing of the life was part of the victory rather than a failure of it.

A victory made of refusals. Note what they conquered, listed in three parts: the beast and its image and the number of its name. Not an army, but a demand. They were not asked to defeat anything. They were asked to bow, to worship an image, and to take a number that would have let them keep buying and selling (13:16–17). Their whole victory consists of things they did not do. They said no to a formality, again and again, at rising cost, and heaven files that under conquered.

Beside the sea of glass. The preposition can mean beside or upon, and the picture is Israel on the far shore of the Red Sea with the water behind them and Egypt at the bottom of it, which is exactly what the next verse makes explicit. They have come through the great tribulation (7:14), and the first thing they do is sing.

Harps of God. Harps given by God for his worship (5:8; 14:2). Even the instruments are his gift. The people who were stripped of everything on earth, their freedom, their trade, their lives, are handed something in heaven, and what they are handed is a way to praise him.

What is the beast today, and what is its mark? In Revelation the beast is the power of the state or culture when it sets itself up as God, demanding the loyalty that belongs to Christ alone; Rome was its form in John’s day, and it takes new forms in every age until the end. Its mark is not a microchip or a tattoo that someone could receive by accident. It is the stamp of belonging, seen in what a person thinks (the forehead) and does (the hand), the opposite of the seal of God on his servants (7:3; 14:1). So the question is not whether you have been scanned but whom you worship, and whether you will keep your loyalty to Christ when it costs you.

I have never been persecuted. Am I really among the conquerors? If you belong to Christ and are holding fast to him, yes. Conquering in this book is not measured by how dramatic the pressure was but by whether faith held. For most believers the beast’s demands come quietly: the colleague who expects you to laugh along, the promotion that requires a lie, the cultural script that says your faith must stay private, the slow pull of comfort and money. Every time you choose Christ over those, you are refusing the image and the number. And the strength to do it is his gift, not your achievement. He keeps his people, and every one of them will stand on that shore (John 10:28–29).

On a Tuesday. When a fellow believer is losing something real for Christ, a job, a friendship, a reputation, tell them what this verse tells you: from the street it looks like defeat, but from the sea of glass it is victory.

verseByVerse.quote: And they sing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, "Great and amazing are your deeds, O Lord God the Almighty! Just and true are your ways, O King of the nations! Who will not fear, O Lord, and glorify your name? For you alone are holy. All nations will come and worship you, for your righteous acts have been revealed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. The song of Moses in Exodus 15 celebrated God’s victory over Pharaoh: who is like you, O LORD, among the gods? Who is like you, majestic in holiness? (Exodus 15:11). Deuteronomy 32, another song of Moses, says that God’s work is perfect, that all his ways are justice, that he is a God of faithfulness, without iniquity, just and upright (Deuteronomy 32:4). Psalm 98:1–2 and Malachi 1:11 also stand behind the new song.

The song of Moses and of the Lamb. Probably not two songs but one. The grammar allows a single song called by two names, and the content suggests it: what follows is sung by both at once, because there is only one deliverance and it has two chapters. The song of Moses is Exodus 15, sung on the far side of the sea with Pharaoh’s army drowned behind them. Israel came out of Egypt through water; these have come out of the beast’s empire through fire and death; and the song is the same song, because the God who did the first did the second.

Moses the servant, Christ the Lamb. Moses is called the servant of God, which is his great title in the Old Testament (Numbers 12:7; Joshua 1:2). The letter to the Hebrews draws the line exactly: Moses was faithful in all God’s house as a servant, but Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son (Hebrews 3:5–6). The servant led the people through the sea; the Lamb led them through death by going into it first. The redeemed sing both names because the whole Bible is one story, and Moses was always pointing to the one whose song this finally is.

The redeemed sing in quotations. Here is something surprising. The words that follow hardly quote Exodus 15 at all. They are a mosaic of the Psalms and the prophets, stitched together. Great and amazing are your deeds (Psalm 111:2; 139:14). Just and true are your ways (Deuteronomy 32:4; Psalm 145:17). Who would not fear you, O King of the nations? (Jeremiah 10:7). All the nations shall come and worship (Psalm 86:9). The worship of heaven is made out of the Scriptures God’s people were given on earth, which is a quiet argument for filling a mind with them now. The Bible you read this morning is the hymnbook of eternity.

Every line is about God. Look at what the song is about, because it is not what a persecuted church would have been expected to sing. There is not one word in it about the beast, about the persecution, about what they suffered, or about their own endurance. Four clauses, and every one of them is about God: his deeds, his ways, his name, his righteous acts. The singers have forgotten themselves entirely; their own story has become a footnote to his. Much of our singing and praying is about our own feelings and needs. Heaven reverses that, and the people who stop making themselves the subject are not made smaller. They are freer and happier than they have ever been.

Great and amazing. His deeds in creation, redemption and judgement. Almighty, as in 1:8, is the one who holds all things. The beast seemed to rule the world for forty-two months; the singers know who was holding it the whole time.

Just and true. True here is faithful, genuine, real. Before the bowls are poured out, the redeemed declare that God’s ways are just. His judgements are not arbitrary or cruel; they are right. Anybody can affirm the justice of God from a comfortable chair. These people were killed for refusing a number, they have come out the other side, and the first thing they say about the way God ran history is that it was just. No complaint. Not because the question was never asked: it was asked, loudly, under the altar in 6:10, how long, O Lord? But it has been answered.

Who will not fear, O Lord, and glorify your name? The question is rhetorical and expects the answer nobody: everyone ought to fear him and give him glory. To fear God here is not to cower but to stand in awe, to take him with the seriousness he deserves. The song has just praised his justice and now calls the whole world to respond to it.

You alone are holy. The ground given is not power but holiness, a word used of God in Revelation only here and in 16:5. You alone: there is one of him, and the beast that demanded worship for forty-two months is not in the category. Every rival claim to ultimate loyalty, ancient or modern, is answered by those four words.

All nations will come. This is the widest sentence in the chapter, and it is startling in a book so full of judgement. The nations who raged (11:18), who drank Babylon’s wine (14:8), over whom the beast was given authority (13:7), will come and worship. It is Psalm 86:9 quoted almost straight, and it is the promise made to Abraham that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3). Righteous acts are God’s just deeds, his judgements and his saving acts. What finally brings the nations in is not that God overwhelmed them, but that his righteous acts were seen clearly. This looks to the great multitude from every nation (7:9) and to the nations walking by the light of the new Jerusalem (21:24–26). God will have the nations, and the multitude is not a consolation prize.

In the flow. Behind the song is the warning of 14:9–11, and ahead of it the seven bowls, so the reader enters the plagues already knowing heaven’s verdict on them. Chapter 16 will repeat that verdict from inside the judgement, when the angel of the waters and the altar answer in the same words, just and true (16:5–7).

Textual note. The manuscripts differ on God’s title in v. 3. The best manuscripts read “King of the nations”; others read “King of the ages”; later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “King of saints”. All three are true of God; “nations” fits the song’s theme of all nations coming to worship.

Where Christians differ: will all nations, and so all people, be saved? Universalists sometimes cite “all nations will come and worship you” as proof that everyone will finally be saved. This commentary’s view: “all nations” means people from every nation, not every individual in every nation. The great multitude comes from every nation, tribe, people and language (7:9), but Revelation is clear that those who worship the beast and refuse to repent are judged for ever (14:9–11; 21:8; 22:15). The song celebrates the worldwide scope of God’s salvation, fulfilling his promise to Abraham, and the universal acknowledgement of his justice. Every knee will bow (Philippians 2:10–11), but not every knee bows in love.

How can people in heaven praise God for judging people they loved? Because in heaven they will see what we only believe now: that God has been perfectly fair to every person, that no one is condemned who did not freely refuse him, and that his patience was longer than anyone deserved. Our hesitation comes partly from our love, which is good, and partly from our limited sight and our sense that sin is not so bad, which is not. The redeemed will not love less. They will love as God loves, and see as God sees. Until then, the right response to the thought of the lost is not to doubt God’s justice but to plead with people while there is time, and to trust the Judge of all the earth to do right (Genesis 18:25).

Should we still sing of God’s justice in church? Yes. The songs of heaven are full of it, and a church that sings only of God’s comfort and never of his holiness and justice is singing a smaller God than the one who is there. It matters especially for persecuted and wronged believers, for whom the justice of God is not a threat but a hope: no evil will go unanswered. Songs like this teach us to rest in his rule. And it should always be sung with the cross in view, because the justice that will judge the world is the justice that was satisfied for us in Christ.

On a Tuesday. When you cannot understand what God is doing, in your own life or in the world, say this song before you say anything else: your ways are just and true. You may still bring the question; the martyrs did. But bring it as someone who already knows how the song ends.
verseByVerse.note: As Israel sang beside the sea after the exodus, so God’s redeemed sing after their deliverance.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–8 — The Sanctuary Filled with Smoke
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 5–6: the sanctuary of the tent of witness, where the covenant law is kept, opens, and seven angels in priestly linen and golden sashes come out of it.

Verses 7–8: one of the four living creatures hands them seven golden bowls full of God’s wrath, and smoke from his glory fills the sanctuary, so that no one can enter until the plagues are finished.
verseByVerse.theology:
Judgement as Liturgy

The bowls come out of the tent of witness, carried by angels in priestly linen and handed over by a worshipper. The golden bowls that once held prayers now hold wrath, and the sanctuary is closed until the plagues are finished.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The judgement rests on the covenant kept since Sinai.

Now: The sanctuary is open today, with a high priest interceding inside it: pray while it is.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I looked, and the sanctuary of the tent of witness in heaven was opened, and out of the sanctuary came the seven angels with the seven plagues, clothed in pure, bright linen, with golden sashes around their chests.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. The tabernacle in the wilderness was called the tent of witness or testimony (Numbers 17:7; 18:2), because it held the ark containing the tablets of the law, the testimony of God’s covenant (Exodus 25:16; 31:18; 38:21; Numbers 1:50). The priests wore white linen when they entered the holy place (Leviticus 16:4). Christ in 1:13 wore a golden sash around his chest, and Daniel’s heavenly man was clothed in linen with a belt of fine gold (Daniel 10:5).

The tent of witness. The sanctuary is the inner shrine, the holy place itself, and the tent of witness is the heavenly reality of which the earthly tabernacle was a copy (Hebrews 8:5). The phrase is precise and old. The ark held the two tablets of the law, which are called the testimony because they are God’s witness to the covenant, and his witness against a people who agreed to keep it and did not.

Wrath from the place where the covenant is kept. So the bowls of wrath come out of the place where the covenant is kept. Not out of an armoury and not out of a prison, but out of the tent that holds God’s law. That is the difference between the judgements of this book and mere destruction. What is coming has a legal basis, and the document it rests on has been in the same box since Sinai.

The lid on the box. In the tabernacle the tablets of the testimony lay inside the ark, and over them was the mercy seat, where once a year the high priest sprinkled the blood of the sin offering (Leviticus 16:14–15). The law was never meant to stand in that tent without blood above it. Paul uses that very word of Christ: God put him forward as a propitiation by his blood (Romans 3:25), using the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the mercy seat. A propitiation is a sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath by bearing it. It is not a bribe that changes God’s mind; it is God himself providing the blood that covers the sin (1 John 4:10). So the tent that sends out the bowls also holds the answer for anyone in Christ: the law’s witness against them is covered by his blood. The bowls fall on those who refused the covering, and they face the testimony bare.

Out of the sanctuary. At 11:19 the sanctuary opened to show the ark; now it opens again to release seven angels from God’s very presence. The judgements are holy acts, carried out by those who stand before God.

Pure, bright linen. They are dressed as priests. Linen was what the priest wore into the holy place (Leviticus 16:4), and a golden sash across the chest is exactly how the risen Christ was dressed in the first chapter of this book (1:13). The sashes show their dignity and their connection with him. And the linen is pure and bright: the second word is the one used of the Bride’s dress at 19:8. Nothing that comes out of that door is dirty. Whatever a reader has to say about the severity of chapter 16, he will not be able to say that the hands carrying it were.

Judgement as liturgy. That combination refuses two easy pictures at once. These are not demons let loose, and they are not soldiers. They are ministers in priestly dress, coming out of a sanctuary, carrying out a service. The angels do not act on their own initiative; the judgement of God is not a loss of control. It is worship. The same holiness that is praised in the song is carried out in the plagues.

Why does God’s law still matter if Christians are not saved by keeping it? Because the law is the expression of God’s own holy character, and it is the standard by which the world is judged (Romans 2:12–16; 3:19–20). It cannot save us; it shows us our need of Christ, who kept it perfectly and bore its curse for us (Galatians 3:13). But for the believer it remains the good and holy rule of life, now written on the heart by the Spirit (Jeremiah 31:33; Romans 8:4). The tent of witness in heaven tells us that God has not lowered his standard. What he has done is meet it himself, in his Son.

On a Tuesday. Take God’s law seriously in your own life: not as a price to pay for God’s favour, but as the shape of the life he is making in you. Read the Ten Commandments this week and ask, honestly, where your heart is out of step with them. Then take each failure to the one who kept them all for you.

verseByVerse.quote: And one of the four living creatures gave to the seven angels seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God who lives forever and ever, and the sanctuary was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power, and no one could enter the sanctuary until the seven plagues of the seven angels were finished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Golden bowls were used in the temple for carrying incense and the blood of sacrifices (1 Kings 7:50; 2 Chronicles 4:22). The golden bowls of 5:8 were full of incense, the prayers of the saints.

Seven golden bowls. The handover is made by one of the four living creatures, the beings nearest the throne, full of eyes, who have been saying holy, holy, holy day and night without ceasing (4:8). The worshippers are the ones who pass the bowls. Nothing in this chapter allows judgement to be handled by anybody outside the worship of God.

A bowl, not a trumpet. The bowl is a shallow, wide dish used for pouring out an offering, not a jug or a jar. It empties in a moment. Compare the trumpets: a trumpet is a warning, blown to be heard, giving time to respond. A bowl is tipped once, and it is gone. The instrument itself says that the time of warnings is running out.

The same bowls. The reader has seen golden bowls in this book before, and the connection is deliberate and almost unbearable. At 5:8 the elders held golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints. Golden bowls went up full of prayer; golden bowls come down full of wrath. God’s judgement is the answer to his people’s prayers. The martyrs asked how long? and these are the vessels in which the answer is delivered.

Full of the wrath of God. Filled to the brim. This wrath is not a mood that passes. It is holiness set against evil, and it belongs to the one who lives for ever and ever, which means no tyrant can outlive it and no evil can wait it out.

Smoke from the glory of God. Smoke filling the sanctuary is an old and glorious sight. When the tabernacle was finished, the cloud covered the tent of meeting, the glory of the LORD filled it, and Moses was not able to enter (Exodus 40:34–35). When Solomon dedicated the temple, the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of the LORD filled the house (1 Kings 8:10–11). Isaiah saw the house filled with smoke and cried, woe is me (Isaiah 6:4–5). It is God’s glory and power in overwhelming holiness, as at Sinai.

No one could enter. At the tabernacle and the temple the smoke meant God had come to dwell, and the exclusion was brief and joyful. Here it means something colder. Consider what the sanctuary is for. It is where a priest goes in to intercede, where blood is brought and pleading is done and mercy is asked for somebody else. And for the duration of the seven bowls, nobody goes in. On this reading the moment is deeply solemn: the door of intercession closes. There comes a point at which the door is shut, not because God has become unwilling to hear, but because the case has been closed, the warnings have been given, and the answering has begun.

Until. But note the exact wording, because it is also the mercy in the verse: until. The closure has a limit, and the limit is the one given in verse 1, when the wrath of God is finished. Even the shutting of the sanctuary has an end date, and beyond it lies the new creation, where the dwelling of God is with man (21:3) and no one is ever shut out of his presence again.

The curtain that was torn. This verse marks the end of an age that began on the afternoon Jesus died. Then the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom (Mark 15:38), and the letter to the Hebrews explains what that meant: we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh (Hebrews 10:19–20). The whole age in which the church prays and the gospel is preached is the age of the open sanctuary, held open by a crucified High Priest. The smoke in this verse marks the day that age is over. Until then, the way in is his body, and it has never once been closed to anyone who came.

What it does not mean. This does not mean that today it is too late to pray or to turn to God. The scene describes the final judgement at the end of history. Today is still the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2), and Christ still intercedes for all who come to God through him (Hebrews 7:25).

Should I pray for God to judge my enemies? Pray first, as Jesus commanded, for their good and their salvation (Matthew 5:44), as Stephen did for the men stoning him (Acts 7:60). That is the Christian’s first prayer. Yet it is also right to pray for God’s kingdom to come and for evil to be ended, and the martyrs’ cry for justice is not rebuked (6:9–11). The answer is to leave vengeance with God (Romans 12:19). He will judge rightly, and he may answer your prayer for justice by turning your enemy into a brother, as he did with Saul of Tarsus. Either way, you do not have to carry the score.

Could it already be too late for me? If you are worried that you have gone too far, that worry is itself a sign that the door is still open. The people shut out in this verse are not anxious seekers; they are those who refused every warning to the end. As long as you are alive and Christ is still offered to you, the sanctuary is open and the High Priest is inside it, praying for those who come to God through him. No one who comes to Christ is ever turned away (John 6:37). Do not wait to feel ready. Come now.

On a Tuesday. While the sanctuary stands open, pray: for yourself, and for the people whose names you would not want read out on the day the smoke fills the room. They are why the open door matters, and why today is a good day to speak of Christ.

For worship. The God of this chapter lives for ever and ever, and his glory fills his temple so completely that no creature can stand in it. Yet the end of the story is not a shut door. In the city to come John saw no temple, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb (21:22), and his servants will see his face (22:4). The glory that drove even priests out of the sanctuary will be the light his people live by. The golden bowls rose full of their prayers, and not one was lost; and the answer to every one of them is this: to be with him, unveiled, for ever.

15.text: <sup>1</sup>Then I saw another sign in heaven, great and amazing, seven angels with seven plagues, which are the last, for with them the wrath of God is finished.<sup>2</sup>And I saw what appeared to be a sea of glass mingled with fire—and also those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name, standing beside the sea of glass with harps of God in their hands.<sup>3</sup>And they sing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, “Great and amazing are your deeds, O Lord God the Almighty! Just and true are your ways, O King of the nations!<sup>4</sup>Who will not fear, O Lord, and glorify your name? For you alone are holy. All nations will come and worship you, for your righteous acts have been revealed.”<sup>5</sup>After this I looked, and the sanctuary of the tent of witness in heaven was opened,<sup>6</sup>and out of the sanctuary came the seven angels with the seven plagues, clothed in pure, bright linen, with golden sashes around their chests.<sup>7</sup>And one of the four living creatures gave to the seven angels seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God who lives forever and ever,<sup>8</sup>and the sanctuary was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power, and no one could enter the sanctuary until the seven plagues of the seven angels were finished.

16.title: The Seven Bowls: The Completion of Divine Justice
16.overview:
Revelation 16 is the last of the book’s three series of seven judgements, and the fullest. The seals struck a quarter of the earth and the trumpets a third; the bowls strike the whole, without fraction. These are the last plagues, and with them God’s answer to the rebellion of history is complete.

More closely than the seals or the trumpets, the bowls follow the plagues on Egypt: sores, water turned to blood, darkness, frogs and hail. The God who brought Israel out of Egypt is acting in the final exodus.

The seventh bowl brings the cry from the throne, It is done!, and the greatest earthquake in history. The cry echoes Christ’s word on the cross, It is finished, and from here everything moves toward the new creation of chapters 21–22.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1: the order to pour comes from the temple, almost certainly from God himself, since no one else could enter it (15:8). Verses 2–4: the first three bowls fall on the beast’s worshippers, the sea and the fresh waters, as the plagues fell on Egypt.

Verses 5–7 pause the sequence: the angel of the waters, and then the altar, declare God’s judgements just. Verses 8–11: the sun scorches and the beast’s throne goes dark, and those struck curse God and do not repent.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Same Ground, Undiluted

The bowls strike earth, sea, rivers, sun and the beast’s throne: the trumpets’ targets, now without limit. The angel of the waters and the altar itself declare God’s judgements true and just. Those struck curse God and do not repent.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The plagues of Egypt return in one chapter, and the mark becomes the wound.

Now: Suffering drives some to their knees and hardens others; it depends which way a person was already facing.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I heard a loud voice from the temple telling the seven angels, "Go and pour out on the earth the seven bowls of the wrath of God." So the first angel went and poured out his bowl on the earth, and harmful and painful sores came upon the people who bore the mark of the beast and worshiped its image.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Revelation 16 pours out the seven bowls of God’s wrath, the last and fullest judgements on a world that has chosen the beast. Sores fall on the beast’s worshippers (vv. 1–2); the sea, then the rivers and springs, become blood, and heaven declares God just, for those who shed the saints’ blood are given blood to drink (vv. 3–7). The sun scorches and the beast’s kingdom goes dark, and still people curse God and do not repent (vv. 8–11). The Euphrates dries up, and three frog-like spirits gather the kings of the world for battle at Armageddon, while Christ warns that he comes like a thief (vv. 12–16). The seventh bowl brings the cry It is done!, the greatest earthquake ever known, the fall of Babylon and huge hailstones, and still people curse God (vv. 17–21). Like the seals and trumpets, the bowls reach the end of history; unlike them, they are complete, not partial.

The setting. The bowls follow the plagues on Egypt closely: sores (the sixth plague, Exodus 9:8–12), water turned to blood (the first, Exodus 7:17–21), darkness (the ninth, Exodus 10:21–23), frogs (the second, Exodus 8:1–15), and hail (the seventh, Exodus 9:22–26). Five of the ten, in one chapter. The empire is Egypt, and the God who broke Egypt has not changed his methods. As Pharaoh hardened his heart, so do the beast’s worshippers. The trumpets struck a third; the bowls strike all.

Three things that govern the chapter. First, the targets match the trumpets almost item for item and in the same order (8:7–12; 9:13–14), which is one of the strongest arguments for reading the three sevens as recapitulation, the same ground covered again at greater intensity (other careful readers take them as successive stages, and the warning of the chapter is the same either way). Second, Egypt is here more densely than anywhere else in the book. Third, and this is the drumbeat of the chapter: three times John records that the people struck by these plagues cursed God, and twice that they did not repent (vv. 9, 11, 21).

A loud voice from the temple. Nobody in the previous chapter could enter the sanctuary (15:8), and the voice comes out of it anyway. It is almost certainly God’s own: the temple is full of the smoke of his glory and closed to everybody else. Whoever else is involved in what follows, the order to begin is given by the one on the throne.

Pour out. The verb (ekcheete, pour out) is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for blood poured out at the base of the altar (Leviticus 4:7). Psalm 79:6 prayed for exactly this: pour out your anger on the nations that do not know you. The prayer of the psalmist and the prayers of the saints in 5:8 are being answered.

Harmful and painful sores. The word for sores (helkos, an ulcer, a festering wound) is the word used in the Greek Old Testament for the boils on the Egyptians. Harmful and painful (kakon kai ponēron) is literally bad and evil. The sixth plague on Egypt was boils breaking out in sores on man and beast (Exodus 9:8–11), and in it the magicians could not even stand before Moses, because the boils were on them too. Whatever else Egypt’s wisdom could imitate, it could not imitate health.

The mark becomes the wound. The bowls are not indiscriminate. Chapter 13 said that anyone who refused the mark could not buy or sell; the mark was the ticket to a working life. Here those who took the beast’s mark bear another mark on their bodies. What was taken as a passport turns out to be the wound. That removes the sense of arbitrariness, because it is how judgement usually works in Scripture. God rarely invents a punishment unconnected to the offence. He hands people over to what they insisted on having: God gave them up, three times in one paragraph (Romans 1:24, 26, 28).

Plagues of an exodus. The Egyptian shape of the bowls tells the reader what story he is in. The plagues on Egypt were not random disasters; they were the blows by which God set his people free, and they ended on the night when the blood of a lamb on the doorposts turned the destroyer away (Exodus 12:13). Paul says plainly who that lamb was: Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7). So when these last plagues fall, the redeemed are not waiting anxiously in the land of the beast. They have already been seen on the far shore, singing the song of Moses and of the Lamb (15:2–3). The bowls are the last chapter of an exodus the Lamb has already won.

Are the bowls still future, or happening now? Both, in a sense. Revelation shows the whole age between Christ’s comings several times over, and the bowls are the final and fullest view, pressing hard toward the end. The kinds of judgement they picture, sickness, disaster, the collapse of proud powers, recur throughout history as warnings, and they will reach their climax in the last days before Christ returns. So we should neither treat every disaster as one specific bowl, nor imagine that the God of these bowls is idle now. He is ruling history, and its end is already written.

If disaster strikes everyone, how are believers protected? Christians live in the same world and can suffer the same illnesses, floods and wars as their neighbours, and sometimes the beast’s hatred besides. The protection promised is not that nothing will touch us, but that nothing that touches us is God’s wrath. For the believer, the same events are a Father’s discipline, a trial of faith, or a share in Christ’s sufferings, and all of them are working for good (Romans 8:28). The sealed belong to God (7:3), and no plague can separate them from his love (Romans 8:35–39).

On a Tuesday. Whatever mark people choose, they will bear its consequences. Most of the marks on offer are small: the habit everyone in the office has, the shaded truth that keeps a sale, the loyalty that slowly crowds out Christ. Each promises to open doors and ends by festering. It is a quiet relief to remember, on an ordinary working day, that you already bear another name, and that the Lamb is able to show you any mark you have been carrying that is not his.
verseByVerse.note: The bowls are the last and fullest judgments; unlike the trumpets, they are not limited to a third.

verseByVerse.quote: The second angel poured out his bowl into the sea, and it became like the blood of a corpse, and every living thing died that was in the sea. The third angel poured out his bowl into the rivers and the springs of water, and they became blood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like the blood of a corpse. The comparison is deliberately revolting: not bright blood from a wound but the blood of a corpse (haima hōs nekrou, blood as of a dead man), dark, thickened, going bad. It is a horrifying image of death, and it is meant to be.

Every living thing died. Every (pasa). Set it against the second trumpet, which turned a third of the sea to blood and killed a third of its creatures (8:8–9). Here there is no fraction. The restraint that has governed every judgement since chapter 6, a fourth, a third, a tenth, forty-two months, a fence around the winds, is gone. The bowls are complete.

Rivers and springs. Fresh water, essential for life, is gone. The first plague on Egypt turned the Nile to blood so that the Egyptians could not drink from it (Exodus 7:20–21), and the Nile was the river into which Pharaoh had ordered every Hebrew boy thrown (Exodus 1:22). The river was given back to Egypt in the condition Egypt had put it in. And the world that rejected the living water (7:17; 21:6) loses even ordinary water.

What the world lives on and lives by. Take the two bowls together and see what has been removed. The sea is where the beast came from (13:1) and where the world’s trade ran; the rivers and springs are where a settlement gets its drinking water. And the springs have been touched once before. At the third trumpet a star called Wormwood made a third of them bitter (8:10–11). Bitter water can still be drunk by a desperate man. Blood cannot. The trumpet made the water unbearable; the bowl makes it impossible, and the distance between the two is the distance between a warning and a verdict.

Everything belongs to somebody. The sea a merchant sails on and the spring a village was built around are not neutral machinery that happens to be reliable. They are upheld, moment by moment, by the Son, in whom all things hold together and who upholds the universe by the word of his power (Colossians 1:17; Hebrews 1:3). A civilisation can spend centuries assuming the water will be there, and be right every single day, and still be wrong about why. And the one who keeps every spring running once hung on a cross and said, I thirst (John 19:28). The Maker of the rivers went without water while he bore the judgement of God, so that those who trust him would not be left to thirst under it.

Is every natural disaster a judgement on the people it strikes? No, and Jesus forbids that conclusion. When a tower fell and killed eighteen people, he said they were not worse sinners than anyone else, and then turned the question round: unless you repent, you will all likewise perish (Luke 13:1–5). Disasters are signs that the whole world lies under the curse of sin and that God’s final judgement is coming, and they call every one of us, not just the victims, to repent. They are never a licence to point at a particular town or person and say God is punishing them. The right response to a flood on the news is compassion, help and self-examination.

On a Tuesday. Every glass of clean water is a gift from God. A tap turned on in the morning can be a small act of worship: the God who could withhold everything is giving you this, today, though you did not earn it. And somewhere today a Christian family is walking a long way for water that is not clean; remembering them, and helping where you can, is part of receiving the gift rightly.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard the angel in charge of the waters say, "Just are you, O Holy One, who is and who was, for you brought these judgments. For they have shed the blood of saints and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink. It is what they deserve!" And I heard the altar saying, "Yes, Lord God the Almighty, true and just are your judgments!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Jewish writings spoke of angels with charge over different parts of creation, such as fire (14:18), winds (7:1) and waters. The principle of fitting judgement runs through Scripture: whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed (Genesis 9:6). Isaiah 49:26 says God will make the oppressors drunk with their own blood. Psalm 19:9 says the rules of the LORD are true, and righteous altogether.

Heaven answers whether this is fair. Here the bowl sequence pauses for the first time. The fourth bowl does not follow the third; three verses of worship follow instead, because heaven has something to say about whether this is fair. And the answer is not given by an argument. It is sung, in the middle of the plague.

Just are you, O Holy One. Just (dikaios, righteous). Holy One (hosios, as in 15:4). The angel in charge of the waters is the one who has just watched every river and spring under his care turn to blood. If anybody in the universe had grounds to file an objection, it is him. He does not complain. He declares God just.

Who is and who was. As in 11:17, the threefold name has lost its third term. The words and is to come are missing, because now he has come in judgement. And the angel names him holy, not powerful. The angel is not saying God has the right to do this because he is strong enough. He is saying it is consistent with what God is.

For you brought these judgments. The verb (ekrinas) is simply you judged. God is the judge, and he judges in person.

Blood to drink. The grounds are stated in one sentence, and it is the oldest principle of justice there is. The punishment fits the crime: it is the crime, served back. These people made the earth run with the blood of God’s people, and now there is nothing else to drink. This is the answer to the martyrs’ cry (6:10).

It is what they deserve! Two words in Greek (axioi eisin, they are worthy), and they are not comfortable. They are a grim echo of the praise of the Lamb: worthy are you (5:9, 12). The Lamb is worthy of glory; the persecutors are worthy of judgement. But see who is not saying them: no human being in this book ever pronounces that sentence over another. The martyrs under the altar asked how long? and left the verdict to God (6:10). Vengeance is God’s, and the reason it is his alone is that only he can be trusted to get it exactly right (Romans 12:19).

Blood for blood, and one exception. By the principle of this verse, blood for blood, the men who shed the blood of the Son of God had earned the worst cup of all. Yet he prayed for them as the nails went in, Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (Luke 23:34), and seven weeks later Peter told a Jerusalem crowd that they had crucified the one God made Lord and Christ, and about three thousand of them were baptised (Acts 2:36–41). The blood they shed became the blood that washed them. That is why the Lamb’s blood speaks a better word than the blood of Abel (Hebrews 12:24). The bowl of blood falls only where that blood has been refused.

The altar answers. The altar speaks, and the reader who has been following knows why. Under that altar are the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God, who cried, O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood? (6:9–10). From it the saints’ prayers rose (8:3–5). There they were clothed in white and asked to wait a little while longer. This is the altar answering its own question. The same words come back, holy and true there, true and just here (alēthinai kai dikaiai, as the redeemed sang in 15:3), and the verdict of the people who actually paid for the injustice is yes. Not at last, and not it took long enough. Yes.

Nobody in heaven thinks God has overdone it. That is the most important thing this chapter has to say to a Christian who finds these plagues hard to look at. The one group whose opinion might be thought to carry most weight, the murdered, who waited for this, are the ones who declare it just when it comes.

Textual note. In v. 5 the King James Version reads “which art, and wast, and shalt be”, following a late reading; the best manuscripts read “who is and who was, the Holy One”. In v. 7, the King James Version reads “I heard another out of the altar say”, but the best manuscripts read simply “I heard the altar saying”.

What it does not mean. Praising God’s judgement is not rejoicing in suffering for its own sake. It is the recognition that God has put things right, that evil has not had the last word, and that the blood of the innocent has not been forgotten. Without God’s justice, the world’s victims would have no hope.

How does this fit with loving my enemies? Perfectly, once we see who does what. Our task is to love, bless and pray for those who wrong us (Matthew 5:44; Romans 12:14), and to leave vengeance entirely to God (Romans 12:19–21). We can do that precisely because we know God will judge. If there were no judge, every wrong would either have to be avenged by us or swallowed as if it did not matter. Because there is a just God, we can forgive without pretending evil is nothing. And we pray, meanwhile, that our enemies will be saved, as many persecutors have been. The praise of this verse belongs to the day when God himself has acted.

On a Tuesday. When you see injustice that is never put right in this life, the abuser who is never charged, the regime that is never toppled, the lie that is never exposed, bring it to God in prayer, and trust that his judgements will be true and just. Name it to him honestly. Then put it down, and do good to the people in front of you. You are not the judge, and you do not need to be.

verseByVerse.quote: The fourth angel poured out his bowl on the sun, and it was allowed to scorch people with fire. They were scorched by the fierce heat, and they cursed the name of God who had power over these plagues. They did not repent and give him glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Allowed to scorch. It was allowed (edothē, it was given). Even here, at full strength, with the limits off, the divine passive holds. Nothing in this book acts on its own authority, and the sun is no exception. To scorch (kaumatisai) is to burn. The sun, which God made to give light and life, becomes an instrument of judgement.

Two companies, one sun. The fourth trumpet darkened the sun; the fourth bowl turns it up. And the reversal is pointed, because the great promise made to the multitude in 7:16 was that the sun would not strike them, nor any scorching heat. For the sealed it is shaded by the tent of God spread over them; for these it is a furnace. What the redeemed are spared, the beast’s worshippers suffer. The same created thing behaves differently depending on whose you are.

They cursed the name of God. The Greek for fierce heat is kauma mega, great heat. Then comes the sentence that is repeated three times in this chapter, and it is a sobering diagnosis. They cursed (eblasphēmēsan, blasphemed, slandered): the same verb used of the beast’s mouth in 13:6. Under the plague they have started to sound like the thing they worshipped. They know. There is no ignorance here, no confusion about the source, no atheism. They have correctly identified who is doing this and they curse him for it. Suffering has not hidden God from them; it has revealed him, and they have decided against him with the evidence in front of them.

They did not repent and give him glory. Did not repent (ou metenoēsan), as in 9:20–21. And see what repentance is called here: repent and give him glory. Not repent and feel sorry. To give God glory is the response called for by the eternal gospel (14:7), and given by some in 11:13. To repent is to hand God back the glory that was given to something else, which is precisely what these people will not do, because they gave it to a beast and they are not taking it back.

Pain does not produce repentance. This is the answer, given for the second time in the book, to a hope most people carry quietly: that if things got bad enough, people would turn. Chapter 9 said it after a third of mankind died. Chapter 16 says it three times more. Pain reveals what was already there, and it hardens as reliably as it softens. And every Christian meets small versions of this: the illness, the loss, the disappointment that could go either way. Two men lose the same thing in the same week, and one is driven to his knees and the other never prays again. The difference is not the weight. It is which direction a person was already facing when it landed. (A believer whose prayers have gone quiet in grief or depression is not the man in this verse: numbness is not cursing, and the people here have no wish for God at all. The Lord who does not break a bruised reed waits for the quiet one, Isaiah 42:3.)

The one who did not curse. There was once a man under the heavy hand of God who did not curse. On the day Jesus died he bore not a plague he had earned but the judgement his people had earned. Yet when he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23), and he died praying, Father, into your hands I commit my spirit (Luke 23:46). Every curse in this chapter is answered by that prayer. He gave God glory under the full weight of wrath, so that people who had cursed God could be forgiven and taught to bless.

Is it fair for God to harden hearts? Scripture holds two things together, as Exodus does with Pharaoh. People harden themselves: they see God’s hand, refuse him, and are fully responsible for it. And God, as judge, confirms them in the path they chose, giving them over to it (Romans 1:24; 9:17–18). He never hardens a soft heart that is seeking him; he hands a rebellious heart over to its own rebellion. So no one in this chapter is a seeker who wanted to repent and was not allowed. If you want to turn to God, that desire is the sign he is softening you, not hardening you. Follow it now.

Why do some people turn to God in suffering and others away from him? Because suffering does not create faith; it tests and exposes what is there, and only the Spirit of God makes a heart new (John 3:5–8; Ezekiel 36:26). That is why we must pray for people in suffering, not merely wait for the trouble to bring them round. And it is why a Christian who is hurting should run to God with the hurt, as the Psalms do, rather than away from him. Lament, honest complaint, even confused anger brought to God in prayer is the very opposite of the cursing in this verse. The cursers turn their backs; the lamenter turns his face.

verseByVerse.quote: The fifth angel poured out his bowl on the throne of the beast, and its kingdom was plunged into darkness. People gnawed their tongues in anguish and cursed the God of heaven for their pain and sores. They did not repent of their deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
