The setting. The ninth plague on Egypt was a darkness that could be felt, three days in which nobody rose from his place, but all the people of Israel had light where they lived (Exodus 10:21–23). Jesus spoke of the outer darkness where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matthew 8:12; 22:13).

The throne of the beast. The first four bowls fell on creation: earth, sea, rivers, sun. The fifth falls on a government. And it is aimed with precision: not at the beast’s subjects, or its armies, but at the throne of the beast (ton thronon tou thēriou), the seat of its power, given by the dragon (13:2). The reader last heard of such a throne in Pergamum, where Satan’s throne is (2:13). Christians had been living under its shadow for the whole book. It goes dark.

Plunged into darkness. The word (eskotōmenē) is simply darkened. In Egypt the darkness was probably a blow at the sun god Ra, often treated as chief of the Egyptian gods; Pharaoh bore the title son of Ra (compare Exodus 12:12). To darken the empire is to show that its god cannot keep a lamp lit. That is what makes the fifth bowl different from the four before it. The others damaged the world; this one exposes the regime. Every empire that demands worship rests on an appearance of permanence: the lights are on, the courts sit, the coins are minted, and it is inconceivable that any of it should stop. One bowl, and the kingdom is in the dark.

Gnawed their tongues. Gnawed (emasōnto, chewed); anguish (ponou, pain). Gnawing the tongue is a small, physical, entirely credible detail: what a person does with pain he cannot get away from and cannot usefully cry out about.

For their pain and sores. The sores are the ones from the first bowl, still there. The plagues in this chapter accumulate; nothing has healed. Not for anything they have thought about, and not for any account of who he is. The entire content of their complaint is their own discomfort. It is possible to spend a life measuring God only by how one feels, and this is what that comes to in the end.

Of their deeds. The third time this refusal is mentioned (9:20–21; 16:9), with one word changed. In verse 9 they did not repent and give him glory. Here they did not repent of their deeds. The first is about worship, the second about behaviour, and together they cover the ground: they will not change what they adore and they will not change what they do. Their hearts are set.

Darkness at noon. The Gospels record one other darkness over a kingdom. When the King of the Jews hung on a cross with his title fixed above his head, there was darkness over the whole land from the sixth hour until the ninth (Mark 15:33), as Amos had said of the day of the LORD: I will make the sun go down at noon (Amos 8:9). The true King went into the darkness of judgement in the place of his people. The beast’s throne goes dark because it is under judgement; Christ’s throne was a cross because he was bearing judgement for others, and on the third day he rose, the light that will never go out. Whoever follows him will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life (John 8:12).

Is it wrong to be angry with God? It depends what you do with it. Scripture is full of believers who brought anger, confusion and grief to God: Job, Jeremiah, the psalmists (Psalm 13; 88). They argued with him, but they argued with him, to his face, in prayer, and they did not let go of him. That is faith in pain. What this verse describes is different: cursing God and refusing to turn, with no desire to know him, only resentment that life is uncomfortable. If you are angry with God, tell him so, ask him to help you understand, open the Psalms, and talk to a mature Christian. Do not let anger become a wall.

On a Tuesday. God has already transferred you into the kingdom of his beloved Son (Colossians 1:13), so you need not live as a citizen of one that ends in the dark. When you last had a grievance against God, what was it actually about? If it was that he had not arranged your comfort as you would have arranged it, that is the same complaint, at a survivable scale, and there is still time to tell him so and turn; the Father who moved you into his Son’s kingdom will not throw you out of it for being honest.

For worship. God is light, and in him is no darkness at all. Thrones rise and fall at his word, and the empires that demanded worship cannot keep their own lamps lit when he withdraws his hand. In Egypt the darkness could be felt, and in Goshen there was light; so it is still. He has called his people out of darkness into his marvellous light, and in the city to come there will be no night, for the Lord God will be their light, and the Lamb is its lamp. The beast’s kingdom ends in the dark. His kingdom ends in a morning that never fades.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–21 — The Sixth and Seventh Bowls
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 12–14: the sixth bowl dries the Euphrates, the river by which old Babylon once fell, and three frog-like spirits from the dragon, the beast and the false prophet gather the kings of the world for battle. Verse 15: Christ breaks in with his own warning and the book’s third beatitude. Verse 16: the place of gathering is named Armageddon.

Verses 17–21: the seventh bowl is poured into the air, the voice from the throne declares it done, the great city splits, Babylon is given the cup of wrath, and under the hail people curse God for the third time.
verseByVerse.theology:
It Is Done

The Euphrates is dried, and frog-like spirits from the mouths of the dragon, beast and false prophet gather the kings to Armageddon. Christ breaks in: stay awake. The seventh bowl brings the voice from the throne, It is done!, the great earthquake, and Babylon remembered for judgement.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Babylon had fallen once before when its river was diverted.

Now: Stay awake and clothed in Christ; ask how much of what you lean on can be shaken.

verseByVerse.quote: The sixth angel poured out his bowl on the great river Euphrates, and its water was dried up, to prepare the way for the kings from the east. And I saw, coming out of the mouth of the dragon and out of the mouth of the beast and out of the mouth of the false prophet, three unclean spirits like frogs. For they are demonic spirits, performing signs, who go abroad to the kings of the whole world, to assemble them for battle on the great day of God the Almighty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. The second plague on Egypt was frogs (Exodus 8:1–15). Under the law, creatures of the water without fins and scales were unclean (Leviticus 11:9–12), and frogs were probably counted among them. The prophets foretold a final gathering of the nations against God and his people, which God would defeat (Joel 3:2; Zechariah 12:3; 14:2; Ezekiel 38–39).

On the great river Euphrates. The Euphrates was the eastern frontier of the empire and the direction from which Israel’s great invaders, Assyria and Babylon, had come, and the reader has been here before: at the sixth trumpet four angels were released who had been bound at this same river (9:14). Now the river itself goes. The barrier that held back invasion is removed.

A road cleared by God. A dried-up river is one of Scripture’s standard pictures of God clearing a road. He dried the Red Sea for Israel to walk through (Exodus 14:21) and the Jordan for them to enter the land (Joshua 3:16). And when Cyrus the Persian took Babylon in 539 BC, his engineers diverted the Euphrates and his troops walked into the city up the lowered riverbed, as the Greek historian Herodotus tells it (Babylonian records speak more simply of the city taken without a battle; compare Jeremiah 50:38; 51:36). Isaiah had spoken of the God who says to the deep, be dry, in the same breath as he named Cyrus (Isaiah 44:27–28). A first-century reader hearing that the Euphrates had been dried for kings from the east would very likely think of how the old Babylon on the Euphrates fell. Babylon is about to fall again.

The kings from the east. From the east (apo anatolēs hēliou) is literally from the rising of the sun. In John’s day the Parthians beyond the Euphrates were the empire’s nightmare. Here they stand for the forces of the world gathering against God. And the irony is that the water is removed to make an invasion easier. God is not defending the beast’s kingdom; he is opening the gate for the thing that will destroy it. Even the enemies of God’s people serve his purposes without knowing it, as in 17:16–17, where the beast and the ten kings turn on the harlot because God has put it into their hearts.

Out of three mouths. The unholy trinity of chapters 12 and 13 (12:3; 13:1, 11) appears together for the first time, and all three do the same thing. They speak. Three mouths, and one thing comes out of each: their words, lies and propaganda. The dragon is the deceiver of the whole world (12:9); the beast was given a mouth uttering haughty and blasphemous words (13:5); the false prophet deceives by signs (13:13–14). The chief weapon of evil in this book is talk.

Like frogs. Unclean spirits (pneumata tria akatharta), and like frogs, which recalls the second plague on Egypt (Exodus 8:6) and, to a Jewish reader, an unclean creature. It is also, deliberately, ridiculous. Everything about this book’s villains has been magnificent so far: seven heads, ten diadems, a mortal wound healed, the worship of the whole earth. And when their propaganda is finally shown, it hops and croaks. Deception is loud and persistent, but worthless. Evil is never as grand as it looks.

Demonic spirits, performing signs. Demonic (daimoniōn). The signs are deceptive wonders, as in 13:13–14. Lies rarely travel alone; they come with something impressive enough to make them believed.

To assemble them for battle. The frogs are a diplomatic service. To assemble (synagagein) is to gather together, and the battle (polemon, with the article in Greek) is the battle, the final one. The great day of God the Almighty is the day of judgement. The rulers of the world think they are gathering to fight; in fact God is gathering them to be judged. The same battle is described in 19:19 and 20:8.

The real battlefield is belief. Set that beside the way people usually imagine spiritual warfare. The decisive struggle in this book is not fought with weapons and is not chiefly about power. It is about what the world is told and whether it believes it. The dragon’s one method, from a conversation in a garden to the last coalition on earth, is to say something untrue convincingly. And the church’s one weapon is the word of truth, the testimony of Jesus (12:11; Ephesians 6:17).

Three temptations, three answers. The pattern was set in a wilderness. The deceiver came to Jesus three times with offers that sounded reasonable, bread, a sign, the kingdoms of the world, and three times Jesus answered with Scripture: it is written (Matthew 4:1–11). Where Adam listened to the lie, the last Adam answered it and won. And before Pilate, the representative of the empire the beast stands for, he said that he had been born and had come into the world to bear witness to the truth (John 18:37). Against three mouths full of lies the church has one Lord, the faithful and true witness (3:14), and the frogs have never yet outshouted him.

In the flow. Each of Revelation’s series of seven pauses near its end. After the sixth seal came the sealing of God’s people (chapter 7); after the sixth trumpet came the little scroll and the two witnesses (10:1–11:14). After the sixth bowl the pause shrinks to a single verse, Christ’s own warning to stay awake (v. 15), and then the seventh bowl ends it all. The sixth bowl itself fights no battle. It only gathers the armies, and the battle they are gathered for is shown in 19:19–21 and 20:7–10, where it is over in a sentence. What this bowl adds to the book is the reason the world marches against God at all: it has believed a lie.

Where Christians differ: who are the kings from the east? John’s readers feared the Parthian armies beyond the Euphrates. Futurist readers (those who expect most of Revelation to be fulfilled in the last years before Christ returns) look for a literal army from the east, often identified with a modern nation; they want to take John’s geography at face value, and that reverence for the text is right. But the bowls are full of Egypt and Babylon used as pictures, and the river belongs to the same world of images. This commentary’s view: the more likely reading is that John uses that ancient fear as a picture of the nations gathered by the dragon for the final battle (v. 14), not a prediction of a particular invasion.

How do I recognise the frogs’ voice today? Look for the marks this chapter gives. It comes from mouths: it is talk, often loud, repeated and everywhere. It is backed by signs: success, spectacle, numbers, things that look like proof. And it always gathers people against God, persuading them that Christ is the enemy of their freedom and that his people are the problem. It can come from a government, a movement, a media culture, or a false teacher in the church. The test is the same: does it confess Jesus Christ as Lord, and does it agree with Scripture (1 John 4:1–3; Isaiah 8:20)? Fill your mind with God’s word, and the croaking becomes easier to hear for what it is.

On a Tuesday. You belong to the faithful and true witness, so measure what you hear by his word and refuse lies, however loud. Before you share, repeat or believe a message about God, his people or what is right and wrong, ask where it came from and whether it agrees with Scripture. Most days are filled with other voices from the first minute. There is a quiet strength in letting the word of God have the first word in the morning, so that it has the loudest voice in your head.

For worship. The God of this chapter rules even the plans of his enemies. He dries a river, and the kings who think they are marching on his people are marching into his court. The dragon, the beast and the false prophet can gather the whole world, and they cannot gather it one step beyond where God has appointed. And the one who will meet them is the Word of God himself, the Truth in person, who has only to speak and every lie is silenced. Their mouths produce frogs. His mouth holds a sharp two-edged sword, and with it he will judge the world in righteousness.

verseByVerse.quote: ("Behold, I am coming like a thief! Blessed is the one who stays awake, keeping his garments on, that he may not go about naked and be seen exposed!") And they assembled them at the place that in Hebrew is called Armageddon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Megiddo, overlooking the plain of Jezreel (Esdraelon) on the main route between Egypt and Mesopotamia, saw many decisive battles. There Deborah and Barak defeated Sisera (Judges 5:19), Ahaziah died (2 Kings 9:27), and King Josiah was killed fighting Pharaoh Neco, and all Judah mourned (2 Kings 23:29–30; 2 Chronicles 35:22–25; Zechariah 12:11). Nearby Mount Carmel was where Elijah defeated the prophets of Baal (1 Kings 18).

Christ interrupts his own book. In the middle of a sentence about demonic frogs assembling the kings of the world, a different voice cuts in, and the ESV rightly marks it with brackets. Christ has scarcely spoken in his own voice since chapter 3, and will not again until chapter 22; here, at the darkest point of the story, he breaks in without introduction to speak directly to his church. The interruption is itself the message. The armies are gathering, the frogs are going out to the kings, the last battle is being assembled, and the Lord’s concern at that exact moment is a Christian in Sardis or Laodicea staying awake and keeping his clothes on. The cosmic scale of this chapter never once displaces the person reading it.

Behold, I am coming like a thief! He said it to Sardis in the same words (3:3) and on the Mount of Olives (Matthew 24:43), and Paul and Peter both repeat it (1 Thessalonians 5:2; 2 Peter 3:10). The point of the image is never stealth. A thief does not sneak so much as arrive on a night nobody expected. It is unpredictability, and its practical consequence is that there is no point in a person planning to get ready later.

Blessed is the one who stays awake. The third of the book’s seven beatitudes. Stays awake (grēgorōn) means keeps watch. Keeping his garments on (tērōn ta himatia autou) is literally guarding his clothes. A later Jewish tradition gives a vivid parallel: the captain of the temple guard in Jerusalem went round at night, and a Levite found asleep at his post could be beaten and have his clothes burned, as the Mishnah records. Being caught asleep meant public shame.

Seen exposed. Exposed (tēn aschēmosynēn) is shame, disgrace. And garments in this book have a settled meaning: white robes given to those who conquer (3:4–5), robes washed and made white in the blood of the Lamb (7:14), the fine linen of the Bride which is the righteous deeds of the saints (19:8). Laodicea was told to buy white garments so that the shame of its nakedness might not be seen (3:18), the same phrase. The garments are the righteousness of Christ received by faith, and the faithful life that flows from it. A Christian, then, is covered before God not by his own record but by Christ’s, as a robe is given to someone who has nothing fit to wear (Isaiah 61:10), and that covering then shows in how he lives. To keep one’s garments on is to keep trusting Christ, and to keep living like it.

Not complicated and not heroic. So the instruction is simple. Stay awake. Keep your clothes on. That is what is asked of a Christian while the kings are assembled for Armageddon: not that he do anything about the coalition, but that he be found alert and dressed. Nor is he left to his own willpower. The robe was never his work: no Christian keeps watch perfectly, but Christ watched and prayed in Gethsemane while his friends slept, and his obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19). And the Spirit he has given is the one who keeps waking us.

Armageddon. This is the only occurrence of the word in the Bible, and an enormous popular literature rests on one verse. Honesty requires saying that its meaning is not certain. The likeliest derivation is har Megiddo, the mountain of Megiddo. Megiddo was a fortress town guarding the pass into the plain of Jezreel, and one of the most fought-over places in the land. To say Megiddo was to say the battlefield. The difficulty is that there is no mountain of Megiddo, only a plain and a mound (a tel). Some therefore connect it with Mount Carmel nearby, or read mountain of assembly, the phrase Isaiah puts in the mouth of the fallen day star who says he will sit on the mount of assembly (Isaiah 14:13). John says it is called this in Hebrew, a signal to look for its meaning. It fits a book that has already told the reader that Sodom and Egypt are symbolic names for the great city (11:8).

Where Christians differ: is Armageddon a literal battle in northern Israel? Many futurists, including premillennial Christians (who expect Christ to return before an earthly reign of a thousand years) and dispensational Christians (a form of premillennialism that keeps God’s plans for Israel and for the church distinct), expect the armies of the world to gather literally in the valley of Megiddo for a final war in the Middle East, before Christ returns. They take the place name as a real address, and they read Zechariah 12–14 as pointing to a real siege in the land; they are faithful brothers and sisters, reading with reverence. This commentary’s view: Armageddon is a symbolic name for the final conflict between the powers of the world and God, drawn from Israel’s history of decisive battles at Megiddo. The battle is described three times in Revelation (16:14–16; 19:17–21; 20:7–10), and each time no battle is actually fought: the enemies are gathered and then destroyed instantly by Christ at his coming. It is the same final event, seen from different angles. It may involve a literal gathering of hostile powers, but its location and form are not the point; its outcome is. Christ wins without a fight.

The shortest battle in the book. What is not uncertain is who wins, and how little of a battle it turns out to be. The kings are assembled here in chapter 16 and nothing happens; the end is described in 19:19–21, it lasts a few lines, and the only weapon is a sword out of a mouth. Armageddon is the most famous battle in the world’s imagination and the shortest in the Bible.

What it does not mean. “Armageddon” in Revelation does not mean nuclear war or a global catastrophe caused by human beings, as the word is often used today. It means the day when God judges the world’s rebellion.

Does coming like a thief mean a secret rapture? No. The thief image is about timing, not visibility: his coming will be unexpected for those who are not watching, not invisible. Revelation says every eye will see him (1:7), and Jesus said his coming will be like lightning flashing across the sky (Matthew 24:27). Paul uses the thief picture in the same passage where the Lord descends with a cry of command and the sound of the trumpet (1 Thessalonians 4:16; 5:2). There is one return of Christ, public and glorious, at the end of the age, when he raises the dead, gathers his people and judges the world. And here, in chapter 16, the church is still on earth being told to stay awake. Christians who expect a rapture before the tribulation usually answer that these are people converted after the church has been taken, and they hold that view out of a real desire to honour God’s distinct promises to Israel and to the church; they are our brothers and sisters. But nothing in the text marks out a second group, and the warning is the one Christ gave to the churches (3:3).

If he comes like a thief, can anyone know when? No. Jesus said that no one knows the day or the hour (Matthew 24:36), and every attempt to set dates has failed and done harm. But Paul adds that believers are not in darkness, for that day to surprise them like a thief (1 Thessalonians 5:4). The difference is not that Christians know the date but that they are ready whatever the date. A watchman does not know when the attack will come; he simply does not fall asleep.

On a Tuesday. Staying awake means keeping short accounts with God, confessing sin the day you see it; keeping your hope fixed on Christ’s righteousness and not your own; and living each ordinary day, at the desk, the sink or the hospital bed, as if he might come before evening.
verseByVerse.note: Armageddon probably means “mountain of Megiddo,” a hill fortress overlooking the plain where many of Israel’s famous battles were fought.

verseByVerse.quote: The seventh angel poured out his bowl into the air, and a loud voice came out of the temple, from the throne, saying, "It is done!" And there were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, and a great earthquake such as there had never been since man was on the earth, so great was that earthquake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Into the air. The last bowl is poured into the air (aera), the one element the first six left alone, and the one nobody can stand outside of. Paul calls the devil the prince of the power of the air (Ephesians 2:2), the realm where demonic powers operate. The final judgement falls on the atmosphere the whole world has been breathing, the whole environment of human life.

It is done! The voice comes from the temple and from the throne, which in this book means God himself. One word in Greek: gegonen, it has happened, it stands accomplished. The tense is perfect: a completed act whose result is permanent.

Three announcements of completion. The cry echoes two others, and they are the frame of everything. On the cross, Jesus said it is finished (John 19:30), a different verb with the same force. At 21:6, on the throne, God says of the new creation it is done, almost the same word as here. Christ’s word on the cross accomplished salvation; God’s word here completes judgement; and the same word opens the new creation. What was accomplished at the first makes the second bearable and the third certain.

What exactly is done? Chapter 15 said it in advance: with them the wrath of God is finished (15:1). This is that sentence arriving. There is no eighth bowl. God’s judgement on this age has a stopping point, and the seventh angel has just reached it.

Lightning, rumblings, thunder. John’s standing signal that God has acted, and it has been growing all through the book. At 4:5 it was three elements, coming out of the throne. At 8:5, when the censer of the saints’ prayers was thrown down, an earthquake was added. At 11:19, when the ark was seen, hail was added. Here it is the full list, with the earthquake described in a clause of its own.

A great earthquake. The prophets had promised exactly this, and the letter to the Hebrews quotes it to make the point Christians most need from this verse. God said through Haggai that he would shake the heavens and the earth (Haggai 2:6), and Hebrews comments that the words yet once more mean the removal of things that are shaken, so that the things that cannot be shaken may remain; therefore let us be grateful for receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken (Hebrews 12:26–28). That is what the greatest earthquake in history is for. It is not demolition for its own sake. It is a sorting: everything that can be shaken is being shaken, so that what is left standing afterwards is only what was never going to fall.

What counts as shakeable in my life? Anything that belongs only to this age: money and property, reputation, health, career, national power, the approval of others, even the outward shapes of church life. None of them is evil, and many are God’s good gifts, but none can bear the full weight of a soul. What cannot be shaken is God himself, his word, Christ’s finished work, the kingdom he gives, and the people he has made his own. A believer’s honest question on reading this verse is therefore not, will I survive this? but, how much of what I am leaning on is in the shakeable category? Hold the first loosely and the second with both hands.

verseByVerse.quote: The great city was split into three parts, and the cities of the nations fell, and God remembered Babylon the great, to make her drain the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath. And every island fled away, and no mountains were to be found. And great hailstones, about one hundred pounds each, fell from heaven on people; and they cursed God for the plague of the hail, because the plague was so severe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. The seventh plague on Egypt was the worst hailstorm the country had ever seen (Exodus 9:18–26). God threw great hailstones from heaven on the Amorite kings fleeing from Joshua (Joshua 10:11). Ezekiel 38:22 promises hailstones, fire and sulphur against Gog. The Greek says the hailstones were talent-weight (talantiaia); a talent varied from place to place, but the ESV’s about one hundred pounds (some 45 kilograms) is a fair figure.

Split into three. The great city is Babylon (v. 19; 17:18), the phrase used at 11:8 of the place that symbolically is called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified. It is completely shattered. Ezekiel was told to divide his hair into three parts as a sign of Jerusalem’s ruin (Ezekiel 5:1–2).

The cities of the nations. Every human city and civilisation built without God collapses with Babylon. They were all built on her plan, and they all fall with her.

God remembered Babylon. Remembered (emnēsthē). In Scripture, God remembering never means that something had slipped his mind. It is covenant language, and it usually means that he is about to act on what he has long known. God remembered Noah, and the waters went down (Genesis 8:1). God remembered his covenant with Abraham, and the exodus began (Exodus 2:24). The thief on the cross asked to be remembered, and was told that today he would be with Christ in paradise (Luke 23:42–43). So the sentence means that a file which has been open for a very long time has come to the top of the pile. God had not forgotten her sins (18:5). Delayed judgement is not cancelled judgement. And this verse is a hinge: Babylon was announced fallen in 14:8 but her fall has not yet been described, and chapters 17 and 18 will do nothing else.

Drain the cup. Not sip it, not drink from it, but drain it to the bottom. It is the cup of 14:10, poured full strength, and it is the cup Babylon herself had been passing round, she who made all nations drink the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality (14:8). She poured; she drinks; and she finishes the cup.

Islands and mountains. Two things that do not move. The sixth seal had already said that every mountain and island was removed from its place (6:14), and at the final judgement earth and sky flee from God’s presence (20:11), which is more evidence that the seals and the bowls are covering the same ground. Islands and mountains are what people steer by and shelter behind, and there are none. The old creation passes away.

Great hailstones. There may be an echo of the law here: stoning was the penalty for blasphemy (Leviticus 24:16), and the chapter has recorded three times that these people blasphemed. If so, the sky returns the sentence.

They cursed God. The final act of humanity in this chapter, with the sky falling on it, is to curse. This is the true horror of sin: it hardens until it cannot turn.

What changes people. That is where the bowls end, and the placement is deliberate. Revelation gives its reader no consoling picture of a world that finally comes round under pressure. It has now said four times that judgement by itself changes nobody. What changes people is what was shown at 11:13, where the two witnesses were killed and raised and the rest of the city gave glory to the God of heaven, and what was announced at 14:6, an eternal gospel flown where every nation could hear it. The instrument of salvation is a Lamb who was slain, and he has been in the middle of the throne since chapter 5. Until the day these bowls picture arrives, he is still saving.

Could a Christian end up like this? A true believer will not, because God keeps his own and finishes what he began in them (Philippians 1:6; John 10:28–29). But Scripture warns Christians about hardness precisely as one of the means by which he keeps us: exhort one another every day, so that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin (Hebrews 3:13). Hardening is gradual: one sin excused, one warning ignored, one prayer neglected. So if your heart feels cold, do not despair and do not drift. Confess it, go back to God’s word and God’s people, and ask him to soften you. A heart worried about being hard is not yet the heart in this verse.

For worship. God remembers. Nothing evil escapes his memory, and nothing done for his name is forgotten. And for those who are in Christ, he has made a promise that turns the whole chapter on its head: their sins and lawless deeds he will remember no more. The cup Babylon must drain to the bottom, the Son of God drained first, in Gethsemane and at Golgotha, for everyone who trusts him. There is no wrath left in it for us. There is only a cup of blessing, and a feast waiting at the wedding of the Lamb.
