17.title: Babylon the Great: The Seductive City
17.overview:
Chapter 17 shows the first of Revelation’s two great women: the prostitute seated on many waters, dressed in purple and scarlet and gold, holding a golden cup full of abominations. She is the counterpart of the Bride of the Lamb (chapters 19 and 21): two women, two cities, two ways of ordering human life, and every person belongs finally to one or the other.

For the first readers she was plainly Rome, the city on seven hills that ruled the kings of the earth (vv. 9, 18). Readers differ on how far she reaches beyond Rome. This commentary takes her as Rome and as the type of every civilisation built on wealth, power and the seduction of the nations away from the living God: Babylon is Rome, and Babylon is every Rome.

The chapter has two movements: the vision of the woman on the beast (vv. 1–6) and the angel’s explanation (vv. 7–18). The details of the seven kings and the eighth have produced more proposals than almost any passage in the book; the main options are set out honestly, without forcing an identification the text does not make certain.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Woman on the Beast
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: one of the bowl angels invites John to see the judgement of the great prostitute, so tying this chapter to 16:19. The same invitation will come at 21:9, to see the Bride.

Verses 3–6: in the wilderness John sees the woman riding the scarlet beast of chapter 13, magnificently dressed, with a name on her forehead and the blood of the saints on her lips, and he marvels at her.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Great Prostitute

John is shown Babylon, magnificent in purple and gold, riding the beast, holding a golden cup full of abominations, drunk with the blood of the saints. She is Rome for the first readers, and the mother of every city built to make a name for itself.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Kings made the arrangements; ordinary people simply drank what was poured.

Now: The cup always looks better than its contents, and even an apostle had to be asked why he marvelled.

verseByVerse.quote: Then one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and said to me, "Come, I will show you the judgment of the great prostitute who is seated on many waters, with whom the kings of the earth have committed sexual immorality, and with the wine of whose sexual immorality the dwellers on earth have become drunk."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Revelation 17 zooms in on Babylon, whose fall was announced in 14:8 and 16:19, and shows her as a great prostitute who sits on many waters, with whom the kings of the earth have committed immorality (vv. 1–2). John sees her in the wilderness riding a scarlet beast with seven heads and ten horns, dressed in purple and jewels, holding a golden cup of abominations, and drunk with the blood of the saints (vv. 3–6). The angel explains: the beast was, is not, and will rise and go to destruction (vv. 7–8); its heads are seven hills and seven kings (vv. 9–11); its ten horns are ten kings who make war on the Lamb, but the Lamb conquers them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and his people are called, chosen and faithful (vv. 12–14). In the end the beast and the kings turn on the prostitute and destroy her, because God put it in their hearts (vv. 15–17). The woman is the great city that rules the kings of the earth (v. 18): Rome in John’s day, and every glittering, godless civilisation since.

The setting. In John’s day Rome was the centre of a vast trading empire, rich, luxurious, and the seat of the emperor cult; Roman writers themselves called it a city of vice. The goddess Roma was worshipped in Asia, and a coin of Vespasian showed her seated on Rome’s seven hills.

One of the seven angels. The guide is one of the bowl angels, which ties this chapter to the last. In 16:19 God remembered Babylon the great, to make her drain the cup, and no further detail was given. Chapters 17 and 18 expand on the seventh bowl: they are that detail.

Come, I will show you. Judgement (krima) is the verdict, the sentence. The same invitation will be issued once more, four chapters later, by another bowl angel in almost identical words: come, I will show you the Bride, the wife of the Lamb (21:9). Two women, two cities, two invitations from the same rank of angel: Babylon and the new Jerusalem. That is the architecture of the rest of the book, and the frame this chapter must be read in. Every human being is finally a citizen of one of two cities and belongs to one of two households, and Revelation is going to describe both so that a reader can tell them apart.

Why a prostitute? The word (pornēs, harlot) is not chosen for shock. It is the settled prophetic word for covenant unfaithfulness, and it is used most often of the people of God themselves: Israel is the wife who played the whore (Jeremiah 3:6–10; Ezekiel 16; Hosea 1–3), and Isaiah raises a lament, in his first chapter, over the faithful city that has become a whore (Isaiah 1:21). It was also used of pagan cities. Nineveh and Tyre are both called prostitutes for selling themselves to whoever would trade (Nahum 3:4; Isaiah 23:15–17). The point of the word is transaction. A prostitute offers what belongs inside a covenant, without the covenant, for a price. That is what Babylon does with every good thing there is, beauty, security, belonging, significance, and it is why she is a more dangerous enemy than the beast. The beast demands. She offers.

Without money and without price. Set what she sells beside what Christ gives. Babylon offers beauty, security and belonging for a price, outside the covenant. The Lamb offers them freely, inside one. Through Isaiah God called, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price (Isaiah 55:1), and the last invitation of this book is that whoever desires may take the water of life without price (22:17). John the Baptist spoke of Jesus as the bridegroom (John 3:29), and a bridegroom does not sell himself; he gives himself, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25). The prostitute takes everything and gives nothing that lasts. The Bridegroom gives everything, and asks for the heart.

Seated on many waters. Verse 15 will interpret it: the waters are peoples, multitudes, nations and languages. She rules over the world. But the image comes first from Jeremiah’s oracle against the original Babylon, which literally sat on the Euphrates and its canals: you who dwell by many waters, rich in treasures, your end has come (Jeremiah 51:13). John takes a geographical fact about one city and makes it a statement about influence.

The kings of the earth. The kings have joined her in idolatry and in the pursuit of wealth and power: political and economic alliances with the godless world system. This is the deal made at the top, the arrangement between power and money that every empire runs on.

Drunk with her wine. Drunk (emethysthēsan). Two groups, and the distinction matters. The kings committed immorality with her; the dwellers on earth merely got drunk, the ordinary population who never signed anything and simply drank what was poured. That is a fair description of how a civilisation actually corrupts the people in it. Very few of them are in the room where the arrangements are made. What reaches them is a mood: what everyone assumes, what is obviously worth having, what only a strange person would refuse. And the effect named is drunkenness, intoxication by her luxury, pleasures and values, which is not primarily wickedness but the loss of judgement: the inability to think clearly about God, or to walk in a straight line while being quite certain that you are.

What does Babylon look like where I live? Wherever a culture offers you everything good, comfort, pleasure, status, security, belonging, without God, and then asks for your heart in return, you are looking at her. In a modern Western city she rarely persecutes with swords. She advertises. She tells you that you are what you own, that your worth is your success, that sex is a right without a covenant, that a sensible person keeps religion private, and that the good life is always one purchase away. She is in the shopping centre, the screen in your pocket, the career ladder and the endless feed. None of those things is evil in itself. The question is whether they are being offered to you as substitutes for God.

On a Tuesday. The world’s seductions are attractive, and most of them arrive as assumptions rather than temptations. Picture an ordinary evening: the conversation at dinner, the programmes on the screen, the plans for the next holiday. Somewhere in all of it is a quiet picture of what a good life must include. It is worth wondering, now and then, where that picture came from, from the word of God or from the wine everyone else is drinking.
verseByVerse.note: “Many waters” recalls ancient Babylon, built on the Euphrates and its canals.

verseByVerse.quote: And he carried me away in the Spirit into a wilderness, and I saw a woman sitting on a scarlet beast that was full of blasphemous names, and it had seven heads and ten horns. The woman was arrayed in purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and jewels and pearls, holding in her hand a golden cup full of abominations and the impurities of her sexual immorality.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Jeremiah 51:7 calls Babylon a golden cup in the LORD’s hand, making all the earth drunk. Jeremiah 4:30 pictures unfaithful Jerusalem dressing in scarlet and adorning herself with gold to attract lovers.

Carried away in the Spirit. In the Spirit (en pneumati), as in 1:10 and 4:2: the third of John’s four times in the Spirit (1:10; 4:2; 17:3; 21:10), each marking a new section. And the location is deliberate. To see the Bride he will be carried to a great, high mountain (21:10); to see the prostitute he is taken into a desert. The wilderness is where the woman of chapter 12 fled and was fed for 1,260 days (12:6). The same landscape shelters the true woman and exposes the false one. From the wilderness, the place of the faithful church, John sees Babylon clearly for what she is.

A woman on a scarlet beast. Sitting on (kathēmenēn epi): riding, supported by, controlling. It is the beast of chapter 13, political power empowered by Satan, and she is riding it. Babylon, the world’s culture and economy, rides on the back of political power. She does not own the beast; she is carried by it. Her whole position depends on a creature she does not control, and verse 16 will show what that arrangement is worth.

Seven heads and ten horns. As in 13:1. The scarlet of the beast matches the scarlet of the woman, and of the dragon (12:3). They are dressed for each other.

Purple and scarlet. She is magnificent. Purple dye came from a Mediterranean shellfish and was fabulously costly; a purple garment was the mark of an emperor. Scarlet dye was costly too. Gold, precious stones and pearls are exactly the list that will reappear in chapter 18 as the cargo the merchants of the earth weep over (18:12, 16). This is not a squalid figure in a doorway. She is the best-dressed woman in the world.

Nobody is seduced by something repulsive. That is the point of the whole picture. The beast is frightening and can be recognised by a child; Babylon is beautiful, expensive, cultured and hospitable, and it takes a prophet in the Spirit to see what she is. The church has often found it easier to resist persecution than prosperity, and this chapter knows it.

A counterfeit Bride. Her finery is a parody of the Bride, who wears fine linen, bright and pure (19:8), and of the new Jerusalem, adorned with gold, jewels and pearls (21:18–21). Babylon offers a counterfeit glory. John stops to say what the Bride’s linen is: the righteous deeds of the saints, and it was given her to wear (19:8). One woman is covered in what she bought; the other is dressed in what was given her. And the giver is her Bridegroom: the robes of his people were washed and made white in the blood of the Lamb (7:14). Her beauty is the fruit of his sacrifice, and that is why it lasts.

A golden cup. Abominations (bdelygmatōn) are detestable things, especially idols; impurities (akatharta) are unclean things. Outwardly golden, inwardly filthy. It is precisely the charge Jesus laid against the Pharisees: they cleaned the outside of the cup while inside it was full of greed and self-indulgence (Matthew 23:25).

The vessel is worth more than the contents. Nobody would drink from a cup that looked like what is in it. That is the entire mechanism of temptation, and it has not needed updating in nineteen centuries. And the contents are always worse than they look.

How can I enjoy good things without being seduced by them? By receiving them as gifts and not as gods. Everything God made is good and to be received with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:4), and Paul tells the rich not to set their hopes on riches but on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17). The danger signs are when a good thing begins to define you, when you cannot imagine being content without it, when getting or keeping it bends your conscience, or when it crowds out God and his people. A simple safeguard is generosity: give freely of what you most enjoy. A thing you can give away has not yet captured you.

verseByVerse.quote: And on her forehead was written a name of mystery: "BABYLON THE GREAT, MOTHER OF PROSTITUTES AND OF EARTH'S ABOMINATIONS." And I saw the woman, drunk with the blood of the saints, the blood of the martyrs of Jesus. When I saw her, I marveled greatly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. One Roman writer suggests that prostitutes in Rome might wear a band on the forehead bearing their name. Jeremiah 3:3 tells unfaithful Israel that she has the forehead of a prostitute and refuses to be ashamed.

A name of mystery. A name on a forehead, in a book where that is never incidental. The servants of God are sealed on the forehead (7:3); the 144,000 carry the Lamb’s name and his Father’s there (14:1); the beast’s worshippers take its mark in the same place (13:16). The forehead shows identity, and everyone is labelled. Mystery (mystērion) means a name with a hidden meaning that must be understood spiritually. Babylon is not literally the ancient city on the Euphrates, which was largely in ruins in John’s day.

BABYLON THE GREAT. The ESV prints the name in capital letters, and it is not decoration; it is how a placard reads. Babylon is the city of pride and rebellion, the destroyer of Jerusalem, and her story goes back to Babel, where people said, let us make a name for ourselves (Genesis 11:4). Here at last is that name, written on her forehead for everyone to read. John uses it the way he used Sodom and Egypt at 11:8, as a type: in every age she is the human city organised against God.

MOTHER OF PROSTITUTES AND OF EARTH’S ABOMINATIONS. Mother: the source, the origin. All the world’s idolatries and corruptions flow from her. She is not one city but the source of a family of them, reproducing in every generation. Rome was a daughter. So was the old city on the Euphrates. There will be others.

Who is she? For John’s first readers she is unmistakably Rome. Verse 9 says the seven heads are seven mountains, and Rome was famous throughout the empire as the city on seven hills. Verse 18 calls her the great city that has dominion over the kings of the earth, which in the AD 90s named exactly one place. Peter, writing from the same city, sends greetings from she who is at Babylon (1 Peter 5:13). A minority reading, held by some preterists (readers who see most of Revelation fulfilled in the first century), takes her as apostate Jerusalem, pointing to verse 6 and to Jesus’ words that Jerusalem kills the prophets (Matthew 23:37). It has real evidence behind it, but it does not explain the seven mountains or verse 18 as naturally.

Drunk with the blood of the saints. She has been serving a cup all chapter, and now the reader is told what she has been drinking. The word is drunk, not merely stained: she has killed God’s people in great numbers, and revels in it, past the point where it serves any purpose. Martyrs (martyrōn) is the word for witnesses. Nero blamed Christians for the fire of Rome in AD 64 and had many killed horribly, and early Christian tradition says that Peter and Paul died there.

Persecuted in his people. The blood is called the blood of the martyrs of Jesus, and the Lord takes it personally. When Saul of Tarsus was on the road to Damascus with warrants against Christians, the risen Christ did not ask him why he was persecuting the church. He asked, Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:4). Every drop Babylon drinks is drawn from the body of which he is the head. And before any of them, she killed him: Jesus Christ is the faithful witness (1:5), condemned by a Roman governor and crucified by Roman soldiers. The martyrs of Jesus died as he died, and they will rise as he rose.

I marveled greatly. The angel pauses over this, and so should we. The Greek is emphatic (ethaumasa … thauma mega, I wondered with a great wonder), and it is the same verb used twice in this book of the world’s reaction to the beast: the whole earth marvelled (13:3), and the dwellers on earth will marvel to see the beast (17:8). John, an apostle, in the Spirit, on assignment, has just had the reaction that the earth-dwellers have. The text does not say why: it may have been horror. It may have been that a figure so magnificent was so foul. It may, uncomfortably, have been fascination. The world’s glamour can fascinate even believers. The next verse opens with a rebuke, why do you marvel?, which suggests he should not have.

Where Christians differ: who is the prostitute? Many Reformers and later Protestants identified the prostitute with the Roman Catholic Church and the papacy, seeing in her purple and scarlet the robes of cardinals, and in her drunkenness the blood of the persecuted Reformers. Others see her as apostate Christianity in general, or a future one-world religion. Preterists see first-century Jerusalem. This commentary’s view: the prostitute is Rome, the great city of John’s day (v. 18), seen as the centre of a seductive world system of wealth, idolatry and persecution; and she stands for the godless world system in every age, the culture, commerce and false religion that seduce people from God and persecute his people. Wherever a church becomes rich, worldly and persecuting, as the Reformers saw in their day, it takes on Babylon’s features. But the image is wider than any one church: she is the whole seductive world, which Christians are called to come out of (18:4).

The Reformers’ reading. It is worth understanding why Luther, Calvin, Knox and the Westminster divines saw the papacy in these chapters. They lived under a church seated in Rome, clothed in purple and scarlet, enormously rich, allied with kings, and burning Bible-believing Christians. They rightly saw that a church can become a harlot, as Israel did. Their reading is not foolish; it is too narrow. Babylon was already there before the papacy, and she is still there wherever Christ’s people are seduced or persecuted. Nor does it license suspicion of Roman Catholic neighbours today, many of whom love Christ; the warning of the chapter is aimed at every church, Protestant ones included, that grows rich and worldly.

What it does not mean. Seeing Babylon in the world does not mean Christians should withdraw from society, hate their cities, or treat individuals as enemies. They are called to seek the welfare of the city where they live (Jeremiah 29:7), while refusing its idols.

Will ancient Babylon in Iraq be rebuilt? Some popular teachers expect the literal city on the Euphrates to be rebuilt as a world capital. The text itself points another way, and says so plainly in two places: the name is a mystery, to be understood spiritually, and the angel identifies her as the great city that ruled the kings of the earth in John’s day, on seven hills (vv. 9, 18). The ruins in Iraq are not the issue. The issue is the spirit of Babel, which is alive in every capital and every heart that says, let us make a name for ourselves.

Can a Christian be fascinated by Babylon? Yes, and John shows it. It is possible to spend a great deal of time appalled by a culture and still be more interested in it than in God: reading every outrage, watching every scandal, knowing every detail of the world’s sin and very little of God’s word. The line between prophetic concern and simple fascination is thinner than it looks, and an apostle needed to have it pointed out to him. If you find your mind full of Babylon, turn it deliberately to the Lamb. You become like what you gaze at.

On a Tuesday. Christ counts the wounds of the persecuted church as his own, so pray for it by name: a particular country where Christians are suffering, and one believer there if you know of one.

For worship. Babylon’s name is written on her forehead for shame, and every daughter in her family bears it. The Lamb writes a different name on his people: his own and his Father’s, and his new name besides (14:1; 3:12). She is drunk on the blood of the saints; he counts their death precious (Psalm 116:15), and he will raise every witness she killed. Hers is the mystery of lawlessness (2 Thessalonians 2:7). His is the great mystery of godliness: he was manifested in the flesh and taken up in glory (1 Timothy 3:16), and he will bring with him all who bore his name to the death.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 7–18 are the most explicitly interpretive passage in the book. Verses 7–8: the angel rebukes John’s marvelling and explains the beast that was and is not, and those who marvel at it. Verses 9–11: the seven heads are seven hills and seven kings, and the beast is an eighth.

Verses 12–14: ten kings rule for one hour, make war on the Lamb, and lose. Verses 15–18: the beast and the kings turn on the woman and destroy her, because God put it in their hearts, and she is named as the great city.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lamb Will Conquer

The beast was, and is not, a parody of God’s name — and goes to destruction. The seven kings cannot be identified with certainty, but their time is short. The kings make war on the Lamb and lose, and the beast turns on the woman it carried; God put it in their hearts.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Those with the Lamb are called, chosen and faithful, in that order.

Now: Evil is not loyal: whatever you ride for safety will one day devour its passengers.

verseByVerse.quote: But the angel said to me, "Why do you marvel? I will tell you the mystery of the woman, and of the beast with seven heads and ten horns that carries her. The beast that you saw was, and is not, and is about to rise from the bottomless pit and go to destruction. And the dwellers on earth whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world will marvel to see the beast, because it was and is not and is to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the angel said to me, Why do you marvel? A gentle rebuke. The world’s power and glamour should not impress the people of God. They should see through it. And the cure for staring at Babylon is being told what she is, which the angel supplies for the rest of the chapter.

The mystery of the woman. Mystery here means what it always means in the New Testament: not a riddle nobody can solve but a secret now disclosed. Verses 7 to 18 are the most explicitly interpretive passage in Revelation; again and again the angel says this is, or these are.

Was, and is not, and is about to rise. Set that clause against the divine name in this book. God is him who is and who was and who is to come (1:4, 8; 4:8). The beast was, and is not, and is about to rise. It is a parody of the eternal name, and a bad one, because the middle term has collapsed: where God says I am, the beast can only say is not. It is also a counterfeit of Christ’s death and resurrection (13:3). Its comings and goings, its apparent defeats and revivals, all end in destruction (apōleian, perdition). The beast appears in one empire, falls, reappears in another, and finally rises for a last time before its end.

Evil has no being of its own. That is a concentrated statement about evil. Whatever the beast is, it does not have being in the way God has being. It was; it is not; it will make an appearance; and its journey ends at one destination which the sentence names before the journey starts: and go to destruction. Four verbs, and the last one is the only certainty among them. Historically, the phrase probably plays on the Nero legend, an emperor who died and whom many in the eastern empire expected back. John takes the popular rumour and turns it into a theological joke.

Slain, and standing. The beast’s career is a parody, and a parody tells you what the original looks like. The beast was wounded and seemed to come back (13:3); it rises from the abyss only to go to destruction. The Lamb was slain in truth, not seemingly, and John first saw him standing, still bearing the marks of slaughter, in the midst of the throne (5:6). His death was real, his rising was real, and where he went after it was not destruction but the right hand of God. The world marvels at a revival that ends in the pit. Heaven sings to the one whose death was the defeat of death, and who will never die again (Romans 6:9).

Written in the book of life. The same safeguard as 13:8, and it is the counterweight to everything alarming in the chapter. There is a register. It belongs to the Lamb. The entries were made from the foundation of the world, before anyone had done anything to earn or forfeit a place. Those not written in the Lamb’s book are fascinated by the beast. Those whose names are written are protected from its deception. Election protects. Election is God’s choice, made before the world began, of a people to belong to Christ, a choice rooted in his free love rather than in any merit he saw in them (Ephesians 1:4–5). That choice, not their own cleverness, is why they are not finally deceived.

Am I in danger of being taken in? That is the fear this chapter is most likely to produce in a sincere reader, and the answer should be given plainly. The verse does not say the enrolled are cleverer or more discerning than others. It says they are written, and it says who wrote them, and it says when. John himself marvelled and had to be corrected. The security is not in his reaction but in the register. Jesus said that the false christs would lead astray, if possible, even the elect (Matthew 24:24), and the words if possible are the point: it is not possible. The Lamb keeps those the Father gave him.

How can I know my name is written in the Lamb’s book? Not by looking into the book, which no one can do, but by looking to the Lamb whose book it is. Scripture gives election not as a puzzle to solve but as a comfort to those who believe. If you have come to Christ, trusting him alone for forgiveness, and you love him and want to follow him, however weakly, that is the evidence that God chose you (1 Thessalonians 1:4–5; John 6:37). The Father draws, the Son receives, and none of them is lost. Make your calling and election sure (2 Peter 1:10), not by anxious introspection but by continuing to trust and follow him.

On a Tuesday. When the news makes you anxious that evil keeps reviving and the church is losing, read 1:17–18 aloud: the one who died and is alive for ever holds the keys of death and Hades. Your safety is written in his book, not in your strength.

verseByVerse.quote: This calls for a mind with wisdom: the seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman is seated; they are also seven kings, five of whom have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come, and when he does come he must remain only a little while. As for the beast that was and is not, it is an eighth but it belongs to the seven, and it goes to destruction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Rome was known throughout the ancient world as the city on seven hills (the Palatine, Capitoline, Quirinal, Viminal, Esquiline, Caelian and Aventine). Roman writers such as Virgil, Horace and Cicero refer to it this way, and an old festival, the Septimontium (seven hills), kept the idea alive. The emperors from Augustus to Domitian were Augustus, Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius, Nero, then Galba, Otho and Vitellius (in AD 68–69), then Vespasian, Titus and Domitian.

This calls for a mind with wisdom. As in 13:18, where the number of the beast was set as a puzzle, spiritual discernment is needed. Both times John invites calculation, and both times readers have been more confident than the evidence allows. Honesty is more useful here than ingenuity.

Seven mountains. A clear reference to Rome, the city on seven hills. The first readers could not have missed it.

They are also seven kings. The symbols have more than one meaning: the heads are both hills and kings. Seven is completeness, the full line of rulers of the beastly empire.

Five have fallen, one is. This is where certainty has to stop. Many attempts have been made to match these to specific emperors, but they depend on where one starts counting and whether one includes the three short-lived emperors of AD 68–69, and no scheme fits perfectly. Depending on the choices, the sixth, the one who is, can be made to come out as Nero, or Vespasian, or Domitian, and each reconstruction requires decisions the text does not authorise. More likely, John’s point is that most of the beast’s rule is already past, the present ruler is in power now, and only a short time remains. History is nearer its end than its beginning.

An eighth. One beyond the seven, a final ruler, yet belonging to the same line and spirit. Possibly a reference to the expectation of Nero returning in a new form; possibly Domitian, often seen as a second Nero. Early Christians saw eight as the number of new beginning, because Christ rose on the day after the Sabbath, the eighth day; if John has that in mind, the beast’s eighth is a counterfeit resurrection, heading only for destruction. The beast is not a new thing; it is the seven again, one more time, wearing a new number. That is what chapter 13 said by giving one animal the features of Daniel’s beasts. Empires are not a series of separate problems. They are one problem with a changing letterhead.

The destination, twice. And it goes to destruction, for the second time in three verses. The angel has now given the beast’s past, its present, its future and its destination, and he has named the destination twice. A reader who cannot reconstruct the emperor list, and nobody can with certainty, has still been given the one piece of information the chapter most wants him to have. The angel’s emphasis is not on who the kings are but on how long they last: a little while, and then destruction.

A kingdom that shall not pass away. The heads and horns come from Daniel 7, and that chapter does not end with beasts. After the beasts have had their season, Daniel sees one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven, and to him is given dominion and glory and a kingdom, an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away (Daniel 7:13–14). Jesus took that title for himself, and at his trial he told the high priest that he would be seen coming with the clouds of heaven (Mark 14:62). So a reader who cannot work out the seventh king can still know the last King. Theirs is a little while; his is for ever.

Should I try to work out who the kings are? It is not wrong to study the history, and it helps to see how clearly the first readers would have recognised Rome. But be very wary of anyone who claims certainty, and still more of anyone who matches the kings to present-day leaders. Every such scheme in church history has failed, and many have damaged faith when the dates passed. The wisdom John calls for is not cleverness with lists but the spiritual insight to recognise the beast’s character in any age, refuse its claims, and remember that its time is short.

On a Tuesday. Do not put your hope in any political leader, and do not despair over any either. When an election or a regime fills you with fear or with excitement, put the name of the leader alongside this verse: one is, another is to come, a little while, and then destruction. Pray for those in authority (1 Timothy 2:1–2), obey what is lawful, and keep your hope where it cannot be voted out.
verseByVerse.note: Rome was famous as the city on seven hills.

verseByVerse.quote: And the ten horns that you saw are ten kings who have not yet received royal power, but they are to receive authority as kings for one hour, together with the beast. These are of one mind, and they hand over their power and authority to the beast. They will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are called and chosen and faithful."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ten kings. The ten horns come from Daniel 7, where the fourth beast had ten horns and the interpretation given was ten kings (Daniel 7:24). Ten in this book is a large, complete number, a full set of a lesser kind: the devil throws some into prison for ten days (2:10). So this is most likely the complete roster of the beast’s client rulers, future from John’s point of view, rather than a list to be filled in with names.

For one hour. One hour (mian hōran): a very short time. It will be used three more times in the next chapter, each time of Babylon’s ruin: in a single hour your judgement has come (18:10, 17, 19). Their reign and her ruin are measured in the same tiny unit.

Of one mind. One mind (mian gnōmēn): one purpose, a single settled opinion. They unite with the beast against God, the nations of the world united in rebellion (Psalm 2:2). And nobody takes anything from them. They give away the one thing a king exists to hold. That is what totalitarian arrangements have often looked like from the inside: not a conquest of the powerful, but a queue of them agreeing to hand something over in exchange for a share.

They will make war on the Lamb. Make war (polemēsousin). The final battle of 16:14 and 19:19. Ten kings, the full authority of the empire, a beast with seven heads and the dragon’s throne behind it, against a Lamb. John does not switch to the Lion for the battle. The word he uses (arnion) is the one he uses of Christ throughout, the Lamb standing as though it had been slain.

The Lamb will conquer. Conquer (nikēsei). The Lamb, who conquered by his death (5:5–6), conquers his enemies at his return. And there is no description of the fighting: they are simply defeated. The reason given is not a strategy or a weapon or a number of troops. It is a title.

Lord of lords and King of kings. The outcome follows from who he is. Nothing has to happen for this to be true, which is why the verse can state it before the event. The title is the highest there is, an Old Testament name for God: the LORD your God is God of gods and Lord of lords (Deuteronomy 10:17; Psalm 136:2–3). And it is applied here to the Lamb without a word of explanation, as this book does everything else concerning his deity. It will be written on his robe and his thigh at 19:16, in reverse order. Every emperor’s claim is answered. The Babylonian and Persian rulers who called themselves king of kings were borrowing a title that belongs to him.

Called and chosen and faithful. Three words describing believers, almost in passing, and the order is the whole doctrine. Called (klētoi): summoned by God’s effective call (Romans 8:30), the call that does not merely invite but actually brings a person to come. They did not volunteer; God summoned them. Chosen (eklektoi, elect): chosen by God before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4). Behind the calling is a choosing, and behind the choosing is nothing but God’s own decision. Faithful (pistoi): trusting and loyal to the end. This is the one they do, but it comes third. God calls and chooses, and those he calls and chooses prove faithful. Their faithfulness is the visible end of a chain God began before they existed: chosen before the foundation of the world, called in time, and kept faithful by his power. Many Christians, often called Arminian, understand God’s choice as resting on his foreknowledge of who would believe, and they love the same Lamb; this commentary follows the order of this verse and of Romans 8:29–30, where God’s choosing and calling come before anything we do.

In the flow. Verse 14 is a flash forward set in the middle of Babylon’s chapter. The angel is explaining the beast and its kings, and before he reaches the woman’s ruin (vv. 16–17) he tells how their war ends: the Lamb wins. Chapter 19 will show the same victory in full, with the same title written on his robe (19:16) and the same kings gathered against him (19:19). Set here, it means that John’s readers learn who wins before they learn how the beast’s alliances fall apart, so that nothing in the rest of the chapter can frighten them.

Outnumbered, and on the winning side. This is the answer for a Christian who reads the chapter and feels outnumbered, which is the correct arithmetic and the wrong conclusion. Ten kings, one beast, the whole world drunk, and a handful of congregations meeting in houses. The verse does not encourage them by disputing the numbers. It tells them who is at the front and who put them there.

What is the difference between being called here and in Matthew 22? In Matthew 22:14 the call is the gospel invitation, which goes out to everyone who hears it and which many refuse. In Revelation 17:14, as in Romans 8:30, the called are those whom God has effectually drawn, whose hearts he has opened so that they come (John 6:44; Acts 16:14). The first is the voice of the preacher; the second is the voice of God through the preacher, raising the dead. So we must offer Christ freely to all, and we can be confident that God’s sheep will hear his voice.

I do not feel faithful. Am I really with the Lamb? Faithfulness here is not a feeling or a flawless record but a heart that keeps trusting and returning to Christ. Peter denied him three times and was restored; Thomas doubted and was met. If you are still holding to Christ, still confessing your sins to him and wanting to follow him, you are with the Lamb. And remember the order: you are faithful because you were called and chosen, not the other way round. God does not abandon what he starts: the one who began the good work in you will carry it through to the day of Jesus Christ (Philippians 1:6).

For worship. Lord of lords and King of kings, and still the Lamb. The highest name in heaven was not laid aside when he took our flesh, and the wounds were not laid aside when he took the throne. The kings of the earth hold power for one hour, and even the hour is his to give; he holds his kingdom for ever, and he shares it, for he has made his called and chosen ones a kingdom, priests to his God and Father (1:6). Every crown on earth is borrowed from his, and every one will be laid at his feet.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel said to me, "The waters that you saw, where the prostitute is seated, are peoples and multitudes and nations and languages. And the ten horns that you saw, they and the beast will hate the prostitute. They will make her desolate and naked, and devour her flesh and burn her up with fire,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Ezekiel 23:25–29 describes how the lovers of unfaithful Jerusalem would turn on her, strip her naked and leave her bare. In AD 68–69, Rome itself was torn apart in civil war, and the Capitol was burned by rival Roman armies. The fire of AD 64 had already destroyed much of the city.

The waters are peoples. The angel interprets his own image, and the fourfold phrase is a form of the one used since 5:9 of the whole human race (5:9; 7:9), the same people the Lamb ransomed. Babylon’s influence is worldwide, and her seat is popular support. She rules by being wanted.

A throne set on water. Water in this book is not solid ground. The sea is chaos; a river was poured out of the dragon’s mouth to sweep the woman away (12:15); the Euphrates dried up in a single bowl (16:12). A throne set on water is a throne set on a mood, and a mood can go out as fast as it came in, which is what the next verse describes.

They will hate the prostitute. Hate (misēsousin). This is the turn of the chapter and it is the last thing a reader expects. Babylon is not destroyed by the armies of heaven. She is destroyed by the beast she was riding and the kings who were her clients.

Desolate and naked. Desolate (ērēmōmenēn): laid waste, made a wilderness. Naked: stripped of her finery and exposed, the woman in purple and scarlet and gold with nothing on.

Devour her flesh. Like Jezebel, eaten by the dogs by the wall of Jezreel (2 Kings 9:36); like a city sacked and burned. Under the law, burning was the penalty for a priest’s daughter who became a prostitute (Leviticus 21:9). The four verbs escalate, and each one answers something she did. She sold beauty and is left desolate; she traded on being clothed and is stripped; she drank the blood of the saints and is eaten; she lit Nero’s gardens with burning Christians, as the Roman historian Tacitus records, and is burned.

The one who was stripped. Her nakedness is the exposure of guilt: she is stripped of what she sold herself for. There is one other figure in the New Testament stripped and shamed outside a city, and he had nothing to be ashamed of. The soldiers divided Jesus’ garments and cast lots for his tunic (John 19:23–24), and he hung on the cross despising the shame (Hebrews 12:2). She is stripped for her own unfaithfulness; he was stripped for the unfaithfulness of others, so that people who had gone after other lovers could be clothed in white and their shameful nakedness never be seen (3:18).

Evil is not loyal. It has no capacity for loyalty. The alliance between the corrupt system and the brute power that carries it holds only while both are getting something, and when it stops paying, the beast eats the woman. Nobody who has ever climbed onto the beast has been carried all the way.

Should Christians ever seek political power or allies? Christians may serve in government and should seek justice and the good of their city (Jeremiah 29:7; Romans 13:1–7). Joseph and Daniel served pagan kings faithfully. The warning here is against climbing on the beast: making an alliance that requires us to compromise Christ’s truth, or trusting a political power to secure the church’s future. Whenever the church has bought favour by silence or sold its witness for protection, it has eventually been devoured. Serve honestly, speak truthfully, and never make any party, ruler or nation your saviour.

On a Tuesday. The world’s alliances and pleasures do not last; those who serve them are eventually devoured by them. Christ already holds you, and no one will snatch you out of his hand (John 10:28), so you need buy no safety elsewhere. If you are tempted this week to make a small accommodation for the sake of safety, a silence to keep your place, a compromise to keep the peace with someone powerful, remember that the thing you are riding to keep your position has an appetite, and it is not sentimental about passengers.

For worship. The Lamb is faithful to the end. The beast devours its friends, and the world consumes those who love it, but Christ has never once betrayed one who trusted him. He laid down his life for his friends, and he did it while they were still his enemies (John 15:13; Romans 5:10). His love is not a contract that ends when it stops paying; it is a covenant sealed in his blood. The beast carries its riders only as far as suits it. He carries his own all the way home, and he will never leave them nor forsake them.

verseByVerse.quote: for God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose by being of one mind and handing over their royal power to the beast, until the words of God are fulfilled. And the woman that you saw is the great city that has dominion over the kings of the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Scripture often shows God using the free actions of wicked people to accomplish his purposes: Joseph’s brothers (Genesis 50:20), Cyrus (Isaiah 45:1–4), and above all those who crucified Jesus, who did what God’s hand and plan had predestined to take place (Acts 4:27–28). Proverbs 21:1 says the king’s heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will.

God has put it into their hearts. The verse explains the one before it, and it is a daring sentence. Put it into their hearts (edōken eis tas kardias autōn, gave into their hearts); purpose (gnōmēn, mind, plan). The reason the kings agreed, the reason they handed everything to the beast, and the reason the beast turned on the woman, is that God has put it into their hearts. God is sovereign even over the evil intentions of the beast and its kings. They act freely and wickedly, and they are responsible for what they do; yet God directs it to his own ends.

Free, wicked, and directed. Not that God tempted anybody, and not that anybody in this chapter is innocent; every one of them is doing exactly what he wants and will answer for it. But the deepest cause of the collapse of Babylon is a decision taken in heaven, carried out through the free and wicked choices of men who thought they were serving themselves. Scripture says this repeatedly and without embarrassment: God hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and Pharaoh hardened his own. Assyria was the rod of his anger and did not know it (Isaiah 10:5–7). And Peter said of the worst act in human history that Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and in the same breath that lawless men crucified him (Acts 2:23).

Handing over their royal power. Even their alliance with the beast serves God’s plan. The very unity they formed against him is the instrument he uses.

Until the words of God are fulfilled. Fulfilled (telesthēsontai, completed). God’s word sets the limit. Nothing happens apart from it. There is an end point, and it is not the exhaustion of the kings or the collapse of the system. It is the completion of what God said. The permission runs exactly as far as the promise and not one hour further.

The great city. Has dominion (echousa basileian): has a kingdom, rules. In John’s day there was only one city that ruled the kings of the earth: Rome. The angel makes the identification about as clear as it could perhaps safely be made in a letter that might fall into Roman hands. But the description is about what she does rather than where she is, and the office has never been vacant for long. Babylon is whatever, in a given century, sits on the peoples, trades with the kings, dresses beautifully, offers everything a person wants without the God who made it, and is prepared to shed blood to keep its position.

Where Christians differ: is God the author of evil? Some worry that saying God put it into their hearts makes God responsible for their sin, and so they soften the verse to mean only that God permits it; they are right to guard God’s goodness, and Scripture guards it too. This commentary’s view: Scripture teaches that God ordains all that comes to pass, including the evil acts of creatures, without himself being the author of sin, and without taking away their responsibility (Genesis 50:20; Acts 2:23; 4:27–28). He does not tempt anyone to evil (James 1:13), nor infuse wickedness into their hearts; but he directs their evil desires to fulfil his good purpose. This mystery is not a reason for fear but for comfort: even the beast’s schemes serve God’s plan.

How does this help a persecuted church? The practical weight of it is considerable, and it is why the verse is here rather than in a theological appendix. A believer watching a hostile power arrange itself has two possible accounts. Either history is a contest whose outcome depends on whether the good side can hold out, or the arrangements being made against the church are themselves the means by which God dismantles what is arrayed against her. The second is harder to look at and is the only one with a floor under it. It means that no plot against you is outside his plan, and none can go one hour beyond his word.

Two women, side by side. So the chapter ends where it began, with an angel showing John a woman. There will be another woman, and another angel, and another invitation in the same words (21:9). Both are cities and both are brides, and a reader is asked to look at them side by side and see which he has been dressing for. One is arrayed in purple and scarlet and gold, rides a beast she does not control, and is stripped and burned by the thing she was sitting on. The other is clothed in fine linen, bright and pure, and comes down out of heaven from God, and her husband is the Lamb who was slain and is Lord of lords and King of kings.

On a Tuesday. When world events seem out of control, remember that God directs even the plans of the wicked, and pray specifically: for rulers to be restrained, for the persecuted to be kept, for enemies of the gospel to be converted, and for God’s words to be fulfilled. Then go about your ordinary duties in peace. The king’s heart is in the LORD’s hand, and so is yours.

When I saw her, I marveled greatly.<sup>7</sup>But the angel said to me, “Why do you marvel? I will tell you the mystery of the woman, and of the beast with seven heads and ten horns that carries her.<sup>8</sup>The beast that you saw was, and is not, and is about to rise from the bottomless pit and go to destruction. And the dwellers on earth whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world will marvel to see the beast, because it was and is not and is to come.<sup>9</sup>This calls for a mind with wisdom: the seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman is seated;<sup>10</sup>they are also seven kings, five of whom have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come, and when he does come he must remain only a little while.<sup>11</sup>As for the beast that was and is not, it is an eighth but it belongs to the seven, and it goes to destruction.<sup>12</sup>And the ten horns that you saw are ten kings who have not yet received royal power, but they are to receive authority as kings for one hour, together with the beast.<sup>13</sup>These are of one mind, and they hand over their power and authority to the beast.<sup>14</sup>They will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are called and chosen and faithful.”<sup>15</sup>And the angel said to me, “The waters that you saw, where the prostitute is seated, are peoples and multitudes and nations and languages.<sup>16</sup>And the ten horns that you saw, they and the beast will hate the prostitute. They will make her desolate and naked, and devour her flesh and burn her up with fire,<sup>17</sup>for God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose by being of one mind and handing over their royal power to the beast, until the words of God are fulfilled.<sup>18</sup>And the woman that you saw is the great city that has dominion over the kings of the earth.”

18.title: Fallen, Fallen Is Babylon the Great
18.overview:
Chapter 18 is a funeral song over the great city, one of the longest chapters in the book. It is shaped like the prophets’ dirges over Babylon and Tyre (Isaiah 13–14; Ezekiel 26–28), and its cargo list is adapted from Ezekiel 27.

It has three movements: the angel’s announcement of Babylon’s fall and the call for God’s people to come out of her (vv. 1–8); the laments of kings, merchants and sailors, who mourn from a safe distance as the city burns (vv. 9–20); and the millstone and the silence that follows (vv. 21–24).

Chapter 17 showed Babylon as a religious and political power; chapter 18 shows her as an economy. Her cargo list ends with slaves, that is, human souls, and the charge reaches beyond Rome’s slave markets to every economy that treats people as goods.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Announcement and the Call
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–3: a glorious angel announces that Babylon has fallen and become a haunt of demons, and names the nations, kings and merchants who shared her sins. Verses 4–5: a voice from heaven calls God’s people to come out of her, for her sins are heaped high as heaven.

Verses 6–8: she is to be repaid in the cup she mixed, and her boast that she will never see mourning is answered by death, mourning and famine in a single day.
verseByVerse.theology:
Come Out of Her

Babylon is fallen and left a haunt of unclean things. God’s people are called to come out of her, not by emigrating but by refusing to share her sins. She said she would never see mourning; death, mourning and famine come in a single day.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: What the beast enforced by law, Babylon sustained by trade.

Now: Coming out of Babylon happens in small daily refusals; beware the unspoken belief that your comforts will simply go on.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I saw another angel coming down from heaven, having great authority, and the earth was made bright with his glory. And he called out with a mighty voice, "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great! She has become a dwelling place for demons, a haunt for every unclean spirit, a haunt for every unclean bird, a haunt for every unclean and detestable beast. For all nations have drunk the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality, and the kings of the earth have committed immorality with her, and the merchants of the earth have grown rich from the power of her luxurious living."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Revelation 18 is a funeral song over Babylon, the world city of wealth, luxury and persecution, written in the style of the prophets’ laments over Babylon and Tyre. An angel announces that Babylon has fallen and become a haunt of demons (vv. 1–3). A voice from heaven calls God’s people to come out of her, and calls for her to be repaid double for her pride, for she said, I sit as a queen (vv. 4–8). Kings, merchants who traded in every luxury and even in human beings, and sailors lament from a distance that in a single hour she is ruined (vv. 9–19), while heaven and the saints are told to rejoice, because God has judged her for them (v. 20). A mighty angel throws a millstone into the sea: music, craft, the mill, the lamp and the voices of bride and groom will be heard in her no more, for she deceived the nations and in her was found the blood of the prophets and saints (vv. 21–24). Chapter 17 showed Babylon as a religious and political power; chapter 18 shows her as an economy, and the charge sheet is a cargo list.

The setting. The chapter draws heavily on Isaiah 13, 21 and 47, Jeremiah 50–51 (oracles against Babylon) and Ezekiel 26–28 (the laments over Tyre, the great trading city of the ancient world). In John’s day, Rome imported vast quantities of goods from across the empire, by sea through its port at Ostia, to supply the luxury of its elite, and the wealth of the provinces flowed to it. Roman writers such as Pliny the Elder complained about the extravagance of Roman luxury and its drain on the empire.

Another angel, having great authority. Great authority (exousian megalēn). Babylon claimed great authority; this angel’s is greater. And it is the authority of one sent, coming down from heaven, which is where every true authority in this book comes from.

Made bright with his glory. Ezekiel saw the same thing when the glory of God returned to the temple: the earth shone with his glory (Ezekiel 43:2). The city about to be described as the most magnificent in the world is about to be lit by something that makes it look like a candle at noon. And the contrast runs to the end of the chapter, where Babylon’s lamps go out (v. 23).

And he called out with a mighty voice, Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great! The announcement made in one verse at 14:8 is made again, and this time the chapter does not move on: it fills the whole chapter. The words are Isaiah’s watchman on the wall (Isaiah 21:9). And they are in the past tense: so certain that it is as good as done.

Fallen because the Lamb has conquered. Why can the angel speak in the past tense before the fall has even been described? Because the decisive battle has already been fought. The previous chapter promised that when the kings make war on the Lamb, the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings (17:14). On the eve of the cross Jesus said, now is the judgement of this world; now will the ruler of this world be cast out (John 12:31). Babylon’s fall is not a separate victory still waiting to be won. It is the victory of the cross working itself out in history, and the angel can announce it as done because, at Calvary, it was.

A dwelling place for demons. This is exactly what the prophets said would happen to the first Babylon, and John is quoting deliberately. Isaiah said that wild animals would lie down there, howling creatures fill its houses, hyenas cry in its towers and jackals in its pleasant palaces (Isaiah 13:21–22; also 34:11–14 of Edom; Jeremiah 50:39). Picture a ruin at night: the great houses still standing, the streets still laid out, and nothing moving in them but owls and jackals. The buildings make it terrible, because they were built for people and there are no people. The glittering city becomes a desolate ruin, and her true nature, demonic all along, is revealed. What does demonic all along mean? Not that every citizen was possessed, but that worship given to anything other than God is never neutral: Paul says that what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons and not to God (1 Corinthians 10:20). The ruin simply shows who had been living there. The word haunt (phylakē) can also mean a prison: the city that offered the world its freedom has become a cage for unclean things.

The wine of her immorality. As in 14:8 and 17:2: the nations drank what she poured, and lost their judgement. Three groups shared her sin and will lament her fall: kings, merchants and sailors (vv. 9–19). This verse is the chapter’s table of contents, and it has a new group. In chapter 17 the parties to Babylon’s business were the kings and the drunken population. Here the merchants arrive (emporoi, wholesale traders), and from verse 11 onward they dominate the chapter. Chapter 17 showed a prostitute demanding worship, riding a beast, drunk on the blood of the saints. Chapter 18 shows a market. And they are the same city, which is the point: what the beast enforces by law, Babylon sustains by trade.

The power of her luxurious living. The word (strēnous) means arrogant luxury, excess, the strength that comes from having far more than is needed. Babylon’s hold on the merchants is not that she threatened them. It is that she made them rich. That is still how she holds people: not chiefly by fear but by comfort, the quiet promise that a little more will make life secure, which is why her grip is so seldom felt.

Has Babylon already fallen? In John’s day Babylon was Rome, and Rome did eventually fall, but slowly, over centuries, not in a single hour (v. 10). Some expect a literally rebuilt city of Babylon. The more likely reading is that Babylon is the world system of wealth, power and false worship that Rome embodied, which has risen and fallen in many forms, and whose final fall comes at Christ’s return. Every collapse of a proud empire in history is a rehearsal of this chapter, and the last one will be the performance.

Is it wrong for a Christian to be wealthy? No. Abraham, Job and Joseph of Arimathea were rich and godly, and Paul does not tell the rich to give up everything but to be rich in good works, generous and ready to share, and to set their hope on God rather than on uncertain riches (1 Timothy 6:17–19). The danger is real, though: Jesus said it is hard for a rich person to enter the kingdom (Mark 10:23–25), because wealth so easily becomes the thing we trust. The questions to ask are how you got it, what you trust in, whether you are generous, and whether you could lose it and still praise God.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I heard another voice from heaven saying, "Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues; for her sins are heaped high as heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. The prophets called the Jewish exiles to flee from Babylon before its fall: go out of the midst of her, my people! Let every one save his life from the fierce anger of the LORD! (Jeremiah 51:45; also 50:8; 51:6; Isaiah 48:20; 52:11). Lot was urged to flee Sodom before its destruction (Genesis 19:12–22). Paul quoted Isaiah 52:11 to the Corinthians: go out from their midst, and be separate from them (2 Corinthians 6:17).

Come out of her, my people. Come out (exelthate). The command is quoted from the prophets almost word for word, and Paul used the same line to a church living in a Greek port. And the possessive matters: my people. God’s people are still in Babylon, in the world system, living among its temptations, and he claims them there. They are called to come out.

Lest you take part in her sins. Take part (synkoinōnēsēte): share, have fellowship with. The danger is not just living in Babylon, but sharing her sins: idolatry, greed, luxury, immorality, injustice.

Lest you share in her plagues. Those who share her sins will share her judgement. When a system falls, the people profiting from it fall with it, and they get no separate hearing on the grounds that they were only doing what everyone did.

It is not emigration. Two things need saying about what the command means, because it has been misused in both directions. It cannot mean physical withdrawal, and the New Testament settles that. Christians stayed in Rome; Paul greeted a congregation there and told them to pay their taxes (Romans 13:6–7). Whatever coming out of Babylon is, it is not a compound in the hills.

It is non-participation. The verse says what it is: lest you take part in her sins. A Christian lives in the city, works in it, pays for it and prays for it, and does not join in what it does, or want what it wants. That is far harder than moving house. Every Christian has to decide, repeatedly and in small instalments, whether to make the arrangement that everyone makes: the invoice adjusted, the thing not mentioned, the standard that quietly relaxes because it is costing too much. Coming out of Babylon happens on Tuesday afternoons, and nobody photographs it.

Outside the gate. The New Testament tells us where coming out leads. Jesus suffered outside the gate of Jerusalem to sanctify the people through his own blood, and Hebrews draws the conclusion: let us go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured, for here we have no lasting city (Hebrews 13:12–14). Coming out of Babylon is not first a moving away from something; it is a moving towards someone. Christians can refuse Babylon’s sins because they have a better treasure, and they can bear her contempt because he bore it first. The church does not leave the city by its own resolve. It follows its Lord, who went out ahead of it carrying a cross.

Heaped high as heaven. Heaped high (ekollēthēsan): glued together, piled up. The image is a tower of sins stacked up until they reach the sky, and it takes the reader straight back to where Babylon began, at a tower whose builders wanted its top in the heavens (Genesis 11:4). She always did want to reach heaven. She has managed it at last, and it is her record that arrived. God’s patience has an end.

In the flow. Verse 4 is the first word in the chapter spoken to the church, and the only command it gives them before the call to rejoice in verse 20. It explains why the chapter was written. The book has warned its churches about Babylon’s ways from the start, in Pergamum’s compromise, Thyatira’s Jezebel and Laodicea’s riches (2:14, 20; 3:17), and here the warning reaches its climax. Revelation is not given to satisfy curiosity about the end of empires. It is given so that Christ’s people will not be found sharing the sins of a city that is about to fall.

Where Christians differ: does this mean Christians should withdraw from society? Some groups, such as some Anabaptists and monastic movements, have taken such passages to call for physical separation from the world, forming separate communities; their seriousness about holiness is a rebuke to comfortable Christians. Others have used the verse to call believers out of particular churches they regard as Babylon. This commentary’s view: coming out of Babylon is mainly spiritual and moral: refusing to share the world’s idolatry, greed and sin, while still living in the world as salt and light. Jesus prayed not that his disciples would be taken out of the world, but that they would be kept from the evil one (John 17:15). Paul told the Corinthians not to leave the world, but not to share the sins of professing believers (1 Corinthians 5:9–11). Sometimes faithfulness will require leaving a particular job, relationship or even church that demands compromise. But the call is to holiness, not withdrawal.

What it does not mean. Coming out of Babylon does not mean God’s people can lose their salvation if they are found in the city when it falls. It is a call to be what they are: God’s holy people, not Babylon’s.

What does coming out look like on an ordinary day? It looks like honesty in your accounts when everyone else rounds up; refusing to laugh at what degrades people; keeping sex within marriage when the culture treats it as recreation; turning off what fills your mind with greed or lust; paying fairly and giving generously; and speaking of Christ when silence would be safer. It also means rhythms that keep your heart in the other city: the Lord’s Day, the church gathered, the word of God and prayer. You come out of Babylon not by moving away but by belonging somewhere else while you live there.

When should a Christian actually leave something? When staying would require you to sin, or when you cannot remain without being drawn into sin you have repeatedly failed to resist. A job that requires dishonesty, a relationship that pulls you from Christ, a business deal that depends on exploitation, or a church that has abandoned the gospel itself, not merely one with faults: these are places where coming out may mean walking out. Seek counsel from mature believers, pray, and act with humility rather than pride. But do not stay in sin because leaving is costly.

On a Tuesday. Where are you being drawn into the world’s sins, at work, online or in your spending? God already calls you my people, so come out of her, not by leaving the world, but by refusing her ways. Name one specific arrangement you have quietly made with Babylon, and end it this week, in the strength of the Spirit he has given you rather than your own resolve. No one comes out cleanly; but the one who went outside the gate obeyed perfectly in our place, and his record, not ours, is what stands before God.

verseByVerse.quote: Pay her back as she herself has paid back others, and repay her double for her deeds; mix a double portion for her in the cup she mixed. As she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so give her a like measure of torment and mourning, since in her heart she says, 'I sit as a queen, I am no widow, and mourning I shall never see.' For this reason her plagues will come in a single day, death and mourning and famine, and she will be burned up with fire; for mighty is the Lord God who has judged her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Jeremiah 50:15, 29 says of Babylon: repay her according to her deeds; do to her as she has done. In Isaiah 47:7–9, Babylon says that she will be mistress for ever, that she will not sit as a widow or know the loss of children; but God replies that these two things will come to her in a moment, in one day: the loss of children and widowhood. Double repayment was a principle of restitution in the law (Exodus 22:4, 7, 9).

Pay her back. Pay back (apodote): render, give back. The imperatives are plural and unattributed, addressed perhaps to the agents of God’s judgement, and the reader should not assume they are the church, because 17:16 has already said who actually destroys Babylon: the beast and the ten kings. Whoever is being commanded, no Christian in this book ever repays anybody. This is the principle of just retribution: what she did to God’s people will be done to her.

Repay her double. Double (diplōsate ta dipla, double the double). That raises a fair question about justice. If the punishment is twice the crime, is it just? Many scholars think the prophets’ use of the word answers it: double can mean the full corresponding measure, a matching copy, rather than twice as much. Isaiah 40:2, where Jerusalem has received double for all her sins, is often read in this way (compare 61:7). And the rest of the sentence makes it explicit. It is her own cup, her own recipe, folded back on her. Nothing new has been added. Her judgement fits her sin precisely and completely.

A cup he never mixed. Babylon’s judgement is her own cup handed back to her, and the reader of the Gospels knows that cup. In Gethsemane Jesus asked that a cup might pass from him (Mark 14:36), and it was not his own: he had mixed nothing in it. It was the cup of God’s wrath, which this book pours out on Babylon (14:10; 16:19), filled by his people’s sins, and he drank it to the bottom so that it would never be handed to them. That wrath is no outburst. It is perfect goodness answering evil, as steady as his love (Romans 1:18). That is the only way out of this verse. Every sinner either receives the measure of his own deeds, or is one of those for whom Christ has already drained it. There is no third cup.

As she glorified herself. Glorified herself (edoxasen hautēn): the root sin is pride, taking the glory that belongs to God. Lived in luxury (estrēniasen). Self-glorification and self-indulgence go together. The measure of her judgement is the measure of her self-exaltation.

I sit as a queen. Here is Babylon in her own words, and the boast is quoted from Isaiah’s taunt against the original city (Isaiah 47:7–8). Three claims, each a denial of something ordinary. I sit as a queen: permanent authority. I am no widow: nothing she depends on can die. Mourning I shall never see: she is exempt from grief. It is the boast of the city that called itself eternal (Roma aeterna).

The assumption of every prosperous society. That is not chiefly arrogance but the unexamined assumption of every prosperous society, which is why a comfortable church finds this chapter so hard to feel. The claim is not, I am better than others; it is, this will go on. Anyone who has never reckoned with the possibility that his country, his savings or his health might simply stop has said this sentence in his heart. And Laodicea said the same thing in different words: I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing (3:17). The sentence can be said inside a church as easily as inside an empire.

In a single day. Sudden collapse. The three-part list echoes the horsemen (6:8). And her boast is answered item by item. She will not be a widow, and death comes; she will never see mourning, and mourning comes; she lived in luxury, and famine comes. The judgement is her own boast, itemised and reversed. Something built over centuries goes in an afternoon (vv. 10, 17, 19), which is often how these things happen: slowly, then all at once. And she will be burned up with fire, as 17:16 foretold.

Mighty is the Lord God. Mighty (ischyros). Babylon was called the mighty city (v. 10), but the Lord God is mightier. Her strength was borrowed and temporary; his is his own and eternal. And his might is never raw force. It is the strength of the God of whom the conquerors sing, you alone are holy (15:4), and it is his holiness, not power alone, that makes his judgement of her right.

What it does not mean. The call for repayment is not a call for Christians to take revenge. It is God’s own sentence on Babylon, carried out by his agents. Believers are forbidden to repay evil for evil (Romans 12:17–19); they leave vengeance to God, who will repay.

How do I know if I am saying I sit as a queen? Watch for the signs of quiet self-sufficiency: you rarely pray except in crisis; you assume your income, health and comfort will continue; you plan your future without reference to God (James 4:13–16); you feel little need of the church; and other people’s suffering seems far away. The cure is not anxiety but humility: thank God daily for what you have as gifts that could be withdrawn, hold your plans with if the Lord wills, and let the needs of others interrupt your comfort.

For worship. Mighty is the Lord God who judges, and the boast of every proud city breaks against him. Babylon said, I am no widow, and mourning I shall never see. The true King said nothing of the kind. He became a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief, and stooped to the death she thought she would never meet. Babylon glorified herself and was brought low; he humbled himself, and God has given him the name above every name. And because he did, a Bride who looked forsaken in Babylon’s streets will never be a widow: her husband died once and lives for ever, and every tear she shed in that city God himself will wipe away.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 9–19: three sets of mourners, in descending rank, as in Ezekiel’s lament over Tyre: kings, merchants and sailors. All stand far off, and all weep for what they have lost. At the centre is the merchants’ cargo list (vv. 12–13), and a word to the city about the fruit her soul longed for (v. 14).

Verse 20 opens a window in the funeral: heaven and the saints are told to rejoice, because God has given judgement for them.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Threefold Lament

Kings, merchants and sailors stand far off and weep, for their trade, not for her. The cargo list ends with slaves, that is, human souls. Heaven and the saints are called to rejoice because God has given judgement for them.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The whole Roman world was arranged to supply one city.

Now: Ask whose hands made what you hold, and whether your deepest grief would be for a person or for a market.

verseByVerse.quote: And the kings of the earth, who committed sexual immorality and lived in luxury with her, will weep and wail over her when they see the smoke of her burning. They will stand far off, in fear of her torment, and say, "Alas! Alas! You great city, you mighty city, Babylon! For in a single hour your judgment has come." And the merchants of the earth weep and mourn for her, since no one buys their cargo anymore,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Ezekiel 26:16–18 and 27:29–36 describe the princes of the sea, merchants and sailors lamenting the fall of Tyre, the great trading city, standing on the shore, crying bitterly, throwing dust on their heads. Revelation 18 follows the same pattern, with three groups of mourners in descending order of rank: kings, merchants and sailors.

They will weep and wail. The first mourners are the kings of the earth, the rulers who shared her idolatry and luxury. Weep (klausousin) and wail (kopsontai, beat their breasts). Their grief is for themselves, for what they have lost. Not one of them grieves for her victims or repents.

Far off. The detail that governs all three laments is in this clause, and it is repeated at verses 15 and 17. Nobody goes near. Nobody attempts a rescue. Her lovers, her business partners and her carriers all watch from a safe distance, afraid of sharing her fate, and that is the exact measure of what Babylon’s relationships were worth. She had the kings of the earth and the merchants of the earth and every shipmaster afloat, and at the end not one of them will cross the road. Jesus did not watch our ruin from a safe distance, afraid of sharing it; he walked into the middle of it, took the judgement on himself, and was forsaken so that his people never would be. Every loyalty in Babylon lasts only while it pays. His held all the way to death.

Alas! Alas! Alas! You great city, you mighty city, Babylon! For in a single hour your judgment has come. Alas (ouai) is the same word as woe, doubled in lament. Single hour (mia hōra), repeated three times (vv. 10, 17, 19). The suddenness of her collapse is astonishing: centuries of power undone in an hour. And something is absent from all three laments: not one word of repentance, not one word about the blood of the saints, which verse 24 says was found in her. They weep because they are afraid, and because their trade is finished.

No one buys their cargo. The second group: the traders. Their grief is openly economic. They mourn the end of the market, not the city. John does not need to comment; the reason for the tears is comment enough.

Is it wrong to work in business or finance? No. Trade, banking and enterprise can be honourable callings that serve neighbours and glorify God; the woman of Proverbs 31 considers a field and buys it, and Lydia was a dealer in purple cloth (Acts 16:14). The merchants here are condemned because they grew rich from Babylon’s sin, did not care whom they hurt, and loved the market more than God or people. A Christian in business serves God by dealing honestly, paying fairly, refusing exploitation, and treating profit as a means of serving others rather than as the measure of a life.

Is this chapter just the resentment of the poor against the rich? No. A sceptic might call it a persecuted minority dreaming of its oppressors in flames, but the chapter never tells the church to seize Babylon’s wealth or burn anything. It tells them to come out of her sins (v. 4) and leaves the judgement to God (vv. 8, 20). Envy wants what the rich have. This chapter calls Christians not to want it, and the same warning is aimed at a wealthy church, Laodicea, as squarely as at Rome (3:17). The charge against Babylon is not that she was rich but that she was proud and cruel, trading even in human lives (v. 13). And the door is not yet shut: the eternal gospel goes out to every nation, tribe, language and people (14:6), including those who now trade in Babylon’s markets.

On a Tuesday. Ask what you would grieve if the world’s economy collapsed tomorrow. If the thing you would find hardest to lose were taken away, would the grief be for a person or for a market? The kings and merchants are not condemned for feeling loss; they are shown up by the reason for it. Treasure laid up in heaven is the one kind no fire reaches (Matthew 6:19–21).
verseByVerse.note: The laments echo Ezekiel’s dirge over the trading city of Tyre.

verseByVerse.quote: cargo of gold, silver, jewels, pearls, fine linen, purple cloth, silk, scarlet cloth, all kinds of scented wood, all kinds of articles of ivory, all kinds of articles of costly wood, bronze, iron and marble, cinnamon, spice, incense, myrrh, frankincense, wine, oil, fine flour, wheat, cattle and sheep, horses and chariots, and slaves, that is, human souls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting.
