The list matches the luxury imports of first-century Rome: gold and silver from Spain, pearls from the Indian Ocean, silk from China, citron wood from North Africa (prized for expensive tables), ivory from Africa and India, marble from Greece, cinnamon and spices from India and Arabia, wine from Italy and Greece, wheat from Egypt (Rome depended on Egyptian grain), horses and chariots from many provinces. Rome had an enormous slave population, by some estimates a quarter or more of the city, bought and sold in markets across the empire. Ezekiel 27:12–24 contains a similar list of Tyre’s trade, which also included human beings (Ezekiel 27:13).

Read it as a list. The manifest must be read, not skimmed, because its last item is the point of the chapter. There are some twenty-eight items, in groups: precious metals and stones, fabrics, materials for fine furniture, spices and perfumes, foodstuffs, livestock, and finally people. The order runs downward from the most luxurious to the most basic: it begins with what nobody needs and ends with what everybody does.

Gold, silver, jewels, pearls. Precious metals and stones, the adornments of the prostitute (17:4). The list opens with exactly what she was wearing. And in the new Jerusalem, gold, jewels and pearls are the building materials (21:18–21), freely given. What Babylon traded at a fortune, God paves the streets with.

Fine linen, purple cloth, silk, scarlet cloth. Luxury fabrics. Silk came overland from China along the trade routes and was enormously expensive; under Tiberius the Roman Senate forbade men to wear it, as Tacitus records, on the grounds that it was effeminate extravagance.

Scented wood, ivory, marble. Materials for luxurious furniture and buildings. Scented wood (xylon thyinon) is citron wood from North Africa, whose grained table tops could sell, Pliny says, for the price of an estate.

Cinnamon, spice, incense. Exotic spices and perfumes, some used in worship, brought up the incense road from Arabia or by sea from India. Frankincense and myrrh were among the gifts brought to the infant Jesus (Matthew 2:11). The same goods that were laid at the feet of the true King were burned in Babylon for her own pleasure.

Wine, oil, flour, wheat. Food, from luxury (fine flour) to staples (wheat). Rome imported, by modern estimates, hundreds of thousands of tonnes of grain a year from Egypt and North Africa because it could not feed itself. The horses and chariots (rhedōn, four-wheeled carriages, a Latin word borrowed into Greek) are transport and luxury.

Slaves, that is, human souls. Here, at the very end, after the horses and carriages, is the climax of the list and its deepest condemnation. The word translated slaves (sōmatōn) is literally bodies, the trade term for slaves, and a merchant’s list could set bodies beside livestock without a second thought. Then come words that no merchant’s manifest carried: that is, human souls (psychas anthrōpōn, lives of human beings). John takes them from Ezekiel’s lament over Tyre, where the Greek Old Testament says the traders dealt in the souls of men (Ezekiel 27:13), and sets them at the end of the list like a correction written into somebody else’s paperwork. The market says bodies, in the same column as the cattle, priced by weight and condition. The apostle stops the list to say what they actually are: people, made in God’s image. It is the last thing named before the lament resumes, and it is the charge that hangs over the entire economy.

Another purchase. Revelation has already described a second market. In the song of chapter 5 the Lamb is worthy because by his blood he ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation (5:9), and the verb is a market word (agorazō, to buy in the marketplace). Babylon’s merchants buy bodies to use them up. The Lamb buys people to set them free, and the price is not reckoned by the weight of a body but paid with his own blood. The contrast is the book’s own: two buyers and two cities, one where human beings are the last line of a cargo list, and one where every one of them is written in the Lamb’s book of life (21:27).

Every generation has its own version. The sin named here is not wealth. It is an arrangement in which people become a line item, and the profit is reason enough not to enquire who is at the far end of it. The question the manifest puts to a reader is not whether he owns anyone. It is whether he knows whose hands made what he is holding, and whether he has ever wanted to.

What can an ordinary Christian do about modern slavery and exploitation? More than nothing. Slavery still exists, in forced labour, trafficking and debt bondage, and it touches ordinary supply chains. Pray for the enslaved and for those who rescue them. Learn where common goods come from, and where you reasonably can, buy from companies that treat workers justly, even if it costs more. Support Christian and other agencies that fight trafficking. Treat the people who serve you, cleaners, delivery drivers, shop workers, as souls rather than services. And remember that the gospel itself is the great liberator: Christians like William Wilberforce opposed the slave trade because they believed that every human being bears God’s image. To the church’s shame, other professing Christians defended slavery with the Bible in their hands; this verse, which calls the cargo human souls, stands against them.

For worship. The King of kings let himself be priced. Judas sold him for thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 26:15), the sum the law set on a slave (Exodus 21:32), and he went into the market of this world as one more body on the manifest, so that bodies and souls could be carried out of it. Babylon’s list ends with human beings sold. The Father’s house is full of human beings welcomed, sons and daughters where there were slaves, and not one of them is a line item: every name is known, and every soul is held in a hand no merchant can open.
verseByVerse.note: The cargo list ends with human beings — the slave trade on which Rome’s economy depended.

verseByVerse.quote: "The fruit for which your soul longed has gone from you, and all your delicacies and your splendors are lost to you, never to be found again!" The merchants of these wares, who gained wealth from her, will stand far off, in fear of her torment, weeping and mourning aloud, "Alas, alas, for the great city that was clothed in fine linen, in purple and scarlet, adorned with gold, with jewels, and with pearls!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fruit for which your soul longed. A single verse to the city, breaking into the lament. Fruit (opōra) is ripe fruit, the late summer harvest; longed (epithymias) is craving, desire, lust. The Greek is the fruit of the desire of your soul. It is a word about appetite, and it says that all of this, the silk, the citron wood, the frankincense, the bodies, was never really about commerce. It was about wanting: the whole system was built to feed a longing in the soul.

A diagnosis of prosperity. That is not an attack on prosperity but a diagnosis of what prosperity is usually being asked to do. Nobody accumulates in order to have more objects. People accumulate because something in them is hungry and the objects are what is nearest. Augustine opened his Confessions by telling God that he had made us for himself. Babylon is that God-shaped hunger fed with things instead of God, organised, with a shipping fleet.

Delicacies and splendours. Delicacies (ta lipara) are rich, fat things, luxuries; splendours (ta lampra) are bright, glittering things. Never (ouketi ou mē) piles negatives on one another, as Greek can: never again, not ever. Not merely lost, but unfindable. The fruit her soul longed for did not last, and was never going to satisfy the longing even while she had it.

Alas, alas, for the great city. The second lament is put in almost the words used of the woman in 17:4. The merchants describe her as a dressed body. Six items, and every one of them was for sale in the manifest they have just lost. So their eulogy for a civilisation is a description of her clothes. They knew her wardrobe and nothing else. There is no mention of anything she did, made, believed or was, and there is nothing else to say, because there was nothing else there.

Two women in fine linen. The merchants’ eulogy describes a woman dressed in fine linen, and in the next chapter another woman appears in fine linen, the Bride of the Lamb (19:8). The difference is in how each got her clothes. Babylon bought hers, and they are lost in an hour. The Bride’s were granted to her, and they are bright and pure because her robes have been washed white in the blood of the Lamb (7:14). The King whose Bride she is was once dressed in purple by soldiers as a joke (Mark 15:17) and then stripped at the cross. Babylon dressed herself at the expense of others. Christ was stripped at his own expense, so that his people would be clothed.

Why do the things I want never satisfy for long? Because you were made for God, and every created good, however lovely, is too small to fill a space shaped for him. C. S. Lewis observed that if we find in ourselves a desire no experience in this world can satisfy, the most probable explanation is that we were made for another world. The answer is not to stop desiring but to desire rightly: to receive good things with thanks as signposts, and to bring the deepest longing to Christ, who said that whoever comes to him will never hunger (John 6:35). Contentment is learned, Paul says (Philippians 4:11–13), and it is learned in him.

On a Tuesday. The pull to buy, scroll or snack in an empty moment is usually a hunger in disguise, and there is freedom in naming it and bringing it in a short prayer to Christ, who is never lost, before reaching for anything else.

verseByVerse.quote: For in a single hour all this wealth has been laid waste." And all shipmasters and seafaring men, sailors and all whose trade is on the sea, stood far off and cried out as they saw the smoke of her burning, "What city was like the great city?" And they threw dust on their heads as they wept and mourned, crying out, "Alas, alas, for the great city where all who had ships at sea grew rich by her wealth! For in a single hour she has been laid waste.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Throwing dust on the head was a sign of grief and mourning (Joshua 7:6; Job 2:12; Ezekiel 27:30, where the sailors throw dust on their heads over Tyre). Rome’s grain and luxury goods came by sea, through the port of Ostia and the Bay of Naples.

All this wealth laid waste. Laid waste (ērēmōthē): made desolate, turned into a wilderness. It is the merchants’ cry, the second single hour. Then come the shipmasters, sailors and all whose trade is on the sea, the third group of mourners, and the humblest: not kings and not merchant princes, but captains, crews and dockworkers, everyone whose living came off the water. The whole economy of the sea was bound up with Babylon. Ezekiel’s lament over Tyre has the same cast standing on the shore, throwing dust on their heads and crying, who is like Tyre? (Ezekiel 27:29–32).

Stood far off and cried out as they saw the smoke of her burning, What city was like the great city? That question is a parody, and the reader of Scripture has heard its form more than once before. Israel sang at the Red Sea, who is like you, O LORD, among the gods? (Exodus 15:11). The worshippers of the beast chanted, who is like the beast? (13:4). And here sailors on a beach ask it of a burning city. It is the question of worship, and it keeps being asked of the wrong subject. They had made the city their god.

The question with one true answer. Revelation has asked one other question of this kind and answered it. In chapter 5 an angel asks who is worthy to open the scroll, and no one in heaven or on earth is found, until the Lamb who was slain takes it, and heaven and earth sing his worth (5:2–13). That is the answer the sailors miss. They ask what city was like Babylon while they watch it burn, and the honest reply is that many cities have been like her, and all of them burn. Nothing in history is like the Lamb, because nothing else has conquered by dying and stayed on the throne.

Grew rich by her wealth. Grew rich (eploutēsan). Three social classes, three laments, and one reason between them. Nobody mourns Babylon. They mourn their share of her.

In a single hour. The third and final single hour, from the third group. All three laments say it, because all three have understood the one thing that actually frightens them: not that Babylon was wicked, but that she was quick. Men who spent their lives on a trade route lost it in an hour. The chapter is not saying that trade is wrong. It is saying that everything in the manifest, and the city that consumed it, and the fleet that carried it, belongs to the category of things that can end between breakfast and lunch.

Should a Christian save, invest or plan for the future? Yes, wisely. Scripture commends the ant that stores up in summer (Proverbs 6:6–8) and the person who provides for his family (1 Timothy 5:8). The problem is not prudence but trust. Saving is wise; making savings your security is idolatry. Jesus called the rich man a fool not because he had barns but because he was rich toward himself and not toward God (Luke 12:16–21). So plan, save and work hard, but give generously, hold it all loosely, and remember that it could all be gone in an hour, while what you have given to Christ is kept for ever.

On a Tuesday. Christ is the one foundation already laid (1 Corinthians 3:11), and nothing built on him burns. So finish this sentence honestly: I would not know who I was if I lost my... Whatever completes it is the thing to hand to God this week, thanking him for it and telling him that he, not it, is your life.

For worship. The question the sailors asked of a burning city belongs to the LORD alone, glorious in holiness and without rival among the gods. Babylon’s wealth went up in an hour of smoke; the riches of Christ are unsearchable, and no fire reaches them. Men who had spent their lives on the water watched their whole living disappear from a beach. Those who belong to him have an anchor that no storm can drag, sure and steadfast, fixed behind the curtain where Jesus has gone ahead of them as their forerunner (Hebrews 6:19–20), and their treasure lies in a harbour that will never burn.

verseByVerse.quote: Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you saints and apostles and prophets, for God has given judgment for you against her!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Jeremiah 51:48 says that the heavens and the earth, and all that is in them, will sing for joy over Babylon. Deuteronomy 32:43 calls the nations to rejoice with God’s people, for he avenges the blood of his children. This verse leads into the great hallelujahs of 19:1–5.

Rejoice over her, O heaven. Rejoice (euphrainou): be glad, celebrate. One verse, and it stands in the middle of the funeral like a window opened in a closed room.

Saints and apostles and prophets. All God’s people, and especially those who led and suffered: apostles, such as Peter and Paul, who by early tradition were killed in Rome, and prophets. Their blood was found in her (v. 24). Nobody who has not been wronged is invited to this celebration, and there is a great difference between a victim relieved that justice has finally been done and a bystander enjoying somebody’s ruin.

God has given judgment for you. The Greek is a legal phrase (ekrinen ho theos to krima hymōn ex autēs): God has judged your case against her. The saints brought their case to God’s court (6:10), and he has ruled in their favour. Babylon condemned them; now God has condemned her and vindicated them. What is being celebrated is not suffering, and not destruction as such, but a verdict.

Their case is his case. The saints do not stand in this court alone. Babylon’s courts condemned Jesus first: a Roman governor sentenced him, and God overturned the verdict by raising him from the dead, which is why Paul says he was vindicated by the Spirit (1 Timothy 3:16). The martyrs go down the same road and receive the same reversal. And the risen Lord counts what is done to them as done to him: Saul, why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:4). When God gives judgement for his people against Babylon, he is finishing what he began on Easter morning, ruling in favour of his Son and of everyone joined to him.

Where Christians differ: is it right to rejoice over judgement? Many Christians are uneasy with this verse, feeling that rejoicing over anyone’s destruction contradicts Christ’s command to love our enemies. Scripture does say, do not rejoice when your enemy falls (Proverbs 24:17). This commentary’s view: the joy here is not delight in suffering, nor personal revenge. It is joy that God has kept his promise, that justice has been done, that evil has been defeated, and that the persecuted have been vindicated. God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11), and neither should we. But when the judgement is final, his people will see clearly that it was right, and rejoice in God’s justice. Now, before that day, we love our enemies, pray for them and seek their salvation, leaving vengeance to God (Romans 12:19–21).

The alternative is worse than it looks. A universe in which the murder of the innocent is finally shrugged at is not a kinder universe; it is one in which nothing matters. To be unable to rejoice that wrong has been put right is not compassion but a failure to believe that the wrong was real. And there is a safeguard: the rejoicing follows the judgement; it never produces it. No Christian in this book lifts a hand against Babylon. They pray, they endure, they refuse the mark, they die, and God settles the account. The joy of verse 20 is the joy of people who were told to leave it with him and did.

What about the wrong done to me that was never put right? This verse has a quiet pastoral word for anyone still carrying something unresolved: a crime nobody was charged with, a reputation destroyed by someone who prospered afterwards, an abuse that was covered up, a person who died and was never accounted for. A day is coming when heaven will name your case out loud and tell you to be glad. Not because you were owed revenge, but because you were owed a verdict, and it will be delivered. Meanwhile, you may seek justice through proper means, the courts, the church’s discipline, the authorities God has appointed (Romans 13:4), and you may bring your grief to him. You are not required to pretend it did not matter. It matters to God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–24 — The Millstone and the Sixfold Silence
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 21: a mighty angel throws a great millstone into the sea, repeating the sign Jeremiah gave against the first Babylon (Jeremiah 51:59–64). Verses 22–23: music, craft, the mill, the lamp and the voices of bridegroom and bride will be heard in her no more.

Verses 23–24: the reasons are her merchants’ pride, her sorcery, and the blood of prophets and saints found in her.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Millstone and the Silence

An angel throws a millstone into the sea: so Babylon sinks. Music, craft, the mill, the lamp, and the voice of bride and bridegroom are heard in her no more, and in her is found the blood of the prophets and saints.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Jeremiah had sunk Babylon’s doom in the Euphrates; John’s angel repeats the sign.

Now: The ordinary goods of life, bread, lamplight and weddings, were always worth more than the cargo. Nothing hidden stays unlooked-for.

verseByVerse.quote: Then a mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone and threw it into the sea, saying, "So will Babylon the great city be thrown down with violence, and will be found no more; and the sound of harpists and musicians, of flute players and trumpeters, will be heard in you no more, and a craftsman of any craft will be found in you no more, and the sound of the mill will be heard in you no more, and the light of a lamp will shine in you no more, and the voice of bridegroom and bride will be heard in you no more, for your merchants were the great ones of the earth, and all nations were deceived by your sorcery. And in her was found the blood of prophets and of saints, and of all who have been slain on earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. In Jeremiah 51:59–64, Jeremiah had his prophecy against Babylon written on a scroll, and told his messenger Seraiah, when he had read it aloud in Babylon, to tie a stone to it and throw it into the Euphrates, saying that so Babylon would sink, to rise no more. A large millstone, of the kind turned by a donkey, could weigh hundreds of kilograms. Jeremiah 25:10 says God will banish from Judah the voice of mirth, the voice of the bridegroom and the bride, the grinding of the millstones and the light of the lamp.

A stone like a great millstone. An acted prophecy borrowed from Jeremiah. A millstone is the heaviest ordinary thing in an ancient town, the stone an animal turned all day to grind the community’s grain, and it is the last thing in the world that floats. When it goes into deep water there is one splash and then nothing at all. It sinks instantly and is never recovered.

Found no more. With violence means with sudden force. Her destruction is total and permanent.

The millstone Jesus spoke of. The angel’s act is Jeremiah’s, but the reader of the Gospels has heard of a millstone and the sea before. Jesus said it would be better for anyone who causes one of his little ones to stumble to have a great millstone hung round his neck and be drowned in the depth of the sea (Matthew 18:6). Babylon did far worse than make them stumble: she killed them, and their blood was found in her. So the fate the Lord pronounced falls on the city, in his own image. The one who warned with a millstone was not exaggerating, and he has not forgotten one of the little ones he spoke for.

The sixfold silence. The phrase no more (ou mē … eti) tolls six times in three verses: once over the city itself, and then over five things that will be heard or found in her no more.

Harpists and musicians. Music goes first. No concerts, no processions, nobody practising badly through an open window. The city of entertainment is quiet.

A craftsman of any craft. No workshops. Nobody making anything. The particular satisfaction of skilled hands producing something that did not exist before is gone from the whole city.

The sound of the mill. In an ancient town the grinding of the handmills began before dawn and was the ordinary background of being alive, the sound that told you the day had started and there would be bread.

The light of a lamp. Not a public illumination: a lamp, the small light in one room where a family sits after dark. Every window in the city is black. In the new Jerusalem, God is the light (21:23; 22:5).

Bridegroom and bride. This is the last and the heaviest. No more weddings, no more joy, no future: nobody is being married, so nobody is being born, so there will be no next generation. Jeremiah used this same group of images as the sum of everything a judged city loses (Jeremiah 25:10). And in contrast, the marriage of the Lamb is about to be announced (19:7).

Where Babylon’s true wealth was. Not palaces, armies, temples or treasuries. Music, craftsmanship, bread, lamplight and weddings. The things named are the ordinary goods of human life, and the chapter that has spent so many verses on gold and silk and ivory ends by mourning the loss of the mill and the lamp. That is where Babylon’s true wealth was the whole time, and she spent it on cargo.

The great ones of the earth. The first reason for her judgement: her merchants were exalted and wealth was worshipped. Isaiah 23:8 says of Tyre that her merchants were princes. The traders had become the aristocracy, which is what happens when a society decides that money is the only real rank.

Deceived by your sorcery. Sorcery (pharmakeia): magic, drugs, enchantment, the word used at 9:21. The second reason: she bewitched the nations, intoxicating them with her seductive power so that they could not see the truth.

The blood of prophets and of saints. The third and deepest reason: murder. The last verse is the indictment, and it is enormous. Not merely the blood of the martyrs she killed herself, but of all who have been slain on earth. Jesus said something with the same reach over Jerusalem: that on that generation would come all the righteous blood shed on earth, from Abel onward (Matthew 23:35). The logic is not that one city committed every murder. Babylon is the name for the human project of building without God, in every century and place, and every drop of innocent blood ever spilled was spilled somewhere inside it.

Found. Babylon did not report it. Somebody looked, and it was there. This city was brilliant, cultured and beautifully dressed, and at the end the search was conducted anyway and the blood was in the foundations. Nothing was ever really hidden. It was only unlooked-for.

In the flow. These verses close the long vision of Babylon that began when one of the seven angels said to John, come, I will show you the judgement of the great prostitute (17:1). The same words will open the vision of the new Jerusalem: come, I will show you the Bride, the wife of the Lamb (21:9). So the millstone does not end the story; it clears the stage. Chapter 18 ends in silence, and chapter 19 opens with the roar of heaven’s hallelujah: the city where no bridegroom’s voice is heard gives way to the marriage of the Lamb.

Will there be music, work and marriage in the new creation? Music, certainly: heaven in this book is full of harps and new songs (5:8–9; 14:2–3; 15:2–3). Meaningful work too, it seems: the nations bring their glory into the city (21:24–26), and his servants will serve him (22:3). Marriage is different. Jesus said that in the resurrection people neither marry nor are given in marriage (Matthew 22:30), because the marriage that every human marriage pointed to will have arrived: Christ and his Bride, the church (Ephesians 5:31–32; Revelation 19:7). Nothing good is lost. Every true joy is either kept or fulfilled in something greater.

For worship. Every good and perfect gift comes down from the Father of lights. The song and the craft, the bread and the lamp, the voice of the bridegroom and the bride: all of them were his before Babylon ever touched them, and all of them will be his when Babylon is a millstone at the bottom of the sea. He will not leave his gifts in the hands of those who despised him. He will gather them into a new creation where the music never stops, where the Lamb is the lamp, where his servants work with joy, and where the voice of the Bridegroom is heard calling his Bride home to the marriage supper. Nothing hidden will stay hidden, and nothing good will be lost.
verseByVerse.note: Jeremiah had a scroll against Babylon tied to a stone and thrown into the Euphrates.

18.text: <sup>1</sup>After this I saw another angel coming down from heaven, having great authority, and the earth was made bright with his glory.<sup>2</sup>And he called out with a mighty voice, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great! She has become a dwelling place for demons, a haunt for every unclean spirit, a haunt for every unclean bird, a haunt for every unclean and detestable beast.<sup>3</sup>For all nations have drunk the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality, and the kings of the earth have committed immorality with her, and the merchants of the earth have grown rich from the power of her luxurious living.”<sup>4</sup>Then I heard another voice from heaven saying, “Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues;<sup>5</sup>for her sins are heaped high as heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities.<sup>6</sup>Pay her back as she herself has paid back others, and repay her double for her deeds; mix a double portion for her in the cup she mixed.<sup>7</sup>As she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so give her a like measure of torment and mourning, since in her heart she says, ‘I sit as a queen, I am no widow, and mourning I shall never see.’<sup>8</sup>For this reason her plagues will come in a single day, death and mourning and famine, and she will be burned up with fire; for mighty is the Lord God who has judged her.”<sup>9</sup>And the kings of the earth, who committed sexual immorality and lived in luxury with her, will weep and wail over her when they see the smoke of her burning.<sup>10</sup>They will stand far off, in fear of her torment, and say, “Alas! Alas! You great city, you mighty city, Babylon! For in a single hour your judgment has come.”<sup>11</sup>And the merchants of the earth weep and mourn for her, since no one buys their cargo anymore,<sup>12</sup>cargo of gold, silver, jewels, pearls, fine linen, purple cloth, silk, scarlet cloth, all kinds of scented wood, all kinds of articles of ivory, all kinds of articles of costly wood, bronze, iron and marble,<sup>13</sup>cinnamon, spice, incense, myrrh, frankincense, wine, oil, fine flour, wheat, cattle and sheep, horses and chariots, and slaves, that is, human souls.<sup>14</sup>“The fruit for which your soul longed has gone from you, and all your delicacies and your splendors are lost to you, never to be found again!”<sup>15</sup>The merchants of these wares, who gained wealth from her, will stand far off, in fear of her torment, weeping and mourning aloud,<sup>16</sup>“Alas, alas, for the great city that was clothed in fine linen, in purple and scarlet, adorned with gold, with jewels, and with pearls!<sup>17</sup>For in a single hour all this wealth has been laid waste.” And all shipmasters and seafaring men, sailors and all whose trade is on the sea, stood far off<sup>18</sup>and cried out as they saw the smoke of her burning, “What city was like the great city?”<sup>19</sup>And they threw dust on their heads as they wept and mourned, crying out, “Alas, alas, for the great city where all who had ships at sea grew rich by her wealth! For in a single hour she has been laid waste.<sup>20</sup>Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you saints and apostles and prophets, for God has given judgment for you against her!”<sup>21</sup>Then a mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone and threw it into the sea, saying, “So will Babylon the great city be thrown down with violence, and will be found no more;<sup>22</sup>and the sound of harpists and musicians, of flute players and trumpeters, will be heard in you no more, and a craftsman of any craft will be found in you no more, and the sound of the mill will be heard in you no more,<sup>23</sup>and the light of a lamp will shine in you no more, and the voice of bridegroom and bride will be heard in you no more, for your merchants were the great ones of the earth, and all nations were deceived by your sorcery.<sup>24</sup>And in her was found the blood of prophets and of saints, and of all who have been slain on earth.”

19.title: Hallelujah! The Wedding and the Rider
19.overview:
Chapter 19 is the hinge between Babylon’s fall and the new creation. It opens with heaven’s fourfold hallelujah over God’s justice and the coming marriage of the Lamb, and closes with the rider on the white horse, named Faithful and True, the Word of God, and King of kings and Lord of lords.

It has two movements. The first (vv. 1–10) is celebration: the multitude, the elders and the living creatures praise God, and the Bride is ready in fine linen. The second (vv. 11–21) is Christ’s return: heaven opens, the rider comes out with the armies of heaven behind him, and the beast and the false prophet are captured and thrown into the lake of fire.

The praise comes before the battle is described, as so often in this book: the outcome is declared before it is worked out. The Lamb has already conquered, and the rider shows that victory made visible.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Hallelujah and the Marriage Supper
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–3: a great multitude sings hallelujah, because God has judged the prostitute and avenged his servants, answering the martyrs’ prayer of 6:10. Verses 4–5: the elders and living creatures add their Amen, and a voice from the throne calls all God’s servants, small and great, to praise him.

Verses 6–8: the last hallelujah announces that God reigns and the marriage of the Lamb has come, and the Bride’s linen is explained. Verses 9–10: the fourth beatitude blesses those invited to the wedding supper, and the angel stops John from worshipping him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Hallelujah and the Wedding

Heaven’s hallelujahs answer the martyrs’ prayer: God has judged and avenged. The marriage of the Lamb has come; the Bride is granted fine linen, which is the righteous deeds of the saints. Blessed are those invited, and worship God, not his messengers.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The prayer under the altar was not lost; it was answered.

Now: The hidden faithfulness of ordinary believers is being woven into the Bride’s dress.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I heard what seemed to be the loud voice of a great multitude in heaven, crying out, "Hallelujah! Salvation and glory and power belong to our God, for his judgments are true and just; for he has judged the great prostitute who corrupted the earth with her immorality, and has avenged on her the blood of his servants." Once more they cried out, "Hallelujah! The smoke from her goes up forever and ever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Revelation 19 moves from Babylon’s fall to the Lamb’s wedding and Christ’s return. Heaven bursts into hallelujahs, because God’s judgements are true and just: he has judged the prostitute and avenged his servants’ blood, and the elders and living creatures say Amen (vv. 1–5). A great multitude sings that the Lord our God the Almighty reigns and the marriage of the Lamb has come; his Bride is clothed in fine linen, the righteous deeds of the saints, and those invited to the marriage supper are blessed; John falls to worship the angel and is told to worship God (vv. 6–10). Then heaven opens and Christ rides out on a white horse: Faithful and True, eyes like fire, many crowns, a robe dipped in blood, named the Word of God, followed by the armies of heaven, with a sword from his mouth, treading the winepress of God’s wrath, King of kings and Lord of lords (vv. 11–16). The birds are summoned to the great supper of God; the beast and the false prophet are thrown alive into the lake of fire, and the rest are killed by the sword from his mouth (vv. 17–21). Two suppers stand at the end of history, the marriage supper of the Lamb and the great supper of God, and between them rides Christ in his single, glorious, victorious return. Chapter 18 ended with a city gone silent; this is heaven’s answer, and it is some of the loudest worship in the Bible.

The setting. Hallelujah is a Hebrew word meaning praise the LORD (hallelu, praise; Yah, the short form of God’s name). In the New Testament it occurs only in this chapter, four times. In the Psalms it often begins or ends a psalm, especially Psalms 104–106, 111–117 and 146–150. Psalms 113–118, the Hallel, were sung at Passover, and Jesus and his disciples sang a hymn, probably from these psalms, after the Last Supper (Matthew 26:30). Psalm 104:35 is the first Hallelujah in the Psalter: let sinners be consumed from the earth, and let the wicked be no more! Bless the LORD, O my soul! Praise the LORD!

A great multitude in heaven. Great multitude (ochlou pollou), as in 7:9: the redeemed, from every nation, tribe, people and language, more than anyone could count.

Hallelujah! Praise the LORD. Hallelujah is Hebrew, not Greek, and it is left untranslated, so that a Jewish Christian hearing this read aloud would likely have heard his own liturgy. And in contrast with the earth’s alas, alas (18:10, 16, 19), heaven sings hallelujah. Earth’s last word over Babylon is a groan; heaven’s is praise.

A hallelujah at a funeral. The thing it is shouted over is the fall of a city, and that takes some facing. The word most associated with Christian praise makes its only New Testament appearance at the funeral of an empire. But look at the reasons given, because the verses supply them at once, and they are not what a modern reader fears.

Salvation and glory and power. As in 7:10 and 12:10. All credit belongs to God. The praise is for the character of God, not for the suffering of anybody. Three nouns are said to belong to him, and Babylon had claimed all three, offering security, glamour and influence to whoever would drink with her. Every one of them turns out to have been his.

True and just. As the redeemed (15:3) and the altar (16:7) declared. God’s justice is the ground of their praise. Three times now heaven has said the same two words about his ways and judgements, before the bowls, during them, and after Babylon’s fall, and it has never once had to take them back.

He has judged the great prostitute. Corrupted (ephtheiren): ruined, destroyed. She was destroying the earth (11:18), and now she is destroyed.

Avenged the blood of his servants. Avenged (exedikēsen). That answers a question asked thirteen chapters ago. Under the altar in 6:10 the souls of the martyrs cried, O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth? Each was handed a white robe and asked to wait a while. Here are the same two verbs, judged and avenged, in the past tense, in the mouth of a multitude nobody can number. Prayer answered. That is the whole content of the first hallelujah, and it is the thing a persecuted church most needs and most doubts: the prayer prayed under the altar was not filed and lost, but answered at the time appointed.

Salvation by the blood of the Lamb. The first word heaven sings is salvation, and this book has already said what it cost. When the same cry was heard at 12:10, it went on: the authority of his Christ has come, and the brothers have conquered the accuser by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony (12:10–11). At 7:10 salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb. So the hallelujah over Babylon is not the cheer of the winning side in a war between equals. The decisive battle was fought on a cross outside Jerusalem, and the fall of Babylon is that victory made visible. The servants whose blood is avenged had already conquered, by his blood and their testimony, before Babylon ever fell.

Her smoke goes up forever. The smoke from her goes up forever and ever. As with Sodom (Genesis 19:28) and Edom, where the smoke of the land goes up for ever (Isaiah 34:10). It is the language of a verdict that will not be reversed: no rebuilding, no restoration, no second edition. The city that said, I sit as a queen and mourning I shall never see (18:7), got the permanence she asked for, but not the kind she wanted.

Does smoke for ever mean that the punishment of the lost is eternal? Yes. The same phrase, for ever and ever, is used of the worship of God (4:9–10; 5:13) and of the torment of those who worship the beast (14:11) and of the devil (20:10). The fall of Babylon as a system is final, and the punishment of those who belonged to her and refused to repent is conscious and without end (Matthew 25:46). That is a terrible truth, and it should make us tremble and plead with people. Some careful Christians, called annihilationists, believe instead that the lost are finally destroyed and cease to exist, and they read for ever as the permanence of the result; they hold this out of reverence for God’s justice and mercy, and they are brothers and sisters in Christ. This commentary holds the conscious reading because the same words at 14:11 and 20:10 speak of no rest, day or night. But it is also why the hallelujah is right: evil is never coming back, and nothing will ever again corrupt God’s world.

On a Tuesday. Next time you pray about an injustice that seems to have gone unanswered for years, remember that the martyrs waited from chapter 6 to chapter 19, and that their prayer was not lost. Keep praying, and add a hallelujah before the answer comes: praise the LORD, because his judgements are true and just.
verseByVerse.note: “Hallelujah” means “praise the LORD” (Hebrew). In the New Testament it appears only here, four times in this chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: And the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fell down and worshiped God who was seated on the throne, saying, "Amen. Hallelujah!" And from the throne came a voice saying, "Praise our God, all you his servants, you who fear him, small and great."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Psalm 106:48 ends: and let all the people say, Amen! Praise the LORD! Psalm 115:13 says the LORD will bless those who fear him, both the small and the great. Psalm 135:1, 20 calls all the servants of the LORD to praise him.

The elders and living creatures. This is the last appearance of the elders and living creatures in Revelation. They have been there from the first throne vision (4:4–11), and they close the worship of this age. These are figures with thrones of their own who have spent this book throwing their crowns on the floor (4:10). The posture has not changed.

Amen, Hallelujah. Amen means it is true, it is firm, so be it. Hallelujah means praise the LORD. Two words, both Hebrew, and together they are one of the oldest congregational responses in Scripture: all the people said Amen and praised the LORD (1 Chronicles 16:36; Psalm 106:48). The beings closest to the throne of God add nothing original. They agree. The entire contribution of the highest creatures in the universe at this moment is to say that what the multitude has just said is true.

Praise our God. A voice from the throne, and the striking thing is the pronoun: our God. The speaker stands alongside the worshippers, so the summons comes from inside the company rather than being shouted down onto it. Servants (douloi): all believers.

A voice that says our God. If the voice is Christ’s, as many have thought, the pronoun is deeply moving. The risen Jesus sent word to his brothers that he was ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God (John 20:17), and Hebrews hears him say to the Father, I will tell of your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise (Hebrews 2:12). The one who shares the Father’s throne stands among his servants and calls them to worship as one who has shared their flesh. Whoever the speaker is, the church sings under a leader who is not ashamed to call them brothers (Hebrews 2:11).

Small and great. Fear (phoboumenoi) means revere. Small and great means everyone, whatever their status, and the phrase appears several times in this book, always to refuse a ranking. It was used of the beast’s mark, which reached both small and great (13:16); it is used at 11:18 of the servants God rewards; and it will be used of the dead standing before the throne (20:12). In God’s presence, distinctions of rank disappear; all praise him together.

No back row. A great deal of Christian discouragement comes from a suspicion that there are tiers. The people summoned here are described in exactly two ways: they serve him and they fear him. Not those who did notable things. Not those who understood this book. The choir is assembled by a single qualification, and the smallest voice in it is not standing at the back. That suspicion is often the old idol of approval in religious clothes: the hope that God will rate us higher because we have done more, or the fear that he rates us lower because others have. Heaven’s choir answers both, because nobody in it is there on his record.

Will there be degrees of reward in heaven? Scripture does speak of rewards for faithfulness (Matthew 25:21; 1 Corinthians 3:12–15; 2 Corinthians 5:10), and many Reformed teachers have held that capacities for joy may differ, as vessels of different sizes may all be full. But there are no degrees of acceptance. Every believer is welcomed on exactly the same ground, the righteousness of Christ, and every one is equally a child, a servant and a member of the Bride. Rewards themselves are gifts of grace, God crowning his own work in us. No one in heaven will feel second-class, and no one will want anything but to praise.

What am I saying when I say Amen? You are saying, this is true, and I put my weight on it. It is not a way of ending a prayer but a confession of faith. In the early church the whole congregation said it aloud after prayers and readings (1 Corinthians 14:16), and Christ himself is called the Amen, the faithful and true witness (3:14), because every promise of God is yes in him, and through him we say our Amen to God for his glory (2 Corinthians 1:20). So say it on purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I heard what seemed to be the voice of a great multitude, like the roar of many waters and like the sound of mighty peals of thunder, crying out, "Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns. Let us rejoice and exult and give him the glory, for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready; it was granted her to clothe herself with fine linen, bright and pure"—for the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Jesus told parables of wedding feasts (Matthew 22:1–14; 25:1–13). A Jewish wedding had two stages: betrothal, a binding commitment, and then, after a period of preparation, the wedding itself, when the groom came to take his bride to his home, followed by a feast. Isaiah 61:10 says, he has clothed me with the garments of salvation; he has covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bride adorns herself with her jewels.

Like the roar of many waters. The fourth and last hallelujah, and the volume is described in three ways: a multitude, a waterfall and thunder. John reaches for the loudest things he knows and says the sound was like all of them at once. It is overwhelming sound, like Christ’s own voice (1:15) and the song of the 144,000 (14:2).

The Lord our God the Almighty reigns. The verb (ebasileusen) means has begun to reign, has taken up his reign. It is one word in Greek, and it is the great announcement of the Psalms: the LORD reigns (Psalm 93:1; 97:1; 99:1). The tense points to a reign that has begun. This is what the seventh trumpet announced at 11:15–17, now sung by the whole company. God’s reign is now openly established. These are the great words of Handel’s Hallelujah Chorus.

Let us rejoice and exult. Rejoice (chairōmen) and exult (agalliōmen, be overjoyed). As Jesus told the persecuted: rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven (Matthew 5:12). The same people who were told to rejoice in their suffering now rejoice at its end.

The marriage of the Lamb. Marriage (ho gamos): the wedding. The image is not new and it is not an ornament. God is the husband of his people all through the Old Testament: your Maker is your husband (Isaiah 54:5); I will betroth you to me for ever (Hosea 2:19). Jesus called himself the bridegroom and said the guests could not fast while he was with them (Mark 2:19). Paul told husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church, and then said the whole arrangement had been about Christ and the church all along (Ephesians 5:25–32). This is the goal of all history: the union of Christ with his people, perfect and permanent. Betrothed now by faith (2 Corinthians 11:2), the church will be united with Christ at his return.

His Bride has made herself ready. Bride (gynē, wife, woman), in contrast with the prostitute. Made herself ready (hētoimasen heautēn). The church prepares for Christ by faithful living, holiness and perseverance, worked in her by his Spirit. One woman was dressed by her lovers and stripped by them; this one has been waiting for one husband.

It was granted her. This is a carefully balanced sentence, and both halves have to be held or it collapses. The dress was given (edothē). She did not buy it, weave it or earn it, and the divine passive that has governed this whole book governs the Bride’s wedding clothes too. She clothes herself, but only with what is given her. Set it beside Laodicea, who was counselled to buy white garments from Christ (3:18), and beside the multitude who washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb (7:14). Nobody in this book is wearing anything he produced. Fine linen (byssinon), in contrast with the prostitute’s purple and scarlet, gold and jewels (17:4). The bride’s beauty is purity.

The righteous deeds of the saints. And yet the dress is made of something. John stops the sentence to say what the fabric is, and it is not an abstraction. Righteous deeds (dikaiōmata, righteous acts): the plural is concrete, the deeds themselves, the faithful lives of believers, their works of obedience and love. Their deeds follow them (14:13).

Where Christians differ: is the bride’s righteousness her own deeds or Christ’s? Some read “righteous deeds of the saints” as meaning that believers are made acceptable to Christ by their own good works. Others, emphasising imputed righteousness (Christ’s righteousness counted to the believer as his own), are uneasy with the phrase. This commentary’s view: both grace and works are in the verse. The linen was given to her (granted), and her robes were washed white in the Lamb’s blood (7:14): her standing before God rests wholly on Christ’s righteousness credited to her by faith (2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 3:9). And the linen is her righteous deeds, the fruit of that grace, the good works God prepared beforehand for her to walk in (Ephesians 2:10). Justification by faith alone is the root; sanctification is the fruit, and both are gifts. The bride is dressed by her bridegroom.

Both clauses are true. Paul held the two together without difficulty: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Philippians 2:12–13). What do the two words in the verdict mean? Justification is God’s once-for-all verdict that a sinner is right with him, not because of anything in the sinner but because Christ’s righteousness is counted as his (Romans 4:5). Sanctification is the lifelong work by which the Spirit actually makes him holy, so that his life begins to look like his Lord’s (2 Corinthians 3:18). The first never changes; the second grows. And the second is never finished here: even the saints’ best deeds are mixed with sin (James 3:2), yet the Father accepts them for his Son’s sake, because Christ’s perfect obedience is counted as theirs (Romans 5:19; Westminster 16.6). So the linen is a gift twice over: the righteousness that covers her is his, and the deeds woven into it are his Spirit’s work, received with delight though they were never spotless.

Textual note. The King James Version reads “the Lord God omnipotent reigneth”, following later manuscripts. The best manuscripts read “the Lord our God the Almighty reigns”. The meaning is the same.

What it does not mean. The marriage does not mean that individual believers are each married to Christ in a romantic sense. The bride is the church together, the whole people of God.

If God already reigns, why does it say he has begun to reign? God has always been King over all; nothing has ever been outside his rule (Psalm 103:19). But in this fallen world his reign has been resisted and hidden, and his people have prayed, your kingdom come. What begins here is the open, undisputed exercise of his rule, when every rival is removed and every knee bows. It is like a rightful king who has ruled from exile and now enters his capital and is crowned in public. He was always King; now everyone sees it.

My life seems to have produced so little. What will I have to wear? There is great comfort in this verse for a believer who suspects his life has amounted to nothing. The visits nobody recorded, the giving that hurt, the years of patience with a difficult person, the prayers for a wayward child, the refusal to say the profitable untrue thing: those are not evaporating. They are being woven. Nothing done for Christ is wasted (1 Corinthians 15:58; Matthew 10:42). And remember the first half: the dress is granted. Your place at the wedding does not depend on the size of your contribution but on the Bridegroom who washed you. When the Bride finally appears, what you did in his name will be part of what she has on.

On a Tuesday. The church is preparing for her wedding, and every act of faithfulness and love today is part of the Bride’s dress. That changes how the church herself looks on an ordinary weekday: the awkward member, the tired minister, the rota nobody wants. A bride being prepared for her husband is not someone to gossip about or walk away from lightly. She is someone to help get ready.

For worship. The Lord our God the Almighty reigns, and the first thing his open reign brings is a wedding. Before the foundation of the world the Father chose a bride for his Son; in the fullness of time the Son came to win her, not with gifts but with his blood; and through the ages the Spirit has been calling her, washing her and making her ready. Kings marry to gain kingdoms. This King already had all things, and married to share them. On the wedding day he will rejoice over her as a bridegroom over his bride (Isaiah 62:5), and she will never stop singing hallelujah.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel said to me, "Write this: Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb." And he said to me, "These are the true words of God." Then I fell down at his feet to worship him, but he said to me, "You must not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers who hold to the testimony of Jesus. Worship God." For the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Isaiah 25:6–8 promises that the LORD will make for all peoples a feast of rich food and well-aged wine, and swallow up death for ever. Jesus said many will come from east and west and recline at table with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom (Matthew 8:11). Colossians 2:18 warns against the worship of angels.

Blessed are those who are invited. Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb. The fourth of the book’s seven beatitudes (1:3; 14:13; 16:15), and like 14:13 and 21:5 it comes with a command to write it down. Each of those three times the command is given, it is given over something a suffering church would find hard to believe. Invited (keklēmenoi) is called, from the same root as the called (klētoi) of 17:14. Marriage supper (deipnon tou gamou) is the wedding feast. The feast pictures the joy of the new creation, fellowship with Christ, and the fulfilment of the Lord’s Supper, which looks forward to it (1 Corinthians 11:26).

The least deserved document in the world. Not those who earned a place, or arranged one, or arrived early. A wedding invitation is the least deserved document in the world; it says only that somebody wanted you there. Jesus told a parable about a wedding feast where the invited guests would not come, and the servants were sent into the streets to bring in whoever they found, both bad and good (Matthew 22:9–10).

The true words of God. True (alēthinoi): genuine, reliable. A guarantee: this promise will happen. And the guarantee is aimed at the reader. It is the wedding, not the beast, that strains belief.

I fell down at his feet. Overwhelmed, John makes a mistake, and he records it honestly. He does it again in 22:8. An apostle, in the Spirit, who has already seen the throne and the Lamb and the sea of glass, twice goes down in front of a messenger. That is a comfort as well as a warning: the mistake is easily made, and it is not a stupid one. The angel is truly glorious, has truly brought the word of God, and has just said something overwhelming. The instinct to worship is right; only the direction is wrong.

But he said to me, You must not do that! The words (hora mē) mean see that you do not: an urgent warning. Fellow servant (syndoulos). Angels, however glorious, are servants like us (Hebrews 1:14). Not senior. Alongside.

Worship God. Worship belongs to God alone. This is crucial evidence for Christ’s deity: the angel refuses worship, but the Lamb receives it (5:8–14). The book that forbids worshipping the highest angel shows the whole of heaven falling down before the Lamb, and no one tells them to stop.

A permanent hazard for the church. It is recorded twice because it is a permanent danger. The people through whom God speaks are always in danger of being given what belongs to God: the preacher whose congregation depends on him rather than on Christ, the writer quoted more readily than Scripture, the movement that becomes the thing believed in. The angel’s answer settles it: worship God. And his self-description is the one every faithful minister has to make: I am a fellow servant with you.

The spirit of prophecy. The testimony of Jesus (hē martyria Iēsou) is the testimony that Jesus gave, and the testimony about Jesus; both are true in this book. The spirit of prophecy is its essence, its heart. All true prophecy bears witness to Jesus. And the sentence explains why the angel refused: everyone who holds the testimony of Jesus is in the prophetic company, so the apostle on the floor and the angel standing over him are colleagues. The angel, John and the church share one task: witnessing to Christ. There is one rank in that room above them both, and neither of them holds it.

Where Christians differ: does this mean prophecy continues in the church? Some read “the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy” as meaning that every witnessing believer has a gift of prophecy, so that new revelations continue today. Many Pentecostal and charismatic Christians believe God still gives prophetic words, always to be tested by Scripture (1 Thessalonians 5:20–21), and they hold this out of love for Christ and a longing to hear him. This commentary’s view: the verse teaches that the heart of all prophecy is witness to Jesus, and that every believer who bears that witness shares in the prophetic calling of the church (11:3). It does not promise new revelation. The prophetic word that John received is now written and closed (22:18–19). Today the church bears the testimony of Jesus by proclaiming the completed Scriptures, and that, this commentary holds with charity towards those who differ, is how the prophetic gift functions now.

Am I invited to the marriage supper? If you will come, yes. The invitation of the gospel goes out to everyone who hears it: the Spirit and the Bride say, come, and let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price (22:17). You do not need to qualify first, clean yourself up, or prove you are chosen. You come by trusting Christ, the Bridegroom who paid for the feast. Those who are truly called are those who accept the call, and no one who comes to him will be turned away (John 6:37). The only people missing will be those who refused.

How is the Lord’s Supper connected to this? The Lord’s Supper is a foretaste and a promise of the marriage supper. Every time the church eats the bread and drinks the cup, it proclaims the Lord’s death until he comes (1 Corinthians 11:26), looking back to the cross and forward to the feast. Jesus said he would not drink the cup again until he drank it new with us in his Father’s kingdom (Matthew 26:29). So come to the Lord’s Table as a guest rehearsing for a wedding: humbled by what it cost him, and glad about where it is leading.

For worship. The King of heaven has prepared a wedding for his Son and filled the hall with guests who had no claim to be there. He did not wait for worthy guests; he made them worthy, washing them in the blood of the Lamb whose wedding it is. And at that table the roles are reversed beyond imagining: Jesus said that the master would dress himself for service, have his servants recline at table, and come and serve them (Luke 12:37). The angel would not take John’s worship. The Lamb receives it, and then serves the guests. He is the Bridegroom, the host and the price of the feast, and the only one in the room worthy of worship.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–21 — The Rider on the White Horse
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 11–16: heaven opens and Christ rides out on a white horse, with eyes of fire, many crowns, a robe dipped in blood and a sword from his mouth, followed by the armies of heaven in white linen, and bearing the name King of kings and Lord of lords.

Verses 17–18: an angel in the sun calls the birds to the great supper of God, the dark counterpart of the Lamb’s wedding feast. Verses 19–21: the beast and the kings gather for war, and the beast and the false prophet are captured without a battle and thrown alive into the lake of fire.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Rider on the White Horse

Faithful and True, crowned with many diadems, robed in blood, named the Word of God and King of kings and Lord of lords, the Rider strikes the nations with the sword of his mouth. The beast and false prophet are captured without a battle and thrown into the lake of fire.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The churches had no army; the armies of heaven ride out in wedding clothes and strike no blow.

Now: There are two suppers in this chapter: at one people are guests, at the other they are the meal.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw heaven opened, and behold, a white horse! The one sitting on it is called Faithful and True, and in righteousness he judges and makes war. His eyes are like a flame of fire, and on his head are many diadems, and he has a name written that no one knows but himself. He is clothed in a robe dipped in blood, and the name by which he is called is The Word of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Roman generals celebrated victory in a triumph, riding into Rome in a chariot, often said to be drawn by white horses, followed by their army, displaying captives and spoil. Isaiah 63:1–3 describes the LORD coming from Edom in crimson garments, stained from treading the winepress of his wrath. Psalm 45:3–6 describes the king riding out victoriously for the cause of truth and righteousness.

Heaven opened. Heaven has been opened once before in this book, at 4:1, when a door stood open and John was called up. This time it is not a door. Heaven itself is opened, and something comes out. This is Christ’s return.

A white horse! The horse of victory. A reader will remember a white horse from 6:2, and the two must not be confused; that rider was a counterfeit conqueror. The differences are deliberate and decisive. That rider had a bow; this one has a sword from his mouth. That rider was given a crown, a single stephanos, a victor’s wreath; this one wears many diadems, royal crowns, and nobody hands them to him. That rider was unnamed; this one has four names in six verses.

Faithful and True. As in 3:14, where Christ introduced himself to Laodicea as the faithful and true witness, and 1:5. The rider coming out of heaven with a sword is the same person who wrote the seven letters. Christ keeps every promise and speaks only truth. His coming is the fulfilment of God’s word.

In righteousness he judges. Righteousness (dikaiosynē). Almost every war ever fought has been declared righteous by the people fighting it, and history is a graveyard of holy causes. This is the one case in which the claim is true, and it is true because of who is making it. Isaiah promised a shoot from the stump of Jesse who would judge the poor with righteousness and strike the earth with the rod of his mouth (Isaiah 11:3–4).

Eyes like a flame of fire. As in 1:14 and 2:18: the eyes that searched the hearts of Thyatira (2:18, 23) and saw what Sardis and Laodicea could not see about themselves (3:1, 17). He sees through everything. No disguise survives his gaze, and no faithful act goes unseen by it.

Many diadems. The dragon wore seven (12:3) and the beast ten (13:1). This rider wears an uncounted number, and every crown either of them claimed is on his head.

A name no one knows. Three names are given in these verses and another is withheld, a striking restraint. There is a depth in Christ that no creature fully comprehends: no one knows the Son except the Father (Matthew 11:27). After every doctrine has been correctly stated there is something in Christ that no creature has been given, and Revelation says so at the moment of his greatest self-disclosure. He is more than all his titles.

A robe dipped in blood. Dipped means soaked. Here is the crux of the scene, because the battle has not been fought yet. He is already covered in blood before a single enemy appears in verse 19. Whose blood is it? The immediate source is Isaiah 63, where a figure comes from Edom in crimson garments and explains that he has trodden the winepress alone, and their lifeblood has spattered his garments (Isaiah 63:1–3). John quotes the winepress two verses later, so Isaiah is unmistakably in view, and on that reading the blood is his enemies’, before the battle has even begun, pointing to his certain victory. Or it is his own blood, shed on the cross, by which he conquered (5:9; 12:11).

His own blood, most likely. Revelation regularly reinterprets Old Testament war imagery in the light of the cross, and the robe is mentioned before any battle, so his own blood is most likely, with a hint of judgement as well. The whole book has turned on a Lamb standing as though it had been slain (5:6), and every victory in Revelation has been won by blood already shed: they conquered him by the blood of the Lamb (12:11). Whichever way the image is weighted, the rider arrives already bloodied, and the outcome of the battle was settled before the battle began. The one who judges is the one who was slain.

The Word of God. Outside this book, the only New Testament writings that use that title of Christ are the Gospel and first letter that bear John’s name: in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God (John 1:1, 14; compare 1 John 1:1). It is like a family signature, and it makes the rider unmistakable. He is God’s final self-revelation and speech. In other words, everything God wants to say to us about himself, he has said in a person: long ago he spoke by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2). To look at Jesus is to hear God, and there is no further word behind him to wait for. And it explains the weapon: the conqueror whose name is the Word fights with his mouth (v. 15).

Where Christians differ: is this Christ’s return before a millennium, or his final coming? Premillennialists read 19:11–21 as Christ’s return to defeat the antichrist, followed in chapter 20 by a thousand-year reign on earth before the final judgement. They do so because John’s and I saw seems to carry the story forward, and because they want to take the thousand years and the two resurrections of chapter 20 at face value; a number of the earliest church fathers read it this way, and many faithful Christians do today. Dispensational premillennialists add a rapture of the church before a seven-year tribulation. Postmillennialists, by contrast, often read this rider as a picture of the gospel’s conquering advance through history before Christ returns. This commentary takes the amillennial view (that the thousand years picture the present age, with no separate earthly reign after Christ’s return). This commentary’s view: this is Christ’s one, final, visible return, which brings the last battle, the final judgement and the new creation. Revelation is a series of parallel visions, and chapter 20 goes back to describe the whole church age again from another angle. The same final battle appears in 16:14–16, 19:19–21 and 20:7–10, described in almost the same words, drawn from Ezekiel 38–39 (the birds’ feast here, the fire there). There is one return, one battle, one final judgement.

The pattern of going back. This is not special pleading for chapter 20. Revelation has done it before: chapter 12 goes back to the birth of Christ after chapter 11 has reached the end (11:15–18), and the seals, trumpets and bowls each reach the end in turn. So on this reading the return of Christ in chapter 19 is the end of the thousand years, not the start of them, and chapter 20 shows the same age from the side of Satan bound and the saints reigning with Christ.

How can the Prince of Peace make war? Because there can be no lasting peace while evil is free to destroy. The Christ who came the first time as a Lamb, to suffer and to offer peace to all who will receive it, comes the second time as Judge, to end the rebellion of those who have refused it (Acts 17:31). His war is not against the weak but against the beast, the false prophet and those who make war on him and his people. It is the war that ends all wars, and it is fought with perfect justice, by one who himself bore the judgement for every enemy who repents. The same hands that hold the reins bear the marks of the nails.

verseByVerse.quote: And the armies of heaven, arrayed in fine linen, white and pure, were following him on white horses. From his mouth comes a sharp sword with which to strike down the nations, and he will rule them with a rod of iron. He will tread the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty. On his robe and on his thigh he has a name written, King of kings and Lord of lords.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Zechariah 14:5 says the LORD will come, and all the holy ones with him. Jesus said the Son of Man will come in his glory, and all the angels with him (Matthew 25:31). Paul says Christ will come with his saints (1 Thessalonians 3:13) and with his mighty angels (2 Thessalonians 1:7). Isaiah 11:4 and 49:2 speak of the Messiah’s mouth like a sharp sword, striking the earth with the rod of his mouth. In the ancient world, a name or title might be written on a statue’s thigh, or on the part of a rider’s robe that covered the thigh, where it would be seen as he rode.

The armies of heaven. Armies (strateumata). Look at what this army is wearing, because John has just told the reader what fine linen means: the righteous deeds of the saints (v. 8). This is the same fabric in almost the same words. The armies of heaven are dressed as the Bride, and those with the Lamb are the called, chosen and faithful (17:14). They include his saints and his angels. Which means the church rides out to the last battle in its wedding clothes. Not armour, not uniform: linen.

They carry no weapons. They do not fight. They simply follow, and nothing in these verses says the army strikes a single blow. Its entire role in the greatest battle in Scripture is to be present and to be with him. That is the last word of this book on Christian militancy. The saints have been told to endure, to hold fast, to keep their garments on, and to conquer by the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony. They have never once been told to fight, and when the fighting finally happens they are spectators in white. It also answers the charge that faith in a coming Judge breeds violence. The book that ends with the most terrible battle in Scripture forbids its readers to fight it: vengeance stays in the hands of the one person who can be trusted with it.

A sharp sword from his mouth. Sword (rhomphaia), as in 1:16 and 2:16: his word. He conquers by speaking, as God created by speaking (Genesis 1). One word from him, and his enemies fall: the Lord Jesus will kill the lawless one with the breath of his mouth (2 Thessalonians 2:8). In a chapter full of horses and armies and a coming slaughter, the conqueror carries nothing in his hands. What kills is what he says. The word of testimony the saints have used all along is a small version of the one he will finish with.

A rod of iron. As in Psalm 2:9, quoted at 2:27 and 12:5. The Son whom the kings of the earth set themselves against is the one who breaks them.

The winepress. As in 14:19–20 and Isaiah 63:3. Christ himself carries out God’s final judgement. The Father has given all judgement to the Son (John 5:22), and the one who drank the cup of wrath for his people now treads the winepress for his enemies.

King of kings and Lord of lords. The supreme title, as in 17:14, where the order is reversed: either way round, the two halves say one thing. It is placed where a rider’s thigh is visible above the horse to everyone standing on the ground: a title worn where it can be read. And it is God’s own title. Moses said the LORD your God is God of gods and Lord of lords (Deuteronomy 10:17). Every emperor, king and lord is under him.

What it meant to the first hearers. Think of the seven congregations who first heard them read out. They lived in a province where the emperor was called lord, where his image was on every coin they handled, and where their neighbours had been asked to say a few words about him that they could not say. Some in that room may well have known someone in prison for it. And into that room came a sentence written on the thigh of a rider coming out of an open heaven: King of kings and Lord of lords. Not a hope, not a slogan, and not a consolation. A name, already written, on someone already riding.

Will I be in that army? If you belong to Christ, yes. The armies are dressed in the Bride’s linen, and the Bride is the whole church. Paul says that when Christ appears, we will appear with him in glory (Colossians 3:4), and that God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep (1 Thessalonians 4:14). Believers who have died are with Christ now, and will come with him; believers still living will be caught up to meet him (1 Thessalonians 4:17). There is one coming, and the whole people of God, living and dead, will share in it, not as soldiers who win the victory but as the Bride who shares it.

On a Tuesday. When an employer, a government or the culture demands something Christ forbids, remember the name on his thigh. Be respectful and obedient wherever you can, but where you cannot, say graciously and firmly that you belong to a higher Lord, and leave the outcome to him.

For worship. King of kings and Lord of lords: the title is written where everyone can see it, and one day everyone will. He needs no army to win, yet he will not ride out without his Bride. The mouth that strikes the nations is the mouth that said to a dead man, Lazarus, come out, and to a dying thief, today you will be with me in paradise. He rules the nations with a rod of iron, and he leads his own people gently, like a shepherd. Every knee will bow to him, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw an angel standing in the sun, and with a loud voice he called to all the birds that fly directly overhead, "Come, gather for the great supper of God, to eat the flesh of kings, the flesh of captains, the flesh of mighty men, the flesh of horses and their riders, and the flesh of all men, both free and slave, both small and great."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Ezekiel 39:17–20 describes God summoning the birds and wild beasts to a great sacrificial feast on the bodies of Gog’s defeated armies, to eat the flesh of the mighty and drink the blood of the princes of the earth. To be left unburied was a curse under the law (Deuteronomy 28:26). Jesus said, wherever the corpse is, there the vultures will gather (Matthew 24:28).

An angel standing in the sun. Blazing, visible to all, at the highest point, so that the summons reaches everything with wings. He calls to the birds that fly directly overhead (en mesouranēmati): in mid-heaven, at the zenith, the same phrase used of the eagle in 8:13 and the gospel angel in 14:6. Three times in this book something is announced from the highest point of the sky where nobody can miss it: a warning, a gospel, and now this. The birds are birds of prey, vultures.

The great supper of God. The scene is Ezekiel 39, almost word for word, and John’s readers knew the passage. And the placement is the horror of it. Eight verses ago an angel told John to write: blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb (v. 9). Here is the other supper, and the invitation goes out to carrion birds. There are two suppers at the end of history: one where the redeemed feast with Christ, and one where his enemies become the feast. Everyone will be at one supper or the other. That is the arrangement the chapter is built on, and it should not be softened: the birds are a picture, but the ruin they picture is real. At one, people are the guests. At the other, they are the meal.

The flesh of kings. The word flesh five times, and a list that starts at the top: kings, commanders, strong men, cavalry, the whole apparatus of power. Every class of people who opposed Christ is here, as at the sixth seal (6:15). Then the phrase that has run through this book refusing every ranking: both small and great. As the redeemed include small and great (v. 5), so do the lost. Rank gives no protection.

The last word on human greatness. To be left unburied and eaten by birds was, in the ancient world, the most complete disgrace there was, the fate David threatened Goliath with (1 Samuel 17:46), and the thing every army feared more than dying. A king in that condition is indistinguishable from a slave. And that is the last thing this book says about human greatness built against God. The chapter has just given a rider four names and an army in wedding linen; it now takes the rival aristocracy, kings, captains, mighty men, and lists them by their flesh.

The disgrace he carried. The image is meant to horrify, and the gospel meets it at the point of horror. To die exposed, a body left in the open to public shame, was the curse of the ancient world, and the law said that a man hanged on a tree was under God’s curse (Deuteronomy 21:23). Jesus died under that curse. Paul says Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). Stripped, hung up in public outside the city, mocked by passers-by, he took that disgrace on himself, though loving hands then buried him, so that everyone who comes to him can be moved from the one table to the other. No one at the marriage supper got there by escaping the curse. They got there because he bore it.

What it does not mean. This is not a literal description of birds eating corpses at the end of the world, to be imagined in detail. It is a vivid, shocking symbol, drawn from Ezekiel, of total and shameful defeat for those who fight against God.

Why would Scripture use such a shocking image? Because we need to be shocked. We easily think of God’s judgement as a polite disappointment, and of rebellion against Christ as a harmless difference of opinion. The image strips away the illusion: to set oneself against the King of kings is to choose utter ruin and disgrace. It is also deliberately placed beside the marriage supper, so that no reader can miss the choice. God does not show us this to frighten us into despair, but to drive us to the other table while the invitation is still open (Ezekiel 33:11).

On a Tuesday. There are two suppers. Make sure you have accepted the invitation to the Lamb’s, and urge others to accept it too (Luke 14:16–24). Who in your life has not yet answered the invitation? Pray for that friend every day this week. Ask God for an opening, and when it comes, tell them about the wedding.
