verseByVerse.quote: And I saw the beast and the kings of the earth with their armies gathered to make war against him who was sitting on the horse and against his army. And the beast was captured, and with it the false prophet who in its presence had done the signs by which he deceived those who had received the mark of the beast and those who worshiped its image. These two were thrown alive into the lake of fire that burns with sulfur. And the rest were slain by the sword that came from the mouth of him who was sitting on the horse, and all the birds were gorged with their flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Psalm 2:2 says the kings of the earth set themselves against the LORD and his Anointed. The gathering was announced in 16:14–16 (Armageddon) and 17:14. Daniel 7:11 says the beast was killed and its body destroyed and given over to be burned with fire. Korah, Dathan and Abiram went down alive into Sheol (Numbers 16:33).

The beast and the kings gathered. Gathered (synēgmena), as in 16:14, 16 and 20:8. This is the muster of 16:14–16 arriving, the kings assembled by three frog-spirits at the place called Armageddon. All the forces of evil gathered in one place. The most famous battle in the world’s imagination is joined: watch how long it lasts.

The beast was captured. That is the battle. There is no engagement and no account of the fighting at all. The verb is passive, and the beast that was worshipped by the whole earth (13:4), that was given authority over every tribe and people and language and nation, that made war on the saints for forty-two months, is simply taken. John has built thirteen chapters of dread and then refuses to give the confrontation a single sentence of drama. That is not carelessness; it is the argument. A thing that requires no fight was never the equal of the one who ends it, and every reader who has been frightened by the beast is being told what the beast actually weighs when the rider arrives.

And with it the false prophet. The second beast of 13:11–17. He is named by the charge sheet: deception is what he is arrested for. In a book whose enemy is the deceiver of the whole world, that is the charge that matters.

Thrown alive into the lake of fire. Alive (zōntes). Lake of fire (tēn limnēn tou pyros): the place of final, eternal punishment, first mentioned here. Later the devil is thrown there (20:10), then death and Hades, and all whose names are not in the book of life (20:14–15). It was prepared for the devil and his angels (Matthew 25:41). Alive is deliberate: this is not annihilation on a battlefield.

Slain by the sword. By his word alone. And all the birds were gorged (echortasthēsan, filled) with their flesh: the great supper of God (v. 17) has been served.

Where Christians differ: are the beast and false prophet persons, and is the lake of fire eternal? Some say that since the beast and false prophet are symbols of systems, not individuals, the lake of fire may mean only their abolition, not eternal punishment. Others, sometimes called annihilationists or conditionalists, hold more generally that the lost are finally destroyed rather than punished for ever; they are often careful students of Scripture, moved by its words destroy and perish, and they are not denying the gospel. This commentary’s view: the beast and false prophet represent systems of persecuting power and deception, and also, finally, the persons who lead them. Their being thrown into the lake of fire shows the total end of those systems, and the eternal punishment of the persons who embody them, together with all who follow them. Revelation 20:10 says the devil, the beast and the false prophet will be tormented day and night for ever and ever: the punishment is conscious and endless. Christ’s victory over every evil power is complete and permanent.

In the flow. The enemies of God entered the book in an order: the dragon in chapter 12, the beast and the false prophet in chapter 13, Babylon in chapter 17. They leave it in reverse. Babylon fell in chapter 18; the beast and the false prophet are thrown into the lake of fire here; and the dragon is still to come. Chapter 20 will step back to show him bound during the age of the gospel, and then bring him to the same final battle and the same lake (20:7–10). The last enemy of all, death itself, follows him there (20:14).

Is the lake of fire literal fire? The language is picture language, and Scripture uses several pictures for hell: fire, outer darkness, the worm that does not die (Mark 9:48; Matthew 8:12). Fire and darkness cannot both be literal at the same time in the ordinary sense. But the pictures do not soften the reality; they point to something worse than any image can convey: conscious, unending separation from the goodness of God, under his just wrath. The right response is not curiosity about its physics but fear of God, gratitude to Christ who bore that wrath for all who trust him, and urgency in warning others.

What the seven churches were being told. This is the final answer of the book to a question the seven churches were living inside. They had no army, no legal standing, no leverage, and no way of resisting the power arranged against them. Nothing in Revelation ever tells them to acquire any of those things. It tells them to endure, to keep their garments on, to hold the testimony, and to conquer by blood already shed. And then it shows them the end, in which they ride out in wedding clothes behind someone who does not need them, and wants them anyway.

Salvation and glory and power belong to our God,<sup>2</sup>for his judgments are true and just; for he has judged the great prostitute who corrupted the earth with her immorality, and has avenged on her the blood of his servants.”<sup>3</sup>Once more they cried out, “Hallelujah! The smoke from her goes up forever and ever.”<sup>4</sup>And the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fell down and worshiped God who was seated on the throne, saying, “Amen. Hallelujah!”<sup>5</sup>And from the throne came a voice saying, “Praise our God, all you his servants, you who fear him, small and great.”<sup>6</sup>Then I heard what seemed to be the voice of a great multitude, like the roar of many waters and like the sound of mighty peals of thunder, crying out, “Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns.<sup>7</sup>Let us rejoice and exult and give him the glory, for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready;<sup>8</sup>it was granted her to clothe herself with fine linen, bright and pure”—for the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints.<sup>9</sup>And the angel said to me, “Write this: Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.” And he said to me, “These are the true words of God.”<sup>10</sup>Then I fell down at his feet to worship him, but he said to me, “You must not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers who hold to the testimony of Jesus. The one sitting on it is called Faithful and True, and in righteousness he judges and makes war.<sup>12</sup>His eyes are like a flame of fire, and on his head are many diadems, and he has a name written that no one knows but himself.<sup>13</sup>He is clothed in a robe dipped in blood, and the name by which he is called is The Word of God.<sup>14</sup>And the armies of heaven, arrayed in fine linen, white and pure, were following him on white horses.<sup>15</sup>From his mouth comes a sharp sword with which to strike down the nations, and he will rule them with a rod of iron. He will tread the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty.<sup>16</sup>On his robe and on his thigh he has a name written, King of kings and Lord of lords.<sup>17</sup>Then I saw an angel standing in the sun, and with a loud voice he called to all the birds that fly directly overhead, “Come, gather for the great supper of God,<sup>18</sup>to eat the flesh of kings, the flesh of captains, the flesh of mighty men, the flesh of horses and their riders, and the flesh of all men, both free and slave, both small and great.”<sup>19</sup>And I saw the beast and the kings of the earth with their armies gathered to make war against him who was sitting on the horse and against his army.<sup>20</sup>And the beast was captured, and with it the false prophet who in its presence had done the signs by which he deceived those who had received the mark of the beast and those who worshiped its image. These two were thrown alive into the lake of fire that burns with sulfur.<sup>21</sup>And the rest were slain by the sword that came from the mouth of him who was sitting on the horse, and all the birds were gorged with their flesh.

20.title: The Thousand Years and the Great White Throne
20.overview:
Chapter 20 is the only passage in the Bible that speaks of a thousand-year reign, and it has divided Scripture-loving Christians for centuries. This commentary follows the amillennial reading and sets out the others with respect. Beneath the debate lies what all the views share: Christ will return, the dead will be raised, the wicked will be judged, the righteous will be glorified, and God will be all in all.

The main views, briefly. Dispensational premillennialism (Walvoord, Ryrie, MacArthur, Swindoll): after a pre-tribulation rapture and a seven-year tribulation, Christ returns and reigns on earth for a thousand years from Jerusalem, with national Israel restored. Historic premillennialism (Ladd, Grudem): the same earthly reign after Christ’s return, but the church goes through the tribulation. Postmillennialism (Jonathan Edwards, Charles Hodge, Warfield in some respects): the thousand years is an era of spreading Christian influence through the gospel before Christ returns. Amillennialism (Augustine, Calvin, Vos, Berkhof, Hoekema, Beale): the thousand years is the whole church age; Satan was bound at the cross so that the gospel can reach the nations; believers who have died reign with Christ in heaven; and Satan’s brief release comes just before Christ’s one return.

The chapter has two sections: the thousand years and Satan’s end (vv. 1–10), and the great white throne (vv. 11–15). On what matters most it is clear: no one escapes the final judgement, only those written in the book of life are safe, and Death and Hades themselves are thrown into the lake of fire.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–3: an angel binds the dragon for a thousand years, so that he can no longer deceive the nations, until he is released for a little while. Verses 4–6: John sees thrones and the souls of the faithful dead, who reign with Christ; this is the first resurrection, and over them the second death has no power.

Verses 7–10: released at the end, Satan gathers the nations, Gog and Magog, against the camp of the saints; fire from heaven consumes them, and the devil is thrown into the lake of fire.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Thousand Years

An angel binds the dragon so that he may no longer deceive the nations; those who refused the beast reign with Christ; and after a brief release Satan’s last host is consumed and he is thrown into the lake of fire. Premillennial, amillennial and postmillennial readers differ on the timing, and agree on all that the creeds require.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The people the world beheaded and shut out of the market are seen on thrones.

Now: Over those who share in the first resurrection the second death has no power; on that there is no dispute.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw an angel coming down from heaven, holding in his hand the key to the bottomless pit and a great chain. And he seized the dragon, that ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years, and threw him into the pit, and shut it and sealed it over him, so that he might not deceive the nations any longer, until the thousand years were ended. After that he must be released for a little while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Revelation 20 is the only passage in the Bible that speaks of a thousand years, and it shows Satan’s defeat and the final judgement. An angel binds Satan with a chain and seals him in the abyss for a thousand years, so that he can no longer deceive the nations, after which he must be released for a little while (vv. 1–3). John sees thrones, and the souls of those beheaded for Jesus and of those who refused the beast; they come to life and reign with Christ for a thousand years. This is the first resurrection, and over such the second death has no power; they are priests reigning with Christ (vv. 4–6). When the thousand years end, Satan is released and gathers Gog and Magog, as numerous as the sand, against the camp of the saints and the beloved city; but fire from heaven consumes them, and the devil is thrown into the lake of fire with the beast and false prophet, to be tormented for ever (vv. 7–10). Before a great white throne the dead, great and small, are judged by their works; Death and Hades are thrown into the lake of fire, the second death, and so is anyone not found in the book of life (vv. 11–15). In the amillennial reading this commentary follows, the chapter goes back to the beginning of the church age once more: Satan was bound at Christ’s first coming so that the gospel could go to the nations; the martyrs and faithful dead now reign with Christ in heaven; at the end Satan is released briefly for a final assault; and then Christ returns, once, to raise all the dead and judge all people. And the whole chapter, read rightly, is a hymn to the Lamb: the serpent of Genesis 3 is finished, death itself is thrown away, and the only thing that decides anyone’s destiny is a name written in the Lamb’s book.

The setting. Jesus said no one can enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man (Matthew 12:29), and he did this by casting out demons through the Spirit of God, showing that the kingdom of God had come. On the eve of the cross he said, now will the ruler of this world be cast out, and I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself (John 12:31–32). Through death he destroyed the one who has the power of death, the devil (Hebrews 2:14), and disarmed the rulers and authorities, triumphing over them in the cross (Colossians 2:15). Jude 6 speaks of angels kept in eternal chains under gloomy darkness until the judgement. When John hears of a chain and a pit, his readers would have heard all of this behind it.

An angel coming down from heaven. “Then I saw” (kai eidon) is John’s regular formula for a new vision. It marks the order of the visions, not necessarily the order of events. John has already done this more than once: chapter 12 went back to Christ’s birth after the seventh trumpet had announced the end of the world.

The key and a great chain. Every reader agrees on three things here, and they are easily lost in the argument. First, the arrest is effortless. One angel, one key (kleida), one chain (halysin), and five verbs done to the dragon: seized, bound, threw, shut, sealed. This is the creature who had seven heads and seven diadems, who gave the beast its throne, who made war on the woman and on the rest of her offspring, and who deceived the whole world. He is handled by a single unnamed angel with a set of keys. A spiritual being cannot literally be chained; the key and the chain are pictures of authority and restraint, and they say that Satan’s power is limited by God, whenever and however God pleases.

That ancient serpent. Second, the four names are the ones from 12:9, in the same order: the dragon, the ancient serpent, the devil, Satan. The same enemy, all his titles read out at his arrest. John is deliberately reaching back to the garden, to the serpent who spoke to Eve, and closing the file that was opened in Genesis 3.

Bound for a thousand years. “Bound” (edēsen) is the same word Jesus used of binding the strong man (Matthew 12:29). The Lord had told his disciples what he was doing in his ministry, and John now shows it from heaven’s side. “A thousand years” (chilia etē; millennium is simply Latin for a thousand years). In Revelation numbers are symbolic: seven lampstands, twelve thousand from each tribe, a woman nourished for twelve hundred and sixty days. A thousand is ten cubed, often read as the number of completeness raised to its fullest. A long, complete period, its length set entirely by God.

Shut and sealed. “Sealed” (esphragisen) is the word used of the tomb of Jesus, when the authorities sealed the stone to keep a dead man in (Matthew 27:66). That seal failed, because the man inside was the Lord of life. This one holds, because the one who placed it is the same Lord.

That he might not deceive the nations. Third, and this is the clause that decides the whole chapter, the binding is given a stated purpose. Not so that he could do nothing at all. Whatever the binding is, John defines it himself, and it is specific. It does not mean Satan is inactive in every way; he still prowls (1 Peter 5:8), tempts and persecutes. It means he cannot prevent the gospel from going to the nations, or gather the nations for the final assault on the church until God permits. Since Christ, people from every nation have been turned from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God (Acts 26:18), which is what a dragon prevented from deceiving the nations would look like.

A dog on a chain. A chained dog is still dangerous to anyone who wanders within reach of it; you would not put your hand near its mouth. But it cannot stop the house being plundered, and it cannot follow the plunderers down the road. Satan can still bite, and Christians are told to resist him firm in the faith (1 Peter 5:9). What he cannot do is keep the nations locked in his house while Christ carries his captives out of it, one by one, from every people on earth.

Released for a little while. After that he must be released for a little while. “Must” (dei) is the divine must that has governed this book since 1:1, the things that must soon take place. Even the release is on a permission and has a term. “A little while” (mikron chronon) is a short time at the end of history, a final outburst of deception and persecution before Christ returns (2 Thessalonians 2:3–12). Nothing the dragon does, including his final rampage, is outside the timetable God has written.

The thousand years: three readings. The phrase occurs six times in six verses, and godly readers have understood it in three main ways. Each deserves to be set out with what genuinely favours it.

The premillennial reading. This takes the chapter in the order it is written. Christ returns at the end of chapter 19; then Satan is bound; then Christ reigns on the earth for a thousand years; then Satan is released, the last rebellion is crushed, and the final judgement follows. Two forms of it are held. Historic premillennialism (George Eldon Ladd, Wayne Grudem) has the church go through the tribulation before Christ returns. Dispensational premillennialism (John Walvoord, Charles Ryrie, John MacArthur and the Scofield tradition) adds a rapture (a catching up of believers to meet the Lord) before a seven-year tribulation, a final period of great distress, and understands the millennium as the period in which God’s promises to national Israel are fulfilled. A form of it was held by a number of the earliest church fathers. What favours it is considerable. The narrative flows straight on from chapter 19 with then I saw. The Old Testament promises of a messianic kingdom on the earth, a wolf lying down with a lamb, a child playing over a snake’s hole, a man building a house and living in it (Isaiah 11:6–9; 65:20–25), are given somewhere to land. And the strongest argument is at verse 5, where the same verb used of the martyrs coming to life is used of the rest of the dead, whom everyone agrees are raised bodily.

The postmillennial reading. This holds that the gospel will succeed so widely that a long era of Christianised civilisation follows, and that Christ returns at the end of it. It was held by Jonathan Edwards and Charles Hodge, and today by writers such as Kenneth Gentry. What favours it is the trajectory of Jesus’ own parables, a mustard seed becoming the largest of garden plants and leaven working through the whole lump (Matthew 13:31–33), along with Psalm 2, Psalm 72 and Isaiah 2:2–4, the sheer scope of the Great Commission, and Paul’s statement that Christ must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet (1 Corinthians 15:25). Its hope has fuelled great missionary labour. Its difficulty is the New Testament’s equally consistent expectation of apostasy and tribulation before the end (Matthew 24:9–13; 2 Timothy 3:1–5), and the final deception described in this very chapter.

The amillennial reading. Amillennial means no millennium, in the sense of no separate earthly reign after Christ’s return; the view takes the thousand years as the whole period between the first and second comings: the age the church is in now. On this view Satan was bound at the cross, in exactly the sense verse 3 specifies: he can no longer keep the nations in the dark. The reign of the saints is their reign with Christ in heaven, which is why verse 4 says John saw souls. Christ returns once, at the end, and there is one resurrection and one judgement. This is the position of Augustine, the Reformers broadly, Geerhardus Vos, William Hendriksen and G. K. Beale, and it is the position this commentary follows. What favours it is also considerable. Numbers in this book are symbolic throughout. The chapter never says Christ is on the earth during these years, and never mentions his physical presence at all. Its hardest point is the verb of verse 5, and it should face that honestly.

Where Christians differ: what is the thousand years? Premillennialists, including dispensationalists, hold that Christ will return before (pre-) a literal thousand-year reign on earth, during which Satan is bound and Christ rules from Jerusalem; then Satan is released, defeated, and the final judgement follows. Postmillennialists hold that the gospel will gradually triumph in the world, bringing a long golden age of Christian influence, after (post-) which Christ returns. Amillennialists hold that the thousand years is a symbol for the present church age, between Christ’s first and second comings: Satan is now bound so that he cannot stop the gospel; believers who have died reign with Christ in heaven; and Christ’s return brings the end, with no separate earthly millennium. This commentary’s view: the amillennial view fits Revelation best. Revelation repeatedly goes back over the same period in parallel visions, and chapter 20 does so again. The binding of Satan is what Jesus and the apostles say happened at the cross. The reign is with Christ, who already reigns from heaven. The final battle of 20:7–10 is the same as 16:14–16 and 19:19–21, all drawn from Ezekiel 38–39, and gathered in almost the same words. And the rest of the New Testament teaches one return of Christ, bringing the resurrection of both righteous and wicked together (John 5:28–29; Acts 24:15), the final judgement and the new creation (2 Peter 3:10–13), with no interval of a thousand years. Premillennial and postmillennial believers are brothers and sisters in Christ, and this is a matter where Christians may charitably differ; but the amillennial reading is the most faithful to the text.

What all three agree on. All three hold everything the historic creeds require. Every one of them affirms that Christ has decisively defeated Satan; that he will return bodily, visibly and personally; that the dead will be raised; that there will be a final judgement; that the wicked will be condemned and the redeemed will live in a new creation; and that the church’s duty now is faithfulness under pressure. The disagreement is about the timing and sequence of things all three are certain will happen. The right response to a brother who reads it differently is not suspicion but an open Bible and a warm handshake.

If Satan is bound, why does the world look so dark? Because the binding is specific, not total. John never says the world will become pleasant; the same book that binds the dragon has the beast making war on the saints. What has changed is that the gospel cannot be stopped. Look at the map: in John’s day the church was a few scattered congregations in one corner of the Roman Empire, and today there are believers in nearly every nation, worshipping in thousands of languages. That did not happen with Satan free to keep the nations blind. So when the news is grim, read it inside this verse. Darkness is real, but it is no longer in charge of who hears about Christ.

But does the rapture not come before all this? This commentary holds that there is no secret rapture. The New Testament knows one coming of Christ, and it is anything but secret: the Lord descends with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel and the sound of the trumpet of God (1 Thessalonians 4:16). Believers who are alive are caught up to meet him, and the dead in Christ rise first, but this is the public meeting of the King, not a quiet removal years before the end. Christians who hold a pre-tribulation rapture are brothers in Christ, and many of them love the Lord’s appearing more than we do. They hold it because God promises to keep his church from the hour of trial (3:10) and says that he has not destined us for wrath (1 Thessalonians 5:9), and those promises are precious. But being kept from wrath is not the same as being kept from trouble: the church should expect to go through trouble, as it always has, and to be kept in it rather than taken out of it (John 17:15). Christ’s coming is near, and we are to watch for it every day; yet the New Testament also names things that come first, the gospel preached to all nations, a great falling away and the man of lawlessness (Matthew 24:14; 2 Thessalonians 2:1–4), and in this chapter the dragon’s brief release.

Does it matter which view I hold? It matters, but not as much as some arguments make it seem. It matters because how you read this chapter shapes how you read the whole of Revelation, and whether you expect the world to get better, worse or both. It does not matter in the sense of dividing Christians. You can belong to a church whose pastor reads it differently, pray with brothers who disagree, and sing the same hymns about the coming King. What you must not do is let the chart replace the Christ. All three views wait for the same person.

On a Tuesday. The colleague who seems hardest, the neighbour who mocks, the relative who has refused for thirty years: none of them is beyond the reach of a gospel the dragon cannot block. So pray for them this week, and for the missionaries your church knows, because the binding of the strong man is the reason those prayers are not in vain.
verseByVerse.note: The thousand years (the millennium) is read in three main ways: Christ’s present reign from heaven through the church age (amillennial); a future reign on earth after his return (premillennial); or a golden age of gospel success before his return (postmillennial).

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw thrones, and seated on them were those to whom the authority to judge was committed. Also I saw the souls of those who had been beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God, and those who had not worshiped the beast or its image and had not received its mark on their foreheads or their hands. They came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Daniel 7:9 and 22 say thrones were placed, and judgement was given for the saints of the Most High, and the time came when the saints possessed the kingdom. Jesus promised the Twelve that they would sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes (Matthew 19:28), and the overcomer that he would sit with Christ on his throne (3:21). Paul asked the Corinthians, apparently expecting them to know, whether they did not know that the saints will judge the world (1 Corinthians 6:2). Beheading with a sword was the Roman method of executing citizens, and tradition says Paul died this way.

Thrones. Plural, and John does not say at once who is on them. “Authority to judge” (krima edothē autois, judgement was given to them) can mean either that they were given authority to judge, or that judgement was given in their favour, as in Daniel 7:22, vindicating them. Both are true of the same people. They were judged by earthly courts; now heaven’s court has found for them, and they sit with the Judge.

The souls of the beheaded. “Souls” (psychas): the same word as 6:9, the souls under the altar. These are believers who have died, now alive in God’s presence. They were killed on earth; now they reign in heaven. “Beheaded” is a specific word, execution by the axe or sword. John does not merely say killed. He says how, because he wants us to see the cost.

Those who had not worshiped the beast. Two groups, or one company described twice? The Greek allows either, and it may well be one company seen from two sides: those who died for refusing, and those who lived without yielding, all who conquered the beast (15:2). If so, the reign belongs to everyone who did not take the mark, not to a sub-class of martyrs. And there is a phrase here the reader has met before. Chapter 13 said nobody could buy or sell without the mark. These people could not buy or sell, and here they are on thrones.

They came to life and reigned. Everything turns on that verb. The Greek is ezēsan, and it means simply they lived, or they came to life. On the reading this commentary follows, it is not their bodily resurrection, which comes at the end (1 Corinthians 15:23, 52), but their entry into life with Christ when they died. Though their bodies were killed, they live and reign with him, for God is not God of the dead but of the living, for all live to him (Luke 20:38; John 11:25–26). “Reigned with Christ” (ebasileusan meta tou Christou): sharing his rule from heaven, where he reigns now (Ephesians 1:20–22). This is the answer to 6:9–11. The martyrs who waited under the altar, crying how long, are now seen on thrones.

Where Christians differ: is this a bodily resurrection to rule on earth? Premillennialists read “came to life” as a bodily resurrection of believers at Christ’s return, followed by a literal thousand-year reign on earth, and their argument from verse 5 is the strongest single argument in the debate: the identical verb is used one sentence later of the rest of the dead, and nobody disputes that their coming to life is bodily. Some amillennial readers take the coming to life of the new birth, for God made us alive together with Christ and seated us with him in the heavenly places (Ephesians 2:5–6), and Jesus said the hour is coming and is now here when the dead will hear his voice and live (John 5:25). This commentary’s view: John sees souls, not bodies, on thrones, which in Revelation are, apart from Satan’s and the beast’s, in heaven. The scene is the heavenly reign of believers who have died, during the present age, while Satan is bound on earth. The verb simply means lived or came to life: it is used of the beast who was wounded by the sword and yet lived (13:14), and of Christ who was dead and is alive (1:18; 2:8), so the word alone does not settle whether a bodily resurrection is meant. What points to life after death here is that John says he saw the souls of those who had been beheaded (v. 4); premillennial readers answer that the parallel with the bodily resurrection of v. 5 favours their view, and that is the strongest point on their side. The bodily resurrection of all believers comes at Christ’s single return at the end (1 Thessalonians 4:16). This is the great comfort of the passage for persecuted believers: those who die for Christ are not defeated; they reign with him now.

The verdict reversed. Whatever a reader concludes about the verb, what the verse is for is not in dispute at all. Look at who is reigning. Not one of them held any office. They were beheaded, boycotted, shut out of the market, unable to buy bread, tried in courts that found against them and buried by people who were afraid to say why. The world’s verdict on them was delivered and recorded and is still on file. And John sees them on thrones, with the authority to judge committed to them, reigning with Christ. The verse reverses that verdict, as the whole book has been doing since chapter 1. The people the world disposed of are the people on the thrones, and the arrangement is already in force.

What happens to a Christian the moment he dies? He goes at once to be with Christ, conscious, at rest and full of joy. Paul calls it far better (Philippians 1:23), and to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). The thief on the cross was told, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43). There is no purgatory where the believer must pay off what Christ left unpaid, and no sleep of the soul in which he knows nothing until the last day: John sees souls who are alive and reigning. The body rests in the grave until the resurrection; the person is with the Lord (the Westminster Confession 32.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.1). That is why Christians may grieve at a graveside, but not as those who have no hope.

Do my loved ones in heaven see me, and should I talk to them? Scripture does not tell us what the departed see of earth, and it is wise not to build on guesses. It does tell us where they are and what they are doing: they are with Christ and reigning with him, and that is enough to know. We should not pray to them or seek to speak with them; the Bible forbids consulting the dead (Deuteronomy 18:10–12), and the one Mediator between God and men is Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). Speak to the Lord about them, thank him for them, and look forward to the morning when you will see them again in a body that cannot die.

verseByVerse.quote: The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were ended. This is the first resurrection. Blessed and holy is the one who shares in the first resurrection! Over such the second death has no power, but they will be priests of God and of Christ, and they will reign with him for a thousand years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Jesus said that an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgement (John 5:28–29). He also said, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life; he does not come into judgement, but has passed from death to life (John 5:24). Paul says believers have been raised with Christ and seated with him in the heavenly places (Ephesians 2:6; Colossians 3:1).

The rest of the dead. That is, unbelievers. They do not share the life and reign with Christ during the present age; they come to life only to be judged, at the end (vv. 12–13). On the premillennial reading the parallel is decisive: two groups, two comings to life, a thousand years apart, and the same verb for both. On the amillennial reading John distinguishes them by calling only one of them the first resurrection, and by reserving for the other the plain statement that it happens at the end.

The first resurrection. The phrase occurs only here. If there is a first resurrection, there is implicitly a second: the bodily resurrection at the end. On the reading this commentary follows, just as there is a first death (physical) and a second death (eternal), so there is a first resurrection (spiritual, entering life with Christ, at conversion and at death) and a second (bodily, at Christ’s return). Believers share both resurrections and only the first death; unbelievers share both deaths and only the second resurrection, to judgement.

First and second of different kinds. There is a feature of John’s vocabulary in this very passage that bears on it. He speaks of a second death in verse 6 and again at verse 14, and the second death is plainly not a death of the same kind as the first: the first is a body in a grave, the second is a lake of fire. If second death can name something of a different order from the first death, then first resurrection may name something of a different order from the second. That is the amillennial answer, and it is a real one.

Textual note. One important early manuscript (Codex Sinaiticus) and some others omit the first sentence, “The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were ended”. Most manuscripts include it, and it is probably original.

Where Christians differ: are there two bodily resurrections a thousand years apart? Premillennialists read the first resurrection as a bodily resurrection of believers before the millennium, and the second as a bodily resurrection of unbelievers after it. This commentary’s view: the rest of the New Testament teaches one bodily resurrection of both righteous and unrighteous at the same time, on the last day (John 5:28–29; Acts 24:15; Daniel 12:2). Jesus says he will raise up believers on the last day (John 6:39–40, 44, 54), which leaves no room for a thousand years after their resurrection. The first resurrection is the believer’s sharing in Christ’s resurrection life, beginning at new birth and carried into heaven at death, while the body awaits the last day.

Blessed and holy. The fifth of the book’s seven beatitudes, and the only one that adds a second adjective. Not merely blessed: blessed and holy (hagios), set apart, belonging to God. Three things are said about this person, and they should be taken one at a time, because they are among the great promises of Scripture.

The second death has no power. Not they will probably escape it, and not they will be forgiven at the trial. It has no authority over them. The word is exousia, authority, the right to act. The second death has no jurisdiction; it cannot bring a case. “Second death”: the lake of fire (v. 14). Smyrna was promised this in almost the same words: the one who conquers will not be hurt by the second death (2:11). And that is the answer to the deepest fear underneath everything in this chapter. A Christian may reasonably be uncertain about the timing of the millennium; he may not reasonably be uncertain about this. Whatever is coming at the great white throne, one kind of person is outside its reach altogether, and the reason is not their record. It is that their names are in a book that belongs to a Lamb who was slain.

Priests of God and of Christ. The kingdom of priests of 1:6 and 5:10, arriving. A priest has access, offers worship, and carries other people’s names into the presence of God. That is what these people will be doing: not standing about being rewarded, but serving in the nearest place there is. And see the phrase of God and of Christ. Christ is served with the same priestly service as God. No creature is ever rightly worshipped in this book; the Lamb is, because he is God.

They will reign with him. The reign is with him, which is the qualifier that keeps it from being a fantasy of revenge. Nobody in this chapter reigns on his own account or over his own patch. The whole substance of the thousand years is being where he is and doing what he does. And note the two offices together: priests, and reigning. That is the combination Israel was promised at Sinai, a kingdom of priests (Exodus 19:6), and never managed. It is held in one person only, the one who is both King of kings and the Lamb who was slaughtered. His people get both because they are with him.

How do I know I share in the first resurrection? If you have been born again, you have. The first resurrection begins when the Spirit makes a dead heart alive and joins it to the risen Christ, and you know it by its fruit: you trust Christ for your salvation and not your record, you love him and want to obey him, you hate the sin you once enjoyed, and you love his people (1 John 3:14). None of that is perfect in anyone. A sin you still fall into can be hated and loved at the same time, and the fight against it is itself the Spirit’s work in you (Romans 7:22–25; Galatians 5:17). None of it grows naturally in a dead soul. If those things are in you, however weakly, the second death has no claim on you, and Christ will not lose you (John 10:28).

Does reigning with Christ start only after I die? In its full form, yes; but it has already begun. Paul says God has raised us up with Christ and seated us with him in the heavenly places (Ephesians 2:6), present tense. A believer on earth already shares Christ’s victory: sin no longer has dominion over him (Romans 6:14), he may come boldly to the throne of grace (Hebrews 4:16), and his prayers are part of how Christ rules the world (8:3–5). The reign John sees in heaven is what this becomes when the struggle is over. So reign now, by saying no to sin and yes to God, and by praying as one who has the King’s ear.
verseByVerse.note: The fifth of the seven “blessed” sayings in Revelation.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the thousand years are ended, Satan will be released from his prison and will come out to deceive the nations that are at the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, to gather them for battle; their number is like the sand of the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. In Ezekiel 38–39, Gog of the land of Magog leads a vast coalition of nations from the far north against God’s restored people Israel, living securely in unwalled villages; God destroys them with fire and brimstone, and the birds and beasts feast on their bodies (Ezekiel 39:4, 17–20). In Jewish tradition, Gog and Magog became names for the final enemies of God’s people.

Satan will be released. The passive again, and 20:3 has already said he must be, using the word of divine necessity. Even the last rebellion is on a licence issued from the throne. God allows a final, brief period of satanic deception and persecution at the end of the age, which Jesus and Paul also foretold (Matthew 24:21–24; 2 Thessalonians 2:3–12).

To deceive the nations. Released from restraint, he goes straight back to the work he was bound to stop doing. The verb has defined him since 12:9, where he was named the deceiver of the whole world. Nothing has been learned, nothing has changed, and after a thousand years in a sealed pit the first thing he does is start talking. He does not repent or reconsider. Evil in this book has no capacity for growth; it only ever repeats itself with a larger audience. “Four corners”: the whole world, every direction at once.

Gog and Magog. In Ezekiel, Gog is a ruler and Magog his land. Here both are names for the nations. And he uses them the way he has used every other name in this book: as a type rather than an address. Babylon was not the city on the Euphrates; Sodom and Egypt in chapter 11 were not Sodom and Egypt; here Gog and Magog is not a country but the last coalition of everything opposed to God.

To gather them for battle. “The battle” (ton polemon, with the definite article): the battle already described in 16:14 and 19:19, in nearly identical words. The same event, seen a third time. John has been showing us the last day from different windows, and this is the last window.

Like the sand of the sea. Countless. The church will seem overwhelmed. And the phrase is heavy with meaning, because it echoes the promise God made to Abraham about his offspring: I will surely multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven and as the sand that is on the seashore (Genesis 22:17). The enemy assembles a counterfeit of Abraham’s promise. That is the last thing the dragon does in Scripture, and it is what he has done at every stage: a beast who parodies the Lamb’s resurrection, a false prophet with horns like a lamb, a mark answering a seal, a prostitute answering a bride, and now a countless host answering the countless family promised to a childless old man standing outside his tent at night.

The true seed of Abraham. A counterfeit can only be measured against the original, and Paul says who the original is. The promise was made to Abraham and to his offspring, singular, who is Christ (Galatians 3:16); and if you are Christ’s, you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise (Galatians 3:29). The multitude before the throne in chapter 7, which no one could number, is that promise kept. So there are two uncountable crowds at the end of the book, and what divides them is not size but a person. One is gathered by the deceiver for war. The other has been gathered by the Son, through faith in him, for a city. Only that one lasts; the other is destroyed in a single verse.

Where Christians differ: is Gog and Magog a specific nation, such as Russia? Some popular prophecy teachers identified Gog and Magog with Russia, linking Rosh (Ezekiel 38:2, in some translations) with Russia and Meshech with Moscow. This commentary’s view: those connections are based on sound-alike words, not on language or history; Rosh is a Hebrew word meaning chief, and Meshech and Tubal were peoples in what is now Turkey. In Revelation, Gog and Magog are explicitly the nations at the four corners of the earth: not one nation but the whole world in rebellion. The point is not geography but the final, worldwide assault on God’s people, and its sure defeat.

Why would God let Satan out at all? Scripture does not give every reason, but it gives enough. The release shows that the human heart, left to itself, does not become good with time or better surroundings: after a whole age of the gospel going out, the nations still gather against God the moment the deceiver speaks. It brings every hidden rebellion into the open, so that the final judgement is seen by all to be just. And it shows the church, one last time, that her safety never rested on Satan being chained but on God himself. A God who can chain the dragon with one angel loses nothing by letting him go for a little while.

How should I read prophecy headlines? With a calm mind and an open Bible. Every generation has had preachers who named the nation of Gog, the identity of the beast and the year of the end, and every one of them has been wrong, and their wrong guesses have made the church look foolish and left believers frightened or cynical. Jesus said no one knows the day or the hour (Matthew 24:36). What we know is enough: opposition to God will gather, it will be worldwide, and it will be destroyed by Christ at his coming. So watch the news without fear, pray for persecuted believers, and be found faithful whenever he comes.
verseByVerse.note: Gog and Magog come from Ezekiel’s vision of a last great attack on God’s people.

verseByVerse.quote: And they marched up over the broad plain of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city, but fire came down from heaven and consumed them, and the devil who had deceived them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur where the beast and the false prophet were, and they will be tormented day and night forever and ever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Ezekiel 38:22 says God will rain upon Gog torrential rains and hailstones, fire and sulphur. Fire came down from heaven on Sodom (Genesis 19:24), on Elijah’s sacrifice at Carmel (1 Kings 18:38), and at Elijah’s word on soldiers sent against him (2 Kings 1:10–12). Psalm 87:2 says the LORD loves the gates of Zion. Israel camped around the tabernacle in the wilderness, tribe by tribe, with the presence of God in the middle (Numbers 2).

Over the broad plain of the earth. Literally the breadth of the earth. This is not a march on one valley in the Middle East but a tide covering every land.

The camp of the saints and the beloved city. Two images for the people of God in one clause, and they should be separated. “The camp” (parembolēn) is Israel in the wilderness: tents, no walls, a people on the move, defended by nothing but the presence in the middle of them. “The beloved city” is Jerusalem, Zion, the city God loves (Psalm 78:68; 87:2), here the people of God, the new Jerusalem in its present form, the church. Pilgrim camp and settled city held together, which is what the church always is: on the way, and already home. And they are surrounded. Not attacked at one point but encircled on every side, by a host like the sand of the sea. If John had wanted to describe a hopeless military position he could not have done it more completely.

Fire came down from heaven. That is the battle. One clause, no engagement, and the saints do not lift a hand, exactly as in chapter 19, where the armies of heaven rode out in white linen and struck no blow. This is Christ’s return: the Lord Jesus revealed from heaven with his mighty angels in flaming fire (2 Thessalonians 1:7–8). The image is Ezekiel again, and behind it Sodom, and behind that Elijah. And it is the one thing James and John once wanted to call down on a Samaritan village, and Jesus rebuked them for it (Luke 9:54–55). The fire is real, and it is not the church’s to call.

The devil thrown into the lake. The beast and false prophet were thrown there in 19:20, the same final event; now their master joins them. The unholy trinity is together for the last time. And the dragon is described one last time by what he does rather than what he is: the devil who had deceived them. That is his epitaph. Not the great red dragon with seven diadems, not the accuser of the brothers, not the prince of the power of the air: the one who told lies, thrown into a lake, in the passive voice, by someone the verse does not even bother to name.

Tormented day and night forever. Conscious and endless. The verb is plural: they will be tormented, the devil with the beast and the false prophet. The lake of fire is pictured not as an incinerator and not as a momentary end. The devil’s defeat, begun at the cross, is completed. So the serpent that spoke in a garden in Genesis 3 has said his last word here. He was cast out at the cross, thrown down to the earth, given a short time, bound in a pit, released for a little while, and is now finished. And the head that was promised to be crushed (Genesis 3:15) is under the heel of the child the dragon once stood waiting to devour (12:4).

Textual note. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “fire came down from God out of heaven”. The meaning is the same.

Is this the same battle as 19:19–21? The more likely reading is yes. Both draw on Ezekiel 38–39, both gather the nations for the battle with the definite article, and both end at once with God’s judgement, without any fighting. Premillennial Christians see two battles a thousand years apart, one before the millennium and one after it. But John has shown the end of history several times already, at the sixth seal, the seventh trumpet and the seventh bowl, and this is one more view of the same day. It is not a literal siege of the city of Jerusalem but the world’s final assault on the camp of the saints and the beloved city, God’s people wherever they are.

Does this teach that punishment is conscious and unending, for lost people as well as the devil? Yes. For ever and ever is the strongest phrase for duration in the New Testament, the same phrase used of God’s own life (4:9–10) and of the reign of the saints (22:5). And the lost share the same lake of fire (v. 15; 14:10–11), the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels (Matthew 25:41). Some evangelicals hold that the wicked will finally be destroyed and cease to exist, and that the torment is only for the devil and his agents; they are often moved by real compassion. But Jesus sets eternal punishment beside eternal life in the same sentence (Matthew 25:46), and if one is endless, so is the other. The punishment of the lost, like that of the devil, is conscious and without end. Those who disagree point to Scripture’s words destroy and perish (Matthew 10:28; 2 Thessalonians 1:9) and to pictures of chaff burned up, and they remain brothers and sisters who trust the same Saviour; the question between us is how to read those words, not whether Christ saves. This commentary holds the conscious reading with grief, not with satisfaction.

How can the lake of fire last for ever if God is loving? This is a real question, and it deserves a real answer, not a shrug. First, sin is not a small thing made large; it is rebellion against an infinitely holy and good God, and its seriousness is measured by the one sinned against. Second, Scripture never pictures anyone in the lake of fire becoming sorry there; the devil goes in still deceiving, and the impenitent in this book go on refusing God even under judgement (16:9, 11). Third, the punishment is just, according to what each has done, with no one punished beyond what he deserves. And fourth, the clearest proof that God is loving is not that hell is empty but that his own Son went to the cross to bear it for sinners. The same Jesus who spoke most about hell wept over Jerusalem and prayed for his executioners from the cross. And the chapter itself settles who goes there at the book of life (20:15): the only way to be outside that lake is to belong to the Lamb, and the Lamb still welcomes everyone who comes to him (22:17).

On a Tuesday. When you feel surrounded, by illness, by opposition at work, by a family that mocks your faith, by a culture that seems to have closed in, you are standing where the saints stand in this verse. You are not asked to break out by your own strength. You are asked to stay in the camp, near the presence, and trust.

For worship. Once before, the beloved of God was surrounded. The Son of God hung outside Jerusalem with enemies on every side, the bulls and dogs of his own psalm closing in (Psalm 22:12–16), and no fire fell, though he had said that twelve legions of angels were his for the asking (Matthew 26:53). He let the enemy close over him so that the camp of his people would never fall. That is why the saints at the end stand empty-handed and unafraid: the judgement that falls on the deceiver can never fall on them, because their Saviour has already borne theirs. The God who loves the gates of Zion has never yet lost a single tent in the camp.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 11–12: before a great white throne earth and sky flee, and the dead, great and small, are judged from the books, while another book, the book of life, is opened. Verses 13–15: the sea, Death and Hades give up their dead and each is judged; Death and Hades are thrown into the lake of fire, the second death, and so is anyone whose name is not found in the book of life.
verseByVerse.theology:
Judged by Works, Saved by a Name

Before the great white throne earth and sky flee, and all the dead, great and small, are judged by what is written in the books. Death and Hades are thrown into the lake of fire, and anyone whose name is not found in the book of life follows them.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Even the sea gives up its dead; nobody is missing, and each is judged by name.

Now: The question is not whether you have done enough, but whether your name is in the Lamb’s book, and the water of life is offered without price.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw a great white throne and him who was seated on it. From his presence earth and sky fled away, and no place was found for them. And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne, and books were opened. Then another book was opened, which is the book of life. And the dead were judged by what was written in the books, according to what they had done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. Daniel 7:9–10 says thrones were placed, the Ancient of Days took his seat, his throne was fiery flames, the court sat in judgement, and the books were opened. Psalm 62:12 says God will render to a man according to his work. Jesus said the Father has given all judgement to the Son (John 5:22), and that he will sit on his glorious throne and all the nations will be gathered before him (Matthew 25:31–32). Paul says we must all appear before the judgement seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10).

A great white throne. The book has been full of thrones since chapter 4: the throne, twenty-four thrones, the throne of the beast, the thrones of verse 4. This is the last one, and it is described with two adjectives. Great, so that its size settles who is in charge. White, which in this book is the colour of purity, holiness and verdicts: white robes, white linen, white horses. The one seated on it is God, who judges the world through Christ (Acts 17:31; Romans 2:16). The Father and the Son share one throne (22:1, 3). John does not describe him; even in chapter 4 he gave only colours, jasper and carnelian (4:3), and no form. He says instead what happens in his presence.

Earth and sky fled away. It is a quietly terrifying sentence. Nothing is said to be destroyed. The universe simply cannot remain in the room. The ground under a reader’s feet and the sky over his head, the two things that have always been there, the very definition of what is permanent, get up and leave, and there is nowhere for them to go. The old creation passes away before God’s holiness (2 Peter 3:10; 21:1). Nowhere to hide (6:14–16). Which means the last judgement has no scenery. Every human court sits somewhere: a room, a building, a country whose laws apply. This one has no location, because the location has gone. There is nothing in the frame but a throne, the one seated on it, and the people standing.

The dead, great and small. “The dead”: all humanity, raised for judgement. “Great and small” for the last time in this book, and it flattens the last hierarchy there is. Emperors and slaves, the men whose statues filled the forum and the women whose names were never written down anywhere, standing on the same floor. No one is too important to be judged or too insignificant to be overlooked.

Books were opened. Books, plural, and then a book, singular, and the distinction is the gospel. Daniel saw the same scene: the court sat in judgement, and the books were opened (Daniel 7:10). They are records of every person’s deeds. God knows everything people have done, said and thought (Ecclesiastes 12:14), and Jesus said every careless word would be accounted for on the day of judgement (Matthew 12:36). Nothing is missing from them.

The book of life. The Lamb’s book (13:8; 21:27), with the names of those chosen before the foundation of the world (17:8). The first shows what each person deserves; the second shows who belongs to the Lamb. The book of life is not a second, better record of the same kind. It is a register of names, and verse 15 says it is the only thing that finally decides anything.

According to what they had done. The judgement is perfectly just, based on the evidence. No one will be condemned unfairly. And the record is the standard by which the dead are judged, which raises the question a Christian reader must have answered rather than hurried past. The New Testament holds both sides without flinching: nobody is justified by works of the law (Galatians 2:16), and each will be repaid according to what he has done (Romans 2:6; 2 Corinthians 5:10). They are not in tension once it is clear what each is answering. The books of deeds establish the case, and the case is unanswerable; every person standing there is guilty on the record. The book of life answers a different question: not what did you do, but whose are you. That cuts both ways. The moralist who hopes his file is good enough will find that it is not, and the sceptic who assumes there is no file will find that there is. Both are offered the same thing, and neither earns it: a name written by grace in the Lamb’s book.

In the flow. The last enemy outside humanity has just been thrown into the lake (v. 10); now the scene turns to humanity itself. And the flight of earth and sky clears the ground for what comes next, a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away (21:1). Judgement is not the end of the story. It is the doorway into the new creation.

Where Christians differ: if judgement is by works, how is salvation by grace? Some take judgement according to works as meaning that final salvation depends on our works. Others think that believers are not judged at all. This commentary’s view: everyone is judged according to works, because works reveal what is in the heart. For unbelievers, their works condemn them, because all have sinned (Romans 3:23). For believers, their names are in the book of life; they are saved by grace through faith alone, because Christ has borne their condemnation (Romans 8:1; John 5:24), and their works are the evidence of their faith and the basis of their rewards (1 Corinthians 3:12–15). No one is saved by works; but no one is saved without the works that true faith produces (James 2:14–26). The book of life is what finally decides (v. 15).

Do believers stand before this throne? All the dead stand there, great and small. For believers, the book of life decides: their names are written, and they are acquitted in Christ, while their works are reviewed for reward (2 Corinthians 5:10). Premillennial Christians often distinguish a judgement of believers from this one, separated by a thousand years; the more likely reading is that there is one final judgement, where the book of life separates the saved from the lost, as the shepherd separates the sheep from the goats in a single scene (Matthew 25:31–46).

What it does not mean. The books of deeds do not mean believers will be shamed by a public display of their forgiven sins. Their sins are removed as far as the east is from the west (Psalm 103:12), blotted out (Isaiah 43:25). They stand clothed in Christ’s righteousness.

Should a Christian be afraid of this day? Serious, yes; terrified, no. A believer should feel the weight of it: every word and deed is known, and how we live matters to the Lord who will review it. But fear of condemnation is not for those in Christ. The Judge on that throne is the Saviour who died for you, and he will not condemn the people he bought. John says that whoever abides in God may have confidence for the day of judgement, because perfect love casts out fear (1 John 4:17–18). If you find yourself dreading the throne, do not try to make your file look better. Go to Christ again, today, and rest in what he has done.

Can my name be removed from the book of life? No, if it is truly there. And if you are afraid that yours is not, that fear is itself a reason to come to Christ now, for no one who comes to him is turned away (John 6:37). The names were written before the foundation of the world (17:8), by God who does not change his mind, and the Lord Jesus promised the one who conquers, I will never blot his name out of the book of life (3:5). The book is the Lamb’s book because it lists the people he bought with his own blood, and he does not lose what he has paid for (John 6:39). The warnings of Scripture are real, and they are among the means by which God keeps his people trusting; but the believer who heeds them is not one whose name is in pencil.

On a Tuesday. Nothing done for Christ in secret is wasted, not the cup of cold water, not the patient answer, not the hidden prayer; it is all in the books, and the Lord who reads them is generous. And nothing done against your neighbour in secret is hidden either. No Christian’s file is clean, not even its best pages; but for those in Christ the worst of it has been answered at the cross, and his perfect obedience is counted in its place. So put right this week, without dread, whatever you would not want read aloud.

verseByVerse.quote: And the sea gave up the dead who were in it, Death and Hades gave up the dead who were in them, and they were judged, each one of them, according to what they had done. Then Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire. This is the second death, the lake of fire. And if anyone's name was not found written in the book of life, he was thrown into the lake of fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. In the ancient world, people feared being lost at sea, because the body could not be buried, and many thought the dead might be lost for ever. Isaiah 25:8 says God will swallow up death for ever. Paul says the last enemy to be destroyed is death (1 Corinthians 15:26), and that death is swallowed up in victory (1 Corinthians 15:54). Christ holds the keys of Death and Hades (1:18).

The sea gave up the dead. Three custodians, and every one of them hands over what it was holding. The sea is named separately for a reason that any first-century reader would have felt at once: to be lost at sea was to have no grave, no body, no name on a stone, the most complete disappearance available. The chapter says the sea gives them up. No one is lost.

Death and Hades gave up the dead. Personified, as in 6:8. This is the general resurrection, and nobody is missing. That is the point of listing three, and it reaches every kind of forgotten person: the man whose ship went down, the woman in an unmarked grave, the child in a plague pit, the soldier whose body was never found, the person whose family died out and whose name nobody has said aloud for eight hundred years. Death and Hades kept their records perfectly and hand over the whole file.

Each one of them. John will not let it be a mass. In a scene involving every human being who has ever lived, the judgement is individual: one at a time, on the evidence, by name. Every person answers for himself or herself.

Death and Hades thrown into the lake. The two figures who rode out at the fourth seal (6:8), the reaper and the one who followed him. The risen Christ said in the first chapter of this book, I have the keys of Death and Hades (1:18), and this is what he does with them. They are not merely disarmed; they are executed. The last enemy is gone. In the new creation, death shall be no more (21:4). Death is not going to be managed, or explained, or made bearable. It is going to be killed. What can it mean to throw death, which is not a creature, into a lake? It means that dying itself will never happen again: no illness will end in a funeral, and no one will ever again be parted from someone he loves, for God will swallow up death for ever and wipe away tears from all faces (Isaiah 25:8). Everything a reader has lost to it, the funerals attended, the diagnosis that came back, the phone call at four in the morning, was inflicted by something that is itself going to be thrown into a lake and will not be coming back.

The second death. John defines his own term, here and again at 21:8, after using it without definition at 2:11 and 20:6. The first death separates soul from body; the second is the final, eternal punishment of the whole person, body and soul, separated from all God’s goodness and under his wrath. The promise made to Smyrna, that the one who conquers will not be hurt by the second death (2:11), now has its definition attached, and it is the last thing a reader will want to be uncertain about.

Not found written in the book of life. One sentence, and it is the last word of the chapter. It is stated negatively: not whoever was found, but if anyone’s name was not. And the verb is found: the search is made, and nothing is left to chance. This is the decisive question. Not whether a person’s good deeds outweigh their bad, not sincerity, not how a person compares with his neighbour. A name, in a book, belonging to the Lamb. The book has spent twenty chapters saying that there are two companies and two destinations and that everyone is in one of them, and here the criterion is stated in a single sentence.

The question it leaves. This is either a most frightening sentence or a most reassuring one, depending on a single question, which every reader is now in a position to ask. It is not, have I done enough? Nobody standing at that throne has. It is whether a person has come to the one who says, two chapters later, let the one who desires take the water of life without price (22:17).

Where Christians differ: is anyone saved apart from faith in Christ? Inclusivists hold that some may be saved through Christ’s work without consciously knowing or believing in him, by responding to the light they have; they are usually moved by concern for those who never heard, and they too confess Christ as the only Saviour. Pluralists hold that many religions lead to God. This commentary’s view: the book of life is the Lamb’s book (21:27), and salvation is found in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). Those who are saved are those who hold the testimony of Jesus and are washed in his blood (7:14; 12:11). This is why the church must take the gospel to every nation, tribe and language (14:6; Romans 10:13–15). God will judge every person justly, according to the light they had (Romans 2:12–16), and no one will be condemned unfairly; but salvation is through Christ alone, received by faith.

Is the lake of fire literal fire? The fire is a picture, but what it pictures is worse, not milder. Scripture describes hell as fire and also as outer darkness (Matthew 25:30), which cannot both be literal in the ordinary sense; both are pointing at something real: conscious, unending suffering under God’s just anger, cut off from every good thing he gives, light, love, rest, friendship, hope. A picture is used because the reality is beyond our words. No one should take comfort from the fact that the language is symbolic. The symbols of heaven in the next chapters are not less than gold and pearls; they are more. The same is true here.

What about babies, and people who never heard? Infants who die in infancy are in the hands of a merciful God, and the Reformed confessions teach that elect infants dying in infancy are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where and how he pleases (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.3; the Westminster Confession 10.3). Many parents have rested on David’s words about his dead child: I shall go to him (2 Samuel 12:23). If you have lost a child, you may grieve with hope, and leave that little one with a God who is kinder than all our fears. For adults who never heard, God will judge justly by the light they had, and none will be condemned for not believing a gospel they never heard, but for the sins they knowingly committed (Romans 1:20; 2:12). That does not make them safe; it makes the missionary task urgent. The answer to the question is not speculation but sending.

What about someone I love who died without Christ? This is one of the heaviest griefs a Christian carries, and Scripture does not ask you to pretend. Three things can be said honestly. First, you do not know everything that passed between that soul and God in the last hours; the thief was saved on a cross. Do not pronounce what you cannot see. Second, the Judge of all the earth will do right (Genesis 18:25), and on the last day no one, including you, will think him unjust. Third, your grief is not a lack of faith; Paul had great sorrow and unceasing anguish for his own people (Romans 9:2). Bring it to the Lord, who wept at a grave, and let it drive you to pray for the living.

On a Tuesday. If you are trusting Christ, your name is in the Lamb’s book. So at the next funeral of a believer you attend, remember the end of this chapter: the grave you are standing beside is going to give back what it holds, and the thing that dug it is going into the lake.

For worship. The sea gives up its dead, and Death and Hades hand over every name they ever took, and then they are thrown away like broken tools. The Lord Jesus once lay in a borrowed grave himself, in the grip of the very enemy he now destroys, and he came out of it as the firstborn of the dead (1:5); every grave that opens on the last day opens because his did. And when the other books are closed, one book remains, written before the world was made, a list of people bought with his blood, and nothing in all the other books can get a name off it. The last enemy dies, and the Lamb lives for ever.

After that he must be released for a little while.<sup>4</sup>Then I saw thrones, and seated on them were those to whom the authority to judge was committed. Also I saw the souls of those who had been beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God, and those who had not worshiped the beast or its image and had not received its mark on their foreheads or their hands. They came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years.<sup>5</sup>The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were ended. This is the first resurrection.<sup>6</sup>Blessed and holy is the one who shares in the first resurrection!
